q: What is the IUPAC name of the ester shown?
h: An ester is named alkyl alkanoate: the group on the single-bonded O comes first, then the acyl part (which includes the C=O carbon) with -oate.
w: Split the ester at the single-bonded oxygen. The O-alkyl group is CH(CH3)2, isopropyl. The acyl part is CH3CH2C(=O)–, three carbons counting the carbonyl carbon, so it is propanoate: isopropyl propanoate.
x: This swaps the two halves: here the branched group is on the oxygen, not on the acyl side, and the O-alkyl group is not a straight propyl.
The acyl part has three carbons including the C=O carbon, not four; counting the oxygen-bearing CH as part of the acid chain gives the wrong parent.
1-Methylethyl is a correct name for isopropyl, but the acid part has three carbons (propanoate), not two (ethanoate); the C=O carbon must be counted.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the amide shown?
h: The parent chain is the acyl chain that includes the C=O carbon (C1). Groups on nitrogen get the locant N.
w: The acyl chain is C(=O)–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH3: four carbons with C1 = C=O, so butanamide with a methyl on C3. Nitrogen carries one ethyl and one methyl, each labeled N. Alphabetizing (ethyl before methyl) and combining the two methyls gives N-ethyl-N,3-dimethylbutanamide.
x: Numbering of an amide always starts at the carbonyl carbon, so the branch is at C3, not C2.
Only one group on nitrogen is ethyl; the other is methyl.
The N-ethyl group is not part of the parent chain; the parent is only the acyl chain, which has four carbons.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: When a –COX group is attached to a ring, the carbonyl carbon is not part of the ring. Which suffix handles that case?
w: The C(=O)Cl carbon is outside the ring, so the ring name takes the suffix -carbonyl (as in cyclohexanecarboxylic acid → cyclohexanecarbonyl chloride). The answer is cyclohexanecarbonyl chloride.
x: The carbonyl carbon is not one of the ring atoms, so the compound is not a seven-carbon ring acyl chloride.
A chloroformate is Cl–C(=O)–O–R, with an oxygen between the ring and the carbonyl; here the ring carbon is bonded directly to C=O.
This is a ring ketone with Cl on a ring carbon; the compound shown has Cl on the carbonyl carbon outside the ring.

q: What is the name of the compound shown?
h: Look at what links the two C=O groups. Then name each acyl half as its acid.
w: Two acyl groups joined through one oxygen make an anhydride. One half is acetyl (2 C), the other propanoyl (3 C). A mixed anhydride lists both acids alphabetically: acetic propanoic anhydride.
x: Propanoic anhydride has two propanoyl groups (six carbons); this compound has five carbons, with one acetyl half.
Acetic anhydride has two acetyl groups (four carbons); one half here is propanoyl.
Propyl acetate is an ester (one C=O); the compound shown has two C=O groups joined by an oxygen.

q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>C≡N?
h: In the -nitrile suffix the C≡N carbon is counted as C1 of the chain.
w: The chain is N≡C(1)–CH2(2)–CH(3)(CH3)–CH3(4): four carbons including the nitrile carbon, so butanenitrile, methyl at C3: 3-methylbutanenitrile.
x: This leaves out the nitrile carbon. With the -nitrile suffix the C≡N carbon is C1, so the chain has four carbons.
Numbering starts at the nitrile carbon, which puts the branch at C3, not C2.
There are only four carbons in the longest chain that contains the C≡N carbon (five carbons in total, one being the methyl branch).

q: Which structure is a δ-lactam?
h: Lactam = cyclic amide; the Greek letter names the carbon bonded to nitrogen (α is next to C=O).
w: In a lactam the ring N is bonded to the C=O. Greek letters count from the carbon next to C=O: α, β, γ, δ. A δ-lactam has N on the δ-carbon, so the ring holds C=O + 4 carbons + N = a six-membered ring: A, piperidin-2-one.
x: This is a five-membered cyclic amide (N on the γ-carbon): a γ-lactam.
C has a ring oxygen, not nitrogen: it is a δ-lactone (cyclic ester).
This is a four-membered cyclic amide, the β-lactam ring of penicillins.

q: Which carboxylic acid is the strongest acid?
h: An electronegative atom stabilizes the carboxylate by induction, and that effect fades quickly with distance.
w: The C–Cl dipole pulls electron density from the carboxylate and stabilizes it. Induction weakens sharply with each intervening σ bond, so the Cl on the α-carbon has the biggest effect: A, 2-chlorobutanoic acid (pKa ≈ 2.9) vs 3-chloro (≈ 4.1), 4-chloro (≈ 4.5) and butanoic acid (≈ 4.8).
x: Cl on the β-carbon still helps, but one more bond away from the carboxylate it has a much smaller effect than α-Cl.
Cl on the γ-carbon is so far away that the pK<sub>a</sub> is only slightly lower than butanoic acid.
Butanoic acid has no electron-withdrawing group and is the weakest of the four.

q: Rank the three acids in order of increasing acidity (weakest first).
h: Compare the inductive pull of one F with one Cl first, then ask what a second Cl adds.
w: All three are stabilized by induction at the α-carbon. F is more electronegative than Cl, so FCH2COOH (pKa 2.6) is stronger than ClCH2COOH (2.9). Two Cl atoms add their effects, so Cl2CHCOOH (1.3) is much stronger than either monohalo acid. Order: I < III < II.
x: This makes Cl more withdrawing than F; fluorine is the more electronegative atom, so fluoroacetic acid is the stronger of the two monohalo acids.
This puts fluoroacetic acid above dichloroacetic acid. Two α-chlorines together outweigh one fluorine.
This reverses the effect of halogens: more and stronger electron-withdrawing groups make the acid stronger, not weaker.

q: Which benzoic acid has the highest pKa?
h: A para substituent that donates electrons by resonance destabilizes the carboxylate anion.
w: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the benzoate anion (lower pKa); electron donors destabilize it (higher pKa). Para-OCH3 donates by resonance more than it withdraws by induction, so A, 4-methoxybenzoic acid is the weakest acid (pKa ≈ 4.5) vs benzoic acid (4.2), 4-chlorobenzoic acid (4.0) and 4-nitrobenzoic acid (3.4).
x: Benzoic acid is the reference (4.2); a para-methoxy group makes the acid weaker still.
Cl withdraws inductively more than it donates, so 4-chlorobenzoic acid is a slightly stronger acid than benzoic acid.
NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws strongly by induction and resonance, so 4-nitrobenzoic acid is the strongest acid of the four (lowest pK<sub>a</sub>).

q: A mixture of benzoic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.2) and phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.0) is dissolved in diethyl ether. Which aqueous solution extracts the benzoic acid but leaves the phenol in the ether layer? (H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> 6.4, H<sub>2</sub>O 15.7, CH<sub>3</sub>OH 15.5)
h: A base deprotonates an acid substantially only when the conjugate acid of the base is weaker (higher pK<sub>a</sub>) than the acid.
w: Bicarbonate's conjugate acid is H2CO3 (pKa 6.4). Benzoic acid (4.2) is stronger, so it is converted to water-soluble sodium benzoate; phenol (10.0) is weaker than H2CO3, so it stays neutral in the ether. The answer is NaHCO3.
x: Hydroxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) deprotonates both acids, so both would move into the water.
Methoxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> 15.5) is also strong enough to deprotonate phenol, so it does not separate the two.
Acid keeps both compounds neutral, so neither moves into the aqueous layer.

q: Rank the compounds in order of decreasing reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution (most reactive first).
h: Two factors: how much the group on the acyl carbon donates by resonance, and how good it is as a leaving group.
w: II (acid chloride): Cl donates very little into the C=O and Cl− is an excellent leaving group. IV (anhydride): the bridging O is shared by two C=O groups, so it donates less to each, and a carboxylate leaves well. I (ester): OR donates more and RO− is a poorer leaving group. III (amide): N is the best π donor and R2N− is the worst leaving group. Order: II > IV > I > III.
x: An anhydride is less reactive than an acid chloride: its carboxylate leaving group is poorer than chloride, and its oxygen donates more into the C=O than Cl does.
This makes the amide more reactive than the ester. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so it donates its lone pair more strongly, and amide ions are terrible leaving groups.
This puts the ester above the anhydride. The anhydride's bridging oxygen is split between two carbonyls and its leaving group is a resonance-stabilized carboxylate, so it is more reactive.

q:
Which statements help explain why amides are the least reactive carboxylic acid derivatives toward nucleophiles?
I. The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the C=O, making the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic.
II. The amide C–N bond has partial double-bond character.
III. An amide ion (R2N−) is a very poor leaving group.
IV. Amides cannot form a tetrahedral intermediate because nitrogen has no lone pair.
h: Draw the resonance form of an amide that has C=N. Then ask how basic each possible leaving group is.
w: The N lone pair donates strongly into the C=O (I), which is exactly why the C–N bond has partial double-bond character (II, planar amide, restricted rotation). The leaving group would be R2N−, conjugate base of an amine (pKa ≈ 35), so it leaves very poorly (III). Statement IV is false: amide nitrogen does have a lone pair (that is the source of I), and amides do react through tetrahedral intermediates under forcing conditions. Answer: I, II and III only.
x: Statement II is true and is a direct consequence of I: the resonance donation shows up as C–N double-bond character.
Statement IV is false: amide nitrogen has a lone pair, and amides are hydrolyzed through tetrahedral intermediates on heating with acid or base.
Statement IV is false, so the set with all four cannot be right.

q: Which reaction proceeds in good yield simply by mixing the two reagents (with a weak base such as pyridine where HCl forms)?
h: Nucleophilic acyl substitution runs downhill: from a more reactive derivative to a less reactive one.
w: Acyl substitutions go from a higher rung of the reactivity ladder to a lower one, because the nucleophile must be a poorer leaving group than the group it replaces. Acid chloride → ester is downhill (Cl− leaves, the alcohol stays): CH3COCl + ethanol → ethyl acetate.
x: Ester → acid chloride is uphill: chloride is a much better leaving group than methoxide, so Cl<sup>−</sup> cannot push out CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>.
Amide → ester is uphill: a neutral alcohol cannot displace NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, a far worse leaving group than an alkoxide.
A carboxylate is the least reactive acyl species of all (its negative charge repels nucleophiles), so methanol cannot add to it.

q: Acetyl chloride reacts with methylamine. Which species is the first-formed tetrahedral intermediate?
h: The amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons go onto oxygen. Nothing has left yet.
w: Addition of the neutral amine to the C=O gives a tetrahedral carbon bearing O<sup>−</sup>, Cl and a positively charged N (it has given its lone pair to carbon). Next the C=O re-forms and expels Cl<sup>−</sup>, then a base removes the N–H proton to give the amide.
x: This is formed after the tetrahedral intermediate collapses and chloride leaves; its carbon is trigonal, not tetrahedral.
This is the neutral amide product, after loss of both Cl<sup>−</sup> and a proton.
An acylium ion is not on this pathway; an amine attacks the neutral acid chloride directly by addition–elimination.

q: The energy diagram shows the hydrolysis of methyl acetate by hydroxide. What does point B represent?
c: the transition state for addition of hydroxide
the acylium ion formed when methoxide leaves
the carboxylate ion formed by proton transfer
h: Points at maxima are transition states; local minima between maxima are intermediates.
w: Nucleophilic acyl substitution is addition–elimination. A is the TS for hydroxide adding to C=O, B is the minimum between the two barriers: the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. C is the TS for loss of methoxide. The final deep drop is the fast proton transfer that gives acetate.
x: A transition state sits at an energy maximum; B is a local minimum.
No acylium ion forms in base; the C=O re-forms as methoxide is expelled from the tetrahedral intermediate.
The carboxylate forms at the end of the reaction (the products), after the second barrier, not between the two barriers.

q: Fischer esterification of acetic acid with 1-butanol (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst) has K ≈ 4. Which change most increases the yield of butyl acetate?
c: Use excess 1-butanol and remove water as it forms
Add water so the acetic acid dissolves completely in the mixture
Replace H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> with NaOH as the catalyst so the acid reacts faster
Double the amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst to speed up the reaction
h: The reaction is an equilibrium with water as a product. Think Le Châtelier.
w: With K near 4, equimolar reactants stop at about 2/3 conversion. Adding excess alcohol (a reactant) and removing water (a product, e.g. with a Dean–Stark trap or drying agent) both shift the equilibrium toward ester: excess 1-butanol plus water removal.
x: Water is a product, so adding it pushes the equilibrium back toward acid and alcohol (ester hydrolysis).
NaOH deprotonates the acid to a carboxylate, which no alcohol can attack; base also hydrolyzes esters. Fischer esterification needs acid catalysis.
A catalyst speeds up the approach to equilibrium in both directions but does not change K or the equilibrium yield.

q: Benzoic acid is heated with CH<sub>3</sub><sup>18</sup>OH and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Where is the <sup>18</sup>O found once the reaction reaches equilibrium?
c: in the ester, as the O bonded to the CH<sub>3</sub> group
in the ester, as the C=O oxygen
in the water that is formed
spread equally between the ester's two oxygens
h: Which bond of the alcohol breaks: C–O or O–H? The alcohol oxygen is the nucleophile.
w: In Fischer esterification the alcohol oxygen attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon, so the CH3–18O bond is never broken. After proton transfers, one of the acid's original OH groups leaves as water. The label ends up in the ester as the C–18O–CH3 oxygen.
x: The C=O oxygen of the ester comes from the benzoic acid; the alcohol oxygen becomes the single-bonded alkoxy oxygen.
Water is formed from an oxygen of the carboxylic acid, not from the alcohol; the alcohol's C–O bond stays intact.

The tetrahedral intermediate can lose either of the acid-derived OH groups, but the alcohol-derived OCH<sub>3</sub> is retained; it cannot become the carbonyl oxygen while staying bonded to CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Ethyl acetate is heated in H<sub>2</sub><sup>18</sup>O containing H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> until hydrolysis is complete. Which product(s) contain <sup>18</sup>O?
c: acetic acid only; the ethanol contains no <sup>18</sup>O
ethanol only; the acetic acid contains no <sup>18</sup>O
neither; the label remains in the water
h: Acid hydrolysis is Fischer esterification run backward. Water attacks which atom, and which bond to oxygen breaks?
w: Labeled water adds to the protonated C=O carbon, so 18O becomes bonded to the acyl carbon. The tetrahedral intermediate then expels ethanol, breaking the acyl–O bond; the CH3CH2–O bond is never touched. So 18O ends up in acetic acid only, and the ethanol keeps its original oxygen.
x: Ethanol would carry the label only if water attacked the ethyl carbon (an S<sub>N</sub>2 at the alkyl group, alkyl–oxygen cleavage), which does not happen for a primary ethyl ester.
Ethanol's oxygen is the original ester alkoxy oxygen; its C–O bond never breaks, so the label cannot get into it.
Water is the nucleophile that adds to the carbonyl, so its oxygen is incorporated into the acid.

q: Acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis is reversible, but saponification (ester + NaOH, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> workup) goes to completion. Why?
c: The acid formed is deprotonated by base, and the carboxylate cannot be attacked by alkoxide
Hydroxide is a better leaving group than alkoxide, so the reverse step cannot occur at all
The alkoxide leaving group is protonated by water and evaporates from the hot mixture as an alcohol
Hydroxide forms a more stable tetrahedral intermediate than water does, so the forward step is irreversible
h: Look at what happens right after the alkoxide leaves the tetrahedral intermediate. What acid and base are now together?
w: Loss of RO− gives a carboxylic acid (pKa ≈ 5) next to a strong base (RO− or HO−, conjugate-acid pKa ≈ 16). Proton transfer is essentially complete and gives a resonance-stabilized carboxylate. The carboxylate is negatively charged and the least electrophilic acyl species, so the alcohol cannot attack it to re-form the ester: the deprotonation drives the reaction to completion.
x: Hydroxide and alkoxides are similar leaving groups; the irreversibility comes from the acid–base step, not leaving-group ability.
Most alcohols do not evaporate under these conditions; the reaction is irreversible even in a closed flask.
The tetrahedral intermediate is a high-energy species in either case; its stability does not decide whether the overall reaction is reversible.

q: The ester shown (pure R) is heated with aqueous NaOH. What alcohol is obtained?
h: In saponification, which bond to the ester oxygen breaks: acyl–O or alkyl–O? Is the stereocenter's C–O bond involved?
w: Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon; the tetrahedral intermediate expels the alkoxide by breaking the acyl–O bond. The bond from oxygen to the stereocenter is never broken, so the configuration is retained: (R)-butan-2-ol.
x: Inversion would require an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack of hydroxide at the stereocenter with carboxylate leaving; saponification instead occurs at the carbonyl carbon.
Racemization would require a carbocation at the stereocenter (S<sub>N</sub>1); no C–O bond to that carbon breaks.
Saponification is not an oxidation; forming a ketone would require an oxidizing agent.

q: A carboxylic acid is converted to the acid chloride with thionyl chloride (SOCl<sub>2</sub>). What are the by-products?
h: Balance RCO<sub>2</sub>H + SOCl<sub>2</sub> → RCOCl + ?
w: RCO2H + SOCl2 → RCOCl + SO2 + HCl. Both by-products are gases, which leave the mixture and help drive the reaction to completion.
x: Thionyl chloride is the reagent, not a by-product, and no water forms (water would destroy the acid chloride).
Sulfur stays in the +4 state and ends up as SO<sub>2</sub>; no Cl<sub>2</sub> or sulfuric acid forms.
This is not balanced: the Cl atoms and the acid's H must go somewhere, and they leave as HCl.

q: Benzoyl chloride is treated with dimethylamine to make N,N-dimethylbenzamide. Why are at least two equivalents of dimethylamine used (when no other base is added)?
c: The second equivalent neutralizes HCl, which would otherwise protonate the amine and stop it reacting
The first equivalent attacks the carbonyl, and the second is needed to break the C–Cl bond in the intermediate
Two amine molecules must add to the C=O to form the tetrahedral intermediate
The second equivalent reduces the acid chloride to benzaldehyde before the amide forms
h: Write the by-product of acyl substitution on an acid chloride. What does it do to an amine?
w: Each acylation releases one HCl. Dimethylamine is a base, so the HCl converts it to (CH3)2NH2+ Cl−, which has no lone pair and cannot attack. With one equivalent, the yield would stop near 50%. The second equivalent (or pyridine/Et3N) is a sacrificial base for HCl.
x: Chloride leaves on its own when the tetrahedral intermediate collapses; no second amine is needed to break the C–Cl bond.
Only one amine adds to the carbonyl carbon; the tetrahedral intermediate has one N.
Amines are not reducing agents; aldehydes from acid chlorides need a hydride donor such as LiAl(OtBu)3H.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: Gilman reagents (R<sub>2</sub>CuLi) are softer and less reactive than Grignard reagents. How many times do they add to an acid chloride?
w: Lithium dimethylcuprate transfers one methyl to the acid chloride, replacing Cl and giving a ketone. It reacts with acid chlorides but only very slowly with ketones, so the reaction stops: A, 1-cyclopentylethan-1-one.
x: The 3° alcohol results from two additions, which happens with excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, not with a cuprate.
A secondary alcohol would need a hydride to reduce the ketone; no hydride source is present.
Cuprates do not reduce acid chlorides; the methyl group, not hydride, is transferred.

q: Which reagent(s) carry out the conversion shown?
h: You need exactly one hydride and a product that survives the reagent.
w: Lithium tri-tert-butoxyaluminum hydride has only one, bulky, weakly reactive hydride. At −78 °C it reduces the very reactive acid chloride but reacts only slowly with the aldehyde product, so the reduction stops there: LiAl(OtBu)3H, −78 °C.
x: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the aldehyde as fast as it forms, so the product is 2-phenylethanol.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> also reduces aldehydes rapidly, so any aldehyde formed would go on to the primary alcohol (and methanol itself reacts with the acid chloride to give an ester).
A cuprate transfers a methyl, not a hydride, giving the methyl ketone 1-phenylpropan-2-one.

q:
Benzoyl chloride is converted to ethyl benzoate with ethanol in pyridine. Which statements about pyridine are correct?
I. It neutralizes the HCl formed.
II. It can attack the acid chloride to give an acylpyridinium ion, which ethanol then attacks.
III. It must deprotonate ethanol to ethoxide before any reaction can occur.
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of pyridinium (≈ 5) with that of ethanol (≈ 16).
w: Pyridine (I) scavenges HCl as pyridinium chloride and (II) can act as a nucleophilic catalyst, forming a highly electrophilic acylpyridinium ion. Statement III is false: pyridine (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 5) is far too weak to deprotonate ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), and none is needed because acid chlorides react with neutral alcohols. Answer: I and II only.
x: Statement II is also correct: pyridine is a good nucleophile toward acid chlorides, and the acylpyridinium ion it forms is even more reactive.
Statement III is false: an acid chloride is reactive enough to acylate neutral ethanol, and pyridine is too weak a base to make ethoxide.
Statement III is false, so all three cannot be right.

q: Aniline reacts with acetic anhydride. Besides acetic acid, what organic product forms?
h: An anhydride transfers one acyl group; the other half leaves as a carboxylate (then acid).
w: Aniline's nitrogen attacks one carbonyl; the tetrahedral intermediate expels acetate, and proton transfer gives A: acetanilide (N-phenylacetamide) plus acetic acid.
x: Only one acyl group is transferred to nitrogen; the second acetyl leaves as acetate, so a diacetylated amine is not the product (and no water is formed).
Anhydrides acylate the nitrogen; they do not do Friedel–Crafts acylation of the ring without a Lewis acid, and the NH<sub>2</sub> group would react first anyway.
Aniline is not converted to phenol, and acetamide is not formed; the amine nitrogen becomes the amide nitrogen.

q: Succinic anhydride is warmed in methanol (no catalyst). What is the main product?
h: A cyclic anhydride opens after one acyl substitution. Where does the leaving group end up?
w: Methanol attacks one carbonyl of the cyclic anhydride. When the tetrahedral intermediate collapses, the leaving carboxylate is still tethered to the molecule, so the ring opens and one end becomes a methyl ester while the other becomes a carboxylic acid: A, 4-methoxy-4-oxobutanoic acid (monomethyl succinate).
x: The second CO<sub>2</sub>H would need Fischer esterification (acid catalyst, heat) to become an ester; a carboxylic acid is much less reactive than the anhydride.
Ring opening with water would give succinic acid; here methanol is the nucleophile, so one end becomes CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
γ-Butyrolactone would require reduction of one carbonyl; no reducing agent is present.

q: Benzoic acid and methylamine are mixed in ether at room temperature. What forms?
h: Before any acyl substitution can happen, what does an amine do with a carboxylic acid?
w: The fastest reaction between a carboxylic acid (pKa 4.2) and an amine (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 10.6) is proton transfer, giving methylammonium benzoate. The carboxylate is too unreactive to be attacked, so making the amide needs strong heating to drive off water, or better, conversion to an acid chloride (SOCl2) or activation with DCC first.
x: Direct amide formation from the acid and amine requires prolonged heating above ~150 °C (or a coupling agent); at room temperature only the salt forms.
No ester can form without an alcohol, and the amine nitrogen does not give up its methyl group.
There is no chlorine source; acid chlorides are made with SOCl<sub>2</sub>, (COCl)<sub>2</sub> or PCl<sub>5</sub>.

q: Which sequence converts butanoic acid into hexan-3-one, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count carbons: the acid supplies four, including the future C=O. What must be added, and which organometallic stops at the ketone?
w: Hexan-3-one = butanoyl (4 C, with the C=O) + ethyl (2 C). Convert the acid to butanoyl chloride with SOCl2, then add one ethyl with the Gilman reagent, which does not add again to the ketone: 1. SOCl2 2. (CH3CH2)2CuLi.
x: Excess Grignard adds twice to an acid chloride, giving the 3° alcohol 3-ethylhexan-3-ol, not the ketone.
A Grignard reagent simply deprotonates the carboxylic acid (giving ethane and a carboxylate salt); no C–C bond forms.
Dimethylcuprate adds a methyl, not an ethyl, giving pentan-2-one (five carbons), one carbon short.

q: 4-Aminophenol is treated with one equivalent of acetic anhydride. What is the major product?
h: Which is the stronger nucleophile, an aryl NH<sub>2</sub> or a phenol OH? With only one equivalent, which reacts?
w: Both groups can be acylated, but nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so its lone pair is more available: the amine is far more nucleophilic than the neutral phenol. With one equivalent of anhydride, N-acetylation wins, giving A, N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide (acetaminophen). The amide product is also more stable than an aryl ester.
x: O-Acetylation of the phenol is slower because a neutral OH is a weaker nucleophile than NH<sub>2</sub>; this ester is not the major product.
Diacetylation needs at least two equivalents of anhydride; with one equivalent the more nucleophilic N reacts selectively.
Ring acylation (Friedel–Crafts) needs a Lewis acid such as AlCl<sub>3</sub>; an anhydride alone acylates N or O, not the ring carbon.

q: Ethyl benzoate is treated with excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in ether, followed by aqueous workup. What are the organic products?
h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> delivers hydride twice to an ester. What happens to the OR group?
w: The first hydride gives a tetrahedral intermediate that expels ethoxide, forming benzaldehyde. The aldehyde is more reactive than the ester and is reduced at once by a second hydride. Workup protonates both alkoxides: benzyl alcohol (PhCH2OH) and ethanol.
x: Benzaldehyde is an intermediate, but with excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub> it is reduced further to the primary alcohol.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent; it does not hydrolyze the ester to the acid.
The C–O bond to the acyl carbon is broken and the ethoxy group leaves; the oxygen is not retained as an ether link.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: DIBAL-H delivers one hydride. At −78 °C the tetrahedral intermediate does not collapse until workup.
w: One equivalent of DIBAL-H at −78 °C adds one hydride to the ester; the aluminum-bound tetrahedral intermediate is stable at that temperature, so no aldehyde is present while active hydride remains. Aqueous workup collapses it to A, hexanal (plus methanol).
x: Hexan-1-ol is the LiAlH<sub>4</sub> product (or DIBAL-H in excess at room temperature), where the aldehyde is reduced again.
DIBAL-H is a reducing agent; it does not hydrolyze the ester to the acid.
Hydride replaces OCH<sub>3</sub> on the carbonyl carbon; the C=O oxygen is not removed to form an ether.

q: Why must the reduction of an ester to an aldehyde with DIBAL-H be run at −78 °C?
c: The Al-bound tetrahedral intermediate survives at −78 °C and gives the aldehyde only at workup
At −78 °C DIBAL-H attacks only the ester oxygen, not the carbonyl carbon, so it cleaves the C–O bond
At higher temperature DIBAL-H reduces the ester all the way to an alkane, removing both oxygens
At −78 °C the aldehyde product freezes out of solution as it forms, so it is protected
h: The danger is a second hydride addition. What species would have to be present for that to happen?
w: An aldehyde is more reactive than an ester, so if it formed while DIBAL-H was still present it would be reduced to the primary alcohol. At −78 °C the tetrahedral intermediate (O–Al(iBu)2 on carbon, with OR still attached) is stable; it collapses to the aldehyde only during aqueous workup, after the hydride is destroyed.
x: DIBAL-H is a Lewis acid that coordinates to the C=O oxygen, but the hydride is delivered to the carbonyl carbon at any temperature.
The over-reduction product at higher temperature is the primary alcohol; aluminum hydrides do not remove the oxygen to give an alkane.
Selectivity comes from the stability of the tetrahedral intermediate in solution, not from precipitation of the aldehyde.

q: What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: A lactone is a cyclic ester. Reduce it the way you would any ester, then remember both ends belong to one molecule.
w: LiAlH4 reduces an ester to two alcohols: the acyl carbon becomes CH2OH and the alkoxy oxygen becomes an OH. In a lactone both pieces are in one molecule, so the ring opens to A, butane-1,4-diol.
x: The lactol (cyclic hemiacetal) is what one hydride gives, e.g. DIBAL-H at −78 °C; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces on through the open-chain aldehyde.
Tetrahydrofuran would require removing the carbonyl oxygen completely while keeping the ring; hydride reduction does not do that.
Butan-1-ol has lost an oxygen; the ring oxygen is retained as the second OH group.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: A Grignard reagent adds to an ester, the alkoxide leaves, and a ketone forms. Is the ketone more or less reactive than the ester?
w: CH3MgBr adds, methoxide leaves, and acetophenone forms. A ketone is more electrophilic than an ester, so it consumes a second CH3MgBr right away. Workup gives the 3° alcohol with two new methyls: A, 2-phenylpropan-2-ol.
x: Acetophenone is the intermediate; it cannot be stopped at with a Grignard reagent because it reacts faster than the ester.
A secondary alcohol would need one methyl and one hydride; no hydride source is present.
This hemiketal-like structure is the first tetrahedral intermediate; it loses methoxide before workup and is not isolated.

q: Which ester and Grignard reagent (excess, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) give the alcohol shown?
h: An ester + excess RMgBr makes a 3° alcohol with two identical R groups from the Grignard. Which two groups on the carbinol carbon match?
w: The carbinol carbon carries Ph, CH2CH3 and CH2CH3. The two identical groups (two ethyls) come from the Grignard reagent; the different one (phenyl) comes from the ester's acyl group. So methyl benzoate + excess CH3CH2MgBr gives 3-phenylpentan-3-ol.
x: Ethyl propanoate + excess PhMgBr gives two phenyls and one ethyl on the carbinol carbon (1,1-diphenylpropan-1-ol).
Methyl propanoate + excess EtMgBr gives three ethyls (3-ethylpentan-3-ol); there is no phenyl.
Ethyl acetate + excess PhMgBr gives 1,1-diphenylethanol (two phenyls and one methyl).

q: What is the product after aqueous workup?
h: Treat the lactone like any ester: the acyl carbon gets two R groups; the ring oxygen becomes a separate alcohol.
w: The first CH3MgBr adds to the C=O; the tetrahedral intermediate opens the ring, releasing an alkoxide on the far end and leaving a methyl ketone. The ketone adds a second CH3MgBr. Workup protonates both alkoxides: A, 4-methylpentane-1,4-diol.
x: The hydroxy ketone is the intermediate after one addition; with excess Grignard the ketone reacts again.
A cyclic ether would need a separate ring-closing step (e.g. strong acid and heat); the mild workup simply protonates the two alkoxides.
Pentane-1,4-diol has only one methyl on C4 and an H; forming it would require a hydride reduction step.

q: Ethyl formate is treated with excess phenylmagnesium bromide, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. What is the product?
h: A formate ester is HC(=O)OR. The acyl carbon keeps its H.
w: PhMgBr adds to the formyl carbon and ethoxide leaves, giving benzaldehyde. The aldehyde is more reactive than the ester and adds a second PhMgBr. The carbinol carbon carries H, Ph and Ph: A, diphenylmethanol, a secondary alcohol. Formate esters are the one ester that gives 2° rather than 3° alcohols with Grignard reagents.
x: Benzaldehyde is the intermediate; it reacts with the excess Grignard faster than the ester does.
A third phenyl would require replacing the formyl H; the C–H bond is not a leaving group.
Benzyl alcohol would require hydride, not phenyl, to add to benzaldehyde.

q: N-Methylbenzamide is heated at reflux in 6 M HCl for several hours. What species are present at the end, before any neutralization?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond. Then ask what form each product takes in strong acid.
w: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis cleaves the amide C–N bond, giving benzoic acid and methylamine. In 6 M HCl the amine is protonated to methylammonium; this protonation is what makes acidic amide hydrolysis irreversible. The acid stays un-ionized at low pH: benzoic acid and CH3NH3+.
x: Benzoate and free methylamine are the forms present under basic conditions; at low pH the acid is neutral and the amine is protonated.
The methyl group is on nitrogen, not oxygen; hydrolysis cannot transfer it to make a methyl ester.
Hydrolysis does not change the oxidation state of the carbonyl carbon; no aldehyde forms.

q: What is the product?
h: With amides, LiAlH<sub>4</sub> removes the carbonyl oxygen instead of the nitrogen. Why is N not lost?
w: Hydride adds to the C=O, but the poorer leaving group is the amide nitrogen, so the oxygen (as an O–Al species) is expelled instead, giving an iminium ion. A second hydride reduces the iminium. The C=O becomes CH2 and the carbon count is unchanged: A, N,N-dimethyl(cyclohexylmethyl)amine.
x: Losing the nitrogen to give a primary alcohol is the ester pattern; for amides the oxygen leaves because R<sub>2</sub>N<sup>−</sup> is a far worse leaving group.
An aldehyde is not the product of LiAlH<sub>4</sub> with an amide; the iminium ion that forms is reduced again.
The carbonyl carbon is retained as CH<sub>2</sub>; this structure has lost a carbon.

q: What does LiAlH<sub>4</sub> (then H<sub>2</sub>O) convert the lactam shown into?
h: Amide + LiAlH<sub>4</sub>: C=O → CH<sub>2</sub>, nitrogen kept.
w: LiAlH4 reduces an amide C=O to CH2 and keeps the C–N bond. For a cyclic amide the ring stays closed, so piperidin-2-one becomes A, piperidine.
x: 5-Aminopentan-1-ol would require cleavage of the C–N bond; with amides the oxygen is lost, not the nitrogen.
Pentan-1-amine has lost an oxygen and opened the ring; the ring stays intact because no ring bond to N is cut.
This cyclic hemiaminal still carries an oxygen; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> removes the carbonyl oxygen completely, so it is not the product.

q: N,N-Diethylacetamide is heated at reflux in aqueous NaOH. What are the products?
h: Hydrolysis cuts the C–N bond. What form does each fragment take in strong base?
w: Hydroxide adds to the amide C=O and the C–N bond breaks on prolonged heating. In base, the acid ends up as the carboxylate and the amine as the free amine: sodium acetate and diethylamine.
x: These are the forms under acidic conditions; in NaOH the acid is deprotonated and the amine is neutral.
Hydrolysis breaks the acyl C–N bond; the ethyl groups stay on nitrogen and are not converted to ethanol.
Hydrolysis does not reduce the carbonyl carbon; no aldehyde forms.

q:
Which statements about amides are correct?
I. When an amide is protonated by a strong acid, the proton goes mainly to the oxygen.
II. The C–N bond in an amide is shorter than the C–N bond in an amine.
III. Amides are stronger bases than amines because their nitrogen is sp2 hybridized.
h: Use the C=N resonance form of the amide. Where is the electron density, and is the N lone pair available?
w: Because the N lone pair is delocalized onto oxygen, O is the most basic site: O-protonation gives a cation stabilized by resonance with N (I true). The same delocalization gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, so it is shorter (about 1.34 Å vs 1.47 Å in an amine) (II true). Delocalization makes the N lone pair less available, so amides are far weaker bases than amines (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 0 vs ≈ 10) (III false). Answer: I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true: resonance gives the amide C–N bond partial double-bond character, so it is shorter than an amine C–N single bond.
Statement III is false: the delocalized lone pair makes amides very weak bases, much weaker than amines.
Statement III is false, so all three cannot be correct.

q: Rank the esters in order of increasing rate of hydrolysis with NaOH (slowest first).
h: All three are acetates, so the acyl part is the same. Compare the leaving groups by the pK<sub>a</sub> of their conjugate acids: CH<sub>3</sub>OH 15.5, phenol 10.0, 4-nitrophenol 7.2.
w: The weaker the base that leaves, the better the leaving group, and the more electron-withdrawing the OR group, the more electrophilic the C=O. Methoxide (from CH3OH, pKa 15.5) is the poorest leaving group, phenoxide (10.0) is better, and 4-nitrophenoxide (7.2), stabilized by resonance into NO2, is best. Slowest to fastest: I < II < III. (4-Nitrophenyl esters are used as 'activated esters' for this reason.)
x: This reverses the trend: a more stable (weaker-base) leaving group makes hydrolysis faster, not slower.
Phenoxide is a better leaving group than methoxide because its negative charge is delocalized into the ring, so phenyl acetate reacts faster than methyl acetate.
The para-nitro group stabilizes the phenoxide by resonance, making it the best leaving group, so III is fastest.

q: What is the major product?
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a mild hydride donor. Which carbonyl is more electrophilic: a ketone or an ester?
w: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones readily but reacts only very slowly with esters, whose C=O is stabilized by resonance donation from the OCH3 oxygen. Only the ketone is reduced: A, methyl 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoate (racemic).
x: Reducing the ester while leaving the ketone reverses the reactivity order; ketones are more reactive than esters.
Reducing both carbonyls is the LiAlH<sub>4</sub> result; NaBH<sub>4</sub> is not strong enough to reduce the ester.
Converting C=O to CH<sub>2</sub> requires Wolff–Kishner or Clemmensen conditions, not NaBH<sub>4</sub>.

q: Phenylacetonitrile is heated at reflux in aqueous H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> for several hours. What is the organic product?
h: Full hydrolysis of a nitrile goes through an amide. Where does it end?
w: Water adds to the protonated C≡N to give an amide, which under prolonged heating in acid is hydrolyzed further (NH4+ released). The nitrile carbon becomes the CO2H carbon, so no carbon is lost: A, phenylacetic acid.
x: The amide is the intermediate; several hours at reflux in strong acid hydrolyze it on to the carboxylic acid.
An amine would require a reducing agent such as LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; aqueous acid only hydrolyzes.
The nitrile carbon is kept as the carboxyl carbon; benzoic acid has one carbon too few.

q: Which sequence converts 1-bromopropane into butan-1-amine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>?
h: The product has one more carbon than the starting halide. Which group adds a carbon that can become CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>?
w: SN2 with cyanide gives butanenitrile (one new carbon). LiAlH4 adds two hydrides to C≡N, and workup gives the primary amine with the nitrile carbon as CH2: 1. NaCN 2. LiAlH4 3. H2O.
x: Ammonia substitution gives propan-1-amine (three carbons), and over-alkylation gives di- and tripropylamines.
Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile gives butanoic acid, not the amine.
A Grignard adds to the nitrile and, after hydrolysis, gives a ketone (pentan-2-one).

q: What is the product after aqueous acid workup?
h: The Grignard adds once to C≡N. What does the resulting C=N species become in aqueous acid?
w: EtMgBr adds to the nitrile carbon to give an imine magnesium salt (C=N–MgBr). Aqueous acid protonates it to the imine, which hydrolyzes to the ketone: A, 1-phenylpropan-1-one (propiophenone).
x: Two additions do not occur: the negatively charged imine salt is not electrophilic enough to react with a second Grignard.
No hydride source is present to reduce C=N to an amine.
The imine is an intermediate; aqueous acid hydrolyzes it to the ketone.

q: An ester and excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr give a 3° alcohol, but a nitrile and excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr give a ketone after workup. What is the best explanation?
c: The nitrile adds once to give an imine anion salt, which does not react again; the ketone forms only at workup
Nitriles are more reactive than ketones, so the Grignard is used up by the nitrile before any of the ketone forms
The ketone formed from the nitrile is protected because it is immediately deprotonated to an enolate
Nitrogen is a better leaving group than oxygen, so the C=N bond is never formed in the intermediate
h: Follow the nitrile reaction step by step. When does the ketone C=O actually appear?
w: With an ester, the tetrahedral intermediate expels the alkoxide in the flask, so a ketone forms in the presence of Grignard and is attacked again. With a nitrile, addition gives R2C=N− MgBr+. There is no leaving group, and the negatively charged imine salt is not electrophilic, so it waits. The ketone appears only when aqueous acid hydrolyzes the imine, after the Grignard has been destroyed.
x: Nitriles are actually less electrophilic than ketones; the explanation is that no ketone is present until workup.
No ketone exists in the flask before workup, so enolization is not what protects it.
Nothing leaves from the nitrile adduct; that is exactly why it stops at the imine salt. Amide ions are also very poor leaving groups.

q: What is the product?
h: DIBAL-H delivers one hydride to C≡N. What does the resulting imine-aluminum species become in water?
w: One hydride adds to the nitrile carbon, giving an aluminum-bound imine (C=N–Al). It cannot accept a second hydride easily, and aqueous workup hydrolyzes the imine to A, 3-methylbutanal.
x: Two hydrides (from LiAlH<sub>4</sub>) give the primary amine; DIBAL-H stops after one.
DIBAL-H reduces; it does not hydrolyze the nitrile to an acid.
The nitrogen is lost as NH<sub>3</sub> during hydrolysis of the imine; the carbon ends as CHO, not CH<sub>2</sub>OH.

q: Which sequence best converts 2-bromo-2-methylpropane into 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCO<sub>2</sub>H?
h: Both the nitrile route and the Grignard/CO<sub>2</sub> route add one carbon. Which one needs an S<sub>N</sub>2 step?
w: Making a tertiary Grignard is fine (no SN2 needed); it adds to CO2 to give a carboxylate, and acid gives the acid: 1. Mg 2. CO2 3. H3O+. The cyanide route needs SN2 at a tertiary carbon, which fails; cyanide acts as a base and gives 2-methylpropene by E2.
x: Cyanide cannot do S<sub>N</sub>2 at a tertiary carbon; elimination to 2-methylpropene dominates, so little nitrile forms.
At best this route forms tert-butyl alcohol (with much 2-methylpropene), which has no H on the carbinol carbon and cannot be oxidized; it also never adds the needed extra carbon.
Besides the failed S<sub>N</sub>2 step, LiAlH<sub>4</sub> would reduce a nitrile to an amine, not a carboxylic acid.

q: What is the final organic product?
h: Two things happen in hot aqueous acid: both esters are hydrolyzed, and then one structural feature of the diacid makes it unstable to heat.
w: Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes both ethyl esters to give benzylmalonic acid. A malonic acid has a C=O β to the other CO2H, so on heating it loses CO2 through a cyclic six-membered transition state, giving an enol of a carboxylic acid that tautomerizes: A, 3-phenylpropanoic acid.
x: Benzylmalonic acid forms first, but a 1,3-diacid decarboxylates on heating; it does not survive the conditions.
Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester, so the ethyl ester does not remain.
Only one CO<sub>2</sub> is lost; after the first decarboxylation there is no longer a β-carbonyl to allow a second one. Phenylacetic acid has one carbon too few.

q: Which acid loses CO<sub>2</sub> readily when warmed to about 100 °C?
h: Easy thermal decarboxylation needs a C=O two carbons away from the carboxyl carbon, so that a six-membered cyclic transition state can form.
w: A β-keto acid has the ketone C=O β to the CO2H. The carboxyl H is transferred to the ketone oxygen through a six-membered cyclic transition state while the C–C bond breaks, giving CO2 and an enol. A, 3-oxobutanoic acid (acetoacetic acid), is the β-keto acid; it decarboxylates to acetone.
x: Pyruvic acid is an α-keto acid; the C=O is too close to form the six-membered cyclic transition state.
4-Oxopentanoic acid is a γ-keto acid; the ketone is too far away for the cyclic transition state, and the C–C bond breaking would not give a stabilized enol.
Benzoic acid has no β-carbonyl; aryl carboxylic acids need much harsher conditions to lose CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: 3-Oxobutanoic acid loses CO2 on heating through a cyclic transition state. What is the first-formed organic product (before any tautomerization)?
h: In the cyclic transition state the carboxyl H moves to the ketone oxygen while the C–CO<sub>2</sub> bond breaks. Where do those C–C bonding electrons go?
w: Six electrons move around a ring: the ketone oxygen takes the carboxyl H, the O–H bond electrons become the second C=O of CO2, and the breaking C–C bond electrons form a C=C between the α-carbon and the former ketone carbon. No charged intermediate forms; the first product is the neutral enol, A (prop-1-en-2-ol), which then tautomerizes to acetone.
x: Acetone is the final product, formed by keto–enol tautomerization of the enol; it is not the first-formed species.
The concerted cyclic pathway is neutral throughout; no carbanion is produced (that would be very unstable without a counter-ion).
Methylketene would require losing water, not CO<sub>2</sub>, and has the wrong connectivity.

q: A carboxylic acid derivative has the IR spectrum shown (two strong C=O bands at 1820 and 1760 cm<sup>−1</sup>; no O–H or N–H bands). Which compound is it?
h: Which derivative has two C=O groups that can stretch in phase and out of phase?
w: An anhydride has two coupled C=O groups, giving a symmetric and an asymmetric stretch, typically near 1820 and 1760 cm−1. The pair of strong high-frequency bands identifies A, propanoic anhydride.
x: An acid chloride shows one C=O band near 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not a pair.
An ester shows a single C=O near 1735–1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
A carboxylic acid would show a very broad O–H band from about 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=O near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Rank the compounds by C=O stretching frequency, lowest to highest wavenumber.
h: Resonance donation into C=O lengthens and weakens it (lower wavenumber); inductive withdrawal shortens and strengthens it.
w: In the amide (III) the N lone pair donates strongly, giving the C=O much single-bond character: ~1650 cm−1. In the ester (I) oxygen donates less and withdraws inductively: ~1740 cm−1. In the acid chloride (II) Cl hardly donates and withdraws strongly: ~1800 cm−1. Order: III < I < II.
x: This reverses the order. More resonance donation means a weaker C=O and a lower wavenumber, so the amide is lowest.
The ester's oxygen donates less than the amide nitrogen, so the ester C=O is at higher wavenumber than the amide.
Chlorine is the poorest π donor and withdraws inductively, so the acid chloride has the highest C=O stretch, not the ester.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows strong IR bands at 1742 and 1240 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no band above 3100 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. What is the compound?
h: The IR says ester. Then look at where the CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is: on oxygen (~4 ppm) or next to C=O (~2.3 ppm)?
w: 1742 and 1240 cm−1 (C=O and C–O) with no O–H band mean an ester. A 3H singlet at 2.05 ppm is a CH3 on C=O. The 2H quartet at 4.12 ppm is an OCH2 next to a CH3 (triplet at 1.26). So the ethyl is on oxygen and the methyl is on the carbonyl: A, ethyl acetate.
x: Methyl propanoate would show an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near 3.7 ppm and a CH<sub>2</sub> quartet near 2.3 ppm (next to C=O), not 4.1 ppm.
Propyl formate would show a formyl H singlet near 8.0 ppm (1H) and an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet, not a quartet.
Butanoic acid would show a very broad O–H band in the IR (2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and a CO<sub>2</sub>H proton near 11–12 ppm.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR spectrum shown: two medium bands at 3360 and 3180 cm<sup>−1</sup>, C–H at 2960 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and strong bands at 1660 and 1630 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: Two N–H stretches mean NH<sub>2</sub>. A C=O near 1660 cm<sup>−1</sup> is much lower than a ketone's.
w: Two N–H bands (symmetric and asymmetric stretch) show an NH2 group. A C=O at 1660 cm−1 (lowered by N donation) with an N–H bend near 1630 cm−1 is a primary amide: A, butanamide.
x: A secondary amide (N–H) shows only one N–H stretch, near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
A tertiary amide has no N–H bond, so it would show no bands at all above 3100 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
This amino ketone has NH<sub>2</sub> bands but a ketone C=O near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not 1660 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which sequence converts hexanoic acid into hexan-1-amine, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, with no change in the number of carbons?
h: Make an amide first. Then find the step that turns C=O into CH<sub>2</sub> while keeping the C–N bond.
w: SOCl2 gives hexanoyl chloride; excess NH3 gives hexanamide (the second equivalent takes up HCl). LiAlH4 reduces the amide C=O to CH2, keeping all six carbons: 1. SOCl2 2. NH3 3. LiAlH4 4. H2O.
x: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the acid to hexan-1-ol, and OH<sup>−</sup> is too poor a leaving group for ammonia to displace it.
Br<sub>2</sub>/NaOH on a primary amide is the Hofmann rearrangement, which loses the carbonyl carbon and gives pentan-1-amine.
Hot aqueous acid simply hydrolyzes the amide back to hexanoic acid.

q: Compound X, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>N, has a sharp IR band at 2250 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no bands above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>. X reacts with 1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr 2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> to give 2-methylpentan-3-one. What is X?
h: Grignard + nitrile → ketone: the nitrile carbon becomes the C=O; the ethyl comes from the Grignard. What is on the other side of the C=O?
w: 2-Methylpentan-3-one is (CH3)2CH–CO–CH2CH3. The ethyl came from the Grignard, so the nitrile must be (CH3)2CH–C≡N. The 2250 cm−1 band (C≡N) and the formula C4H7N fit: A, 2-methylpropanenitrile.
x: Butanenitrile + EtMgBr gives hexan-3-one (unbranched), not 2-methylpentan-3-one.
An isocyanide (R–N≡C) absorbs near 2140 cm<sup>−1</sup> and does not give a ketone with a Grignard reagent.
A primary amine would show N–H stretches above 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and an internal alkyne C≡C is weak; it would not give a ketone with EtMgBr.

q: Which compound is the strongest acid?
h: Compare the stability of each conjugate base. Where can the negative charge on oxygen spread?
w: Acidity tracks the stability of the conjugate base. A phenoxide ion delocalizes its charge into the ring (phenol pKa ≈ 10), while cyclohexoxide keeps it on one oxygen (pKa ≈ 16–18). A para-nitro group adds one more resonance form that places the negative charge on the nitro oxygens, so 4-nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 7.2) is the strongest acid.
x: Phenol is a good deal more acidic than an alcohol, but it lacks the electron-withdrawing nitro group that further stabilizes the phenoxide (pK<sub>a</sub> 10 vs 7.2).
The methyl group is weakly electron-donating, which slightly destabilizes the phenoxide; 4-methylphenol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10.3) is a little weaker than phenol.
An alkoxide has no resonance delocalization, so cyclohexanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 18) is the weakest acid of the four.

q: Rank these phenols in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
h: For each para substituent, decide whether its resonance effect or its inductive effect dominates on the phenoxide.
w: Approximate pKa values: 4-methoxyphenol 10.2, phenol 10.0, 4-chlorophenol 9.4, 4-nitrophenol 7.2. A para OCH3 donates lone-pair density by resonance, which outweighs its inductive pull and destabilizes the phenoxide slightly. Chlorine is inductively withdrawing, and that outweighs its weak resonance donation, so it stabilizes the anion a little. NO2 withdraws by both resonance and induction. Order: I < II < III < IV.
x: This treats OCH<sub>3</sub> as electron-withdrawing because oxygen is electronegative; at the para position its resonance donation wins, so 4-methoxyphenol is slightly weaker than phenol.
This makes chlorine stronger than nitro. Nitro can delocalize the phenoxide charge onto its own oxygens by resonance; chlorine only pulls inductively.
This treats chlorine as a net donor. For halogens, induction outweighs resonance, so 4-chlorophenol is more acidic than phenol.

q:
Rank these alcohols in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
I. CH3CH2OH   II. ClCH2CH2OH   III. CF3CH2OH   IV. (CH3)3COH
h: None of these alkoxides has resonance. Think about induction from halogens and about how well the solvent can surround each alkoxide.
w: Electron-withdrawing halogens stabilize the alkoxide by induction, and three fluorines on the adjacent carbon pull far harder than one chlorine one carbon farther away. A bulky tert-butoxide is poorly solvated, which makes tert-butyl alcohol the weakest acid. Approximate pKa: (CH3)3COH 18, CH3CH2OH 16, ClCH2CH2OH 14.3, CF3CH2OH 12.4. Order: IV < I < II < III.
x: This swaps ethanol and tert-butyl alcohol. The crowded tert-butoxide ion is solvated less well, so tert-butyl alcohol is the weaker acid.
One chlorine is not stronger than three fluorines: the CF<sub>3</sub> group exerts a much larger inductive pull on the alkoxide oxygen.
This is the reverse order; halogen substituents make alcohols more acidic, not less.

q: Which base deprotonates phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.0) essentially completely but deprotonates ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> 16) far less than completely? (The pK<sub>a</sub> of each base's conjugate acid is in parentheses.)
h: An acid–base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid. Compare each conjugate acid's pK<sub>a</sub> with 10 and with 16.
w: Keq = 10(pKa of conjugate acid of the base − pKa of the acid). For phenol + NaOH, Keq ≈ 105.7, essentially complete. For ethanol + NaOH, Keq ≈ 10−0.3 ≈ 0.5, so ethanol is only partly deprotonated, far from complete. NaOH separates the two; this is why phenols dissolve in aqueous NaOH as phenoxide salts, while ordinary alcohols are not converted to alkoxides there.
x: Bicarbonate is too weak: for phenol, K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>6.4−10</sup> ≈ 10<sup>−3.6</sup>, so phenol is barely deprotonated.
Hydride is so strong (H<sub>2</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 35) that it deprotonates ethanol completely too.
Amide (NH<sub>3</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> 38) deprotonates both phenol and ethanol essentially completely.

q: Rank these compounds from highest to lowest boiling point.
h: Count the O–H groups first; then, among isomers with one O–H, consider shape and surface area.
w: Butane-1,4-diol has two O–H groups and forms an extended hydrogen-bond network (bp ≈ 230 °C). Butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol each have one O–H, but the straight chain has more surface contact and less steric shielding of the OH (117 °C vs 82 °C). Diethyl ether cannot donate a hydrogen bond (35 °C). Order: I > II > III > IV.
x: A second O–H group roughly doubles the hydrogen bonding, so the diol boils far above butan-1-ol.
Branching lowers the boiling point: the compact tert-butyl alcohol has less surface area and a more hindered OH than butan-1-ol.
Diethyl ether is a hydrogen-bond acceptor only; it cannot donate, so it boils well below tert-butyl alcohol.

q: What is the major organic product of this reaction?
h: Which carbonyl is more electrophilic, the ketone or the ester? How strong a hydride donor is NaBH<sub>4</sub>?
w: NaBH4 is a mild hydride donor. It reduces aldehydes and ketones quickly but leaves esters essentially untouched, because the ester carbonyl is stabilized by donation from the OCH3 oxygen. Only the ketone becomes a secondary alcohol: methyl 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoate (racemic).
x: Reducing both groups needs LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; NaBH<sub>4</sub> in methanol does not reduce the ester at a useful rate.
This reverses the selectivity: the ester is the less reactive carbonyl, so it cannot be reduced while the ketone survives.
Removing the oxygen completely (C=O → CH<sub>2</sub>) requires Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner conditions, not a hydride reagent.

q:
Which functional groups are reduced by NaBH4 in methanol at room temperature?
I. aldehyde   II. ketone   III. ester   IV. carboxylic acid
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is the gentle hydride reagent. Which carbonyls are the most electrophilic?
w: NaBH4 reduces the most electrophilic carbonyls, aldehydes (to 1° alcohols) and ketones (to 2° alcohols). Esters are resonance-stabilized and react too slowly, and a carboxylic acid is simply deprotonated to an unreactive carboxylate. Answer: I and II only. LiAlH4 reduces all four.
x: Ketones are reduced by NaBH<sub>4</sub> as well; they are only slightly less reactive than aldehydes.
Esters are not reduced at a useful rate by NaBH<sub>4</sub> in methanol; that takes LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.
A carboxylic acid is deprotonated by the basic hydride to a carboxylate, which is far too electron-rich to accept hydride from NaBH<sub>4</sub>.

q: The ketone below is a single enantiomer. Which statement best describes the product mixture after reduction with NaBH<sub>4</sub>?
c: (2R,3R) and (2S,3R) diastereomers in unequal amounts; optically active
(2R,3R) and (2S,3S) enantiomers in equal amounts; optically inactive
(2R,3S) and (2S,3R) enantiomers in equal amounts; optically inactive
(2R,3R) and (2S,3R) diastereomers in equal amounts; optically inactive
h: Hydride does not touch C3. With C3 fixed, how are the two possible C2 products related?
w: The starting ketone is (R)-3-phenylbutan-2-one. Hydride adds to C2 from either face, creating a new stereocenter, while C3 keeps its (R) configuration. The products, (2R,3R)- and (2S,3R)-3-phenylbutan-2-ol, are diastereomers. The two faces of the carbonyl are diastereotopic (the existing stereocenter makes them different), so the transition states differ in energy and the products form in unequal amounts. A mixture of chiral, non-mirror-image molecules is optically active.
x: C3 is not touched by NaBH4, so it cannot become (S); a (2S,3S) product would require inverting a carbon that never reacts.
This inverts C3, which does not react; every product molecule keeps the (3R) configuration of the starting ketone.

Diastereomers form through transition states of different energy, so equal amounts are not expected; and even a 1:1 mixture of diastereomers would still rotate light because they are not mirror images.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: A lactone is a cyclic ester. What does LiAlH<sub>4</sub> do to both the acyl carbon and the alkoxy oxygen of an ester?
w: LiAlH4 reduces an ester to two alcohols: the acyl carbon becomes a CH2OH and the alkoxy oxygen becomes a second OH. In a lactone both pieces are in the same molecule, so the ring opens to one diol: butane-1,4-diol.
x: The aldehyde formed after the first hydride is more reactive than the ester and is reduced at once; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not stop at the aldehyde.
Tetrahydrofuran would need the carbonyl oxygen removed while the ring stays closed; hydride reduction instead opens the ring at the C–O bond to give a diol.
The ring oxygen is not lost: it becomes an O–H after workup, so the product keeps both oxygens.

q: What is the major organic product after treatment with excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub> followed by aqueous workup?
h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces both carbonyls. For the amide, which group leaves from the tetrahedral intermediate: oxygen or nitrogen?
w: Excess LiAlH4 reduces the ketone to a secondary alcohol. Amides are reduced too, but differently from esters: the oxygen (bound to aluminum) is expelled to give an iminium ion, which takes a second hydride, so C=O becomes CH2 and the nitrogen stays. Product: 1-[4-(dimethylaminomethyl)phenyl]ethan-1-ol.
x: This treats the amide like an ester. In amide reduction nitrogen stays attached and the oxygen is removed, giving an amine, not an alcohol.
Amides are less reactive than ketones but are still reduced by excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; leaving the amide intact is the NaBH<sub>4</sub> result.
The ketone is the most reactive carbonyl present; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> cannot reduce the amide while leaving the ketone untouched.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane reacts with NaOH in DMSO. What is the substitution product?
h: A strong nucleophile, a secondary substrate and a polar aprotic solvent: which substitution mechanism, and what does it do to configuration?
w: Hydroxide is a strong nucleophile and DMSO is polar aprotic, so substitution goes SN2 with backside attack and inversion. OH takes the place of Br, which had the same priority rank (highest), so inversion changes the label: (S)-butan-2-ol.
x: Retention would require frontside attack or two inversions; a single S<sub>N</sub>2 step inverts the stereocenter.
Racemization comes from a planar carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1), which is not favored with a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent.
S<sub>N</sub>2 does not move the functional group; the OH ends up on the carbon that carried the Br.

q: Which reagents carry out this conversion in good yield?
h: The OH goes to the more substituted alkene carbon, and the carbon skeleton must not change. Which Markovnikov method avoids a free carbocation?
w: The target has Markovnikov regiochemistry and the same skeleton. Acid hydration would form a secondary carbocation next to a quaternary carbon, which undergoes a methyl shift. Oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, gives Markovnikov addition and does not rearrange. Answer: 1. Hg(OAc)2, H2O 2. NaBH4.
x: Acid hydration goes through a free 2° carbocation that undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to a 3° cation, giving mainly 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov and gives the primary alcohol 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol.
Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C; reduction of the resulting aldehyde gives 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol, with one carbon fewer.

q: Which compound is the weakest acid?
h: Draw the resonance forms of each phenoxide. In which isomer can the negative charge reach the carbon bearing the nitro group?
w: The phenoxide charge is delocalized to the ortho and para carbons. A nitro group at an ortho or para position can accept that charge onto its own oxygens (pKa ≈ 7.2 for both 2- and 4-nitrophenol), and two such groups do even better (2,4-dinitrophenol, pKa ≈ 4.1). A meta nitro group is never on a carbon that carries the charge, so it helps only by induction: 3-nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 8.4) is the weakest acid of the four.
x: In 4-nitrophenol the charge delocalizes onto the nitro oxygens by resonance, which makes it more acidic than the meta isomer.
An ortho nitro group also stabilizes the phenoxide by resonance (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 7.2), so 2-nitrophenol is more acidic than 3-nitrophenol.
Two resonance-withdrawing nitro groups (ortho and para) make 2,4-dinitrophenol the strongest acid here, not the weakest.

q: Acetophenone is treated with NaBD<sub>4</sub> in ether, then with H<sub>2</sub>O. Where are the deuterium atoms in the product?
h: Follow each hydrogen: one comes from the hydride reagent, one from the workup.
w: Borodeuteride delivers D− to the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide. The O–H proton comes later from the H2O workup. Product: PhCD(OH)CH3 (racemic, since D adds equally to both faces).
x: The nucleophile is the deuteride; it bonds to carbon, not oxygen. The oxygen is protonated by H<sub>2</sub>O.
The workup uses H<sub>2</sub>O, not D<sub>2</sub>O, so the O–H ends up as O–H; only the carbon carries D.
Hydride attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, not the methyl carbon; the CH<sub>3</sub> is untouched.

q: Which sequence carries out this conversion?
h: You must reduce the less reactive carbonyl and keep the more reactive one. What can temporarily hide a ketone from LiAlH<sub>4</sub>?
w: Any hydride that reduces an ester also reduces a ketone, so the ketone must be protected. Ethylene glycol and acid convert the ketone to a cyclic acetal, which is inert to LiAlH4. LiAlH4 then reduces the ester to CH2OH, and aqueous acid removes the acetal and restores the ketone. Answer: 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH 2. LiAlH4 3. H3O+.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> has the opposite selectivity: it reduces the ketone to an alcohol and leaves the ester untouched.
Unprotected, both carbonyls are reduced, giving the diol 4-(hydroxymethyl)cyclohexan-1-ol.
PCC re-oxidizes both alcohols of the diol, giving the keto aldehyde (4-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde), not the keto alcohol.

q: Which compound, treated with CH3CH2MgBr in ether and then H3O+, gives a primary alcohol?
h: The carbonyl carbon becomes the carbinol carbon. How many carbon groups will it carry after the Grignard adds?
w: In a Grignard addition the carbonyl carbon becomes the C–OH carbon, carrying the new alkyl group plus whatever it already had. Formaldehyde has only H atoms, so the carbinol carbon ends up with one carbon group: CH3CH2CH2OH, a primary alcohol. Answer: formaldehyde.
x: Acetaldehyde already has one methyl group, so adding ethyl gives the secondary alcohol butan-2-ol.
Acetone carries two methyl groups, so adding ethyl gives the tertiary alcohol 2-methylbutan-2-ol.
An ester takes two equivalents: methyl formate gives pentan-3-ol, a secondary alcohol with two ethyl groups on the carbinol carbon.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: After the first addition, methoxide leaves. What carbonyl is left, and is it more or less reactive than the ester?
w: The first CH3MgBr adds to the ester carbonyl; the tetrahedral intermediate expels CH3O− to give acetophenone. The ketone is more electrophilic than the ester, so it captures a second CH3MgBr at once. Workup gives the tertiary alcohol 2-phenylpropan-2-ol, with two identical methyl groups that both came from the Grignard.
x: The ketone intermediate is more reactive than the starting ester, so it cannot be isolated with excess Grignard; it is converted to the tertiary alcohol.
A secondary alcohol would require a hydride as the second nucleophile; here both nucleophiles are methyl groups.
Grignard reagents add C–C bonds; they do not hydrolyze the ester to benzoic acid.

q: (R)-2-Methyloxirane is treated with phenylmagnesium bromide, followed by H3O+. What is the major product?
h: A Grignard opens an epoxide by an S<sub>N</sub>2-like attack. Which carbon is less hindered, and does any bond to the stereocenter break?
w: Under basic (Grignard) conditions the epoxide opens by backside SN2 attack at the less hindered CH2. No bond to the stereocenter breaks, so it keeps its spatial arrangement. Its priorities stay in the same order (O > CH2R > CH3 > H), so the label stays the same: (R)-1-phenylpropan-2-ol.
x: Inversion happens only at the carbon that is attacked. The CH2 is attacked, so the stereocenter is untouched and stays (R).
Attack at the more substituted carbon is the acid-catalyzed pattern; a strongly basic Grignard attacks the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub>.
This places phenyl on the more substituted carbon (the wrong regiochemistry) and also keeps the old arrangement, which an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack there could not do.

q: Which compound cannot be converted into a useful Grignard reagent by treatment with Mg in dry ether?
h: A Grignard reagent is a very strong base. Look for an acidic hydrogen in the same molecule.
w: A Grignard carbon is strongly basic (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 50). Any O–H, N–H, S–H or CO2H in the same molecule protonates it immediately, destroying the reagent. 4-Bromobutan-1-ol has an O–H (pKa ≈ 16), so its OH must be protected first, for example as a TBS ether.
x: An ether oxygen has no acidic hydrogen; ethers are the usual solvents for Grignard reagents.
Aryl bromides form Grignard reagents readily, and the methoxy group has no acidic hydrogen.
Secondary alkyl bromides such as bromocyclohexane form Grignard reagents without difficulty.

q: Which sequence prepares the diol below from 4-bromobutan-1-ol and benzaldehyde?
c: 1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. Mg, ether  3. PhCHO  4. NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, H<sub>2</sub>O  5. TBAF
1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. Mg, ether  3. PhCHO  4. NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, H<sub>2</sub>O  5. PCC  6. TBAF
1. TBAF  2. Mg, ether  3. PhCHO  4. NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, H<sub>2</sub>O  5. TBSCl, imidazole
h: The Grignard reagent cannot coexist with a free O–H. When must the OH be masked, and when should it be released?
w: The free OH would protonate the Grignard as soon as it formed. So: (1) protect the OH as a TBS ether, (2) form the Grignard, (3) add it to benzaldehyde, (4) protonate the new alkoxide with a mild workup, and (5) remove the silyl group with fluoride (TBAF), which frees the primary OH. Answer: TBSCl/imidazole; Mg; PhCHO; NH4Cl; TBAF.
x: Without protection, the Grignard is quenched by its own O–H as soon as it forms, giving butan-1-ol (as its alkoxide), not the diol.
PCC oxidizes the new secondary alcohol to a ketone, so the product would be 5-hydroxy-1-phenylpentan-1-one, not the diol.
TBAF removes a silyl group; using it first does nothing, so the OH is still free when Mg is added. Protection must come before the Grignard step.

q: Which ester, treated with excess CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr and then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, gives 3-methylpentan-3-ol?
h: Two equivalents of the Grignard end up on the ester carbonyl carbon. Which of the three groups on the carbinol carbon is not ethyl?
w: An ester plus excess RMgX gives a tertiary alcohol in which two of the three groups on the carbinol carbon are the Grignard's R and the third is the ester's acyl group. 3-Methylpentan-3-ol has two ethyls and one methyl on the carbinol carbon, so the acyl group must be acetyl: ethyl acetate.
x: The propanoyl group contributes a third ethyl, giving 3-ethylpentan-3-ol.
Formate contributes H, so two ethyls give the secondary alcohol pentan-3-ol.
A carbonate loses both ethoxy groups and adds three ethyl groups, giving 3-ethylpentan-3-ol.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: Treat the lactone as an ester whose alkoxy group is tethered to the same chain. How many methyl groups add?
w: Like any ester, the lactone takes two equivalents of CH3MgBr. The first addition opens the ring (the ring oxygen leaves as an alkoxide, still attached to the chain) and gives a methyl ketone; the second adds to that ketone. Workup protonates both alkoxides: 5-methylhexane-1,5-diol.
x: The ketone formed after ring opening is more reactive than the lactone, so with excess Grignard it does not survive.
The ring oxygen leaves the carbonyl carbon during the reaction and ends up as a free primary OH after workup; it does not stay bonded in a ring.
This product has only one new methyl group and an H on the carbinol carbon, which would need a hydride donor; both added groups here are methyls.

q: Which combination, followed by H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> workup, gives 2-phenylethan-1-ol?
h: Count the carbons between the ring and the OH. Which electrophile adds a two-carbon unit with the OH on the far carbon?
w: A Grignard opens ethylene oxide at a CH2, adding –CH2CH2O−; after protonation the OH sits two carbons from the original nucleophilic carbon. PhMgBr + oxirane gives PhCH2CH2OH.
x: With acetaldehyde the phenyl bonds to the carbonyl carbon, so the OH ends up on the carbon next to the ring: 1-phenylethanol.
Formaldehyde adds only one carbon, giving benzyl alcohol (PhCH<sub>2</sub>OH).
Methyl adds to the benzaldehyde carbonyl carbon, giving the secondary alcohol 1-phenylethanol.

q: 4-Hydroxyacetophenone is treated with 1.0 equivalent of CH3MgBr in THF, followed by H3O+. What is the main organic compound isolated?
h: Before the Grignard can act as a nucleophile, does anything in the molecule react with it faster as a base?
w: Proton transfer is much faster than carbonyl addition. The phenolic O–H (pKa ≈ 8) protonates CH3MgBr, releasing CH4 and using up the single equivalent. The phenoxide salt has no Grignard left to add to the ketone, and workup reprotonates it, so the starting material, 4-hydroxyacetophenone, is recovered.
x: This would need at least two equivalents: the first is consumed by the acidic phenol O–H.
A Grignard reagent does not methylate oxygen; the phenoxide is only reprotonated on workup.
A Grignard reagent delivers a carbon nucleophile, not a hydride; it cannot reduce the ketone to a secondary alcohol.

q: Cyclohexene oxide is treated with CH<sub>3</sub>Li in ether, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. What is the product?
h: Organolithium opening of an epoxide is S<sub>N</sub>2-like. From which face does the nucleophile attack, relative to the C–O bond that breaks?
w: The methyl anion attacks one epoxide carbon from the backside, opposite the C–O bond that breaks. The oxygen stays on the neighboring carbon, on the face where it started, so CH3 and OH end up anti: trans-2-methylcyclohexanol. The two epoxide carbons are equivalent mirror-image sites in this achiral epoxide, so attack at either gives the two enantiomers equally: racemic.
x: A cis product would require frontside attack; SN2 opening places the nucleophile anti to the departing oxygen.
The methyl bonds to an epoxide carbon, and the oxygen remains on the other carbon; both cannot end up on the same carbon.
Cyclohexylmethanol would need the new carbon inserted between the ring and the oxygen; instead the methyl bonds to a ring carbon and the OH stays on the adjacent ring carbon.

q: Using bromobenzene and reagents with no more than two carbons, which sequence gives 2-phenylbutan-2-ol?
c: 1. Mg, ether  2. CH<sub>3</sub>CHO  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC  5. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr  6. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. Mg, ether  2. oxirane  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC  5. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr  6. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. Mg, ether  2. HCHO  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC  5. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr  6. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: Disconnect one C–C bond at the carbinol carbon. The ketone you need has to be made first; which secondary alcohol oxidizes to it?
w: The target is a tertiary alcohol carrying Ph, CH3 and CH2CH3. Disconnecting the ethyl group leaves acetophenone + EtMgBr. Acetophenone comes from oxidizing 1-phenylethanol, which is PhMgBr + acetaldehyde. Sequence: Mg; CH3CHO; H3O+; PCC; EtMgBr; H3O+.
x: After step 2 the carbinol carbon is an alkoxide, not a carbonyl, so EtMgBr has nothing to add to; workup gives only 1-phenylethanol.
Oxirane puts a CH<sub>2</sub> between the ring and the new carbinol carbon; the route ends at 1-phenylpropan-2-ol.
Formaldehyde gives benzyl alcohol, then benzaldehyde; adding EtMgBr gives the secondary alcohol 1-phenylpropan-1-ol.

q: Ethyl acetate reacts with only 1.0 equivalent of C6H5MgBr. The mixture contains mostly 1,1-diphenylethanol (after workup) and unreacted ethyl acetate, with little acetophenone. What is the best explanation?
c: Acetophenone, once formed, is more electrophilic than the ester and captures PhMgBr faster than the remaining ester does
Acetophenone is less electrophilic than ethyl acetate but forms in higher concentration, so it reacts first with PhMgBr
PhMgBr adds twice to the same ester molecule in a single concerted step, so no ketone ever forms
The ethoxide released in the first step converts acetophenone back into ethyl acetate
h: Compare the electrophilicity of a ketone and an ester. What does the OR group donate to the ester carbonyl?
w: An ester carbonyl is stabilized by resonance donation from the OR oxygen, which makes it less electrophilic than a ketone. When the first addition expels ethoxide, the ketone formed competes for the remaining Grignard and wins, so most of it goes on to the tertiary alcohol while some ester is left. The ketone is more reactive than the ester. This is why stopping at a ketone requires a different method (for example a Weinreb amide or a nitrile).
x: Ketones are more, not less, electrophilic than esters; a ketone formed in small amounts still reacts faster.
The two additions are separate steps: addition, loss of ethoxide to give the ketone, then a second addition.
Ethoxide does not convert ketones into esters; the observed result comes from the ketone's higher reactivity.

q: Which is a suitable solvent for preparing and using a Grignard reagent?
h: The solvent must not protonate the reagent and must not be attacked by it.
w: A Grignard reagent is both a strong base and a strong nucleophile. Ethers such as diethyl ether and THF have no acidic hydrogen and no electrophilic carbonyl, and their oxygen lone pairs coordinate and stabilize magnesium.
x: Ethanol's O–H protonates RMgX at once, converting it to the alkane R–H.
Acetone's carbonyl is an electrophile; the Grignard would add to the solvent to give a tertiary alcohol.
Ethyl acetate's ester carbonyl reacts with Grignard reagents (two equivalents each), consuming the reagent.

q: What is the major organic product of this sequence?
h: First build the tertiary alcohol. Then ask which alkene E1 dehydration of that alcohol favors.
w: Methyl adds to the carbonyl to give 1,2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol. Hot sulfuric acid dehydrates it by E1 through a tertiary carbocation at C1. Loss of the C2 hydrogen gives the most substituted (tetrasubstituted) alkene, which is the Zaitsev product: 1,2-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene.
x: The exocyclic alkene is only disubstituted; under thermodynamic E1 conditions the more substituted endocyclic alkene is favored.
Losing a C6 hydrogen gives a trisubstituted alkene, but removing the C2 hydrogen gives the more stable tetrasubstituted alkene.
This is the alcohol after step 2; hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> dehydrates a tertiary alcohol readily.

q:
Which combinations, after H3O+ workup, give 1-phenylpropan-1-ol?
I. C6H5MgBr + propanal
II. CH3CH2MgBr + benzaldehyde
III. C6H5CH2MgBr + acetaldehyde
h: For each pair, the carbonyl carbon becomes the C–OH carbon. Which groups end up on that carbon?
w: The carbinol carbon of the target carries Ph, CH2CH3 and H. Either group can come from the Grignard: Ph adds to propanal (I) or ethyl adds to benzaldehyde (II). In III the carbinol carbon (from acetaldehyde) carries CH3 and CH2Ph, giving 1-phenylpropan-2-ol. Answer: I and II only.
x: II also works: ethyl adds to the benzaldehyde carbonyl carbon, which already carries the phenyl.
III puts a CH<sub>2</sub> between the ring and the carbinol carbon, giving 1-phenylpropan-2-ol.
III gives the constitutional isomer 1-phenylpropan-2-ol, not the target.
