q: What is the product of this two-step sequence, and why?
c: (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile: retention in the TsCl step, inversion in the SN2 step
(R)-2-methylbutanenitrile: inversion in the TsCl step, inversion again in the SN2 step
Racemic 2-methylbutanenitrile: the tosylate ionizes to a carbocation
h: In tosylation, which bond is made: C–O or O–S? Then decide what cyanide does at carbon.
w: Tosylation forms an O–S bond; the C–O bond of the stereocenter is not touched, so the (R) tosylate forms with retention. Cyanide, a good nucleophile in polar aprotic DMSO, then displaces tosylate by SN2 with inversion. In the product, CN takes the top priority that OTs had, so the label changes: (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile.
x: Tosylation does not invert: the alcohol oxygen attacks sulfur, and the C–O bond stays intact.
The S<sub>N</sub>2 step with cyanide inverts the stereocenter, so the configuration cannot be retained overall.
A secondary tosylate with a strong nucleophile in DMSO reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2, not through a free carbocation.

q: (S)-Pentan-2-ol is treated with PBr3. What is the major product?
h: PBr<sub>3</sub> turns OH into a leaving group, then bromide attacks. By which mechanism, and from which side?
w: The OH attacks phosphorus, becoming –OPBr2, a good leaving group. Bromide then displaces it by SN2 with backside attack and no carbocation. The stereocenter inverts, and since Br takes the top priority that O had, the label changes: (R)-2-bromopentane.
x: Retention would require frontside attack; the S<sub>N</sub>2 step in the PBr<sub>3</sub> reaction inverts the stereocenter.
PBr<sub>3</sub> does not form a carbocation, so there is no hydride shift to C3.
The bromine replaces the OH on the same carbon (C2); it does not migrate to the chain end.

q: (R)-Butan-2-ol is taken through the sequence below. What is the final product?
h: Track the stereocenter step by step. In ester hydrolysis by hydroxide, which bond breaks: acyl C–O or alkyl C–O?
w: Step 1 makes the (R) tosylate with retention (only the O–S bond forms). Step 2: acetate displaces tosylate by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-butan-2-yl acetate. Step 3: saponification attacks the acyl carbon and breaks the acyl C–O bond, so the alkyl C–O bond, and the stereocenter, are untouched. Net result: the alcohol is inverted, giving (S)-butan-2-ol.
x: This assumes the hydrolysis step inverts the stereocenter again. Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, not the stereocenter, so there is only one inversion overall.
No step forms a carbocation: the displacement is S<sub>N</sub>2 and the hydrolysis occurs at the acyl carbon.
This is the product after step 2; hot aqueous NaOH saponifies the acetate ester to the alcohol.

q: cis-4-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol is treated with PBr3. What is the major product?
h: The ring carbon with the OH reacts by backside attack. If OH was on the same face as CH<sub>3</sub>, where does Br end up?
w: PBr3 converts OH into –OPBr2, and bromide displaces it by SN2 from the opposite face. OH was cis to the methyl, so Br ends up trans: trans-1-bromo-4-methylcyclohexane. Neither compound is chiral; the stereochemistry shows up as cis/trans.
x: Keeping the cis relationship would need retention; PBr<sub>3</sub> reactions proceed with inversion at the carbinol carbon.
Moving Br to the methyl-bearing carbon would need a carbocation and hydride shifts, which do not occur with PBr<sub>3</sub>.
PBr<sub>3</sub> is a substitution reagent; it does not dehydrate the alcohol to an alkene.

q: Why is an alcohol usually converted to a tosylate before an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction with a nucleophile such as N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>?
c: Hydroxide is a strong base and poor leaving group; tosylate is a weak, resonance-stabilized base that leaves easily
The tosyl group makes the carbon less hindered, so the nucleophile can reach it from the back side
Tosylation converts the alcohol into a carbocation, which the nucleophile then traps in a fast second step of the reaction
The tosylate makes the nucleophile stronger by deprotonating it before it attacks the carbon
h: Good leaving groups are the conjugate bases of strong acids. Compare H<sub>2</sub>O (pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) with TsOH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −3).
w: A leaving group must be able to carry away the electron pair. HO− is a strong base (conjugate acid H2O, pKa 15.7), so it is a very poor leaving group. TsO− is the conjugate base of a strong acid and spreads its charge over three oxygens. Tosylation turns a poor leaving group into an excellent one without touching the stereocenter.
x: The tosyl group is large; it does not reduce steric hindrance at the carbon.
Tosylation forms a neutral sulfonate ester; no carbocation is formed, which is why stereochemistry is kept in this step.
The tosylate is on the substrate; it does not change the nucleophile.

q: Butane-1,3-diol is taken through the sequence below. What is the final product?
h: The bulky silyl chloride reacts with the least hindered OH first. Which OH is left for PCC?
w: TBSCl is bulky, so one equivalent silylates the primary OH much faster than the secondary one. PCC then oxidizes the free secondary OH to a ketone (the TBS ether is inert). TBAF cleaves the Si–O bond and frees the primary OH: 4-hydroxybutan-2-one.
x: This assumes the secondary OH was protected. The bulky TBS group goes on the less hindered primary OH, so the secondary carbon is the one oxidized.
Only one OH is free during the PCC step; the silyl ether is not oxidized.
PCC does not oxidize alcohols to carboxylic acids, and the primary OH was protected during the oxidation.

q: Why does tetrabutylammonium fluoride (TBAF) remove a TBS protecting group under mild conditions?
c: The Si–F bond formed is much stronger than the Si–O bond broken
Fluoride is a strong base that deprotonates the silyl ether to cleave it
Fluoride reduces silicon, breaking the Si–O bond
TBAF is a strong acid that hydrolyzes the silyl ether
h: Compare bond strengths to silicon.
w: Silicon forms an exceptionally strong bond to fluorine (about 135 kcal/mol for Si–F vs about 110 for Si–O). Fluoride attacks silicon, forming a pentacoordinate intermediate that releases the alkoxide; workup gives the alcohol. The driving force is the strong Si–F bond. Carbon-based groups (esters, ketones, alkenes) are untouched, which makes TBS removal very selective.
x: A silyl ether has no acidic hydrogen to remove; fluoride acts as a nucleophile at silicon.
No redox occurs; silicon stays in the +4 oxidation state.
TBAF is a salt of fluoride, not an acid; acid can also cleave silyl ethers, but that is a different method.

q: Which reagent converts cyclohexylmethanol into cyclohexanecarbaldehyde in good yield?
h: You need an oxidant that stops at the aldehyde. Which oxidants work without water?
w: Primary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes by anhydrous oxidants that cannot form the aldehyde hydrate: PCC, Swern, or Dess–Martin periodinane.
x: Aqueous chromic acid oxidizes the aldehyde (through its hydrate) on to cyclohexanecarboxylic acid.
Hot permanganate is a strong aqueous oxidant that takes a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent; it cannot oxidize an alcohol.

q: What is the major organic product with excess Jones reagent?
h: Classify each OH as 1°, 2° or 3°. Oxidation needs an H on the carbinol carbon.
w: Chromic acid oxidizes a primary alcohol through the aldehyde hydrate all the way to a carboxylic acid. The tertiary alcohol has no H on its carbinol carbon, so it cannot form the C=O and is untouched. Product: 4-hydroxy-4-methylcyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid.
x: Stopping at the aldehyde needs an anhydrous oxidant such as PCC; aqueous Jones reagent goes on to the acid.
Oxidizing the tertiary carbon would require breaking a C–C bond (losing the methyl); Cr(VI) does not do this.
The primary alcohol is readily oxidized; only the tertiary OH is inert.

q: Which alcohol is not oxidized by PCC in CH2Cl2?
h: Look at the carbon carrying the OH. Does it have a hydrogen?
w: Oxidation to a carbonyl removes the H from the carbinol carbon. 2-Methylbutan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol with no such H, so PCC does not react with it.
x: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol; PCC oxidizes it to 3-methylbutan-2-one.
2-Methylbutan-1-ol is primary; PCC oxidizes it to 2-methylbutanal.
Cyclohexanol is secondary; PCC oxidizes it to cyclohexanone.

q: Which sequence carries out this conversion?
c: 1. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  2. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, ether  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. H<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>, acetone  2. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, ether  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
h: Work backward: a methyl ketone comes from oxidizing a secondary alcohol, which comes from CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + an aldehyde.
w: Retrosynthesis: the methyl ketone ⇐ 1-cyclohexylethanol (oxidation) ⇐ cyclohexanecarbaldehyde + CH3MgBr ⇐ cyclohexylmethanol (oxidation that stops at the aldehyde). Forward: PCC; CH3MgBr; H3O+; PCC.
x: Jones reagent takes the primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid, which simply protonates CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr; no ketone or secondary alcohol forms.
This stops at the secondary alcohol 1-cyclohexylethanol; a final oxidation is needed to reach the ketone.
The Grignard reagent is destroyed by the alcohol's O–H before any oxidation is done; Grignard addition needs a carbonyl present.

q: Why does PCC in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> stop at the aldehyde when it oxidizes a primary alcohol, while aqueous Jones reagent gives the carboxylic acid?
c: Without water the aldehyde cannot form its hydrate, the form that Cr(VI) oxidizes to the acid
PCC is too weak to oxidize any C–H bond on a carbon that already bears an oxygen atom
The pyridinium ion reduces the carboxylic acid back to the aldehyde as fast as the acid forms
In CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> the aldehyde evaporates from the flask before it can be oxidized any further
h: Chromium oxidizes an O–H-bearing carbon that also has a C–H. What must happen to the aldehyde before it fits that description?
w: Cr(VI) oxidation requires a carbon that bears both an OH (to form the chromate ester) and an H. An aldehyde becomes such a species only after adding water to form the hydrate, R–CH(OH)2. In aqueous Jones conditions the hydrate forms and is oxidized to the acid; in anhydrous CH2Cl2 it cannot. No water, no hydrate, no over-oxidation.
x: PCC does oxidize a C–H on an oxygen-bearing carbon: that is exactly how it converts the alcohol to the aldehyde.
Pyridinium is not a reducing agent; no acid is formed in the first place.
Most aldehydes made this way are not volatile; the selectivity is chemical, not physical.

q: The racemic trans alcohol below is converted to its tosylate and then heated with NaOCH2CH3 in ethanol. What is the major product?
h: E2 in a cyclohexane needs the leaving group and the β-H both axial (trans-diaxial). Put OTs axial: where is the methyl, and which neighbor still has an axial H?
w: Tosylation keeps the configuration, so the tosylate is trans to the methyl. For E2 the OTs must be axial; in that chair the trans methyl on C2 is also axial, so C2's only H is equatorial and cannot be anti-periplanar. The only axial β-H is on C6, so elimination goes toward C6 and gives the less substituted alkene: 3-methylcyclohexene, not the Zaitsev product.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene needs loss of the C2 hydrogen, which is never anti-periplanar to the OTs in the trans isomer.
An exocyclic alkene would need a C=C to the methyl carbon, which is not β to the leaving group.
A strong base with heat on a secondary tosylate favors E2; the S<sub>N</sub>2 ether is at most a minor product.

q:
Which conditions would remove (cleave) a TBS ether?
I. TBAF in THF
II. aqueous HCl in methanol
III. CH3MgBr in ether
IV. PCC in CH2Cl2
h: Silyl ethers are chosen because they survive bases, nucleophiles and oxidants. What two kinds of reagent do take them off?
w: TBS ethers are cleaved by fluoride (strong Si–F bond) and by aqueous acid (protonation of oxygen, then attack at silicon). They survive strong bases and carbon nucleophiles such as Grignard reagents, and they cannot be oxidized because there is no O–H. Answer: I and II only.
x: Aqueous acid also removes silyl ethers; that is why a mild workup (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) is often used when a TBS group must survive.
Grignard reagents do not cleave TBS ethers; that stability is why TBS is used to protect OH groups during Grignard reactions.
Neither a Grignard reagent nor PCC cleaves a TBS ether; PCC needs a free O–H to oxidize.

q: Which reagent converts 3-methylbutan-2-ol into 2-chloro-3-methylbutane without rearrangement?
h: Which method avoids a free carbocation next to a carbon that carries a hydrogen it could shift?
w: With HCl/ZnCl2 a secondary alcohol ionizes to a 2° carbocation, which undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the tertiary cation and gives 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Thionyl chloride with pyridine forms a chlorosulfite ester that chloride displaces by SN2, with no carbocation: SOCl2, pyridine.
x: The Lucas reagent goes through a carbocation; the hydride shift gives mainly the rearranged tertiary chloride.
Radical chlorination replaces C–H bonds, not the OH, and gives a mixture.
Hydroxide is a very poor leaving group, so chloride cannot displace OH without activation.

q: What is the major product when this diol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: After one OH leaves, the neighboring carbon still carries an OH. What can migrate to the cation, and what does the remaining oxygen become?
w: Pinacol rearrangement: protonation and loss of water give a tertiary carbocation. A methyl on the adjacent carbon shifts (1,2-shift) to that cation, leaving a cation on the carbon bearing the OH, which is strongly stabilized as a protonated carbonyl (oxocarbenium ion). Loss of H+ gives 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one (pinacolone).
x: Double dehydration can compete, but the pinacol pathway is favored because the oxygen-stabilized cation formed after the methyl shift is especially stable and leads to a C=O.
An epoxide would form only by the neighboring OH attacking the cation; under hot acid the 1,2-shift to a carbonyl dominates and an epoxide would itself open again.
Forming this alkene would require removing both oxygens; the second oxygen is kept and becomes the ketone C=O.

q: What is the major product of pinacol rearrangement of this diol?
h: Decide first which OH leaves: which carbocation is more stable? Then see which groups are available to migrate from the other carbon.
w: Loss of water from the diphenyl carbon gives a doubly benzylic tertiary cation, much more stable than the dimethyl tertiary cation. The groups on the neighboring carbon are two methyls and an OH, so a methyl migrates. The carbinol carbon becomes the C=O: 3,3-diphenylbutan-2-one.
x: This product comes from ionizing at the dimethyl carbon and then shifting a phenyl. Ionization occurs at the carbon that gives the more stable, diphenyl-stabilized cation.
Simple dehydration is not the main path; the 1,2-shift leads to a strongly stabilized oxocarbenium ion and a ketone.
The epoxide is not the product of this reaction under hot acid; the 1,2-methyl shift and loss of H<sup>+</sup> give the ketone.

q: What is the major product when this diol is treated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Only a C–C bond of the other ring can migrate to the cation. How does the size of that ring change when one of its bonds shifts?
w: Loss of water gives a tertiary cation on one ring carbon. On the neighboring carbinol carbon the migrating group must be a ring C–C bond; when it shifts, that carbon's ring gains the cationic carbon and expands from five to six members. The carbinol carbon becomes the C=O, and the original carbocation carbon becomes the spiro atom: spiro[4.5]decan-6-one.
x: Losing both oxygens is not the main path; the 1,2-shift gives an oxocarbenium ion that becomes a ketone.
A ketone flanked by two intact cyclopentyl groups would need a hydride shift, but neither carbinol carbon has a hydrogen.
Simple dehydration of one OH is outcompeted by the alkyl shift, which also relieves ring strain as the five-membered ring grows to six.

q: What is the product of NaIO<sub>4</sub> cleavage of this diol?
h: Periodate breaks the C–C bond between the two OH carbons; each becomes a C=O. Keep every other bond.
w: NaIO4 forms a cyclic periodate ester with the 1,2-diol and cleaves the C1–C2 bond. C1 (bearing CH3) becomes a ketone and C2 (bearing H) becomes an aldehyde, opening the ring: 6-oxoheptanal. Periodate does not oxidize the aldehyde further.
x: Periodate stops at the aldehyde; further oxidation to the acid would need an oxidant such as hot KMnO<sub>4</sub>.
The methyl group stays attached to C1, so that end becomes a methyl ketone, not an aldehyde.
A ring-contracted or methyl-shifted ketone is a pinacol-type (acid) product; periodate cleaves the C–C bond instead.

q: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is treated with excess NaIO<sub>4</sub>. What products form, per mole of glycerol?
h: Two C–C bonds have an OH on both ends. Cleave both, and count how many C–O bonds the middle carbon ends up with.
w: Both C1–C2 and C2–C3 are vicinal-diol bonds, so periodate cleaves both. Each terminal CH2OH becomes formaldehyde. The middle carbon loses both C–C bonds and keeps its H and OH, gaining one more bond to oxygen from each cleavage: it ends at the formic acid oxidation level. Products: 2 HCHO + 1 HCO2H (2 equiv NaIO4 consumed).
x: The middle carbon keeps a C–H bond, so it stops at formic acid; periodate does not oxidize it to CO<sub>2</sub>.
This stops after one cleavage. Both C–C bonds of glycerol are vicinal-diol bonds, so excess periodate cleaves the second one too.
No carbon is reduced in a periodate cleavage, so methanol cannot form; every carbon is oxidized or unchanged.

q: Which alkene gives only cyclohexanone and formaldehyde after 1. OsO4, NMO 2. NaIO4?
h: OsO<sub>4</sub> makes a 1,2-diol at the C=C; NaIO<sub>4</sub> then cuts where the double bond was. Reconnect the two carbonyl carbons with a C=C.
w: Dihydroxylation followed by periodate cleavage splits the C=C into two C=O groups, like ozonolysis. Joining cyclohexanone's carbonyl carbon to formaldehyde's carbon with a double bond gives methylenecyclohexane.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene has its C=C in the ring, so cleavage opens the ring to one product, 6-oxoheptanal.
Vinylcyclopentane gives cyclopentanecarbaldehyde and formaldehyde; the ring is five-membered and the ring carbon becomes an aldehyde, not a ketone.
Ethylidenecyclohexane gives cyclohexanone and acetaldehyde, not formaldehyde.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol is heated with H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Acid-catalyzed dehydration is E1 and gives the most stable alkene available.
w: Protonation and loss of water give a secondary carbocation (which can also shift a hydride to the tertiary C2 cation). Loss of a proton gives the most substituted, most stable alkene (Zaitsev): 1-methylcyclohexene.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexene is disubstituted and forms only as a minor product under thermodynamic E1 conditions.
The exocyclic alkene is disubstituted and less stable than the trisubstituted ring alkene.
4-Methylcyclohexene cannot form directly from either carbocation; the C=C must include C1 or C2.

q: What is the major alkene formed when 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: The first cation is secondary and sits next to a quaternary carbon. What can shift, and which alkene is most substituted after the shift?
w: Loss of water gives a 2° cation next to a C(CH3)3 group. A 1,2-methyl shift gives the more stable 3° cation, (CH3)2C+–CH(CH3)2. Loss of the H from the isopropyl CH gives the tetrasubstituted alkene: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.
x: 3,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene would need loss of a proton before any shift; under E1 conditions the cation rearranges first. (That product comes from E2 methods such as POCl<sub>3</sub>/pyridine.)
2,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene comes from the rearranged cation but is only disubstituted; the tetrasubstituted isomer is favored.
Water capture of the rearranged cation gives this alcohol, but under hot concentrated acid the elimination product is favored.

q: What is the major product when 1-cyclobutylethan-1-ol is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: A cation next to a strained ring can shift a ring bond. What ring size results, and is there a further shift to a better cation?
w: Loss of water gives a secondary cation next to the cyclobutane. A ring C–C bond shifts to it, expanding the four-membered ring to a five-membered ring and relieving strain; the new cation is secondary, on the carbon next to the CH(CH3). A 1,2-hydride shift then gives the tertiary 1-methylcyclopentyl cation, and loss of H+ gives the trisubstituted alkene: 1-methylcyclopentene.
x: Ethylidenecyclobutane keeps the strained four-membered ring; ring expansion is faster than proton loss from the unrearranged cation.
Vinylcyclobutane is a monosubstituted alkene from the unrearranged cation; it is both less stable and kinetically bypassed by ring expansion.
3-Methylcyclopentene is disubstituted; the tertiary cation formed after the hydride shift gives the more substituted 1-methylcyclopentene.

q: What is the major product when 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol is treated with POCl<sub>3</sub> in pyridine?
h: POCl<sub>3</sub> makes the OH a leaving group and pyridine removes a β-H in one step. Is there a carbocation? Which β carbons carry hydrogens?
w: POCl3 converts the OH to a dichlorophosphate leaving group, and pyridine removes a β-H in a concerted E2 step, so no carbocation forms and no methyl shift occurs. The only β-hydrogens are on the CH3 at C1 (C3 is quaternary), so the product is 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.
x: The tetrasubstituted alkene requires a methyl shift through a carbocation, which the E2 pathway avoids.
This also needs the rearranged carbon skeleton, which forms only through a carbocation.
Pyridine is used to promote elimination; under these conditions the dichlorophosphate is eliminated rather than displaced by chloride.

q: Hexan-1-ol was treated with reagent X. The product shows the IR spectrum below and gives no broad band at 2500–3600 cm<sup>−1</sup>. What is X?
h: Read the spectrum: what do the two weak bands near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus a C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup> indicate?
w: The strong C=O at 1728 cm−1 with the pair of weak aldehyde C–H stretches (about 2820 and 2720 cm−1), and no O–H band, identify an aldehyde, hexanal. An anhydrous oxidant that stops at the aldehyde was used: PCC.
x: Aqueous chromic acid gives hexanoic acid, which shows a very broad O–H band from about 2500 to 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not react with an alcohol; the spectrum would still show the broad O–H stretch near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Hot permanganate also oxidizes to the carboxylic acid, which shows the broad acid O–H band.

q: What is the major organic product of this sequence?
h: Make the alcohol first. In the E1 step, which alkene is most stable: think about conjugation and about E vs Z.
w: Ethyl adds to benzaldehyde to give 1-phenylpropan-1-ol. Hot acid ionizes it to a benzylic cation, and loss of a proton from the adjacent CH2 gives an alkene conjugated with the ring. The E isomer avoids the steric clash between phenyl and methyl and is favored under these equilibrating conditions: (E)-prop-1-en-1-ylbenzene.
x: The Z isomer puts the phenyl and methyl on the same side; under thermodynamic E1 conditions the less hindered E isomer dominates.
Allylbenzene is not conjugated with the ring and would need loss of a proton from a carbon not adjacent to the cation.
This is the alcohol after step 2; hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> dehydrates a benzylic alcohol readily.

q: An ether solution of benzoic acid, 4-methylphenol and cyclohexanol is extracted first with aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, then with aqueous NaOH. Where does each compound end up?
c: NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid; NaOH layer: 4-methylphenol; ether: cyclohexanol
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid and 4-methylphenol; NaOH layer: cyclohexanol; ether: nothing
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid; NaOH layer: 4-methylphenol and cyclohexanol; ether: nothing
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: nothing; NaOH layer: benzoic acid and 4-methylphenol; ether: cyclohexanol
h: A compound moves into water only if the base deprotonates it. Compare each pK<sub>a</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (6.4) and H<sub>2</sub>O (15.7).
w: Bicarbonate (conjugate acid H2CO3, pKa 6.4) deprotonates only acids with pKa below about 6, so only benzoic acid moves into that layer as sodium benzoate. Hydroxide (H2O, 15.7) then deprotonates the phenol (10.3) but not cyclohexanol (≈ 18), which stays in the ether. Answer: benzoic acid / 4-methylphenol / cyclohexanol.
x: 4-Methylphenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.3) is far less acidic than H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, so bicarbonate barely deprotonates it.
Cyclohexanol is less acidic than water, so hydroxide leaves it mostly protonated and it stays in the ether.
Bicarbonate is basic enough to deprotonate a carboxylic acid (K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>2</sup>), so benzoic acid is removed in the first extraction.

q: Diol A (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) reacts with NaIO<sub>4</sub> to give a single product, heptane-2,6-dione. Which structure is A?
h: Work backward: join the two carbonyl carbons of the product with a C–C bond and put an OH on each. Is the result a ring?
w: Periodate cleavage turns each carbon of a 1,2-diol into a C=O. Reconnecting C2 and C6 of heptane-2,6-dione gives a five-membered ring with a methyl and an OH on each of the two joined carbons: cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane-1,2-diol (C7H14O2). The cis isomer forms the cyclic periodate ester easily.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexane-1,2-diol is cleaved too, but its secondary carbinol carbon becomes an aldehyde: the product is 6-oxoheptanal.
This is a 1,3-diol; periodate cleaves only vicinal (1,2) diols, so it does not react.
Cycloheptane-1,2-diol has only secondary OH carbons, so cleavage gives the dialdehyde heptanedial.

q: Alcohol X (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O) is oxidized by PCC to a ketone. When X is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, the major alkene is 2-methylbut-2-ene. What is X?
h: Use each clue to eliminate choices: the PCC result tells you the alcohol class; the alkene skeleton (possibly after a shift) tells you the branching.
w: A ketone from PCC means X is secondary, which rules out the 1° and 3° choices. Of the secondary alcohols, pentan-2-ol has an unbranched chain and gives pent-2-ene. 3-Methylbutan-2-ol ionizes to a 2° cation that undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the 3° cation, and Zaitsev loss of H+ gives 2-methylbut-2-ene. X is 3-methylbutan-2-ol.
x: Pentan-2-ol is secondary but has no branch, so dehydration gives pent-2-ene, not 2-methylbut-2-ene.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol does give 2-methylbut-2-ene, but as a tertiary alcohol it is not oxidized by PCC.
3-Methylbutan-1-ol is primary; PCC gives the aldehyde 3-methylbutanal, not a ketone.

q: Which compound is a secondary (2°) amine?
h: Amine class counts the carbons bonded to nitrogen, not the substitution of the carbon that carries the N.
w: An amine is classified by how many carbon groups are attached to N. N-Methylcyclohexanamine has two (cyclohexyl and methyl) on an N–H nitrogen, so it is 2°. The common trap is 1-methylcyclohexan-1-amine: its NH2 sits on a tertiary carbon, but nitrogen itself carries only one carbon, so it is a 1° amine (the alcohol rule, which looks at the carbon, does not apply to amines).
x: 1-Methylcyclohexan-1-amine has an NH<sub>2</sub> group with one carbon on N: a 1° amine on a tertiary carbon, not a 2° amine.
N,N-Dimethylcyclohexanamine has three carbons on N and no N–H: a 3° amine.
Cyclohexylmethanamine (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) has only the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon on N: a 1° amine.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Aniline is the parent. Groups on nitrogen get the locant N; ring positions are counted from the carbon bearing N (C1).
w: The parent is aniline (benzenamine), with the ring carbon bonded to N as C1. Nitrogen carries an ethyl and a methyl group (each gets the locant N); the ring carries a methyl group at C4, para to N. Alphabetical order (ethyl before methyl, the multiplier "di" ignored) gives N-ethyl-N,4-dimethylaniline.
x: This name puts the ethyl on the ring and both methyls on N; that is a different compound (an isomer).
The ring methyl is para to N (C4), not meta (C3).
The ring is aromatic, so the parent is aniline, not cyclohexanamine (which would be a saturated ring).

q: What is the IUPAC name of the amine shown?
h: Pick the longest carbon chain that contains the carbon bearing N, then number to give that carbon the lowest locant. Groups on N are N-substituents, not part of the chain.
w: The longest chain through the C–N carbon has five carbons (pentane). Numbering from the end nearer the C–N carbon puts the amine at C2 and the branch methyl at C4. The two methyls on nitrogen are N-substituents. Combining all three methyl prefixes in alphabetical-locant order gives N,N,4-trimethylpentan-2-amine.
x: Numbering from the wrong end gives the amine carbon locant 4; the principal group must get the lowest possible number (2).
An N-methyl group cannot be counted as part of the carbon chain because the chain would have to pass through nitrogen; this name also describes a different compound with an N–H.
Butane is not the longest chain, and "1,1-dimethyl" on a chain end means the chain was not extended; the parent must be pentane.

q: Rank the compounds in order of increasing basicity (weakest base first).
h: Ask where each nitrogen lone pair goes: into a carbonyl, into a benzene ring, or nowhere. Compare with NH<sub>3</sub> (conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> 9.2).
w: Conjugate-acid pKa values track the basicity: acetanilide (I, an amide) about −0.5 because the N lone pair is delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen; aniline (II) 4.6 because the lone pair is delocalized into the ring (and the N is attached to an sp2 carbon); ammonia (IV) 9.2; cyclohexylamine (III) about 10.6 because the alkyl group donates electron density and there is no resonance. Order: I < II < IV < III.
x: An amide is a far weaker base than an aniline: the C=O pulls the N lone pair much more strongly than the ring does (pK<sub>a</sub>H about −0.5 vs 4.6).
Aniline (pK<sub>a</sub>H 4.6) is a weaker base than ammonia (9.2) because its lone pair is shared with the aromatic ring.
Alkylamines are slightly stronger bases than ammonia (10.6 vs 9.2): the alkyl group donates electron density and stabilizes the ammonium ion.

q: Rank these anilines in order of increasing basicity (weakest base first).
h: A para substituent that donates electrons by resonance pushes density toward N; one that withdraws by resonance pulls the lone pair farther from N.
w: Conjugate-acid pKa values: 4-nitroaniline (II) 1.0, aniline (I) 4.6, 4-methoxyaniline (III) 5.3. A para NO2 group accepts the N lone pair by resonance (a resonance form puts negative charge on the nitro oxygens), so the lone pair is much less available. A para OCH3 donates by resonance, which outweighs its inductive withdrawal at the para position, so the amine is slightly more basic than aniline. Order: II < I < III.
x: The para methoxy group is a net donor by resonance, so 4-methoxyaniline is more basic than aniline, not less.
This order is reversed: the nitro group makes the weakest base, not the strongest.
Oxygen is electronegative, but at the para position its resonance donation dominates; 4-methoxyaniline (5.3) is more basic than aniline (4.6).

q: Which compound is the strongest base?
h: Look for a nitrogen whose lone pair is in an sp<sup>3</sup> orbital and is not delocalized.
w: Piperidine is a saturated cyclic 2° amine: its lone pair sits in an sp3 orbital and is not delocalized, so its conjugate acid has pKa about 11. Pyridine (5.2) holds its lone pair in an sp2 orbital with more s character; aniline (4.6) delocalizes it into the ring; pyrrole (about −3.8) uses it in the aromatic sextet.
x: Pyridine's lone pair is in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital, held closer to N, so its conjugate acid has pK<sub>a</sub> only 5.2.
Aniline's lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring, giving a conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> of 4.6.
Pyrrole's lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet; protonation destroys aromaticity, so pyrrole is barely basic (pK<sub>a</sub>H about −3.8).

q: Which nitrogen in the molecule shown is the most basic?
h: Classify each N: pyridine-type, amide, alkylamine or arylamine. Then recall a typical conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> for each.
w: N a is a pyridine nitrogen (pKaH about 5); N b is an amide N–H (its lone pair is delocalized into C=O; amides protonate on O, pKaH about −0.5); N d is an N-methylaniline nitrogen whose lone pair is shared with the ring (pKaH about 5); N c is a 3° alkylamine (a pyrrolidine N) with an undelocalized sp3 lone pair (pKaH about 10). Acid adds to N c first.
x: The pyridine N is only weakly basic (pK<sub>a</sub>H about 5) because its lone pair is in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital.
The amide nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl; amides are the weakest bases here.
An arylamine N shares its lone pair with the benzene ring (pK<sub>a</sub>H about 5), about 10<sup>5</sup> times less basic than an alkylamine.

q: An ether solution of acetanilide, 4-methylaniline and naphthalene is shaken with 1 M HCl. Which compound moves into the aqueous layer, and how is it recovered?
c: 4-methylaniline, as ArNH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> Cl<sup>−</sup>; add NaOH to the aqueous layer and extract the free amine back into ether
4-methylaniline and acetanilide, as N-protonated salts; add NaOH to the aqueous layer and extract both back into ether
4-methylaniline, as ArNH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> Cl<sup>−</sup>; evaporate the aqueous layer to dryness to obtain the neutral amine
acetanilide, as its O-protonated salt; add NaHCO<sub>3</sub> to the aqueous layer and extract the amide back into ether
h: 1 M HCl protonates only a base whose conjugate acid has pK<sub>a</sub> well above 0. After extraction, the salt must be converted back to the neutral compound.
w: 4-Methylaniline (pKaH about 5.1) is protonated by 1 M HCl to a water-soluble anilinium chloride, so it leaves the ether layer. Acetanilide is an amide (pKaH about −0.5): it is not protonated appreciably and stays in ether with the neutral hydrocarbon naphthalene. Making the aqueous layer basic with NaOH deprotonates ArNH3+, and the neutral amine is extracted back into ether. Key: 4-methylaniline as its salt, recovered by basifying and extracting.
x: The amide N lone pair is tied up in resonance with C=O; amides are far too weakly basic to be extracted by dilute aqueous acid.
Evaporating the water leaves the ammonium chloride salt, not the neutral amine; a base is needed to free the amine.
Acetanilide is not protonated by 1 M HCl to any useful extent, and it is the amine, not the amide, that enters the water.

q: An ether solution of aniline (conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> 4.6) and 4-nitroaniline (conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> 1.0) is shaken with an aqueous buffer at pH 3.0. Which statement best describes the result?
c: Aniline is about 98% protonated and moves into the water; 4-nitroaniline is about 99% neutral and stays in ether
Both amines are more than 90% protonated at pH 3.0, so both move into the water
4-Nitroaniline is mostly protonated and moves into the water layer; aniline is mostly neutral and stays in the ether
Neither amine is protonated appreciably, because pH 3.0 is above both conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> values
h: Use [BH<sup>+</sup>]/[B] = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> − pH)</sup> for each amine.
w: For aniline, [BH+]/[B] = 10(4.6 − 3.0) = 101.6 ≈ 40, so about 98% is the anilinium ion, which is water-soluble. For 4-nitroaniline, [BH+]/[B] = 10(1.0 − 3.0) = 0.01, so about 99% is the neutral amine, which stays in ether. A pH between the two pKa values separates them: aniline goes to the water, 4-nitroaniline stays in ether.
x: At pH 3.0, which is two units above its conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> of 1.0, 4-nitroaniline is only about 1% protonated.
This reverses the basicities: the nitro group makes 4-nitroaniline the weaker base, so it is the one left neutral.
pH 3.0 is below aniline's conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> (4.6), so aniline is mostly protonated; only 4-nitroaniline (1.0) stays neutral.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N gives the IR spectrum shown, with two sharp medium bands near 3380 and 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a band near 1610 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: Count the N–H bonds. How many N–H stretching bands does each class of amine show?
w: A primary amine has an NH2 group whose two N–H bonds stretch in phase (symmetric) and out of phase (asymmetric), giving two N–H bands near 3300–3500 cm−1; the NH2 scissoring bend appears near 1600 cm−1. A 2° amine shows one weak N–H band and a 3° amine none. Only pentan-1-amine is primary.
x: N-Methylbutan-1-amine is a 2° amine with one N–H bond: one N–H stretching band, not two.
N,N-Dimethylpropan-1-amine is a 3° amine with no N–H bond, so it shows no band above 3100 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
N-Ethylpropan-1-amine is a 2° amine: a single weak N–H band.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>11</sub>N gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. The broad singlet at 1.0 ppm disappears when the sample is shaken with D<sub>2</sub>O. Which compound is it?
h: A 3H singlet near 2.4 ppm is a CH<sub>3</sub> on nitrogen. How many N–H protons does the exchangeable signal show?
w: The exchangeable 1H broad singlet is a single N–H, so the amine is 2°. The 3H singlet at 2.43 ppm is an N–CH3 (no neighbors), and the 2H triplet at 2.55 ppm is an N–CH2 next to a CH2; the 2H sextet and 3H triplet complete a propyl group. The compound is N-methylpropan-1-amine, CH3NHCH2CH2CH3.
x: Butan-1-amine has an NH<sub>2</sub> (a 2H exchangeable signal) and no 3H singlet.
N,N-Dimethylethanamine has a 6H singlet, a quartet and a triplet, and no N–H signal at all.
N-Methylpropan-2-amine would show a 6H doublet and a 1H septet for the isopropyl group, not a sextet and a triplet.

q: Pyridine and pyrrole both contain a ring nitrogen, yet the conjugate acid of pyridine has pK<sub>a</sub> 5.2 and protonated pyrrole about −3.8. What best explains the difference?
c: Pyrrole’s N lone pair is part of its aromatic sextet, so protonating N destroys aromaticity; pyridine’s lone pair is in the ring plane, outside the π system
Pyrrole's nitrogen is sp hybridized, so its lone pair has more s character and is held more tightly than pyridine's sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair
Pyridine’s nitrogen bears a partial negative charge from resonance with the ring, while pyrrole’s nitrogen bears a partial positive charge from induction alone
Pyrrole is antiaromatic with 4 π electrons, and protonation at nitrogen would relieve the antiaromaticity only partly
h: Count the π electrons in each ring and ask where the N lone pair must be for the ring to have six.
w: Pyrrole has four π electrons from its two C=C bonds; the N lone pair, in a p orbital, supplies the other two for the aromatic sextet. Using it to bond H+ removes it from the π system, so the cation is not aromatic (pyrrole actually protonates on C2). Pyridine already has six π electrons from three C=C/C=N bonds; its lone pair is in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, perpendicular to the π system, and can bond H+ without affecting aromaticity. Answer: pyrrole's lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet.
x: Pyrrole's N is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridized with its lone pair in a p orbital; it is not sp.
Pyrrole's nitrogen actually donates electron density into the ring by resonance; the difference is about whether the lone pair belongs to the aromatic sextet, not partial charges.
Pyrrole is aromatic (4n + 2 = 6 π electrons), not antiaromatic.

q: Acetamide (CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>) is about 10<sup>11</sup> times less basic than ethylamine. Which statement about acetamide is correct?
c: It is protonated on O, giving a cation stabilized by resonance with the N lone pair, which is delocalized into the C=O
It is protonated on nitrogen, but the N–H<sup>+</sup> bond is weak because nitrogen in an amide is sp hybridized, not sp<sup>3</sup>
It is protonated on nitrogen, and the cation is destabilized only by the inductive effect of the methyl group
It cannot be protonated at all, because an amide has no lone pairs left after resonance with the C=O
h: Draw the resonance form of an amide that puts a negative charge on oxygen. Which atom is then the electron-rich one?
w: In an amide the N lone pair is delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen (C=N+–O− resonance form), so N is planar and poorly basic, while O carries extra electron density. Protonation on oxygen gives a cation whose positive charge is shared between C, O and N by resonance; protonation on N would remove the amide resonance. The conjugate-acid pKa is about −0.5, compared with 10.7 for CH3CH2NH3+.
x: Amide nitrogen is sp<sup>2</sup> (planar, lone pair in a p orbital), and amides protonate on oxygen, not nitrogen.
A methyl group is weakly donating, not withdrawing; the low basicity comes from resonance with the carbonyl.
Amides are weak bases but can be protonated by strong acids (that is the first step of acid-catalyzed amide hydrolysis).

q: Which ion is the strongest acid?
h: The strongest conjugate acid belongs to the weakest base. Which neutral amine has the least available lone pair?
w: The ions are conjugate acids of 4-nitroaniline (pKa 1.0), pyridine (5.2), aniline (4.6) and methylamine (10.6). The weakest base, 4-nitroaniline, gives the strongest conjugate acid: its free amine is stabilized by resonance donation of the N lone pair into both the ring and the para nitro group, so losing H+ is most favorable.
x: Pyridinium (pK<sub>a</sub> 5.2) is a weaker acid than 4-nitroanilinium (1.0) by about four pK<sub>a</sub> units.
Anilinium (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.6) lacks the nitro group that further stabilizes the free amine, so it is about 4000 times weaker as an acid.
Methylammonium (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.6) is the weakest acid here because methylamine is the strongest base.

q: Rank the three anilines in order of increasing basicity (weakest base first).
h: A methoxy group donates by resonance only to ortho/para positions; at a meta position only its inductive effect acts on the carbon bearing N.
w: From the meta position, OCH3 cannot donate by resonance to the carbon bearing NH2; only its inductive withdrawal (electronegative O) acts, so 3-methoxyaniline (I, pKaH 4.2) is slightly less basic than aniline (II, 4.6). From the para position, resonance donation dominates, so 4-methoxyaniline (III, 5.3) is more basic. Order: I < II < III.
x: This is the exact reverse; the para isomer is the strongest base and the meta isomer the weakest.
At the meta position OCH<sub>3</sub> withdraws inductively and cannot donate by resonance, so 3-methoxyaniline is weaker than aniline, not stronger.
Para resonance donation makes 4-methoxyaniline a stronger base than aniline, so it cannot be in the middle.

q: Which primary amine cannot be prepared in good yield by the Gabriel synthesis (potassium phthalimide, then an alkyl halide, then hydrazine)?
h: The key C–N bond forms when the phthalimide anion displaces a halide. What substrate does that step need?
w: The Gabriel synthesis forms the C–N bond by SN2 attack of the phthalimide anion on an alkyl halide, so it works for methyl, primary and some unhindered secondary halides. 1-Methylcyclohexan-1-amine would require 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane, a tertiary halide that cannot undergo SN2; the basic phthalimide anion instead causes E2 elimination to an alkene.
x: Benzylamine comes from benzyl bromide, an excellent S<sub>N</sub>2 substrate.
Butan-1-amine comes from 1-bromobutane, an unhindered primary halide.
2-Phenylethan-1-amine comes from (2-bromoethyl)benzene, a primary halide that reacts well by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: What is the final organic product of the sequence shown?
h: The phthalimide N is alkylated once; hydrazine then releases the nitrogen with its new alkyl group.
w: KOH removes the acidic N–H of phthalimide (pKa about 8.3). The anion alkylates 1-bromo-3-methylbutane by SN2 to give an N-alkylphthalimide, which cannot be alkylated again because its N has no H and its lone pair is delocalized into two carbonyls. Hydrazine cleaves the imide, releasing 3-methylbutan-1-amine (and phthalhydrazide).
x: A dialkylamine forms in direct alkylation of an amine; the imide nitrogen can be alkylated only once, which is the point of the Gabriel method.
This N-alkylphthalimide is the intermediate before step 3; hydrazine cleaves it to the free amine.
Hydroxide is used only to deprotonate phthalimide; the alkyl halide reacts with the phthalimide anion, so no alcohol forms.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is treated with NaN3 in DMSO, and the product is reduced with LiAlH4 and worked up with water. What is the final product?
h: Decide the mechanism (and stereochemical result) of the azide step. Does the reduction step touch the stereocenter?
w: Azide is a strong nucleophile and DMSO is polar aprotic, so the secondary bromide reacts by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-2-azidobutane (the N3 group takes priority 1, as Br did, so inversion changes R to S). LiAlH4 reduces R–N3 to R–NH2 with loss of N2; no bond to the stereocenter is broken, so the product is (S)-butan-2-amine.
x: Retention would require two inversions or a front-side attack; S<sub>N</sub>2 by azide inverts the stereocenter once.
2-Azidobutane is the intermediate; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the azide to the amine.
Racemization requires a planar carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1); a strong nucleophile in DMSO reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 with clean inversion.

q: Treating ammonia with one equivalent of bromoethane gives a mixture of ethylamine, diethylamine, triethylamine and tetraethylammonium bromide. Why?
c: Each alkylation product is at least as nucleophilic as the amine it came from, so it competes for the bromoethane
Ammonia is too weak a nucleophile to react with bromoethane, so only the amine products react with it
Bromoethane reacts by S<sub>N</sub>1, and the ethyl carbocation is captured by every amine present at equal rates, giving all four
Ethylamine is a weaker base than ammonia, so its salt is deprotonated faster and it is alkylated again
h: Compare the nucleophilicity of NH<sub>3</sub> with that of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.
w: Alkyl groups donate electron density, so ethylamine is a better nucleophile than ammonia, and diethylamine is comparable or better still. As soon as some ethylamine forms, it competes with NH3 for bromoethane, and the process continues to the quaternary salt. That is why each product competes for the alkyl halide, and why indirect routes (Gabriel, azide reduction, reductive amination) are used to make primary amines cleanly.
x: Ammonia does react with bromoethane by S<sub>N</sub>2; it is simply out-competed by the more nucleophilic products.
A primary halide does not ionize to a primary carbocation; the alkylations are S<sub>N</sub>2 reactions.
Ethylamine is a slightly stronger base than ammonia, and over-alkylation results from its greater nucleophilicity, not faster deprotonation.

q: Which carbonyl compound and amine give the target compound shown by reductive amination with NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN (pH about 6)?
h: Reductive amination joins the amine N to the former carbonyl carbon, which ends up as a CH that came from C=O.
w: Disconnect the C–N bond to the benzylic CH2: that carbon was the C=O of an aldehyde, and the N came from a secondary amine. Benzaldehyde and piperidine condense to an iminium ion, which NaBH3CN reduces to N-benzylpiperidine.
x: An alcohol has no C=O, so it cannot condense with the amine to form an iminium ion.
Pyridine is aromatic with no N–H; it cannot form an iminium ion and would not give a saturated piperidine ring.
A carboxylic acid simply forms an ammonium carboxylate salt with the amine, and NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN does not reduce acids or amides.

q: In the reductive amination shown, why is NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN used instead of NaBH<sub>4</sub>?
c: Near pH 6, NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN reduces iminium ions far faster than ketones, so the ketone survives to form the imine
NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN is a stronger hydride donor than NaBH<sub>4</sub>, so it can reduce the C=N bond, which NaBH<sub>4</sub> cannot touch at all
NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN supplies the nitrogen atom of the product through its cyanide ligand, which is reduced to an amine
NaBH<sub>4</sub> would reduce the N–H bond of methylamine to give H<sub>2</sub> gas, so no amine product could form
h: The electron-withdrawing CN makes this borohydride milder. Which electrophile in the flask is the most reactive?
w: The cyano group withdraws electron density from boron, making NaBH3CN a weaker, more selective hydride donor that is stable at mildly acidic pH. Under those conditions the iminium ion (C=N+) formed from cyclohexanone and methylamine is far more electrophilic than the neutral ketone, so the iminium ion is reduced selectively to N-methylcyclohexanamine. NaBH4 would reduce much of the ketone to cyclohexanol before the imine formed.
x: NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN is the weaker hydride donor; its selectivity, not its strength, is the point.
The nitrogen in the product comes from methylamine; cyanide stays on boron.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce N–H bonds of amines; the problem with NaBH<sub>4</sub> is that it reduces the ketone too.

q: Which sequence converts benzyl bromide into 2-phenylethan-1-amine (PhCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>)?
h: Count carbons: the product has one more carbon between the ring and N than the starting material.
w: The target has two carbons between the ring and nitrogen, but benzyl bromide supplies only one. Cyanide adds the extra carbon by SN2 (PhCH2CN), and LiAlH4 reduces the nitrile C≡N to CH2NH2, giving PhCH2CH2NH2.
x: The azide route adds nitrogen but no carbon; it gives benzylamine (PhCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>).
Ammonia gives benzylamine, and CH<sub>3</sub>I then methylates the nitrogen instead of adding a carbon to the chain.
Acid hydrolysis converts the nitrile into phenylacetic acid, not an amine.

q: What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> treats amides differently from esters: the C–N bond survives.
w: LiAlH4 reduces an amide all the way to an amine: hydride adds to C=O, the oxygen leaves as an aluminate to give an iminium ion, and a second hydride reduces it. The C=O becomes CH2 and the N keeps its substituents, so N-methylbenzamide gives N-methyl-1-phenylmethanamine (PhCH2NHCH3).
x: Losing the N-methyl group would require breaking an N–C(alkyl) bond, which LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not do.
Esters are reduced to alcohols because the alkoxy group leaves; in an amide the nitrogen is a much poorer leaving group than the oxygen (expelled as an aluminate), so the C–N bond is kept.
An imine or iminium ion is only an intermediate; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces it on to the amine before workup.

q: Which sequence gives 3-bromoaniline from benzene as the major product?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Fe, HCl; then NaOH
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Fe, HCl; then NaOH
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; then H<sub>2</sub>O
h: The two groups are meta. Which of NO<sub>2</sub>, NH<sub>2</sub> and Br is a meta director? Then choose a reducing agent that turns ArNO<sub>2</sub> into ArNH<sub>2</sub>.
w: Only the nitro group directs meta, so it must be on the ring when bromine is introduced: nitration, then Br2/FeBr3 gives 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene. A dissolving-metal reduction (Fe or Sn with HCl, then base to free the amine) converts NO2 into NH2 and leaves the aryl C–Br intact: nitrate, brominate, then Fe/HCl.
x: Reducing first gives aniline, a strong o,p-director that is brominated at 2, 4 and 6, not at the meta position.
Bromine is an o,p-director, so nitrating bromobenzene gives mainly 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene and the para amine after reduction.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce aryl nitro groups cleanly to anilines (it gives azo compounds); Fe, Sn or SnCl<sub>2</sub> with acid, or catalytic hydrogenation, is used.

q: Which sequence converts aniline into 4-bromoaniline as the major product?
c: 1. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O, pyridine  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H  3. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. HCl (to form the anilinium ion)  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. NaOH
1. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O, pyridine  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H  3. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; then H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Free NH<sub>2</sub> is so activating that bromination does not stop after one Br. How can its activating power be turned down temporarily?
w: Aniline reacts with bromine at every open ortho and para position, giving 2,4,6-tribromoaniline even with limited Br2. Acetylating the nitrogen makes the less-activating acetamido group (the N lone pair is shared with C=O), and its bulk favors the para position, so monobromination occurs para. Base hydrolysis then removes the acetyl group: acetylate, brominate, hydrolyze.
x: Unprotected aniline is so activated that bromination continues to 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.
The anilinium ion (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) is a strongly deactivating meta director, so it cannot deliver bromine to the para position.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the amide C=O to CH<sub>2</sub>, giving 4-bromo-N-ethylaniline instead of removing the acetyl group.

q: Treating 4-aminophenol with one equivalent of acetic anhydride gives which compound as the main product?
h: Two nucleophiles compete for one acylating agent. Which is more nucleophilic, a neutral aryl NH<sub>2</sub> or a neutral phenol OH?
w: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so the neutral NH2 lone pair is more available and the amine is the better nucleophile. With one equivalent of anhydride, N-acetylation wins and gives N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide (acetaminophen); the amide formed is also no longer nucleophilic, so the reaction stops there.
x: O-Acylation needs a phenoxide or a large excess of acylating agent; the neutral amine reacts faster.
Acetylating both groups would need two equivalents of anhydride.
Ring acylation is a Friedel–Crafts reaction requiring an acyl chloride and AlCl<sub>3</sub>; acetic anhydride alone acylates the heteroatom.

q: When an amide is made from an acid chloride and an amine, two equivalents of the amine (or one equivalent plus pyridine) are used. Why?
c: The HCl formed would protonate the amine to a non-nucleophilic ammonium salt, so a second base takes it up
The first equivalent of amine adds to the C=O and the second displaces chloride from the intermediate
Two amine molecules are incorporated into each amide product, one on each side of the C=O
The excess amine reduces the acid chloride to an aldehyde, which then reacts with more amine
h: Write the by-product of the substitution and ask what it does to the remaining amine.
w: RCOCl + R′NH2 → RCONHR′ + HCl. The HCl immediately protonates any free amine, and an ammonium ion has no lone pair, so it cannot attack the acid chloride. A second equivalent of the amine, or a cheaper base such as pyridine or Et3N, neutralizes the HCl so all of the valuable amine can react.
x: A single amine molecule both adds to the C=O and, after chloride leaves, loses H<sup>+</sup>; the second equivalent only takes up HCl.
Each amide contains one nitrogen from one amine molecule.
Amines are not reducing agents for acid chlorides; this is a nucleophilic acyl substitution.

q: What is the major alkene formed in the Hofmann elimination sequence shown?
h: A trimethylammonium leaving group removed by E2 behaves differently from a halide: think about which β-hydrogen is removed.
w: Excess CH3I converts the NH2 into –N(CH3)3+ I−; Ag2O/H2O exchanges iodide for hydroxide; heating causes E2 elimination of trimethylamine. Hofmann elimination gives the least substituted alkene: the β-hydrogens on the CH3 group (C1) are removed rather than the single hindered H on C3, so the product is 3-methylbut-1-ene.
x: 2-Methylbut-2-ene is the Zaitsev (more substituted) alkene; the bulky ammonium leaving group steers elimination away from it.
2-Methylbut-1-ene would need a double bond at a carbon that was never bonded to nitrogen.
This 3° amine is the product of incomplete methylation; excess CH<sub>3</sub>I takes N on to the quaternary salt, and heat then eliminates it.

q: N-Methylpiperidine is put through one cycle of Hofmann elimination as shown. What is the organic product?
h: In a ring, losing the ammonium leaving group breaks a ring C–N bond, and the nitrogen stays attached to the other end of the chain.
w: Methylation gives N,N-dimethylpiperidinium ion. On heating with hydroxide, a β-H on a ring carbon is removed and the C–N bond to the adjacent α carbon breaks. Because N is still attached to the carbon on its other side, the ring opens to an acyclic alkenyl amine: N,N-dimethylpent-4-en-1-amine, CH2=CHCH2CH2CH2N(CH3)2. Nitrogen is removed completely only after a second cycle of methylation and elimination.
x: Penta-1,4-diene forms only after a second cycle (CH<sub>3</sub>I, Ag<sub>2</sub>O, heat) on the ring-opened amine.
Hydroxide acts as a base, not a nucleophile, in Hofmann elimination; an alcohol is not formed.
The quaternary hydroxide does eliminate on heating; stopping at the ammonium ion ignores step 3.

q: Heating the ammonium hydroxide shown gives mainly but-1-ene rather than but-2-ene. What is the best explanation?
c: The bulky –N(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group hinders removal of an internal β-H, and the carbanion-like E2 transition state favors the CH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens
Hydroxide is a bulky base, so it can reach only the hydrogens on the terminal CH<sub>3</sub> group of the butyl chain
The reaction goes through a carbocation (E1), and the less substituted alkene forms faster from that carbocation by loss of H<sup>+</sup>
But-1-ene is more stable than but-2-ene, so it accumulates as the thermodynamic product of the elimination on heating
h: The base here is small. What is unusual about this substrate compared with 2-bromobutane?
w: The base (OH−) is small, so the selectivity comes from the leaving group. The large, positively charged –N(CH3)3+ group is a poor leaving group, so C–H breaking runs ahead of C–N breaking (a carbanion-like E2 transition state that favors the more acidic primary hydrogens), and its size makes the anti-periplanar conformations for removing an internal C3 hydrogen crowded. Both effects favor removal of a CH3 hydrogen, giving but-1-ene (Hofmann product).
x: Hydroxide is a small base; the steric bulk that matters belongs to the trimethylammonium leaving group.
Hofmann elimination is an E2 reaction; a 2° carbocation would not form, and E1 would favor the more substituted alkene anyway.
But-2-ene, being more substituted, is the more stable alkene; Hofmann elimination gives the less stable product under kinetic control.

q: What is the product when aniline is treated with NaNO<sub>2</sub> and aqueous HCl at 0–5 °C?
h: HNO<sub>2</sub> in acid generates the nitrosonium ion, NO<sup>+</sup>. A primary arylamine has two N–H bonds to lose.
w: NaNO2 and HCl form HNO2, which gives NO+. The NH2 nitrogen attacks NO+ to give an N-nitrosamine, which tautomerizes and loses water to form the benzenediazonium ion, Ar–N≡N+ (here as its chloride). Aryl diazonium salts are stable enough to use in solution below about 5 °C.
x: Phenol forms only when the diazonium solution is warmed in water; at 0–5 °C the diazonium salt persists.
The N-nitroso compound is the first intermediate for a 1° amine; it loses water to the diazonium ion. Stable N-nitrosamines come from 2° amines.
Nitrous acid does not oxidize the amine nitrogen to a nitro group; it transfers NO<sup>+</sup>.

q: What is the major product when N-methylaniline is treated with NaNO<sub>2</sub> and aqueous HCl at 0 °C?
h: A 2° amine has only one N–H. After NO<sup>+</sup> bonds to nitrogen, can it lose water to form N≡N?
w: The secondary nitrogen attacks NO+ and loses its single N–H proton, giving an N-nitrosamine, Ar(CH3)N–N=O. With no second N–H, it cannot tautomerize and lose water, so no diazonium ion forms; the N-nitrosamine is the stable product (and such compounds are potent carcinogens).
x: Ring C-nitrosation at the para position is typical of 3° arylamines such as N,N-dimethylaniline, which have no N–H.
Forming a diazonium ion requires a 1° amine; this nitrogen would have to lose its methyl group.
Nitrous acid nitrosates (adds N=O); it does not deliver an NO<sub>2</sub> group to nitrogen.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Follow each step in turn: diazotization, a Sandmeyer reaction, then a nitrile reaction under hot aqueous acid.
w: Diazotization converts 4-methylaniline into its diazonium salt. CuCN replaces N2+ with CN (Sandmeyer), giving 4-methylbenzonitrile. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile completely, through the amide, to the carboxylic acid: 4-methylbenzoic acid.
x: 4-Methylbenzonitrile is the product after step 2; heating with H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> hydrolyzes the C≡N.
The diazonium group was already replaced by CN in step 2, so no diazonium is left to be converted into a phenol in step 3.
The amide is an intermediate in nitrile hydrolysis; prolonged heating with aqueous acid takes it on to the acid.

q: Which sequence gives 1,3,5-tribromobenzene from benzene?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (excess), H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (excess), H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. CuBr
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (excess), H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C  5. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
h: The three Br atoms are meta to each other, yet Br is an o,p-director. Which group could place them, and then be removed without a trace?
w: Bromines that are mutually meta can all be ortho/para to one strongly activating group. Nitration and reduction give aniline; aqueous Br2 brominates every ortho and para position, giving 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. Diazotization and then H3PO2 replace N2+ with H, removing the directing group: 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.
x: Bromine directs ortho/para, so successive brominations of benzene give mainly 1,2,4-tribromobenzene, not the 1,3,5 isomer.
CuBr replaces N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> with Br, giving 1,2,3,5-tetrabromobenzene; H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> is needed to replace it with H.
Heating the diazonium salt in water replaces N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> with OH, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

q: Which sequence converts aniline into fluorobenzene?
h: Fluoride is introduced from a non-nucleophilic counterion that the dry diazonium salt carries with it.
w: Adding HBF4 to the diazonium solution precipitates the arenediazonium tetrafluoroborate. Heating the dry salt releases N2 and BF3 and delivers fluoride to the ring (the Balz–Schiemann reaction), giving fluorobenzene. Copper(I) fluoride is not used; Sandmeyer reactions cover Cl, Br and CN.
x: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> replaces the diazonium group with hydrogen, giving benzene.
In hot water, the solvent captures the aryl cation and gives phenol; fluoride ion is a poor nucleophile in water.
CuCl is the Sandmeyer reagent for chlorobenzene, not fluorobenzene.

q: What is the major product of the sequence shown?
h: Sulfuric acid is used instead of HCl in step 1. Which nucleophile is left to capture the aryl group in step 2?
w: Diazotization gives the arenediazonium hydrogen sulfate. On warming in water the diazonium group leaves as N2, and water (the only good nucleophile present; HSO4− is very weak) bonds to the ring carbon. Loss of H+ gives 4-ethylphenol. H2SO4 rather than HCl is used to avoid aryl chloride by-products.
x: Replacement by H needs a reducing agent such as H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>; hot water gives the phenol.
No chloride is present (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> was used), and replacing N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> by Cl efficiently needs CuCl.
Nitrous acid converts a 1° arylamine into a diazonium ion; it does not oxidize the amine to a nitro group.

q: Benzenediazonium chloride is added to phenol in mildly basic solution (pH about 9). What is the major product?
h: The diazonium ion is a weak electrophile that attacks only a strongly activated ring. Where does the phenoxide ion direct, and which position is least hindered?
w: At pH 9 some phenol is present as phenoxide, a very strongly activated ring. The terminal nitrogen of the diazonium ion is the electrophile in an electrophilic aromatic substitution, and coupling occurs para to O−, the least hindered activated position, giving 4-hydroxyazobenzene (an azo dye, drawn as the more stable E isomer).
x: Ortho coupling occurs only when the para position is blocked; the bulky electrophile prefers the open para position.
The meta position is not activated by OH or O<sup>−</sup>, so the weakly electrophilic diazonium ion does not attack there.
O-attack to form a diazo ether is not the observed outcome; diazonium ions couple at ring carbon to give the conjugated azo compound.

q: Which arenediazonium ion reacts fastest in azo coupling with N,N-dimethylaniline?
h: In azo coupling the diazonium ion is the electrophile. Which para substituent makes its terminal nitrogen most electron-poor?
w: The rate depends on the electrophilicity of the terminal diazonium nitrogen. A para electron-withdrawing group increases the positive character of that nitrogen, while donors (CH3, and especially OCH3, which donates by resonance into the N≡N+ group) make the ion more stable and less electrophilic. The 4-nitrobenzenediazonium ion couples fastest.
x: A para OCH<sub>3</sub> donates electron density by resonance into the diazonium group, making it the least electrophilic and slowest to couple.
A para methyl group is weakly donating, so this ion is slightly less reactive than the unsubstituted one.
The unsubstituted ion lacks the electron-withdrawing nitro group that raises electrophilicity.

q: Which sequence converts nitrobenzene into 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene?
c: 1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  4. CuBr
1. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  2. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  3. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  4. CuBr
1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  4. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  4. HBF<sub>4</sub>, heat
h: Use the nitro group as a meta director first, then turn it into something that can be swapped for Br.
w: The nitro group directs chlorination meta (1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene). Reduction gives 3-chloroaniline, diazotization gives the 3-chlorobenzenediazonium ion, and the Sandmeyer reaction with CuBr replaces N2+ with Br: chlorinate, reduce, diazotize, CuBr.
x: Reducing first makes aniline, an o,p-director that is chlorinated at ortho and para positions (and more than once), so the meta relationship is lost.
Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> brominates ring C–H positions; it does not replace a diazonium group. CuBr is needed.
HBF<sub>4</sub> and heat replace the diazonium group with F, giving 1-chloro-3-fluorobenzene.

q: Imidazole is protonated by one equivalent of HCl. Which atom accepts the proton?
c: N a and N b equally, giving two different cations
h: One nitrogen's lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet; the other's lies in the ring plane.
w: N a (the N–H nitrogen) is pyrrole-like: its lone pair is in a p orbital and is part of the six π electrons. N b is pyridine-like: its lone pair is in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, so N b can bond H+ without disturbing aromaticity. The resulting imidazolium ion is aromatic and symmetric (the charge is shared equally by both N atoms by resonance), which is why imidazole (conjugate-acid pKa about 7.0) is a stronger base than pyridine (5.2).
x: Protonating the N–H nitrogen would use its lone pair, which is part of the aromatic sextet, giving a non-aromatic cation.
Protonating C2 would destroy aromaticity; ring carbon protonation is not competitive with the available nitrogen lone pair.
The two nitrogens are not equivalent in neutral imidazole: only N b has a lone pair outside the π system.

q:
Consider these statements about nitrogen heterocycles.
I. The nitrogen lone pair of pyridine occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane and is not part of the aromatic π system.
II. The nitrogen lone pair of pyrrole occupies a p orbital and is one of the six π electrons of the ring.
III. Pyrrole is protonated mainly on nitrogen, giving an aromatic cation.
IV. Imidazole contains one pyridine-like nitrogen and one pyrrole-like nitrogen.
Which statements are true?
h: For each ring, count π electrons and decide whether the N lone pair is needed to reach six.
w: I is true: pyridine already has six π electrons from its three double bonds, so the lone pair lies in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane. II is true: pyrrole needs the N lone pair in a p orbital to complete its sextet. III is false: N-protonation would remove the lone pair from the π system and destroy aromaticity, so pyrrole is a very weak base and protonates (when forced) on C2. IV is true: imidazole has an N–H nitrogen like pyrrole and an N= nitrogen like pyridine. Answer: I, II and IV only.
x: Statement IV is also true: imidazole has one nitrogen of each type.
Statement I is true and statement III is false; protonating pyrrole on N destroys its aromaticity.
Statement III is false: an N-protonated pyrrole is not aromatic, and pyrrole is protonated on carbon.

q: Which sequence gives 3-bromotoluene (1-bromo-3-methylbenzene) from toluene? (Assume the para isomer is separated after nitration.)
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O  4. Br<sub>2</sub>  5. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O, heat  6. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  7. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub>  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>

1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O  4. Br<sub>2</sub>  5. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O, heat  6. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C  7. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
h: CH<sub>3</sub> directs ortho/para, so a temporary, stronger director para to CH<sub>3</sub> must steer Br meta to CH<sub>3</sub>. Tame it so only one Br adds, then remove it.
w: Nitration and reduction give 4-methylaniline. Acetylation makes the acetamido group, which still outranks CH3 as a director but is mild enough for monobromination; Br enters ortho to NHAc, which is meta to CH3. Hydrolysis frees the amine, and diazotization followed by H3PO2 replaces the nitrogen with H, leaving 3-bromotoluene.
x: Without acetylation, the free NH<sub>2</sub> directs bromine to both of its ortho positions; after deamination the product is 3,5-dibromotoluene.
Hot water replaces the diazonium group with OH, giving 2-bromo-4-methylphenol instead of removing it.

With the nitro group still in place, bromination is directed by CH<sub>3</sub> (ortho to it, which is also meta to NO<sub>2</sub>); after removing the nitrogen the product is 2-bromotoluene, not 3-bromotoluene.

q: 4-(Dimethylamino)pyridine (DMAP, conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> 9.6) is a much stronger base than pyridine (5.2). Which nitrogen is protonated, and why is DMAP so basic?
c: N b; the N a lone pair donates into the ring by resonance, spreading the cation’s positive charge onto N a
N a; it is a 3° alkylamine nitrogen with an undelocalized sp3 lone pair, like trimethylamine
N a; the pyridine ring withdraws electrons from N b, leaving N a as the only basic site in the molecule
N b; the dimethylamino group withdraws electron density inductively, which stabilizes the cation formed at N b
h: Draw the cation from protonating the ring nitrogen. Can the dimethylamino lone pair share the positive charge?
w: N a is attached to an aromatic ring, so its lone pair is conjugated with the ring like that of an aniline; it is not an ordinary alkylamine nitrogen. Protonation at the ring nitrogen N b gives a cation with a resonance form C=N+(CH3)2, in which the positive charge is shared by both nitrogens (an amidinium-like ion). That extra resonance stabilization of the conjugate acid raises the pKa from 5.2 to 9.6.
x: N a is bonded to an aromatic carbon, so its lone pair is delocalized into the ring (like an aniline); protonating it would also lose that conjugation.
The ring nitrogen N b becomes more, not less, electron rich because N a donates into the ring.
The dimethylamino group raises the basicity by resonance donation; an inductive withdrawal would lower it.

q: In which compound is the nitrogen lone pair not part of an aromatic π system?
h: Count the π electrons from double bonds alone. If the ring already has six, the lone pair stays out of the π system.
w: In pyridine the three ring double bonds supply six π electrons; the N lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, perpendicular to the p orbitals. In pyrrole, N-methylpyrrole and indole the five-membered ring has only four π electrons from C=C bonds, so the N lone pair must sit in a p orbital to complete the aromatic sextet.
x: Pyrrole needs the N lone pair to give six π electrons, so it is part of the aromatic system.
N-Methylpyrrole is aromatic in the same way as pyrrole; the methyl group does not change where the lone pair is.
In indole the nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic π system of the five-membered (and the fused ten-electron) ring.

q: An amine C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N gives the mass spectrum shown, with a weak M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 87 and the base peak at m/z 30. Which structure fits?
h: Amines fragment by α-cleavage: the C–C bond next to the C–N carbon breaks, leaving a resonance-stabilized iminium ion. Work out the iminium mass for each candidate.
w: An odd molecular ion (87) fits one nitrogen (nitrogen rule). α-Cleavage of pentan-1-amine breaks the C1–C2 bond and gives CH2=NH2+, m/z 30, the base peak for amines with an unbranched RCH2NH2 group. Each other isomer gives a heavier iminium ion because it carries extra carbon on the α carbon or on nitrogen.
x: Pentan-2-amine loses the propyl radical by α-cleavage to give CH<sub>3</sub>CH=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, m/z 44.
N-Methylbutan-1-amine loses a propyl radical to give CH<sub>2</sub>=NHCH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, m/z 44.
N,N-Dimethylpropan-1-amine loses an ethyl radical to give CH<sub>2</sub>=N(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, m/z 58.

q: Which of these ions is aromatic? (Assume each ring could be planar.)
h: For each ion, decide the hybridization of the charged carbon, then count the π electrons in the ring and test 4n + 2.
w: Hückel's rule: a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring is aromatic with 4n + 2 π electrons and antiaromatic with 4n. In the cycloheptatrienyl (tropylium) cation the C+ is sp2 with an empty p orbital, so the ring holds the 6 π electrons of its three C=C bonds: 4n + 2 with n = 1, aromatic. The other three ions have 8, 4 and 4 π electrons (4n), so none can be aromatic.
x: The cycloheptatrienyl anion has 6 electrons from the C=C bonds plus 2 from the carbanion lone pair: 8 π electrons, a 4n count.
The cyclopentadienyl cation has only the 4 π electrons of its two C=C bonds (the C<sup>+</sup> p orbital is empty): 4n, antiaromatic if planar.
The cyclopropenyl anion has 2 π electrons from the C=C plus 2 from the lone pair: 4 π electrons, a 4n count. It is the cyclopropenyl cation (2 π) that is aromatic.

q: Cyclooctatetraene (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> like an ordinary alkene, and its C–C bonds alternate between about 1.33 and 1.47 Å. Which classification and reason fit these facts best?
c: Nonaromatic: its tub shape keeps the p orbitals from overlapping all the way around the ring
Antiaromatic: it is planar and cyclic with 8 π electrons, a 4n count, so it is strongly destabilized
Aromatic: it is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated with 8 π electrons in the ring
Antiaromatic: it is tub-shaped, and the 8 π electrons overlap continuously around the tub
h: Hückel's rule applies only to rings that are planar. What does an 8-membered ring do to avoid a 4n π count?
w: If cyclooctatetraene were planar it would have 8 π electrons in a continuous loop (4n) and be antiaromatic. A planar 8-membered ring would also have 135° bond angles. The molecule escapes both problems by folding into a tub: adjacent C=C bonds are twisted so their p orbitals barely overlap, the double bonds become localized (alternating bond lengths) and react like isolated alkenes. Because there is no continuous cyclic overlap, it is nonaromatic.
x: A planar 8π ring would be antiaromatic, but the observed localized bonds and alkene reactivity show the molecule is not planar; it avoids antiaromaticity by puckering.
8 is a 4n number, not 4n + 2, so the ring could not be aromatic even if planar; aromatic rings also show equal bond lengths, not alternation.
Antiaromaticity requires continuous cyclic overlap in a planar ring; in the tub the p orbitals of neighboring C=C bonds are nearly perpendicular, so there is no continuous overlap.

q: Cyclooctatetraene reacts with 2 equivalents of potassium metal in THF to give K<sub>2</sub>C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, whose eight C–C bonds are all the same length and whose eight H give one <sup>1</sup>H NMR singlet near 5.7 ppm. Which description of the C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup> ion is correct?
c: A planar, aromatic ring with 10 π electrons
A tub-shaped, nonaromatic ring with 10 π electrons
A planar, antiaromatic ring with 8 π electrons
A planar, aromatic ring with 8 π electrons and two lone pairs outside the π system
h: Each potassium atom gives one electron to the π system. Count again and apply 4n + 2.
w: Two electrons added to the 8 π electrons of cyclooctatetraene give 10 π electrons (4n + 2, n = 2). Ten electrons fill the planar ring's three bonding MOs and its two nonbonding MOs, a closed shell, so the dianion flattens to a planar, aromatic octagon. Equal bond lengths and the single NMR environment both point to full delocalization.
x: With 10 π electrons the ion gains aromatic stabilization by becoming planar; the equal bond lengths show it is no longer a localized tub.
The added electrons go into the π system, so the count is 10, not 8; an 8π planar ring would show bond alternation, not equal bonds.
The added electrons occupy p orbitals of the ring (the nonbonding π MOs), not in-plane lone pairs, so they are part of the π count of 10.

q: How many electrons are in the aromatic π system of furan?
h: Oxygen has two lone pairs. Can both sit in a p orbital perpendicular to the ring?
