w: The two C=C bonds give 4 π electrons. The ring oxygen is sp2: one lone pair sits in the p orbital parallel to the carbon p orbitals and joins the π system, and the other lone pair lies in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring. Total: 6 π electrons, so furan is aromatic.
x: Only one oxygen lone pair can occupy the p orbital; the second lies in the ring plane, perpendicular to the π system.
4 counts only the two C=C bonds and leaves out the oxygen lone pair that completes the sextet.
Lone pairs contribute two electrons, not one; an odd count would mean a radical.

q: Use a Frost circle (inscribed-polygon) picture of the planar cyclopentadienyl cation, C5H5+. Which description of its π-electron configuration is correct?
c: Two electrons in the lowest MO and one electron in each of the two degenerate bonding MOs: an open-shell, antiaromatic ion
Two electrons in the lowest MO and two paired electrons in one of the degenerate bonding MOs: a closed-shell, aromatic ion
Six electrons filling all three bonding MOs: a closed-shell, aromatic ion
Two electrons in the lowest MO and two in a single nonbonding MO: a closed-shell, nonaromatic ion
h: Draw a pentagon point-down in a circle: the corners are the MO energies. Then place 4 π electrons, remembering Hund's rule for degenerate orbitals.
w: A pentagon inscribed point-down gives one low bonding MO, a degenerate pair of bonding MOs just below the midline, and a degenerate antibonding pair above it (no nonbonding level). The cation has 4 π electrons: 2 fill the lowest MO and the other 2 go one into each degenerate bonding MO with parallel spins (Hund's rule). A half-filled degenerate pair is the signature of an antiaromatic (4n) ring.
x: Degenerate orbitals fill singly first (Hund's rule), so the two electrons do not pair in one MO; the ion is not closed-shell.
Six π electrons describes the cyclopentadienyl anion, not the cation; the cation has only the 4 electrons of its two C=C bonds.
A five-membered ring has no nonbonding MO; in the Frost picture of a pentagon no corner sits on the midline.

q: Which statement correctly describes the π molecular orbitals of the cyclopentadienyl anion?
c: Its 6 π electrons fill the three bonding MOs, leaving the two antibonding MOs empty
Its 6 π electrons fill the three bonding MOs and place one electron in each antibonding MO
Its 4 π electrons half-fill the degenerate bonding MOs, leaving two unpaired electrons
Its 6 π electrons fill one bonding MO and two nonbonding MOs of equal energy
h: Five p orbitals give five π MOs. How many are bonding, and how many electrons does the anion have?
w: Five p orbitals give five π MOs: one lowest bonding MO, a degenerate bonding pair, and a degenerate antibonding pair. The anion has 4 electrons from the two C=C bonds plus 2 from the carbanion lone pair: 6. They exactly fill the three bonding MOs, giving a closed shell with empty antibonding MOs, the electronic signature of an aromatic ring.
x: Six electrons fit exactly into the three bonding MOs (two each), so none spill into the antibonding MOs.
The lone pair on the anionic carbon adds 2 electrons, so the anion has 6 π electrons, not 4; the 4-electron case is the cation.
A pentagon in the Frost circle has no corner on the midline, so there are no nonbonding MOs; the three filled MOs are all bonding.

q: Which [n]annulene is expected to be aromatic and is observed to be essentially planar with a strong aromatic ring current?
h: Two tests: is the π count 4n + 2, and can the ring actually be planar without severe strain or H–H crowding?
w: [18]Annulene has 18 π electrons (4n + 2, n = 4) and its ring is large enough to be nearly planar with six H atoms pointing into the cavity without serious crowding, so it is aromatic. [10]Annulene also has a 4n + 2 count, but any planar form suffers either large angle strain (all-cis) or a clash of the two inward-pointing H atoms, so it puckers and is nonaromatic. [12] and [16]annulene have 4n counts.
x: 10 is a 4n + 2 number, but a planar [10]annulene has either severe angle strain or two inner H atoms that collide, so the real molecule is nonplanar and nonaromatic.
16 π electrons is a 4n count; [16]annulene is not aromatic.
12 π electrons is a 4n count; [12]annulene is not aromatic.

q: Azulene, an isomer of naphthalene, is deep blue and has an unusually large dipole moment (about 0.8 D) for a hydrocarbon. Which statement best explains the direction of its dipole?
c: The negative end is at the five-membered ring: a dipolar form with a cyclopentadienyl anion fused to a tropylium cation has two aromatic 6π rings
The negative end is at the seven-membered ring, because the larger ring holds more of the 10 π electrons and more of the charge
The negative end is at the five-membered ring, because the five-membered ring is antiaromatic and withdraws electrons from the seven-membered ring
There is no permanent dipole; the blue color comes from its extended system of 10 π electrons alone
h: Move one π electron pair's worth of charge from one ring to the other on paper. When is each separate ring a 6π system?
w: Azulene has 10 π electrons in total. In the charge-separated resonance contributor, the five-membered ring carries a negative charge (6 π electrons, like the cyclopentadienyl anion) and the seven-membered ring carries a positive charge (6 π electrons, like tropylium). Because each ring is then an aromatic sextet, this contributor is significant, so electron density shifts toward the five-membered ring: the negative end of the dipole is at the five-membered ring.
x: Ring size alone does not decide where π density goes; shifting density to the seven-membered ring would give it 8 π electrons, a 4n count.
The direction is right but the reason is wrong: in the polarized form the five-membered ring is a 6π aromatic anion, not antiaromatic.
Azulene has a measurable dipole; a hydrocarbon with no polar bonds shows one only because of this charge-separated aromatic contributor.

q: Which compound is nonaromatic?
h: Look for an atom in the ring that has no p orbital available for conjugation.
w: Cycloheptatriene contains an sp3 CH2 carbon. That carbon has no p orbital, so the cyclic π system is interrupted and the ring cannot be aromatic or antiaromatic: it is nonaromatic. Removing hydride from that carbon gives the tropylium ion, which is aromatic.
x: The tropylium ion's C<sup>+</sup> is sp<sup>2</sup> with an empty p orbital, so the ring is fully conjugated with 6 π electrons: aromatic.
Pyridine is a planar, fully conjugated ring with 6 π electrons (the N lone pair is in the plane, outside the π system): aromatic.
Thiophene uses one sulfur lone pair in its π system to reach 6 π electrons: aromatic.

q: Which species is antiaromatic?
h: Antiaromatic means planar, cyclic, fully conjugated and 4n π electrons. Check planarity as well as the count.
w: Cyclobutadiene is a square-planar (rectangular) ring with 4 π electrons in a continuous loop, a 4n count, and a four-membered ring cannot pucker enough to escape the overlap. It is the classic antiaromatic molecule: so unstable that it dimerizes almost at once unless it is trapped at very low temperature.
x: The cyclopropenyl cation has 2 π electrons (4n + 2, n = 0) in a planar ring: aromatic.
Cyclooctatetraene has 8 π electrons, but it avoids antiaromaticity by adopting a nonplanar tub shape: nonaromatic.
The cyclopentadienyl anion has 6 π electrons in a planar ring: aromatic.

q: Rank these hydrocarbons in order of increasing acidity of their most acidic C–H.
h: Draw each conjugate base. Which one is aromatic, which is a delocalized but 4n system, and which is a localized alkyl carbanion?
w: Removing H+ from the CH2 of cyclopentadiene (I) gives the cyclopentadienyl anion, a 6π aromatic ion, so I is remarkably acidic for a hydrocarbon (pKa ≈ 16). Cycloheptatriene (II) gives an 8π anion that cannot gain aromatic stabilization, but its charge is still spread over a conjugated system (pKa ≈ 36). Cyclopentane (III) gives a localized sp3 carbanion (pKa ≈ 50). Increasing acidity: III < II < I.
x: The cycloheptatrienyl anion is not aromatic, but it is still delocalized over several sp<sup>2</sup> carbons, so II is far more acidic than the alkane III.
This is the reverse order: the compound with the aromatic conjugate base (I) is the most acidic, not the least.
A larger conjugated ring does not mean a more stable anion: the seven-membered anion has 8 π electrons, while the five-membered anion has an aromatic 6.

q: Cyclopentadiene has pKa ≈ 16. Which base will convert it essentially completely to the cyclopentadienyl anion?
h: An acid–base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid. Compare each base's conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> with 16.
w: Deprotonation is essentially complete when the conjugate acid of the base is much weaker than cyclopentadiene. NH3 (pKa ≈ 38) is about 1022 times weaker an acid than cyclopentadiene, so NaNH2 drives the equilibrium fully to the aromatic anion. The other three bases have conjugate acids far stronger than cyclopentadiene, so equilibrium lies on the cyclopentadiene side.
x: Et<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>+</sup> (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.7) is a stronger acid than cyclopentadiene (16), so equilibrium favors the starting hydrocarbon.
H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (pK<sub>a</sub> 6.4) is about 10<sup>10</sup> times stronger an acid than cyclopentadiene, so bicarbonate deprotonates almost none of it.
Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8) is a much stronger acid than cyclopentadiene, so acetate cannot remove its proton to any useful extent.

q: How many electrons are in the aromatic π system of indole?
h: Count the C=C π bonds in a Kekulé structure, then decide whether the N lone pair is in a p orbital.
w: A Kekulé structure of indole has four C=C bonds (8 π electrons). The N–H nitrogen is pyrrole-like: it is sp2, and its lone pair sits in a p orbital and is part of the ring π system, adding 2 more. Total: 10 π electrons (4n + 2, n = 2), delocalized over both rings.
x: 8 leaves out the nitrogen lone pair, which must be in the π system because the N–H nitrogen has no double bond in the ring.
A lone pair contributes two electrons, not one; the N in indole is not pyridine-like (it has no ring double bond).
Twelve would require another lone pair or π bond; the nine ring atoms hold only four C=C bonds and one N lone pair.

q: Imidazole has two ring nitrogens, labeled a and b. Which statement is correct?
c: The lone pair on a is part of the aromatic sextet; b is the basic site that is protonated by acid
The lone pair on b is part of the aromatic sextet; a is the basic site that is protonated by acid
Both lone pairs are part of the sextet, so imidazole is not basic
The lone pair on a is part of the aromatic sextet, and a is also the basic site that is protonated by acid
h: Which N looks like the N of pyrrole (N–H, no ring double bond) and which looks like the N of pyridine?
w: Na (the N–H) is pyrrole-like: its lone pair occupies a p orbital and supplies 2 of the 6 π electrons. Nb is pyridine-like: it already contributes one electron to the π system through its C=N bond, and its lone pair lies in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane. Protonating b leaves the aromatic sextet intact, so b is the basic site and a's lone pair is in the sextet.
x: This reverses the roles: the N–H nitrogen has no ring double bond, so its lone pair must supply the π electrons.
Only one lone pair is needed to reach 6 π electrons; the second (on b) is in the plane and is basic (imidazole's conjugate acid pKa ≈ 7).
Protonating a would remove its lone pair from the π system and destroy aromaticity, so that site is not basic.

q: Suppose cyclooctatetraene were forced to be a planar regular octagon. According to its Frost circle, how would its 8 π electrons be arranged?
c: Six fill the bonding MOs, and the last two singly occupy the two degenerate nonbonding MOs
Six fill the three bonding MOs, and the last two pair up in one nonbonding MO, giving a closed shell
Eight fill four bonding MOs, giving a closed shell like benzene with no unpaired electrons
Six fill the three bonding MOs, and the last two pair in the lowest antibonding MO
h: An octagon drawn point-down in a circle has two corners exactly on the midline. What are those MOs called?
w: An octagon inscribed point-down gives 1 bonding MO at the bottom, a degenerate bonding pair, a degenerate nonbonding pair on the midline, a degenerate antibonding pair and 1 antibonding MO at the top. Six electrons fill the three bonding MOs; the remaining two go one into each nonbonding MO with parallel spins (Hund's rule). This open-shell, diradical configuration is the hallmark of an antiaromatic 4n ring, which is why real cyclooctatetraene puckers into a tub instead.
x: Degenerate orbitals are filled singly before any pairing (Hund's rule), so the two electrons do not pair in one nonbonding MO.
A planar eight-membered ring has only three bonding π MOs, not four; the fourth-lowest level is nonbonding.
The nonbonding pair lies below the antibonding MOs, so electrons fill the nonbonding level first.

q: Rank these nitrogen compounds in order of increasing basicity.
h: For each N, ask where the lone pair is (in the π sextet? sp<sup>2</sup>? sp<sup>3</sup>?) and what protonation would cost.
w: Pyrrole (I): the N lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet, so N-protonation would destroy aromaticity; pyrrole is a very weak base (conjugate acid pKa ≈ −4). Pyridine (II): the lone pair is in an sp2 orbital outside the π system, so it is available, but the higher s character holds it tightly (pKa of pyridinium ≈ 5.2). Piperidine (III): an sp3 amine lone pair, the most available (pKa of piperidinium ≈ 11.1). Order: I < II < III.
x: Pyrrole is far less basic than pyridine: its lone pair is tied up in the aromatic sextet, while pyridine's lone pair is free in the ring plane.
Pyridine is less basic than piperidine because an sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair (33% s) is held closer to N than an sp<sup>3</sup> lone pair (25% s).
This is the order of decreasing basicity; the question asks for increasing.

q: Pyridine is protonated by HCl to give the pyridinium ion. Which description of pyridinium is correct?
c: Aromatic with 6 π electrons; the N–H bond uses the in-plane sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair, which was never in the π system
Nonaromatic; protonation removes two electrons from the π system and leaves only four
Antiaromatic with 4 π electrons; the positive charge empties one ring p orbital on nitrogen
Aromatic with 8 π electrons; the new N–H bond adds two electrons to the π system
h: Where is pyridine's lone pair pointing: perpendicular to the ring or in the ring plane?
w: Pyridine's six π electrons come from its three ring double bonds; the N lone pair is in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring. Protonation uses that in-plane pair to form the N–H bond, so the π system is untouched: pyridinium is still aromatic with 6 π electrons. That is why pyridine is a reasonable base, unlike pyrrole.
x: The lone pair used for bonding to H<sup>+</sup> was never in the π system, so the π count stays at 6.
The N in pyridinium is still sp<sup>2</sup> with a p orbital holding one π electron from the C=N bond; no ring p orbital is emptied.
The N–H σ bond lies in the ring plane and cannot contribute to the π system; the count stays at 6.

q: 4-(Dimethylamino)pyridine (DMAP) is about 10<sup>4</sup> times more basic than pyridine. Which nitrogen is protonated first, and why?
c: a; NMe2 donates into the ring, raising electron density on a and spreading the + charge over both N
b; it is a trialkyl-type sp3 amine, and amines are always more basic than pyridines
b; the lone pair on a is part of the aromatic sextet, so it cannot be protonated at all
a; it is sp3 hybridized, so its lone pair is held less tightly than the lone pair of b
h: Draw a resonance form in which the NMe<sub>2</sub> lone pair pushes into the ring. Where does the negative charge end up?
w: Nb is an aniline-type nitrogen: its lone pair is conjugated with the ring (it is nearly planar, sp2-like), so it is not very basic. That donation pushes electron density onto the para ring nitrogen a. After a is protonated, the positive charge is shared with b through an amidinium-like resonance form (C=N+Me2). So a is protonated, and DMAP (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 9.6) is much more basic than pyridine (5.2).
x: Nb is attached to an aromatic ring, so its lone pair is delocalized into the ring like aniline's; protonating it would destroy that conjugation and give no charge sharing.
Ring nitrogen a is pyridine-like: its lone pair is in the ring plane, outside the sextet, and is available for protonation.
Ring nitrogen a is sp2, not sp3; the extra basicity comes from resonance donation by the NMe2 group, not hybridization.

q: In thiophene, how many of the sulfur lone pairs are part of the aromatic π system?
c: One; the other lies in the plane of the ring
Two; both are needed to reach 6 π electrons
None; the 3p orbitals of sulfur are too large to overlap with carbon
h: Two C=C bonds give 4 π electrons. How many more are needed for a sextet?
w: The two C=C bonds supply 4 π electrons, and one sulfur lone pair in a p orbital supplies the other 2 for an aromatic sextet. The second lone pair occupies an orbital in the ring plane, perpendicular to the π system. Thiophene is therefore aromatic.
x: Two lone pairs would give 8 π electrons (4n); only one p orbital on S is aligned with the ring p orbitals.
Sulfur's 3p orbital does overlap with carbon 2p orbitals well enough; thiophene is clearly aromatic.
For the lone pair to sit in a p orbital parallel to the ring, sulfur must be described as sp<sup>2</sup>, not sp<sup>3</sup>.

q: In which compound is a nitrogen lone pair part of the aromatic π system?
h: A nitrogen that is part of a ring C=N bond already gives one electron to the π system. Look for a nitrogen with no ring double bond.
w: In indole, the N–H nitrogen has only single bonds in the ring; to keep the ring fully conjugated its lone pair occupies a p orbital and is part of the 10-electron π system (pyrrole-like N). In quinoline, pyrimidine and isoquinoline every ring N is part of a C=N bond (pyridine-like), so each lone pair lies in the ring plane, outside the π system.
x: Quinoline's nitrogen is pyridine-like: it contributes one electron through its C=N bond and its lone pair is in the ring plane.
Both nitrogens of pyrimidine are pyridine-like; their lone pairs are in the plane and make pyrimidine a (weak) base.
Isoquinoline's nitrogen is pyridine-like, with its lone pair in the plane of the ring.

q: The conjugate acid of imidazole has pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 7.0, while pyridinium has pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 5.2. Which statement best explains why imidazole is the stronger base?
c: In imidazolium the positive charge is shared equally by both nitrogens by resonance, and the ring stays aromatic
Imidazole is protonated on the N–H nitrogen, whose lone pair is held less tightly than an sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair
The basic nitrogen of imidazole is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridized, while pyridine’s nitrogen is sp<sup>2</sup>, so its lone pair is more available
Protonation of pyridine destroys its aromaticity, but protonation of imidazole does not
h: Draw the resonance forms of the imidazolium ion. Compare them with pyridinium.
w: Imidazole is protonated at its pyridine-like N (the one without H), using an in-plane lone pair, so aromaticity is kept, just as in pyridine. The difference is the conjugate acid: in imidazolium the N–H nitrogen's π lone pair can push into the ring to give an equivalent resonance form with the + charge on the other nitrogen (an amidinium-type cation). Charge shared over two nitrogens in an aromatic ring stabilizes the conjugate acid, raising its pKa to about 7.
x: Protonating the N–H nitrogen would use the lone pair that belongs to the aromatic sextet and destroy aromaticity; it is not the basic site.
Both nitrogens of imidazole are sp<sup>2</sup>; the basic one has its lone pair in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital, just like pyridine.
Pyridinium is aromatic: pyridine's lone pair is outside the π system, so protonation does not disturb the sextet.

q: (S)-Nicotine has two nitrogens, a and b. When one equivalent of HCl is added, which nitrogen is protonated?
c: a, because its lone pair is in an sp3 orbital and is the more available
b, because its lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet
b, because aromatic nitrogens are always the most basic site
a, because protonating b would destroy the aromaticity of the pyridine ring
h: Compare a trialkylamine (sp<sup>3</sup> N) with a pyridine-type (sp<sup>2</sup> N). Typical conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> values are about 10 vs 5.
w: Nitrogen a is a tertiary amine in a pyrrolidine ring: its lone pair is in an sp3 orbital (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 8 in nicotine). Nitrogen b is pyridine-like: its lone pair is in an sp2 orbital with more s character and is held more tightly (pKa ≈ 3). So a is protonated first because its sp3 lone pair is more available.
x: Pyridine's lone pair is in the ring plane, not in the sextet; b can be protonated, it is simply less basic than a.
Pyridine-type nitrogens are weaker bases than alkylamines because of the greater s character of their lone-pair orbital.
The site is correct but the reason is wrong: protonating the pyridine N does not destroy aromaticity, because that lone pair is outside the π system.

q: Which of these oxygen heterocycles is aromatic?
h: Check every ring atom for a p orbital, then count π electrons. A positively charged oxygen with a double bond behaves like the N of pyridine.
w: The pyrylium ion is isoelectronic with pyridine: the O+ is sp2, part of a ring double bond, and contributes one electron to the π system, while its remaining lone pair lies in the ring plane. Three ring double bonds give 6 π electrons in a planar, fully conjugated ring: aromatic. 4H- and 2H-pyran each contain an sp3 CH2 that breaks the cycle, and 1,4-dioxin would have 8 π electrons (4 from the C=C bonds, 2 from each O), so it is not aromatic.
x: 4H-Pyran has an sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub> carbon in the ring, so conjugation is not continuous: nonaromatic.
If each O donated one lone pair, 1,4-dioxin would have 8 π electrons (4n); it is not aromatic.
2H-Pyran has an sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub> next to oxygen, which interrupts the cyclic π system: nonaromatic.

q: Tropone (cycloheptatrienone) has a much larger dipole moment than cycloheptanone, and its carbonyl oxygen is protonated far more easily than that of an ordinary ketone. Which explanation is best?
c: The dipolar resonance form, with O<sup>−</sup> and a positive seven-membered ring, contains a 6π aromatic tropylium ring and contributes strongly
The dipolar resonance form, with O<sup>−</sup> and a positive seven-membered ring, is antiaromatic, which forces even more negative charge onto oxygen
The ring contains 8 π electrons including the C=O, so tropone itself is aromatic without any charge separation
The carbonyl carbon of tropone is sp<sup>3</sup>, so the C=O bond is unusually long and polar
h: Push the C=O π electrons onto oxygen. Count the π electrons left in the seven-membered ring.
w: In the charge-separated resonance form C–O−, the ring carbon becomes C+, and the ring holds the 6 π electrons of its three C=C bonds: a tropylium-like aromatic sextet. Because this form gains aromatic stabilization, it contributes much more than the corresponding form of an ordinary ketone. More negative charge on O means a larger dipole and a more basic oxygen (its conjugate acid is a hydroxytropylium ion, also aromatic).
x: With 6 π electrons in the ring, the dipolar form is aromatic, not antiaromatic.
Counting the C=O as part of the ring gives 8 π electrons, a 4n count, which would not be aromatic; the stabilization comes only from the charge-separated form.
The carbonyl carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, as in any ketone; hybridization is not the source of the large dipole.

q: What is the correct name of this compound?
h: Count the carbons between the two substituents. When locants tie, the substituent cited first in alphabetical order gets the lower number.
w: The two groups are separated by one ring carbon, a 1,3 (meta) relationship. Neither chloro nor nitro is a suffix group, so both are prefixes in alphabetical order, and when the locant sets tie ({1,3} either way) the first-cited group, chloro, gets C1: 1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene, or m-chloronitrobenzene.
x: 1,4 (para) would put the groups directly across the ring; here one CH sits between them.
1,2 (ortho) would put the groups on adjacent carbons; here they are separated by one carbon.
The meta relationship is right, but with tied locants the alphabetically first prefix (chloro) gets the lower number, C1.

q: What is the IUPAC name of this compound?
h: Which group has higher priority and becomes the parent name (suffix)? Its ring carbon is C1.
w: The carboxylic acid outranks the OH, so the parent is benzoic acid and the carbon bearing COOH is C1. Number toward the OH by the shorter path: it is at C3 (one CH between them, meta). Name: 3-hydroxybenzoic acid (m-hydroxybenzoic acid).
x: Numbering the long way around gives 5; the rule is to give the substituent the lowest possible locant, 3.
A carboxylic acid outranks an alcohol/phenol, so COOH is named as the parent (benzoic acid), not as a carboxy prefix.
In 4-hydroxybenzoic acid the OH would be directly across from COOH (para); here the relationship is meta.

q: Which structure is p-nitroanisole (1-methoxy-4-nitrobenzene)?
h: Anisole is methoxybenzene. Para means the 1,4 positions.
w: Anisole is C6H5OCH3; para places the NO2 group on the carbon directly across the ring (1,4) from OCH3. The answer is the 1,4-disubstituted methoxy/nitro benzene.
x: This is the 1,3 (meta) isomer, m-nitroanisole.
This is the 1,2 (ortho) isomer, o-nitroanisole.
This has OH instead of OCH3: it is p-nitrophenol, not an anisole.

q: What is the IUPAC name of this compound (common name o-cresol)?
h: The OH group outranks CH<sub>3</sub>, so it is named as the suffix and its carbon is C1.
w: Phenol is the parent, so the OH carbon is C1. Numbering toward the methyl group the short way puts it at C2 (ortho): 2-methylphenol.
x: Numbering the long way gives 6; the methyl must get the lowest locant, 2.
When a ring carries OH, the compound is named as a phenol (suffix), not with a hydroxy prefix on benzene.
3-Methylphenol is the meta isomer (m-cresol); here the groups are on adjacent carbons.

q: Which compound gives no benzoic acid when heated with aqueous KMnO4 (then acidified)?
h: Side-chain oxidation begins at the benzylic carbon. What must the benzylic carbon carry?
w: Hot KMnO4 oxidizes an alkyl side chain to COOH only if the benzylic carbon has at least one C–H bond. The benzylic carbon of tert-butylbenzene is quaternary (no benzylic H), so the side chain is not oxidized.
x: Isopropylbenzene has one benzylic H, so its side chain is cleaved to COOH, giving benzoic acid.
Ethylbenzene has two benzylic H; the whole side chain is oxidized down to a COOH on the ring.
Benzyl alcohol already has an oxidized benzylic carbon with two H; KMnO<sub>4</sub> takes it on to benzoic acid.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: Check each benzylic carbon for an H atom.
w: The isopropyl group has a benzylic C–H, so hot KMnO4 oxidizes it all the way to a carboxylic acid (the two methyl carbons are lost). The tert-butyl group has no benzylic H and survives. Product: 4-tert-butylbenzoic acid.
x: The tert-butyl group cannot be oxidized because its benzylic carbon has no H, so only one COOH forms.
This oxidizes the wrong group: the tert-butyl carbon lacks a benzylic H and is untouched, while the isopropyl group is the one that reacts.
Hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> does not stop at a tertiary benzylic alcohol; it cleaves the side chain to COOH.

q: What is the major organic product when indane is heated with excess aqueous KMnO<sub>4</sub> and the mixture is then acidified?
h: Indane has two benzylic CH<sub>2</sub> groups, one on each ring-fusion carbon. Each benzylic carbon ends up as what group?
w: Hot KMnO4 converts every alkyl carbon attached to the ring that has a benzylic H into a COOH group and removes the rest of the chain. Indane has two benzylic carbons (C1 and C3), one on each of two adjacent ring carbons, so the five-membered ring is cleaved and two ortho COOH groups result: phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid). The middle CH2 is lost.
x: A benzylic ketone is the product of milder oxidants; hot, excess KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves the side chain all the way to COOH.
Both benzylic carbons are attached to the ring and both carry H, so both become COOH groups, not just one.
Each benzylic carbon becomes a COOH bonded directly to the ring; a CH<sub>2</sub>COOH group cannot survive because its CH<sub>2</sub> is itself benzylic.

q: What is the major organic product? (Stereochemistry is not shown.)
h: NBS supplies a low concentration of Br<sub>2</sub> for a radical chain. Which C–H gives the most stable radical?
w: Under radical conditions, NBS abstracts the H whose removal gives the most stable radical. A benzylic radical is resonance-stabilized by the ring, so the benzylic C–H (bond energy ≈ 375 kJ/mol) reacts selectively. The benzylic radical then takes Br from Br2: (1-bromopropyl)benzene, formed as a racemate.
x: The C2 radical is an ordinary secondary radical with no resonance stabilization; the benzylic radical forms much faster.
A primary radical at the chain end is the least stable choice; NBS bromination is selective for the benzylic position.
Ring bromination is an electrophilic substitution that needs Br<sub>2</sub> with a Lewis acid such as FeBr<sub>3</sub>; NBS with light does radical substitution on the side chain.

q: What is the major monobromination product? (Stereochemistry is not shown.)
h: There are two kinds of benzylic H. Compare the radicals they would give.
w: Both the CH3 and the CH2 of the ethyl group are benzylic. Abstracting a CH2 hydrogen gives a secondary benzylic radical (stabilized by the ring and by an extra alkyl group); abstracting a CH3 hydrogen gives only a primary benzylic radical. The more stable radical forms faster, so the major product is 1-(1-bromoethyl)-4-methylbenzene (racemic).
x: This product comes from the primary benzylic radical, which is less stable than the secondary benzylic radical at the ethyl CH<sub>2</sub>.
The terminal CH<sub>3</sub> of the ethyl group is not benzylic; its primary radical is the least stable possible.
Substitution on the ring requires electrophilic conditions (Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>); NBS with a radical initiator brominates the benzylic side chain.

q: What is the major product of the Birch reduction of anisole?
h: Birch reduction gives a nonconjugated 1,4-cyclohexadiene. Electron-donating groups end up on a double bond; electron-withdrawing groups end up on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.
w: Birch reduction adds two electrons and two protons to opposite (para) ring carbons, giving a 1,4-cyclohexadiene. Electron-donating groups such as OCH3 destabilize the carbanion intermediates at the carbon they are attached to, so protonation occurs elsewhere and the donor stays on a C=C: 1-methoxycyclohexa-1,4-diene.
x: Putting OCH<sub>3</sub> on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon is the pattern for electron-withdrawing groups (like COOH), not donors.
Birch reduction gives the unconjugated 1,4-diene, not a conjugated 1,3-diene.
Na/NH<sub>3</sub> reduces the ring only to the diene stage; isolated C=C bonds are not reduced further.

q: What is the major product of the Birch reduction of benzoic acid (after acidic workup)?
h: An electron-withdrawing group stabilizes a negative charge on the carbon it is attached to. Where is that carbon protonated?
w: A carboxyl (carboxylate under the conditions) group stabilizes carbanion character on its own ring carbon, so that carbon is reduced and protonated, ending up sp3. The two remaining double bonds are not conjugated with each other: cyclohexa-2,5-diene-1-carboxylic acid.
x: Keeping COOH on a C=C is the pattern for electron-donating groups; electron-withdrawing groups end up on the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.
Birch reduction does not give the conjugated 1,3-diene.
Na/NH<sub>3</sub> stops at the cyclohexadiene; it does not fully saturate the ring.

q: What is the major product of the Birch reduction of 4-methylanisole?
h: Both substituents are electron donors. In a 1,4-cyclohexadiene, which pairs of ring positions are sp<sup>3</sup>?
w: In the 1,4-diene from a Birch reduction, the two sp3 carbons are para to each other. Both OCH3 and CH3 are electron donors and prefer to remain on double-bond carbons. Because they are para to each other, both can stay on sp2 carbons at once, with C3 and C6 reduced: 1-methoxy-4-methylcyclohexa-1,4-diene.
x: This places both donors on the sp<sup>3</sup> carbons, the pattern for electron-withdrawing groups.
Birch reduction gives a nonconjugated 1,4-diene, not a conjugated 1,3-diene.
Na/NH<sub>3</sub> does not reduce isolated alkenes, so the reduction stops at the diene.

q: The Birch reduction of benzene (Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l), EtOH) gives cyclohexa-1,4-diene, even though cyclohexa-1,3-diene is the more stable isomer. Which statement best explains this outcome?
c: The cyclohexadienyl anion is protonated at its central carbon, where charge density is greatest, and the 1,4-diene does not isomerize
The 1,3-diene forms first and then isomerizes to the 1,4-diene, which is the more stable product under these conditions
Ethanol protonates the radical anion at both ends of a conjugated system at once, which can only give a 1,4-diene
The 1,4-diene is the only product in which every carbon remains sp<sup>2</sup> hybridized, as in benzene
h: The product forms in the last, irreversible step. Which carbon of a pentadienyl anion carries the most negative charge?
w: Sequence: electron transfer gives a radical anion, ethanol protonates it, a second electron gives a cyclohexadienyl (pentadienyl) anion, and ethanol protonates again. A pentadienyl anion has its largest coefficient (charge density) at the central carbon (C3 of the five-carbon system), so protonation there gives the unconjugated 1,4-diene. The result is under kinetic control; the conjugated 1,3-diene would be more stable but is not formed (and would be reduced further if it were).
x: The 1,3-diene is more stable than the 1,4-diene, so a reaction under thermodynamic control would not favor the 1,4 isomer.
The two protons are added in separate steps, one to the radical anion and one to the later carbanion.
A cyclohexadiene has two sp<sup>3</sup> carbons whichever isomer forms; this is not what distinguishes 1,4 from 1,3.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: Which is easier to hydrogenate, an alkene or a benzene ring?
w: An alkene C=C is hydrogenated rapidly over Pd/C at room temperature and 1 atm, but the aromatic ring is not reduced under these mild conditions; its aromatic stabilization means ring hydrogenation needs high pressure, heat and an active catalyst (Rh, Pt or Ni). Product: propylbenzene.
x: Saturating the ring as well requires forcing conditions (for example high-pressure H<sub>2</sub> with Rh/C or Pt and heat), not 1 atm and 25 °C.
The ring is much harder to reduce than the alkene, so it cannot be reduced while the alkene survives.
A 1,4-cyclohexadiene is the product of a Birch reduction (Na/NH<sub>3</sub>), not catalytic hydrogenation.

q: Use the heats of hydrogenation in the table (each reduced to cyclohexane) to estimate the aromatic stabilization (resonance energy) of benzene, using cyclohexene as the model for an isolated C=C.
h: What would a hypothetical cyclohexatriene with three isolated C=C bonds release? Compare with what benzene actually releases.
w: Three isolated C=C bonds would release 3 × 120 = 360 kJ/mol. Benzene actually releases only 208 kJ/mol, so it is more stable than the localized model by 360 − 208 = 152, about 150 kJ/mol. This extra stabilization is why benzene resists hydrogenation and addition reactions.
x: 232 − 208 compares benzene with cyclohexadiene, which is not the model for three isolated double bonds.
208 kJ/mol is benzene's measured heat of hydrogenation, not the difference from the localized model.
232 − 120 compares the diene with the monoene (two C=C vs one); it says nothing about benzene's three C=C.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum below. Which structure fits?
h: Two 2H doublets in the aromatic region signal a particular substitution pattern. Then match the 3H singlets to their neighbors.
w: Two aromatic doublets of 2H each are the classic pattern of a para-disubstituted ring with two different groups. The doublet at 7.93 ppm belongs to the H ortho to the electron-withdrawing ester carbonyl. The singlet at 3.90 ppm (3H) is an OCH3 on an ester oxygen, and the singlet at 2.40 ppm (3H) is an aryl CH3. Structure: methyl 4-methylbenzoate.
x: A meta-disubstituted ring has four different aromatic H, which would give four aromatic signals (1H each), not two 2H doublets.
This para ester has two CH<sub>3</sub> singlets near 2.1–2.3 ppm (acetyl and aryl CH<sub>3</sub>); nothing would appear at 3.90 ppm.
Methyl phenylacetate has a monosubstituted ring (5 aromatic H) and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub> singlet; the spectrum shows 4 aromatic H and no 2H singlet.

q: Benzene protons appear at 7.3 ppm, while the vinyl protons of cyclohexene appear near 5.7 ppm. What is the main reason the aromatic protons are farther downfield?
c: The circulating π electrons of the ring create an induced field that reinforces the applied field at the ring's outer protons
The circulating π electrons of the ring create an induced field that opposes the applied field at the ring's outer protons
Aromatic C–H protons are acidic and partly ionized in the NMR solvent
Aromatic protons hydrogen-bond to the π cloud of neighboring benzene molecules
h: Think about the ring current in the applied magnetic field: which way do its field lines point outside the ring?
w: In a magnetic field, the delocalized π electrons of an aromatic ring circulate (a diatropic ring current). The induced field opposes B0 inside the ring but its field lines loop back parallel to B0 outside the ring, where the H atoms sit. These protons feel a larger effective field, so they are deshielded and resonate downfield, about 7–8 ppm.
x: An induced field that opposed B<sub>0</sub> at the outer protons would shield them and move them upfield; outside the ring the induced field adds to B<sub>0</sub>.
Benzene C–H bonds are not acidic (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 43); chemical shift does not come from ionization.
Weak intermolecular contacts do not explain a consistent shift of about 1.6 ppm; the ring current does.

q: At low temperature, [16]annulene shows its 4 inner protons near 10.5 ppm and its 12 outer protons near 5.4 ppm. Reduction with potassium gives the [16]annulene dianion. What <sup>1</sup>H NMR change is expected?
c: The inner protons move far upfield (below 0 ppm) and the outer ones downfield: the 18π dianion has an aromatic (diatropic) ring current
The inner protons move farther downfield and the outer protons farther upfield, because the dianion is a more strongly antiaromatic 18π system
Both sets of protons merge into one signal near 5.4 ppm, because the dianion puckers into a nonaromatic tub shape
The spectrum is unchanged, because the two added electrons go into σ orbitals and leave the π system alone
h: Count π electrons before and after. Then recall which way an aromatic ring current shifts inner and outer protons.
w: Neutral [16]annulene has 16 π electrons (4n); its paratropic ring current deshields the inner H (10.5 ppm) and shields the outer H (5.4 ppm), the reverse of the aromatic pattern. The dianion has 18 π electrons (4n + 2) and is aromatic, so its diatropic ring current strongly shields the inner protons (they appear well below 0 ppm) and deshields the outer ones.
x: 18 is a 4n + 2 count, so the dianion is aromatic, not antiaromatic; the neutral 16π ring is the antiaromatic one.
An 18π dianion gains aromatic stabilization by being planar and conjugated, so it does not become a nonaromatic tub, and its inner and outer protons stay distinct.
Electrons added by potassium go into the lowest empty π MO, so they change the π count and the ring current.

q: Which compound best fits this IR spectrum?
h: Look for evidence of sp<sup>2</sup> C–H, ring C=C stretches near 1600 and 1500, and check what is missing.
w: Weak absorption just above 3000 cm−1 (3030) is aromatic sp2 C–H stretch; the pair near 1605 and 1495 cm−1 is the aromatic ring C=C stretch; the strong bands near 730 and 690 cm−1 are C–H out-of-plane bends typical of a monosubstituted benzene; and 2920 is sp3 C–H. There is no O–H and no C=O band. Answer: toluene.
x: Methylcyclohexane has only sp<sup>3</sup> C–H (below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and no ring C=C bands near 1600 and 1500.
Benzyl alcohol would show a strong, broad O–H stretch near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which is absent.
Acetophenone would show a strong conjugated C=O stretch near 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which is absent.

q: Which C8H10 isomer gives only two sets of chemically equivalent hydrogens (two 1H NMR signals)?
h: Use the symmetry of each ring. How many different kinds of ring H does each isomer have?
w: In p-xylene the two CH3 groups are equivalent and all four ring H are equivalent (by its two perpendicular mirror planes), so it shows exactly two signals: 6H near 2.3 ppm and 4H near 7.0 ppm.
x: o-Xylene has two kinds of ring H (2H each) plus the CH3 groups: three sets.
m-Xylene has three kinds of ring H (1H, 1H, 2H) plus the CH3 groups: four sets.
Ethylbenzene has CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub> and three kinds of ring H (ortho, meta, para): five sets.

q: Which compound shows exactly two signals in its 13C NMR spectrum?
h: Find the symmetry elements of each ring and group the six ring carbons into equivalent sets.
w: In 1,4-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl carbons are equivalent and the four C–H carbons are equivalent, so there are exactly 2 carbon environments.
x: 1,2-Dichlorobenzene has three carbon environments: the two C–Cl, the two C–H next to them, and the remaining two C–H.
1,3-Dichlorobenzene has four environments: C–Cl (×2), C2 between the chlorines, C4/C6, and C5.
Chlorobenzene has four environments: the ipso carbon, two ortho, two meta and one para carbon.

q: Which sugar is shown in the Fischer projection?
h: The D/L label comes from one carbon only: the stereocenter farthest from C1. Then compare the whole pattern of –OH groups with the D-sugar you know best.
w: The highest-numbered stereocenter (C5) has its –OH on the left, so this is an L-sugar. Every stereocenter is the mirror image of D-glucose (right, left, right, right becomes left, right, left, left), so the compound is L-glucose, the enantiomer of D-glucose.
x: D-Idose has the same C2–C4 pattern as this drawing but its C5 –OH points right. It differs from the drawing at C5 only, so it is a diastereomer (C5 epimer), not this sugar.
D-Glucose has the C2, C4 and C5 –OH groups on the right. Every center here is inverted, so this is its enantiomer.
L-Mannose has its C2 –OH on the right (the mirror image of D-mannose, whose C2 –OH points left). Here the C2 –OH points left.

q: What are the CIP configurations of the four stereocenters of open-chain D-glucose (shown)?
h: At each center rank OH first and H last, then compare the carbon branches. In a Fischer projection H points toward you, so reverse the direction you read.
w: At every center OH ranks 1 and H ranks 4. The carbon toward C1 outranks the carbon toward C6 at C2 (CHO: O,O,H), C3 and C4 (O,C,H vs O,C,H, decided further out toward the aldehyde), and at C5 the C4 branch (O,C,H) beats CH2OH (O,H,H). So priority 2 is always the upward carbon. With H on a horizontal bond, a right-side OH traces 1→2→3 counterclockwise on paper, which reverses to R; a left-side OH gives S. Right, left, right, right gives (2R,3S,4R,5R) (confirmed with CIP software).
x: This is every center inverted, the descriptor set of L-glucose. It comes from forgetting that the H on a horizontal bond points toward you.
'Right side = R' is not a rule. C3 has its OH on the left, which makes it S here.
At C5 the C4 branch (O,C,H) outranks CH<sub>2</sub>OH (O,H,H). Ranking CH<sub>2</sub>OH higher flips the C5 label to S.

q: The Fischer projection shows D-galactose. Which Haworth projection is β-D-galactopyranose?
h: Right-side Fischer groups point down in the Haworth ring; left-side groups point up. For a D-sugar, β puts the anomeric –OH on the same face as CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
w: Fischer → Haworth: right → down, left → up. D-Galactose has C2 –OH right (down), C3 –OH left (up), C4 –OH left (up), and C5 bonded to the ring O with CH2OH up. β means the C1 –OH is cis to the C5 CH2OH, so it points up. Drawing II matches all five carbons.
x: I has the C4 –OH down: that is β-D-glucopyranose, the C4 epimer of galactose.
III has the C1 –OH down, trans to CH<sub>2</sub>OH: that is the α anomer.
IV has the C2 –OH up as well, which corresponds to a left-side C2 –OH in the Fischer projection (β-D-talopyranose, the C2 epimer).

q: At equilibrium in water, D-glucose is about 64% β-pyranose and 36% α-pyranose. What best explains why the β anomer is the major form?
c: In the <sup>4</sup>C<sub>1</sub> chair of the β anomer every ring substituent, including the C1 –OH, is equatorial
The anomeric effect stabilizes an equatorial –OH at C1, so it strongly favors the β anomer
The β anomer forms faster when the ring closes, and it cannot reopen once it has formed
Only the β anomer can hydrogen bond to its own ring oxygen, which holds it in the closed ring form
h: Put β-D-glucopyranose in the chair that has CH<sub>2</sub>OH equatorial. Where does every other group sit?
w: β-D-Glucopyranose is the one aldohexopyranose in which all five ring substituents (C1 –OH, C2 –OH, C3 –OH, C4 –OH and C5 CH2OH) can be equatorial at once. The α anomer has to place the C1 –OH axial, with 1,3-diaxial interactions. The all-equatorial chair is why β dominates. The anomeric effect actually works the other way: it favors an axial electronegative group at C1, which is why α is still 36% rather than a few percent.
x: Backwards: the anomeric effect stabilizes an axial C1 substituent (the α anomer in glucose), so it opposes the β preference.
Mutarotation shows the opposite: both anomers reopen to the aldehyde and re-close, so the ratio is an equilibrium (thermodynamic) value.
Both anomers have –OH groups that can hydrogen bond, and water competes for those bonds. It is not the factor that sets the ratio.

q: How are the two D-glucopyranoses shown related?
c: Anomers: diastereomers that differ only at C1
C2 epimers that differ only at C2
Conformers that interconvert by a chair flip
h: Compare the two drawings carbon by carbon. How many stereocenters differ, and which carbon is it?
w: The two rings match at C2, C3, C4 and C5 and differ only at C1, the hemiacetal carbon that became a new stereocenter when the ring closed. Stereoisomers that differ only at the anomeric carbon are anomers, a special case of diastereomers (α is I, β is II).
x: Enantiomers differ at every stereocenter. Here four of the five centers are the same.
The C2 –OH points down in both drawings. The difference is at C1.
A chair flip cannot change configuration. Converting α to β requires breaking the C1–O ring bond (mutarotation).

q: Freshly dissolved α-D-glucopyranose slowly changes its specific rotation from +112° to +52.7° as it converts partly to the β anomer. Through which species does the α → β conversion pass?
h: To change the configuration at C1 of a cyclic hemiacetal, which bond has to break, and what does C1 become when it does?
w: Mutarotation is ring opening and reclosing of the hemiacetal. Acid or base catalysis breaks the C1–O5 bond to give the open-chain aldehyde. The C5 –OH can then add to either face of the planar C=O, giving α or β. No other bond to a stereocenter is broken, so C2–C5 keep their configurations.
x: The 1,2-enediol forms in base by enolization (Lobry de Bruyn–van Ekenstein). It scrambles C2 (glucose ⇌ mannose ⇌ fructose), not just C1, and is not needed to switch anomers.
This is β-D-glucofuranose, a minor five-membered-ring form. It is itself reached only through the open-chain aldehyde, so it is not the link between the two pyranoses.
This is D-glucono-1,5-lactone, an oxidation product. Forming it would require an oxidizing agent; water alone cannot do it.

q: Pure methyl β-D-glucopyranoside (shown) is dissolved in neutral water. What happens to the specific rotation of the solution over time, and why?
c: It stays constant: C1 is an acetal, which does not open to an aldehyde in neutral water
It drifts to an equilibrium value: the ring opens and recloses to give some of the α anomer
It stays constant: the β anomer is already the most stable form, so no α forms
It drifts as water rapidly hydrolyzes the –OCH<sub>3</sub> group to give free glucose
h: Is C1 a hemiacetal or an acetal? What does each need in order to open the ring?
w: In a glycoside C1 carries two –OR groups (the ring O and OCH3): it is an acetal. A hemiacetal opens readily under mild acid or base catalysis, but an acetal is stable in neutral and basic water and is hydrolyzed only by aqueous acid. With no ring opening there is no α/β interconversion, so the rotation stays constant. Glycoside formation locks the anomer.
x: That is what a free sugar with a hemiacetal C1 does. Here C1 bears OCH<sub>3</sub>, not OH.
Stability is not the reason. Even pure β-glucose (a hemiacetal) mutarotates to a 64:36 β:α mixture. The glycoside cannot reach that equilibrium at all.
Acetals need an acid catalyst to hydrolyze. In neutral water a glycoside is kinetically stable.

q:
Which of these give a positive Tollens test (Ag+, NH3, H2O)?
I. methyl α-D-glucopyranoside
II. D-fructose
III. sucrose
IV. lactose
h: A reducing sugar has a hemiacetal (or hemiketal) carbon that can open to a free carbonyl. Remember that Tollens reagent is basic.
w: Lactose (IV) has a free hemiacetal on its glucose unit and is reducing. D-Fructose (II) is a ketose, but in the basic Tollens reagent it tautomerizes through an enediol to aldoses, so it is also reducing. Methyl glucoside (I) is an acetal, and sucrose (III) joins the anomeric carbons of glucose (C1) and fructose (C2), so neither has a hemiacetal. Answer: II and IV only.
x: Fructose is also oxidized: base-catalyzed enolization converts it to glucose and mannose, which reduce Ag<sup>+</sup>.
Sucrose is nonreducing. Its glycosidic bond uses both anomeric carbons, so neither ring can open.
Methyl α-D-glucopyranoside is an acetal at C1 and cannot open to an aldehyde.

q: Which D-aldohexose gives an optically inactive alditol when reduced with NaBH<sub>4</sub>?
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> turns CHO into CH<sub>2</sub>OH, so both ends become identical. Look for a horizontal mirror plane through the middle of the chain.
w: Reduction gives HOCH2–(CHOH)4–CH2OH. The product is meso if the top half mirrors the bottom half across a horizontal plane: C2 must match C5 and C3 must match C4. In III (D-galactose) C2 and C5 are both right and C3 and C4 are both left, so galactitol has an internal mirror plane and is meso (optically inactive).
x: I is D-glucose: C2 right / C5 right match, but C3 left / C4 right do not. D-Glucitol is chiral.
II is D-mannose: C2 left / C5 right do not match. D-Mannitol is chiral (it has a C2 axis, not a mirror plane).
IV is D-altrose: C2 left / C5 right do not match, so its alditol is chiral.

q: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduction of D-glucose (shown) gives D-glucitol. Reduction of which other aldohexose gives the identical alditol?
h: After reduction both ends are CH<sub>2</sub>OH. Turn the alditol 180° in the plane so C6 is on top, and read it as if C6 were the new aldehyde carbon.
w: Rotate D-glucitol 180° in the plane (allowed for a Fischer projection). Old C6 is now on top, and from the top the –OH groups read left, left, right, left (old C5, C4, C3, C2). Oxidizing the new top carbon to CHO gives an aldose whose last stereocenter has its –OH on the left: an L-sugar. Its mirror image (right, right, left, right) is D-gulose, so the sugar is L-gulose. D-Glucose and L-gulose differ only in which end is the aldehyde, so they give the same alditol (confirmed: identical SMILES).
x: D-Gulose gives D-gulitol, which is the enantiomer of D-glucitol (the mirror image of L-gulitol).
L-Glucose gives L-glucitol, the enantiomer of D-glucitol, not the same compound.
D-Mannose differs from glucose at C2, so D-mannitol is a diastereomer of D-glucitol.

q: Warm dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> oxidizes both ends of an aldose to COOH. Which two D-aldopentoses give optically inactive aldaric acids?
h: In HOOC–CHOH–CHOH–CHOH–COOH the two ends are identical. Is there a mirror plane through C3?
w: An aldaric acid from a pentose is meso when C2 and C4 match (C3 sits on the mirror plane). I (D-ribose: right, right, right) and III (D-xylose: right, left, right) both have C2 = C4, so ribaric and xylaric acids are meso and optically inactive.
x: II (D-arabinose) and IV (D-lyxose) have C2 on the left and C4 on the right, so their aldaric acids are chiral. In fact both give the same optically active aldaric acid.
II, D-arabinose, has C2 left and C4 right, so its aldaric acid is chiral.
IV, D-lyxose, has C2 left and C4 right, so its aldaric acid is chiral.

q: Which reagent oxidizes D-glucose to D-gluconic acid but leaves D-fructose unchanged, and so can tell the two sugars apart?
h: Ketoses are oxidized by the basic reagents only because base converts them to aldoses. Which oxidant works without base?
w: Bromine water is a mild oxidant used near neutral pH. It oxidizes the aldehyde of an aldose to a carboxylic acid (an aldonic acid) and does not touch ketoses, because without base a ketose cannot isomerize to an aldose. Tollens and Benedict's reagents are basic, so fructose enolizes to aldoses and also tests positive.
x: Tollens reagent is basic, so fructose isomerizes through an enediol to aldoses and also reduces Ag<sup>+</sup>.
Benedict's reagent is basic too, and fructose is a reducing sugar toward it.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent. It reduces both sugars (to alditols) rather than oxidizing either one.

q:
D-Aldopentose X has these properties:
• Kiliani–Fischer synthesis gives two aldohexoses. HNO3 converts one to an optically active aldaric acid and the other to a meso aldaric acid.
• Wohl degradation of X, then HNO3, gives an optically active tartaric acid.
What is X?
h: Kiliani–Fischer adds a new C2 (both configurations) above the old chain. Wohl removes C1, so old C3 and C4 become tetrose C2 and C3. Test each pentose.
w: Kiliani–Fischer products: D-ribose → D-allose + D-altrose; D-arabinose → D-glucose + D-mannose; D-xylose → D-gulose + D-idose; D-lyxose → D-galactose + D-talose. A meso aldaric acid comes from allose or galactose, so X is ribose or lyxose. Wohl degradation: ribose → D-erythrose → meso-tartaric acid (inactive); lyxose → D-threose → (−)-tartaric acid (active). Only D-lyxose fits both clues.
x: D-Ribose fits the first clue (allaric acid is meso) but its Wohl product, D-erythrose, gives meso-tartaric acid, which is optically inactive.
D-Arabinose gives glucose and mannose, and both glucaric and mannaric acids are optically active, so neither product gives a meso acid.
D-Xylose gives gulose and idose, whose aldaric acids are both optically active.

q: What is the product of a Wohl degradation (1. NH<sub>2</sub>OH 2. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O, NaOAc 3. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>) of D-galactose (shown)?
h: The Wohl degradation removes C1 (as HCN from the cyanohydrin-like intermediate). Old C2 becomes the new aldehyde carbon. Which stereocenters survive?
w: The Wohl sequence makes the oxime, dehydrates it to a nitrile, and then base reverses cyanohydrin formation, losing C1 as cyanide. Old C2 becomes the new CHO, so its stereocenter is destroyed. The surviving centers are old C3 (left), C4 (left) and C5 (right), which become C2, C3 and C4 of the pentose: left, left, right = D-lyxose.
x: D-Xylose (right, left, right) would require old C2 to keep its configuration as the new C2. Old C2 becomes the aldehyde carbon and loses its stereocenter.
D-Arabinose (left, right, right) does not match the left, left pattern of galactose C3 and C4.
D-Ribose has all –OH groups on the right. Galactose has its C3 and C4 –OH groups on the left, and those survive the degradation.

q: Which sugar is the C4 epimer of D-glucose?
h: Epimers are diastereomers that differ at exactly one stereocenter.
w: Inverting only C4 of D-glucose (C4 –OH from right to left) gives D-galactose. The other stereocenters, including C5, are unchanged, so it is still a D-sugar.
x: D-Mannose is the C2 epimer of D-glucose.
D-Allose is the C3 epimer of D-glucose (all four –OH groups on the right).
L-Glucose differs at all four stereocenters: it is the enantiomer, not an epimer.

q: What are the CIP configurations of the three stereocenters of open-chain D-fructose (shown)?
h: Rank OH first and H last at each center, then decide which carbon branch (up or down) wins. H is on a horizontal bond, toward you.
w: At C3 the C2 branch (C=O: O,O,C) beats C4 (O,C,H). At C4, C3 (O,C,H) ties C5 (O,C,H) at the first atoms, but further out C3 leads to the ketone carbon while C5 leads to CH2OH, so C3 wins. At C5, C4 (O,C,H) beats CH2OH (O,H,H). So the upward carbon is always priority 2. With H toward the viewer, a right-side OH gives R and a left-side OH gives S: left, right, right = (3S,4R,5R) (confirmed with CIP software).
x: This inverts every center: it is L-fructose. It comes from forgetting that the horizontal H points toward you.
C3 has its –OH on the left, which gives S, not R.
C4 has its –OH on the right; with the C3 branch outranking C5 that center is R.

q: β-D-Mannopyranose is shown. In its more stable chair (the <sup>4</sup>C<sub>1</sub> chair, with CH<sub>2</sub>OH equatorial), which ring substituent is axial?
c: None; all five substituents are equatorial
h: Start from β-D-glucopyranose, where every substituent is equatorial in this chair. How does mannose differ from glucose?
w: In the 4C1 chair β-D-glucopyranose has all substituents equatorial. D-Mannose is the C2 epimer of glucose, so inverting C2 moves only that –OH, from equatorial to axial. β-D-Mannopyranose therefore has the C2 –OH axial and everything else equatorial.
x: The C1 –OH is axial in α anomers. In β-mannose it is cis to CH<sub>2</sub>OH and equatorial, as in β-glucose.
The C4 –OH of mannose has the same configuration as in glucose (equatorial). An axial C4 –OH is the mark of galactose.
That is true only for β-D-glucopyranose. Mannose differs from glucose at C2, so one group must be axial.

q: Heating D-glucose in methanol with a little HCl converts only the C1 –OH into –OCH<sub>3</sub> (giving a mixture of methyl α- and β-glucosides). Why does only the anomeric –OH react?
c: Loss of water from C1 gives an oxocarbenium ion stabilized by the ring oxygen
The C1 –OH is the most acidic, so methoxide attacks C1 by S<sub>N</sub>2 and displaces it
The other –OH groups are protected by hydrogen bonds to the methanol solvent
C1 is the only primary carbon in the ring, so it reacts fastest with methanol
h: Under acid, which carbon can lose –OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> to give the most stabilized cation?
w: Acid protonates the anomeric –OH, and water leaves to give a cyclic oxocarbenium ion, in which the ring O lone pair forms a C=O+ π bond. No other ring carbon has an adjacent oxygen that can stabilize a cation, so only C1 ionizes (an SN1-like acetal formation). Methanol adds to either face of the planar ion, which is why both anomers form.
x: The conditions are acidic: there is no methoxide, and an S<sub>N</sub>2 at C1 would give only one anomer, not a mixture.
Hydrogen bonding to solvent does not protect an alcohol. The other OH groups are simply not ionized because their cations would not be stabilized.
C1 is a secondary carbon bonded to two oxygens. The only primary carbon is C6 (CH<sub>2</sub>OH), which does not react under these conditions.

q: A disaccharide made of two D-glucopyranose units is treated with excess CH3I and Ag2O, then hydrolyzed with aqueous acid. The products are 2,3,4,6-tetra-O-methyl-D-glucose and 2,3,4-tri-O-methyl-D-glucose. What is the glycosidic linkage?
h: Methylation caps every free –OH. Acid hydrolysis then cleaves only acetal bonds (the glycosidic bond and any methyl glycosides). Which –OH groups were not free before methylation?
w: After hydrolysis an unmethylated –OH marks an oxygen that was tied up in a ring or a glycosidic bond. The tetramethyl unit has free C1 and C5 only: it is the nonreducing end, joined through its C1 and closed through C5. The trimethyl unit has free C1 and C5 (ring and anomeric carbon) plus a free C6 –OH, so its C6 oxygen carried the glycosidic bond. The linkage is 1→6 (as in isomaltose or gentiobiose).
x: A 1→4 link would leave the second unit's C4 –OH unmethylated, giving 2,3,6-tri-O-methylglucose, not 2,3,4-.
A 1→1 link (as in trehalose) uses both anomeric carbons, so both units would come out as 2,3,4,6-tetramethyl glucose.
A 1→2 link would leave C2 free, giving 3,4,6-tri-O-methylglucose.

q: The disaccharide shown (lactose) is treated with Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O and then hydrolyzed with aqueous acid. What are the products?
h: Bromine water oxidizes only a free aldehyde, which comes from a hemiacetal. Which ring still has one?
w: The galactose unit is joined through its anomeric carbon (an acetal), so it cannot open. The glucose unit (right) has a free hemiacetal at C1, which opens to an aldehyde and is oxidized by Br2/H2O to a carboxylic acid (a lactobionic acid). Acid hydrolysis of the glycosidic bond then releases D-galactose and D-gluconic acid.
x: The galactose C1 is locked in the β(1→4) glycosidic acetal, so it is the unit that cannot be oxidized.
Only one anomeric carbon is free. The galactose C1 is protected as an acetal during the oxidation step.
Lactose is a reducing sugar: its glucose hemiacetal is oxidized before hydrolysis, so glucose comes out as gluconic acid.

q: Alanine has pKa values of 2.34 (α-COOH) and 9.70 (α-NH3+). What is its isoelectric point?
h: For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, the neutral zwitterion is the major form between the two pKa values.
w: The pI is the pH where the average charge is zero. The zwitterion exists between the two pKa values, and the pI is their average: (2.34 + 9.70)/2 = 6.02.
x: 3.68 is half the difference of the pKa values, not their average.
pH 7.00 is neutral water. An amino acid's pI depends on its own pKa values.
12.04 is the sum of the two pKa values; it still has to be divided by 2.

q: What is the isoelectric point of glutamic acid?
h: Write the charge of each form as the pH rises past each pKa. The pI is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the neutral form.
w: Charges: +1 (below 2.19) → 0 (2.19–4.25) → −1 (4.25–9.67) → −2. The neutral form is flanked by pKa 2.19 and 4.25, so pI = (2.19 + 4.25)/2 = 3.22. An acidic side chain pulls the pI well below 6.
x: 6.96 averages the two pKa values around the −1 form, not the neutral form.
Averaging all three pKa values has no physical meaning; only the two that border the zwitterion count.
5.93 averages the α-COOH and α-NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> values and ignores the side chain, which ionizes before the amino group.

q: What is the isoelectric point of histidine?
h: Is the imidazolium side chain positive or neutral when it holds its proton? Track the net charge from the fully protonated form.
w: Fully protonated histidine is +2 (NH3+ and imidazolium, COOH neutral). Charges: +2 → +1 after 1.82 (COO−) → 0 after 6.00 (neutral imidazole) → −1 after 9.17 (NH2). The neutral form lies between 6.00 and 9.17, so pI = (6.00 + 9.17)/2 = 7.59.
x: 3.91 treats the side chain like a carboxylic acid that becomes negative. Imidazolium goes from +1 to 0 when it loses its proton.
5.50 ignores the side chain. Histidine has an extra positive charge at low pH, which pushes the pI up.
Averaging all three pKa values is not how a pI is found.

q: Aspartic acid has pKa values of 1.88 (α-COOH), 3.65 (side-chain COOH) and 9.60 (α-NH3+). Which form is the major species at pH 3.0?
h: Compare pH with each pKa: a group is mostly deprotonated when pH > pKa and mostly protonated when pH < pKa.
w: At pH 3.0: the α-COOH (1.88) is above its pKa, so it is mostly COO−; the side-chain COOH (3.65) is below its pKa, so it is mostly COOH; the amine (9.60) is NH3+. The major species is the zwitterion with a neutral side-chain COOH.
x: Fully protonated (+1) aspartic acid is the major form only below pH 1.88.
The α-COOH (pKa 1.88) is more acidic than the side-chain COOH (3.65), because the nearby NH3+ withdraws electron density. It loses its proton first.
The −1 form, with both carboxylates, is major between pH 3.65 and 9.60.

q: What is the approximate net charge of the tripeptide Gly-His-Asp at pH 7.0?
h: Only the two termini and the side chains ionize; the amide N–H groups do not. Compare pH 7.0 with each pKa.
w: At pH 7.0: C-terminal COO− (−1); Asp side-chain COO− (−1); His is 1 unit above its pKa, so only about 9% is protonated (≈ 0); the N-terminal NH3+ is 1 unit below its pKa, so about 91% is protonated (≈ +1). Net ≈ −1.
x: This counts His as +1. At pH 7.0, one unit above its pKa, the imidazole is mostly neutral.
This counts His as +1 and misses the Asp side-chain carboxylate.
This forgets the N-terminal NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, which is still mostly protonated at pH 7.0.

q: L-Serine is (S) but L-cysteine is (R), although the two have the same spatial arrangement at the α carbon. What is the reason?
c: Sulfur outranks oxygen, so CH<sub>2</sub>SH outranks CO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>; in serine CH<sub>2</sub>OH ranks below it
L-Cysteine has its NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> on the opposite side of the Fischer projection from L-serine
The SH group is the lowest-priority group in cysteine, so the H moves to priority 3
D and L are defined by the CIP rules, so the two labels must agree for every amino acid
h: Rank the four groups at each α carbon. At the first point of difference, compare (O,O,O) for the carboxylate with (S,H,H) or (O,H,H) for the side chain.
w: Both have NH3+ = 1 and H = 4. In serine, CO2− (O,O,O) beats CH2OH (O,H,H). In cysteine, CH2SH has (S,H,H), and S (Z = 16) beats O (Z = 8) at the first point of difference, so the side chain outranks the carboxylate. Priorities 2 and 3 swap, so the same arrangement is labeled R.
x: Both are L amino acids: in the Fischer projection (COOH on top) the NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> is on the left for both. The spatial arrangement is the same.
H is always lowest priority. The SH is not even on the stereocenter; it is on the β carbon.
D/L describes the Fischer arrangement relative to glyceraldehyde; R/S comes from CIP priorities. The two systems are independent, which is exactly why they can disagree.

q: Which amino acid is shown in the Fischer projection?
h: With COOH on top and the side chain on the bottom, which side does the amino group of an L amino acid occupy?
w: With COOH on top, L amino acids have NH2 on the left; here it is on the right, so this is a D amino acid. CIP: NH2 > COOH > CH3 > H. NH2 (right) → COOH (top) → CH3 (bottom) runs counterclockwise, and H is on a horizontal bond toward the viewer, so the label reverses to R: D-alanine, (R).
x: L-Alanine has NH<sub>2</sub> on the left. This drawing is its mirror image.
The counterclockwise path must be reversed because the H points toward the viewer, which gives R.
L and R do not go together for alanine; natural L-alanine is S.

q: Natural L-threonine is (2S,3R)-2-amino-3-hydroxybutanoic acid. Which Fischer projection represents it?
h: Assign each center separately. At C3 rank OH > C2 (N,C,H) > CH<sub>3</sub> > H.
w: C2: an L amino acid has NH2 on the left (S). C3: OH > C2 > CH3; with OH on the right, OH → C2 (up) → CH3 (down) runs counterclockwise, reversed to R because H points toward the viewer. NH2 left and OH right is IV, (2S,3R) (confirmed with CIP software).
x: I is (2S,3S): L-allothreonine, the C3 epimer.
II is (2R,3S): D-threonine, the enantiomer of L-threonine.
III is (2R,3R): D-allothreonine.

q: Which carbonyl compound gives valine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)–COOH, in a Strecker synthesis (1. NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, KCN 2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat)?
h: The carbonyl carbon becomes the α carbon (it gains NH<sub>2</sub> and CN, and the CN becomes COOH). Work backward from the side chain.
w: In the Strecker synthesis the aldehyde forms an imine with NH3, cyanide adds to give an α-aminonitrile, and hydrolysis converts CN to COOH. The aldehyde carbon becomes the α carbon, and everything attached to it becomes the side chain. Valine's side chain is isopropyl, so the aldehyde is 2-methylpropanal. The product is racemic, because cyanide adds equally to both faces of the planar imine.
x: 3-Methylbutanal has one more CH<sub>2</sub>, so it gives leucine (isobutyl side chain).
Propanal gives 2-aminobutanoic acid, with an ethyl side chain.
Acetone is a ketone. It gives 2-amino-2-methylpropanoic acid, with two methyls on the α carbon.

q: In the chair, the α anomer of D-glucopyranose has its C1 –OH axial. Based on A-values alone it should be only a few percent of the equilibrium mixture, but it is about 36%. What extra stabilization does an axial electronegative group at C1 receive?
c: Donation of a ring-oxygen lone pair into the σ* orbital of the axial C1–O bond
Hydrogen bonding of the axial C1 –OH to the axial hydrogens on C3 and C5
Conjugation of the C1 –OH with the C2–C3 bond, which is possible only when it is axial
A lower steric demand for –OH than for H, so –OH prefers the axial position
h: This is the anomeric effect. Which orbitals are antiperiplanar when the C1–O bond is axial?
w: When the C1–O bond is axial, it is antiperiplanar to a lone pair on the ring oxygen. That filled n orbital overlaps with the empty σ*(C1–O) orbital (hyperconjugation), which stabilizes the axial anomer. Dipole repulsion between the ring C–O bonds is also smaller. This anomeric effect offsets part of the steric penalty, so α-glucose is 36% instead of a few percent.
x: Axial hydrogens on C3 and C5 are C–H bonds and are not hydrogen-bond acceptors. The axial –OH actually suffers 1,3-diaxial steric strain from them.
C2–C3 is a σ bond with no π system, so there is nothing to conjugate with.
–OH is larger than H (A-value about 0.9 kcal/mol in cyclohexane), so steric effects favor the equatorial position, not the axial one.

q: In peptide synthesis, what is the role of dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC, shown)?
c: It activates the carboxyl group as an O-acylisourea, a good acylating agent
It deprotonates the amine so it becomes a stronger nucleophile
It protects the N-terminal amine so it cannot react twice
It reduces the carboxylic acid to an aldehyde that then forms an imine with the amine
h: A carboxylic acid and an amine just form a salt. What does a coupling reagent do to the COOH?
w: The carboxylic acid adds across a C=N of DCC to give an O-acylisourea, in which the acyl group carries a good leaving group. The amine then attacks the acyl carbon (nucleophilic acyl substitution), forming the amide and releasing dicyclohexylurea (DCU). DCC is a dehydrating agent: the water lost in forming the amide ends up in DCU.
x: DCC is not a base. Without activation the acid and amine only form an ammonium carboxylate salt.
N-terminal protection is the job of Boc, Fmoc or Cbz groups, not DCC.
DCC is not a reducing agent, and peptide bonds are amides, not imines.

q: Which route gives the dipeptide Ala-Gly (shown) selectively?
c: Couple Boc-Ala with Gly-OCH<sub>3</sub> (DCC); then TFA; then NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O
Couple Ala-OCH<sub>3</sub> with Boc-Gly (DCC); then TFA; then NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O
Couple Boc-Ala with Boc-Gly (DCC); then TFA
Couple Ala with Gly (DCC) in one step; no protecting groups
h: Ala-Gly means alanine is the N-terminal residue: the Ala carboxyl must be the one activated, and the Gly amine the one that attacks.
w: In Ala-Gly the amide is made from the Ala COOH and the Gly NH2. So the Ala amine must be blocked (Boc) and its COOH left free for DCC activation, while the Gly carboxyl is blocked (methyl ester) and its amine left free. After coupling, TFA removes Boc and NaOH hydrolyzes the methyl ester, giving Ala-Gly only.
x: This activates the Gly carboxyl and lets the Ala amine attack, which gives Gly-Ala, the wrong sequence.
Both amines are blocked, so there is no nucleophile to attack the activated carboxyl. No peptide bond forms.
With both partners unprotected, either amine can attack either activated acid. The result is Ala-Ala, Ala-Gly, Gly-Ala, Gly-Gly and longer chains.

q: Fmoc-alanine is shown. Which reagent removes the Fmoc group while leaving Boc groups and tert-butyl esters intact?
h: Fmoc is the base-labile group. The fluorene C9–H is unusually acidic. Why?
w: Removing the C9–H of the fluorene gives an aromatic anion (a cyclopentadienyl-type 6π ring fused to two benzene rings). A mild amine base, piperidine, removes that proton, and the carbamate is eliminated (E1cB) to give dibenzofulvene, CO2 and the free amine. Boc and t-Bu esters are cleaved only by acid, so they survive. This orthogonality is the basis of Fmoc/t-Bu solid-phase synthesis.
x: TFA is the acid that removes Boc and t-Bu esters. It is the reagent that would destroy the groups we want to keep.
HF is an even stronger acid. It removes Boc, t-Bu and benzyl groups and cleaves peptides from Merrifield resin.
Hot aqueous acid cleaves Boc and t-Bu groups and also hydrolyzes amide (peptide) bonds.

q: The tripeptide Ala-Leu-Gly undergoes one cycle of Edman degradation (1. PhN=C=S, base 2. CF<sub>3</sub>COOH 3. aqueous acid). Which compound is identified by chromatography?
h: Phenyl isothiocyanate reacts with the free N-terminal amine. The released residue is converted to a stable five-membered heterocycle that still contains sulfur.
w: PhN=C=S adds to the N-terminal NH2 (Ala) to give a phenylthiourea. In acid, the thiourea sulfur attacks the neighboring amide C=O, cleaving off only the first residue as an anilinothiazolinone. Aqueous acid then rearranges it to the stable phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) of alanine, which is identified by HPLC. Leu-Gly remains for the next cycle.
x: This is PTH-glycine. Glycine is the C-terminal residue; Edman removes residues from the N-terminus.
This phenylthiocarbamoyl (PTC) amino acid is only a short-lived intermediate of the aqueous-acid step; it cyclizes to the PTH, which is the stable compound identified.
This is a phenylhydantoin (C=O instead of C=S). The sulfur from PhN=C=S is retained, so the product is a thiohydantoin.

q: A heptapeptide gives the data below. Trypsin cleaves on the C-terminal side of Lys and Arg; chymotrypsin cleaves on the C-terminal side of Phe, Tyr and Trp. What is the sequence?
h: Start with the N-terminal fragment and then use the overlapping fragments from the other enzyme to decide which piece comes next.
w: Gly is N-terminal, so the trypsin fragment Gly-Phe-Lys comes first. The chymotrypsin fragment Lys-Ala-Tyr shows Ala-Tyr follows Lys, so trypsin's Ala-Tyr-Arg is next. Arg-Leu (chymotrypsin) places Leu last, and the single Leu from trypsin confirms it is the C-terminus. Sequence: Gly-Phe-Lys-Ala-Tyr-Arg-Leu.
x: Trypsin would cut this after Lys to give a Leu-Ala-Tyr-Arg fragment, and chymotrypsin would give Lys-Leu-Ala-Tyr. Neither was observed.
Trypsin would give Gly-Phe-Arg and Ala-Tyr-Lys; the observed fragments have Lys third and Arg sixth.
Trypsin would release Arg as a single residue and give Leu-Ala-Tyr, not Ala-Tyr-Arg.

q: Before sequencing, a protein is treated first with HSCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (excess) and then with ICH<sub>2</sub>COOH. What does the iodoacetic acid step accomplish?
c: It alkylates the free Cys thiols by S<sub>N</sub>2, so the disulfides cannot re-form
It oxidizes the free thiols to sulfonic acids so they cannot be oxidized again
It cleaves the peptide chain on the C-terminal side of each Cys
It reduces the remaining disulfide bonds that the thiol did not break
h: 2-Mercaptoethanol has already reduced S–S to two –SH groups. What happens to those –SH groups if they are left alone in air?
w: 2-Mercaptoethanol reduces each disulfide (thiol–disulfide exchange) to two Cys–SH groups. Those thiols would be reoxidized by air to disulfides. A thiolate is an excellent nucleophile and displaces iodide from ICH2COOH in an SN2 reaction, giving stable Cys–S–CH2COOH (carboxymethylcysteine). Capping the thiols this way prevents the disulfides from re-forming.
x: Oxidation to sulfonic acids (cysteic acid) is done with performic acid. Iodoacetic acid is an alkylating agent, not an oxidant.
Iodoacetic acid does not cut peptide bonds; chain cleavage needs a protease or BrCN (at Met).
Iodoacetic acid cannot reduce S–S bonds. The reducing agent here is the excess 2-mercaptoethanol.

q: Rank these C<sub>18</sub> fatty acids from lowest to highest melting point.
h: Melting requires breaking London forces between packed chains. Which shape packs best: straight, slightly kinked, or sharply bent?
w: Stearic acid (I) is a fully extended saturated chain that packs tightly (mp about 70 °C). Elaidic acid (III, E) has a double bond, but the trans geometry keeps the chain nearly straight (mp about 45 °C). Oleic acid (II, Z) has a 30° kink that disrupts packing (mp about 13 °C). Lowest to highest: II < III < I.
x: The Z (cis) acid, not the E, has the kink that disrupts packing, so II melts lower than III.
This is the order reversed. Fewer contacts between kinked chains mean a lower melting point.
The trans acid cannot pack better than the saturated chain: a C=C still shortens and stiffens part of the chain, so I melts highest.

q: The triglyceride shown is heated with aqueous NaOH. What are the products?
c: Glycerol, 2 sodium palmitate and 1 sodium oleate
Glycerol, 2 palmitic acid and 1 oleic acid
Glycerol, 2 methyl palmitate and 1 methyl oleate
h: Saponification is base hydrolysis of all three esters. In what form does each fatty acid come out in excess NaOH?
w: Hydroxide attacks each ester C=O (nucleophilic acyl substitution). The carboxylic acid that forms is immediately deprotonated by the base, so the products are glycerol plus the sodium carboxylates: two sodium palmitate (C16, saturated, from C1 and C3) and one sodium oleate (C18, Z, from C2). The carboxylates are soaps.
x: Free fatty acids form only if the mixture is acidified afterward. In NaOH they are carboxylate salts.
The middle chain has 18 carbons and a Z C=C: it is oleate, not a third palmitate.
Methyl esters come from transesterification with CH<sub>3</sub>OH (biodiesel), not from aqueous NaOH.

q: Partial catalytic hydrogenation (H2, Ni) of a vegetable oil leaves some C=C bonds, and many of them are now E (trans) although every C=C in the oil was Z. What explains the isomerization?
c: Adding one H gives a surface-bound alkyl that can lose H again, re-forming the C=C as the more stable E isomer
H2 adds anti across the C=C, and the anti addition product then eliminates H2 to give the E alkene
The nickel catalyst oxidizes the C=C to an epoxide, which opens and recloses to give the E alkene
Heat alone rotates the C=C bond, because the π bond is weakened by the nearby ester group
h: Hydrogenation on a metal surface adds the two H atoms one at a time, and the steps are reversible.
w: On the metal surface the alkene adds one H to give a half-hydrogenated alkyl.
