If the second H does not arrive, the step can reverse: β-hydrogen loss can remove an H from either neighboring carbon, and the C–C single bond can rotate first. The re-formed alkene can therefore be the more stable E isomer or a positional isomer. This is the source of trans fats in partially hydrogenated oils.
x: Catalytic hydrogenation is a syn addition on the metal surface, and its alkane product cannot eliminate back to an alkene under these conditions.
H<sub>2</sub>/Ni is reducing; no epoxide forms.
Thermal cis/trans rotation of an isolated C=C needs breaking the π bond (about 65 kcal/mol), which does not happen at hydrogenation temperatures, and the ester is too far away to matter.

q: Farnesol (shown) is a terpene. How many isoprene units does it contain, and what class of terpene is it?
h: Count carbons. Each isoprene unit has 5, and a monoterpene (C<sub>10</sub>) has two.
w: Farnesol is C15H26O, so it contains 15/5 = 3 isoprene units joined head to tail. Terpene classes count C10 units: monoterpene C10, sesquiterpene C15 (1½ × C10), diterpene C20, triterpene C30. Farnesol is a sesquiterpene.
x: A monoterpene has 10 carbons (2 units), such as geraniol or limonene. Farnesol has 15.
A diterpene has 20 carbons, such as retinol or phytol.
'Tri' in triterpene counts C<sub>10</sub> units: three of them make C<sub>30</sub> (six isoprene units), such as squalene.

q: How many stereocenters does cholesterol (shown) have, and what is the maximum number of stereoisomers with this constitution?
h: Check every sp<sup>3</sup> ring-fusion carbon, including the two quaternary ones that carry methyl groups, and the side chain.
w: The stereocenters are C3 (OH), C8, C9, C14 (ring-fusion CH), C10 and C13 (quaternary ring-fusion carbons bearing the angular methyls), C17 (side-chain attachment) and C20 (in the side chain). That is 8, so the maximum is 28 = 256 stereoisomers (no meso forms are possible). Nature makes only one.
x: Six misses the two quaternary ring-fusion carbons, C10 and C13. A quaternary carbon is a stereocenter when its four groups differ.
Seven usually misses C20 in the side chain, which carries H, CH<sub>3</sub>, the ring and the C<sub>5</sub> chain.
2 × 8 = 16 confuses addition with powers. Each stereocenter doubles the count, so it is 2n.

q: In adenine (9H tautomer, shown), which tagged ring nitrogen(s) contribute their lone pair to the aromatic π system?
h: A ring N already in a ring double bond keeps its lone pair in the plane (pyridine-like). An N–H with only single ring bonds donates its lone pair (pyrrole-like).
w: Nb (N7) and Nc (N1) each sit in a ring C=N; their π electron is in the double bond, and their lone pairs are in sp2 orbitals in the ring plane, pointing out (pyridine-like, basic and H-bond acceptors). Na (N9–H) has only σ bonds in the ring, so its lone pair is in a p orbital and is part of the π system (pyrrole-like). With it the bicyclic purine has 10 π electrons (4n + 2, n = 2). Answer: a only.
x: Nb (N7) is pyridine-like: its lone pair is in the ring plane, which is why N7 accepts H bonds and gets alkylated.
Only the N–H nitrogen donates its pair. Counting Nb's lone pair too would give 12 π electrons.
Nc (N1) is also pyridine-like. In an A·T pair its in-plane lone pair accepts the H bond from thymine N3–H.

q: Which tautomer of thymine predominates in water and in DNA, where it pairs with adenine?
h: Compare amide (lactam) with imidic acid (lactim), the N analog of keto vs enol. Which is more stable for 2-pyridone-type rings?
w: Like simple amides and 2-pyridone, thymine strongly prefers the lactam (diketo) tautomer A, with two C=O groups and two N–H groups. The C=O bond and amide resonance make it far more stable than the lactim (enol-like) forms. In the A·T pair, thymine N3–H donates to adenine N1, and thymine C4=O accepts from adenine's 6-NH2. The rare enol tautomers change the donor/acceptor pattern and can cause mispairing (with G).
x: This 4-lactim has C4–OH and no N3–H. It is a rare tautomer whose donor/acceptor pattern pairs with guanine, a source of mutations.
This 2-lactim (C2–OH, no N1–H) is a minor tautomer; the lactam C=O is much more stable.
The dilactim has no amide C=O groups at all. Lactim (C=N–OH) forms are much less stable than lactams, so it is a very minor tautomer in water.

q: A Watson–Crick G·C base pair has three hydrogen bonds. In how many of them is guanine the H-bond donor (supplies the N–H)?
h: List the edge facing the partner for each base: guanine has O6, N1–H and the 2-NH<sub>2</sub>; cytosine has the 4-NH<sub>2</sub>, N3 and O2.
w: Guanine's Watson–Crick edge is C6=O (acceptor), N1–H (donor) and 2-NH2 (donor). Cytosine's edge is 4-NH2 (donor), N3 (acceptor, pyridine-like lone pair) and C2=O (acceptor). The pairs are G O6···H–N4 C, G N1–H···N3 C and G N2–H···O2 C. Guanine donates in two.
x: Only one H bond has cytosine as the donor (its 4-NH<sub>2</sub> to guanine O6); guanine donates in the other two.
Cytosine's 4-NH<sub>2</sub> donates to guanine O6, so guanine cannot be the donor in all three.
Guanine's N1–H and 2-NH<sub>2</sub> both point at cytosine acceptors (N3 and O2).

q: Dilute NaOH at room temperature cleaves RNA into nucleotides but leaves DNA intact. The two sugars are shown. What is the main reason?
c: The ribose 2'-O<sup>−</sup> attacks the adjacent phosphorus intramolecularly, forming a 2',3'-cyclic phosphate and breaking the chain
RNA is single-stranded, so hydroxide reaches its phosphates; the DNA double helix blocks them from attack
Uracil in RNA is a better leaving group than thymine, so the N-glycosidic bond breaks and the chain falls apart
Ribose is a pyranose in RNA, and its ring opens in base to give a reactive aldehyde that cleaves the chain
h: Compare the two sugars at C2. What nucleophile sits right next to the 3'-phosphodiester in RNA but not in DNA?
w: In RNA the 2'-OH is next to the 3'-phosphodiester. Base deprotonates it, and the 2'-alkoxide attacks phosphorus intramolecularly (a fast five-membered-ring cyclization), displacing the 5'-O of the next nucleotide. The 2',3'-cyclic phosphate then hydrolyzes to 2'- and 3'-phosphates. DNA lacks the 2'-OH, so it has no internal nucleophile, and intermolecular attack of hydroxide on a phosphodiester anion is extremely slow.
x: Single-stranded DNA is also stable in dilute base, so strandedness is not the reason; the internal nucleophile is.
Base hydrolysis cleaves phosphodiester bonds, not N-glycosidic bonds, and the bases do not act as leaving groups here.
Ribose in RNA is a furanose (five-membered ring), and its C1' is an N-glycoside that does not open in base.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Find the highest-priority group first. Between an aldehyde and a ketone, which one becomes the suffix, and which carbon must then be C1?
w: An aldehyde outranks a ketone, so the parent is a pentanal and the CHO carbon is C1. Counting from the CHO carbon, the ketone C=O is at C4 and is named as the prefix oxo: 4-oxopentanal.
x: This gives the ketone the suffix, but an aldehyde has higher priority than a ketone, so the suffix must be -al.
The aldehyde carbon is C1, so the ketone sits at C4, not C2. 2-Oxopentanal is a different compound (a 1,2-dicarbonyl).
A CHO is named as a 'formyl' prefix only when the aldehyde is not the principal group; here it is the principal group, and the chain also includes the CHO carbon.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Ketone vs. alcohol: which group earns the suffix? Then number to give that group the lowest locant.
w: A ketone outranks an alcohol, so the suffix is -one and the OH becomes the prefix hydroxy. Numbering so the C=O gets the lowest number puts it at C2 and the OH at C4: 4-hydroxypentan-2-one.
x: The principal group (the ketone) must get the lowest possible locant; numbering from the other end gives it 4 instead of 2.
An alcohol ranks below a ketone, so -ol cannot be the suffix while a ketone is present.
The compound has no aldehyde (no H on the carbonyl carbon), and an internal carbon cannot carry -al.

q: What is the complete name of the compound shown, including its configuration?
h: The carbonyl carbon is C1; go around the ring in the direction that reaches the methyl soonest. For CIP, compare the two ring branches atom by atom until they differ.
w: The ring carbonyl carbon is C1 and numbering toward the methyl gives it locant 3 (not 5). At C3 the priorities are: CH2 toward C=O (C2, whose next atom is the carbonyl C bearing O,O,C) > CH2 on the other side (C4) > CH3 > H. With the lowest-priority H pointing away from the viewer, 1 → 2 → 3 runs clockwise: (R)-3-methylcyclohexan-1-one.
x: This reverses the configuration: with the C2 branch ranked over C4 and the H in back, the path turns clockwise, which is R.
Numbering the other way gives locant 5 instead of 3; lowest locants are required.
Both the locant (5 instead of 3) and the descriptor are wrong.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: When a CHO group is attached to a ring, the ring cannot absorb the aldehyde carbon into its name. What suffix is used then?
w: The aldehyde is the principal group. Because the CHO carbon is outside the ring, the suffix is -carbaldehyde and the ring carbon bearing it is C1. The ring ketone is a prefix, oxo, at C4: 4-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde.
x: This makes the ketone the principal group, but an aldehyde outranks a ketone.
The -al suffix is used only when the CHO carbon is part of the parent chain; a CHO on a ring needs -carbaldehyde.
The ketone is not the principal group, and the locants are inverted as well.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The ketone gets the lowest locant, ahead of the C=C. Then compare the higher-priority group on each alkene carbon.
w: The ketone is the principal group, so C1 is the methyl and the C=O is C2; the C=C is C3–C4 with the phenyl on C4. On C3 the higher-priority group is the acyl carbon; on C4 it is the phenyl. They are on opposite sides: (E)-4-phenylbut-3-en-2-one.
x: The acyl group and the phenyl lie on opposite sides of the C=C, which is E, not Z.
Numbering must give the principal group (the ketone) the lowest locant, so the ketone is at 2, not 3.
There is no aldehyde: the carbonyl carbon carries a methyl, not an H.

q: Rank these carbonyl compounds from most to least reactive toward nucleophilic addition.
h: Two effects: alkyl groups donate electron density to the carbonyl carbon, and they crowd the tetrahedral product. Count and size the groups.
w: Each alkyl group lowers the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon (donation) and raises steric strain in the sp3 addition product. Formaldehyde (two H) is most reactive, then acetaldehyde (one alkyl), then acetone (two methyls), and pinacolone (methyl + bulky tert-butyl) is least: I > III > II > IV.
x: Formaldehyde has no alkyl groups at all, so it is more electrophilic and less hindered than acetaldehyde.
Acetone has two alkyl groups and acetaldehyde only one, so aldehydes rank above ketones.
A tert-butyl group crowds the tetrahedral product far more than a methyl, so pinacolone is less reactive than acetone, not more.

q: Which compound has the largest equilibrium constant for hydrate (gem-diol) formation in water?
h: What does an electron-withdrawing group next to the C=O do to the stability of the carbonyl compared with the hydrate?
w: Three chlorines pull electron density from the carbonyl carbon by induction, destabilizing the C=O and favoring the sp3 hydrate. Chloral (Cl3CCHO) exists almost entirely as the stable hydrate in water.
x: Acetaldehyde is roughly half hydrated in water, far less than chloral, because a methyl donates rather than withdraws electrons.
Acetone is a ketone with two donating methyls; its hydrate is only a tiny fraction at equilibrium.
Benzaldehyde's C=O is stabilized by conjugation with the ring, which disfavors hydrate formation.

q: Rank these compounds from largest to smallest equilibrium constant for cyanohydrin formation with HCN.
h: Addition destroys the conjugation between the C=O and the ring. Which para substituent makes the carbonyl carbon most electron-poor, and which donates into it? Where do ketones fall?
w: A para-nitro group withdraws electron density by resonance and induction, raising the carbonyl's electrophilicity (I largest). A para-methoxy group donates by resonance, stabilizing the C=O and lowering K (III below II). Acetophenone is a ketone: an extra methyl donates and crowds the adduct, so its K is far smaller than any of the aldehydes: I > II > III > IV.
x: This reverses the substituent effects: OCH<sub>3</sub> donates electron density into the C=O, making it less electrophilic, while NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws.
Even a donor-substituted benzaldehyde has a much larger K than a ketone; the extra alkyl group of acetophenone lowers K sharply.
An electron-withdrawing nitro group increases, not decreases, K relative to benzaldehyde.

q:
Consider these statements about the hydration of chloral, Cl3CCHO.
I. The CCl3 group withdraws electron density inductively and destabilizes the C=O.
II. In water, chloral lies mostly on the hydrate side, whereas acetone lies mostly on the carbonyl side.
III. The CCl3 group donates electrons to the carbonyl carbon by resonance, which stabilizes the hydrate.
Which statements are correct?
h: Can an sp<sup>3</sup> CCl<sub>3</sub> carbon take part in resonance with the C=O at all?
w: Statement I is the reason chloral hydrates so well: the inductive pull of three Cl atoms makes the C=O less stable relative to the gem-diol. Statement II is a true comparison (chloral is almost fully hydrated; acetone is <0.2% hydrated). Statement III is false: the sp3 CCl3 carbon has no π system to donate through, and donation would stabilize the carbonyl, not the hydrate. I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true: chloral is essentially all hydrate in water, while acetone is almost all ketone.
Statement III is false; CCl<sub>3</sub> acts only inductively (withdrawing), and it is not a resonance donor.
Statement III is false, so not all three can be correct.

q: Acetone is dissolved in H<sub>2</sub><sup>18</sup>O with a trace of acid. After some time, the acetone is recovered. Where is the <sup>18</sup>O label?
c: In the carbonyl oxygen of the recovered acetone
Nowhere; the hydrate equilibrium lies so far toward acetone that no exchange occurs
Only in the hydrate, which cannot lose water to re-form acetone
On the methyl carbons, by acid-catalyzed enolization
h: Hydrate formation is reversible. When the gem-diol loses water, which of its two OH groups can leave?
w: Even a small, fast hydrate equilibrium exchanges oxygen. Acetone + H218O ⇌ (CH3)2C(OH)(18OH); the gem-diol can lose either OH as water, so half the time it returns to acetone with 18O in the carbonyl. Repeated cycles enrich the label.
x: A small equilibrium constant does not stop exchange; the hydrate forms and reverts quickly, and that is all exchange requires.
Hydrate formation is reversible; the gem-diol readily loses water to re-form the C=O.
Enolization exchanges α-hydrogens, not oxygen; oxygen never moves onto a carbon.

q: Cyanohydrins are usually made from an aldehyde with NaCN (or KCN) and a controlled amount of acid, rather than with pure HCN. Why?
c: HCN is a weak acid, so free CN<sup>−</sup> (the real nucleophile) is needed; the acid then protonates the alkoxide
Pure HCN protonates the carbonyl oxygen so strongly that the aldehyde polymerizes instead of adding cyanide
CN<sup>−</sup> is a poor nucleophile, so the acid must first convert it into the more nucleophilic HCN
Acid is needed afterward to dehydrate the cyanohydrin to an α,β-unsaturated nitrile
h: Which species actually attacks the carbonyl carbon, and how much of it is present in pure HCN (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 9)?
w: The nucleophile is cyanide ion, and HCN (pKa ≈ 9.2) is barely ionized on its own, so the reaction with pure HCN is very slow. Supplying CN− from NaCN gives a good nucleophile; the alkoxide formed then takes a proton from HCN or the added acid, regenerating CN−. CN− is the nucleophile, and acid protonates the alkoxide.
x: HCN is too weak an acid to protonate a carbonyl significantly; the problem is the lack of cyanide ion, not polymerization.
This is backwards: the anion CN<sup>−</sup> is the nucleophile, while neutral HCN is a far weaker one.
Cyanohydrins are the desired products and are not dehydrated under these mild conditions.

q: Butan-2-one is treated with NaCN and HCl (aq). Which statement best describes the product?
c: Only (R)-2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile, because CN− attacks from the less hindered face
An achiral cyanohydrin, because the carbonyl carbon carries two alkyl groups
A meso cyanohydrin with two stereocenters
h: Is the new sp<sup>3</sup> carbon a stereocenter? Are the two faces of the planar C=O in butan-2-one different in any way that a cyanide ion could detect?
w: Addition creates C2 bearing OH, CN, CH3 and CH2CH3: a new stereocenter. The two faces of the planar C=O are enantiotopic, so with an achiral nucleophile and no chiral catalyst each face is attacked equally: a racemic mixture of 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile.
x: Methyl and ethyl do not make one face of the C=O more hindered in a way an achiral reagent can tell apart; the faces are mirror images, so both enantiomers form equally.
The new carbon carries four different groups (OH, CN, CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), so it is a stereocenter and the product is chiral.
Only one stereocenter forms, so a meso compound is impossible.

q: What is the final product of this sequence?
h: Step 1 adds CN and OH to the same carbon. What does LiAlH<sub>4</sub> do to a nitrile, and does it touch an alcohol?
w: Step 1 forms the cyanohydrin 1-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carbonitrile. LiAlH4 reduces the C≡N to CH2NH2 and leaves the tertiary OH in place: 1-(aminomethyl)cyclohexan-1-ol, a β-amino alcohol.
x: This is the product of nitrile hydrolysis (H3O+, heat), not reduction with LiAlH4.
The OH and CN were both on the ring carbon; reduction converts CN into CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, so the NH<sub>2</sub> ends up one carbon away, with the OH still on the ring.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not remove a tertiary OH; the alcohol survives.

q: Which species is an intermediate in the base-catalyzed (OH−) hydration of acetone?
h: Under base, the strong nucleophile attacks first. What does hydroxide add to, and what is formed directly?
w: In base, hydroxide attacks the neutral carbonyl carbon directly, giving the tetrahedral alkoxide (CH3)2C(OH)O−, which is then protonated by water to give the hydrate and regenerate OH−.
x: The protonated carbonyl is the activated electrophile in the acid-catalyzed path; there is no strong acid in basic solution.
A protonated gem-diol (oxonium) is an acid-catalyzed intermediate, not one formed in hydroxide solution.
The enol forms by tautomerization, a different process; it is not on the path to the hydrate.

q: Cyclohexanone gives a high yield of cyanohydrin with HCN/CN<sup>−</sup>, but 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexanone gives almost none. What is the best explanation?
c: The three α-methyl groups crowd the tetrahedral adduct, so the reversible equilibrium favors the ketone
The methyl groups make the ketone so acidic that CN<sup>−</sup> deprotonates it at the α-carbon instead of adding to C=O
The trimethyl ketone has no α-hydrogens left, so it cannot form a cyanohydrin by any path
The methyl groups withdraw electron density, making the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic
h: Cyanohydrin formation is reversible. What happens to steric strain when the carbonyl carbon goes from sp<sup>2</sup> (120°) to sp<sup>3</sup> (109.5°)?
w: Cyanohydrin formation is an equilibrium. On going from sp2 to sp3, the new OH and CN groups are pressed against the three neighboring α-methyl groups; that strain makes the adduct much less stable, so the equilibrium lies toward the hindered ketone.
x: α-Methyl groups do not make the ketone notably more acidic, and cyanide is too weak a base to enolize it significantly.
C6 still bears one α-hydrogen, and cyanohydrin formation does not need α-hydrogens anyway (benzaldehyde has none).
Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating; their electronic effect is small here compared with the steric strain.

q: What is the main organic product of this reaction (water removed with a Dean–Stark trap)?
h: A diol supplies both oxygens needed for the full acetal. Removing water drives the reaction past the hemiacetal stage.
w: Acid-catalyzed reaction of a ketone with ethylene glycol, with water removed, gives the cyclic acetal (a 1,3-dioxolane): 1,4-dioxaspiro[4.5]decane. The ring carbon becomes the spiro carbon bonded to both glycol oxygens.
x: The hemiacetal is an intermediate; with acid and water removal it closes onto the second OH to give the cyclic acetal.
An enol ether is not the product; the oxocarbenium ion is trapped by the second OH of the diol, not deprotonated.
This 1,3-dioxane would require propane-1,3-diol; ethylene glycol has only two carbons between its oxygens.

q: Which sequence converts the keto ester into the hydroxy ketone shown?
c: 1. HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, TsOH  2. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, then H<sub>2</sub>O  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: The ester must be reduced while the more reactive ketone is left untouched. Which reagent reduces esters, and how do you hide the ketone from it?
w: LiAlH4 is needed to reduce an ester, but it would also reduce the ketone. Protect the ketone first as an ethylene glycol acetal (stable to strong base and hydride), reduce the ester to CH2OH with LiAlH4, then remove the acetal with aqueous acid: 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH 2. LiAlH4 3. H3O+.
x: Without protection LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces both the ester and the ketone, giving a diol.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone, the very group that must survive, and leaves the ester essentially untouched.
After protection, NaBH<sub>4</sub> is too weak to reduce the ester at a useful rate, so the starting keto ester is recovered after deprotection.

q: Which sequence converts 4-bromobenzaldehyde into the hydroxy aldehyde shown?
c: 1. HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, TsOH  2. Mg, THF  3. CH<sub>3</sub>CHO  4. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, TsOH  2. Mg, THF  3. CH<sub>3</sub>CHO  4. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, TsOH  2. Mg, THF  3. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH  4. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: A Grignard reagent and an aldehyde cannot coexist in the same molecule. What must be done before Mg, and what must the last step accomplish?
w: The CHO must be masked before the Grignard reagent is formed, or the ArMgBr would attack another molecule's aldehyde. Make the ethylene glycol acetal, form the Grignard, add it to acetaldehyde (new C–C bond, secondary alkoxide), then aqueous acid both protonates the alkoxide and removes the acetal: 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH 2. Mg 3. CH3CHO 4. H3O+.
x: Without protection the aryl Grignard reacts with the unprotected aldehyde of other molecules, giving oligomers instead of a clean product.
Acetals are stable to base, so NaOH/H<sub>2</sub>O leaves the CHO protected; the aldehyde is never released.
Ethanol is an acid toward a Grignard reagent; it simply protonates ArMgBr (giving the protected benzaldehyde) and forms no C–C bond.

q: A ketone was protected as its ethylene glycol acetal. Under which condition is the acetal cleaved back to the ketone?
c: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in ether, then aqueous workup at pH 7
h: Acetal hydrolysis needs a leaving group to depart from the acetal carbon. Under which conditions can an alkoxy group become a good leaving group?
w: An acetal's oxygens must be protonated before they can leave, forming an oxocarbenium ion that water then attacks. That requires acid: dilute aqueous HCl (H3O+) regenerates the ketone and the diol. This is why acetals protect carbonyls only under neutral and basic conditions.
x: Acetals are stable to hydroxide; RO<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group and nothing protonates it in base.
Hydrides do not attack acetals; this is exactly why acetals are used to protect ketones during LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reductions.
Grignard reagents do not attack acetals; acetals are a standard protecting group in Grignard chemistry.

q: 5-Hydroxypentanal exists in solution mainly as a cyclic hemiacetal. Which structure is that hemiacetal?
h: The OH oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon. Count the ring atoms: the carbons from C1 through C5 plus that oxygen.
w: The C5 oxygen attacks C1. The ring contains C1–C5 (five carbons) plus the oxygen: a six-membered ring. The former carbonyl carbon now carries OH and is bonded to the ring O: tetrahydropyran-2-ol (oxan-2-ol).
x: This five-membered ring has only four carbons; 5-hydroxypentanal has five, so one carbon has been lost.
This seven-membered ring has six carbons, one more than the starting material.
This is a lactone (an ester), an oxidation product; hemiacetal formation is not an oxidation, and the anomeric carbon keeps its H.

q: Which hydroxy aldehyde exists in solution predominantly as an intramolecular (cyclic) hemiacetal?
h: Work out the ring size for each (ring = the carbons from C1 to the OH carbon, plus O). Which ring sizes form easily and without strain?
w: Intramolecular hemiacetals are favored only when the ring is five- or six-membered: low strain and a favorable entropy of ring closure. 5-Hydroxypentanal closes to a six-membered ring, so 5-hydroxypentanal is mainly cyclic.
x: Ring closure would give a strained four-membered ring (oxetane), so the open chain dominates.
Ring closure would give a three-membered ring (an epoxide-like ring), which is far too strained.
Ring closure would give a nine-membered ring; medium rings are strained and entropically unfavorable, so the open-chain form dominates.

q: Acetaldehyde reacts with excess methanol and a catalytic amount of H2SO4 to give 1,1-dimethoxyethane. Which species does not appear as an intermediate in this mechanism?
h: In acidic methanol, would a free alkoxide (a strong base) survive long enough to be an intermediate?
w: Acid-catalyzed acetal formation runs: protonate C=O → methanol adds → hemiacetal → protonate the OH and lose water → oxocarbenium ion → second methanol adds → deprotonate. Every intermediate is neutral or cationic. The tetrahedral alkoxide CH3CH(OCH3)O− belongs to a base-catalyzed pathway and does not form in acid.
x: The protonated carbonyl is the first intermediate: acid activates the weakly electrophilic C=O toward weakly nucleophilic methanol.
The hemiacetal is the neutral intermediate formed after the first methanol adds and loses a proton.
The resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion forms when the protonated hemiacetal loses water; it is attacked by the second methanol.

q: A hemiacetal forms when an aldehyde is mixed with methanol and a little NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, but no acetal forms however long the mixture stands. Why?
c: Making the acetal requires OH to leave, and in base it cannot be protonated to leave as water
Methoxide is too weak a nucleophile to add to an aldehyde, even with heating
Acetals form in base but are immediately hydrolyzed back to the hemiacetal by the methoxide
In base the hemiacetal is fully deprotonated and reverts entirely to the aldehyde, so none is present
h: Compare the two halves of acetal formation. The first is an addition; what kind of step does the second half need?
w: The second half of acetal formation is a substitution at the hemiacetal carbon: the OH must leave to form an oxocarbenium ion. Hydroxide is a poor leaving group; only acid can convert it into H2O. In base, the OH cannot be protonated to leave, so the reaction stops at the hemiacetal.
x: Methoxide is a strong nucleophile and adds readily to aldehydes; that is why the hemiacetal does form.
Acetals are stable to base; methoxide does not hydrolyze them.
The stem says the hemiacetal does form; base catalyzes its formation and reversal, but it is still present at equilibrium.

q: What is the main organic product of this reaction?
h: A primary amine has two N–H bonds. After the water is lost, which hydrogen is removed to give the neutral product?
w: A primary amine adds to the C=O (carbinolamine), the protonated OH leaves as water, and the resulting iminium ion loses its N–H proton to give the imine, N-methylcyclohexanimine. Primary amines give imines (C=N).
x: An enamine forms when the amine is secondary and the iminium ion has no N–H to lose; a primary amine gives the more stable imine.
The carbinolamine is the tetrahedral intermediate; under these acidic, dehydrating conditions it loses water.
This amine would require a reducing agent (reductive amination, e.g. NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN); no reductant is present.

q: What is the main organic product of this reaction?
h: Pyrrolidine is a secondary amine. After loss of water, the iminium nitrogen carries no H. Where must a proton be lost from instead?
w: Pyrrolidine adds to the C=O, water is lost, and the iminium ion that results has no N–H. A proton is removed from the α-carbon instead, giving the neutral enamine, 1-(cyclohex-1-en-1-yl)pyrrolidine.
x: The iminium ion is an intermediate; it is a cation and loses an α-proton to give the neutral enamine.
The carbinolamine is the tetrahedral intermediate; with acid and water removal it dehydrates and does not accumulate.
This saturated amine is a reductive-amination product; no reducing agent is present.

q: The rate of imine formation from a ketone and a primary amine is greatest near pH 4–5 and drops at both lower and higher pH. Which explanation is correct?
c: Below pH ≈ 4 most amine is protonated and non-nucleophilic; above pH ≈ 6 the carbinolamine OH is not protonated, so water cannot leave
Below pH ≈ 4 the ketone is fully protonated and cannot react with the amine; above pH ≈ 6 the imine is hydrolyzed back
Below pH ≈ 4 the carbinolamine cannot form because water is a better nucleophile; above pH ≈ 6 the amine is deprotonated to an amide ion
Acid is needed only to protonate the C=O in the first step; the pH maximum reflects how fast the ketone is protonated
h: Acid helps one step and hurts another. Which species must stay unprotonated, and which group must be protonated?
w: Two opposing needs: the amine must be a free base to attack the C=O, but the carbinolamine OH must be protonated to leave as water (usually the slow step near neutral pH). Too acidic: the amine is tied up as R–NH3+. Too basic: dehydration of the carbinolamine is too slow. The compromise is pH ≈ 4–5.
x: Ketones are very weak bases (pK<sub>a</sub> of the protonated form ≈ −7); at pH 3 almost none is protonated, so that is not what slows the reaction.
Amines are not deprotonated to amide ions (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 35) at pH 6–7; the problem at higher pH is the slow loss of OH from the carbinolamine.
The key acid-dependent step is protonating the carbinolamine OH so water can leave, not protonating the C=O.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is heated with pyrrolidine and catalytic TsOH, with water removed. Which enamine is the major product?
h: The N lone pair must overlap with the C=C, so the nitrogen's ring CH<sub>2</sub> groups lie in the alkene plane. What would they bump into on the more substituted side?
w: For the nitrogen lone pair to conjugate with the C=C, the pyrrolidine ring must lie in the alkene plane. In the tetrasubstituted enamine, the pyrrolidine CH2 groups clash with the methyl on the adjacent alkene carbon (A1,3 strain). Forming the C=C toward the unsubstituted C6 avoids this, so the less substituted enamine (double bond away from the methyl) is major, unlike Zaitsev alkenes.
x: This tetrasubstituted enamine suffers severe A<sup>1,3</sup> strain between the methyl and the planar pyrrolidine, so it is the minor isomer despite the more substituted C=C.
The iminium ion is an intermediate; it loses an α-proton to give the neutral enamine.
An exocyclic C=C would require deprotonating the methyl, and the nitrogen would no longer be attached to an alkene carbon, so this is not an enamine.

q: The imine shown is stirred in dilute aqueous HCl. Which pair of compounds forms (the amine as its ammonium salt)?
h: Hydrolysis reverses imine formation: the C=N carbon becomes the C=O carbon, and the nitrogen keeps every group attached to it.
w: Water adds to the protonated C=N carbon and the amine is expelled, the reverse of imine formation. The imine carbon bears CH3 and phenyl, so it becomes acetophenone; the nitrogen bears a benzyl group, so it leaves as benzylamine (as PhCH2NH3+ in acid).
x: This splits the molecule on the wrong side of N; benzaldehyde + 1-phenylethanamine would give PhCH=N–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)Ph, a different imine.
The nitrogen bears a CH<sub>2</sub>Ph (benzyl) group, not a phenyl group bonded directly to N.
Only the C=N bond is hydrolyzed; the C–N single bond to the benzyl group is not cleaved.

q: 5-Aminopentan-2-one cannot be isolated as such; it spontaneously cyclizes with loss of water. What is the product?
h: The NH<sub>2</sub> nitrogen attacks the ketone carbon. Count the ring atoms from N to the carbonyl carbon, then decide what a primary amine gives after water is lost.
w: The amine nitrogen attacks C2; the ring contains N, C5, C4, C3 and C2: five atoms. Loss of water from the cyclic carbinolamine gives a C=N within the ring: 5-methyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-pyrrole (2-methyl-1-pyrroline), a cyclic imine.
x: This six-membered ring contains one carbon too many; N, C5, C4, C3 and C2 close a five-membered ring.
The cyclic carbinolamine is the intermediate; the stem says water is lost, giving the C=N.
This saturated pyrrolidine is a reduction product; forming it would require a hydride source such as NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN.

q: Which compound is a hemiketal (the hemiacetal of a ketone)?
h: Look for one carbon bonded to both an OH and an OR, and check whether that carbon also has a hydrogen.
w: A hemiketal carbon carries one OH, one OR and two carbon groups (no H). In 2-methyloxan-2-ol, C2 bears OH, the ring O, CH3 and a ring CH2: a cyclic hemiketal.
x: C2 carries two OR groups (OCH<sub>3</sub> and the ring O) and an H: that is an acetal of an aldehyde, not a hemiketal.
C2 carries two OR groups and no OH: a ketal (full acetal), not a hemiketal.
The OH and the ring oxygen are on different carbons, so this is simply an ether and a primary alcohol.

q: Which reagent(s) best convert the ketone C=O into a CH<sub>2</sub> group while leaving the acetal intact?
h: Both classic C=O → CH<sub>2</sub> reductions work on this ketone. Which survives the other functional group: strongly acidic or strongly basic conditions?
w: Acetals are stable to base but hydrolyze in aqueous acid. The Wolff–Kishner reduction runs in hot KOH, so it reduces the ketone to CH2 and leaves the acetal alone: H2NNH2, KOH, heat.
x: The Clemmensen reduction uses hot concentrated HCl, which would hydrolyze the acetal to an aldehyde (and reduce it too).
NaBH<sub>4</sub> stops at the alcohol (C=O → CH–OH); it does not remove the oxygen.
H<sub>2</sub>/Pd does not reduce an ordinary aliphatic ketone to CH<sub>2</sub>; at most it slowly gives the alcohol.

q: Which sequence gives propylbenzene from benzene in good yield?
h: Friedel–Crafts alkylation with a primary halide goes through a cation-like species. What happens to a primary carbocation? How does an acylium ion avoid that?
w: Direct alkylation with 1-chloropropane rearranges (hydride shift) to give mainly isopropylbenzene. Acylation with propanoyl chloride gives propiophenone through a resonance-stabilized acylium ion that does not rearrange, and Clemmensen reduction converts the C=O to CH2: 1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3 2. Zn(Hg), HCl.
x: The primary carbocation-like species rearranges to the 2° isopropyl cation, so cumene (isopropylbenzene) is the main product, and polyalkylation also occurs.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone only to the alcohol, 1-phenylpropan-1-ol, not to CH<sub>2</sub>.
Acetyl chloride adds only two carbons; Wolff–Kishner then gives ethylbenzene, not propylbenzene.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: These are Wolff–Kishner conditions. The hydrazone is only an intermediate at 200 °C; what gas is lost?
w: The Wolff–Kishner reduction forms a hydrazone, which in hot base loses N2 and is protonated by the solvent, converting C=O into CH2: propylbenzene.
x: Wolff–Kishner removes the oxygen completely; an alcohol would come from a hydride reagent such as NaBH<sub>4</sub>.
The hydrazone forms first, but at 200 °C in KOH it loses N<sub>2</sub>; it is not the final product.
No alkene forms; the carbanion left after N<sub>2</sub> loss is simply protonated by the solvent.

q: In the Wolff–Kishner reduction of acetophenone, which species forms immediately after N2 is lost?
h: The reaction runs in hot KOH. When the diazene anion R–N=N<sup>−</sup> fragments, which atom keeps the bonding pair from the C–N bond?
w: Base deprotonates the hydrazone N–H, the diazene forms, and a second deprotonation gives R–N=N−. That anion expels N2 and leaves the electron pair on carbon: the benzylic carbanion PhCH−CH3, which is protonated by the solvent to give ethylbenzene. Loss of very stable N2 drives the step.
x: A carbocation would require the carbon to lose the bonding electrons; in a basic medium the electrons stay on carbon, giving a carbanion.
Styrene is not formed; the carbanion is simply protonated by the solvent.
An azine is a side product from hydrazone + ketone condensation; it is not formed by loss of N<sub>2</sub>.

q: What is the product of this Wittig reaction?
h: A Wittig reaction swaps the carbonyl oxygen for the ylide carbon. The new C=C is exactly where the C=O was.
w: The ylide carbon (CHCH3) bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and Ph3P=O is lost. The C=C forms exactly where the C=O was, outside the ring: ethylidenecyclohexane.
x: Wittig reactions do not move the double bond to the more substituted position; that thinking applies to E1/E2 eliminations.
This puts the C=C between the two ylide-derived atoms; the new double bond must join the former carbonyl carbon to the ylide carbon.
An alcohol would come from a Grignard reagent (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr); the Wittig reaction removes the oxygen as Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O.

q: A student wants to make 1-phenylprop-1-ene (PhCH=CHCH3) by a Wittig reaction using benzaldehyde as the carbonyl partner. How should the ylide be prepared?
h: Split the C=C: the benzaldehyde provides PhCH=. What must the ylide carbon carry, and which reagent removes the proton from the phosphonium salt?
w: Disconnect PhCH=CHCH3 at the C=C: benzaldehyde supplies PhCH=, so the ylide must be Ph3P=CHCH3. Make it by SN2 of Ph3P on bromoethane (phosphonium salt), then deprotonate the carbon α to phosphorus with a strong base: 1. Ph3P + CH3CH2Br 2. BuLi.
x: Bromomethane gives Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub>, which converts benzaldehyde into styrene (PhCH=CH<sub>2</sub>), one carbon short.
1-Bromopropane gives Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and hence PhCH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, one carbon too many.
Water cannot deprotonate the phosphonium salt (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 22 or higher); a strong base such as BuLi is needed to form the ylide.

q: Which alkyl halide is the poorest choice for preparing a phosphonium salt (and then a Wittig ylide) with triphenylphosphine?
h: Ph<sub>3</sub>P reacts with the alkyl halide by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which substrate cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2?
w: Phosphonium salts form by SN2 attack of Ph3P on the alkyl halide. A tertiary halide is too hindered for SN2 (and would give no α-H on the P-bearing carbon to make an ylide anyway): 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is the poorest choice.
x: Methyl halides are the best S<sub>N</sub>2 substrates; CH<sub>3</sub>Br gives the widely used Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub>.
A primary halide reacts well with Ph<sub>3</sub>P by S<sub>N</sub>2.
Benzylic halides are excellent S<sub>N</sub>2 substrates and give stabilized benzylic ylides.

q: Which route gives methylenecyclohexane as the major product?
h: Elimination reactions favor the more substituted alkene. Which method fixes the position of the C=C regardless of stability?
w: The Wittig reaction places the C=C exactly where the C=O was, so cyclohexanone + Ph3P=CH2 gives the exocyclic, less substituted alkene: methylenecyclohexane. Every elimination route gives mainly the more stable trisubstituted 1-methylcyclohexene.
x: Acid-catalyzed E1 dehydration gives the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene, as the major product.
The Grignard step gives 1-methylcyclohexanol, whose dehydration again gives mainly the Zaitsev product, 1-methylcyclohexene.
Ethoxide is a small base, so E2 gives mainly the Zaitsev alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene; a bulky base would be needed even to favor the exocyclic isomer.

q: What is the main product of this reaction?
h: Hard, highly reactive organolithium and Grignard reagents add fastest to the most electrophilic atom, the carbonyl carbon. Which reagent class is used for 1,4-addition?
w: Organolithium reagents add directly (1,2-addition) to the carbonyl carbon of an α,β-unsaturated ketone. Workup gives the tertiary allylic alcohol 1-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol. Conjugate (1,4) addition would require a cuprate such as (CH3)2CuLi.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexanone is the 1,4-addition product expected from (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CuLi, not from CH<sub>3</sub>Li.
CH<sub>3</sub>Li does not reduce the C=C; this saturated alcohol has two more H atoms than any addition product.
No oxidation or substitution of a vinyl H occurs; the methyl adds and the C=O becomes an alcohol.

q: 4-tert-Butylcyclohexanone is reduced with NaBH4 in methanol. Which statement best describes the product?
c: Mainly trans-4-tert-butylcyclohexanol (OH equatorial), from axial attack of the small hydride
Mainly cis-4-tert-butylcyclohexanol (OH axial), from equatorial attack of the small hydride reagent
A racemic mixture, because hydride attacks the two faces of the planar C=O equally
Equal amounts of cis and trans alcohols, because the tert-butyl group is far from the C=O
h: The tert-butyl group locks the chair. A small nucleophile like BH4− prefers the approach that avoids torsional strain with the neighboring C–H bonds. Then ask: is either product chiral?
w: The tert-butyl group is locked equatorial. Small hydride donors attack mainly from the axial direction (equatorial approach would develop torsional strain with the neighboring C2 and C6 C–H bonds), which pushes the oxygen equatorial. Equatorial OH and equatorial tert-butyl at C1/C4 are trans: mainly trans-4-tert-butylcyclohexanol (about 90:10). Bulky hydrides (L-Selectride) reverse this.
x: Equatorial attack (giving the axial-OH cis isomer) is preferred by bulky hydrides such as L-Selectride, not by small NaBH4.
Both cis and trans products have a mirror plane through C1 and C4, so they are achiral; the two faces of this C=O are not mirror images but are diastereotopic.
The locked chair makes the two faces different (axial vs equatorial approach), so the two diastereomers form in unequal amounts.

q: Enantiopure (R)-2-phenylpropanal is treated with CH3MgBr, then aqueous NH4Cl. Which statement best describes the product mixture?
c: Two diastereomers of 3-phenylbutan-2-ol, formed in unequal amounts
Two diastereomers of 3-phenylbutan-2-ol, formed in exactly equal amounts
h: The existing stereocenter is untouched. Are the two faces of this C=O enantiotopic or diastereotopic?
w: The new stereocenter (C2) forms next to an existing one (C3, which keeps its R configuration). Attack on the two faces of the C=O gives (2R,3R) and (2S,3R) products, which are diastereomers. Because the adjacent stereocenter makes the faces diastereotopic, the transition states differ in energy (Felkin–Anh/Cram selectivity): two diastereomers in unequal amounts.
x: The C3 stereocenter is not touched, so every product molecule is 3R; a racemic mixture would require the 3S enantiomers too.
The two stereocenters carry different groups (OH/CH<sub>3</sub> vs Ph/CH<sub>3</sub>), so no internal mirror plane is possible; the compound cannot be meso.
The faces are diastereotopic, so the competing transition states are diastereomeric and differ in energy; exactly equal amounts would be a coincidence.

q: Which combination, followed by aqueous acid workup, gives 2-phenylbutan-2-ol?
h: Find the carbinol carbon in the target and list its three carbon groups. One must come from the Grignard reagent; the other two must already be on the carbonyl carbon.
w: The carbinol carbon of the target carries phenyl, methyl and ethyl. Ethyl Grignard adding to acetophenone (PhCOCH3) supplies exactly those three groups: CH3CH2MgBr + acetophenone.
x: An aldehyde gives a secondary alcohol: this pair gives 1-phenylbutan-1-ol, not a tertiary alcohol.
In 1-phenylpropan-2-one the phenyl is on CH<sub>2</sub>, not on the carbonyl carbon; the product is 2-methyl-1-phenylpropan-2-ol.
Benzaldehyde gives a secondary alcohol, 1-phenylpropan-1-ol.

q: 4-Hydroxybutan-2-one is treated with one equivalent of CH3MgBr, then aqueous NH4Cl. What is recovered mainly?
h: Before it can add to the C=O, the Grignard reagent meets a far faster reaction partner in the same molecule.
w: A Grignard reagent is a strong base (pKa of CH4 ≈ 50), and the alcohol O–H (pKa ≈ 16) is protonated much faster than the C=O is attacked. The single equivalent is consumed making CH4 and the magnesium alkoxide; workup returns mostly unreacted hydroxy ketone. Using a second equivalent, or protecting the OH, would allow addition.
x: This diol would form only if enough Grignard reagent were present to deprotonate the OH and add to the C=O (at least 2 equivalents).
Grignard reagents do not methylate oxygen; the methyl group ends up as CH<sub>4</sub>, not as an ether.
Grignard reagents are not hydride donors here; butane-1,3-diol would require NaBH<sub>4</sub> or LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.

q: What is the main product when the keto ester is treated with NaBH<sub>4</sub> in methanol at 0 °C, followed by water?
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a mild hydride donor. Which carbonyl in this molecule is the more electrophilic?
w: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones readily but esters only very slowly, because the ester C=O is stabilized by resonance donation from the OR oxygen. The ketone is reduced and the ester survives: methyl 4-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carboxylate (as a cis/trans mixture).
x: Reducing the ester as well requires LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; NaBH<sub>4</sub> leaves esters essentially untouched at 0 °C.
This reverses the chemoselectivity: the ketone is more electrophilic than the ester and is the group NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces.
A hemiacetal-like reduced ester is not a product of NaBH<sub>4</sub>; the ester is not attacked at all.

q: Acetophenone is reduced with NaBD<sub>4</sub> in ether, and the mixture is then worked up with ordinary H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the product?
h: Track each hydrogen: one is delivered by the borohydride, the other by the workup. Which one goes to carbon?
w: The borodeuteride delivers D− to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide; H2O then supplies the proton on oxygen. The product is PhCD(OH)CH3 (racemic, since D attacks either face).
x: The deuteride goes to the electrophilic carbon, not the oxygen; the O–H proton comes from the water workup.
The workup is ordinary H<sub>2</sub>O, so the oxygen picks up H, not D.
Hydride (deuteride) attacks the carbonyl carbon, not the methyl carbon; the methyl is not electrophilic.

q: What is the product of this Baeyer–Villiger oxidation?
h: An oxygen is inserted between the carbonyl carbon and one of its groups. Which group migrates better: phenyl or methyl?
w: In the Baeyer–Villiger oxidation, the group with the higher migratory aptitude moves from carbon to oxygen. Phenyl migrates far better than methyl, so the O is inserted between the C=O and the ring: phenyl acetate.
x: Methyl benzoate would require the methyl group to migrate, but methyl has the lowest migratory aptitude.
Peroxy acids do not hydroxylate the ring of a ketone; the reaction inserts O next to the carbonyl carbon.
The Baeyer–Villiger reaction gives an ester; no C–C bond to methyl is lost to form benzoic acid.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: The ring grows by one atom (an O). Of the two ring carbons attached to the C=O, which is more substituted and therefore migrates?
w: Baeyer–Villiger oxidation inserts O on the side of the better migrating group. The secondary ring carbon (bearing the methyl) migrates in preference to the primary CH2, so the O ends up next to CH(CH3): the seven-membered lactone 7-methyloxepan-2-one.
x: This lactone results from migration of the CH<sub>2</sub> (primary) carbon; the more substituted secondary carbon migrates preferentially.
α-Hydroxylation is not what a peroxy acid does to a ketone; the oxygen is inserted into a C–C bond next to the C=O.
This six-membered lactone has a different carbon skeleton (an ethyl side chain); Baeyer–Villiger only inserts O and does not rearrange the carbons.

q: 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one (pinacolone) is treated with a peroxy acid. Which ester is the major product?
h: Migratory aptitude: 3° alkyl > 2° alkyl ≈ aryl > 1° alkyl > methyl. Which group moves from C to O?
w: In the Criegee intermediate, the group best able to stabilize partial positive charge migrates. A tert-butyl (3°) group migrates far better than methyl, so O is inserted between the C=O and the tert-butyl group: tert-butyl acetate.
x: Methyl pivalate would require the methyl to migrate, but methyl has the lowest migratory aptitude.
This carboxylic acid would need the carbon skeleton to rearrange; Baeyer–Villiger only inserts an O next to the C=O and gives an ester.
Baeyer–Villiger inserts only an O; it does not insert a CH<sub>2</sub> group between the carbonyl and the alkyl group.

q: Enantiopure (S)-3-phenylbutan-2-one is oxidized with mCPBA. What is the major product?
h: Decide which group migrates (secondary benzylic vs methyl). Then: the migrating carbon moves with its bonding electrons, never becoming a free ion. What does that mean for its configuration?
w: The secondary (benzylic) carbon migrates in preference to methyl, so O is inserted between the C=O and the stereocenter, giving 1-phenylethyl acetate. The migration is concerted and intramolecular, so the migrating carbon keeps its configuration (retention). The product is (S)-1-phenylethyl acetate; here the descriptor stays S because the priority order (O-substituent > Ph > CH3 > H) parallels the original order.
x: Baeyer–Villiger migration occurs with retention of configuration, not inversion, so the enantiomer does not form.
Methyl ester formation would require the methyl group to migrate; the secondary benzylic carbon migrates far better.
This combines the wrong migrating group (methyl) with an unexplained change of configuration.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: Ozonolysis cuts the ring C=C. Each alkene carbon becomes a C=O; with a reductive workup, a carbon that carried an H becomes an aldehyde.
w: Ozone cleaves the C=C, and dimethyl sulfide is a reductive workup. The methyl-bearing alkene carbon becomes a ketone and the CH alkene carbon becomes an aldehyde, giving one open-chain molecule: 6-oxoheptanal.
x: An oxidative workup (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) would convert the aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S is reductive, so the CHO survives.
The methyl carbon is not lost; the alkene carbon that carries it becomes a methyl ketone.
Ozonolysis breaks the C=C completely; no ring survives and no ketone forms on the ring.

q: Which reagent converts hexan-1-ol into hexanal without significant over-oxidation to hexanoic acid?
h: Over-oxidation of an aldehyde goes through its hydrate. Which reagent works in the absence of water?
w: Aldehydes are over-oxidized via their hydrates, which need water. PCC in anhydrous CH2Cl2 stops at the aldehyde because no hydrate can form.
x: Aqueous chromic acid (Jones-type conditions) oxidizes the aldehyde's hydrate further, giving the carboxylic acid.
Hot basic KMnO<sub>4</sub> is a strong aqueous oxidant that gives the carboxylic acid (as its salt).
NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent; it does not oxidize alcohols.

q: Which alkyne gives a single ketone when treated with HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O?
h: An internal alkyne can place the oxygen on either alkyne carbon. When do both choices lead to the same compound?
w: Hydration of an internal alkyne gives an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone; with an unsymmetrical internal alkyne the oxygen can go to either sp carbon, giving two ketones. Hex-3-yne is symmetrical, so both pathways give the same product, hexan-3-one.
x: Hex-2-yne is unsymmetrical; hydration gives a mixture of hexan-2-one and hexan-3-one.
4-Methylpent-2-yne is unsymmetrical; it gives a mixture of 4-methylpentan-2-one and 2-methylpentan-3-one.
Pent-2-yne is unsymmetrical (methyl vs ethyl); it gives both pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one.

q: What is the product of this sequence?
h: The Grignard reagent adds once to the C≡N. What is the charge on the intermediate, and why can't a second equivalent add? What does aqueous acid do to the imine?
w: The Grignard reagent adds once to the nitrile carbon, giving an imine anion (N−MgBr+). This negatively charged species does not react with a second equivalent. Aqueous acid protonates it and hydrolyzes the imine to a ketone: propiophenone (1-phenylpropan-1-one).
x: Double addition happens with esters, not nitriles: the imine anion is not electrophilic enough to accept a second Grignard.
No reducing agent is present; acid hydrolyzes the C=N to C=O rather than reducing it to an amine.
Nitrile hydrolysis to the acid needs hot aqueous acid or base; here the Grignard first forms a new C–C bond.

q: Anisole is treated with one equivalent of acetyl chloride and AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: OCH<sub>3</sub> is an o,p-director; which of those positions is less hindered? Then consider what the new acyl group does to the ring's reactivity.
w: The methoxy group activates the ring and directs ortho/para; the bulky acylium–AlCl3 electrophile prefers the less hindered para position. The acyl group then deactivates the ring, so a second acylation does not occur: 4-methoxyacetophenone.
x: OCH<sub>3</sub> donates by resonance to the ortho and para positions, not meta, so the meta isomer is minor.
The first acyl group is strongly deactivating (and complexes AlCl<sub>3</sub>), so polyacylation does not occur, unlike Friedel–Crafts alkylation.
Friedel–Crafts acylation leaves a C=O; converting it to CH<sub>2</sub> would need a separate Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner step.

q:
Consider these statements about nucleophilic addition to aldehydes and ketones.
I. Under basic conditions, a strong nucleophile adds to the neutral C=O, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.
II. Under acidic conditions, the carbonyl oxygen is protonated first, making the carbon a better electrophile for weak nucleophiles such as water or alcohols.
III. Under acidic conditions, the tetrahedral intermediate is an alkoxide ion that is later protonated.
Which statements are correct?
h: Ask what each pathway's tetrahedral intermediate looks like. Could a strongly basic alkoxide accumulate in acidic solution?
w: Statement I describes base conditions (OH−, CN−, RO− attack the C=O directly and give an alkoxide). Statement II describes acid catalysis: protonation activates the C=O for weak, neutral nucleophiles. Statement III is false: in acid the nucleophile adds to the protonated carbonyl, so the tetrahedral intermediate is neutral or protonated (an oxonium ion), never an alkoxide. I and II only.
x: Statement II is also correct: acid catalysis works by protonating the carbonyl oxygen.
Statement III is false: an alkoxide would be immediately protonated in acid; the acid-pathway intermediates are neutral or cationic.
Statement III is false, so not all three statements can be correct.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown (key bands labeled by wavenumber)?
h: Look just to the right of the sp<sup>3</sup> C–H stretches. Which C–H bond gives a pair of weak bands near 2820 and 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>?
w: A strong C=O near 1730 cm−1 plus the two weak aldehyde C–H stretches at about 2820 and 2720 cm−1 (a Fermi doublet) identify an aliphatic aldehyde: butanal. There is no O–H band and no strong C–O band near 1200 cm−1.
x: A ketone has a C=O band (≈1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>) but no aldehyde C–H bands near 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
An ester shows a C=O near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> but also a strong C–O stretch near 1200 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and it has no 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup> band.
An alcohol would show a strong, broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no C=O band.

q: Which compound shows its C=O stretch at the lowest wavenumber (≈1685 cm−1)?
h: Two effects shift a C=O stretch: conjugation (more single-bond character) and ring strain (in small rings). Which way does each move the band?
w: Conjugation with a C=C delocalizes the π electrons and gives the C=O partial single-bond character, lowering its stretching frequency by about 30 cm−1. Ring strain raises it (cyclohexanone ≈1715, cyclopentanone ≈1745, cyclobutanone ≈1780 cm−1). Cyclohex-2-en-1-one absorbs lowest, near 1685 cm−1.
x: Cyclohexanone is an unstrained, unconjugated ketone; its C=O stretch is near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Ring strain in the five-membered ring raises the C=O stretch to about 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
The strained four-membered ring raises the C=O stretch to about 1780 cm<sup>−1</sup>, the highest of these.

q: A compound C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O shows a strong IR band at 1725 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum below. What is it?
h: The 9.8 ppm signal is diagnostic. Its splitting and the splitting of the 2H signal tell you what is attached to the CHO carbon.
w: The 1H signal at 9.82 ppm is an aldehyde H; it is a triplet, so the CHO is attached to a CH2. That CH2 (2.31 ppm, α to C=O) is a doublet, coupled only to the CHO H, so its other neighbor has no H: a quaternary carbon bearing three equivalent methyls (9H singlet). 3,3-Dimethylbutanal.
x: Pinacolone is a ketone: it has no 9–10 ppm signal and shows a 3H singlet near 2.1 ppm instead.
Here the CHO is attached to a quaternary carbon, so its signal would be a singlet, and there would be an ethyl group (a triplet and a quartet).
This methyl ketone has no aldehyde H and would show an isopropyl doublet (6H), not a 9H singlet.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives a strong IR band at 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> (no band near 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum below. What is it?
h: DBE = 5; a 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> C=O suggests conjugation. Any aldehyde H? How many aromatic H? What does the 3H singlet near 2.6 ppm sit next to?
w: C8H8O has 5 degrees of unsaturation (ring + 3 C=C + C=O). The conjugated C=O (1685 cm−1), no aldehyde H (no 9–10 ppm signal, no 2720 cm−1 band), five aromatic H in a monosubstituted pattern (2:1:2) and a 3H singlet at 2.60 ppm (CH3 next to C=O) fit acetophenone.
x: Phenylacetaldehyde would show an aldehyde H near 9.7 ppm (t) and a CH<sub>2</sub> doublet near 3.7 ppm, and its C=O is not conjugated (≈1725 cm<sup>−1</sup>).
4-Methylbenzaldehyde would show a CHO singlet near 9.9 ppm, two 2H doublets (para pattern), and a CH<sub>3</sub> near 2.4 ppm.
An epoxide has no C=O, so it cannot account for the 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> band, and it would show three 1H ring signals near 2.8–3.9 ppm.

q: Which species appears in the acid-catalyzed formation of a hemiacetal from acetaldehyde and methanol, but not in the base-catalyzed (CH3O−) formation?
h: In acid, what happens to the aldehyde before the weak nucleophile attacks? Then check whether each other species is on either pathway at all.
w: In acid, the C=O is protonated first, giving the resonance-stabilized protonated aldehyde CH3CH=OH+, which neutral methanol then attacks. In base, methoxide attacks the neutral C=O directly, so no protonated carbonyl forms.
x: This tetrahedral alkoxide is the base-pathway intermediate (methoxide adds to the neutral C=O); it does not form in acid.
The hemiacetal is the product of both pathways, so it appears in both.
The oxocarbenium ion forms only when the hemiacetal goes on to an acetal (loss of water in acid); it is not on the path to the hemiacetal itself.

q: Each C5H8 diene below is hydrogenated to pentane with 2 equiv H2/Pt. Which one releases the least heat (smallest |ΔH°hydrog|)?
h: All four give the same product, so the least heat comes from the most stable starting diene. Think conjugation first, then sterics.
w: Because every isomer ends at pentane, the most stable diene has the smallest heat of hydrogenation. Conjugated dienes are stabilized by π overlap across the central C2–C3 bond (and a stronger sp2–sp2 σ bond), and the E isomer avoids the steric clash of the Z isomer. So (E)-1,3-pentadiene releases the least heat (about −226 kJ/mol, versus about −254 kJ/mol for 1,4-pentadiene and nearly −300 kJ/mol for the allene).
x: 1,4-Pentadiene has two isolated C=C bonds with no delocalization, so it releases more heat than a conjugated isomer.
1,2-Pentadiene is a cumulated diene (allene); its sp central carbon makes it the least stable isomer, so it releases the most heat.
(Z)-1,3-Pentadiene is conjugated, but its methyl crowds the C3 hydrogen, so it is slightly less stable than the E isomer and releases a little more heat.

q: Use the heats of hydrogenation in the table to estimate the extra stabilization (delocalization energy) of 1,3-butadiene relative to a hypothetical diene with two isolated monosubstituted C=C bonds.
h: Two isolated C=C bonds would each release about the same heat as one 1-butene. Compare that sum with the measured value.
w: Two isolated monosubstituted C=C bonds would release about 2 × (−127) = −254 kJ/mol. Butadiene releases only −237 kJ/mol, so it starts 254 − 237 = about 17 kJ/mol lower in energy (more stable). That difference is the conjugation (delocalization) energy.
x: Less heat released means the diene started lower in energy, so it is more stable, not less.
110 kJ/mol is the difference between butadiene and a single 1-butene (237 − 127), which compares one C=C with two.
127 kJ/mol is just the heat of hydrogenation of one C=C; it is not a stabilization energy.

q:
Which statements about cumulated dienes (allenes) are correct?
I. The central carbon of an allene is sp hybridized.
II. The two π bonds of an allene lie in perpendicular planes.
III. 2,3-Pentadiene (CH3CH=C=CHCH3) is chiral even though it has no stereocenter.
IV. Among C5H8 diene isomers, allenes have the smallest heats of hydrogenation.
h: Picture the central carbon using one p orbital for each π bond. What does that do to the planes of the two end groups?
w: The central allene carbon forms two π bonds with two different p orbitals, so it is sp (I true) and the two π bonds are perpendicular (II true). That puts the H/CH3 pair on one end in a plane perpendicular to the pair on the other end, so CH3CH=C=CHCH3 has no mirror plane and is chiral (axial chirality, III true). Allenes are the least stable dienes and have the largest heats of hydrogenation, so IV is false. Answer: I, II and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: the perpendicular end groups make 2,3-pentadiene a chiral molecule with a chiral axis.
Statement II is omitted and IV is false: allenes release the most heat on hydrogenation, not the least.
Statement I is true and IV is false; cumulated dienes are less stable than both isolated and conjugated dienes.

q: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with 1 equiv of HBr at −80 °C. Which is the major product?
h: Protonate a terminal carbon to make an allylic cation. At low temperature the product that forms fastest wins.
w: H+ adds to C1, giving an allylic cation with positive character on C2 and C4. At −80 °C the addition is irreversible, so the product that forms fastest dominates: bromide attacks C2, which is right next to it in the ion pair and carries more of the positive charge (secondary). The kinetic 1,2-product 3-bromo-1-butene is major.
x: 1-Bromo-2-butene is the 1,4-product; it is more stable but forms more slowly, so it is major only when the reaction can equilibrate at higher temperature.
4-Bromo-1-butene would need protonation at C2 to give a primary, non-allylic cation (or a radical anti-Markovnikov path); neither happens here.
2-Bromo-1-butene has Br on an sp<sup>2</sup> (vinylic) carbon; capture of the allylic cation always puts Br on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.

q: The same HBr addition to 1,3-butadiene is run at 40 °C and allowed to reach equilibrium. Which statement best describes the outcome?
c: Mostly 1-bromo-2-butene, because the products interconvert and it has the more substituted C=C
Mostly 3-bromo-1-butene, because attack at C2 has the lower activation energy and is faster
Mostly 1-bromo-2-butene, because attack at C4 has the lower activation energy and is faster
About 1:1, because both products come from the same allylic cation and Br<sup>−</sup> attacks either end equally
h: At higher temperature the products can re-ionize. When that happens, which property of a product decides how much of it you get?
w: At 40 °C the C–Br bonds re-ionize back to the allylic cation, so the system reaches equilibrium (thermodynamic control). The product ratio then reflects product stability, and 1-bromo-2-butene, with a disubstituted internal C=C, is the major product. The 1,2-product still forms faster, but it keeps reverting.
x: Lower activation energy explains the low-temperature (kinetic) result; under equilibrium the faster-forming product is not the one that accumulates.
The 1,4-product is major for the right reason only if you cite stability; attack at C4 actually has the higher barrier.
A shared intermediate does not force equal amounts: the two paths have different barriers and the two products have different stabilities.

q: The energy diagram shows 1,3-butadiene + HBr → 3-bromo-1-butene. Which statement is correct?
c: B is the allylic carbocation, and the step through A is rate-determining
A is the allylic carbocation, and the step through C is rate-determining
B is a transition state in which the C–H bond is partly formed
C is the highest point, so bromide attack is rate-determining
h: Maxima are transition states and minima between them are intermediates. The rate-determining step has the highest transition state.
w: Minima between two maxima are intermediates, so B is the allylic carbocation. A is the transition state for protonation of the diene and C is the transition state for bromide attack. A is the highest point on the path, so protonation (through A) is rate-determining; bromide capture of the cation is fast.
x: A is a maximum, so it is a transition state, not an intermediate; and C is lower than A.
B is a minimum, so it is an intermediate (the cation), not a transition state.
C is lower than A in the diagram, so the bromide-attack step is not rate-determining.

q: The table gives free energies (kJ/mol) relative to the allylic cation + Br<sup>−</sup> formed from 1,3-butadiene and HBr. On warming, the 1,2-product gradually converts into the 1,4-product. Which explanation is consistent with these data?
c: The 1,2-product re-ionizes over a 49 kJ/mol barrier, lower than the 61 kJ/mol for the 1,4-product, so material drains to the more stable 1,4-product
The 1,4-product forms over a smaller barrier (13 kJ/mol) than the 1,2-product (9 kJ/mol), so it is favored at all temperatures
The 1,2-product rearranges directly to the 1,4-product by a 1,3-shift of Br, without ever forming the allylic cation
The 1,2-product re-ionizes over a 9 kJ/mol barrier, so it is never formed or isolated at any temperature
h: For each product, calculate the barrier to go back up to its transition state. Which product escapes more easily, and which one traps the material?
w: Reverse barriers: 1,2-product → cation, 9 − (−40) = 49 kJ/mol; 1,4-product → cation, 13 − (−48) = 61 kJ/mol. When warmed enough to cross these barriers, the 1,2-product returns to the cation much more often than the 1,4-product does, and each return gives another chance to form the 1,4-product. Material therefore drains into the more stable 1,4-product (lower G, larger reverse barrier), the thermodynamic product. At low temperature the 4 kJ/mol difference in forward barriers (9 vs 13) makes the 1,2-product the kinetic product.
x: 13 kJ/mol is the larger forward barrier, not the smaller; the 1,4-product forms more slowly, so it cannot be favored at all temperatures.
The data describe a path through the allylic cation; the interconversion is ionization and recombination, not a direct Br shift.
9 kJ/mol is the forward barrier from the cation; the 1,2-product is the major product at low temperature.

q: Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) reacts with 1 equiv of HBr at −78 °C (kinetic control). Which is the major 1,2-addition (kinetic) product?
h: Compare the two terminal carbons you could protonate. Which choice gives an allylic cation that is also tertiary? Then decide 1,2 vs 1,4.
w: Protonating C1 (the CH2 next to the methyl-bearing carbon) gives an allylic cation whose positive charge is shared by a tertiary carbon (C2) and a primary carbon (C4). Protonating C4 instead gives a secondary/primary allylic cation, which is less stable. At −78 °C bromide traps the cation fastest at the carbon with the most positive charge, next to it in the ion pair, so the kinetic 1,2-product is 3-bromo-3-methyl-1-butene.
x: 1-Bromo-3-methyl-2-butene is the 1,4-product, with a trisubstituted C=C; it is the thermodynamic product seen at higher temperature.
3-Bromo-2-methyl-1-butene comes from protonating the other terminal carbon, which makes a less stable secondary allylic cation.
4-Bromo-2-methyl-1-butene is an anti-Markovnikov product that would need a radical (HBr/ROOR) mechanism.

q: 1,3-Cyclohexadiene is treated with 1 equiv of HBr. How many constitutional isomers are obtained as products?
h: Draw the allylic cation formed by protonating C1, add Br at each cationic carbon, and number both products from scratch.
w: Protonating C1 gives an allylic cation with positive charge on C2 and C4 (double bond C3=C4 ↔ C2=C3). Bromide at C2 leaves C3=C4: Br is on the carbon next to the C=C. Bromide at C4 leaves C2=C3: Br is again on the carbon next to the C=C. Because the ring makes the two ends equivalent, both are 3-bromocyclohexene (one constitutional isomer) (formed as a racemate).
x: 4-Bromocyclohexene would need Br two carbons from the C=C; neither cationic carbon is in that position.
1-Bromocyclohexene has Br on a vinylic carbon, which no step of this mechanism produces.
Only one constitutional product forms; the 4-bromo and 1-bromo isomers are not reachable from the allylic cation.

q: In the carbocation shown, which labeled carbons share the positive charge?
h: Draw the second resonance form by moving the π electrons toward the cationic carbon.
w: Shifting the Ca=Cb π electrons toward Cc gives the resonance form CH3CH+–CH=CH2. The charge alternates, so it is shared by the two end carbons, a and c; the central carbon b carries none. The form with the charge on a (secondary) contributes more.
x: The charge is delocalized; ignoring resonance leaves it only on c.
In an allylic system the central carbon never carries the positive charge in any resonance form.
Carbon b is a node of the allyl nonbonding orbital, so it bears no positive charge.

q: Which alkene gives only one constitutional isomer of monobromide when treated with NBS and light (ignore stereoisomers)?
h: Find every allylic hydrogen, form each allylic radical, and draw both resonance forms. Count distinct bromides.
w: NBS/hν abstracts an allylic H to give a resonance-stabilized allylic radical, and Br can attach at either end. In cyclohexene both allylic CH2 groups are equivalent and the two ends of the allylic radical are equivalent, so the only product is 3-bromocyclohexene (racemic).
x: 1-Butene gives an allylic radical with unequal ends, so 3-bromo-1-butene and 1-bromo-2-butene both form.
(E)-2-Pentene has two different allylic positions (C1 and C4), and each radical has two different ends, giving several bromides.
1-Methylcyclohexene has three different allylic positions (CH<sub>3</sub>, C3 and C6), giving a mixture of constitutional isomers.

q: In the allyl radical (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•), where is the unpaired electron found, according to π MO theory?
c: In ψ<sub>2</sub>, a nonbonding MO with a node at C2, so the spin is on C1 and C3
In ψ<sub>1</sub>, a bonding MO spread evenly over all three carbons
In ψ<sub>2</sub>, a nonbonding MO concentrated on the central carbon, C2
In ψ<sub>3</sub>, an antibonding MO with a node between each pair of adjacent carbons
h: Three p orbitals give three MOs. Fill three electrons from the bottom and look at the shape of the singly occupied one.
w: Three p orbitals combine to give ψ1 (bonding, 0 nodes), ψ2 (nonbonding, 1 node) and ψ3 (antibonding, 2 nodes). Three π electrons fill ψ1 twice and ψ2 once. The node of ψ2 passes through C2, so the unpaired electron is in ψ2 and resides on C1 and C3, matching the two resonance forms.
x: ψ<sub>1</sub> holds two paired electrons; the third electron must go into the next orbital.
ψ2 has its node at C2, so it has zero coefficient there, not a concentration.
ψ<sub>3</sub> is empty in the radical; it would only be occupied in an excited state.

q: How many nodes (perpendicular to the carbon chain, not counting the molecular plane) does ψ<sub>3</sub> of 1,3-butadiene have?
h: In a linear π system, ψ<sub>n</sub> has n − 1 nodes.
w: For a linear conjugated system, the number of nodes grows by one per MO: ψ1 0, ψ2 1, ψ3 2, ψ4 3. ψ3 (the LUMO of ground-state butadiene) has 2 nodes.
x: One node is ψ<sub>2</sub>, the HOMO of butadiene.
Three nodes is ψ<sub>4</sub>, the highest antibonding MO.
Zero nodes is ψ<sub>1</sub>, the lowest bonding MO.

q: 1,3,5-Hexatriene absorbs UV light, promoting one electron from the HOMO to the LUMO. In this excited state, which MO is the highest occupied orbital, and how many nodes does it have?
h: Six π electrons fill ψ<sub>1</sub>–ψ<sub>3</sub> in the ground state. Move one electron up one level.
w: Six p orbitals give ψ1–ψ6. In the ground state six electrons fill ψ1–ψ3, so the HOMO is ψ3 (2 nodes) and the LUMO is ψ4. After excitation one electron sits in ψ4, so the highest occupied MO is ψ4, with 3 nodes. This is why photochemical electrocyclic reactions follow the opposite rotation to thermal ones.
x: ψ<sub>3</sub> with 2 nodes is the ground-state HOMO, before excitation.
ψ<sub>4</sub> is correct, but it has n − 1 = 3 nodes, not 4.
ψ<sub>5</sub> is empty in both the ground state and the first excited state.

q: Which compound has the longest-wavelength UV absorption (largest λ<sub>max</sub>)?
h: More conjugated π bonds in a row mean a smaller HOMO–LUMO gap.
w: Each added conjugated C=C raises the HOMO and lowers the LUMO, shrinking the gap, so absorption moves to longer wavelength (lower energy). 1,3,5,7-Octatetraene, with four conjugated C=C bonds, has the largest λmax (near 290 nm) compared with hexatriene (about 258 nm) and butadiene (217 nm).
x: 1,3,5-Hexatriene has three conjugated C=C bonds, one fewer than octatetraene, so its gap is larger.
1,3-Butadiene has only two conjugated C=C bonds; it absorbs near 217 nm.
1,5-Hexadiene has isolated C=C bonds, so it absorbs below 200 nm like a simple alkene.

q: Rank compounds I–III by λ<sub>max</sub> in the UV spectrum, from shortest to longest wavelength.
h: Count how many C=C bonds are conjugated with each other in each compound; isolated bonds do not count together.
w: λmax increases as the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks with longer conjugation. I (1,4-pentadiene) has isolated C=C bonds and absorbs below 200 nm; II (1,3-pentadiene) is a conjugated diene (about 223 nm); III (2,4,6-octatriene) is a conjugated triene (above 260 nm). So I < II < III.
x: Two isolated C=C bonds do not act like a diene; I absorbs at shorter wavelength than the conjugated diene II.
This is the order by energy of absorption, not wavelength; the longest conjugation absorbs at the longest wavelength.
The triene III has the longest conjugation, so it absorbs at a longer wavelength than the diene II.

q: Isomers X and Y both have formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> and both take up 2 equiv of H<sub>2</sub> to give hexane. X absorbs at 227 nm; Y shows no absorption above 200 nm. Which pair fits?
h: Absorption near 220–230 nm signals a conjugated diene. Also check that Y gives hexane with 2 equiv of H<sub>2</sub>.
w: A λmax above 200 nm needs conjugation, so X is a conjugated diene: (E)-2,4-hexadiene fits (about 227 nm). Y has two C=C bonds (2 H2 → hexane, so no ring) but no conjugation, so it is an isolated diene such as 1,5-hexadiene. Answer: X = (E)-2,4-hexadiene; Y = 1,5-hexadiene.
x: This reverses the assignment: the conjugated diene is the one that absorbs at 227 nm.
1,4-Hexadiene is an isolated diene, so it would not absorb at 227 nm.
Cyclohexene takes up only 1 equiv of H<sub>2</sub> and gives cyclohexane, not hexane.

q: What is the product of the Diels–Alder reaction shown?
h: A Diels–Alder makes a six-membered ring with the new C=C between the old C2 and C3 of the diene, and it is stereospecific for the dienophile.
w: The diene's C1 and C4 bond to the two dienophile carbons, forming a cyclohexene whose C=C sits between the old diene C2 and C3, two carbons away from each ring-fusion carbon. Maleic anhydride is a cis dienophile and the reaction is a concerted suprafacial addition, so the two carbonyl groups stay cis: the product is cis-4-cyclohexene-1,2-dicarboxylic anhydride (a meso compound).
x: The trans-fused anhydride would require the dienophile substituents to change their relationship; a concerted [4+2] keeps cis groups cis.
Here the C=C is next to a ring-fusion carbon; in a Diels–Alder adduct the new π bond is between the old diene C2 and C3, flanked by two CH<sub>2</sub> groups.
This cyclobutane is a [2+2] product, which is thermally forbidden; butadiene and maleic anhydride give the six-membered [4+2] ring.

q: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with dimethyl fumarate (dimethyl (E)-but-2-enedioate). What is the product? (For a racemic product only one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: The geometry of the dienophile is kept in the product: groups trans on the alkene end up trans on the ring.
w: The Diels–Alder is stereospecific: both new σ bonds form on the same face of the dienophile at once, so substituents that are trans on the C=C end up trans on the ring. Dimethyl fumarate therefore gives racemic trans-dimethyl cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylate (the (1R,2R) enantiomer is drawn).
x: The cis diester (meso) comes from dimethyl maleate, the Z dienophile, not from fumarate.
A 1,4-cyclohexadiene forms when the dienophile is an alkyne such as dimethyl acetylenedicarboxylate, not an alkene.
The two esters come from two different carbons of the dienophile, so they end up on adjacent ring carbons, not on the same carbon.

q: (2E,4E)-Hexa-2,4-diene reacts with maleic anhydride. What is the relationship of the two methyl groups in the adduct?
c: Cis to each other, whether the adduct is endo or exo
Trans to each other, whether the adduct is endo or exo
Cis in the endo adduct but trans in the exo adduct
A 1:1 mixture of cis and trans, because the diene can rotate during the reaction
h: Classify each methyl as an 'outside' or 'inside' group in the s-cis diene. Do two outside groups end up on the same face or opposite faces?
w: In the s-cis conformation of the (E,E)-diene both methyls point 'outside'. As the diene termini rotate to bond to the dienophile, both outside groups swing toward the same face of the new ring, so they end up cis to each other.
