Endo vs exo only changes where the anhydride sits relative to the methyls, not the methyl–methyl relationship; the concerted reaction leaves no chance for rotation. (An (E,Z)-diene, with one outside and one inside methyl, would give trans methyls.)
x: Trans methyls come from a diene with one outside and one inside methyl, the (2E,4Z) isomer.
The diene's own stereochemistry fixes the methyl relationship; endo/exo selectivity affects only the dienophile substituents relative to them.
The reaction is concerted, with no intermediate in which a bond could rotate, so it is stereospecific.

q: (E)-1-Methoxy-1,3-butadiene reacts with acrolein (propenal). What is the major constitutional product (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: Find the most nucleophilic diene carbon (use a resonance form that puts negative charge on carbon) and the most electrophilic dienophile carbon. Bond those two.
w: Resonance donation from OCH3 on C1 puts the most negative charge (largest HOMO coefficient) on C4 of the diene. In acrolein, the β carbon (the CH2) is the electrophilic end. Bonding diene C4 to the dienophile CH2 places the CHO-bearing carbon next to the OCH3-bearing carbon: the 'ortho' (1,2) product, 2-methoxycyclohex-3-ene-1-carbaldehyde.
x: This is the 'meta' (1,3) isomer, which forms from the mismatched orientation and is minor.
This 'para' (1,4) pattern with OCH<sub>3</sub> on the ring C=C is what a 2-substituted diene gives; a 1-substituted diene puts the OCH<sub>3</sub> on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.
Here the ring C=C is not next to the OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon; in the adduct the diene C1 (bearing OCH<sub>3</sub>) is allylic to the new C=C.

q: 2-Methoxy-1,3-butadiene reacts with methyl acrylate. What is the major constitutional product (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: With a donor on C2 of the diene, which terminal carbon is most electron-rich? Bond it to the β carbon of the acrylate.
w: An OCH3 on C2 pushes electron density to C1 (the CH2 attached to C2). C1 bonds to the electrophilic β carbon (CH2) of methyl acrylate, so the ester-bearing carbon bonds to C4. Counting around the ring, the OCH3 carbon and the CO2CH3 carbon are 1,4 (the 'para' rule for 2-substituted dienes): methyl 4-methoxycyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate.
x: This is the 1,3 ('meta') isomer, the minor orientation for a 2-substituted diene.
A 1,2 relationship between the OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon and the ester carbon is impossible here: the diene C2 is on the new C=C, and the dienophile carbons attach only to C1 and C4.
The OCH<sub>3</sub> was on C2 of the diene, which becomes part of the new ring C=C, so it must be on an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, not an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.

q: Which diene does not undergo a Diels–Alder reaction with maleic anhydride, even on heating?
h: The diene must reach the s-cis conformation. Look for a diene whose ring holds it permanently in the other conformation.
w: A Diels–Alder needs the diene in the s-cis conformation so C1 and C4 can reach the dienophile together. In 3-methylenecyclohexene the single bond between the two C=C bonds is part of the ring, and the ring locks the exocyclic CH2 and the ring C=C s-trans, so it cannot react.
x: Cyclopentadiene is locked s-cis and is one of the most reactive dienes known.
1,2-Dimethylenecyclohexane holds both exocyclic C=C bonds s-cis, which makes it a reactive diene.
(E)-1,3-Pentadiene rotates freely about C2–C3 and can adopt the s-cis conformation; its methyl is on the outside, so it reacts readily.

q: Rank dienes I–III by their rate of Diels–Alder reaction with maleic anhydride, slowest first.
h: Ask how easily each diene reaches the s-cis conformation, and what is pointing into the space between C1 and C4 when it does.
w: Rate depends on how much s-cis diene is available. III (cyclopentadiene) is held s-cis by its ring, so it is fastest. II, the (E,E) isomer, has both methyls outside and reaches s-cis easily. I, the (Z,Z) isomer, has both methyls 'inside'; in the s-cis form they collide, so very little reactive conformer exists and it is extremely slow. Order: I < II < III.
x: The (Z,Z) diene suffers inside-methyl clash in the s-cis form, so it is slower than the (E,E) diene, not faster.
This is the reverse order; a diene locked s-cis reacts fastest.
An acyclic diene that must rotate into the s-cis form cannot outrun cyclopentadiene, which is permanently s-cis.

q: Cyclopentadiene and maleic anhydride react at room temperature to give mainly the endo adduct. Which description of the endo adduct is correct?
c: The anhydride ring points toward the two-carbon C=C bridge, anti to the one-carbon CH<sub>2</sub> bridge
The anhydride ring points toward the one-carbon CH<sub>2</sub> bridge, anti to the two-carbon C=C bridge
The anhydride carbonyls are trans to each other, one on each face of the ring
The anhydride ring is attached at the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge carbon (C7), not at C2 and C3
h: 'Endo' describes where the dienophile's electron-withdrawing groups sat in the transition state: under the diene π system.
w: In the endo transition state the anhydride carbonyls lie under the diene, where their π orbitals overlap with the developing C2=C3 π bond (secondary orbital interaction). In the norbornene product those diene carbons become the C5=C6 bridge, so the anhydride ring points toward the C=C bridge and away from (anti to) the CH2 bridge. The endo product forms faster even though the exo adduct is slightly more stable.
x: That is the exo adduct, in which the anhydride points toward the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge; it is the minor kinetic product.
Maleic anhydride is a cis dienophile, so both carbonyl carbons stay cis in either the endo or exo adduct.
The dienophile carbons bond to the diene termini (C1 and C4 of the diene), becoming C2 and C3 of the norbornene; C7 is the original CH<sub>2</sub> of cyclopentadiene.

q: Cyclopentadiene reacts with methyl acrylate at 0 °C. Which describes the major product? (Each product forms as a racemate.)
c: the endo adduct: CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the face syn to the C=C (anti to the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge)
the exo adduct: CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the face syn to the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge (anti to the C=C)
a bicyclo[2.2.2]octene: CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> at C2, with a two-carbon CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub> bridge
a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptene: CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the one-carbon bridge (C7)
h: First choose the correct ring skeleton (cyclopentadiene gives a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptene with the substituent at C2). Then decide which face the ester ends up on.
w: Cyclopentadiene's CH2 becomes the one-carbon bridge (C7) of a bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-5-ene, and the acrylate carbons become C2 and C3. Under the endo rule (secondary orbital overlap) the ester lies under the diene in the transition state, so in the product it points toward the C5=C6 bridge and away from C7. The major product is the endo adduct, methyl bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-5-ene-2-carboxylate with CO2CH3 syn to the C=C and anti to the CH2 bridge; its diastereomer with the ester syn to the CH2 bridge is the exo adduct.
x: This is the exo diastereomer, with the ester pointing toward the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge. The endo rule makes it the minor kinetic product.
A bicyclo[2.2.2]octene would come from 1,3-cyclohexadiene, which has one more ring carbon than cyclopentadiene.
The ester cannot end up on the one-carbon bridge; C7 comes from the CH<sub>2</sub> of cyclopentadiene, which forms no new bond.

q: Which diene and dienophile would give this compound as the major Diels–Alder product?
h: The cyclohexene C=C came from diene C2–C3; the two sp<sup>3</sup> carbons across the ring came from the dienophile. Then check the regiochemistry against the 'para' rule.
w: Retro-Diels–Alder: break the two σ bonds that are allylic to the ring C=C, on the side opposite the double bond. The four carbons C=C plus its two allylic CH2 neighbors are the diene, with the methyl on an internal (C2) carbon: isoprene. The remaining two carbons, one bearing C≡N, are acrylonitrile. The 1,4 ('para') relationship of CH3 and CN is exactly what a 2-substituted diene gives, so the answer is isoprene + acrylonitrile.
x: 1,3-Pentadiene has its methyl on a terminal carbon, so the methyl would end up on an sp<sup>3</sup> ring carbon, not on the C=C.
Methacrylonitrile would put CH<sub>3</sub> and CN on the same sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, and the ring C=C would have no methyl.
But-2-enenitrile would put CH<sub>3</sub> and CN on adjacent sp<sup>3</sup> carbons, not CH<sub>3</sub> on the alkene.

q: Which diene and dienophile combine to give this bicyclic compound (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: Count the carbons in each bridge. The bridge containing the C=C and the two bridgeheads came from the diene's four π carbons.
w: The compound is a bicyclo[2.2.2]oct-2-ene with CN on a saturated bridge. A cyclic diene gives a bridged product: its four π carbons become the two bridgeheads and the new C=C bridge, and its remaining CH2CH2 becomes a two-carbon bridge, so the diene is 1,3-cyclohexadiene; the CN-bearing two-carbon bridge came from acrylonitrile.
x: Cyclopentadiene has only one extra CH<sub>2</sub>, so it gives a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptene with a one-carbon bridge.
1,4-Cyclohexadiene is not conjugated, so it cannot act as the diene.
An alkyne dienophile would leave a second C=C in the product (a bicyclo[2.2.2]octadiene), but this product has only one.

q: Cyclopentadiene is sold as its dimer, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. To get the monomer, the dimer is heated to about 170 °C and cyclopentadiene is distilled off. What reaction regenerates the monomer?
h: The dimer formed when one cyclopentadiene acted as a diene and another as a dienophile.
w: At room temperature one cyclopentadiene molecule acts as the diene and a second acts as the dienophile, giving dicyclopentadiene by a Diels–Alder reaction. Heating reverses it: a retro-Diels–Alder breaks the two σ bonds formed in the dimerization. Distilling the volatile monomer (bp 41 °C) pulls the equilibrium toward it.
x: A Cope rearrangement converts one 1,5-diene into another; it does not split a molecule in two.
A 4π electrocyclic opening breaks one σ bond of a cyclobutene; the dimer has no cyclobutene.
A [1,5] H shift moves a hydrogen within one cyclopentadiene; it does not separate two molecules.

q: What is the product when 1,3-butadiene is heated with dimethyl acetylenedicarboxylate (DMAD)?
h: An alkyne dienophile uses only one of its two π bonds. Where does the remaining one end up?
w: The diene forms its usual new C=C between C2 and C3, and the alkyne's second π bond is left in the ring between the two ester-bearing carbons. The product is dimethyl cyclohexa-1,4-diene-1,2-dicarboxylate, with two non-conjugated ring C=C bonds separated by CH2 groups.
x: Dimethyl phthalate would need an extra oxidation (loss of H<sub>2</sub>); the Diels–Alder alone stops at the 1,4-cyclohexadiene.
In this 1,3-diene the two ring C=C bonds are conjugated, but the [4+2] leaves CH<sub>2</sub> groups between them.
This is the adduct of an alkene dienophile (dimethyl maleate); an alkyne leaves a C=C between the ester carbons.

q: In a normal-electron-demand Diels–Alder reaction (electron-rich diene, electron-poor dienophile), which frontier-orbital interaction dominates?
c: HOMO of the diene (ψ<sub>2</sub>) with LUMO of the dienophile (π*)
HOMO of the dienophile (π) with HOMO of the diene (ψ<sub>2</sub>)
LUMO of the diene (ψ<sub>3</sub>) with LUMO of the dienophile (π*)
ψ<sub>1</sub> of the diene with LUMO of the dienophile (π*)
h: A stabilizing two-electron interaction pairs a filled orbital with an empty one. Electron-donating groups raise orbitals; electron-withdrawing groups lower them.
w: Bonding interactions come from a filled orbital mixing with an empty one, and the smaller the energy gap, the stronger the interaction. Donor groups raise the diene HOMO (ψ2) and withdrawing groups lower the dienophile LUMO (π*), making that gap small. So diene HOMO (ψ2) + dienophile LUMO (π*) controls the rate and regiochemistry; the terminal lobes of ψ2 and π* match in phase on the same face, so the reaction is thermally allowed.
x: Two filled orbitals mixing (HOMO + HOMO) gives no net bonding; it is a four-electron, repulsive interaction.
Two empty orbitals mixing contributes no electrons, so it cannot form bonds.
ψ<sub>1</sub> is filled but much lower in energy than ψ<sub>2</sub>, so its gap to π* is large and its interaction is weak.

q: Furan and maleic anhydride give mainly the endo adduct after a few minutes at room temperature, but after a long reaction time the isolated product is almost entirely the exo adduct. Which explanation fits?
c: The adducts readily revert to furan and maleic anhydride, so the more stable exo adduct builds up
The endo adduct isomerizes to exo by rotation about the new C–C σ bonds at room temperature over time
Secondary orbital overlap favors the exo transition state once the furan becomes aromatic
Furan reacts only through its s-trans conformation, which can give only the exo product
h: Furan loses its aromatic stabilization when it reacts. How does that affect the reverse reaction?
w: Furan is aromatic, so its Diels–Alder adducts are only modestly downhill and the retro-Diels–Alder is fast even at room temperature. The endo adduct forms faster (kinetic control, secondary orbital overlap), but it keeps reverting. Over time the system reaches equilibrium and the more stable exo adduct accumulates (thermodynamic control).
x: Converting endo to exo would require breaking a ring bond; bond rotation within the bicyclic framework cannot do it.
Secondary orbital overlap favors the endo transition state; it never favors exo.
Furan's ring locks its diene s-cis; an s-trans diene cannot do a Diels–Alder at all.

q: Rank dienophiles I–III by Diels–Alder reactivity toward cyclopentadiene, slowest first.
h: Electron-withdrawing groups lower the dienophile LUMO, bringing it closer to the diene HOMO.
w: In a normal-demand Diels–Alder the dienophile is the electrophile, and each electron-withdrawing group lowers its LUMO. Ethylene has none and reacts only under forcing conditions; methyl acrylate has one ester; tetracyanoethylene has four cyano groups and reacts almost instantly. Order: I < II < III.
x: This is the reverse order; electron-withdrawing groups speed up the reaction rather than slow it.
Ethylene has no activating group, so it is slower than methyl acrylate.
Four cyano groups make tetracyanoethylene far more electron-poor than methyl acrylate, so it is faster.

q: In the Diels–Alder reaction of 1,3-butadiene with ethylene, how many π bonds are broken and how many new σ bonds are formed?
c: 3 π bonds broken; 2 new C–C σ bonds and 1 new π bond formed
2 π bonds broken; 2 new C–C σ bonds formed
3 π bonds broken; 3 new C–C σ bonds formed
2 π bonds broken; 1 new C–C σ bond and 1 new π bond formed
h: Count all π bonds in the reactants and all π bonds in cyclohexene.
w: The reactants have three π bonds (two in butadiene, one in ethylene). The product cyclohexene has one new π bond (between the old diene C2 and C3) and two new C–C σ bonds that close the ring. So three π bonds are broken, and two σ bonds plus one new π bond are formed. Trading two π bonds for two stronger σ bonds is why the reaction is exothermic.
x: Butadiene's two π bonds and ethylene's one π bond are all broken, which is three, not two.
Only two σ bonds are needed to close the six-membered ring; the third electron pair becomes the new π bond.
Two σ bonds form, not one; the ring has two new connections, C1–C6 and C4–C5.

q: Which combination describes a symmetry-allowed electrocyclic reaction?
h: Thermal: 4n electrons → conrotatory, 4n + 2 → disrotatory. Light reverses each rule.
w: The Woodward–Hoffmann rules for electrocyclic reactions: thermal 4n π electrons go conrotatory, thermal 4n + 2 go disrotatory, and photochemical reactions do the opposite. A hexatriene (6π = 4n + 2) closes thermally in a disrotatory sense, so 6π, thermal, disrotatory is allowed.
x: A 4π (4n) system closes or opens conrotatory under heat; disrotatory is the photochemical mode.
A 6π system under heat is disrotatory; conrotatory is its photochemical mode.
A 4π system under light is disrotatory; conrotatory is its thermal mode.

q: (2E,4Z,6E)-Octa-2,4,6-triene is heated. What is the product?
h: Count the π electrons, choose con- or disrotatory, then follow the two terminal methyls (both 'outside').
w: A triene has 6π electrons (4n + 2), so the thermal ring closure is disrotatory. In the reactive (E,Z,E) conformation both terminal methyls point outward; disrotatory motion turns one clockwise and one counterclockwise, which carries both methyls to the same face. The product is cis-5,6-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene (meso).
x: The trans isomer comes from conrotatory closure, which is the photochemical mode for a 6π system.
A 1,4-cyclohexadiene has its C=C bonds separated by sp<sup>3</sup> carbons; electrocyclic closure of a triene gives a conjugated 1,3-diene with the new σ bond between the old termini.
The methyls were on the terminal carbons, which become the two new sp<sup>3</sup> carbons; they cannot end up on ring C=C carbons.

q: The same (2E,4Z,6E)-octa-2,4,6-triene is irradiated with UV light instead. What is the ring-closure product? (For a racemic product one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: Light promotes an electron so that ψ<sub>4</sub> becomes the highest occupied MO. What rotation does its symmetry require?
w: Under irradiation the highest occupied MO is ψ4, whose terminal lobes have the symmetry that requires conrotatory closure for a 6π system. Conrotation turns both termini the same way, so two outside methyls end up on opposite faces: trans-5,6-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene (racemic).
x: The cis isomer is the thermal (disrotatory) product; light reverses the rotation.
A 1,4-cyclohexadiene is not an electrocyclic product; the new σ bond joins the old termini and leaves a conjugated 1,3-diene.
This cyclobutene would come from closing only a 4π portion of the triene; the full 6π closure to a six-membered ring is the observed electrocyclization.

q: cis-3,4-Dimethylcyclobutene is heated. Which diene forms?
h: A 4π electrocyclic reaction under heat is conrotatory. Rotate both sp<sup>3</sup> carbons the same way and see where each methyl goes.
w: Ring opening of a cyclobutene is a 4π (4n) process, so under heat it is conrotatory. In the cis isomer both methyls start on the same face; conrotation turns one methyl outward and the other inward, so the diene gets one E and one Z double bond: (2E,4Z)-hexa-2,4-diene.
x: (E,E) needs both methyls to rotate outward, which conrotation allows only for the trans-dimethylcyclobutene.
(Z,Z) needs both methyls to rotate inward, which also requires the trans starting material and is sterically disfavored.
Ring opening breaks the C3–C4 bond, so the methyls end up on C2 and C5 of the diene, not at one end.

q: trans-3,4-Dimethylcyclobutene is heated. Which diene is the major product?
h: Thermal 4π opening is conrotatory. For the trans isomer, conrotation sends both methyls the same direction: both out or both in. Which is less crowded?
w: The thermal opening is conrotatory. With the methyls on opposite faces, conrotation moves both methyls outward or both inward. Both-inward would give the badly crowded (Z,Z) diene, so the reaction rotates both methyls out and gives (2E,4E)-hexa-2,4-diene.
x: (E,Z) is the conrotatory product of the cis isomer; from the trans isomer it would need disrotation, which is forbidden thermally.
(Z,Z) is also conrotatory from the trans isomer, but both methyls rotating inward clash, so this path is strongly disfavored.
The methyls stay on the two carbons of the broken σ bond, which become C2 and C5 of the diene, not on one end.

q: (2E,4E)-Hexa-2,4-diene is irradiated with UV light and closes to a cyclobutene. Which stereoisomer forms?
h: Photochemical 4π reactions use the opposite rotation to thermal ones. Both methyls start 'outside'.
w: For 4π electrons, light makes the reaction disrotatory. Disrotation turns the two outside methyls toward the same face, so the product is cis-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene (meso). This is the photochemical counterpart of the thermal results: thermal conrotatory closure of the (E,E) diene would give the trans isomer.
x: The trans isomer results from conrotatory closure of the (E,E) diene, the thermal mode; under light the motion is disrotatory.
Ring closure joins C2 and C5, which become sp<sup>3</sup> carbons; the methyls stay on those carbons, not on the ring C=C.
Closure bonds the two methyl-bearing carbons to each other, so each ring sp<sup>3</sup> carbon keeps one methyl; no ethyl group forms.

q: Why is the thermal ring closure of 1,3,5-hexatriene disrotatory?
c: In the HOMO (ψ<sub>3</sub>), the terminal p lobes on the same face have the same phase, so disrotation brings matching lobes together
In the HOMO (ψ<sub>3</sub>), the terminal p lobes on the same face have opposite phases, so disrotation brings matching lobes together
The LUMO (ψ<sub>4</sub>) controls thermal reactions, and its terminal lobes require disrotation
Disrotatory motion is always less sterically hindered than conrotatory motion
h: Look at the symmetry of the terminal lobes of the thermal HOMO. To form a σ bond, the lobes that meet must have the same phase.
w: A thermal electrocyclic reaction is controlled by the ground-state HOMO. For hexatriene that is ψ3, whose two terminal p orbitals have the same phase on the same face. Rotating the termini in opposite directions (disrotation) turns those matching lobes toward each other, giving bonding overlap, so the closure is disrotatory.
x: If the terminal lobes on the same face had opposite phases (as in butadiene's ψ<sub>2</sub>), conrotation, not disrotation, would be needed.
ψ<sub>4</sub> is empty in the ground state; it becomes the relevant orbital only after photoexcitation, which gives conrotation.
Orbital symmetry, not sterics, sets the rotation; 4π systems go conrotatory under heat regardless of sterics.

q: (2E,4Z,6Z,8E)-Deca-2,4,6,8-tetraene undergoes thermal 8π ring closure at −10 °C. What is the product? (For a racemic product one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: 8 = 4n. Decide con- vs disrotatory under heat, then track two outside methyls.
w: Eight π electrons is a 4n system, so the thermal closure is conrotatory. Both terminal methyls are outside; conrotation sends them to opposite faces, giving trans-7,8-dimethylcycloocta-1,3,5-triene (racemic). (On warming further, this triene can undergo a 6π disrotatory closure to a bicyclo[4.2.0]octadiene.)
x: The cis isomer would need disrotatory closure, which is the photochemical mode for 8π electrons.
This cyclohexadiene comes from a 6π closure of only part of the tetraene; the question asks for the full 8π closure that joins the two terminal carbons.
This cyclobutene comes from a 4π closure of one end of the tetraene; it is not the 8π electrocyclization.

q: 3,4-Dimethylhexa-1,5-diene is heated to 250 °C. Which constitutional isomer is formed by a Cope rearrangement?
h: Number the 1,5-diene C1–C6. A [3,3] shift breaks the C3–C4 σ bond, makes a C1–C6 σ bond and moves both π bonds.
w: In a Cope rearrangement the σ bond between C3 and C4 breaks, a new σ bond forms between C1 and C6, and the π bonds shift to C2=C3 and C4=C5. The methyls on C3 and C4 end up on alkene carbons at each end: CH3CH=CH–CH2CH2–CH=CHCH3, octa-2,6-diene. The product has two disubstituted C=C bonds (the start had two monosubstituted ones), so the equilibrium favors it.
x: 2,5-Dimethylhexa-1,5-diene would require the methyls to move to C2 and C5, which a [3,3] shift does not do.
3-Methylhepta-1,5-diene would require a methyl group to migrate; in a Cope only the σ bond and π bonds move.
A cyclohexene would be a Diels–Alder-type product; the Cope rearrangement gives an acyclic 1,5-diene.

q: The meso isomer of 3,4-dimethylhexa-1,5-diene undergoes a Cope rearrangement through a chair-like transition state. What is the major product?
c: A 1:1 mixture of the (E,E) and (Z,Z) isomers
h: Place the six atoms in a chair. In the meso isomer, can both methyls be equatorial? An equatorial substituent becomes an E double bond; an axial one becomes Z.
w: In the chair transition state, a substituent that is pseudo-equatorial on C3 or C4 ends up E in the new C=C, and one that is pseudo-axial ends up Z. In the meso diastereomer the two methyls cannot both be equatorial: one is equatorial and one axial in any chair. So the meso isomer gives (2E,6Z)-octa-2,6-diene almost exclusively. (The racemic isomer can put both methyls equatorial and gives mainly (E,E).)
x: (E,E) needs both methyls equatorial in the chair, which is possible only for the racemic (R,R/S,S) diastereomer.
(Z,Z) needs both methyls axial, which again requires the racemic diastereomer and is the disfavored chair.
The Cope rearrangement is concerted and stereospecific, so the meso isomer does not give a mixture of (E,E) and (Z,Z).

q: 3-Methylhexa-1,5-diene and hepta-1,5-diene interconvert by a Cope rearrangement on heating. Which statement about the equilibrium is correct?
c: It favors hepta-1,5-diene, which has a more substituted C=C
It favors 3-methylhexa-1,5-diene, which has a branched carbon chain
It lies at 1:1, because both compounds are 1,5-dienes with the same formula
It cannot be reached, because [3,3] shifts are thermally forbidden
h: Count the alkyl groups on each C=C in both compounds. Alkene stability decides the position of a Cope equilibrium.
w: A Cope rearrangement is reversible, so the equilibrium favors the more stable 1,5-diene. 3-Methylhexa-1,5-diene has two monosubstituted C=C bonds; hepta-1,5-diene has one monosubstituted and one disubstituted (E) C=C. More substituted alkenes are more stable, so the equilibrium favors hepta-1,5-diene.
x: Branching of the sp<sup>3</sup> chain matters far less than the substitution of the C=C bonds, which is what changes here.
Same formula does not mean same energy; the alkene substitution differs, so K is not 1.
[3,3] sigmatropic shifts (6 electrons, suprafacial, chair or boat TS) are thermally allowed.

q: Hexa-1,5-dien-3-ol is treated with KH and 18-crown-6 in THF at room temperature, then with aqueous NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. What is the isolated product?
h: The alkoxide speeds up a [3,3] shift of the 1,5-diene. Draw the shifted product with O<sup>−</sup> still on its carbon; what does it become on protonation?
w: This is an anionic oxy-Cope rearrangement. The potassium alkoxide (with 18-crown-6 freeing the anion) undergoes a very fast [3,3] shift: the C3–C4 bond breaks, C1–C6 bonds, and the O-bearing C3 becomes part of an enolate (C3=C2). Protonation gives an enol that tautomerizes to the aldehyde, so the product is hex-5-enal (CH2=CH–CH2CH2CH2–CHO).
x: KH is a base, not an oxidant, so the alcohol is not converted into a ketone.
This places the C=C at C4, but in the shift the C=C forms between the old C4 and C5, which becomes the terminal CH=CH<sub>2</sub> of the product.
The [3,3] shift keeps the chain acyclic; no ring forms because the new σ bond (C1–C6) is made as the C3–C4 bond breaks.

q: Allyl phenyl ether is heated to 200 °C. What is the major product?
h: This is a [3,3] sigmatropic (Claisen) rearrangement: the O–CH<sub>2</sub> bond breaks and the far end of the allyl group bonds to a ring carbon three atoms away from it.
w: In the aromatic Claisen rearrangement, the O–CH2 bond breaks and the terminal CH2 of the allyl group bonds to an ortho carbon through a six-membered cyclic transition state. The resulting cyclohexadienone tautomerizes to restore aromaticity, giving 2-allylphenol.
x: The para product forms only when both ortho positions are blocked (by a further Cope step); here an ortho position is free.
Moving the C=C toward oxygen (to a propenyl ether) is an isomerization, not the [3,3] Claisen rearrangement.
The meta carbon is not three atoms from the allyl terminus in the cyclic transition state, so the allyl group cannot reach it.

q: (E)-But-2-enyl 2,6-dimethylphenyl ether (both ortho positions blocked) is heated. What is the final isolated product?
h: The first [3,3] shift reaches a blocked ortho carbon and cannot tautomerize. A second [3,3] (Cope) shift moves it to para. Track which butenyl carbon is attached each time.
w: Step 1 (Claisen): the O–CH2 bond breaks and the CH(CH3) terminus bonds to a blocked ortho carbon, giving a 6-(1-methylallyl)cyclohexa-2,4-dienone that cannot lose H to rearomatize. Step 2 (Cope): this 1,5-diene shifts the group from the ortho to the para carbon, attaching through its CH2 terminus, so the two inversions cancel. Tautomerization then gives 4-[(E)-but-2-enyl]-2,6-dimethylphenol, with the butenyl group attached at the same carbon that was bonded to O. The Cope shift re-forms an internal C=C, and its chair transition state keeps the CH3 equatorial, so that alkene is (E), as drawn.
x: This para product has the group attached through the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) carbon (one inversion); the second [3,3] shift inverts the allyl unit again.
This dienone is the intermediate after the first shift; it cannot tautomerize at a blocked ortho carbon, so it rearranges on to the para product.
Simple cleavage of the ether to the phenol is not a pericyclic process and does not occur on heating alone.

q: (E)-But-2-enyl vinyl ether is heated. What is the product of the Claisen rearrangement?
h: Number the six atoms C=C–O–C–C=C. The O–C3 bond (atoms 3–4) breaks and atoms 1 and 6 bond. Which carbon of the butenyl group is atom 6?
w: Number vinyl CH2 (1), vinyl CH (2), O (3), OCH2 (4), =CH (5), =CH(CH3) (6). The [3,3] shift breaks O3–C4, bonds C1 to C6, and makes C2=O3 (a carbonyl) and C4=C5. The methyl-bearing C6 is now the carbon attached to the CH2CHO unit and also carries a vinyl group: 3-methylpent-4-enal.
x: This keeps the original attachment through the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon; a [3,3] shift bonds through the far end (C6) and inverts the allyl unit.
Here the methyl is next to the CHO, but the methyl starts on C6 of the six-atom array, which bonds to C1, so it ends up one carbon further out (C3 of the aldehyde).
The methyl ends up on the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon formed in the new σ bond, not on the alkene.

q: At room temperature, 5-methylcyclopenta-1,3-diene isomerizes to 1-methylcyclopenta-1,3-diene (which then forms 2-methyl). How is this first step best classified?
c: A 4π electrocyclic ring opening and closing
h: Find which atom moves and count the atoms along the π path from where it leaves to where it arrives (the starting carbon is 1).
w: The hydrogen on C5 migrates to C4. Counting along the conjugated path from the starting carbon (C5 = 1, C1 = 2, C2 = 3, C3 = 4, C4 = 5), the H moves to position 5, so this is a [1,5] sigmatropic hydrogen shift. It involves 6 electrons (the σ bond plus two π bonds) and is thermally allowed suprafacially, which is why it happens at room temperature.
x: A suprafacial [1,3] H shift is thermally forbidden (4 electrons); in the ring, counting along the π path shows the H moves five atoms, not three.
No ring is opened or closed in this process; the five-membered ring stays intact while one hydrogen moves.
A [3,3] shift needs a 1,5-diene in which a σ bond migrates between two allyl units; here only one hydrogen changes position.

q: Benzene is nitrated with a mixture of concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which species is the electrophile that attacks the ring?
h: Sulfuric acid is the stronger acid. Protonate HNO<sub>3</sub> on an OH oxygen and let a good leaving group depart.
w: H2SO4 protonates the OH of nitric acid; the protonated acid loses water to give the linear nitronium ion, O=N+=O. It is a strong electrophile because nitrogen carries a formal positive charge and the ring's π electrons can attack it to form the arenium ion. Anions such as NO3− and HSO4− are electron-rich and cannot be attacked by an electron-rich ring.
x: Nitrate is an anion with no empty or low-lying acceptor orbital; an electron-rich ring cannot attack it.
NO<sup>+</sup> (from HNO<sub>2</sub>) nitrosates only very activated rings such as phenols; it is not formed from HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> is the conjugate base left behind; it later acts as the base that removes H<sup>+</sup> from the arenium ion.

q: Benzene does not react with Br<sub>2</sub> alone, but it is brominated quickly when FeBr<sub>3</sub> is added. What does FeBr<sub>3</sub> do?
c: It is a Lewis acid that binds Br<sub>2</sub> and polarizes the Br–Br bond, so the terminal Br becomes strongly electrophilic
It is a Brønsted base that removes the ring proton first, giving a phenyl anion that then attacks Br<sub>2</sub>
It is a radical initiator that splits Br<sub>2</sub> into two Br· atoms, which add to the ring by a chain mechanism
It is a reducing agent that converts Br<sub>2</sub> into Br<sup>−</sup>, which then acts as the nucleophile that attacks the benzene ring
h: Iron(III) has an empty orbital. Which atom of Br<sub>2</sub> can donate a lone pair to it?
w: FeBr3 is a Lewis acid: a lone pair on one Br of Br2 coordinates to Fe, giving Br–Br+–FeBr3−. The outer Br now behaves like Br+, and the ring's π electrons attack it to form the arenium ion while FeBr4− leaves. FeBr4− later removes the ring proton, regenerating FeBr3 and releasing HBr.
x: An aryl C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> about 43) is not removed by FeBr<sub>3</sub>, which is not a base; the proton is lost only after the electrophile adds.
Radical bromination needs light or heat and gives benzylic, not ring, substitution; FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalysis is polar.
The ring is the nucleophile in EAS; bromide anion cannot attack an electron-rich π system.

q: The energy diagram shows the bromination of benzene with Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>. Which statement is correct?
c: B is the arenium ion (σ complex); the step through A, which breaks the aromatic π system, is rate-determining
B is the arenium ion (σ complex); the step through C, loss of H<sup>+</sup> to restore aromaticity, is rate-determining
A is the arenium ion; it is the highest-energy point, so it is the rate-determining intermediate of the reaction
B is a cyclohexadienyl radical; the step through A, homolysis of Br–Br, is rate-determining
h: Intermediates sit in valleys, transition states on peaks. Which step costs the ring its aromaticity?
w: Maxima (A, C) are transition states; the valley B is the arenium ion (σ complex). Its formation destroys the aromatic sextet, so the first barrier (A) is the highest and that step is rate-determining. Loss of H+ through C restores aromaticity and is fast, which is why C is lower than A.
x: C is lower than A; deprotonation regains aromatic stabilization and is fast, so it does not limit the rate.
A is a peak, so it is a transition state, not an intermediate; intermediates sit in energy minima.
FeBr<sub>3</sub> bromination is a polar (ionic) process; there is no Br· or cyclohexadienyl radical on this path.

q: Which statement about aromatic sulfonation with fuming sulfuric acid (SO<sub>3</sub> in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) is correct?
c: It is reversible: heating the sulfonic acid in dilute aqueous acid removes the SO<sub>3</sub>H group
It needs FeBr<sub>3</sub> or AlCl<sub>3</sub> as a Lewis acid to turn SO<sub>3</sub> into a strong electrophile
The SO<sub>3</sub>H group it installs is an ortho/para-directing activator, like an OH or OCH<sub>3</sub> group
The electrophile is HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, formed when SO<sub>3</sub> dissolves in the concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
h: Think about what large amounts of water do to the position of the sulfonation equilibrium.
w: SO3 (or its protonated form HSO3+) is the electrophile: sulfur is strongly δ+ between three oxygens, so no metal Lewis acid is needed. Every step of sulfonation is reversible: in concentrated acid with excess SO3 the sulfonic acid forms, but heating in dilute aqueous acid (steam) drives desulfonation. This reversibility is why SO3H works as a removable blocking group in synthesis.
x: SO<sub>3</sub> is already a strong electrophile (S bearing three electronegative O); no metal halide catalyst is used.
SO<sub>3</sub>H is strongly electron-withdrawing; it deactivates the ring and directs meta.
HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> is an anion and a weak base, not an electrophile; the electrophile is SO<sub>3</sub> or HSO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>.

q: Acetyl chloride and AlCl<sub>3</sub> are added to benzene. Which species is the electrophile that attacks the ring?
h: AlCl<sub>3</sub> pulls chloride off the acyl chloride. What cation remains, and how is it stabilized?
w: AlCl3 abstracts Cl− from CH3COCl to give AlCl4− and the acylium ion, CH3C≡O+. Its positive charge is shared by resonance between carbon (CH3–C+=O) and oxygen (C≡O+, all octets complete). Because the cation is resonance-stabilized it does not rearrange, which is why acylation gives clean, unrearranged products.
x: Losing CO to give a methyl cation would trade a resonance-stabilized cation for the least stable carbocation; it does not happen under these conditions.
Ketene forms only when a base removes an α-H from an acyl chloride; it is neutral and is not the Friedel–Crafts electrophile.
There is no proton source to make a protonated acyl chloride; AlCl<sub>3</sub> is a Lewis acid that removes Cl<sup>−</sup>.

q: Anisole is nitrated para to the OCH<sub>3</sub> group. Which structure is the most important resonance contributor to the σ complex (arenium ion) on that pathway?
h: Count the electrons around every atom in each form. A form in which every atom has an octet beats any form with a 6-electron carbon.
w: Para attack puts the positive charge on the two carbons ortho to the new sp3 carbon and on the carbon bearing OCH3 . From that form, an oxygen lone pair forms a C=O+ π bond, giving the oxonium form, in which every atom has a complete octet. A form with all octets outweighs any form with an electron-deficient carbon, even the tertiary-like cation on the OCH3 carbon. This extra contributor is why OCH3 activates the ring and directs ortho/para.
x: This is a real contributor (the cation sits on the carbon bearing OCH<sub>3</sub>), but that carbon has only six electrons; the oxonium form, with all octets, is more important.
This is a real contributor, but its cationic carbon has only six electrons and gets no direct help from the oxygen lone pair.
This is a resonance form of the meta σ complex (the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon is meta to OCH<sub>3</sub>), not of the para σ complex.

q: Rank these compounds from fastest to slowest reaction with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
h: Sort the substituents into strong donors, weak donors, weak withdrawers and strong withdrawers.
w: OCH3 donates a lone pair by resonance (strong activator); CH3 donates weakly by hyperconjugation and induction (weak activator); Cl withdraws inductively more than it donates by resonance (weak deactivator); NO2 withdraws by both induction and resonance (strong deactivator). Order: anisole (II) > toluene (IV) > chlorobenzene (I) > nitrobenzene (III).
x: Resonance donation from an oxygen lone pair (OCH<sub>3</sub>) is much stronger than hyperconjugation from CH<sub>3</sub>; anisole reacts thousands of times faster than toluene.
Chlorobenzene is only mildly deactivated (about 30 times slower than benzene); nitrobenzene is millions of times slower.
Cl lone-pair donation only steers the electrophile ortho/para; overall the C–Cl inductive pull makes chlorobenzene slower than benzene and far slower than toluene.

q: Rank these compounds from fastest to slowest reaction with Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>.
h: In acetanilide, the nitrogen lone pair is shared between the ring and the C=O. In ethyl benzoate, which atom is attached to the ring?
w: OH donates an oxygen lone pair fully into the ring (strong activator). In NHCOCH3 the nitrogen lone pair is partly tied up by amide resonance with C=O, so it is a moderate activator, still faster than benzene. The ester is attached through its carbonyl carbon, so it withdraws electron density (deactivator). Order: phenol (III) > acetanilide (I) > benzene (II) > ethyl benzoate (IV).
x: Amide resonance diverts part of the nitrogen lone pair to the carbonyl oxygen, so NHCOCH<sub>3</sub> activates less than OH.
Acetanilide is still activated: its nitrogen lone pair, though shared with C=O, stabilizes the ortho/para σ complexes, so it reacts faster than benzene.
In ethyl benzoate the ring is bonded to the C=O carbon, not to an oxygen with a lone pair; CO<sub>2</sub>Et withdraws electrons and slows the reaction below benzene.

q: Chlorobenzene reacts more slowly than benzene in EAS, yet it gives mostly ortho and para products. Which explanation is correct?
c: Cl’s inductive pull slows attack everywhere, but its lone pairs stabilize the ortho and para σ complexes, which can put the + charge on the C bearing Cl
Cl donates electrons by induction but withdraws them by resonance, so it slows meta attack more than ortho and para attack
Cl deactivates only the meta positions; the ortho and para positions are activated relative to benzene by its lone pairs
Cl lone pairs make every ring position more electron-rich than in benzene, but the large Cl atom sterically blocks the meta positions
h: Two effects act at once. One sets the overall rate; the other decides which σ complex is least bad.
w: Cl is more electronegative than carbon, so its inductive withdrawal lowers the energy of the ring π electrons and slows reaction at every position (net deactivator). But in the ortho and para σ complexes one resonance form puts the positive charge on the carbon bonded to Cl, and a Cl lone pair can donate into it (a chloronium form with all octets). The meta σ complex never places the charge there, so it gets no such help. Result: slower than benzene, but ortho/para selective.
x: The directions are reversed: Cl withdraws by induction and donates by resonance.
No position of chlorobenzene reacts faster than a position of benzene; the ortho/para positions are simply deactivated less than meta.
Cl does not raise the electron density of the ring overall (it is a deactivator), and meta selectivity is electronic, not steric.

q: Which compound is nitrated mainly at the meta position?
h: Look at the atom bonded directly to the ring. Does it have a lone pair, or is it the δ+ carbon of a C=O?
w: Meta directors have a δ+ atom (often a C=O carbon) bonded to the ring, so they withdraw electrons by resonance. Methyl benzoate has the ester carbonyl carbon on the ring: meta director. Phenyl acetate and acetanilide attach through O and N lone pairs (ortho/para), and bromobenzene is an ortho/para-directing deactivator.
x: Phenyl acetate is attached through an oxygen with a lone pair; the OCOCH<sub>3</sub> group directs ortho/para (a weak activator).
Acetanilide is attached through N, whose lone pair stabilizes ortho/para σ complexes.
Halogens deactivate but direct ortho/para through lone-pair donation.

q: Nitrobenzene reacts with Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> (heat) at the meta position. Each structure below is a resonance form of a σ complex for ortho, meta or para attack. Which form is especially unstable and best explains why ortho and para attack are avoided?
h: Find the form where the ring's positive charge sits right next to the positively charged nitrogen.
w: Ortho and para attack each give one resonance form with the cation on the carbon bonded to the nitro group. That puts a positive carbon directly next to the formally positive nitrogen: two adjacent positive centers, a very high-energy form. The meta σ complex has no such form; its charge is never on the carbon bearing NO2. So the meta σ complex is the least destabilized, and meta substitution wins (slowly, because all paths are destabilized).
x: B (para attack, cation two carbons away from the nitro-bearing carbon) is an ordinary contributor with the charge on a C–H carbon; it is not what makes para attack bad.
C belongs to the meta σ complex (the favored pathway). The cation is next to, not on, the carbon bearing NO<sub>2</sub>, so it lacks the adjacent-positive-charge clash.
D belongs to the ortho σ complex, but its cation is far from the nitro group; the bad form of the ortho complex is the one with the charge on the nitro-bearing carbon.

q: Rank these compounds from fastest to slowest nitration.
h: CF<sub>3</sub> withdraws only by induction; NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws by induction and resonance. Cl withdraws by induction but also has lone pairs.
w: Toluene (IV) is activated. Chlorobenzene (I) is only weakly deactivated because Cl lone-pair donation offsets part of its inductive pull. CF3 (II) is a strong, purely inductive withdrawer with no lone pair on carbon, so it deactivates far more than Cl. NO2 (III) withdraws by induction and resonance and has the positively charged nitrogen next to the ring: the strongest deactivator here. IV > I > II > III.
x: C–F bonds do not hyperconjugate like C–H; CF<sub>3</sub> is strongly electron-withdrawing and makes the ring much slower than chlorobenzene.
The three fluorines are not attached to the ring; CF<sub>3</sub> withdraws only inductively, while NO<sub>2</sub> adds resonance withdrawal and a formal + charge, so nitrobenzene is slowest.
Chlorobenzene reacts more slowly than benzene, so it cannot beat toluene.

q: What is the major product when the trimethylanilinium ion is nitrated with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
c: no reaction: a ring that carries a positive charge cannot react with NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
h: Does the nitrogen in N(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> still have a lone pair to donate?
w: In –N(CH3)3+ the nitrogen uses all four of its electron pairs in σ bonds, so it has no lone pair to donate. Its positive charge withdraws strongly by induction. Ortho and para attack would place the ring cation on the carbon bonded to N+ (two adjacent positive centers), so attack occurs meta. The ring is strongly deactivated but still reacts with the very reactive NO2+.
x: Para attack would put the cation on the carbon bonded to N<sup>+</sup>; with no lone pair on N to help, that σ complex is strongly destabilized.
Ortho attack has the same problem as para, and the bulky N(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group also blocks the ortho positions.
Strongly deactivated rings (even cationic ones) still react with NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> under forcing conditions; they just react slowly and meta.

q: Nitration of aniline in concentrated HNO3/H2SO4 gives a large amount of m-nitroaniline, even though NH2 is an ortho/para director. What is the best explanation?
c: In strong acid aniline is mostly protonated to anilinium, whose NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group has no lone pair and directs meta
NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> first attacks the nitrogen, and the N-nitro group then migrates to the nearest free meta carbon
The NH<sub>2</sub> group is so bulky in acid that both ortho and para positions are sterically blocked
Sulfuric acid sulfonates the para position first, and the nitro group then enters the only free meta position
h: What happens to a basic amine (conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> about 4.6) in concentrated sulfuric acid?
w: Aniline's conjugate acid has pKa ≈ 4.6, so in concentrated H2SO4 nearly all of it is anilinium ion. The –NH3+ group has no lone pair and withdraws by induction, so it deactivates the ring and directs meta. The small amount of free aniline still reacts ortho/para, giving a mixture. Protecting the amine as an acetamide avoids this.
x: N-Nitration and migration is not the main path here; the meta product comes from the protonated amine.
The para position is remote from the substituent and cannot be blocked sterically.
Sulfonation as a blocking step requires a separate SO<sub>3</sub> step and later removal; it does not explain meta product in a nitration mixture.

q: Phenol is treated with excess bromine water (Br<sub>2</sub> in H<sub>2</sub>O, no catalyst). What is the major product?
c: no reaction, because Br<sub>2</sub> needs FeBr<sub>3</sub> to brominate an aromatic ring
h: OH is one of the strongest activators. How many ortho and para positions are open, and is there enough Br<sub>2</sub> for all of them?
w: The OH group is so strongly activating (and in water some phenoxide forms, which is even more activating) that no Lewis acid is needed and the reaction does not stop at one substitution. With excess Br2, all three ortho/para positions are brominated: 2,4,6-tribromophenol, which precipitates as a white solid.
x: 4-Bromophenol forms when bromination is done with one equivalent in a nonpolar solvent at low temperature; with excess bromine water the ring keeps reacting.
The 3- and 5-positions are meta to OH; a strong ortho/para director does not send bromine there.
Strongly activated rings such as phenol and aniline react with Br<sub>2</sub> without any Lewis acid.

q: Toluene is treated with one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub> in the dark. What is the major product?
h: FeBr<sub>3</sub> means a polar ring substitution. CH<sub>3</sub> is an ortho/para director; which of those positions is less crowded?
w: With a Lewis acid and no light, Br2 substitutes on the ring. CH3 is a weak activator that directs ortho/para; the para position is free of steric interaction with the methyl group, so 4-bromotoluene is the major product (2-bromotoluene is the main minor product).
x: CH<sub>3</sub> donates electrons to the ortho and para positions; the meta product forms only in trace amounts.
Benzylic bromination is a radical reaction (light or NBS/peroxide); FeBr<sub>3</sub> in the dark gives ring substitution.
Only one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> is used, so monobromination is the main outcome.

q: What is the major product when methyl benzoate is nitrated with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 0 °C?
h: Which atom of the ester is bonded to the ring, and is it electron-rich or electron-poor?
w: The CO2CH3 group is attached through its δ+ carbonyl carbon; it withdraws electrons by resonance and induction. Ortho/para attack would place the ring cation next to that carbonyl carbon, so substitution occurs meta: methyl 3-nitrobenzoate. The product ring is even more deactivated, so a second nitration does not occur at 0 °C.
x: Para attack gives a σ complex with the cation on the carbon bonded to the electron-poor C=O carbon; it is disfavored.
Ortho attack has the same destabilized form as para attack, plus steric hindrance.
After one nitro group the ring is doubly deactivated; dinitration needs much harsher conditions.

q: What is the major product of this Friedel–Crafts acylation?
h: OCH<sub>3</sub> directs ortho/para, the acylium–AlCl<sub>3</sub> electrophile is bulky, and an acyl group deactivates the ring it joins.
w: OCH3 is a strong ortho/para director. The bulky acylating complex strongly prefers the open para position, giving 4-methoxyacetophenone. The C=O introduced deactivates the product, so acylation stops after one group, and the acyl group is not reduced to an alkyl group by AlCl3.
x: OCH<sub>3</sub> donates a lone pair to the ortho and para positions; meta attack gets no such help.
Friedel–Crafts acylation gives a ketone; turning C=O into CH<sub>2</sub> needs a separate Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner step.
The first acyl group deactivates the ring, so a second acylation does not occur (unlike Friedel–Crafts alkylation).

q: 4-Nitrotoluene is nitrated further with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Find the carbon that is ortho to CH<sub>3</sub> and also meta to NO<sub>2</sub>.
w: CH3 (at C1) directs to its open ortho positions, C2 and C6. NO2 (at C4) directs meta to itself, also C2 and C6. The two groups reinforce each other, so the product is 2,4-dinitrotoluene.
x: Substitution ortho to NO<sub>2</sub> (C3) is meta to CH<sub>3</sub> and ortho to the deactivating nitro group; neither group favors it.
TNT requires a third nitration under much harsher conditions; each nitro group makes the next substitution slower.
Nitration with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> substitutes ring C–H, not the benzylic C–H of the methyl group.

q: 4-Methylanisole is treated with one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: The two groups send the electrophile to different carbons. Which group is the stronger activator?
w: OCH3 directs to its ortho positions (para is taken); CH3 directs to its own ortho positions. These are different carbons, so the directors compete, and the stronger activator wins: lone-pair resonance from oxygen beats hyperconjugation from CH3. Bromine enters ortho to OCH3: 2-bromo-4-methylanisole.
x: This is ortho to the weaker activator (CH<sub>3</sub>) and meta to OCH<sub>3</sub>; the σ complex gets no oxygen lone-pair stabilization.
Benzylic bromination needs radical conditions (NBS, light); FeBr<sub>3</sub> gives ring substitution.
With only one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub>, monobromination is the main result.

q: m-Xylene (1,3-dimethylbenzene) is mononitrated. What is the major product?
h: Three ring positions are activated by both methyl groups or by one. Which of the doubly activated positions is easiest to reach?
w: C2 (between the methyls), C4 and C6 are each ortho or para to both CH3 groups; C5 is meta to both. C2 is flanked by two methyl groups, so attack there is sterically hindered: groups meta to each other block the carbon between them. C4/C6 (equivalent) is ortho to one methyl and para to the other and open, so 2,4-dimethyl-1-nitrobenzene is the major product.
x: C2 is electronically activated by both methyls, but it sits between them; this crowded position gives only a minor product.
C5 is meta to both methyl groups, so neither activator helps the σ complex.
The question asks for mononitration; a second nitro group is not introduced under these conditions.

q: What is the major product when N-(4-methylphenyl)acetamide reacts with Br2 in acetic acid?
h: Both groups direct ortho to themselves. Compare a nitrogen lone pair (even one shared with C=O) with a methyl group.
w: The para position is blocked, so each group directs ortho to itself. NHCOCH3 is a moderate activator (nitrogen lone pair), stronger than CH3 (weak activator). The stronger activator controls: bromine enters ortho to the acetamido group.
x: Ortho to CH<sub>3</sub> is meta to NHCOCH<sub>3</sub>; the stronger activator does not stabilize that σ complex.
Benzylic bromination requires radical conditions; Br<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid is a polar ring bromination.
N-Bromoamides are not the stable product of Br<sub>2</sub>/AcOH with an activated ring; ring C-bromination is observed.

q: 1-Bromo-4-nitrobenzene is heated with Br<sub>2</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
c: no reaction: a ring with two deactivating groups cannot be brominated
h: Br directs ortho/para; NO<sub>2</sub> directs meta. Is there a carbon both groups agree on?
w: Br at C1 directs to C2/C6 (para is taken); NO2 at C4 directs meta to itself, also C2/C6. The directors reinforce, giving 1,2-dibromo-4-nitrobenzene. The ring is deactivated, so heat is needed, but halogenation still occurs.
x: The carbon ortho to NO<sub>2</sub> is meta to Br; bromine's lone pair cannot stabilize that σ complex and the nitro group disfavors it.
Replacing NO<sub>2</sub> by Br (ipso substitution) is not a normal EAS outcome; the electrophile replaces H<sup>+</sup>.
Deactivated rings, even nitrobenzene itself, are brominated with Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> and heat; only Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on strongly deactivated rings.

q: 1-tert-Butyl-4-methylbenzene is mononitrated. What is the major product?
h: Both groups are alkyl activators of similar strength. When electronics nearly tie, what decides?
w: CH3 and C(CH3)3 are both weak ortho/para activators; the para positions are mutually blocked, so each directs ortho to itself. Electronically they are similar, so sterics decide: the carbons next to the huge tert-butyl group are hindered, and nitration occurs ortho to the methyl group.
x: Attack next to the bulky tert-butyl group is sterically hindered and gives only a minor product.
HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> nitrates ring C–H bonds, not benzylic C–H bonds.
The question asks for mononitration; the first nitro group deactivates the ring toward a second substitution.

q: 3-Methoxybenzaldehyde reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid. What is the major product?
h: Let the activator choose among its ortho/para positions; then eliminate the most crowded one and compare the rest.
w: OCH3 (strong activator) controls over CHO (deactivator). It directs to C2, C4 and C6 (numbering the ring from CHO at C1, OCH3 at C3: its ortho carbons are C2 and C4, its para carbon is C6). C2 lies between the two substituents and is sterically blocked. C4 is ortho to OCH3 and para to CHO; C6 is para to OCH3 and ortho to CHO. Attack para to the activator, where its lone-pair donation is most effective and the electrophile is farther from OCH3, is preferred: 2-bromo-5-methoxybenzaldehyde.
x: This carbon is meta to OCH<sub>3</sub>; following the deactivating CHO group's meta preference ignores the stronger director.
This carbon is between the two substituents (meta to each other), the most hindered position on the ring.
This carbon (ortho to OCH<sub>3</sub>) is electronically allowed, but attack para to OCH<sub>3</sub> is favored; this is the minor isomer.

q: 4-Methylbenzoic acid is nitrated. At which labeled carbon does substitution mainly occur?
c: neither; the CO<sub>2</sub>H group prevents nitration
h: Ask each substituent separately where it sends the electrophile.
w: CH3 directs ortho to itself (para is occupied): that is carbon b. CO2H is a meta director: the carbons meta to it are also b (and its mirror). The directors reinforce, so nitration occurs at carbon b, giving 4-methyl-3-nitrobenzoic acid.
x: Carbon a is ortho to the deactivating CO2H and meta to CH3; neither group favors it.
The two carbons are not equivalent; both substituents favor b.
CO<sub>2</sub>H deactivates the ring but does not stop nitration; it only blocks Friedel–Crafts reactions.

q: Which sequence converts aniline into 4-bromoaniline as the major product?
c: 1. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O, pyridine  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH  3. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
h: NH<sub>2</sub> is so activating that it is hard to stop at one bromine. How can you temporarily tone it down without changing its directing effect?
w: Free NH2 activates the ring so strongly that bromination runs to 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. Converting it to the acetamide pulls part of the N lone pair onto C=O: still an ortho/para director, but moderate, and the bulky group favors para. After monobromination, basic hydrolysis removes the acetyl group to give 4-bromoaniline.
x: Unprotected aniline is brominated at all three ortho/para positions even with limited Br<sub>2</sub>; a clean mono product is not obtained.
In excess acid aniline becomes anilinium ion, a meta director, so bromination would favor 3-bromoaniline.
Diazotization replaces the amino group (step 3 would make a phenol), so the target amine is lost.

q: Which compound gives the largest para : ortho product ratio on mononitration?
h: All four are ortho/para-directing alkyl groups of similar electronic strength. What differs?
w: All four alkyl groups activate and direct ortho/para with similar electronic effects, so the ortho share is set by sterics. The bulkier the group, the more it blocks its neighbors. The tert-butyl group is the largest, so tert-butylbenzene gives the highest para : ortho ratio; toluene gives the most ortho product.
x: Isopropyl is bulky but has a benzylic H and can rotate it toward the ring; it hinders the ortho positions less than tert-butyl.
Ethyl is only slightly larger than methyl; ethylbenzene still gives a lot of ortho product.
Methyl is the smallest alkyl group; toluene gives the most ortho product of the four.

q: Biphenyl reacts with one equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>COCl and AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: A phenyl substituent can share its π electrons with the σ complex. Where does that help, and which of those positions is open?
w: A phenyl group is a weak activator and ortho/para director: in the ortho and para σ complexes the positive charge can be delocalized into the second ring. The bulky acylium–AlCl3 electrophile avoids the crowded ortho position (next to the other ring), so 4-acetylbiphenyl is the major product. The ketone deactivates its ring, and one equivalent of reagent gives monoacylation.
x: Meta attack cannot delocalize the cation into the second ring; it gets no help from the phenyl substituent.
The ortho position is electronically allowed but crowded by the other ring, a poor fit for the bulky acylating complex.
With one equivalent of acyl chloride, monoacylation is the main result; the acetyl group also deactivates the molecule.

q: Phenyl benzoate is mononitrated with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Decide first which ring reacts: one is bonded to an oxygen, the other to a carbonyl carbon.
w: The ring bonded to the ester oxygen (–OCOPh) is activated: the O lone pair donates into it (moderately, because it is shared with C=O), so this ring reacts and directs ortho/para. The ring bonded to the carbonyl carbon is deactivated. Nitration therefore occurs on the O-bearing ring, mainly para (less hindered): 4-nitrophenyl benzoate.
x: This is the meta product on the deactivated acyl ring; that ring reacts much more slowly than the oxygen-bearing ring.
Right ring, wrong position: the –OCOPh group directs ortho/para on its own ring, not meta.
The acyl ring is deactivated by the C=O, and even if it reacted it would be meta, not para, substituted.

q: Excess benzene is treated with 1-chloropropane and AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: The electrophile is a primary carbocation (or a cation-like complex). What does a primary carbocation do if a hydride shift is available?
w: AlCl3 pulls Cl− from 1-chloropropane. The developing primary cation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable secondary isopropyl cation, which alkylates the ring: isopropylbenzene (cumene, A) is the major product. Using excess benzene keeps polyalkylation low.
x: Propylbenzene forms only as a minor product; the primary electrophile rearranges faster than it is captured. To make propylbenzene, acylate and then reduce.
Polyalkylation does occur, but a large excess of benzene makes the monoalkylated product the major one.
The chlorine of the alkyl halide leaves as AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>; it is not transferred to the ring.

q: Benzene reacts with 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl chloride) and AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What is the major monoalkylation product?
h: The neopentyl cation has no H on the carbon next to C<sup>+</sup>. What can shift instead, and where does the charge end up?
w: Ionization gives a primary (neopentyl) cation. The adjacent carbon is quaternary, so no hydride can shift, but a 1,2-methyl shift gives the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation, (CH3)2C+CH2CH3. That cation alkylates benzene to give (2-methylbutan-2-yl)benzene (tert-pentylbenzene, A).
x: The unrearranged neopentyl product needs the primary electrophile to be captured before it rearranges; the methyl shift to a tertiary cation is much faster.
The methyl shift gives a tertiary cation; moving on to this secondary attachment would require a further, uphill shift to a less stable cation.
Placing the ring on a CH<sub>2</sub> with the skeleton rearranged would still require capture at a primary carbon; Friedel–Crafts gives the tertiary attachment.

q: Which compound gives no Friedel–Crafts acylation product with CH<sub>3</sub>COCl/AlCl<sub>3</sub>?
h: Friedel–Crafts electrophiles are relatively weak. Which ring is too electron-poor to attack them?
w: Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation fail on rings bearing a strong deactivator (NO2, CN, SO3H, C=O, NR3+). Nitrobenzene is so unreactive that it is even used as a solvent for Friedel–Crafts reactions. Halobenzenes are only weakly deactivated and do react (bromobenzene gives 4-bromoacetophenone).
x: Toluene is activated and is acylated readily, mainly para.
Anisole is strongly activated and is acylated rapidly at the para position.
Halogens are weak deactivators; bromobenzene still undergoes Friedel–Crafts acylation, mostly para.

q: Aniline gives no Friedel–Crafts alkylation or acylation product with AlCl<sub>3</sub>, even though NH<sub>2</sub> is a strong activator. Why?
c: The nitrogen lone pair binds AlCl<sub>3</sub>, and the resulting –NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>–AlCl<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> group strongly deactivates the ring
The NH<sub>2</sub> group is too bulky for the electrophile to reach the ortho and para positions
Aniline is so reactive that the electrophile adds to every carbon and only polymer forms
AlCl<sub>3</sub> oxidizes the amino group to a nitro group, which then blocks the ring from reacting with the electrophile
h: An amine is a Lewis base and AlCl<sub>3</sub> is a Lewis acid. What forms first?
w: The amino nitrogen is a better Lewis base than the ring π system, so it coordinates to AlCl3. The resulting Lewis acid–base complex puts a formal positive charge on nitrogen and removes its lone pair from resonance, turning the strong activator into a strong deactivator, and it also consumes the catalyst. The same problem stops Friedel–Crafts reactions of alkylamino- and other basic amino-substituted rings.
x: The para position is not hindered at all; steric arguments cannot explain a complete failure.
Highly activated rings can polyalkylate, but aniline gives no ring product because the catalyst is captured by nitrogen.
AlCl<sub>3</sub> is a Lewis acid, not an oxidizing agent; it does not convert NH<sub>2</sub> to NO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene often gives di- and trialkylated products, but Friedel–Crafts acylation stops cleanly after one substitution. Why?
c: An alkyl group activates the ring, so the product reacts faster than benzene; an acyl group deactivates it, so it reacts slower
Acylium ions are too bulky to approach a ring that already has a substituent, while carbocations are small
AlCl<sub>3</sub> is consumed in alkylation but regenerated in acylation, so acylation runs out of electrophile
An acyl group activates the ring but blocks the ortho and para positions sterically, so no further substitution is possible on the ring
h: Compare how an alkyl group and a C=O group change the electron density of the product ring.
w: The alkylbenzene product carries an electron-donating alkyl group, so it is more reactive than the starting benzene and competes for the electrophile: polyalkylation. The aryl ketone product carries an electron-withdrawing C=O, so it is less reactive than the starting material, and acylation stops after one group. (In acylation the ketone also ties up a full equivalent of AlCl3.)
x: Steric bulk is not the reason; para positions are open in both products. The electronic effect of the new group decides.
It is the reverse: AlCl<sub>3</sub> is catalytic in alkylation, but in acylation it stays bound to the product ketone, so a full equivalent is needed.
An acyl group is a deactivator (δ+ carbonyl carbon on the ring), not an activator.

q: Which sequence is the best way to prepare propylbenzene from benzene?
h: A straight three-carbon chain cannot be attached through a primary carbocation. Which electrophile cannot rearrange?
w: Direct alkylation with a propyl halide or propene goes through (or toward) a cation that becomes isopropyl, giving cumene. The acylium ion CH3CH2C≡O+ does not rearrange, so acylation gives propiophenone, and Clemmensen reduction (Zn(Hg), HCl) converts the aryl C=O into CH2, giving propylbenzene. Wolff–Kishner (H2NNH2, KOH, heat) would work equally well for step 2.
x: The primary electrophile rearranges by a hydride shift, so the main product is isopropylbenzene, with polyalkylation as well.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone only to the secondary alcohol, 1-phenylpropan-1-ol, not to CH<sub>2</sub>.
Protonating propene gives the secondary (isopropyl) cation, so this makes cumene.

q: Which reagent converts compound X into compound Y in one step?
h: The ketone must become CH<sub>2</sub>, and the cyclic acetal must survive. Is an acetal stable to acid or to base?
w: Turning an aryl ketone C=O into CH2 calls for Clemmensen (strong acid) or Wolff–Kishner (strong base). The 1,3-dioxolane is an acetal, stable to base but hydrolyzed by aqueous acid. So the Wolff–Kishner reduction (H2NNH2, KOH, heat) removes the ketone oxygen while the acetal survives.
x: Hot aqueous HCl would hydrolyze the acetal to an aldehyde (which Clemmensen conditions could then also reduce), so Y would not be obtained.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone only to a secondary alcohol; it cannot remove the oxygen.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> also stops at the alcohol, and the aqueous acid workup can hydrolyze the acetal.

q: Which sequence is best for making 3-bromoaniline from benzene?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, NH<sub>3</sub>  3. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
h: The two groups end up meta. Which nitrogen group is a meta director: NO<sub>2</sub> or NH<sub>2</sub>?
w: To place Br meta to nitrogen, brominate while nitrogen is still a nitro group (a meta director), then reduce: nitration gives nitrobenzene, Br2/FeBr3 gives 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene, and Sn/HCl (then base) reduces NO2 to NH2 without touching the aryl bromide.
x: Reducing first gives aniline, a powerful ortho/para director that is brominated at the 2-, 4- and 6-positions; it also complexes FeBr<sub>3</sub>.
Bromobenzene is nitrated ortho/para (Br is an o/p director), so this route leads to 2- and 4-bromoaniline.
NaNH<sub>2</sub> converts bromobenzene to aniline through benzyne, and aniline is then brominated ortho/para, not meta.

q: Which sequence is best for making 4-nitrobenzoic acid from benzene?
c: 1. CH<sub>3</sub>Cl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  3. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. CH<sub>3</sub>Cl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  3. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. CH<sub>3</sub>Cl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  3. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. CH<sub>3</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  3. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: CO<sub>2</sub>H is a meta director, but the target is para. Which precursor of CO<sub>2</sub>H directs ortho/para?
w: A para relationship needs the nitration to happen while the carbon substituent is still an ortho/para director. Install CH3 (Friedel–Crafts), nitrate (para isomer separated from ortho), and only then oxidize the benzylic CH3 to CO2H with hot KMnO4.
x: Oxidizing first gives benzoic acid, a meta director, so nitration then gives 3-nitrobenzoic acid.
Friedel–Crafts alkylation fails on nitrobenzene, a strongly deactivated ring.
The acetyl group is a meta director, so nitration of acetophenone gives the 3-nitro isomer.

q: Which sequence gives 2-bromotoluene from toluene with the best selectivity?
c: 1. SO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. SO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
h: Bromination of toluene favors para. How can you temporarily occupy the para position with a group that comes off later?
w: Sulfonation of toluene goes mainly para. With para blocked, CH3 directs Br ortho to itself, and SO3H (a meta director) points to the same carbon: reinforcing. Because sulfonation is reversible, heating in dilute aqueous acid removes SO3H, leaving 2-bromotoluene. This is the classic blocking-group strategy.
x: Direct bromination gives mostly 4-bromotoluene; 2-bromotoluene is the minor isomer.
Bromine goes on first (mostly para), so the blocking group arrives too late to help; the final product is still mostly the 4-bromo isomer.
NBS with light brominates the benzylic CH<sub>3</sub> (giving benzyl bromide), not the ring.

q: Which sequence is best for making 1-bromo-3-propylbenzene from benzene?
c: 1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat  3. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
h: An alkyl group is ortho/para-directing, but the target is meta. What could the propyl group be while the bromine goes on?
w: The propyl chain must come from acylation (no rearrangement). The acyl group is a meta director, so brominate while it is still a ketone, giving 1-(3-bromophenyl)propan-1-one; then Clemmensen reduction turns C=O into CH2. The order acylate → brominate → reduce uses the ketone's directing effect before it is removed.
x: Bromobenzene is acylated para (Br is an o/p director), giving the 4-bromo isomer.
Reducing first gives propylbenzene, an ortho/para director, so bromination gives 2- and 4-bromopropylbenzene.
The propyl cation rearranges to isopropyl, and an alkyl group directs o/p anyway, so the meta target is not formed.

q: Which reagent does not reduce nitrobenzene to aniline?
h: Three of these are standard nitro reductions: a dissolving metal in acid, or catalytic hydrogenation.
w: Aryl nitro groups are reduced to amines by metals in acid (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, Zn/HCl; then base to free the amine from its ammonium salt) or by catalytic hydrogenation (H2, Pd/C or Pt). NaBH4 is a mild hydride donor for aldehydes and ketones; it does not reduce an aryl nitro group under ordinary conditions.
x: Tin in HCl is the classic nitro-to-amine reduction; NaOH frees the amine from the anilinium salt.
Catalytic hydrogenation reduces NO<sub>2</sub> to NH<sub>2</sub> cleanly (it would also reduce alkenes if present).
Iron in acid is the cheap industrial method for reducing nitroarenes.

q: Which sequence is best for making 4-chloro-3-nitrobenzoic acid from toluene?
c: 1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  3. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
1. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  3. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  3. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
h: Cl and CO<sub>2</sub>H are para to each other, and NO<sub>2</sub> is ortho to Cl but meta to CO<sub>2</sub>H. Which group should be in place when the nitro group goes on?
w: Chlorinate toluene (CH3 directs para) to get 4-chlorotoluene; oxidize CH3 to CO2H to get 4-chlorobenzoic acid. Now nitrate: Cl directs ortho to itself and CO2H directs meta to itself, and both point to the same carbon, so nitration cleanly gives 4-chloro-3-nitrobenzoic acid. Planning so that the last EAS step has reinforcing directors is the key.
x: Oxidizing first gives benzoic acid, a meta director, so chlorine goes meta: the Cl and CO<sub>2</sub>H would end up 1,3, not 1,4.
4-Nitrotoluene is chlorinated ortho to CH<sub>3</sub> (meta to NO<sub>2</sub>), and oxidation then gives 2-chloro-4-nitrobenzoic acid, not the target.
Zn(Hg)/HCl does not oxidize CH<sub>3</sub> to CO<sub>2</sub>H (it is a reducing agent), so the product is not a carboxylic acid.

q: What is the major product when 4-phenylbutanoyl chloride is treated with AlCl<sub>3</sub>?
h: The acylium ion and the ring are in the same molecule. Count the atoms in the ring that closes.
w: AlCl3 converts the acid chloride into an acylium ion, which is attacked by the ortho carbon of its own phenyl ring (intramolecular Friedel–Crafts acylation). The new ring contains the carbonyl carbon, three CH2 groups and two aromatic carbons: a six-membered ring, α-tetralone. Acylium ions do not rearrange, so the chain stays unbranched.
x: A five-membered ring with a methyl branch would require the chain to rearrange; acylium ions do not rearrange and the chain is unbranched.
This indanone also has a branched carbon skeleton that the starting chain cannot give without rearrangement.
A cyclopropyl ketone would need a C–C bond between the chain carbons, not an attack by the aromatic ring.

q: Which combination can not serve as a Friedel–Crafts alkylating agent for benzene?
h: Every Friedel–Crafts alkylation needs a carbocation (or a cation-like complex). Which halide would have to make an sp<sup>2</sup> carbocation?
w: Carbocation sources for Friedel–Crafts alkylation include alkyl halides + Lewis acid, alkenes + strong acid, and alcohols + strong acid. Vinyl (and aryl) halides do not work: ionizing an sp2 C–Cl bond would give a very unstable vinyl cation, and the C–Cl bond is strengthened by partial double-bond character.
x: 2-Chloropropane and AlCl<sub>3</sub> give the isopropyl cation (complex), which alkylates benzene to cumene.
Protonating isobutylene gives the tert-butyl cation, which alkylates benzene readily.
Protonated tert-butyl alcohol loses water to give the tert-butyl cation, a good Friedel–Crafts electrophile.

q: Which compound reacts fastest with NaOCH<sub>3</sub> in methanol by nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S<sub>N</sub>Ar)?
h: Two questions: where are the nitro groups relative to the leaving group, and which step of S<sub>N</sub>Ar is slow?
w: SNAr is addition–elimination: the nucleophile adds to the carbon bearing the leaving group to form an anionic Meisenheimer complex (slow step), then the halide leaves (fast). Nitro groups ortho and para to the leaving group delocalize the negative charge onto their oxygens. Fluorine's strong inductive pull makes the attacked carbon most electrophilic and stabilizes the anion, so 1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene is fastest; leaving-group order in SNAr is F ≫ Cl ≈ Br > I.
x: Same activation pattern, but Cl is less electronegative than F, so addition (the slow step) is slower.
Iodide is the best leaving group in S<sub>N</sub>2, but C–X bond breaking is not rate-determining in S<sub>N</sub>Ar; the weakly electronegative I gives the slowest addition.
Both nitro groups are meta to F, so the negative charge of the Meisenheimer complex cannot reach their oxygens; this compound reacts very slowly.

q: In S<sub>N</sub>Ar reactions of 1-halo-2,4-dinitrobenzenes, the aryl fluoride reacts much faster than the aryl iodide. What is the best explanation?
c: Addition is rate-determining, and fluorine’s inductive pull makes the ipso carbon more electrophilic and stabilizes the anion
The C–F bond is the weakest carbon–halogen bond, so it breaks fastest in the rate-determining step of the substitution reaction
