Fluoride is the most stable halide ion in methanol, so it is the best leaving group in every substitution reaction
Fluorine donates its lone pairs by resonance into the ring, stabilizing a carbocation intermediate on the ipso carbon
h: Which step of the addition–elimination mechanism is slow, and does that step break the C–halogen bond?
w: In SNAr the slow step is addition of the nucleophile, which destroys aromaticity and forms the Meisenheimer complex. The C–X bond is not broken in that step, so bond strength and leaving-group ability matter little. What matters is how electrophilic the ipso carbon is and how well the anionic intermediate is stabilized; fluorine, the most electronegative halogen, helps both. Loss of X− in the second step is fast because it restores aromaticity.
x: The C–F bond is the strongest carbon–halogen bond; F reacts fastest despite this because the bond is not broken in the slow step.
Fluoride is the poorest leaving group in S<sub>N</sub>2 reactions (a strongly solvated, basic ion); its S<sub>N</sub>Ar advantage comes from the addition step.
S<sub>N</sub>Ar involves an anionic intermediate, not a carbocation; resonance donation from F would destabilize the negative charge, not help it.

q: 1-Chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene reacts with NaOCH<sub>3</sub> to give 2,4-dinitroanisole. Which structure is the key intermediate on this pathway?
h: The nucleophile adds first and the chloride leaves second. Which carbon must carry both OCH<sub>3</sub> and Cl at the same time?
w: SNAr is addition–elimination. Methoxide adds to the carbon bearing Cl, giving a resonance-stabilized anion, the Meisenheimer complex, with an sp3 carbon bonded to both OCH3 and Cl. The negative charge is delocalized to the carbons ortho and para to that carbon, which carry the nitro groups, and from there onto their oxygens. Chloride then leaves and aromaticity returns.
x: A benzyne forms only from unactivated aryl halides with very strong bases such as NaNH<sub>2</sub>; with nitro activation and methoxide, addition–elimination is far faster. Benzyne would also scramble the product position.
Aryl cations are extremely unstable (an empty sp<sup>2</sup> orbital in the ring plane); aryl halides do not ionize in an S<sub>N</sub>1 process.
Here methoxide has added to a carbon that bears H, not Cl; this adduct cannot lose chloride to give 2,4-dinitroanisole.

q: 1,2-Difluoro-4-nitrobenzene reacts with one equivalent of NaOCH<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Both fluorines are leaving groups. For each, ask whether the nitro group is ortho, meta or para to it.
w: SNAr needs the electron-withdrawing group ortho or para to the leaving group so the Meisenheimer anion can be delocalized onto it. The fluorine at C1 is para to NO2; the fluorine at C2 is meta. Methoxide therefore replaces the C1 fluorine, giving 2-fluoro-1-methoxy-4-nitrobenzene. The remaining fluorine is meta to NO2, and the new OCH3 donates electrons, so a second substitution is slow.
x: This replaces the fluorine meta to NO<sub>2</sub>; its Meisenheimer complex cannot place the negative charge on the nitro group.
Nitrite can be displaced in some S<sub>N</sub>Ar reactions, but here a fluorine para to a strong EWG is far more reactive than NO<sub>2</sub> activated only by fluorines.
Only one equivalent of methoxide is used, and the remaining fluorine is meta to NO<sub>2</sub>, so double substitution is not the major result.

q: Which feature is required for an aryl halide to undergo nucleophilic aromatic substitution by the addition–elimination (S<sub>N</sub>Ar) mechanism under mild conditions?
c: A strong electron-withdrawing group ortho or para to the leaving group
A strong electron-donating group ortho or para to the leaving group
A strong electron-withdrawing group meta to the leaving group
A hydrogen ortho to the leaving group and a very strong base such as NaNH<sub>2</sub>
h: The intermediate carries a negative charge in the ring. Where can that charge go?
w: Addition of the nucleophile puts a negative charge on the carbons ortho and para to the attacked carbon. An EWG such as NO2, CN or C=O at one of those positions delocalizes the charge by resonance, lowering the energy of the Meisenheimer complex and of the transition state leading to it. A meta EWG can only help inductively, and donors make things worse.
x: Electron donors destabilize the anionic intermediate and shut down S<sub>N</sub>Ar.
A meta EWG cannot accept the negative charge by resonance, so it activates only weakly.
An ortho H plus NaNH<sub>2</sub> describes the elimination–addition (benzyne) mechanism, not S<sub>N</sub>Ar.

q: Chlorobenzene labeled with 14C at the carbon bearing Cl (carbon a) is treated with KNH2 in liquid NH3. Where is the label in the aniline produced?
c: About half at the carbon bearing NH<sub>2</sub> and half at a carbon ortho to NH<sub>2</sub>
All of it at the carbon bearing NH<sub>2</sub>
About half at the carbon bearing NH<sub>2</sub> and half at the carbon para to NH<sub>2</sub>
All of it at a carbon ortho to NH<sub>2</sub>
h: Unactivated aryl halide plus amide ion: think elimination first, then addition to an intermediate with two equivalent-looking ends.
w: Amide removes the H ortho to Cl and chloride leaves, giving benzyne with the label on one of the two triple-bond carbons. NH2− adds to either end about equally (the isotope barely matters). Adding at the labeled carbon puts the label at C–NH2; adding at the other end puts it ortho to NH2. This roughly 1:1 result is the classic evidence for the benzyne (elimination–addition) mechanism and for cine substitution.
x: That is what a direct substitution (S<sub>N</sub>Ar or S<sub>N</sub>2-like) would give; the scrambled label shows a benzyne intermediate.
The benzyne triple bond joins the labeled carbon and the carbon next to it, so the label can end up only at C1 or ortho, never para.
Addition to the labeled carbon is just as likely as addition to its neighbor, so about half of the label stays at C–NH<sub>2</sub>.

q: 4-Chlorotoluene is heated with NaNH<sub>2</sub> in liquid NH<sub>3</sub>. What is the product?
h: Draw the benzyne first. Which two carbons form the triple bond, and can NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> add to either one?
w: Amide removes an H ortho to Cl (C3), and loss of Cl− gives 4-methylbenzyne with the triple bond between C3 and C4. The methyl group is remote from both ends and barely biases the addition, so NH2− adds to either carbon: at C4 gives 4-methylaniline (p-toluidine), at C3 gives 3-methylaniline (m-toluidine). Result: a mixture of the meta and para isomers.
x: Only direct substitution would give the para isomer alone; the benzyne can be attacked at either end.
Addition at C3 is only half the story; attack at C4 is about as likely.
The triple bond involves C3 and C4, so NH<sub>2</sub> cannot reach C2 (ortho to CH<sub>3</sub>).

q: 2-Bromoanisole is treated with NaNH<sub>2</sub> in liquid NH<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Only one H is ortho to Br. After the benzyne forms, ask which carbanion is more stable: one next to the electronegative OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon, or one farther away?
w: The only H ortho to Br is at C3, so elimination gives 3-methoxybenzyne (triple bond between the old C2 and C3, with OCH3 next to C2). NH2− adds in the ring plane. Addition at the old C3 (the carbon farther from OCH3) leaves the aryl anion at the old C2, right next to the inductively withdrawing oxygen-bearing carbon, which stabilizes it. Protonation gives 3-methoxyaniline essentially as the only product.
x: Direct replacement of Br would give 2-methoxyaniline, but the reaction goes through benzyne, and the inductive effect of OCH<sub>3</sub> sends NH<sub>2</sub> to the other end.
The benzyne triple bond involves C2 and C3 only, so NH<sub>2</sub> cannot end up para to OCH<sub>3</sub>.
The two ends of 3-methoxybenzyne are not equivalent; the anion next to the OCH<sub>3</sub>-bearing carbon is strongly favored, so addition is highly selective.

q: 3-Chlorotoluene reacts with KNH<sub>2</sub> in liquid NH<sub>3</sub>. How many different constitutional isomers of methylaniline (toluidine) can form?
h: Count the hydrogens ortho to Cl: each one can give a different benzyne, and each benzyne has two ends.
w: Number CH3 as C1 and Cl as C3. The hydrogens ortho to Cl are at C2 and C4, so two benzynes can form: C2≡C3 and C3≡C4. Benzyne C2≡C3: NH2 at C2 (2-methylaniline) or C3 (3-methylaniline). Benzyne C3≡C4: NH2 at C3 (3-methylaniline) or C4 (4-methylaniline). Together: ortho, meta and para toluidine, 3 isomers.
x: Two would be right if only one benzyne formed; but Cl has two different ortho hydrogens (C2 and C4).
One isomer would mean direct substitution; benzyne chemistry gives cine products as well.
There are only three toluidine isomers (ortho, meta, para), and each arises here; a fourth is not possible.

q: 2-Bromo-1,3-dimethylbenzene is treated with NaNH<sub>2</sub> in liquid NH<sub>3</sub> under the conditions that convert bromobenzene to aniline. What happens?
c: No substitution occurs, because there is no hydrogen ortho to Br, so no benzyne can form
2,6-Dimethylaniline forms by direct addition–elimination at the carbon bearing Br
A mixture of 2,6-dimethylaniline and 2,4-dimethylaniline forms by way of a benzyne intermediate
3,5-Dimethylaniline forms because NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> adds to the carbon para to Br
h: Benzyne formation starts with removal of a proton. Which proton?
w: The elimination–addition mechanism begins with amide removing an aryl H ortho to the halogen. In 2-bromo-1,3-dimethylbenzene both ortho positions carry CH3 groups, so no benzyne can form. Without nitro-type activation, SNAr is not possible either, so no substitution occurs. Such labeling/blocking experiments helped prove the benzyne mechanism.
x: S<sub>N</sub>Ar needs strong EWGs ortho/para to Br; methyl groups are donors, so addition–elimination does not occur.
A benzyne would need an H on a carbon next to C–Br; both neighbors carry CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
Amide does not add to an ordinary aromatic C–H carbon; nothing activates that position.

q: Benzyne is generated from 2-(trimethylsilyl)phenyl triflate and CsF in the presence of furan. What product is trapped?
h: Benzyne has a strained, reactive π bond, and furan is a diene.
w: Benzyne is a very reactive dienophile: its in-plane π bond is weak because of poor sp2–sp2 overlap. Furan acts as the diene in a Diels–Alder [4+2] cycloaddition, bridging C2 and C5 of furan across the benzyne carbons to give 1,4-dihydro-1,4-epoxynaphthalene, an oxygen-bridged bicyclic alkene.
x: A 2-arylfuran would need substitution at a furan C–H; benzyne reacts with furan by cycloaddition, not substitution.
A 3-arylfuran also implies substitution, and attack at furan C3 is not the pathway; the furan acts as a diene.
A [2+2] adduct is not formed with a good diene such as furan; the thermally allowed [4+2] path dominates.

q: In the second step of bromination of benzene, the arenium ion loses H<sup>+</sup> rather than adding Br<sup>−</sup> (as an alkene-derived carbocation would). Why?
c: Loss of H<sup>+</sup> restores the aromatic sextet; addition of Br<sup>−</sup> would give a nonaromatic cyclohexadiene
Br<sup>−</sup> is a poor nucleophile in the presence of FeBr<sub>3</sub>, so it cannot add to any carbocation
The arenium ion has no carbon able to accept a nucleophile, since every carbon has a full octet of electrons
Loss of H<sup>+</sup> is the rate-determining step, so it must be the step that happens
h: Compare the two possible products of the second step. Which one is aromatic?
w: Both pathways are possible in principle, but substitution gives back the aromatic ring (about 150 kJ/mol of resonance stabilization), while addition would trap the ring as a nonaromatic cyclohexadiene. The substitution product is far more stable, so the arenium ion is deprotonated (by FeBr4−), and the overall reaction is substitution, not addition.
x: Br<sup>−</sup> (as FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>) is available; the choice is driven by product stability, not by a lack of nucleophile.
The arenium ion is a delocalized carbocation with three electron-deficient carbons; a nucleophile could bond to them, but that product would lose aromaticity.
Deprotonation is the fast step; the slow step is formation of the arenium ion.

q: Benzene and hexadeuteriobenzene (C<sub>6</sub>D<sub>6</sub>) are nitrated at essentially the same rate (k<sub>H</sub>/k<sub>D</sub> ≈ 1). What does this show?
c: The C–H bond is not broken in the rate-determining step; forming the arenium ion is slow and losing H<sup>+</sup> is fast
The C–H bond breaks in the rate-determining step, so the reaction is a single concerted step
Deprotonation of the arenium ion is rate-determining, but C–D and C–H bonds break at equal rates
Formation of NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> is rate-determining, so the arene never takes part in the slow step under any reaction conditions
h: A primary kinetic isotope effect (k<sub>H</sub>/k<sub>D</sub> of about 2–7) appears when the C–H bond breaks in the slow step. What does its absence tell you?
w: If C–H(D) bond cleavage were in the rate-determining step, the stronger C–D bond would slow C6D6 noticeably (a primary isotope effect). kH/kD ≈ 1 means the proton is lost after the slow step: the two-step mechanism, with slow formation of the σ complex and fast loss of H+, fits; a concerted one-step substitution does not.
x: A concerted mechanism that breaks C–H in the slow step would show a large primary isotope effect, which is not observed.
C–D bonds have lower zero-point energy and break more slowly than C–H bonds; if deprotonation were slow, k<sub>H</sub>/k<sub>D</sub> would be well above 1.
The rate does depend on the arene (activated rings react faster), so the arene is in the slow step; the experiment only rules out C–H cleavage in that step.

q: Which compound can give only one constitutional isomer when one ring hydrogen is replaced by Br (Br2/FeBr3)?
h: Count the sets of symmetry-equivalent aromatic hydrogens in each compound.
w: Each set of equivalent ring hydrogens gives one possible monobromination product. p-Xylene has four equivalent ring H (each is ortho to one CH3 and meta to the other), so only 2-bromo-1,4-dimethylbenzene can form. o-Xylene has two sets (3- and 4-positions), m-xylene three (2-, 4- and 5-), and ethylbenzene three (ortho, meta, para).
x: o-Xylene has two kinds of ring H (next to a methyl, and one carbon farther away), giving 3-bromo- and 4-bromo-o-xylene.
m-Xylene has three kinds of ring H (between the methyls, ortho/para, and meta to both).
Ethylbenzene has ortho, meta and para ring hydrogens: three possible isomers.

q: Naphthalene is nitrated with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Where does the nitro group mainly go, and why?
c: carbon a, because its σ complex has more resonance forms that keep one benzene ring fully aromatic
carbon b, because its σ complex has more resonance forms that keep one benzene ring fully aromatic
carbon b, because attack there avoids steric strain with the hydrogen on the other ring
carbon a, because its σ complex keeps both rings fully aromatic
h: Draw the σ complex for each site and count the forms in which the other ring is still an intact benzene ring.
w: Attack at C1 (a, the α position) gives an allylic cation that can be delocalized while the second ring remains an intact benzene ring in two resonance forms; attack at C2 (b, β) allows only one such form. The α σ complex is lower in energy, so nitration (a kinetically controlled, irreversible reaction) gives mainly 1-nitronaphthalene.
x: Attack at C2 gives only one resonance form with an intact benzene ring, so its σ complex is less stable.
The peri H interaction disfavors C1 only for bulky or reversible substitutions (such as sulfonation at high temperature); nitration is fast, irreversible and goes to C1.
In any σ complex the attacked ring loses its aromaticity; only the other ring can stay benzenoid.

q: Which structure is the enol tautomer of cyclohexanone?
h: Tautomers differ only in where one H and one π bond sit: the H moves from the α-carbon to the carbonyl oxygen.
w: Keto–enol tautomerism moves one α-H to the carbonyl O and moves the π bond from C=O to C=C between the former carbonyl carbon and the α-carbon. The enol of cyclohexanone is cyclohex-1-en-1-ol, with the OH on an alkene carbon.
x: Here the OH is on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon next to the C=C (an allylic alcohol). It is an isomer, but not an enol, and it cannot form from cyclohexanone by a single proton shift.
This is the enolate, the conjugate base. It has one fewer H than cyclohexanone, so it is not a tautomer.
Cyclohexene oxide has the same formula (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O) but a different carbon–oxygen connectivity; it is a constitutional isomer, not a tautomer.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone can form two different enols. Which enol is present in the larger amount at equilibrium?
h: Enols are alkenes. Which alkene-stability rule decides between the two enols?
w: An enol is an alkene, so the more substituted C=C is more stable (Zaitsev-type stability). Enolization toward C2 puts the C=C between C1 and the methyl-bearing C2, giving a tetrasubstituted enol. Enolization toward C6 gives only a trisubstituted C=C, so that enol is the minor one.
x: This is a real enol of 2-methylcyclohexanone, but its C=C is only trisubstituted, so it is less stable than the tetrasubstituted enol.
The OH is on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, so this is an allylic alcohol, not an enol; it is not a tautomer of the ketone.
The C=C is exocyclic to a carbon that does not carry the OH, so this is an allylic alcohol, not an enol.

q: Acetone contains far less than 0.01% enol at equilibrium, yet pure 2,4-pentanedione is roughly 80% enol. Which statement best explains the large enol content of 2,4-pentanedione?
c: The enol C=C is conjugated with the second C=O, and the enol OH forms a six-membered intramolecular hydrogen bond to that C=O.
An O–H bond is stronger than a C–H bond, which makes every enol more stable than its keto form; acetone simply enolizes too slowly to reach equilibrium.
The central CH<sub>2</sub> has a pK<sub>a</sub> near 9, so the compound exists mainly as its enolate, which is counted as enol.
Water and other protic solvents hydrogen-bond strongly to the enol OH, which is why the enol content is highest in polar solvents.
h: Look at the enol drawn on the right. What can its OH and C=C do with the remaining carbonyl that the enol of acetone cannot?
w: For simple ketones the keto form wins because a C=O π bond is much stronger than a C=C π bond. The enol of a β-diketone gains two extra stabilizations: the C=C–C=O system is conjugated, and the OH is held in a six-membered ring by an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the other carbonyl O. Together these outweigh the usual preference for the keto form.
x: If enols were generally more stable, acetone would be mostly enol at equilibrium; acid or base catalysis establishes that equilibrium quickly, and it lies far on the keto side.
Acidity (pK<sub>a</sub>) describes the enolate, not the neutral enol; with no base present the compound is neutral, and the enol/keto ratio is a separate equilibrium.
The opposite is observed: polar protic solvents compete for the hydrogen bond and lower the enol content (about 15% in water), which supports the intramolecular H-bond explanation.

q: Which labeled hydrogen-bearing carbon in ethyl acetoacetate carries the most acidic hydrogens?
h: Which carbon's conjugate base can spread the negative charge onto two carbonyl oxygens?
w: Removing H from carbon a, between the ketone and the ester C=O, gives an anion delocalized onto both carbonyl oxygens (pKa about 11). The methyl next to the ketone (d) is stabilized by only one C=O (pKa about 20), and the ethyl carbons (b, c) are not α to any carbonyl.
x: Carbon b is bonded to the ester oxygen, not to a carbonyl carbon; its anion has no resonance stabilization.
The terminal CH<sub>3</sub> of the ethyl group is an ordinary alkane-type C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> about 50).
The ketone methyl is α to one carbonyl only (pKa about 20); it is roughly a billion times less acidic than a.

q: Rank the compounds from least to most acidic (most acidic α-hydrogen in each).
h: Count the carbonyl groups that can share the negative charge, then ask whether a ketone C=O or an ester C=O is better at stabilizing an adjacent anion.
w: Typical pKa values: ethyl acetate (I) about 25, acetone (II) about 19–20, diethyl malonate (IV) about 13, 2,4-pentanedione (III) about 9. So I < II < IV < III. The ester OR group donates electrons into its own C=O by resonance, which makes that C=O less able to accept the enolate's negative charge; this is why esters are less acidic than ketones, and why a malonic ester (two ester groups) is less acidic than a β-diketone (two ketone groups).
x: This puts the ester above the ketone. Ester enolates are less stable because the alkoxy O already donates into the C=O, so an ester (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is less acidic than a ketone (≈ 20).

This makes the malonic ester more acidic than the β-diketone. Each ester C=O stabilizes the anion less than a ketone C=O does, so malonate (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 13) is less acidic than 2,4-pentanedione (≈ 9).
Two ester carbonyls still beat one ketone carbonyl: diethyl malonate (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 13) is much more acidic than acetone (≈ 20).

q: Which labeled position carries the most acidic hydrogens?
h: Two of the labeled carbons are α to a carbonyl. Which type of carbonyl stabilizes an enolate better?
w: Carbons a and b are both α to a carbonyl, but a is α to a ketone (pKa about 19) while b is α to an ester (pKa about 25). The ester OCH3 donates into its own C=O, making the ester enolate less stable. So a is most acidic. Neither carbon is between two carbonyls (the carbonyls are 1,4-related), so there is no β-dicarbonyl effect.
x: Carbon b is α to the ester carbonyl; ester α-H's (pKa ≈ 25) are about a million times less acidic than ketone α-H's.
The OCH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens are on a carbon attached to oxygen, not to a carbonyl carbon; their conjugate base has no resonance stabilization.
Aryl C–H bonds have pK<sub>a</sub> near 43; the anion is in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital perpendicular to the π system, so the C=O cannot stabilize it.

q: What is the major product of this sequence?
h: LDA is a strong, bulky base used cold and in a slight excess of base. Which α-H does it remove fastest, and is that step reversible?
w: LDA at −78 °C deprotonates quickly and irreversibly at the less hindered α-carbon (C6, a CH2), forming the kinetic enolate. SN2 attack on allyl bromide at that carbon gives 2-allyl-6-methylcyclohexanone (cis/trans mixture).
x: Alkylation at the methyl-bearing carbon comes from the more substituted (thermodynamic) enolate, which forms under equilibrating conditions such as NaOEt/EtOH, not with LDA at −78 °C.
Lithium enolates react with alkyl halides at carbon, not oxygen; the C-alkylated ketone is the normal product with soft electrophiles such as allyl bromide.
One equivalent of LDA forms one enolate per ketone; dialkylation at both α-carbons would require a second deprotonation and a second equivalent of halide.

q: LDA in THF at −78 °C converts 2-methylcyclohexanone mainly into the less substituted enolate, while NaOEt in ethanol at 25 °C gives mainly the more substituted enolate. Which explanation is correct?
c: LDA removes the less hindered H fast and irreversibly; with NaOEt, proton transfer is reversible, so the more stable, more substituted enolate builds up.
LDA removes the more acidic H on the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, while NaOEt removes the less acidic H next to the methyl group because ethoxide is a weaker base.
Both bases give the same enolate mixture at first, but at −78 °C the more substituted enolate isomerizes to the less substituted one, which is more stable at low temperature.
Ethoxide is bulkier than LDA, so it can only reach the H on the methyl-bearing carbon, which is the less hindered position.
h: Compare pK<sub>a</sub> values: diisopropylamine about 36, ethanol about 16, ketone α-H about 19. Which base deprotonates reversibly?
w: LDA (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 36) deprotonates the ketone completely and irreversibly; the bulky base removes the more accessible H on C6 faster, and at −78 °C nothing equilibrates, so the kinetic (less substituted) enolate is formed. Ethoxide (EtOH pKa ≈ 16) is too weak to deprotonate completely (ketone pKa ≈ 19), so ketone, enolates and ethanol keep exchanging protons and the more substituted, more stable enolate dominates at equilibrium.
x: The two kinds of α-H have similar acidity; the difference comes from the rate of removal (sterics) versus the stability of the product enolate, not from one H being much more acidic.
At −78 °C there is no isomerization, and the less substituted enolate is the less stable one; low temperature preserves the kinetic product.
LDA, with two isopropyl groups on N, is far bulkier than ethoxide, and the methyl-bearing carbon is the more hindered position, not the less hindered one.

q: An enolate is alkylated with each of these halides. Which halide gives the poorest yield of C-alkylated product?
h: Enolate alkylation is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction. Which substrate cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2?
w: Enolate alkylation follows SN2 rules: methyl, primary, allylic and benzylic halides work well. A tertiary halide (2-bromo-2-methylpropane) cannot be attacked from the back side, and the strongly basic enolate instead causes E2 elimination to 2-methylpropene.
x: Methyl halides are the best S<sub>N</sub>2 substrates; enolate methylation with CH<sub>3</sub>I is fast and clean.
Benzylic halides are primary and their S<sub>N</sub>2 transition state is stabilized by the ring; they alkylate enolates very well.
Allylic halides are primary and activated toward S<sub>N</sub>2 by the adjacent π bond; they are excellent alkylating agents.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylcyclohexanone is treated with one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid?
h: Under acid, the halogen reacts with the enol. Which enol of this ketone is present in greater amount?
w: In acid the electrophile Br2 is attacked by the enol, and the more substituted (more stable) enol predominates. Bromination therefore occurs at the more substituted α-carbon, giving 2-bromo-2-methylcyclohexanone. The first Br withdraws electron density, making the carbonyl O less basic, so a second enolization (and a second bromination) is slow; acid-catalyzed halogenation stops after one halogen.
x: Bromination at C6 goes through the less substituted enol, which is the minor enol under acid; this product dominates under kinetic (LDA-type) conditions, not acid catalysis.
Acid-catalyzed halogenation stops after monohalogenation because the α-Br slows further enol formation; polyhalogenation is typical of base, not acid.
The methyl carbon is β to the carbonyl, not α; it cannot become part of an enol and is not brominated.

q: 1-Cyclohexylethan-1-one is treated with excess Br<sub>2</sub> in aqueous NaOH, and the mixture is then acidified. Which organic product (other than CHBr<sub>3</sub>) is isolated?
h: This is the haloform reaction. What happens to a CX<sub>3</sub> group attached to a carbonyl when hydroxide is present?
w: Under base each α-Br makes the remaining H on that carbon more acidic, so the methyl group is brominated three times to give a CBr3 ketone. Hydroxide then adds to the C=O, and the tetrahedral intermediate expels −CBr3 (stabilized by three Br). Proton transfer gives CHBr3 and the carboxylate, which acidification converts to cyclohexanecarboxylic acid.
x: Base-promoted halogenation does not stop at one halogen: the bromomethyl ketone is more acidic than the starting ketone and reacts faster.
Single halogenation at the more substituted α-carbon is the acid-catalyzed outcome; under base with excess Br<sub>2</sub> the methyl group is perhalogenated.
The tribromomethyl ketone is an intermediate; in aqueous NaOH it undergoes acyl substitution, losing <sup>−</sup>CBr<sub>3</sub> as the leaving group.

q: Acid-catalyzed bromination of acetone can be stopped cleanly at bromoacetone, but base-promoted bromination cannot: it continues to CH<sub>3</sub>COCBr<sub>3</sub>. Which single effect of the first α-Br explains both observations?
c: Its electron withdrawal makes the carbonyl O less basic (slowing acid-catalyzed enol formation) but makes the remaining α-H on that carbon more acidic (speeding enolate formation).
Its electron donation by resonance makes the carbonyl O more basic (speeding enol formation) but makes the α-H less acidic (slowing enolate formation).
Its large size blocks the approach of Br<sub>2</sub> to the enol in acid, while hydroxide is small enough to reach the remaining α-H.
It converts the ketone into an acid bromide, which cannot enolize in acid but enolizes rapidly in base.
h: The rate-determining step differs: forming the enol (after C=O protonation) in acid, removing α-H to form the enolate in base. How does an electronegative substituent affect each?
w: The rate-determining step in acid needs the carbonyl O to be protonated first. An α-Br is inductively electron-withdrawing, which lowers the basicity of the C=O oxygen, so enol formation from bromoacetone is slower than from acetone, and the reaction stops at one Br. In base the rate-determining step is removal of an α-H; the same electron withdrawal stabilizes the resulting enolate, so the CH2Br hydrogens are more acidic than those of acetone and each bromination accelerates the next, giving CBr3.
x: Resonance donation by Br into the C=O is minor here; the dominant effect is inductive withdrawal, and the observed trends (faster in base, slower in acid) are the opposite of what this choice predicts.
Steric bulk would slow halogenation in both media; it cannot explain why base halogenation speeds up after each Br.
The C–Br bond is on the α-carbon, not on the carbonyl carbon; bromoacetone is an α-halo ketone, not an acid bromide.

q: Each optically active compound is stirred in NaOH/H<sub>2</sub>O at 25 °C. Which one loses its optical activity?
h: Racemization through an enolate requires a stereocenter that both is an α-carbon and carries an H.
w: Base removes an α-H to form a planar enolate; reprotonation occurs equally from either face. Only a stereocenter that is α to the carbonyl and bears an H is destroyed this way. Only the ketone whose stereocenter is the α-carbon bearing an H racemizes.
x: The stereocenter is the β-carbon. Enolization involves only the α-CH<sub>2</sub>, so the configuration at the β-carbon is unchanged.
This stereocenter is α to the carbonyl but has no H (it carries CH<sub>3</sub>, ethyl and phenyl), so no enolate can form there.
This alcohol has no carbonyl group, so it cannot form an enol or enolate; the C–H at the stereocenter is not acidic.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is stirred in D<sub>2</sub>O containing a catalytic amount of NaOD until no further change occurs. How many hydrogens are replaced by deuterium?
h: Only hydrogens on carbons directly attached to the C=O carbon exchange. Count them on both sides.
w: Exchange occurs through the enolate, so only α-H's are replaced. C2 has one H and C6 has two H's: 3 hydrogens become D. The methyl H's are on a β-carbon and do not exchange; neither do the ring H's at C3–C5.
x: This counts the methyl group or another non-α position. The methyl carbon is attached to C2, not to the carbonyl carbon, so its H's are β-H's.
Five would include all H's on C2, C3 and C6; C3 is a β-carbon and its H's are not acidic.
Two counts only C6. C2 also has one α-H; it is more hindered but still exchanges through the more substituted enolate under equilibrating conditions.

q: Propanal is treated with dilute NaOH at 5 °C. What is the major organic product?
h: Form the enolate at the α-carbon of one molecule and let it add to the C=O of a second molecule. At low temperature, does the product lose water?
w: The enolate forms at C2 (the α-carbon) of one propanal and adds to the carbonyl carbon of another. Protonation gives the β-hydroxy aldehyde 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal: the new C–C bond joins the α-carbon of one unit to the former carbonyl carbon of the other, so the methyl ends up on C2. In the cold, dehydration is slow, so aldol addition (not condensation) is the result.
x: This links the terminal CH<sub>3</sub> carbon to the carbonyl carbon. The CH<sub>3</sub> of propanal is β, not α, so it is not deprotonated; the nucleophile is C2.
This is the aldol condensation product, which forms on heating. At 5 °C the β-hydroxy aldehyde is the main product.
A 1,3-dicarbonyl like this comes from a Claisen-type acyl substitution, which needs a leaving group (an ester). An aldehyde has none, so its enolate adds to the C=O and gives an alcohol.

q: Butanal is heated with aqueous NaOH. What is the major organic product?
h: Two four-carbon units join α-carbon to carbonyl carbon; with heat, water is lost between the α- and β-carbons. Which group ends up on C2 of the product?
w: The enolate (C2 of butanal) adds to the C=O of a second butanal. The β-hydroxy aldehyde then dehydrates by E1cB to the conjugated enal. C2 of the product carries the ethyl group (what remains of the enolate unit), and C3 carries the propyl group of the electrophile: (E)-2-ethylhex-2-enal, C8H14O.
x: This is the aldol addition product. On heating with base it loses water to give the conjugated enal.
A straight-chain product would require the terminal carbon to act as the nucleophile; only the α-carbon (C2) is deprotonated, so the new C–C bond creates a branch.
The branches are swapped: the alkyl group on the α-carbon must be the ethyl (C3–C4 of the enolate unit), and the propyl comes from the electrophile side.

q: Acetophenone and benzaldehyde are heated with NaOH in ethanol. What is the major product?
h: Only one partner has α-hydrogens. Which one forms the enolate, and which carbonyl is the better electrophile?
w: Benzaldehyde has no α-H, so only acetophenone forms an enolate. Aldehydes are more electrophilic than ketones, so the enolate adds to benzaldehyde (crossed aldol, Claisen–Schmidt). Heating dehydrates the β-hydroxy ketone to the conjugated (E)-chalcone, where the C=C is conjugated with both the C=O and a ring.
x: This is the β-hydroxy ketone formed first. With heat and base it dehydrates (E1cB) to the extended conjugated enone.
This is the self-condensation product of acetophenone. Ketones are much poorer electrophiles than aldehydes, so the enolate prefers benzaldehyde.
Benzoin forms from two benzaldehydes with cyanide or thiazolium catalysts, not by an enolate reaction; it also contains no carbons from acetophenone.

q: Which pair, treated with NaOH, gives one major crossed aldol product rather than a mixture?
c: Ethanal with propanal (mixed in equal amounts)
Propanal with butanal (mixed in equal amounts)
h: A clean crossed aldol needs exactly one partner that can form an enolate, and the other partner must be a good electrophile.
w: A crossed aldol is selective when one partner cannot enolize. Benzaldehyde has no α-H, so it can act only as the electrophile; adding propanal slowly keeps its concentration low, so its enolate meets mostly benzaldehyde rather than another propanal. When both partners have α-H's, four aldol products are possible.
x: Both aldehydes have α-H's and both are good electrophiles, so two enolates add to two carbonyls: up to four aldol products.
Both partners are enolizable aldehydes of similar reactivity; the mixture gives four products.
Neither aldehyde has an α-H (the tert-butyl carbon and the ring carbon carry none), so no enolate forms and no aldol reaction occurs.

q: Which pair of carbonyl compounds gives the target by a crossed aldol condensation (NaOH, heat)?
h: Break the C=C. The carbon bonded to the ring came from a C=O; the other alkene carbon was the α-carbon of the enolate partner.
w: Disconnect the C=C of the enone. The alkene carbon bearing the phenyl group was the carbonyl carbon of the electrophile (benzaldehyde). The other alkene carbon, which carries the CH3 and the C(=O)CH2CH3, was the α-carbon of the ketone: CH3CH2C(=O)CH2CH3, i.e., 3-pentanone. Benzaldehyde (no α-H) and 3-pentanone (symmetric, one kind of enolate) give a single product, C12H14O.
x: 2-Butanone would give either PhCH=CHC(=O)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (via its CH<sub>3</sub>) or PhCH=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)C(=O)CH<sub>3</sub> (via its CH<sub>2</sub>); neither has both the α-methyl and the ethyl ketone of the target.
With acetophenone as the enolate and butanal as the electrophile, the phenyl ends up on the carbonyl carbon (PhC(=O)CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), not on the alkene.
Phenylacetaldehyde would place a CH<sub>2</sub> between the ring and the alkene, and it is itself enolizable, giving mixtures.

q: Octane-2,7-dione is heated with aqueous NaOH. What is the major product of the intramolecular aldol condensation?
h: List each possible enolate carbon and count the ring size it would form by attacking the other C=O. Which ring size is favored?
w: Number the chain C1–C8 (C=O at C2 and C7). An enolate at C1 attacking C7 would close a seven-membered ring; an enolate at C3 attacking C7 closes a five-membered ring (C3, C4, C5, C6, C7). Five- and six-membered rings form much faster and are less strained, so the C3 enolate wins. After dehydration the C=C sits in the ring, conjugated with the acetyl group: 1-acetyl-2-methylcyclopentene, C8H12O (starting material minus H2O).
x: This seven-membered ring forms from the terminal CH<sub>3</sub> enolate attacking the far carbonyl. Seven-membered rings close more slowly and are more strained than the available five-membered ring.
This six-membered enone has only seven carbons; it is the product from heptane-2,6-dione, not octane-2,7-dione.
A six-membered ring with these substituents needs nine carbons (it would come from nonane-2,8-dione); the ring is one carbon too large for this substrate.

q: Under NaOH and heat, the β-hydroxy ketone shown loses water to form the conjugated enone. By which mechanism does this dehydration occur?
c: E1cB: deprotonation at the α-carbon gives an enolate, which expels hydroxide
E2: hydroxide removes the α-H while water leaves in the same step
E1: the OH leaves first to form a carbocation, which then loses the α-H to form the C=C
S<sub>N</sub>2: hydroxide displaces the OH group, and the product then isomerizes
h: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group. What stabilized intermediate can form before it leaves?
w: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, but the α-H is acidic (pKa ≈ 20). Base first removes the α-H to give a resonance-stabilized enolate (the conjugate base); the enolate then pushes out −OH from the β-carbon, forming the conjugated C=C. Leaving from the conjugate base in a second step is the E1cB mechanism.
x: A concerted E2 would require hydroxide to leave without help; the stabilized enolate forms first because the α-H is acidic, so the steps are separate.
Carbocation formation needs acid to turn OH into a good leaving group (H<sub>2</sub>O); under basic conditions no carbocation forms.
Substitution of OH by OH would not remove water or create a C=C; an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction cannot form the enone.

q: Which compound cannot form an enolate and therefore can act only as the electrophile in an aldol reaction?
h: Look at the carbon(s) directly attached to the carbonyl carbon. Do they carry any H?
w: An enolate requires an H on an α-carbon. In 2,2-dimethylpropanal the only α-carbon is quaternary (three CH3 groups), so there is no α-H; it can serve only as the electrophile.
x: 2-Methylpropanal has one α-H on its CH carbon, so it can form an enolate (its aldol adduct cannot dehydrate, but addition still occurs).
Phenylacetaldehyde has two α-H's that are especially acidic because the enolate is conjugated with the ring.
Cyclohexanone has four α-H's (two on each α-carbon) and forms enolates readily.

q: What is the major product of this sequence?
h: Which carbonyl compound is present when LDA is added? Once that enolate is formed completely, what can the second carbonyl compound do?
w: LDA converts all the cyclohexanone into its lithium enolate before the aldehyde is added (a directed aldol). Propanal is then added and acts only as the electrophile; there is no free base left to make the propanal enolate. The cyclohexanone enolate carbon bonds to the aldehyde carbon, and acidic workup gives the β-hydroxy ketone 2-(1-hydroxypropyl)cyclohexanone.
x: This has the roles reversed (propanal enolate adding to cyclohexanone). That requires the propanal enolate, but LDA was consumed by cyclohexanone before propanal was added.
Propanal self-aldol needs propanal enolate; with the preformed ketone enolate and no excess base, the ketone enolate traps the aldehyde instead.
Dehydration to the enone needs heat or stronger acid/base; a cold acidic workup after a directed aldol gives the β-hydroxy ketone.

q:
Which statements about the aldol reaction are correct?
I. With NaOH, the aldol addition equilibrium for acetone lies on the side of acetone.
II. Heating drives aldol reactions toward product because dehydration forms a conjugated enone.
III. Once a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound forms, it cannot revert to the two carbonyl compounds.
h: The aldol addition is reversible (retro-aldol). Compare how favorable it is for ketones versus aldehydes, and what dehydration adds.
w: I is true: for ketones the aldol addition is uphill or nearly so (two sterically crowded ketones lose a C=O), so only a few percent of 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one is present at equilibrium. II is true: dehydration to a conjugated enone is favorable and pulls the equilibrium forward. III is false: under the same base the β-hydroxy carbonyl undergoes retro-aldol cleavage back to the starting carbonyls. Answer: I and II only.
x: Statement II is also correct: forming the conjugated C=C–C=O by dehydration makes the overall condensation favorable.
Statement III is false: aldol addition is reversible, and β-hydroxy ketones fragment in base (retro-aldol).
Statement III is false because the aldol addition is an equilibrium; retro-aldol cleavage occurs under the same conditions.

q: Which diketone gives 3-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one by intramolecular aldol condensation (NaOH, heat)?
h: Break the C=C of the enone: put back a C=O on the β-carbon (the one bearing the CH<sub>3</sub>) and two H's on the α-carbon. Count the carbons.
w: The target has six carbons. Retro-aldol at the C2=C3 bond turns C3 back into a ketone (CH3C=O) and C2 back into a CH3, opening the ring: CH3C(=O)CH2CH2C(=O)CH3, hexane-2,5-dione. In the forward reaction the terminal CH3 enolate attacks the other C=O to close a five-membered ring.
x: Heptane-2,6-dione closes a six-membered ring and gives 3-methylcyclohex-2-enone.
4-Oxopentanal has only five carbons; its methyl-ketone enolate attacking the CHO gives cyclopent-2-enone without the methyl group.
Octane-2,7-dione closes a five-membered ring through its internal CH<sub>2</sub> and gives 1-acetyl-2-methylcyclopentene.

q: Acetone is heated with two equivalents of benzaldehyde in aqueous ethanolic NaOH. What is the major product?
h: Acetone has α-H's on both sides. After one condensation, can the other methyl group react too?
w: Acetone's enolate adds to benzaldehyde and dehydrates to benzalacetone. Its remaining CH3 is still enolizable, so with a second equivalent of benzaldehyde the sequence repeats on the other side, giving (1E,4E)-1,5-diphenylpenta-1,4-dien-3-one (dibenzylideneacetone, A), C17H14O.
x: Benzalacetone is the product with one equivalent of benzaldehyde; with two equivalents its remaining CH<sub>3</sub> condenses again.
With heat the β-hydroxy groups are eliminated (E1cB) to give the conjugated dienone; the bis-aldol addition product does not survive.
This would need acetone to self-condense; benzaldehyde is the better electrophile and is present in excess, so acetone's enolate reacts with benzaldehyde.

q: A single aldehyde is heated with NaOH and gives only the aldol condensation product shown (C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O). Which aldehyde was used?
h: Self-condensation doubles the aldehyde and removes H<sub>2</sub>O. Also check the branch on the α-carbon: it is the aldehyde's chain minus its first two carbons.
w: Self-condensation: 2 RCH2CHO → product + H2O, so each unit is C5H10O. The α-carbon of the product carries an n-propyl branch and the β-carbon carries an n-butyl chain, matching CH3CH2CH2CH2CHO: pentanal. The product is (E)-2-propylhept-2-enal.
x: 3-Methylbutanal is also C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O, but it would give branched groups: an isopropyl on the α-carbon and an isobutyl on the β-carbon (2-isopropyl-5-methylhex-2-enal).
Butanal gives a C<sub>8</sub> product, 2-ethylhex-2-enal.
Hexanal gives a C<sub>12</sub> product, 2-butyloct-2-enal.

q: Ethyl propanoate is treated with one equivalent of NaOEt in ethanol, and the mixture is then acidified. What is the Claisen condensation product?
h: The α-carbon (C2) of one ester attacks the C=O of a second ester, and ethoxide leaves. Which carbon of the product carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch?
w: The enolate of one ester (nucleophilic C2, which carries a CH3) attacks the carbonyl of a second ester; the tetrahedral intermediate expels EtO−, giving a β-keto ester. The CH3 stays on the carbon between the two C=O groups: ethyl 2-methyl-3-oxopentanoate, C8H14O3 = 2 C5H10O2 − C2H5OH.
x: This product lacks the CH<sub>3</sub> branch (C<sub>7</sub>); it would come from ethyl acetate plus ethyl propanoate. The nucleophilic carbon of ethyl propanoate is the CH<sub>2</sub>, so it keeps its CH<sub>3</sub>.
This is an aldol-type alcohol. In a Claisen the tetrahedral intermediate is not protonated; it expels ethoxide, regenerating a C=O (a ketone).
Losing both ethoxy groups gives a β-diketone; only one ester undergoes acyl substitution, so the product keeps one OEt.

q: Which ester gives little or no Claisen condensation product when treated with NaOEt in ethanol?
h: The Claisen equilibrium is driven to completion by one last step after the β-keto ester forms. What does that step require of the product?
w: The Claisen addition–elimination steps are uphill. The reaction is pulled forward because ethoxide removes the very acidic H between the two C=O groups of the β-keto ester (pKa ≈ 11). Ethyl 2-methylpropanoate has only one α-H; after condensation the central carbon carries two CH3 groups and no H, so this driving deprotonation is impossible and the equilibrium returns to starting ester.
x: Ethyl acetate has three α-H's; its product, ethyl acetoacetate, has an acidic CH<sub>2</sub> between the carbonyls that ethoxide deprotonates.
Ethyl propanoate has two α-H's; its β-keto ester product still has one H between the carbonyls to drive the reaction.
Ethyl phenylacetate has two benzylic α-H's; its product keeps an acidic H between the carbonyls and condenses well.

q: Diethyl heptanedioate is treated with NaOEt in ethanol and then with dilute acid. What is the product?
h: A Dieckmann reaction is an intramolecular Claisen. Count the atoms from the enolate α-carbon to the other C=O carbon, inclusive.
w: Number the diacid chain C1–C7 (C1 and C7 are the ester carbons). The enolate at C2 attacks C7; the ring contains C2, C3, C4, C5, C6 and C7: a six-membered ring. Loss of ethoxide gives ethyl 2-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylate, C9H14O3 (diester minus EtOH).
x: A five-membered Dieckmann product comes from diethyl hexanedioate (adipate), which has one fewer CH<sub>2</sub>.
A seven-membered product would require diethyl octanedioate; heptanedioate gives a six-membered ring.
Cyclohexanone forms only after ester hydrolysis and decarboxylation with heat; dilute acid workup at room temperature leaves the β-keto ester intact.

q: What is the final product of this sequence?
h: Step 1 is a Dieckmann cyclization (count the ring size). Where is the most acidic H in the product, and what happens to a β-keto acid on heating?
w: Diethyl hexanedioate (adipate) undergoes Dieckmann cyclization to ethyl 2-oxocyclopentane-1-carboxylate, whose enolate (between the two C=O groups) is methylated by CH3I at that carbon. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester to a β-keto acid, which decarboxylates. The product is 2-methylcyclopentanone.
x: Adipate (six-carbon diacid) gives a five-membered ring; a six-membered ring needs heptanedioate.
This omits the methylation. The doubly stabilized enolate is alkylated by CH<sub>3</sub>I before hydrolysis, and the methyl survives decarboxylation.
β-Keto acids lose CO<sub>2</sub> on heating through a cyclic transition state; the carboxylic acid does not survive step 3.

q: Acetone is added slowly to a mixture of NaH and excess ethyl benzoate; the mixture is then acidified. What is the major product?
h: Only one partner can form an enolate. Which C=O is the electrophile, and what leaves from it?
w: Ethyl benzoate has no α-H, so it can only be the electrophile. The acetone enolate attacks the ester carbonyl, ethoxide is expelled, and the β-diketone is deprotonated (driving the reaction) until acid workup. The product of this crossed Claisen is 1-phenylbutane-1,3-dione.
x: Ethyl 3-oxo-3-phenylpropanoate would need an ester enolate (from ethyl acetate). Here the enolate comes from acetone, so the product keeps a methyl ketone, not an ester.
Mesityl oxide is acetone's self-aldol condensation product. Slow addition of acetone into excess, more reactive ethyl benzoate makes the crossed Claisen dominant.
This 1,3-diketone has two benzoyl groups; it would need acetophenone as the enolate partner, and no acetophenone is present.

q: In a crossed Claisen condensation with ethyl acetate, the second ester should be able to act only as the electrophile. Which ester is not suitable for this role?
h: Look for α-hydrogens on each ester.
w: A partner that acts only as an acceptor must lack α-H's. Ethyl phenylacetate (PhCH2CO2Et) has two acidic benzylic α-H's, so it would also form an enolate and give a mixture of self- and crossed-Claisen products.
x: Ethyl benzoate has no α-carbon bearing H (the carbonyl is attached to the ring), so it can only be attacked.
Diethyl carbonate, (EtO)<sub>2</sub>C=O, has no α-carbon at all; it is a standard acylating partner that installs a CO<sub>2</sub>Et group.
Ethyl formate, HCO<sub>2</sub>Et, has no α-carbon; it installs a CHO (formyl) group.

q: Which alkyl halide(s), used in a malonic ester synthesis, give 2-methylbutanoic acid?
c: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br and CH<sub>3</sub>I (one after the other)
h: In the product, find the α-carbon (next to CO<sub>2</sub>H). It was the malonate CH<sub>2</sub>. What groups were added to it?
w: Malonic ester synthesis gives R(R′)CH–CO2H: the malonate CH2 becomes the α-carbon, and one CO2Et becomes the CO2H while the other is lost as CO2. The α-carbon of 2-methylbutanoic acid carries an ethyl and a methyl, so alkylate with CH3CH2Br and then CH3I (either order).
x: A propyl group plus a methyl gives 2-methylpentanoic acid, one carbon too many.
A sec-butyl group on the malonate carbon gives 3-methylpentanoic acid; the branch ends up at C3, not C2 (and secondary halides alkylate poorly).
A single ethyl gives butanoic acid; the methyl branch on C2 needs a second alkylation.

q: Diethyl malonate is treated with two equivalents of NaOEt and one equivalent of 1,4-dibromobutane, then heated with aqueous acid. What is the final product?
h: The first alkylation attaches the four-carbon chain; the second enolate is formed on the same carbon and displaces the other Br intramolecularly. Count the ring atoms.
w: The malonate carbon is alkylated by one end of the dibromide; a second deprotonation at the same carbon lets it displace the other bromide intramolecularly. The ring contains the malonate carbon plus four CH2 groups: a five-membered ring. Hydrolysis and decarboxylation of the 1,1-diacid give cyclopentanecarboxylic acid.
x: A six-membered ring would need 1,5-dibromopentane. The ring holds the four chain carbons plus the malonate carbon.
A four-membered ring would come from 1,3-dibromopropane.
A 1,1-dicarboxylic acid (a malonic acid) loses CO<sub>2</sub> on heating, so only one CO<sub>2</sub>H remains.

q: What is the final product of this acetoacetic ester synthesis?
h: The acetoacetic ester synthesis turns R–X into a methyl ketone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>–R. What happens to the ester group in hot aqueous acid?
w: The enolate (from the CH2 between the two C=O groups) is benzylated by SN2. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester to a β-keto acid, which decarboxylates. The CO2Et carbon is lost, leaving CH3C(=O)CH2–CH2Ph: 4-phenylbutan-2-one.
x: This is one carbon short: the original CH<sub>2</sub> of the acetoacetate stays in the product between the C=O and the new benzyl group.
A carboxylic acid product is the outcome of a malonic ester synthesis. Acetoacetic ester loses the ester carbon and keeps the ketone.
This is the alkylated β-keto ester before step 3. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes and decarboxylates it.

q: Which alkyl halides should be used, in two separate alkylation steps, to make 3-methylhexan-2-one by the acetoacetic ester synthesis?
h: Keep the CH<sub>3</sub>C(=O) unit and the α-carbon from ethyl acetoacetate. Which groups are attached to that α-carbon in the target?
w: In the target, CH3C(=O)– comes from the acetoacetate, and C3 is the original active CH2. C3 carries a methyl and an n-propyl group, so the ester is alkylated with CH3I and CH3CH2CH2Br (in either order) before hydrolysis and decarboxylation.
x: A single butyl group gives heptan-2-one, a straight-chain ketone with no branch at C3.
Methyl plus ethyl gives 3-methylpentan-2-one, one carbon short.

A secondary halide attaches through its C2, giving CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (4-methylheptan-2-one), and secondary halides alkylate enolates poorly.

q: Which carboxylic acid cannot be prepared efficiently by a malonic ester synthesis?
h: Work backward to the halide(s) needed for each acid. Each alkylation is an S<sub>N</sub>2 step.
w: A malonic ester synthesis gives RCH2CO2H or RR′CHCO2H, where each R comes from an SN2 alkylation. 3,3-Dimethylbutanoic acid, (CH3)3C–CH2CO2H, needs R = tert-butyl, i.e., (CH3)3CBr, a tertiary halide that undergoes E2 with the malonate anion instead of SN2.
x: 3-Phenylpropanoic acid needs benzyl bromide, an excellent S<sub>N</sub>2 substrate.
2-Methylpentanoic acid needs 1-bromopropane and CH<sub>3</sub>I, both good S<sub>N</sub>2 substrates.
Pent-4-enoic acid needs allyl bromide, an activated primary halide that alkylates readily.

q: Which compound loses CO<sub>2</sub> most readily when heated to about 100 °C?
h: Decarboxylation on gentle heating requires a carbonyl positioned to accept electrons through a six-membered cyclic transition state.
w: A β-keto acid decarboxylates easily: the acid H is transferred to the ketone O through a six-membered cyclic transition state as CO2 leaves, giving an enol that tautomerizes to the ketone (acetone here).
x: In a γ-keto acid the ketone is too far away to form the six-membered cyclic transition state.
A β-hydroxy acid has no C=O at the β-position to accept the electrons; it may dehydrate but does not lose CO<sub>2</sub> easily.
Benzoic acid has no β-carbonyl and its carboxyl is attached to an sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon; it is stable well above 100 °C.

q: 3-Oxobutanoic acid decarboxylates on warming. What is the organic species formed directly in the CO2-loss step, before any tautomerization?
h: In the cyclic transition state, the carboxyl H moves to the ketone oxygen as the C–C bond to CO<sub>2</sub> breaks. Where does the new π bond form?
w: In the six-membered cyclic transition state, the O–H proton moves to the ketone oxygen, the C–CO2 bond breaks, and its electrons form a C=C between the α-carbon and the former carbonyl carbon. The first product is the neutral enol, prop-1-en-2-ol, which then tautomerizes to acetone.
x: Acetone is the final product, but it forms only after the enol tautomerizes; the concerted CO<sub>2</sub>-loss step gives the enol.
Under these neutral thermal conditions the proton is transferred within the cyclic transition state, so no free carbanion (enolate) forms.
Ketene would require losing water or an alcohol from an acid derivative; decarboxylation removes CO<sub>2</sub> and keeps the ketone oxygen.

q: What is the final product of this sequence?
h: A stabilized malonate anion adds 1,4 to an enone. Then count the carbons that remain after one CO<sub>2</sub>H is lost.
w: The malonate anion is a soft, stabilized nucleophile and adds to the β-carbon of methyl vinyl ketone (Michael addition), giving (EtO2C)2CH–CH2CH2C(=O)CH3. Hydrolysis and decarboxylation leave one CO2H on the former malonate carbon: HO2C–CH2–CH2CH2C(=O)CH3, 5-oxohexanoic acid.
x: This comes from 1,2-addition to the C=O. Stabilized enolates such as malonate add reversibly at C=O and end up in the more stable 1,4 (conjugate) adduct.
4-Oxopentanoic acid is one carbon short; the MVK unit contributes four carbons and the malonate CH<sub>2</sub> plus one CO<sub>2</sub>H contribute two.
This is one carbon too long; only two carbons of malonate remain (CH<sub>2</sub> and one CO<sub>2</sub>H), not three.

q: Cyclohexanone and methyl vinyl ketone are heated with NaOH in ethanol (Robinson annulation). What is the final product?
h: Step 1: Michael addition gives a 1,5-diketone. Step 2: the methyl-ketone enolate attacks the ring C=O to close a six-membered ring. Step 3: heat. Where does the C=C end up?
w: The cyclohexanone enolate adds 1,4 to MVK, giving 2-(3-oxobutyl)cyclohexanone. The enolate of the side-chain CH3 then attacks the ring C=O, closing a new six-membered ring (intramolecular aldol). With heat the β-hydroxy ketone dehydrates (E1cB) so that the new C=C is conjugated with the C=O: the bicyclic enone A (C10H14O, octahydronaphthalen-2-one).
x: This is the Michael adduct, the intermediate after step 1. Under NaOH with heat it continues to the intramolecular aldol condensation.
This β-hydroxy ketone is the aldol addition intermediate; heating with base dehydrates it to the enone.
Here the C=C is β,γ to the carbonyl. E1cB dehydration forms the C=C between the α- and β-carbons, giving the more stable conjugated enone.

q: Which starting materials give the bicyclic enone shown by a Robinson annulation (NaOH, heat)?
h: Undo the aldol (break the C=C, restore the ring C=O), then undo the Michael addition. Which ring carbon bonded to the side chain, and what is on it?
w: Retro-aldol of the enone gives the 1,5-diketone: a cyclohexanone whose α-carbon carries both the CH3 (the angular methyl) and a CH2CH2C(=O)CH3 chain. Retro-Michael splits that into 2-methylcyclohexanone (its more substituted α-carbon was the nucleophile) and methyl vinyl ketone. Michael additions run under equilibrating base, so the more substituted enolate of 2-methylcyclohexanone reacts, placing the methyl at the ring fusion.
x: With pent-3-en-2-one the extra CH<sub>3</sub> ends up on the β-carbon of the acceptor, i.e., on the new ring next to the ring fusion, not on the ring-fusion carbon.
Acrolein has no methyl ketone; after the Michael step there is no CH<sub>3</sub>C=O whose enolate can close the six-membered enone ring.
The 1,3-dione would leave an extra ketone in the product (this route gives the Wieland–Miescher ketone, C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>).

q: Which compound is not a Michael acceptor?
h: A Michael acceptor has its C=C conjugated with an electron-withdrawing group, so the β-carbon is electrophilic.
w: Conjugate addition requires the C=C to be conjugated with the C=O (or C≡N), which makes the β-carbon δ+. In pent-4-en-2-one a CH2 separates the C=C from the C=O (a β,γ-unsaturated ketone), so the alkene is isolated and not electrophilic.
x: Acrylonitrile's C=C is conjugated with C≡N, so its terminal CH<sub>2</sub> is an electrophilic β-carbon.
Ethyl acrylate is an α,β-unsaturated ester, a classic Michael acceptor.
Cyclopent-2-enone is an α,β-unsaturated ketone; nucleophiles add at the ring β-carbon.

q: What is the final product of this Stork enamine sequence?
h: An enamine is a neutral enolate equivalent. Which carbon of the enamine is nucleophilic, and what does aqueous acid do at the end?
w: Pyrrolidine and cyclohexanone form the enamine. Its α-carbon (nucleophilic through the N lone pair) attacks allyl bromide by SN2, giving an iminium ion. Aqueous acid hydrolyzes the iminium back to the ketone, releasing pyrrolidine: 2-allylcyclohexanone. Because the alkylated iminium is not deprotonated again under these conditions, enamine alkylation stops cleanly at one alkyl group.
x: This tertiary alcohol would come from an allyl Grignard adding to the C=O; enamines react at the α-carbon, not at the carbonyl carbon.
Stork enamine alkylation stops after one alkylation because the product is an iminium ion, not a neutral enamine.
Enamines react at carbon; there is no oxygen on the enamine to be alkylated, and hydrolysis regenerates the C=O.

q: Which structure is the product formed when cyclohexanone is heated with pyrrolidine and a catalytic amount of acid, with removal of water?
h: A secondary amine cannot form a neutral imine. After water is lost, where must the proton come from?
w: A secondary amine adds to the C=O to give a carbinolamine, which loses water to form an iminium ion. The iminium N has no H to lose, so an α-H is removed instead, giving the neutral enamine A (C=C–N).
x: This saturated amine is the product of reductive amination (with NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN); no reducing agent is present.
The carbinolamine is an intermediate; with acid and removal of water it loses H<sub>2</sub>O.
The iminium ion is also an intermediate; loss of an α-proton gives the neutral enamine that is isolated.

q: The pyrrolidine enamine of cyclohexanone is heated with methyl vinyl ketone in dioxane, and then aqueous acid is added. What is the product?
h: The enamine is a soft nucleophile. Does it add at the C=O or at the β-carbon of the enone? No hydroxide base is present for a later aldol step.
w: The enamine α-carbon adds to the β-carbon of MVK (Stork–Michael reaction). Hydrolysis of the resulting iminium/enamine with aqueous acid gives the 1,5-diketone 2-(3-oxobutyl)cyclohexanone. Closing the second ring (Robinson annulation) requires a separate base/heat step.
x: This is the Robinson annulation product; it needs base (e.g., NaOH or NaOMe) with heat to effect the intramolecular aldol condensation after the Michael step.
Enamines, like other soft, stabilized nucleophiles, add 1,4 to enones rather than 1,2 to the C=O.
This would be the product of free pyrrolidine adding to MVK. The amine is bound up as the enamine, whose nucleophilic site is carbon.

q: Diethyl malonate and cyclohex-2-en-1-one are treated with catalytic NaOEt in ethanol. What is the major product (before any hydrolysis)?
h: Is the malonate anion a hard or a soft nucleophile? Which carbon of the enone is the soft electrophilic site?
w: The malonate anion is a stabilized (soft) nucleophile, so it adds to the β-carbon of the enone (Michael addition). Protonation of the resulting enolate at the α-carbon gives diethyl 2-(3-oxocyclohexyl)malonate, with the malonate on C3 of the cyclohexanone.
x: 1,2-Addition to the C=O is reversible for stabilized anions; the 1,4-adduct, which keeps the strong C=O bond, is the thermodynamic product.
This attaches the malonate to the α-carbon (C2). In conjugate addition the nucleophile bonds to the β-carbon (C3), and the α-carbon is protonated.
A Knoevenagel-type product requires condensation with the C=O and loss of water; malonate with an enone under catalytic base undergoes Michael addition.

q: 4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one is treated with lithium dimethylcuprate, and the reaction is then quenched with aqueous NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. What is the product?
h: Gilman reagents are soft carbon nucleophiles. Which carbon of an α,β-unsaturated ketone do they attack?
w: Lithium dialkylcuprates add a carbon group to the β-carbon of α,β-unsaturated ketones (1,4-addition), even when that carbon is disubstituted. The enolate is protonated on workup to give 4,4-dimethylpentan-2-one, with a new quaternary carbon.
x: This tertiary allylic alcohol is the 1,2-addition product typical of CH<sub>3</sub>Li or CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, not of a cuprate.
Methyl on the α-carbon with the C=C intact would require substitution of a vinyl H; cuprates add across the C=C instead.
This is the product of reducing the C=C (adding H, not CH<sub>3</sub>); the cuprate delivers a methyl group to the β-carbon.

q: Which reagent carries out the transformation shown?
h: The product is an alcohol with the C=C still in place. Was the methyl added to the carbonyl carbon or to the β-carbon?
w: The methyl group and the OH are on the former carbonyl carbon, and the ring C=C is untouched: this is 1,2-addition. Hard, highly reactive organometallics such as CH3MgBr (or CH3Li) add directly and irreversibly to the C=O of cyclohex-2-enone, giving 1-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol after workup.
x: Gilman reagents add 1,4; the product would be 3-methylcyclohexanone, with the C=O retained.
LDA/CH<sub>3</sub>I alkylates an α-carbon of the ketone (C6) and keeps the C=O; it does not create an alcohol.
Malonate is a soft stabilized nucleophile that gives the Michael (1,4) adduct, and it would add a CH(CO<sub>2</sub>Et)<sub>2</sub> group, not a methyl.

q: What is the major product of this one-pot sequence (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: Conjugate addition leaves an enolate. Which carbon of that enolate is nucleophilic, and is anything there to protonate it before CH<sub>3</sub>I is added?
w: The cuprate adds CH3 to C3 (1,4-addition), generating a specific lithium enolate with its C=C between C1 and C2. No proton source is present, so this enolate is trapped by CH3I at C2, the carbon between the carbonyl and the new methyl. The product is 2,3-dimethylcyclohexanone (mainly trans).
x: 3-Methylcyclohexanone forms if the enolate is protonated (aqueous workup) instead of being alkylated; here CH<sub>3</sub>I traps it.
Methylation at C6 would need the other enolate. Conjugate addition generates the enolate regiospecifically toward C2, and it does not equilibrate at low temperature with no proton source.
This tertiary allylic alcohol is the 1,2-adduct formed by CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr or CH<sub>3</sub>Li, not by a cuprate.

q: Which pair of esters, with NaOEt followed by acid workup, gives the target by a crossed Claisen condensation as the main product?
h: Disconnect the bond between the ketone C=O carbon and the α-carbon (the CH bearing CH<sub>3</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>Et). Which piece is the acyl electrophile and which is the ester enolate?
w: The Claisen bond joins the ketone carbonyl carbon to the α-carbon between the two C=O groups. The acyl piece is PhC(=O)–, from ethyl benzoate (no α-H, so it is only an electrophile; used in excess). The enolate piece is –CH(CH3)CO2Et, from ethyl propanoate. The product still has one H on the central carbon, so the final deprotonation drives the reaction.
x: Ethyl acetate supplies a CH<sub>2</sub>, giving ethyl benzoylacetate (no CH<sub>3</sub> on the central carbon).
Here the ring is on the α-carbon side and a CH<sub>3</sub>CO group is the acyl piece; the product would be ethyl 3-oxo-2-phenylbutanoate or its isomer, not a phenyl ketone.
Ethyl formate transfers a CHO group, giving an aldehyde. The resulting product would also have no H between the carbonyls, so the Claisen would not be driven to completion.

q: A Robinson annulation combines which two reactions, in which order?
c: Michael addition, then intramolecular aldol condensation
Intramolecular aldol condensation, then Michael addition
h: The first step joins a ketone enolate to an α,β-unsaturated ketone; the second step forms the new ring and the C=C.
w: Robinson annulation is a Michael addition of an enolate to an α,β-unsaturated ketone (usually methyl vinyl ketone), giving a 1,5-diketone, followed by an intramolecular aldol condensation that closes a cyclohexenone ring.
x: The order is reversed: the 1,5-diketone needed for ring closure exists only after the Michael step.
No ester or alkoxide leaving group is involved; the new ring forms by enolate addition to a ketone (aldol), not by acyl substitution.
A Dieckmann condensation is an intramolecular Claisen of a diester; the annulation closes the ring by an aldol reaction between two ketones.

q: The pyrrolidine enamine of cyclohexanone is treated with acetyl chloride, and the product is then hydrolyzed with aqueous acid. What is the final product?
h: The enamine's nucleophilic carbon attacks the acyl chloride. What functional group results after hydrolysis of the iminium?
w: The enamine α-carbon attacks the acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution, Cl− leaves), giving an acylated iminium/enamine. Hydrolysis regenerates the ring ketone, producing the β-diketone 2-acetylcyclohexanone. Stork acylation is a mild route to 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds.
x: An enol acetate would need acylation on oxygen; the enamine has no oxygen and reacts at carbon.
One equivalent of acid chloride acylates once; the product iminium is not a nucleophile, so the second α-carbon is not acylated.
This puts an extra CH<sub>2</sub> between the ring and the acetyl group; it would come from alkylation with chloroacetone, not acylation with acetyl chloride.

q: Which pair of compounds gives the 1,5-diketone shown in one C–C bond-forming step (Michael addition, then workup)?
c: Cyclohexanone pyrrolidine enamine and phenyl vinyl ketone
Cyclohex-2-en-1-one and the enolate of acetophenone
Cyclohexanone and ethyl benzoate with NaOEt
h: Number the chain from one C=O carbon (C1) to the other (C5). The Michael bond joins the donor's α-carbon to the acceptor's β-carbon. Which bond is that?
w: A 1,5-dicarbonyl is disconnected at the bond between the α-carbon of one carbonyl and the β-carbon of the other. The ring α-carbon (C2) bonds to CH2CH2COPh, so the donor is cyclohexanone (enolate or enamine) and the acceptor is CH2=CHCOPh; the donor's α-carbon adds to the acceptor's terminal β-carbon.
x: Acetophenone enolate adds to C3 of cyclohexenone, giving 3-(2-oxo-2-phenylethyl)cyclohexanone: the side chain is on C3 and has only one CH<sub>2</sub>.
A crossed aldol with benzaldehyde gives 2-benzylidenecyclohexanone (or its β-hydroxy ketone), a 1,3-relationship, not a 1,5-diketone.
A crossed Claisen with ethyl benzoate gives 2-benzoylcyclohexanone, a 1,3-diketone.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the ether shown?
h: Name an ether as an alkoxy substituent on the larger alkyl group, then find the longest chain of that group.
w: The larger alkyl group (four carbons) is the parent alkane and the smaller group becomes the alkoxy substituent: CH3CH2O– is ethoxy. The four-carbon chain is numbered so the ethoxy carbon gets the lowest number, C2. The name is 2-ethoxybutane (common name: sec-butyl ethyl ether).
x: 1-Ethoxybutane has the oxygen on the end carbon of an unbranched butyl group; here the O is on C2 of the four-carbon chain.
The parent should be the larger alkyl group (butane), with the smaller ethyl group named as ethoxy.
Calling the chain "propane" with a methyl branch misses the longest chain; the C1 methyl plus three more carbons make a butane chain.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Count the ring atoms (including O) and remember that the ring oxygen is position 1.
w: A three-membered ring with one oxygen is an oxirane (epoxide). Numbering starts at the oxygen (O1), so the substituted carbon is C2: 2-methyloxirane (also called propylene oxide or 1,2-epoxypropane).
x: Oxetane is the four-membered cyclic ether; this ring has only two carbons and one oxygen.
The ring oxygen is O1 and numbering goes the short way to the substituent, so the methyl carbon is C2, not C3.
The molecule has three carbons in all, so as an epoxy-alkane it is 1,2-epoxypropane, not epoxybutane.

q: Which pair of reagents gives the best yield of the ether shown by a Williamson synthesis?
h: The Williamson synthesis is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction. Which carbon can be attacked from the back side?
w: A Williamson ether synthesis is SN2: the alkoxide attacks an alkyl halide with a good leaving group. Put the hindered group on the alkoxide and the unhindered group on the halide. tert-Butoxide + bromoethane works because the primary C–Br carbon is open to back-side attack.
x: A tertiary halide cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; ethoxide acts as a base and the main product is 2-methylpropene by E2.
An alcohol has no leaving group (OH<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group), so ethoxide only does an acid–base exchange with it.
Ethanol has no leaving group, so tert-butoxide simply deprotonates it (an acid–base equilibrium), not a substitution.

q: What is the major organic product of this reaction?
h: Can a strong base reach the back side of a tertiary carbon? If not, what else can it do?
w: Ethoxide is a strong base and a good nucleophile, but a tertiary carbon is too hindered for SN2. With a strong base and a 3° halide, E2 wins: ethoxide removes a β-H and bromide leaves, giving 2-methylpropene. This is why a Williamson synthesis must use a methyl or primary halide.
x: This ether would need S<sub>N</sub>2 at a tertiary carbon, which is blocked; it is made instead from tert-butoxide and a primary ethyl halide.
There is no water or hydroxide as a nucleophile, and the strong base favors E2 over the slow S<sub>N</sub>1 path.
Forming this ether would need tert-butoxide and a tertiary electrophile; neither is present, and such a hindered ether is not made by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: Which reagents give the best preparation of the aryl ether shown?
h: One of the two carbons on oxygen is sp<sup>2</sup>. Can that carbon be the S<sub>N</sub>2 electrophile?
w: The Williamson synthesis needs back-side attack on an sp3 carbon. The aryl carbon cannot be the electrophile, so the aryl group must be on the nucleophile: phenoxide (easily made because phenol has pKa ≈ 10) attacks iodoethane by SN2. Sodium phenoxide + iodoethane is the best choice.
x: Aryl halides do not do S<sub>N</sub>2: the ring blocks back-side attack and the C(sp<sup>2</sup>)–Br bond is strong. No ether forms with an unactivated bromobenzene.
Ethoxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) just deprotonates phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10) to give phenoxide and ethanol; no C–O bond forms.
Ethanol has no leaving group, so phenoxide cannot displace anything from it.

q: What is the main product when this bromo alcohol is treated with NaH in THF?
h: NaH makes the alkoxide. Count the atoms that will end up in the ring, including O.
w: NaH deprotonates the OH. The alkoxide then attacks the primary C–Br carbon in the same molecule (intramolecular Williamson, SN2). The new ring holds O plus C1–C5: a six-membered ring, oxane (tetrahydropyran). Five- and six-membered rings form quickly because the chain ends meet easily and there is little ring strain.
x: Oxolane has only four carbons; the ring here includes all five chain carbons plus the oxygen.
Oxepane is a seven-membered ring (six carbons); the chain has only five carbons.
E2 on a primary bromide with an alkoxide is minor; the fast intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2 that forms a six-membered ring wins.

q: (S)-4-Bromopentan-1-ol is treated with NaH in THF. What is the main product?
h: The ring closes by S<sub>N</sub>2 at the carbon bearing Br. What does S<sub>N</sub>2 do to that stereocenter?
w: NaH forms the alkoxide, which attacks C4 from the back side (intramolecular SN2), making a five-membered ring (O + 4 C). Back-side attack inverts C4. The oxygen takes the place of Br as the top-priority group, so the descriptor changes from S to (R)-2-methyloxolane (confirmed with CIP ranking: O > ring CH2 > CH3 > H).
x: Retention would need front-side attack; S<sub>N</sub>2 ring closure inverts the carbon that loses bromide.
Racemization needs a carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1). A secondary bromide with a strong internal nucleophile reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 with clean inversion.
E2 can compete at a secondary bromide, but 5-membered ring closure is intramolecular and fast, so the cyclic ether is the main product.

q: What is the major product of this alkoxymercuration–demercuration?
h: Methanol adds to the alkene carbon that can best carry positive charge in the mercurinium ion.
w: Alkoxymercuration adds RO and H across C=C with Markovnikov regiochemistry and no rearrangement. Methanol opens the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon (the one with more partial positive charge), and NaBH4 replaces Hg with H. The product is 1-methoxy-1-methylcyclohexane.
x: This is the anti-Markovnikov ether; methanol adds to the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, not the secondary one.
The solvent is methanol, not water, so the nucleophile that adds is CH<sub>3</sub>OH and an ether forms, not an alcohol.
Mercurinium ions do not rearrange, so the methoxy group cannot move to C3.

q: What is the major product?
h: Does a bridged mercurinium ion allow a methyl shift the way a free carbocation would?
w: Ethanol opens the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon (C2), and NaBH4 replaces Hg by H. Because the mercurinium ion is bridged, there is no free carbocation and no methyl shift. The product is 2-ethoxy-3,3-dimethylbutane. (Acid-catalyzed addition of ethanol would instead give the rearranged 2-ethoxy-2,3-dimethylbutane.)
x: This rearranged ether forms only through a free 2° carbocation and a 1,2-methyl shift, which the bridged mercurinium ion avoids.
This is anti-Markovnikov addition; the alcohol attacks the more substituted carbon of the mercurinium ion.
An alcohol would form with water as solvent (oxymercuration); in ethanol the nucleophile is ethanol, giving an ether.

q: Methoxybenzene (anisole) is heated with excess HI. What are the products?
h: After protonation, iodide must do an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack. Which carbon on oxygen can it attack?
w: HI protonates the ether oxygen. Iodide then attacks by SN2, and it can only attack the sp3 methyl carbon; aryl carbons do not undergo SN2 or SN1. So the aryl C–O bond stays and the products are phenol + iodomethane. Phenol is not converted further, because its C–O bond cannot be broken this way.
x: Cleaving the aryl C–O bond would need S<sub>N</sub>2 or S<sub>N</sub>1 at an sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon, which does not happen.
Phenol cannot be converted to iodobenzene by HI; only the alkyl side of the ether is cleaved.
With excess HI the methyl group leaves as iodomethane (I<sup>−</sup> attacks the methyl carbon directly), not as methanol.

q: Tetrahydrofuran (oxolane) is heated with excess concentrated HBr. What is the final organic product?
h: The first cleavage opens the ring. What happens to the new OH group with more HBr?
w: Protonation of O and SN2 attack by Br− at a primary carbon opens the ring to 4-bromobutan-1-ol. With excess HBr and heat, that primary alcohol is protonated and displaced by a second bromide. The final product is 1,4-dibromobutane.
x: 4-Bromobutan-1-ol is the intermediate after one equivalent; excess HBr converts its OH to Br as well.
HBr does not reduce C–O to C–H; one carbon end would have to lose its oxygen without gaining bromine.
Water is not the nucleophile here; bromide attacks the protonated ether, and diols are converted to dibromides by excess HBr.

q: tert-Butyl methyl ether is treated with one equivalent of HI. Which products form?
h: After protonation, one C–O bond can break without any nucleophile. Which one gives the more stable cation?
