w: Protonation makes a good leaving group. The tertiary C–O bond ionizes (SN1) to the stable tert-butyl cation and methanol leaves; iodide then traps the cation. Products: 2-iodo-2-methylpropane + methanol. The methyl C–O bond would need an SN2 attack, which is slower than ionization here.
x: This would be S<sub>N</sub>2 at the methyl group. For ethers with a tertiary group, S<sub>N</sub>1 cleavage at the 3° carbon is faster.
Converting both groups to iodides needs a second equivalent of HI; with one equivalent the methanol remains.
The methyl group leaves as methanol, not iodomethane; and E1 (2-methylpropene) would pair with methanol, not iodomethane.

q: The diether shown is heated with excess HBr. Which set of products forms?
h: Treat each C–O bond separately: which ones have an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon that bromide can attack?
w: Each protonated ether is cleaved by SN2 attack of Br− on an sp3 carbon. The Ar–O bond cannot break, so the aryl side gives phenol. The CH3–O and both CH2–O bonds can be attacked; with excess HBr every alkyl alcohol formed is also converted to its bromide, giving 1,3-dibromopropane and bromomethane.
x: Bromobenzene cannot form: the aryl C–O bond is not cleaved because aryl carbons do not do S<sub>N</sub>1 or S<sub>N</sub>2.
HBr cleavage makes alkyl bromides, not alcohols, once excess acid and heat convert the alkyl OH groups.
The aryl C–O bond stays intact, and with excess HBr the 3-bromopropanol OH is also replaced by Br.

q: The crown ether shown (18-crown-6) binds which cation most strongly?
h: Match the size of the cavity to the size of the ion.
w: Crown ethers bind cations whose diameter fits the ring cavity, with all oxygen lone pairs pointing inward. The 18-membered ring with six oxygens fits K+ best. (15-crown-5 fits Na+, 12-crown-4 fits Li+.)
x: Li<sup>+</sup> is too small for the 18-crown-6 cavity; 12-crown-4 is the better size match.
Na<sup>+</sup> is somewhat small for 18-crown-6; 15-crown-5 fits it better.
Mg<sup>2+</sup> is small and very strongly hydrated, and it does not fit the 18-crown-6 cavity well.

q: KF barely reacts with 1-bromooctane in acetonitrile, but adding a little 18-crown-6 gives 1-fluorooctane quickly. What is the best explanation?
c: The crown ether binds K<sup>+</sup>, bringing KF into solution with a poorly solvated, very reactive F<sup>−</sup>
The crown ether binds F<sup>−</sup> through its oxygens and delivers it directly to the carbon
The crown ether hydrogen-bonds to F<sup>−</sup>, making it a stronger base and nucleophile
The crown ether coordinates the Br, making bromide a better leaving group
h: The oxygen lone pairs of a crown ether point into its cavity. Which ion do they attract?
w: The ring oxygens are Lewis bases that wrap around K+. The large organic-coated complex dissolves in the organic solvent and drags F− with it. That fluoride has no tight cation partner and no hydrogen-bonding shell ("naked" fluoride), so it is a much stronger nucleophile and SN2 is fast. The crown ether binds K+.
x: Oxygen lone pairs attract cations, not anions; the crown ether does not bind fluoride.
A crown ether has no O–H groups, so it cannot hydrogen-bond to fluoride; hydrogen bonding would also make F<sup>−</sup> less reactive.
The crown ether does not interact with the alkyl bromide; its role is to bind the potassium ion.

q: (Z)-Hex-3-ene is treated with mCPBA. Which describes the product?
h: Epoxidation is concerted: both C–O bonds form on the same face at the same time.
w: Peroxyacid epoxidation is a concerted syn addition, so the alkene geometry is kept: a Z alkene gives a cis-epoxide. cis-2,3-Diethyloxirane has two stereocenters (R,S) and a mirror plane, so it is a single meso compound; attack on either face gives the same molecule.
x: trans-Epoxides come from E alkenes; the concerted reaction cannot rotate the C–C bond.
A mixture of cis and trans would need a stepwise path with a rotating intermediate; mCPBA epoxidation is stereospecific.
The cis-epoxide here has identical groups on both carbons and a mirror plane, so it is meso; there is no enantiomer pair.

q: (E)-But-2-ene is treated with Br2 in water, and the product is then treated with NaOH. What is the final product?
h: Follow the stereochemistry of two anti steps: anti halohydrin formation, then back-side ring closure.
w: Step 1 adds Br and OH anti (bromonium ion opened by water), giving the bromohydrin. In step 2 the alkoxide attacks the C–Br carbon from the back side (intramolecular SN2), which needs O− and Br anti. Anti addition followed by an anti (back-side) ring closure puts the oxygen on the same face overall, exactly as mCPBA would. The E alkene therefore gives racemic trans-2,3-dimethyloxirane.
x: A cis-epoxide comes from (Z)-but-2-ene; this two-step route keeps the alkene geometry just like mCPBA.
Hydroxide closes the halohydrin to an epoxide; opening it to the diol would need acid or much harsher conditions.
NaOH deprotonates the bromohydrin OH, and the alkoxide quickly displaces the anti bromide to close the epoxide.

q: What is the major product when 2,2-dimethyloxirane reacts with methanol containing a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: In the protonated epoxide, which C–O bond is longer and carries more positive charge?
w: Acid protonates the epoxide oxygen. The C–O bond to the tertiary carbon is weakened most, and that carbon carries most of the positive charge (SN1-like transition state), so methanol attacks the more substituted carbon. Product: 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol.
x: This is the base-catalyzed regiochemistry (attack at the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub>), which applies with CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>, not with acid.
Methanol, not water, is the solvent and nucleophile, so a methyl ether forms rather than the diol.
Only one equivalent of methanol adds; the new primary alcohol is not converted to a methyl ether under these mild conditions.

q: 2,2-Dimethyloxirane is treated with sodium ethanethiolate (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SNa) in ethanol, followed by water. What is the major product?
h: A strong, unprotonated nucleophile opens an epoxide by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which carbon is easier to reach?
w: Thiolate is a strong nucleophile, so the epoxide opens by SN2 without acid. SN2 attack occurs at the less hindered CH2 carbon, and the alkoxide is then protonated. Product: 1-(ethylsulfanyl)-2-methylpropan-2-ol.
x: Attack at the tertiary carbon is the acid-catalyzed regiochemistry; under basic S<sub>N</sub>2 conditions the hindered carbon is avoided.
Water is added only to protonate the alkoxide after the ring has opened; the thiolate is the nucleophile.
Ethanol is a much weaker nucleophile than ethanethiolate, which is large, polarizable and anionic.

q: The racemic epoxide shown (one enantiomer drawn) is treated with CH<sub>3</sub>OH and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which structure is the major product (formed as a racemate; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: Decide two things: which carbon methanol attacks under acid, and from which face relative to the epoxide oxygen.
w: Under acid the nucleophile attacks the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, which carries more positive charge in the protonated epoxide. The attack is still back-side, so OCH3 ends up trans to the OH (anti opening; on the ring the product first forms with OCH3 and OH trans-diaxial). Product: trans-2-methoxy-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
x: B has OCH<sub>3</sub> and OH cis; epoxide opening is back-side (anti), so the two groups must be trans.
C has methanol attacking the secondary carbon, the regiochemistry seen with methoxide (base), not with acid.
Methanol, not water, is the nucleophile, so a methyl ether forms rather than a diol.

q: (R)-2-Ethyl-2-methyloxirane is treated with CH3OH and a catalytic amount of H2SO4. What is the major product?
h: Acid sets the regiochemistry (which carbon); the back-side attack sets the configuration at that carbon.
w: Under acid, methanol attacks the tertiary carbon of the protonated epoxide. The attack is back-side, opposite the leaving oxygen (the ring is still bonded, so no free carbocation forms), so that stereocenter is inverted. Ranking the product carbon: OCH3 > CH2OH > CH2CH3 > CH3; with inversion this gives (S)-2-methoxy-2-methylbutan-1-ol (checked with CIP software).
x: Retention of configuration would need front-side attack; acid-catalyzed epoxide opening is back-side even at a tertiary carbon.
This is the product of attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, the regiochemistry for basic conditions (e.g. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>).
The ring oxygen is still bonded when methanol attacks, so there is no free planar carbocation and no racemization.

q: Cyclohexene oxide reacts with HBr to give 2-bromocyclohexan-1-ol. Which describes the product in the chair conformation in which it is first formed?
h: Bromide attacks anti to the C–O bond. In a half-chair, which direction is anti to the epoxide oxygen?
w: Bromide attacks the protonated epoxide from the side opposite the oxygen (anti opening). In the cyclohexane ring that path keeps the nucleophile and the leaving oxygen on a common axis, so the new C–Br bond and the C–OH bond are both axial on opposite faces: the product forms trans-diaxial. It then ring-flips to the more stable diequatorial chair, but it stays trans.
x: The diequatorial chair is the more stable conformer reached after a ring flip; it is not the chair formed directly by anti opening.
Anti (back-side) opening always puts Br and OH on opposite faces, so the product is trans, not cis.
A cis product would need syn delivery of Br; epoxide opening is anti, giving the trans isomer.

q: Cyclohexene oxide is treated with (1) NaN<sub>3</sub> in aqueous ethanol, then (2) LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, then (3) H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the product (racemic; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: Azide is a strong nucleophile. Track the stereochemistry of the ring opening, then ask what LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does to an azide.
w: Azide opens the epoxide by SN2 from the face opposite the oxygen, giving trans-2-azidocyclohexan-1-ol. LiAlH4 reduces the azide (–N3) to a primary amine (–NH2) without touching the stereocenters. Product: trans-2-aminocyclohexan-1-ol.
x: This is the cis isomer; S<sub>N</sub>2 opening of the epoxide is anti, so N and O end up trans.
This is the intermediate after step 1; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the azide to an amine.
Azide is far more nucleophilic than water, so the epoxide is opened by N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, not hydrolyzed to the diol.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Hydride from LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a strong nucleophile. Where does a strong nucleophile open an epoxide?
w: Hydride (from AlH4−) opens the epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered secondary carbon. The oxygen stays on the tertiary carbon, and acid workup protonates it: 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
x: This would need hydride to attack the tertiary carbon, which is too hindered for S<sub>N</sub>2.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> adds one H; it does not add a second oxygen, so no diol forms.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> opens the ring to an alcohol; it does not remove the oxygen to regenerate the alkene.

q: What is the product after phenylmagnesium bromide reacts with oxirane (ethylene oxide) and the mixture is worked up with aqueous acid?
h: The Grignard carbon bonds to a ring carbon; the oxygen ends up two carbons away.
w: The aryl carbanion attacks one CH2 of oxirane by SN2, opening the strained ring. Workup protonates the alkoxide. The phenyl group gains a two-carbon chain ending in OH: 2-phenylethan-1-ol. Grignard + oxirane adds two carbons, with the OH on the second carbon.
x: 1-Phenylethanol would form from PhMgBr + acetaldehyde (or CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + benzaldehyde), not from oxirane.
Benzyl alcohol has only one carbon between ring and OH; it is the product with formaldehyde, which adds one carbon.
Oxirane adds two carbons, not three; three carbons would need oxetane.

q: Which reagents give the alcohol shown as the major product?
h: For each pair, put the Grignard carbon on the less hindered epoxide carbon and draw what results.
w: Grignard reagents open epoxides at the less hindered carbon. Phenyl attacks the CH2 of 2-methyloxirane, and the O stays on the CH(CH3) carbon: C6H5–CH2–CH(OH)–CH3, 1-phenylpropan-2-ol. The answer is C6H5MgBr + 2-methyloxirane.
x: Attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> of 2-phenyloxirane gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (OH next to the ring), and attack at the benzylic carbon gives 2-phenylpropan-1-ol; neither is the target.
Benzyl + oxirane gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, a primary alcohol (3-phenylpropan-1-ol).
Methyl adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> of 2-benzyloxirane, giving C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, which has one carbon too many (1-phenylbutan-2-ol).

q: (R)-2-Methyloxirane is treated with CH3MgBr, followed by aqueous acid. What is the product?
h: Find which carbon is attacked. Are any bonds to the stereocenter broken?
w: The Grignard attacks the less hindered CH2 carbon, so no bond to the stereocenter is broken and its spatial arrangement is kept. CIP check at that carbon: before, O > CH2(ring, bonded to O) > CH3 > H; after, OH > CH2CH3 > CH3 > H. The priority order maps onto the same positions, so the label stays (R)-butan-2-ol.
x: Inversion happens only at the carbon that is attacked; here the attacked carbon (CH<sub>2</sub>) is not the stereocenter.
Racemization would need the stereocenter to become planar; no bond to it breaks in this S<sub>N</sub>2 opening.
This product would come from attack at the more hindered CH carbon, which Grignard reagents avoid.

q: (2R,3R)-2,3-Dimethyloxirane is treated with NaOCH3 in CH3OH. Which stereoisomer of 3-methoxybutan-2-ol forms?
h: The two epoxide carbons are equivalent here. One carbon is inverted and the other is untouched; then assign R/S.
w: The (R,R) epoxide has C2 symmetry, so attack at either carbon gives the same product. Methoxide attacks one carbon by SN2 and inverts it: that carbon (C3, now bearing OCH3) goes from R to S. The other carbon (C2, keeps the oxygen as OH) is untouched and stays R. Product: (2R,3S)-3-methoxybutan-2-ol as a single enantiomer (assignments checked with CIP software).
x: This is the enantiomer; it would come from the (S,S) epoxide.
Both centers R would mean retention at the attacked carbon; SN2 opening inverts it.
Inverting both centers would need both C–O bonds to break; only one carbon is attacked.

q: With NaOH, trans-2-chlorocyclohexan-1-ol rapidly forms cyclohexene oxide, but the cis isomer does not form an epoxide. What is the best explanation?
c: Ring closure is an internal SN2 that needs O− anti to Cl (both axial); only the trans isomer can do this
The cis isomer would have to give a trans-fused epoxide, which is too strained to form
The cis alcohol is much less acidic, so NaOH cannot form enough of its alkoxide
The trans isomer reacts by E2, which needs an anti-periplanar H that the cis isomer lacks
h: Epoxide closure from a halohydrin is a back-side displacement. Where must the nucleophile sit relative to the leaving group?
w: The alkoxide closes the ring by intramolecular SN2, so it must approach the C–Cl carbon from the back side, anti to Cl. In the trans isomer a ring flip puts OH and Cl trans-diaxial, perfectly anti. In the cis isomer O and Cl are on the same face, so back-side attack is impossible. Only the trans isomer can place O− anti to Cl.
x: Both isomers would give the same cis-fused cyclohexene oxide if they could close; the problem is the approach geometry, not product strain.
Cis and trans chlorohydrins have very similar acidities; both are deprotonated by NaOH.
Epoxide formation is a substitution by oxygen, not an elimination of H and Cl.

q:
Rank these compounds from least acidic to most acidic.
I. CH3CH2OH II. CH3CH2SH III. CF3CH2OH
h: Compare the atom carrying the negative charge first, then the inductive effect.
w: Ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is least acidic. Three fluorines pull electron density away inductively and stabilize CF3CH2O− (pKa ≈ 12.4). Ethanethiol is most acidic (pKa ≈ 10.6) because the charge sits on the larger, more polarizable sulfur atom, and the weaker S–H bond breaks more easily; going down a group outweighs the inductive effect here. Order: I < III < II.
x: Inductive stabilization by CF<sub>3</sub> lowers the pK<sub>a</sub> to about 12, but putting the charge on sulfur lowers it more, to about 10.6.
Fluorination makes the alcohol more acidic than ethanol, not less.
The thiol is the most acidic of the three, not the least: sulfur, being larger, holds the negative charge better than oxygen.

q: 2-Sulfanylethan-1-ol (HSCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is treated with one equivalent of NaOH in water, then one equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I. What is the major product?
h: Which proton does one equivalent of hydroxide remove? Which anion is the better nucleophile anyway?
w: The thiol (pKa ≈ 10) is far more acidic than the alcohol (pKa ≈ 16), so one equivalent of NaOH forms the thiolate. Thiolate is also a much better nucleophile than an alcohol or alkoxide in water, because sulfur is large and polarizable. It attacks CH3I by SN2, giving 2-(methylsulfanyl)ethan-1-ol.
x: O-Methylation would need the alkoxide, but NaOH deprotonates the much more acidic SH, and S<sup>−</sup> is the better nucleophile.
Only one equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I is used, and the neutral OH does not react with CH<sub>3</sub>I in water.
A sulfonium salt needs a second equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I to alkylate the sulfide; only one is available.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is treated with sodium methanethiolate (CH3SNa) in DMF. What is the major product?
h: Thiolates are excellent nucleophiles but weak bases. Which pathway does that favor at a secondary carbon?
w: CH3S− is a weak base (CH3SH pKa ≈ 10) but a very strong, polarizable nucleophile, and DMF is polar aprotic. So even at a secondary carbon SN2 beats E2. Back-side attack inverts the stereocenter; S replaces Br as top priority, so the product is (S)-2-(methylsulfanyl)butane.
x: Retention would require front-side attack; SN2 gives inversion, and the S group takes Br's priority rank, so the label changes to S.
E2 to (E)-but-2-ene needs a strong base such as ethoxide; methanethiolate is too weak a base to compete with its own SN2.
Hofmann-type alkene formation needs a bulky strong base; thiolate gives substitution.

q: What is the product when ethanethiol is treated with I<sub>2</sub> (a mild oxidant) in the presence of a weak base?
h: Mild oxidation of thiols forms an S–S bond.
w: Two thiol molecules are oxidized by I2, each losing an H, and their sulfur atoms join: 2 RSH → RS–SR + 2 HI. The product is diethyl disulfide. This is the same S–S bond that links cysteine residues in proteins.
x: A sulfide (thioether) has one sulfur bonded to two carbons; forming it would need an alkylation, not an oxidation.
Sulfonic acids need strong oxidants such as HNO<sub>3</sub> or KMnO<sub>4</sub>; I<sub>2</sub> stops at the disulfide.
Iodine does not replace the SH group; the thiol is oxidized at sulfur, not substituted at carbon.

q: The disulfide bond in cystine is cleaved by excess 2-mercaptoethanol (or by Zn/HCl) to give two cysteine molecules. Which statement about the sulfur atoms is correct?
c: Their oxidation state does not change; the S–S bond is hydrolyzed
h: Count each sulfur's bonds: S–S counts as zero; S is slightly more electronegative than C and more than H.
w: In the disulfide each S has one bond to C (S is assigned that electron pair: −1) and one bond to S (0), so each S is −1. In the thiol each S has a bond to C (−1) and a bond to H (−1), so S is −2. Going from disulfide to thiols, each sulfur gains a bond to H: reduction from −1 to −2. The reverse (thiols → disulfide) is an oxidation.
x: That is the reverse reaction, thiol to disulfide; breaking the S–S bond and adding H is a reduction.
The disulfide sulfur is −1, not 0, because each sulfur is also bonded to a carbon.
Each S gains an S–H bond in place of an S–S bond, so the oxidation state changes; water does not cleave disulfides.

q: Methyl phenyl sulfide is treated with excess H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid with heating. What is the final product?
h: Each oxidation adds one oxygen to sulfur. How many times can a sulfide sulfur be oxidized without breaking C–S bonds?
w: Sulfides are oxidized at sulfur in two steps: sulfide → sulfoxide (one O) → sulfone (two O). One equivalent of a mild oxidant (NaIO4, or 1 equiv H2O2 at low temperature) stops at the sulfoxide; excess oxidant with heat continues to the sulfone, methyl phenyl sulfone. The C–S bonds are kept.
x: The sulfoxide is the intermediate; with excess H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and heat it is oxidized again to the sulfone.
A sulfonic acid would require breaking the S–CH<sub>3</sub> bond; peroxide oxidation adds O to S and leaves both C–S bonds.
Oxidation adds oxygen to sulfur; it does not replace sulfur by oxygen.

q: Which compound is chiral and can be isolated as a single enantiomer at room temperature?
h: A sulfoxide sulfur is pyramidal with a lone pair as its fourth "group". Look for four different groups.
w: The sulfoxide sulfur is tetrahedral: O, two carbon groups and a lone pair. Its pyramidal inversion is slow at room temperature (barrier about 160 kJ/mol), so a sulfoxide with two different carbon groups is a stable stereocenter. Methyl phenyl sulfoxide has O, CH3, C6H5 and a lone pair, so it is chiral and resolvable.
x: A sulfone has two identical oxygens on sulfur, so the sulfur is not a stereocenter.
Diphenyl sulfoxide has two identical phenyl groups, so it has a mirror plane and is achiral.
DMSO has two identical methyl groups, so it is achiral.

q: Which compound reacts with CH<sub>3</sub>I at room temperature to give a stable, isolable salt?
h: Compare how nucleophilic, and how basic, sulfur and oxygen lone pairs are.
w: Divalent sulfur is large and polarizable, so sulfides are good nucleophiles even though they are weak bases. Dimethyl sulfide attacks CH3I by SN2 to give trimethylsulfonium iodide, (CH3)3S+ I−, a stable salt. Ethers are poor nucleophiles, and trialkyloxonium ions are too reactive to form this way. The answer is dimethyl sulfide.
x: Dimethyl ether's oxygen is a poor nucleophile; a trimethyloxonium salt does not form from CH<sub>3</sub>I.
Diethyl ether is a common solvent for reactions of alkyl halides precisely because it does not react with them.
THF's oxygen lone pairs coordinate to metals (as in Grignard reagents), but THF is not nucleophilic enough to be alkylated by CH<sub>3</sub>I.

q: Which sequence converts (R)-butan-2-ol into (R)-2-methoxybutane?
h: Decide which C–O bond must stay intact to keep the configuration.
w: To keep the configuration, the C–O bond at the stereocenter must not break. NaH forms the alkoxide (the stereocenter is untouched), and the alkoxide attacks CH3I by SN2 at the methyl carbon. The new bond is O–CH3, so the stereocenter keeps its arrangement: 1. NaH 2. CH3I gives (R)-2-methoxybutane (CIP label confirmed).
x: Tosylation keeps the configuration, but methoxide then displaces OTs by SN2 at the stereocenter, giving (S)-2-methoxybutane (plus some E2 alkene).
Acid with a secondary alcohol gives elimination and S<sub>N</sub>1 mixtures that lose the stereochemistry; it is not a clean route to one enantiomer of the ether.
A neutral alcohol reacts very slowly with CH<sub>3</sub>I; the alkoxide must be formed first, so the order of steps matters.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexene into the product shown (racemic; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: The target has two oxygens on adjacent carbons, trans. Which route adds two oxygens anti?
w: Epoxidation adds one oxygen across the double bond. Ethoxide then opens the epoxide by back-side SN2, placing OCH2CH3 trans to the alkoxide, which ethanol protonates. The sequence 1. mCPBA 2. NaOCH2CH3, CH3CH2OH gives trans-2-ethoxycyclohexan-1-ol.
x: OsO4 adds both OH groups syn, so this route gives the cis ether-alcohol (and mixtures from the diol).
Alkoxymercuration adds only one oxygen (ethoxycyclohexane); the product needs an OH on the next carbon.
Hydroboration–oxidation adds only one OH, so this sequence gives ethoxycyclohexane with no second oxygen.

q: Epoxides are opened by hydroxide or alkoxides under mild conditions, while diethyl ether is inert to them. What is the main reason?
c: The three-membered ring is strained, and opening it releases about 110 kJ/mol of strain
Epoxide carbons are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridized, like a carbonyl carbon, so they are very electrophilic
The epoxide oxygen carries a formal positive charge, like a protonated ether
Epoxides are aromatic, and opening the ring relieves antiaromatic strain
h: Compare the C–O–C bond angle in an epoxide with the normal tetrahedral angle.
w: In an epoxide the ring bond angles are about 60°, far from 109.5°, so the ring holds roughly 110 kJ/mol of angle and torsional strain. Opening the ring releases that strain, which makes the alkoxide leaving group acceptable. An acyclic ether has no such driving force. Answer: ring strain.
x: Epoxide carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>; they have no π bond.
A neutral epoxide oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs, so its formal charge is zero.
An epoxide has no π electrons and cannot be aromatic or antiaromatic.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Find the C=O band position first (conjugated or not), then ask whether there is an aldehyde H near δ 9–10.
w: DBE = 5: a benzene ring (4) plus one C=O. The strong band at 1685 cm−1 is a C=O lowered about 30 cm−1 by conjugation with the ring, and there is no aldehyde C–H pair near 2720/2820 cm−1 and no signal at δ 9–10. The aromatic pattern 2H : 1H : 2H (d, t, t) with 5H total is a monosubstituted ring, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.60 is a CH3 on a C=O. The compound is acetophenone.
x: Phenylacetaldehyde has an unconjugated CHO: C=O near 1725 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a 1H triplet near δ 9.7 and a 2H doublet near δ 3.6, none of which appear.
4-Methylbenzaldehyde has a 1H singlet near δ 9.9 (CHO), the C–H pair at 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and only 4 aromatic H as two 2H doublets.
2-Methylbenzaldehyde shows a CHO singlet near δ 10.2 and four separate 1H aromatic signals, not a 2:1:2 pattern for 5H.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 12.0 signal disappears on shaking with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: A very broad band from about 3300 down to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus a 1H signal near δ 12 points to one functional group. Then read the aromatic pattern.
w: The very broad O–H band (3300–2500 cm−1) and the exchangeable 1H at δ 12.0 identify a carboxylic acid; the C=O at 1685 cm−1 is low because the COOH is conjugated with the ring. Two 2H doublets (δ 7.99 and 7.27) are the classic para-disubstituted pattern, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.43 is an aryl CH3. The compound is 4-methylbenzoic acid.
x: Methyl benzoate has no O–H (no broad band, no δ 12 signal); its CH<sub>3</sub> is an O–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.9, and its ring is monosubstituted (5H).
Phenylacetic acid has 5 aromatic H and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.6; its COOH is not conjugated, so its C=O is near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
3-Methylbenzoic acid is meta-substituted: four different aromatic H (four 1H signals), not two 2H doublets.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a strong band at 1230 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Where would a CH<sub>2</sub> appear if it were bonded to both an oxygen and a benzene ring? Where would CH<sub>3</sub> appear on O versus on C=O?
w: 1740 cm−1 with a strong C–O band at 1230 cm−1 is an unconjugated ester (13C 170.9). The 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring. The 2H singlet at δ 5.11 is far downfield because the CH2 is both benzylic and bonded to the ester O (13C 66.3), and the 3H singlet at δ 2.10 is a CH3–C=O (13C 21.0). This is benzyl acetate, PhCH2OC(=O)CH3.
x: Methyl phenylacetate also gives two singlets, but at δ 3.70 (OCH<sub>3</sub>, 13C ≈ 52) and δ 3.63 (ArCH<sub>2</sub>C=O, 13C ≈ 41); nothing would reach δ 5.1 or 66 ppm.
Ethyl benzoate shows an OCH<sub>2</sub> quartet (δ 4.38) and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet (δ 1.38), and its conjugated ester C=O absorbs near 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Methoxyacetophenone is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets, 4 ArH) and its conjugated ketone C=O is near 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup> with 13C near 197 ppm.

q: A compound has molecular formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>7</sub>ClO. Which set of structural features matches its degree of unsaturation?
c: A benzene ring and one C=O
A benzene ring and one C≡C
A benzene ring, one C=O and one more ring
h: DBE = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. A halogen counts like a hydrogen.
w: DBE = (2·8 + 2 − 7 − 1)/2 = 10/2 = 5. A benzene ring accounts for 4 (one ring + three C=C), leaving one more: a benzene ring and one C=O (for example 4-chloroacetophenone).
x: A benzene ring alone is DBE 4; this formula has DBE 5, so one π bond or ring is missing.
A C≡C counts as 2, giving DBE 6, one too many.
Ring + C=O + benzene is DBE 6, one too many; the extra ring is not allowed.

q: A compound gives the mass spectrum and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two molecular-ion peaks 2 units apart in a 1 : 1 ratio identify one halogen. Then count aromatic signals.
w: M+ at m/z 170 and 172 in about a 1 : 1 ratio means one Br (79Br and 81Br are nearly equally abundant); 170 − 79 = 91, the C7H7+ base peak. The two 2H doublets are a para-disubstituted ring and the 3H singlet at δ 2.30 is an aryl CH3: 4-bromotoluene.
x: Benzyl bromide has 5 aromatic H and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>Br singlet near δ 4.5, not a 3H singlet at δ 2.30.
2-Bromotoluene is ortho-disubstituted: four different aromatic H, not two 2H doublets.
4-Chlorotoluene has M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 126 and 128 in a 3 : 1 ratio, not 170/172 at 1 : 1.

q: A compound shows a strong IR band at 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> and gives the mass spectrum and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Check the M : M+2 ratio for the halogen, then the aromatic pattern, then where the CH<sub>3</sub> or CH<sub>2</sub> sits.
w: M+ 154 and M+2 156 in a 3 : 1 ratio means one Cl. The base peak at 139/141 is loss of CH3 (α-cleavage) to give ClC6H4CO+, still carrying Cl. Two 2H doublets mean para substitution, the 3H singlet at δ 2.59 is CH3C=O, and 1685 cm−1 is an aryl ketone: 4-chloroacetophenone.
x: 2-Chloro-1-phenylethanone has 5 aromatic H and a 2H singlet near δ 4.7 for CH<sub>2</sub>Cl; there is no 3H singlet.
4-Bromoacetophenone would give M<sup>+</sup> at 198/200 in a 1 : 1 ratio.
3-Chloroacetophenone is meta-substituted: four different 1H aromatic signals, not two 2H doublets.

q: The most downfield <sup>13</sup>C signal of a compound is at δ 207.5, and it is absent from both the DEPT-90 and DEPT-135 spectra. Which compound is it?
h: Match 13C carbonyl regions: ketone ≈ 205–210, aldehyde ≈ 200, ester/acid ≈ 170–180, nitrile ≈ 118–122. Then use DEPT: which carbons have no H?
w: δ 207.5 is in the ketone window, and a signal missing from DEPT-90 and DEPT-135 belongs to a carbon with no H (quaternary). A ketone C=O has no H; an aldehyde C=O is a CH and would appear in DEPT-90. So the compound is 4-phenylbutan-2-one.
x: 3-Phenylpropanal's CHO carbon is near δ 201 and is a CH, so it would appear (positive) in both DEPT-90 and DEPT-135.
An ester C=O such as that of methyl 3-phenylpropanoate is near δ 173, well upfield of 207.
A nitrile carbon is near δ 119; 3-phenylpropanenitrile has no signal anywhere near 207 ppm.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>7</sub>N gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: What absorbs sharply near 2230 cm<sup>−1</sup> with nothing near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>? Then read the aromatic pattern.
w: DBE = (16 + 2 + 1 − 7)/2 = 6: a benzene ring plus two more, fitting a C≡N. The sharp 2228 cm−1 band (low for a nitrile because it is conjugated with the ring) and the 13C signal at δ 119.1 confirm a nitrile; nothing appears near 3300 cm−1, so there is no N–H or ≡C–H. Two 2H doublets mean para substitution, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.42 is an aryl CH3: 4-methylbenzonitrile. (The 13C at δ 109.3 is the ring carbon bearing CN.)
x: Phenylacetonitrile has 5 aromatic H and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.7; its unconjugated C≡N absorbs near 2250 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Ethynylaniline would show two N–H stretches (3300–3450 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a sharp ≡C–H stretch near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a ≡C–H singlet near δ 3.0.
Indole has an N–H stretch near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>, no triple-bond band, and six different aromatic/heteroaromatic C–H signals.

q: Isomers I and II (both C8H8O2) are shown. Which observation distinguishes them?
c: The CH<sub>3</sub> singlet: near δ 3.9 in I but near δ 2.3 in II
The molecular ion: m/z 136 for I but m/z 150 for II
The <sup>13</sup>C signal count: 6 for I but 5 for II
The aromatic integration: 5H for I but 4H for II in the δ 7–8 region
h: Both are esters with a monosubstituted ring and one CH<sub>3</sub>. What is the CH<sub>3</sub> bonded to in each?
w: In methyl benzoate (I) the CH3 is on the ester oxygen (O–CH3, δ ≈ 3.9). In phenyl acetate (II) the CH3 is on the carbonyl carbon (CH3–C=O, δ ≈ 2.3). So the CH3 singlet position tells them apart. (Their IR also differs: about 1725 cm−1 for I, conjugated with the ring, and about 1765 cm−1 for the aryl ester II.)
x: They are isomers with the same formula, so both have M<sup>+</sup> = 136.
Both have 6 carbon signals: C=O, CH<sub>3</sub>, and four ring signals (ipso, ortho, meta, para).
Both rings are monosubstituted, so both show 5 aromatic H.

q: Which 1H NMR data (CDCl3) belong to the major product of this reaction?
h: OCH<sub>3</sub> is an o/p director, and the bulky acylium ion prefers the less hindered position. What is added: an acetyl or a methyl?
w: Friedel–Crafts acylation puts an acetyl group on the ring. OCH3 directs ortho/para, and para wins on sterics, giving 4-methoxyacetophenone. Its spectrum: two 2H doublets (para), OCH3 at δ 3.87 and the acetyl CH3 at δ 2.55, deshielded by the C=O: δ 7.93 (d, 2H), 6.93 (d, 2H), 3.87 (s, 3H), 2.55 (s, 3H). The doublet at 7.93 is ortho to the electron-withdrawing C=O; the one at 6.93 is ortho to the donating OCH3.
x: Four separate 1H aromatic signals with ortho couplings fit the ortho product (2-methoxyacetophenone), which is the minor isomer.
Four aromatic H with a 1H triplet and a dd fit the meta product (3-methoxyacetophenone), which an o/p director like OCH<sub>3</sub> barely forms.
A CH<sub>3</sub> at δ 2.29 is an aryl methyl, as in 4-methylanisole. Acylation adds CH<sub>3</sub>C=O, whose CH<sub>3</sub> appears near δ 2.5–2.6.

q: Acetophenone is treated with NaBH<sub>4</sub> in CH<sub>3</sub>OH. Which spectral change shows that the reaction worked?
c: The 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> band vanishes and a broad 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> band appears; the CH<sub>3</sub> singlet (δ 2.60) becomes a δ 1.5 doublet, coupled to a new 1H quartet at δ 4.9
The C=O band moves from 1685 to about 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> because conjugation with the ring is lost; the δ 2.60 CH<sub>3</sub> singlet is unchanged
The δ 2.60 CH<sub>3</sub> singlet moves to δ 1.5 and stays a singlet, and a new 1H singlet appears near δ 4.9 for the CH–O proton
A very broad band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears, and a new exchangeable 1H singlet appears near δ 12, as for a COOH group
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces a ketone to a secondary alcohol. What is the new carbon bonded to, and what does the CH<sub>3</sub> now neighbor?
w: NaBH4 gives 1-phenylethanol, PhCH(OH)CH3. The C=O band is gone and an O–H band appears near 3350 cm−1. The CH3 now sits next to a CH (n + 1 = 2, a doublet near δ 1.5), and that CH (next to 3 H, a quartet) is at δ 4.9 because it carries O and Ph. So the C=O is replaced by O–H, and the CH3 singlet becomes a doublet coupled to a new 1H quartet.
x: The product has no C=O at all, so no C=O band remains to shift.
The CH<sub>3</sub> is now on a carbon that carries one H, so it is split into a doublet, and that CH is a quartet, not a singlet.
A 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> O–H and a δ 12 H describe a carboxylic acid; NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces, it does not oxidize.

q: Which compound has the longest-wavelength UV absorption maximum (λ<sub>max</sub>)?
h: Count the C=C bonds that are in one continuous conjugated system (a benzene ring counts).
w: λmax increases as the conjugated π system grows, because the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks. (E)-1-Phenyl-1,3-butadiene has a diene conjugated with a benzene ring (λmax ≈ 280 nm), the largest conjugated system here.
x: 1,3-Cyclohexadiene is a conjugated diene held s-cis (λ<sub>max</sub> ≈ 256 nm), but it has only two C=C in conjugation.
(2E,4E)-2,4-Hexadiene is a conjugated diene (λ<sub>max</sub> ≈ 227 nm); its methyl groups add only a few nm.
1,4-Cyclohexadiene's C=C bonds are separated by CH<sub>2</sub> groups, so they are not conjugated; it absorbs below 200 nm.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>11</sub>N shows two medium IR bands at 3370 and 3290 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (the δ 1.15 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: Two N–H bands mean NH<sub>2</sub>. Then look at the aromatic integration and the coupling of the CH<sub>2</sub> groups.
w: Two N–H stretches (symmetric and asymmetric) mean a primary amine, and the 2H exchangeable signal at δ 1.15 is the NH2 of an alkylamine. The 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring, and two 2H triplets mean –CH2CH2–: δ 2.97 (CH2N) and 2.75 (ArCH2). The compound is 2-phenylethylamine.
x: N-Methylbenzylamine is a secondary amine with one N–H band, and it gives two singlets (CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.75, NCH<sub>3</sub> near δ 2.45), not two triplets.
N,N-Dimethylaniline is tertiary: no N–H band at all, and a 6H singlet near δ 2.9.
4-Ethylaniline is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets) with an ArNH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.5 and an ethyl quartet/triplet, not two triplets.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 7.20 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: How many N–H bands, and where is the C=O? Then decide which CH<sub>3</sub> is on the ring and which is on the carbonyl.
w: DBE = 5: a ring plus one C=O. One N–H stretch (3290 cm−1) and a C=O at 1660 cm−1 with an amide II band at 1540 cm−1 mean a secondary amide (one N–H, 1H broad at δ 7.20). Two 2H doublets mean para substitution. The two 3H singlets are an aryl CH3 (δ 2.31) and an acetyl CH3 (δ 2.16). The compound is N-(4-methylphenyl)acetamide.
x: N,N-Dimethylbenzamide has no N–H (no band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>), and its ring is monosubstituted (5H). Its two N–CH<sub>3</sub> singlets appear near δ 3.0 because of slow C–N rotation.
2-(4-Methylphenyl)acetamide is a primary amide: two N–H bands, a 2H NH<sub>2</sub>, and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.5 instead of a second 3H singlet.
4′-Aminopropiophenone has an NH<sub>2</sub> (two N–H bands) and an ethyl group (quartet near δ 2.9, triplet near δ 1.2), not two singlets.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> shows strong IR bands at 1825 and 1755 cm<sup>−1</sup> (none above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Which carbonyl derivative shows two C=O stretches, one above 1800 cm−1?
w: Two strong C=O bands about 60–70 cm−1 apart, the higher one above 1800 cm−1, are the symmetric and asymmetric stretches of an anhydride. One 6H singlet and only two 13C signals (C=O at δ 166.6, CH3 at δ 22.1) mean a symmetric molecule: acetic anhydride.
x: Methyl pyruvate has two different CH<sub>3</sub> groups (OCH<sub>3</sub> near δ 3.9, CH<sub>3</sub>C=O near δ 2.5) and a ketone 13C near δ 192; its C=O bands are near 1735–1750 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not 1825.
Acetoacetic acid has a carboxylic O–H (broad 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet, and a ketone 13C near δ 200.
(2-Oxopropyl) formate has a formyl H singlet near δ 8.1 and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 4.7 in addition to a CH<sub>3</sub>; three signals, not one.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: A 1H singlet near δ 10 and weak IR bands near 2820 and 2730 cm<sup>−1</sup> point to one group. Then read the ring pattern and the alkyl signals.
w: The 1H singlet at δ 9.97 and the C–H pair at 2820/2730 cm−1 identify an aldehyde; the C=O at 1700 cm−1 is conjugated with the ring. It is a singlet, so the CHO is on the ring (no neighboring H). Two 2H doublets mean para substitution, and the quartet/triplet (δ 2.72, 1.27) is an aryl ethyl group: 4-ethylbenzaldehyde.
x: Propiophenone is a ketone: no δ 9.97 signal, no 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup> band, and a 5H monosubstituted ring.
3-Phenylpropanal's CHO is a triplet near δ 9.8 (coupled to CH<sub>2</sub>), with two CH<sub>2</sub> signals and a 5H ring.
2,4-Dimethylbenzaldehyde would show two separate 3H singlets near δ 2.4–2.6 and three different aromatic H, not an ethyl quartet and triplet.

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O shows a strong IR band at 1686 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a <sup>13</sup>C signal at δ 200.4, and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Is the C=O conjugated with the ring? Then use the splitting of the alkyl signals to build the chain.
w: 1686 cm−1 and δ 200.4 fit an aryl ketone (conjugation lowers the C=O stretch from about 1715 and moves the 13C a little upfield of 207). The 2:1:2 aromatic pattern is a monosubstituted benzoyl group. The alkyl chain is t (2H, δ 2.95, next to C=O) – sextet (2H) – t (3H): CH2CH2CH3. The compound is 1-phenylbutan-1-one (butyrophenone).
x: 1-Phenylbutan-2-one has a CH<sub>2</sub> between ring and C=O that is a singlet near δ 3.7, plus an ethyl q/t; its C=O is unconjugated (≈1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, δ ≈ 209).
4-Phenylbutan-2-one shows a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet near δ 2.1 and two triplets; its C=O is unconjugated (≈1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, δ ≈ 208).
2-Methyl-1-phenylpropan-1-one is also an aryl ketone, but its isopropyl group gives a 1H septet near δ 3.5 and a 6H doublet near δ 1.2.

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1716 cm<sup>−1</sup> and strong bands at 1275 and 1105 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. Which structure fits?
h: An ethyl quartet near δ 4.3 and one near δ 2.5 mean different things. Which side of the ester O is the ethyl on?
w: The C=O at 1716 cm−1 with strong C–O bands is a conjugated (aryl) ester. The ethyl CH2 quartet at δ 4.36 must be on oxygen (O–CH2); a CH2–C=O would be near δ 2.5. Two 2H doublets, with the δ 7.94 pair ortho to the C=O, mean para substitution, and δ 2.40 is an aryl CH3. The compound is ethyl 4-methylbenzoate.
x: In 4-methylphenyl propanoate the ethyl is on the acyl side: its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is near δ 2.6, and an aryl ester C=O absorbs near 1760 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Propyl benzoate has a 5H monosubstituted ring and an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet, a sextet and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet; there is no aryl CH<sub>3</sub> singlet.
Ethyl phenylacetate has a 5H ring, a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.6 and an OCH<sub>2</sub> quartet near δ 4.15; its unconjugated C=O is near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 11.5 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: Identify the functional group from the O–H shape and the δ 11.5 proton. Is the C=O conjugated? Then read the splitting of the CH<sub>2</sub> groups.
w: The broad 3300–2500 cm−1 O–H and the exchangeable δ 11.5 H mean a carboxylic acid. Its C=O at 1710 cm−1 is not lowered, so the COOH is not on the ring. A 5H multiplet (monosubstituted ring) and two 2H triplets (ArCH2CH2COOH) give 3-phenylpropanoic acid.
x: 4-Ethylbenzoic acid has a para pattern (two 2H doublets), an ethyl quartet/triplet, and a conjugated C=O near 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
2-Phenylpropanoic acid shows a 1H quartet near δ 3.7 and a 3H doublet near δ 1.5, not two 2H triplets.
Methyl phenylacetate is an ester: no O–H band and no δ 11.5 signal, and it shows two singlets (OCH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>).

q: An aromatic hydrocarbon C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>10</sub> shows <sup>1</sup>H NMR δ 7.12 (m, 4H), 2.27 (s, 6H) and the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: The 1H spectrum fits more than one isomer. Count unique carbons in each using its symmetry.
w: A 6H singlet means two equivalent aryl CH3 groups, so the compound is a xylene, and the 13C spectrum decides which one. o-Xylene has a mirror plane through the ring between the two CH3 groups: 2 ring C bearing CH3, 2 pairs of ring CH, and 1 CH3 type = 4 signals (δ 136.5, 129.6, 125.8, 19.7). The answer is 1,2-dimethylbenzene.
x: m-Xylene has 5 carbon signals: C1/C3, C2, C4/C6, C5 and CH<sub>3</sub>.
p-Xylene has only 3 carbon signals, and its 4 ring H are equivalent (a sharp singlet).
Ethylbenzene shows an ethyl quartet/triplet in the 1H spectrum, not a 6H singlet, and 6 carbon signals.

q: A compound with molecular formula C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>13</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> contains a benzene ring. What is its degree of unsaturation (DBE)?
h: DBE = (2C + 2 + N − H)/2. Oxygen does not change the count; each N adds one.
w: DBE = (2·10 + 2 + 1 − 13)/2 = 10/2 = 5. The benzene ring uses 4, so there is exactly one more ring or π bond (for example an amide or ester C=O).
x: 4 comes from subtracting the N instead of adding it: (22 − 1 − 13)/2. Nitrogen brings an extra H to a saturated formula, so it is added.
6 comes from treating each O like N; oxygen is divalent and does not change the H count of a saturated formula.
10 is the value of (2C + 2 + N − H) before dividing by 2; each degree of unsaturation removes two H, so the difference must be halved.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. The δ 7.49 doublet and δ 6.72 dd share a 16 Hz coupling, and the δ 6.72 dd and δ 9.70 doublet share a 7.7 Hz coupling. Which structure fits?
h: DBE = 6. Which proton appears near δ 9.7 and why is it a doublet? What does J = 16 Hz say about a C=C?
w: DBE = (18 + 2 − 8)/2 = 6: a benzene ring plus two more (C=O and C=C). The δ 9.70 H with IR 2815/2740 cm−1 is an aldehyde H; it is a doublet because it is coupled to one vinyl H (δ 6.72). That vinyl H is also coupled (J = 16 Hz, trans) to the δ 7.49 H on the carbon bearing the phenyl group. The C=O at 1680 cm−1 is lowered by conjugation. The compound is (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enal (cinnamaldehyde).
x: 1-Phenylprop-2-yn-1-ol would show a broad O–H near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a sharp ≡C–H near 3290 cm<sup>−1</sup>, no C=O band, and no signal near δ 9.7.
1-Indanone has four 1H aromatic signals, two 2H triplet-like CH<sub>2</sub> signals near δ 3.1 and 2.7, and no aldehyde H.
1-Phenylprop-2-en-1-one has a terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> (two vinyl H near δ 5.9 and 6.4 plus a dd near δ 7.1) and no aldehyde H near δ 9.7.

q: Natural chlorine is 75.8% <sup>35</sup>Cl and 24.2% <sup>37</sup>Cl. What relative intensities are expected for the M, M+2 and M+4 peaks of 1,4-dichlorobenzene (ignore <sup>13</sup>C)?
h: Each Cl is independently 35 or 37. Multiply probabilities for the three combinations (35,35), (35,37 two ways), (37,37).
x: 100 : 32 is the pattern for one Cl (3 : 1). With two Cl atoms the chance that at least one is <sup>37</sup>Cl roughly doubles, and an M+4 peak appears.
The M+2 value is right, but a molecule with both Cl atoms as <sup>37</sup>Cl (0.242² ≈ 6%) gives a real M+4 peak.
100 : 196 : 96 (≈ 1 : 2 : 1) is the pattern for two Br atoms, whose isotopes are nearly 50 : 50.

q: A compound gives the mass spectrum and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: The 1 : 1 pair at the top of the spectrum tells you the halogen. The CH<sub>3</sub> splitting tells you its neighbor.
w: M+ at m/z 184/186 in a 1 : 1 ratio means one Br (C8H9Br). The base peak at m/z 105 is M − Br, a stabilized secondary benzylic cation. In the NMR, the 3H doublet (δ 2.04) and 1H quartet (δ 5.21) form a CH–CH3 unit; the CH is far downfield because it carries both Br and Ph. With a 5H ring, the compound is (1-bromoethyl)benzene.
x: (2-Bromoethyl)benzene has –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br: two 2H triplets near δ 3.55 and 3.15, no 3H doublet.
1-Bromo-4-ethylbenzene has the Br on the ring: two 2H doublets (4 ArH) and an ethyl quartet near δ 2.6 and triplet near δ 1.2.
(1-Chloroethyl)benzene would give M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 140/142 in a 3 : 1 ratio.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>11</sub>N shows one medium IR band at 3410 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (the δ 3.55 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: One N–H band means a secondary amine. Then decide whether the CH<sub>2</sub> quartet at δ 3.13 is on N or on the ring, and look at the aromatic shifts.
w: One N–H stretch and a 1H exchangeable signal mean a secondary amine (N–H). The aromatic H are 5H in a 2:1:2 pattern with the ortho (δ 6.61) and para (δ 6.70) H shifted upfield by the electron-donating NH group, so N is on the ring. The ethyl CH2 quartet at δ 3.13 is on N (an Ar–CH2 would be near δ 2.6). The compound is N-ethylaniline.
x: 4-Ethylaniline is a primary amine (two N–H bands, 2H NH<sub>2</sub>), para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets), with its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet near δ 2.55.
N,N-Dimethylaniline has no N–H at all and shows a 6H singlet near δ 2.9.
N-Methylbenzylamine has an ordinary 5H phenyl multiplet near δ 7.3 (N is not on the ring) and two singlets (CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.75, CH<sub>3</sub> near δ 2.45).

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>3</sub> shows strong IR bands at 1725 and 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Assign the two carbonyl carbons (δ 197.6 and 166.3) to carbonyl types. Then decide where each CH<sub>3</sub> is attached from its 1H and 13C shifts.
w: DBE = 6: ring + two C=O. δ 197.6 is a conjugated ketone (1685 cm−1) and δ 166.3 a conjugated ester (1725 cm−1). The 3H singlet at δ 3.95 with 13C δ 52.4 is an ester O–CH3; the 3H singlet at δ 2.64 with 13C δ 26.9 is CH3C=O. Both aromatic doublets are far downfield (δ 8.11, 8.01) because both substituents withdraw electrons, and two 2H doublets mean para. The compound is methyl 4-acetylbenzoate.
x: 4-Acetylphenyl acetate has an aryl ester: C=O near 1765 cm<sup>−1</sup>, ester 13C near 169, an OC(=O)CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.3 (13C ≈ 21) and no OCH<sub>3</sub> near δ 3.9; the ArH ortho to O would be near δ 7.2.
Methyl 3-acetylbenzoate is meta-substituted: four different aromatic H and 10 carbon signals, not two 2H doublets and 8 signals.
Methyl 2-(4-formylphenyl)acetate has an aldehyde (1H singlet near δ 10.0, 13C near 192) and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.7; its ester C=O (≈ 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>, δ ≈ 171) is unconjugated.

q: At room temperature the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of N,N-dimethylacetamide shows three 3H singlets: δ 3.02, 2.94 and 2.09. Why do the two N–CH<sub>3</sub> groups give separate signals?
c: The C–N bond has partial double-bond character, so rotation is slow on the NMR time scale; one CH<sub>3</sub> is cis to O, the other trans
The nitrogen is a stereocenter that inverts slowly, which makes the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups diastereotopic
The two N–CH<sub>3</sub> groups split each other, so the pair at δ 3.02 and 2.94 is really one doublet
Rotation about the bond between C=O and the acetyl CH<sub>3</sub> is slow, which holds one N–CH<sub>3</sub> closer to that CH<sub>3</sub> group
h: Draw the resonance form of an amide that puts a double bond between C and N.
w: Amide resonance (O=C–NR2 ↔ −O–C=N+R2) gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character and a rotation barrier of roughly 75–85 kJ/mol. At room temperature the two N–CH3 groups do not exchange places quickly, so the one cis to O and the one trans to O are in different environments: slow C–N rotation. On heating, the two signals broaden and merge.
x: The amide N is planar (sp<sup>2</sup>, lone pair delocalized) and carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it is not a stereocenter.
Equivalent or not, CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the same N are four bonds apart and do not show resolved coupling; a doublet would also be one 6H signal, not two 3H singlets.
Rotation of a CH<sub>3</sub> about a C–C single bond is fast, and it cannot make the two N–CH<sub>3</sub> groups different.

q: A compound C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>5</sub>BrO<sub>2</sub> shows a very broad IR band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a strong band at 1690 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum (DMSO-d<sub>6</sub>) is shown; the δ 8.05 signal shows only small (≈ 1.8 Hz) couplings, and the δ 7.47 triplet has J ≈ 8 Hz. Which structure fits?
h: Four different 1H aromatic signals rule out para. Which ring H has no ortho neighbor at all?
w: The broad O–H, the exchangeable δ 13.3 H and C=O at 1690 cm−1 mean an aryl carboxylic acid. Four different aromatic H mean the ring is not para. The δ 8.05 H has only meta couplings, so it has no H on either adjacent carbon: it sits between the two substituents (C2 of a 1,3-disubstituted ring). The 1H triplet with J ≈ 8 Hz is H5, which has two ortho neighbors. That is the meta pattern: 3-bromobenzoic acid.
x: 4-Bromobenzoic acid is para-substituted: two 2H doublets, not four 1H signals.
In 2-bromobenzoic acid every ring H has at least one ortho neighbor, so every signal shows a large (≈ 8 Hz) coupling; none has only small couplings.
5-Bromo-2-hydroxybenzaldehyde has an aldehyde H singlet near δ 9.9 and a phenol O–H near δ 11, and only 3 aromatic H; it is not a carboxylic acid.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 4.05 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: Two N–H bands and a 2H exchangeable signal: what kind of nitrogen? The ethyl quartet at δ 4.32 tells you which atom the CH<sub>2</sub> is on.
w: Two N–H stretches (3420, 3340 cm−1) and a 2H exchangeable signal mean an aryl NH2. The C=O at 1680 cm−1 is an ester lowered by conjugation with a ring carrying a strong donor. The CH2 quartet at δ 4.32 is on the ester O (O–CH2CH3). Two 2H doublets, one far upfield at δ 6.64 (ortho to NH2) and one at δ 7.86 (ortho to C=O), mean para. The compound is ethyl 4-aminobenzoate (benzocaine).
x: 4-Aminophenyl propanoate is an aryl ester: C=O near 1750 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the ethyl CH<sub>2</sub> quartet on the acyl side near δ 2.55; no aromatic H would be as far downfield as δ 7.86.
Ethyl 2-aminobenzoate is ortho-substituted: four different 1H aromatic signals, not two 2H doublets.
4-(Ethylamino)benzoic acid has one N–H (one band), a broad carboxylic O–H, an N–CH<sub>2</sub> quartet near δ 3.2, and its exchangeable H are 1H (NH) plus 1H (COOH).

q: Which spectral change best confirms that the reaction shown gave the expected product?
c: The sharp 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears, a strong band appears near 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a new 3H singlet appears near δ 2.57
The sharp 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears, a strong band appears near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a new 3H singlet appears near δ 2.15
The sharp 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears, a broad band appears near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a new 6H singlet appears near δ 1.55
The sharp 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears, two N–H bands appear near 3300–3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a new 2H singlet appears near δ 3.8
h: A Grignard reagent adds once to a nitrile; the imine salt is hydrolyzed in step 2. What functional group results, and is it conjugated?
w: CH3MgBr adds once to C≡N to give an imine anion, which cannot add a second Grignard; aqueous acid hydrolyzes the imine to a ketone, 4-methylacetophenone. The C≡N band disappears and a ketone C=O appears near 1685 cm−1 (conjugated with the ring); the new CH3C=O singlet is near δ 2.57. So: 2228 cm−1 gone, C=O near 1685 cm−1, new 3H singlet near δ 2.57.
x: 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and δ 2.15 describe an unconjugated methyl ketone; here the C=O is attached directly to the ring, which lowers the stretch to about 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> and moves the CH<sub>3</sub> to about δ 2.6.
A 3° alcohol with two new CH<sub>3</sub> groups would need two Grignard additions; the negatively charged imine intermediate does not react a second time.
A primary amine (ArCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) comes from reducing a nitrile with LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, not from a Grignard reagent.

q: Benzaldehyde and acetone react as shown (Claisen–Schmidt condensation). Which data best confirm that the product is (E)-4-phenylbut-3-en-2-one?
c: Two 1H doublets at δ 7.50 and 6.71 with J ≈ 16 Hz, a 3H singlet at δ 2.38, and a C=O band near 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup>
Two 1H doublets at δ 6.90 and 6.20 with J ≈ 11 Hz, a 3H singlet at δ 2.20, and a C=O band near 1690 cm<sup>−1</sup>
A 1H doublet at δ 9.70, a 1H dd at δ 6.72, a 1H doublet at δ 7.49, and a C=O band near 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup>
A 1H dd at δ 5.15, a 2H doublet at δ 2.85, a 3H singlet at δ 2.20, and bands near 3400 and 1712 cm<sup>−1</sup>
h: Condensation (with heat) means dehydration to a C=C conjugated with the C=O. What J value goes with a trans C=C?
w: Heating drives the aldol addition product to dehydrate, giving the conjugated enone PhCH=CHC(=O)CH3. Its two vinyl H are mutually coupled doublets; J ≈ 16 Hz shows they are trans (E). The β H (δ 7.50) is downfield of the α H (δ 6.71) because conjugation puts δ+ on the β carbon. The methyl ketone singlet is at δ 2.38 and the conjugated C=O is near 1670 cm−1. The answer is two doublets with J ≈ 16 Hz, a 3H singlet, C=O near 1670 cm−1.
x: J ≈ 11 Hz is a cis (Z) vinyl coupling; trans coupling is 12–18 Hz, typically about 16 Hz.
A δ 9.70 doublet is an aldehyde H; this describes cinnamaldehyde, not a methyl ketone.
A CH–O dd at δ 5.15, a CH2 doublet, an O–H band and an unconjugated C=O describe the aldol addition product (4-hydroxy-4-phenylbutan-2-one), which has not yet lost water.

q: Acetophenone is treated with mCPBA. The product (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) shows a strong IR band at 1765 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a strong band at 1200 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is the product?
h: In a Baeyer–Villiger oxidation the group with higher migratory aptitude ends up on oxygen. Then check: is the CH<sub>3</sub> on O or on C=O?
w: Phenyl migrates in preference to methyl, so O is inserted between the ring and the C=O, giving phenyl acetate. The data agree: 1765 cm−1 is the high C=O stretch of an aryl ester (the O lone pair is shared with the ring, so it donates less to C=O), and the 3H singlet at δ 2.30 is CH3C=O, not O–CH3. The ring H ortho to O (δ 7.08) are upfield of ordinary benzene H. The product is phenyl acetate.
x: Methyl benzoate (from methyl migration) would show an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.9, ortho ArH near δ 8.0, and a conjugated ester C=O near 1725 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Phenylacetic acid shows a broad O–H (3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a δ 11–12 COOH, and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.6; it is not a Baeyer–Villiger product.
4-Hydroxyacetophenone shows a phenol O–H, a conjugated ketone C=O near 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and two 2H doublets; mCPBA does not hydroxylate the ring.

q: Aniline has a UV absorption band at 280 nm. In dilute aqueous HCl this band disappears and the spectrum looks almost like benzene's (λ<sub>max</sub> ≈ 254 nm). What explains the shift?
c: Protonation ties up the N lone pair, so it no longer conjugates with the ring; the chromophore becomes benzene-like and λ<sub>max</sub> gets shorter
Protonation puts a positive charge in conjugation with the ring, which extends the π system and shrinks the HOMO–LUMO gap
Aqueous acid removes the NH<sub>2</sub> group from the ring, so the solution actually contains benzene and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>
The new N–H bonds of the anilinium ion absorb strongly near 254 nm and hide the 280 nm band beneath them
h: Which electrons on aniline are part of the conjugated π system, and what happens to them on protonation?
w: In aniline the N lone pair is delocalized into the ring, raising the HOMO and shifting λmax to longer wavelength (280 nm). In the anilinium ion, C6H5NH3+, that pair forms an N–H σ bond and is no longer conjugated, so the chromophore is just the benzene ring: loss of lone-pair conjugation gives a shift to shorter wavelength (a hypsochromic or blue shift). Adding base reverses it.
x: A larger conjugated system would shift λmax to longer wavelength, the opposite of what is observed. The NH3+ group has no π electrons or p orbital to conjugate.
Dilute HCl only protonates the amine (an acid–base reaction); adding base restores the 280 nm band, which would be impossible if the C–N bond had broken.
N–H σ bonds absorb only in the far UV (below 200 nm); they do not produce a 254 nm band. That band is the benzene ring's own π → π* absorption.

q: Rank compounds I–III by λmax in the UV, from shortest to longest wavelength.
h: Only C=C bonds in one continuous conjugated system count. A CH<sub>2</sub> between two C=C breaks the conjugation.
w: In 1,4-pentadiene (I) the C=C bonds are separated by CH2, so they absorb like isolated alkenes (below 200 nm). 1,3-Butadiene (II) is a conjugated diene (≈ 217 nm), and 1,3,5-hexatriene (III) has three conjugated C=C (≈ 258 nm). More conjugation means a smaller HOMO–LUMO gap and longer λmax: I < II < III.
x: Having more carbons does not lengthen λ<sub>max</sub>; I has five carbons but no conjugation, so it absorbs at the shortest wavelength.
This is the reverse order; the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks, not grows, as conjugation increases.
I has isolated C=C bonds and absorbs at the shortest wavelength, not the longest.

q: A compound C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O shows a broad IR band at 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (the δ 4.70 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: The broad band and exchangeable H mean O–H. Then count aromatic H and look at the pattern.
w: The broad 3300 cm−1 band and the exchangeable 1H at δ 4.70 mean an O–H. Only 4 aromatic H as two 2H doublets means para substitution, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.27 is an aryl CH3. The compound is 4-methylphenol (p-cresol).
x: Anisole has no O–H, a 5H monosubstituted ring, and an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.8.
Benzyl alcohol has a 5H ring and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>O singlet near δ 4.65, not a 3H singlet at δ 2.27.
2-Methylphenol is ortho-substituted: four different aromatic H, not two 2H doublets.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> (none above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: There are two ethyl groups. One CH<sub>2</sub> is near δ 4.1 and one near δ 2.3. What is each bonded to?
w: 1740 cm−1 with no O–H is an ester. Two quartet/triplet pairs mean two ethyl groups. The CH2 at δ 4.12 is on the ester O (O–CH2CH3); the CH2 at δ 2.32 is on the carbonyl carbon (CH3CH2–C=O). The compound is ethyl propanoate.
x: Methyl butanoate would show a 3H OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.67 and a CH<sub>2</sub> sextet; it has only one CH<sub>3</sub> triplet.
Propyl acetate would show a 3H acetyl singlet near δ 2.05 and an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet near δ 4.0.
Pentanoic acid would show a broad 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> O–H, a C=O near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a δ 11–12 COOH signal.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>9</sub>N shows a sharp, medium IR band at 2245 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a <sup>13</sup>C signal at δ 121.6, and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Identify the group from the 2245 cm<sup>−1</sup> band and the δ 121.6 carbon. Then use the splitting of the alkyl signals.
w: A sharp 2245 cm−1 band and a 13C signal near δ 120 mean a nitrile (DBE 6 = ring + C≡N). The 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring. A 1H quartet (δ 3.89) and 3H doublet (δ 1.64) form a CH–CH3 unit; the CH is benzylic and next to C≡N. The compound is 2-phenylpropanenitrile.
x: 3-Phenylpropanenitrile has –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN: two 2H triplets near δ 2.95 and 2.6, no 3H doublet.
4-Ethylbenzonitrile is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets) with an ethyl quartet near δ 2.7 and triplet near δ 1.25; its aryl nitrile absorbs near 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
2-(4-Methylphenyl)acetonitrile is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets) and shows two singlets (CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.7, CH<sub>3</sub> near δ 2.35).

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 5.6 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: Two N–H bands with C=O near 1655 cm<sup>−1</sup>: which N-containing group? Then check the aromatic integration and what the CH<sub>2</sub> is between.
w: Two N–H stretches (3350, 3170 cm−1) with a low C=O (1655 cm−1) are a primary amide, CONH2 (2H broad at δ 5.6). The 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring, and the 2H singlet at δ 3.57 is a CH2 between the ring and C=O. The compound is 2-phenylacetamide.
x: N-Methylbenzamide is a secondary amide: one N–H band and an N–CH<sub>3</sub> doublet near δ 3.0 (coupled to N–H), with no CH<sub>2</sub>.
Acetanilide is a secondary amide (one N–H) with a 3H acetyl singlet near δ 2.15.
4-Aminoacetophenone also has two N–H bands and a low C=O, but it is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets, 4 ArH) and has a 3H singlet near δ 2.5 instead of a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: Which <sup>1</sup>H NMR data (CDCl<sub>3</sub>) fit the product of the reaction shown?
h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces an amide C=O all the way to CH<sub>2</sub>, keeping the C–N bond.
w: LiAlH4 reduces amides to amines: C(=O)NHCH3 becomes CH2NHCH3, giving N-methylbenzylamine. Its spectrum: 5H phenyl, a benzylic CH2N singlet near δ 3.75, an N–CH3 singlet near δ 2.45 and a small broad N–H: δ 7.30 (m, 5H), 3.75 (s, 2H), 2.45 (s, 3H), 1.4 (br s, 1H). The CH3 is a singlet because N–H coupling is usually not seen in amines (fast exchange).
x: These are the data of the starting amide (ortho ArH near δ 7.75 next to C=O, amide N–H near δ 6.2, N–CH<sub>3</sub> doublet near δ 3.0); LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does reduce amides.
Benzyl alcohol would require breaking the C–N bond. With LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, the oxygen leaves (as an aluminate) and the nitrogen stays.
Benzaldehyde (δ 9.99) is not the product: amide reduction by LiAlH<sub>4</sub> passes through an iminium ion that is reduced again, so it does not stop at an aldehyde.

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Start with the carbonyl carbon in the 13C spectrum and the C=O stretch: which carbonyl class and is it conjugated? Then place the three singlets.
w: The 13C signal at δ 206.9 and the IR band at 1715 cm−1 fit an unconjugated ketone (an ester would be near 170, a conjugated ketone near 197 and 1680 cm−1). The 3H singlet at δ 2.14 (13C 29.1) is CH3C=O, the 2H singlet at δ 3.63 (13C 50.1) is ArCH2C=O, and the 3H singlet at δ 3.79 (13C 55.2) with the strong 1250 cm−1 band is an aryl OCH3. Two 2H doublets mean para. The compound is 1-(4-methoxyphenyl)propan-2-one.
x: 1-(4-Methoxyphenyl)propan-1-one is a conjugated ketone (C=O near 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup>, 13C near δ 200) with an ethyl quartet/triplet, not two singlets.
Methyl 2-(4-methylphenyl)acetate has three similar singlets, but it is an ester: 13C C=O near δ 172, IR near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and no carbon near δ 207.
1-(4-Ethoxyphenyl)ethan-1-one has an OCH<sub>2</sub> quartet near δ 4.1 and a triplet near δ 1.4, and its conjugated ketone has 13C near δ 197 and IR near 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which sequence converts ethyl 4-oxopentanoate into 5-hydroxy-5-methylhexan-2-one?
c: 1. TBSCl, imidazole, DMF  2. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr (excess), ether  3. TBAF, THF
h: The ketone must survive while the ester gains two methyl groups. Which carbonyl is more reactive toward CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, and how can you hide it?
w: The target keeps the ketone and turns the ester carbon into C(CH3)2OH, which needs two equivalents of CH3MgBr at the ester. A ketone is more reactive than an ester toward a Grignard reagent, so the ketone must be protected first. Ethylene glycol with catalytic acid converts the ketone into a cyclic acetal (esters do not form acetals). Excess CH3MgBr then adds twice to the ester (ester → ketone → 3° alkoxide), and aqueous acid both protonates the alkoxide and hydrolyzes the acetal back to the ketone: 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH 2. CH3MgBr (excess) 3. H3O+.
x: Without protection the ketone reacts first and fastest, so the ketone carbon also gains a methyl group and the product is mainly 2,5-dimethylhexane-2,5-diol.
Protection is correct, but LiAlH<sub>4</sub> delivers hydride, not methyl: the ester becomes CH<sub>2</sub>OH and the product is 5-hydroxypentan-2-one.
TBSCl silylates alcohols, not ketones, so the ketone is left unprotected; CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr attacks both carbonyls and TBAF has nothing to remove.

q: Which pairing of functional group, protecting group, and removal conditions is correct?
c: ketone: cyclic acetal (HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, TsOH); removed with H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
alcohol: Boc carbamate (Boc<sub>2</sub>O, Et<sub>3</sub>N); removed with TBAF
amine: TBS ether (TBSCl, imidazole); removed with H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
aldehyde: Cbz carbamate (CbzCl, Et<sub>3</sub>N); removed with CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H
h: Match each protecting group to the atom it bonds to: acetals bond to a carbonyl carbon, silyl groups to O, carbamates to N.
w: A cyclic acetal is the standard protecting group for a ketone or aldehyde: it forms from ethylene glycol with an acid catalyst, survives bases, hydrides and organometallics, and is removed with aqueous acid (H3O+). Silyl ethers (TBS) protect alcohols and come off with fluoride (TBAF); carbamates (Boc, Cbz) protect amines, with Boc removed by CF3CO2H and Cbz by H2, Pd/C.
x: Boc is an amine protecting group (a carbamate on nitrogen), and TBAF removes silyl ethers, not Boc.
A TBS group protects an alcohol oxygen, not an amine, and it is removed with fluoride (TBAF), not hydrogenolysis.
A carbamate needs an N–H to form, so it cannot protect an aldehyde; aldehydes are protected as acetals.

q: Which reagent carries out the conversion shown?
h: Two carbonyls are present, but only one changes. Which hydride reagent is too weak to reduce an ester?
w: Only the aldehyde is reduced to CH2OH; the methyl ester is untouched. NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones quickly but reacts with esters only very slowly, so it is chemoselective here. LiAlH4 is strong enough to reduce both groups.
x: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces esters as well as aldehydes, so both groups become CH<sub>2</sub>OH (1,4-benzenedimethanol).
Clemmensen conditions reduce the aldehyde C=O all the way to CH<sub>3</sub>, giving methyl 4-methylbenzoate, not an alcohol.
A Grignard reagent adds a methyl group (and also attacks the ester), so the product would contain CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>, not CH<sub>2</sub>OH.

q: Which sequence converts ethyl hexanoate into 1-phenylhexan-1-ol?
c: 1. DIBAL-H, toluene, −78 °C  2. H<sub>2</sub>O  3. C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>MgBr, ether  4. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, ether  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  3. C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>MgBr, ether  4. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: The target is a secondary alcohol: one H and one phenyl on the old ester carbon. Which reagent stops an ester at the aldehyde stage?
w: The old ester carbon must end up as CH(OH)Ph, so it needs exactly one hydride and one phenyl. DIBAL-H at −78 °C reduces an ester to an aldehyde (the tetrahedral aluminum intermediate does not collapse until workup), and PhMgBr then adds once to the aldehyde: 1. DIBAL-H, −78 °C 2. H2O 3. C6H5MgBr 4. H3O+. Esters cannot be stopped at the ketone with a Grignard reagent, and an alcohol made first cannot be "added to".
x: The ketone formed after the first addition is more reactive than the ester, so PhMgBr adds twice (1,1-diphenylhexan-1-ol); a Grignard route from an ester never gives a secondary alcohol with an H on carbon.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> takes the ester all the way to hexan-1-ol; PhMgBr then only deprotonates the OH (giving benzene) and adds no carbon.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce the ester, so PhMgBr meets the unchanged ester and adds twice, giving the tertiary diphenyl alcohol.

q: Which sequence converts 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one into 3-ethyl-3-methylcyclohexan-1-one?
h: The new ethyl group appears on the β-carbon of the enone. Which organometallic adds 1,4 rather than 1,2?
w: The ethyl group must bond to C3, the β-carbon of the α,β-unsaturated ketone, so this is a conjugate (1,4) addition. Lithium diorganocuprates (Gilman reagents) add 1,4 to enones; protonation of the enolate on workup gives the saturated ketone with a new quaternary C3: 1. (CH3CH2)2CuLi 2. H3O+.
x: Grignard reagents add mainly 1,2 to the C=O of an enone, giving the tertiary allylic alcohol 1-ethyl-3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
Hydrogenation removes the C=C first; a saturated ketone is not a Michael acceptor, so the cuprate has no electrophilic C3 to attack.
LDA forms the enolate at C6 (α′), so ethyl bromide alkylates C6 (6-ethyl-3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one), not C3.

q: Which starting materials give the bicyclic enone shown by a Robinson annulation (Michael addition, then intramolecular aldol condensation)?
c: 2-methylcyclohexan-1-one + methyl vinyl ketone, NaOEt, EtOH, heat
h: Find the new enone C=C (formed by the aldol) and the bond to the quaternary ring-fusion carbon (formed by the Michael). The carbon that carries the methyl was the nucleophile.
w: Work backward. The C=C–C=O of the new ring came from an intramolecular aldol condensation between a methyl ketone (CH3 → the ring CH=) and the original ring C=O. The quaternary ring-fusion carbon with its methyl was the enolate carbon in the Michael step, and it added to the CH2= end of methyl vinyl ketone. So the donor is 2-methylcyclohexanone, alkylated at its more substituted α-carbon (the thermodynamic enolate under NaOEt), and the acceptor is but-3-en-2-one: 2-methylcyclohexan-1-one + methyl vinyl ketone.
x: With cyclohexanone the ring-fusion carbon carries an H, and the methyl from pent-3-en-2-one ends up on the new ring next to the fusion carbon, not on the fusion carbon.
The 1,3-dione gives the Wieland–Miescher ketone, which has a second C=O in the left-hand ring; the target has only one carbonyl.
Acetone enolate adds to C3 of the enone, so no quaternary carbon bearing a methyl forms at the ring fusion; the connectivity does not match.

q: Which sequence converts ethyl acetoacetate into 5-phenylpentan-2-one?
h: In the acetoacetic ester synthesis the product is CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>–R. What is R here, and must it be an S<sub>N</sub>2-reactive halide?
w: The acetoacetic ester synthesis makes methyl ketones CH3C(=O)CH2–R: ethoxide removes the doubly activated α-H (pKa ≈ 11), the enolate does SN2 on R–X, and hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester and decarboxylates the β-keto acid. Here CH3C(=O)CH2–R = CH3C(=O)CH2CH2CH2Ph, so R = CH2CH2Ph and the halide is 2-phenylethyl bromide: 1. NaOEt 2. PhCH2CH2Br 3. H3O+, heat.
x: Benzyl bromide puts only one CH<sub>2</sub> between the new bond and the ring, giving 4-phenylbutan-2-one (one carbon short).
Decarboxylating first gives acetone, which has lost the second activating group; ethoxide only partly deprotonates acetone, so aldol reactions and multiple alkylations compete.
Bromobenzene cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2 (backside attack is blocked by the ring), so the enolate is not phenylated.

q: Which sequence converts diethyl malonate into cyclopentanecarboxylic acid?
c: 1. NaOEt (1 equiv), Br(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Br  2. NaOEt (1 equiv)  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. NaOEt (1 equiv), Br(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>Br  2. NaOEt (1 equiv)  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. NaOEt (1 equiv), Br(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Br  2. NaOEt (1 equiv)  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
h: Count ring atoms: the malonate α-carbon becomes one ring carbon, and the dibromide supplies the rest.
w: In a malonic ester ring synthesis the malonate carbon is alkylated twice by the same dihalide: first intermolecularly, then (after a second deprotonation) intramolecularly. The ring contains the malonate carbon plus every CH2 of the dihalide, so a five-membered ring needs four CH2 groups, Br(CH2)4Br. Hydrolysis and decarboxylation then leave one CO2H on the ring: 1. NaOEt, Br(CH2)4Br 2. NaOEt 3. H3O+, heat.
x: 1,3-Dibromopropane supplies three CH<sub>2</sub> groups, which with the malonate carbon gives a four-membered ring (cyclobutanecarboxylic acid).
1,5-Dibromopentane gives a six-membered ring (cyclohexanecarboxylic acid).
Without the second equivalent of base the ring never closes; hydrolysis and decarboxylation give the open-chain 6-bromohexanoic acid.

q: A student plans to make 3-nitroacetophenone from benzene as shown. Why does the plan fail, and what fixes it?
c: Step 2 fails: nitrobenzene is too deactivated for Friedel–Crafts acylation; acylate first, then nitrate
Step 2 gives the para isomer because NO<sub>2</sub> is an ortho/para director; nitrate after acylation instead of before
Step 1 fails: nitration requires an FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst; use HNO<sub>3</sub> with FeBr<sub>3</sub> instead of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
Step 2 fails: AlCl<sub>3</sub> reduces the nitro group to an amine, which then complexes it; use FeCl<sub>3</sub> instead
h: Friedel–Crafts reactions have a list of rings they will not touch. Is a nitro-substituted ring on it?
w: Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation fail on rings bearing a strongly deactivating group (NO2, C=O, SO3H, CF3, NR3+), because the acylium ion is too weak an electrophile for such an electron-poor ring. Both substituents of the target are meta directors, so the order can simply be reversed: acylation of benzene gives acetophenone, and the acetyl group directs nitration meta. Step 2 fails; acylate first, then nitrate.
x: NO<sub>2</sub> is a meta director, not ortho/para; the real problem is that the deactivated ring does not undergo Friedel–Crafts acylation at all.
Nitration uses H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to generate NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>; FeBr<sub>3</sub> is the catalyst for bromination, and step 1 works as written.
AlCl<sub>3</sub> is a Lewis acid, not a reducing agent; the nitro group is left intact and simply shuts down the Friedel–Crafts reaction.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown (Stork enamine reaction)?
h: The enamine β-carbon is the nucleophile, and methyl acrylate is a Michael acceptor. What does aqueous acid do to an iminium ion?
w: Pyrrolidine and cyclohexanone form an enamine, a neutral enolate equivalent whose α-carbon is nucleophilic. It adds 1,4 to methyl acrylate (attack at the CH2= β-carbon), giving an iminium ion/enamine that aqueous acid hydrolyzes back to the ketone. The net result is Michael addition of cyclohexanone to methyl acrylate: methyl 3-(2-oxocyclohexyl)propanoate.
x: This is the enamine before hydrolysis; step 3 (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) converts the C=C–N unit back into the C=O.
Enamines add to the C=C of an α,β-unsaturated ester (conjugate addition); they do not substitute at the ester carbonyl to make an acryloyl ketone.
D has the new bond to the α-carbon of the acrylate; in a Michael addition the nucleophile attacks the β-carbon (the CH<sub>2</sub>= end).
