q: Which sequence gives 1-bromo-3-propylbenzene from benzene?
c: 1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat  3. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
h: Br and propyl are meta to each other, yet both are ortho/para directors. Which group could you install that directs meta and later becomes propyl?
w: Both final groups are ortho/para directors, so neither can place the other meta. The trick is to introduce the propyl group as a propanoyl group: acylation (no rearrangement, and C=O is a meta director), then bromination meta to the ketone, then Clemmensen reduction of C=O to CH2: 1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3 2. Br2, FeBr3 3. Zn(Hg), HCl. Friedel–Crafts acylation also avoids the 1° carbocation rearrangement that ruins direct propylation.
x: Friedel–Crafts alkylation with 1-chloropropane rearranges to the isopropyl cation (giving cumene), and the alkyl group then directs bromine ortho/para.
Reducing the ketone before bromination turns the meta director into propyl, an ortho/para director, so Br goes ortho/para.
Bromine is an ortho/para director, so the acylation occurs para to Br; the product is 1-bromo-4-propylbenzene.

q: Which sequence converts benzene into 1,3,5-tribromobenzene?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (excess), H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (excess), H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. CuBr
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
h: Three bromines meta to one another cannot come from bromine directing itself. Which group directs to the three positions ortho/para to it, and can then be removed?
w: Bromine is an ortho/para director, so bromines cannot direct each other into a 1,3,5-pattern. An NH2 group is a powerful ortho/para director: aniline with Br2/H2O brominates both ortho positions and the para position, which are mutually meta (2,4,6-tribromoaniline). The NH2 is then removed by diazotization and reduction with hypophosphorous acid, which replaces N2+ by H: nitrate, reduce, brominate, NaNO2/HCl, H3PO2.
x: Each Br directs ortho/para, so the second and third bromines go ortho/para to the first (mainly 1,2,4-tribromobenzene), never all mutually meta.
CuBr (Sandmeyer) replaces N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> by Br instead of H, giving 1,2,3,5-tetrabromobenzene.
Bromination of nitrobenzene places only one Br meta; after reduction and deamination the product is bromobenzene.

q: Which sequence converts chlorobenzene into 4-methoxyaniline?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, heat  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
1. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, heat  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C  3. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, heat
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, heat  3. NaBH<sub>4</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH
h: Methoxide can replace Cl on a ring only by S<sub>N</sub>Ar. What must be on the ring, and where, while that step runs?
w: Cl is an ortho/para director, so nitration of chlorobenzene gives 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene (separated from the ortho isomer). The para nitro group activates the C–Cl carbon toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution (addition–elimination through a Meisenheimer complex), so methoxide replaces Cl. Only then is the nitro group reduced to NH2: 1. HNO3, H2SO4 2. NaOCH3, heat 3. H2, Pd/C.
x: Plain chlorobenzene has no electron-withdrawing group to stabilize the Meisenheimer complex, so S<sub>N</sub>Ar with methoxide does not occur in step 1.
Reducing first converts the activating NO<sub>2</sub> into an electron-donating NH<sub>2</sub>, so the ring is no longer activated for S<sub>N</sub>Ar and step 3 fails.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce an aromatic nitro group; the product would remain 4-nitroanisole.

q: Which sequence converts 4-piperidinylmethanol into 4-(methoxymethyl)piperidine?
c: 1. Boc<sub>2</sub>O, Et<sub>3</sub>N  2. NaH; then CH<sub>3</sub>I  3. CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. CbzCl, Et<sub>3</sub>N  2. NaH; then CH<sub>3</sub>I  3. CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. Boc<sub>2</sub>O, Et<sub>3</sub>N  2. NaH; then CH<sub>3</sub>I  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
h: Which is the better nucleophile toward CH<sub>3</sub>I, the ring N–H or the O–H? Then check that each protecting group comes off under the conditions chosen.
w: The secondary amine is more nucleophilic than the alcohol, so it would be methylated (and even quaternized) by CH3I. Protect it as a Boc carbamate, which has no N–H and is not nucleophilic. NaH then deprotonates only the OH, and the alkoxide is methylated (Williamson). Boc is acid-labile and is removed with trifluoroacetic acid: 1. Boc2O 2. NaH, CH3I 3. CF3CO2H.
x: With the amine unprotected, nitrogen competes for CH<sub>3</sub>I and gives N-methyl and quaternary ammonium products.
Cbz protects the amine, but it is stable to CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H; Cbz is removed by hydrogenolysis (H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C), so the final step fails.
Boc is not cleaved by hydrogenolysis; it needs acid (CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H), so the product would still carry the Boc group.

q: Which reagent removes the Boc group shown while leaving the benzyl ether intact?
h: Boc is the protecting group that leaves as a tert-butyl cation. What kind of reagent triggers that?
w: A Boc carbamate is cleaved by strong acid: protonation lets a tert-butyl cation leave (it becomes isobutylene), and the carbamic acid loses CO2 to free the amine. Benzyl ethers are stable to these conditions, so CF3CO2H is selective.
x: Hydrogenolysis cleaves benzyl–O bonds (and Cbz groups), so it would remove the benzyl ether and leave the Boc group.
Fluoride removes silyl ethers such as TBS; it does not cleave carbamates.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces aldehydes and ketones; it does not touch carbamates or ethers.

q: Which sequence converts 3-bromopropan-1-ol into 4-methylpentane-1,4-diol?
c: 1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. Mg, ether  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O; then NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (aq)  4. TBAF, THF
1. HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, TsOH (cat.)  2. Mg, ether  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O; then NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (aq)  4. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. Mg, ether  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O; then NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (aq)  4. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
h: A Grignard reagent and an O–H cannot exist in the same flask. How do you hide an alcohol, and what takes the group off?
w: The new C–C bond joins C3 of the bromoalcohol to the carbonyl carbon of acetone, which calls for the Grignard reagent of the bromide. A free OH (pKa ≈ 16) would protonate the Grignard reagent immediately, so the alcohol is first protected as a TBS ether. The protected Grignard reagent adds to acetone, mild workup protonates the alkoxide, and fluoride removes the silyl group: 1. TBSCl 2. Mg 3. acetone; NH4Cl 4. TBAF.
x: The unprotected OH destroys the Grignard reagent by proton transfer, giving propan-1-ol (after workup) instead of adding to acetone.
Ethylene glycol/acid protects aldehydes and ketones as acetals; it does not protect an alcohol, so the OH still quenches the Grignard reagent.
H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C does not cleave silyl ethers, so the product keeps the TBS group on the primary oxygen.

q: Which reagent converts cyclohexanone into methylenecyclohexane?
c: Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub> (from CH<sub>3</sub>PPh<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> Br<sup>−</sup> and n-BuLi), THF
h: You need a C=C exactly where the C=O was. Which reaction puts it there with no choice of position?
w: The Wittig reaction replaces C=O with C=C at the same carbon, so the double bond cannot migrate. Methylidenetriphenylphosphorane converts cyclohexanone into methylenecyclohexane via the oxaphosphetane, with Ph3P=O as by-product.
x: Acid dehydration of 1-methylcyclohexanol forms the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene, not the exocyclic alkene.
The enolate is methylated at the α-carbon, giving 2-methylcyclohexanone; the C=O is unchanged.
This stops at 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol; no alkene is formed.

q: Which combination, followed by H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> workup, gives 4-phenylbutan-2-ol?
h: Grignard reagents open epoxides at the less substituted carbon, and the OH ends up on the other epoxide carbon. Map each choice onto the target.
w: A Grignard reagent opens an epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered carbon, so the OH stays on the more substituted carbon and the chain grows by two carbons. Benzyl Grignard attacks the CH2 of 2-methyloxirane: PhCH2–CH2–CH(OH)–CH3, which is 4-phenylbutan-2-ol.
x: Phenyl adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> of the epoxide, giving PhCH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> (1-phenylpropan-2-ol), one CH<sub>2</sub> short.
Methyl adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> of 2-benzyloxirane, giving CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>Ph (1-phenylbutan-2-ol); the OH is next to the benzyl carbon.
Addition to acetone gives a tertiary alcohol, 2-methyl-4-phenylbutan-2-ol, with an extra methyl group.

q: Which sequence converts diethyl hexanedioate into 2-methylcyclopentan-1-one?
c: 1. NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. NaOEt, CH<sub>3</sub>I  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat  3. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr (1 equiv); then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CuLi; then H<sub>2</sub>O
h: A Dieckmann condensation of a 1,6-diester gives a five-membered β-keto ester. Where is the most acidic C–H, and what should happen to it before decarboxylation?
w: NaOEt cyclizes diethyl hexanedioate (Dieckmann) to ethyl 2-oxocyclopentane-1-carboxylate. Its C–H between the two carbonyls (pKa ≈ 11) is easily deprotonated by ethoxide, and the enolate is methylated by CH3I. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester and decarboxylates the β-keto acid, leaving the methyl on the α-carbon: 1. NaOEt; H3O+ 2. NaOEt, CH3I 3. H3O+, heat.
x: After decarboxylation, CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr adds to the C=O of cyclopentanone, giving the tertiary alcohol 1-methylcyclopentan-1-ol.
CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr is a strong base: it removes the acidic α-H of the β-keto ester (making methane) instead of forming a C–C bond, so decarboxylation gives plain cyclopentanone.
Cyclopentanone is neither an enone nor an acid chloride, so the Gilman reagent does not react with it.

q: Which compound gives 3-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one on heating with NaOH (intramolecular aldol condensation)?
h: Number the carbons of the target ring. The enolate carbon and the carbonyl carbon it attacks must end up five atoms apart in the ring, and one carbonyl must remain.
w: In an intramolecular aldol the enolate carbon bonds to the other carbonyl carbon, which loses OH as water to form the C=C. For hexane-2,5-dione the terminal CH3 (C1) enolate attacks C5: the ring is C1–C2–C3–C4–C5 (five atoms), the C2 carbonyl stays, and dehydration puts the C=C conjugated with it, with C6 as the methyl on the alkene carbon. Hexane-2,5-dione gives 3-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one.
x: Heptane-2,6-dione closes a six-membered ring, giving 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one.
The CH<sub>3</sub> enolate of 4-oxopentanal attacks the aldehyde to close a five-membered ring, but there is no extra carbon left for the methyl: the product is cyclopent-2-en-1-one.
Octane-2,7-dione closes a five-membered ring through its internal C3 enolate, giving 1-(2-methylcyclopent-1-en-1-yl)ethan-1-one, which keeps an acetyl group.

q: Which conditions convert cyclohexanone into N-benzylcyclohexanamine?
c: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> and NaBH<sub>4</sub> mixed at the start, CH<sub>3</sub>OH
h: The C–N bond forms through an imine. Which hydride reduces an iminium ion but leaves the ketone alone?
w: Reductive amination: the ketone and benzylamine form an imine/iminium ion under mildly acidic conditions, and sodium cyanoborohydride reduces the iminium ion much faster than it reduces the ketone, so the imine is trapped as it forms: PhCH2NH2, NaBH3CN, pH ≈ 6.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> first gives cyclohexanol, and an alcohol does not react with an amine (OH<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group).
The imine forms, but aqueous acid hydrolyzes it straight back to cyclohexanone and benzylamine; nothing reduces the C=N.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone faster than the imine forms, so most of the ketone ends up as cyclohexanol.

q: Which sequence converts 1-bromobutane into pentan-1-amine?
c: 1. potassium phthalimide, DMF  2. H<sub>2</sub>NNH<sub>2</sub>, ethanol, heat
1. NaCN, DMSO  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat  3. SOCl<sub>2</sub>  4. NH<sub>3</sub>  5. Br<sub>2</sub>, NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. Mg, ether  2. H<sub>2</sub>C=O  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. NH<sub>3</sub>, heat
h: Count carbons: the amine has one more carbon than the bromide, and the new carbon carries the nitrogen.
w: Pentan-1-amine has five carbons and the NH2 on the new carbon, so the extra carbon and the nitrogen should arrive together, as cyanide. SN2 with NaCN gives pentanenitrile, and LiAlH4 reduces C≡N to CH2NH2: 1. NaCN 2. LiAlH4 3. H2O.

This builds pentanamide, but the Hofmann rearrangement (Br<sub>2</sub>, NaOH) removes the carbonyl carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>, giving butan-1-amine.
The Grignard route gives pentan-1-ol, but NH<sub>3</sub> cannot displace OH (hydroxide is a poor leaving group), so no amine forms.

q: Which reagent carries out the conversion shown?
h: Only the nitro group changes. Which reducing agent is selective for ArNO<sub>2</sub> over a ketone?
w: Dissolving-metal reductions in acid (Sn, SnCl2 or Fe with HCl) reduce an aromatic nitro group to the anilinium ion and leave a ketone untouched; NaOH then frees the amine: SnCl2, HCl; then NaOH.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone to a secondary alcohol and does not reduce the nitro group.
Clemmensen conditions reduce the ketone C=O to CH<sub>2</sub> (and the nitro group as well), giving 4-ethylaniline.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone, and with aromatic nitro groups it gives azo compounds rather than a clean aniline.

q: Which sequence converts butanoic acid into hexan-3-one?
h: You need to add exactly one ethyl group to the acyl carbon and stop at the ketone. Which organometallic reacts with acid chlorides but not with ketones?
w: Converting the acid to the acid chloride makes a strong acylating agent. A Gilman reagent transfers one alkyl group to an acid chloride but reacts only slowly with the ketone it forms, so the reaction stops at the ketone: CH3CH2CH2C(=O)CH2CH3, hexan-3-one.
x: Grignard reagents add to the ketone as fast as it forms, so two ethyls add and the product is 3-ethylhexan-3-ol.
The Grignard reagent simply deprotonates the carboxylic acid; the carboxylate salt does not accept a second Grignard addition, and workup returns butanoic acid.
This makes butanal and then adds ethyl, so the product is the alcohol hexan-3-ol, not the ketone.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Ozonolysis of cyclohexene opens the ring to a six-carbon dialdehyde. Which α-carbon can reach the other C=O to form a strain-free ring, and what does heat do to the aldol?
w: O3 then (CH3)2S cleaves cyclohexene to hexanedial, OHC(CH2)4CHO. In hot NaOH the enolate at C2 attacks C6, closing a five-membered ring (C2–C6); dehydration gives the conjugated cyclopent-1-ene-1-carbaldehyde. NaBH4 reduces the aldehyde (1,2) to the primary alcohol and leaves the C=C: (cyclopent-1-en-1-yl)methanol.
x: B forms only if the aldol product does not dehydrate and the ring C=C is never made; heating with NaOH drives the elimination to the conjugated enal first.
A six-membered ring would need a seven-carbon dialdehyde; hexanedial can only close a five-membered ring (or a strained three-membered one).
Dimethyl sulfide gives a reductive workup, so the ozonide gives the dialdehyde, not adipic acid; adipic acid would also not undergo aldol reactions.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohex-2-en-1-one into 2-(3-oxocyclohexyl)acetic acid?
c: 1. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C  2. CH<sub>2</sub>(CO<sub>2</sub>Et)<sub>2</sub>, NaOEt, EtOH  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. CH<sub>2</sub>(CO<sub>2</sub>Et)<sub>2</sub>, NaOEt, EtOH  2. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, 25 °C
h: The new CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H sits on C3, the β-carbon. Which nucleophile adds 1,4 and is a synthetic equivalent of <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H?
w: Diethyl malonate anion is a soft, stabilized nucleophile that adds 1,4 (Michael addition) to the β-carbon of the enone. Hot aqueous acid then hydrolyzes both esters and decarboxylates the malonic acid, leaving CH2CO2H on C3: 1. CH2(CO2Et)2, NaOEt 2. H3O+, heat.
x: LDA makes the enolate at C6 (α′), so the new CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H ends up on the α-carbon next to the C=O, not on C3.
After hydrogenation there is no C=C to accept a Michael addition, so the malonate cannot bond to C3.
Saponification at 25 °C gives the substituted malonic acid; without heat it does not lose CO<sub>2</sub>, so the product keeps two CO<sub>2</sub>H groups.

q: Which sequence converts toluene into 2-bromo-1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH
h: In the target, Br is ortho to CH<sub>3</sub> and meta to NO<sub>2</sub>. In which intermediate do both groups send Br to that carbon?
w: Nitration of toluene gives 4-nitrotoluene (CH3 directs ortho/para). In 4-nitrotoluene, CH3 directs to C2 (ortho to itself) and NO2 directs meta to itself, which is also C2: the effects reinforce, and bromination gives 2-bromo-1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene.
x: In 4-bromotoluene the activating CH<sub>3</sub> controls nitration, which goes ortho to CH<sub>3</sub>; the product is 4-bromo-1-methyl-2-nitrobenzene (Br and NO<sub>2</sub> swapped).
Br<sub>2</sub> with light brominates the benzylic CH<sub>3</sub> by a radical pathway, giving 4-nitrobenzyl bromide.
The first two steps give the target, but Sn/HCl then reduces the nitro group to NH<sub>2</sub>, giving 3-bromo-4-methylaniline.

q: Which sequence converts benzene into 3-bromophenol?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C  5. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C; then H<sub>2</sub>O, heat  4. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C  5. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
h: OH and Br are both ortho/para directors, yet they are meta in the target. Which meta director can later be turned into OH?
w: Neither OH nor Br directs meta, so a meta director must place the Br and then be converted to OH. NO2 directs bromination meta; reduction gives 3-bromoaniline; diazotization and warming in water replace N2+ with OH: nitrate, brominate, reduce, NaNO2/H2SO4, H2O/heat.
x: Phenol is strongly activated and directs ortho/para; bromination gives 2- and 4-bromophenol (and polybromination), not the meta isomer.
Bromine directs nitration para (and ortho), so the sequence ends with 4-bromophenol.
H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> replaces the diazonium group with H, not OH, so the product is bromobenzene.

q: Which diene and dienophile give the Diels–Alder product shown as the major regioisomer?
h: The new ring C=C is between old diene C2 and C3. Where is the CH<sub>3</sub> relative to that C=C, and how far is it from the ester carbon?
w: In the product the ring C=C came from C2=C3 of the diene and the CO2CH3 sits on a carbon from the dienophile. The methyl is on a carbon of the ring C=C, so it was on C2 of the diene: isoprene. Isoprene and methyl acrylate give mainly the "para" (1,4) adduct, with CH3 and CO2CH3 on C4 and C1 of the cyclohexene: isoprene + methyl acrylate.
x: With methyl methacrylate both the CH<sub>3</sub> and the ester end up on the same sp<sup>3</sup> carbon (methyl 1-methylcyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate).
A 1-substituted diene gives the "ortho" (1,2) adduct, methyl 2-methylcyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate, with the CH<sub>3</sub> on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon next to the ester.
Both substituents come from the dienophile, so they end up on adjacent sp<sup>3</sup> carbons (methyl 6-methylcyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate).

q: Which sequence gives the racemic trans diol shown?
c: 1. buta-1,3-diene + diethyl fumarate, heat  2. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, ether; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. buta-1,3-diene + maleic anhydride, heat  2. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, ether; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. buta-1,3-diene + diethyl maleate, heat  2. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, ether; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. buta-1,3-diene + diethyl fumarate, heat  2. NaBH<sub>4</sub>, ethanol
h: The Diels–Alder reaction is stereospecific: groups trans on the dienophile end up trans on the ring. Then ask which hydride reduces esters.
w: The Diels–Alder reaction keeps the dienophile geometry: a trans (E) dienophile gives trans substituents, a cis (Z) dienophile gives cis. Diethyl fumarate (E) gives racemic trans-diethyl cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylate, and LiAlH4 reduces both esters to CH2OH without touching the stereocenters: diethyl fumarate, then LiAlH4.
x: Maleic anhydride is a cis dienophile, so the adduct and the diol made from it are cis (the meso diastereomer).
Diethyl maleate is the Z isomer, so the two ester groups, and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH groups made from them, are cis.
The stereochemistry is right, but NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce esters, so the diester is recovered.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexene into racemic trans-2-methoxycyclohexan-1-ol?
c: 1. OsO<sub>4</sub>, NMO  2. NaH (1 equiv); then CH<sub>3</sub>I
1. mCPBA, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  2. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH  3. NaH; then CH<sub>3</sub>I
h: Trans-1,2 groups on a ring come from backside opening of a three-membered ring.
w: Epoxidation gives cyclohexene oxide; methoxide then opens it by SN2 from the face opposite the epoxide oxygen, so OCH3 and OH end up trans (anti opening). The product is racemic because attack at either carbon is equally likely: 1. mCPBA 2. NaOCH3, CH3OH.
x: OsO<sub>4</sub> adds both OH groups to the same face (syn), so methylating one of them gives the cis isomer (along with dimethylated product).
Alkoxymercuration–demercuration adds CH<sub>3</sub>O and H across the C=C, giving methoxycyclohexane with no OH.
The first two steps make the target, but NaH/CH<sub>3</sub>I then methylates the remaining OH, giving trans-1,2-dimethoxycyclohexane.

q: A student plans to make 4-ethylaniline from benzene as shown. Which step fails, and why?
c: Step 3: the basic NH<sub>2</sub> group binds AlCl<sub>3</sub>, which strongly deactivates the ring toward Friedel–Crafts alkylation
Step 1: nitration of benzene needs FeBr<sub>3</sub> as the catalyst rather than H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to make NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
Step 2: Sn/HCl reduces the benzene ring to cyclohexane along with the nitro group
Step 3: the primary ethyl cation rearranges, so the product is 4-isopropylaniline, not 4-ethylaniline
h: Friedel–Crafts reactions need a Lewis acid. What does a Lewis acid do when it meets a Lewis base such as an amine?
w: Steps 1 and 2 give aniline normally. In step 3 the nitrogen lone pair binds AlCl3 (a Lewis acid–base complex), turning NH2 into a positively charged, strongly electron-withdrawing –NH2–AlCl3 group, so the ring does not undergo Friedel–Crafts alkylation. Step 3 fails. A workable route alkylates benzene first, nitrates (separating the para isomer), and then reduces.
x: Nitration uses H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to generate the nitronium ion; FeBr<sub>3</sub> is the bromination catalyst, and step 1 works.
Dissolving-metal reduction converts NO<sub>2</sub> to NH<sub>2</sub> and leaves the aromatic ring intact.
An ethyl group cannot rearrange to anything more stable (there is no isopropyl skeleton in two carbons); the problem is the Lewis acid–amine complex.

s.arrow: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH

q: A student plans the route shown to 4-(hydroxymethyl)cyclohexan-1-one. Which step fails, and why?
c: Step 2: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is too weak to reduce an ester; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is needed
Step 1: ethylene glycol reacts with the ester rather than with the ketone
Step 3: aqueous acid cannot remove an acetal; TBAF is needed
Step 2: NaBH<sub>4</sub> attacks the acetal carbon and opens the ring
h: Check each reagent against the group it must change: acetal formation, ester reduction, acetal removal.
w: The plan is sound in outline: protect the ketone as an acetal, reduce the ester to CH2OH, and remove the acetal with aqueous acid. The flaw is the hydride: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones but not (at a useful rate) esters. With LiAlH4 in step 2 the route works. Step 2 fails.
x: Acetal formation is selective for the ketone; an ester carbonyl does not form an acetal under these conditions.
Acetals are hydrolyzed by aqueous acid; TBAF removes silyl ethers.
Acetals are stable to hydride reagents and bases, which is why they work as protecting groups during reductions.

q: What is the product of the sequence shown, starting from (R)-butan-2-ol?
h: Tosylation does not touch the stereocenter; one later step does. Then check what LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does to C≡N, and reassign R/S with the new groups.
w: TsCl/pyridine makes the tosylate with retention (the C–O bond is not broken). Cyanide displaces tosylate by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile (CN outranks ethyl and methyl, like OH did, so the inverted center is S). LiAlH4 reduces C≡N to CH2NH2 without touching the stereocenter; CH2NH2 still outranks ethyl, so the product is (S)-2-methylbutan-1-amine.
x: This is the R amine, which would require retention in the cyanide step; S<sub>N</sub>2 at the secondary tosylate inverts the center.
This is the nitrile from step 2; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> then reduces C≡N to CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, so the nitrile is not the final product.
This is the nitrile with retention; it is wrong at both the stereocenter (S<sub>N</sub>2 inverts) and the functional group (step 3 reduces it).

q: Which sequence converts 1-bromopropane into butanal?
c: 1. Mg, ether  2. H<sub>2</sub>C=O  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. Mg, ether  2. CO<sub>2</sub>  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. Mg, ether  2. ethylene oxide  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
h: Butanal has four carbons. How many does each electrophile add, and which oxidant stops at the aldehyde?
w: Propylmagnesium bromide plus formaldehyde adds one carbon and gives butan-1-ol after workup. PCC (anhydrous) oxidizes a primary alcohol only to the aldehyde: 1. Mg 2. H2C=O 3. H3O+ 4. PCC.
x: Jones reagent is aqueous: the aldehyde forms a hydrate and is oxidized further to butanoic acid.
Carboxylation gives butanoic acid, which PCC cannot convert to an aldehyde (PCC is an oxidant, and the acid is already more oxidized).
Ethylene oxide adds two carbons, so the alcohol is pentan-1-ol and PCC gives pentanal.

q: Which reaction, followed by the workup shown, gives 1,1-diphenylpropan-1-ol?
h: An ester plus excess Grignard reagent gives a tertiary alcohol with two identical groups from the Grignard. Which two groups on the carbinol carbon are identical?
w: Esters react with two equivalents of a Grignard reagent (addition, loss of alkoxide to give a ketone, second addition), so the carbinol carbon carries two identical R groups from RMgX and the acyl group of the ester. The target carbinol carbon has two phenyls and one ethyl: the ethyl comes from the ester (propanoate) and both phenyls from PhMgBr: ethyl propanoate + excess PhMgBr.
x: Here the two identical groups are ethyls, giving 3-phenylpentan-3-ol.
A Gilman reagent adds once to an acid chloride and stops at the ketone, propiophenone; it does not add a second phenyl.
Ethyl benzoate supplies the third phenyl as well, giving triphenylmethanol.

q: Which sequence converts 2-methylcyclohexan-1-one into 2,6-dimethylcyclohexan-1-one (as a mixture of stereoisomers)?
h: The new methyl goes on the less substituted α-carbon. Which conditions form the less substituted enolate?
w: The new CH3 must go on C6, the less substituted α-carbon. LDA, a strong, bulky base at −78 °C, removes the more accessible C6 proton fastest and irreversibly (kinetic enolate); alkylation with CH3I then gives 2,6-dimethylcyclohexanone.
x: Under equilibrating conditions the more substituted (thermodynamic) enolate dominates, so methylation occurs at C2 and gives mainly 2,2-dimethylcyclohexanone.

Acid-catalyzed bromination goes through the more substituted enol, so Br goes on C2; any methyl introduced there ends up at C2, not C6 (and the cuprate does not cleanly substitute a tertiary bromide).
The Grignard reagent adds to the C=O, giving 1,2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol; the ketone is lost.

q: What is compound X, isolated after a neutral aqueous workup?
h: Step 1 protects one carbonyl. Which carbonyl forms an acetal, and what does LiAlH<sub>4</sub> do to the other one?
w: Ethylene glycol and acid convert the ketone (not the ester) of ethyl acetoacetate into a cyclic acetal. LiAlH4 then reduces the ester to a primary alcohol; the acetal, which is stable to hydride and base, survives a neutral workup. X is the acetal-protected 4-hydroxybutan-2-one; aqueous acid would later remove the acetal.
x: Butane-1,3-diol forms only if the ketone is unprotected; the acetal keeps the ketone carbon from being reduced.
4-Hydroxybutan-2-one is what forms after acid removes the acetal; the neutral workup leaves the acetal in place.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not stop at the aldehyde; the aldehyde formed after loss of ethoxide is reduced at once to the alcohol (DIBAL-H at −78 °C would be needed to stop at the aldehyde).

q: Which reaction is the best way to make ethyl 2-methyl-3-oxo-3-phenylpropanoate?
c: ethyl benzoate (excess) + ethyl propanoate, NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
ethyl benzoate (excess) + ethyl acetate, NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
ethyl propanoate alone, NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
benzaldehyde (excess) + ethyl propanoate, NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: A β-keto ester comes from a Claisen condensation. Disconnect the bond between the ketone carbon and the α-carbon: which ester gives the acyl group and which gives the enolate?
w: Disconnecting the C2–C3 bond of the β-keto ester splits it into an acyl donor, PhC(=O)– from ethyl benzoate, and an ester enolate, −CH(CH3)CO2Et from ethyl propanoate. Ethyl benzoate has no α-H, so it can only be the electrophile, and using it in excess limits propanoate self-condensation: crossed Claisen of ethyl benzoate and ethyl propanoate.
x: Ethyl acetate supplies <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Et, so the product lacks the 2-methyl group (ethyl 3-oxo-3-phenylpropanoate).
Self-Claisen of ethyl propanoate puts a propanoyl group on the α-carbon, giving ethyl 2-methyl-3-oxopentanoate, with no phenyl.
An aldehyde acceptor gives an aldol-type β-hydroxy ester (or its dehydration product), not a β-keto ester.

q: Which sequence converts butane-1,3-diol into 4-hydroxybutan-2-one?
c: 1. TBSCl (1 equiv), imidazole, 0 °C  2. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  3. TBAF, THF
1. TBSCl (1 equiv), imidazole, 0 °C  2. TBAF, THF  3. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. TBSCl (1 equiv), imidazole, 0 °C  2. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
h: Only the secondary alcohol is oxidized. Which OH does the bulky TBSCl silylate faster, and when must the TBS group come off?
w: The bulky TBSCl reacts selectively with the less hindered primary OH, protecting it as a TBS ether. PCC then oxidizes the free secondary alcohol to the ketone, and fluoride removes the silyl group to reveal the primary alcohol: 1. TBSCl (1 equiv) 2. PCC 3. TBAF.
x: Without protection PCC oxidizes both alcohols, giving 3-oxobutanal (the primary OH becomes an aldehyde).
Removing the TBS group before oxidation leaves both OH groups free again, so PCC oxidizes both.
Hydrogenation does not cleave a TBS ether, so the product is still the silyl-protected ketone.

q: In the first step of cyanohydrin formation (NaCN, HCN), cyanide ion adds to acetaldehyde. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: Find the nucleophilic atom of cyanide (the one carrying the negative charge), then make sure the carbonyl carbon still has only four bonds after it is attacked.
w: Cyanide is a carbon nucleophile: the lone pair on the negatively charged carbon attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, and because that carbon cannot hold five bonds, the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen at the same time. The correct drawing is an arrow from the cyanide carbon lone pair to the carbonyl carbon plus an arrow from the C=O π bond onto oxygen, giving the tetrahedral alkoxide CH3CH(O−)C≡N, which HCN then protonates.
x: This arrow starts at the nitrogen lone pair, so it would make a C–N bond and an isocyanide (–N≡C) product; the cyanohydrin has a new C–C bond, so the carbon end of cyanide must attack.
This arrow starts at the C=O π bond and points at cyanide, as if the carbonyl were the nucleophile; the carbonyl carbon is the electrophile, and arrows must start at the electron-rich cyanide.
With only the attack arrow, the carbonyl carbon would end up with five bonds (H, CH<sub>3</sub>, CN and a double bond to O); the π bond must move onto oxygen in the same step.

q: In acid-catalyzed acetal formation from acetaldehyde and methanol, the protonated hemiacetal loses water to give a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion. Which drawing correctly shows this step?
h: Under acid, what has to happen to an OH before it can leave? And which neighboring atom can push electrons in to replace the bond that breaks?
w: Water is a good leaving group only after the OH has been protonated. The lone pair on the methoxy oxygen then pushes in to form the C=O+ π bond while the C–OH2+ bond breaks with its electrons going to oxygen: OCH3 lone pair → C–O bond, and C–OH2+ bond → O. The product, CH3CH=O+CH3, is the oxocarbenium ion that a second methanol then attacks.
x: Here the OH has not been protonated, so the leaving group would be hydroxide; in acid, OH<sup>−</sup> is far too poor a leaving group (and cannot exist in acid), so the OH must be protonated first.
The methoxy lone pair forms a new π bond, but no bond breaks, so the central carbon would have five bonds; the C–OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> bond must break in the same step.

This is a direct S<sub>N</sub>2-style displacement by a second methanol; acetal formation goes through the planar oxocarbenium ion (loss of water first, assisted by the OCH<sub>3</sub> lone pair), and methanol adds afterward.

q: Acetone and methylamine form an imine (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> catalyst, pH ≈ 5). Which drawing correctly shows the step in which the carbinolamine loses water to give an iminium ion?
h: Check three things in each drawing: is the leaving group a neutral molecule, does every arrow start at electrons, and does carbon keep four bonds?
w: In the dehydration step the carbinolamine OH has already been protonated (the reason for the mild acid). The nitrogen lone pair pushes in to make the C=N π bond and the C–O bond breaks with both electrons going to the positive oxygen, which leaves as water: N lone pair → C–N bond; C–OH2+ bond → O. This gives the iminium ion (CH3)2C=N+HCH3, which loses an N–H proton to give the imine.
x: The OH is not protonated, so it would leave as hydroxide ion, a strong base and poor leaving group that cannot form in acid; protonation must come first.
Only the C=N bond forms, so the carbon would have five bonds; the C–O bond has to break as the nitrogen pushes in.
The second arrow starts at the carbon atom, which has no lone pair; the electrons that leave are those of the C–O bond, so the arrow must start on that bond and end on oxygen.

q: Cyclohexanone and dimethylamine (a secondary amine) form the iminium ion shown. Because nitrogen has no H to lose, water removes a proton to give the enamine. Which set of arrows correctly converts the iminium ion into the enamine?
h: An enamine has its C=C between the former carbonyl carbon and an α carbon. Which H must be removed, and where do the C=N π electrons go?
w: Water removes a proton from the α carbon; the C–H bond electrons become the new C=C π bond, and the C=N+ π electrons move onto nitrogen, which becomes neutral with a lone pair. Three arrows: H2O lone pair → α H, C–H bond → C–C bond, C=N π bond → N. Every carbon keeps four bonds and the product is 1-(dimethylamino)cyclohexene.
x: Water adding to the iminium carbon gives back the carbinolamine; that is a real step, but it is the reverse of the dehydration (hydrolysis), not the step that forms the enamine.
The new C=C forms but the C=N π bond does not break, so the former carbonyl carbon would carry five bonds; the C=N π electrons must move onto nitrogen.
The C–H electrons are sent to nitrogen, an atom not bonded to that carbon; this would make a three-membered ring and give nitrogen five bonds. Electrons move only to an adjacent atom or bond.

q: In acid-catalyzed hydration of acetone, water adds to the protonated carbonyl. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this addition step?
h: Curved arrows start at an electron source (a lone pair or a bond) and point to where the electrons go. Which species here is the electron source?
w: Water is the nucleophile: one of its oxygen lone pairs attacks the electrophilic carbon of the protonated carbonyl, and the C=O+H π electrons move onto oxygen, neutralizing it. The correct drawing has a water lone pair → carbonyl carbon and the C=O π bond → O, giving the protonated gem-diol (CH3)2C(OH)(OH2+).
x: The first arrow starts at the carbonyl carbon, which has no lone pair to donate; it is the electron-poor atom, so arrows should end there, not start there.
Only the attack arrow is drawn, so the carbonyl carbon would end up with five bonds; the π bond must move onto the oxygen at the same time.
This arrow treats the C=O π bond as the nucleophile attacking water; the protonated carbonyl is the electrophile, and the electrons come from water's lone pair.

q: In saponification of methyl acetate, hydroxide ion first attacks the ester. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this first step?
h: Nucleophilic acyl substitution is addition first, elimination second. What must happen to the C=O π bond when the nucleophile adds?
w: Nucleophilic acyl substitution is an addition–elimination mechanism, not a one-step displacement. In the first step the hydroxide lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen: OH− lone pair → C, C=O π bond → O. The product is the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate CH3C(O−)(OH)OCH3, which collapses in the next step to expel methoxide.
x: This is an S<sub>N</sub>2-style direct displacement at the acyl carbon. A trigonal carbonyl carbon is not attacked from the back side; the π bond accepts the electrons first, forming a tetrahedral intermediate, and methoxide leaves in a separate step.
Only the attack arrow is shown, so the carbonyl carbon would have five bonds; the C=O π electrons must move onto oxygen as hydroxide adds.
The first arrow starts at the carbonyl carbon, which has no lone pair; the electrons come from hydroxide, so the arrow must start at the hydroxide oxygen and point to the carbon.

q: In Fischer esterification of acetic acid with methanol (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst), the tetrahedral intermediate is protonated on one OH and then loses water. Which drawing correctly shows the loss of water?
h: Water leaves only from a protonated oxygen, and the bond electrons go with the leaving group. Which oxygen pushes in to replace the broken bond?
w: Once one OH is protonated, the lone pair of the other OH pushes in to form a C=O+H π bond while the C–OH2+ bond breaks with its electrons going to oxygen: OH lone pair → C–O bond; C–OH2+ bond → O. This releases neutral water and gives the protonated ester CH3C(=O+H)OCH3, which loses H+ to give methyl acetate and regenerate the acid catalyst.
x: Neither OH is protonated, so the leaving group would be hydroxide ion, which is a poor leaving group and cannot form in strongly acidic solution; the OH must be protonated before it leaves.
A new π bond forms but nothing leaves, so the central carbon would have five bonds; the C–OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> bond must break in the same step.

The leaving-group arrow points back to carbon, which would leave the oxygen with only two bonds and a 2+ charge; when a bond breaks heterolytically here, the electrons go to the more electronegative oxygen.

q: Acetyl chloride reacts with methylamine through the tetrahedral intermediate shown. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the collapse of this intermediate that leads toward the amide product?
h: The C=O reforms from the oxygen lone pair. Of the groups on the tetrahedral carbon, which is the best leaving group (the weakest base)?
w: The negatively charged oxygen pushes a lone pair back in to re-form the C=O π bond, and the best leaving group departs with the C–Cl bonding electrons: O− lone pair → C–O bond; C–Cl bond → Cl. Chloride (conjugate base of HCl, pKa ≈ −7) is a far better leaving group than the amine, so this gives the N-protonated amide, which loses H+ to a second equivalent of amine to give N-methylacetamide.
x: The C=O re-forms but nothing leaves, so carbon would have five bonds; a leaving group must depart as the π bond re-forms.
Expelling methylamine just reverses the addition and gives back acetyl chloride; it does not lead to the amide. Chloride is the far better leaving group and is the one lost.
The first arrow starts at the carbon atom, which has no lone pair; the π bond is made from the oxygen's lone pair, so the arrow must start on O<sup>−</sup> and end on the C–O bond.

q: In acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of acetonitrile, water attacks the N-protonated nitrile. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: Which atom of the protonated nitrile is electron-poor and can accept a nucleophile if one π bond moves away?
w: Protonating the nitrile nitrogen makes the nitrile carbon strongly electrophilic. Water attacks that carbon and one C≡N π bond moves onto nitrogen: water lone pair → nitrile C; one C≡N π bond → N. This gives CH3C(=NH)OH2+, which loses a proton to give the imidic acid; tautomerization then gives acetamide, and further hydrolysis gives acetic acid.
x: Water attacks nitrogen here, which already has four bonds and no lone pair to spare in the protonated nitrile; the electrophilic atom is the carbon, and an N–O bond is not formed in nitrile hydrolysis.
Without a π bond moving onto nitrogen, the nitrile carbon would have five bonds after water adds.
The arrow starts at the nitrile carbon, which has no lone pair; the nucleophile is water, so the arrow must start at its oxygen lone pair.

q: When LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces methyl acetate, hydride addition gives the tetrahedral intermediate shown (counterion omitted). Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the next step, which forms an aldehyde that is then reduced again?
h: This is the elimination half of nucleophilic acyl substitution. Which bond to the tetrahedral carbon must break to give acetaldehyde?
w: The tetrahedral alkoxide collapses: the O− lone pair re-forms the C=O and the acyl carbon–OCH3 bond breaks with its electrons going to oxygen, so the arrows are O− lone pair → C–O bond; C–OCH3 bond → O. This releases methoxide and acetaldehyde. An aldehyde is more reactive than the ester, so it is reduced again at once, and after workup the products are ethanol and methanol. This is why LiAlH4 cannot stop at the aldehyde (DIBAL-H at −78 °C can).
x: This breaks the O–CH<sub>3</sub> (alkyl–oxygen) bond instead of the acyl–oxygen bond; the central carbon would still have five bonds and a methyl cation would form. Nucleophilic acyl substitution cleaves the acyl C–O bond.
The C=O re-forms but no group leaves, so the central carbon would have five bonds.
The first arrow starts at the carbon atom, which has no lone pair; the new π bond comes from the oxygen's lone pair.

q: Fischer esterification begins when the acid catalyst (shown as H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) protonates acetic acid to make the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this activating step?
h: Protonating which oxygen gives a cation in which the positive charge is shared with the carbonyl carbon by resonance? And what happens to the H–O bond of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>?
w: The carbonyl oxygen is the more basic site, and protonating it gives a cation whose positive charge is delocalized onto the carbonyl carbon (and the OH oxygen), which activates that carbon toward methanol. Two arrows: carbonyl O lone pair → H, and the H–O bond of H3O+ → its O, releasing water.
x: Protonating the OH oxygen gives a cation with no resonance delocalization onto the carbonyl carbon, so it does not activate the carbonyl toward attack; the carbonyl oxygen is the more basic site.
The new O–H bond forms but the H–O bond of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> never breaks, so the hydrogen would have two bonds.
The arrow runs from the H–O bond to the carbonyl oxygen, as if hydronium donated electrons to oxygen; the carbonyl oxygen's lone pair is the electron source, and it must reach out to the proton.

q: The arrows show the hydride-transfer step when NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces acetophenone. What species is formed directly in this step, before any protonation?
h: Follow each arrow: where does the hydride end up, and where do the C=O π electrons go?
w: The B–H bond electrons (a hydride) form a new C–H bond at the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen, so this step gives the alkoxide ion, 1-phenylethoxide, PhCH(CH3)O−. The neutral alcohol forms only in a later proton transfer (from the alcohol solvent or aqueous workup).
x: The neutral alcohol is the final product, but it needs a separate proton-transfer step; the arrows shown leave a negative charge on oxygen.
This places the hydride on oxygen and the negative charge on carbon; the arrows deliver hydride to the carbonyl carbon and send the π electrons to the more electronegative oxygen.
Complete deoxygenation to ethylbenzene requires Wolff–Kishner or Clemmensen conditions; NaBH<sub>4</sub> adds one hydride and keeps the oxygen.

q: The arrows show methylmagnesium bromide adding to benzaldehyde in ether. After aqueous acid workup, what is the product?
h: Which atom of the Grignard reagent is nucleophilic, which atom does it bond to, and from which face(s) can it approach a planar carbonyl?
w: The C–Mg bond is polarized with carbon δ−, so the methyl carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon and the π electrons go to oxygen, giving a magnesium alkoxide; workup protonates it to PhCH(OH)CH3. The new stereocenter forms from a planar (trigonal) carbonyl that is attacked equally from both faces by an achiral reagent, so the product is racemic 1-phenylethanol.
x: An achiral Grignard reagent attacks the two faces of the planar aldehyde at equal rates, so both enantiomers form equally; a single enantiomer needs a chiral reagent or catalyst.

2-Phenylethanol (PhCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) would come from PhCH<sub>2</sub>MgBr + formaldehyde or from an epoxide; here the methyl bonds to the former carbonyl carbon, so the OH sits on the carbon attached to the ring.
An ether would need the methyl to bond to oxygen; the nucleophilic carbon attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, not the oxygen.

q: The arrows show the second step of cyanohydrin formation: the alkoxide formed by cyanide addition to acetaldehyde reacts with HCN. Besides the neutral cyanohydrin, what does this step produce, and why does it matter?
c: Cyanide ion, which is regenerated, so only catalytic base or cyanide is needed
Hydroxide ion, which makes the mixture basic and drives the reaction to completion
Hydronium ion, which protonates the next aldehyde C=O for the following addition
Hydrogen gas, which bubbles out of the mixture and makes this step irreversible
h: Follow the H–C bond of HCN: after the alkoxide takes the proton, where do that bond's electrons end up?
w: The alkoxide oxygen takes the proton from HCN, and the H–C bond electrons stay on carbon as a lone pair, so the step forms the cyanohydrin and a new cyanide ion. That cyanide can attack another aldehyde, so cyanide acts catalytically: a small amount of base (or NaCN) added to HCN is enough to run the reaction.
x: No hydroxide forms; the proton comes from HCN, so the base left behind is its conjugate base, cyanide.
Nothing here produces H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>; the step is a proton transfer from HCN to the alkoxide, which leaves cyanide. Cyanohydrin formation is base-catalyzed.
H<sub>2</sub> would require a hydride and a proton to combine; the H leaves HCN as a proton and the bonding electrons stay on carbon.

q: In acid-catalyzed acetal formation, a methanol molecule attacks the oxocarbenium ion as shown. What is the product of this step?
h: Count bonds and lone pairs on the oxygen of the attacking methanol after it forms a new bond. What charge does it carry?
w: The methanol oxygen uses a lone pair to bond to the electrophilic carbon, and the C=O+ π electrons return to the original methoxy oxygen, making it neutral. The attacking oxygen now has three bonds (C, CH3, H) and one lone pair, so it carries +1: the product of this step is the protonated acetal, CH3CH(OCH3)O+(H)CH3. A separate proton transfer to a base (methanol) then gives the neutral acetal and regenerates the acid catalyst.
x: The neutral acetal is the final product, but the oxygen that just attacked still carries its H and a + charge; a separate deprotonation step is needed.
The hemiacetal is the intermediate that formed before this step (by addition of the first methanol); the oxocarbenium ion was made from it by loss of water.
An ester has a different oxidation level (three bonds from that carbon to oxygen); acetal formation adds no oxidizing agent and does not create a C=O.

q: In the Wittig reaction of acetone with Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub>, the ylide carbon attacks the carbonyl as the arrows show (drawn here through the stepwise betaine picture). What is the next intermediate, and what drives the reaction to completion?
c: An oxaphosphetane ring, which breaks apart to the alkene and Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O with its very strong P=O bond
An epoxide, which then opens to the alkene with release of its three-membered ring strain
A tertiary carbocation, which then loses a proton to give the more substituted alkene as the product
An enolate, which is then protonated on carbon to give the new alkene
h: The negatively charged oxygen and the positively charged phosphorus end up close together. What ring can they make, and which very strong bond appears in the by-product?
w: The ylide carbanion adds to the carbonyl carbon to give a betaine-like species with O− and P+ on neighboring carbons (many textbooks show a direct [2+2] instead). The O–P bond then forms, giving a four-membered oxaphosphetane, which fragments into 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, and triphenylphosphine oxide. Formation of the very strong P=O bond is the driving force.
x: No epoxide forms in a Wittig reaction; oxygen ends up bonded to phosphorus (in Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O), not to a second carbon. (Sulfur ylides, by contrast, do give epoxides.)
There is no carbocation: the oxygen stays bonded to carbon until the oxaphosphetane fragments, and the C=C forms exactly where the C=O was, with no choice of more substituted alkene.
An enolate would need deprotonation at an α carbon; here the ylide carbon bonds to the carbonyl carbon and the oxygen is removed as Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O.

q: Butanal in methanol forms a hemiacetal with either a catalytic acid or a catalytic base (NaOCH<sub>3</sub>), but the acetal forms only with acid. Why does base not give the acetal?
c: The hemiacetal OH must be protonated to leave as water; in base it would leave as hydroxide, a very poor leaving group
Methoxide is too weak a nucleophile to add to the aldehyde carbonyl of butanal at all
In base the hemiacetal is deprotonated to an alkoxide, which immediately eliminates methoxide to form an ether instead
Base converts the aldehyde to a carboxylate salt before methanol has a chance to add
h: Compare the two halves of acetal formation: addition (which base can help) and substitution of the OH (what does that need?).
w: Hemiacetal formation is only an addition, which base catalyzes by supplying the strong nucleophile CH3O−. Converting the hemiacetal to the acetal requires the OH to leave. In acid it is protonated and leaves as neutral water, helped by the OCH3 lone pair, to give the oxocarbenium ion. In base there is no way to make OH a good leaving group (hydroxide is a strong base), so the substitution step cannot occur. This is also why acetals are stable to base, which makes them useful protecting groups.
x: Methoxide is a strong nucleophile and adds readily to aldehydes; that is how base catalyzes hemiacetal formation.
Deprotonating the hemiacetal gives an alkoxide that can only expel methoxide to re-form the aldehyde (reversing hemiacetal formation); it cannot form an acetal or ether.
Catalytic methoxide does not oxidize an aldehyde; forming a carboxylate requires an oxidizing agent (or the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated hydroxide and a non-enolizable aldehyde).

q: With a trace of acid, 5-hydroxypentanal cyclizes: the OH oxygen attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon of the same molecule. Which cyclic hemiacetal forms?
h: Count the atoms from the hydroxyl oxygen to the carbonyl carbon, including both. The ring contains all of them.
w: The ring includes the hydroxyl oxygen, carbons C5 through C2, and the former carbonyl carbon C1: five carbons and one oxygen, a six-membered ring (2-hydroxytetrahydropyran). The former carbonyl carbon becomes the hemiacetal carbon, carrying both the new OH and the ring oxygen. Five- and six-membered cyclic hemiacetals form readily, as in glucose.
x: A five-membered cyclic hemiacetal (2-hydroxytetrahydrofuran) would come from 4-hydroxybutanal; this chain has one more carbon, so the ring is six-membered.
This is a lactone (cyclic ester), which is at a higher oxidation level; hemiacetal formation adds an O–H across the C=O and does not oxidize the carbonyl carbon.
In this ring the OH sits on a CH<sub>2</sub> outside the ring, so the former carbonyl carbon is not the one bearing both oxygens; in a hemiacetal one carbon carries both the OH and the ring O.

q: A student proposed the step shown for acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of acetaldehyde dimethyl acetal (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>): water attacks the acetal carbon and methoxide leaves in one step. What is wrong with this step?
c: In acid, OCH<sub>3</sub> is protonated and leaves as methanol, giving an oxocarbenium ion that water attacks
Water should attack an oxygen of the acetal, since the oxygens are where the electron density is
Nothing is wrong; acetal hydrolysis is a one-step S<sub>N</sub>2 displacement of methoxide at the acetal carbon
The first step should be loss of a hydride from the acetal carbon to make a carbonyl
h: Under acid, what does a leaving group look like? And is there a neighboring atom that can stabilize a cation on the acetal carbon?
w: Two errors appear. First, methoxide (a strong base) cannot leave in acidic solution; the OCH3 must be protonated so it leaves as neutral methanol. Second, the substitution does not occur by back-side attack: the other OCH3 lone pair pushes in as methanol leaves, giving a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion, and water then adds to it. Repeating the sequence (protonate, lose CH3OH, deprotonate) gives the aldehyde. The real mechanism is the exact reverse of acetal formation.
x: Water as a nucleophile bonds to the electrophilic carbon; the acetal oxygens are electron-rich, and attacking one would make an O–O bond, which does not happen here.
The drawing has a methoxide leaving group in acid and skips the oxocarbenium ion; acetal hydrolysis is an S<sub>N</sub>1-like process through that cation, which is why acetals are stable to base.
Hydride is an extremely poor leaving group and nothing here accepts it; the carbonyl is regenerated by losing methanol twice.

q: In saponification of methyl acetate, the tetrahedral intermediate collapses to acetic acid and methoxide, which then react as the arrows show. Why does this step make saponification effectively irreversible?
c: Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8) is far stronger than methanol (pK<sub>a</sub> 15.5), so K ≈ 10<sup>11</sup> and methanol cannot attack the carboxylate
Methoxide is a better leaving group than hydroxide, so once it has left, the ester cannot re-form from the acid
A new C–O bond forms in this step, and forming a bond is always irreversible, so the ester can never return
Methanol evaporates from the warm reaction mixture as it forms, so Le Châtelier’s principle pulls the equilibrium forward
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of the acid on the left with that of the base's conjugate acid. What does a gap of about 10 pK<sub>a</sub> units mean for K?
w: The arrows show a proton transfer: methoxide takes the O–H proton of acetic acid. Because acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is far stronger than methanol (pKa ≈ 15.5), K ≈ 1015.5−4.8 ≈ 1011. The carboxylate formed is a resonance-stabilized anion and a very poor electrophile, so methanol cannot attack it to reverse the reaction. That is why saponification needs a full equivalent of base and gives the carboxylic acid only after acid workup.
x: Leaving-group ability is not the issue here (methoxide and hydroxide are similar), and the step shown is a proton transfer, not a leaving-group departure.
No C–O bond forms in this step; the arrows move a proton from O to O. Forming a bond does not by itself make a step irreversible.
Saponification is irreversible even in a closed flask; the driving force is the very favorable acid–base reaction, not loss of methanol.

q: A student drew the one-step mechanism shown for Fischer esterification of acetic acid with methanol (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst). Which statement best describes what is wrong?
c: It skips protonating the C=O and has OH<sup>−</sup> leave directly; methanol must add to the protonated C=O, then water leaves
Methanol should attack the carbonyl oxygen, not the carbonyl carbon, because that oxygen is the atom protonated first
Nothing is wrong except that the methanol O–H proton should be shown leaving before the new C–O bond forms
The arrows are backwards: the acid’s OH oxygen should attack the methanol carbon and displace water from it
h: Compare the drawing with the addition–elimination pattern of acyl substitution under acid. What is the leaving group, and is the carbonyl activated?
w: The drawing makes two classic errors. It shows an SN2-like direct displacement at a trigonal acyl carbon, and its leaving group is hydroxide in strongly acidic solution. In the accepted mechanism the carbonyl oxygen is protonated first, methanol adds to give a tetrahedral intermediate, a proton shift puts H+ on an OH, and water (not hydroxide) leaves as the C=O re-forms. Isotope labeling confirms this pathway: the ester oxygen comes from methanol and the water oxygen from the acid.
x: The electrophilic site is the carbonyl carbon; attacking oxygen would make an O–O bond.
The main errors are the direct displacement and the hydroxide leaving group; reordering one proton transfer does not fix them.

Attack by the acid's oxygen on the methanol carbon would be an S<sub>N</sub>2 at a methyl carbon with hydroxide (or water) leaving; labeling shows the ester's alkoxy oxygen comes from methanol, so this is not the pathway.

q: Propanoyl chloride reacts with diethylamine. The arrows show the first step. Why is a second equivalent of diethylamine (or pyridine) normally used?
c: To take up the HCl formed, which would otherwise protonate the amine to an unreactive ammonium salt
To attack the amide carbonyl a second time and convert the amide product into a tertiary amine
To act as the leaving group in place of chloride, since a neutral amine leaves more easily than Cl<sup>−</sup>
To reduce the amide to an amine after it forms, using its own N–H hydrogens as the hydride source
h: Track the protons: what acid is released overall, and what happens to an amine when it meets that acid?
w: After addition and loss of chloride, the amide nitrogen still carries the H that came from the amine, and overall the reaction releases HCl. A second equivalent of base takes that proton. Without it the HCl would protonate unreacted diethylamine to diethylammonium chloride, which has no lone pair and cannot attack, so the yield would stop near 50%.
x: The amide product is far less electrophilic than the acid chloride, and a second acyl substitution on it does not occur under these conditions; no tertiary amine forms.
Chloride is already an excellent leaving group (much better than an amine); the extra base is there to take a proton.
An amine is not a reducing agent; reducing an amide to an amine requires LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.

q: Methyl benzoate is treated with excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr. After the first addition, the tetrahedral intermediate collapses as shown to give acetophenone. Why can the reaction not be stopped at the ketone, and what is the product after aqueous workup?
c: The ketone is more electrophilic than the ester, so it adds a second CH<sub>3</sub> at once; 2-phenyl-2-propanol forms
The ketone is less electrophilic than the ester, so the reaction stops there; acetophenone is isolated
The ketone is more electrophilic than the ester, so it adds a second CH<sub>3</sub>; 1-phenylethanol forms
The Grignard reagent deprotonates the ketone to an enolate, which is unreactive; acetophenone is recovered after workup
h: Compare the electrophilicity of an ester carbonyl (with its electron-donating OCH<sub>3</sub>) and a ketone carbonyl. Then count the methyl groups on the carbinol carbon.
w: The ester carbonyl is stabilized by resonance donation from the OCH3 lone pair, so the ketone formed when the tetrahedral intermediate collapses is more reactive than the remaining ester. With CH3MgBr present it adds a second methyl immediately, and workup gives the tertiary alcohol 2-phenyl-2-propanol, PhC(CH3)2OH, which carries two identical groups from the Grignard reagent.
x: The ester is the less reactive carbonyl, because its OCH<sub>3</sub> donates electron density by resonance; the ketone cannot survive in the presence of excess Grignard reagent.
The reasoning is right, but 1-phenylethanol would require hydride addition; a second methyl addition puts two CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the carbinol carbon, giving a tertiary alcohol.
Enolization is a minor side reaction with very hindered ketones; acetophenone readily adds CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, and with excess reagent the main product is the tertiary alcohol.

q: Propanenitrile is heated in aqueous acid to give propanoic acid. In what order do the neutral organic species form?
c: Nitrile → imidic acid → amide → carboxylic acid
Nitrile → amide → imidic acid → carboxylic acid
h: Water adds across one C≡N π bond first. Which group does that put on carbon, and which tautomer is more stable?
w: Water adds to the protonated nitrile carbon, and loss of a proton gives the imidic acid CH3CH2C(=NH)OH. This tautomerizes to the more stable amide (C=O is stronger than C=N), CH3CH2CONH2. Under the vigorous conditions the amide is then hydrolyzed by acid-catalyzed acyl substitution to propanoic acid and NH4+.
x: An amine would come from reducing the nitrile (LiAlH<sub>4</sub>); hydrolysis adds water and never forms an amine intermediate.
An aldehyde comes from partial reduction of a nitrile (DIBAL-H), not from hydrolysis; hydrolysis keeps the carbon at the carboxylic acid oxidation level.
The order of the middle two is reversed: the imidic acid forms first, by adding water, and then tautomerizes to the more stable amide.

q: Ethyl propanoate labeled with <sup>18</sup>O in the ether oxygen (the O bonded to the ethyl group) is saponified with NaOH. The tetrahedral intermediate collapses as shown. After workup, where is the <sup>18</sup>O label found?
c: Split about equally between the ethanol and the propanoic acid
Only in water, because it is lost as H<sub>2</sub><sup>18</sup>O
h: Which bond breaks in nucleophilic acyl substitution: the acyl carbon–O bond or the O–ethyl bond? The labeled oxygen stays with whichever fragment it remains bonded to.
w: Nucleophilic acyl substitution breaks the bond between the acyl carbon and the ether oxygen, as the second arrow shows. The labeled oxygen keeps its bond to the ethyl group and leaves as ethoxide, which is protonated to ethanol. So the 18O appears only in the ethanol, and the propanoic acid (after workup) contains only unlabeled oxygens, one from the original C=O and one from hydroxide. This labeling result is classic evidence for acyl–oxygen cleavage.
x: That would require breaking the O–ethyl bond (alkyl–oxygen cleavage, an S<sub>N</sub>2 at the ethyl carbon), which does not happen in saponification.
The two possible bond cleavages are not equally likely; saponification occurs almost entirely by acyl–oxygen cleavage, so the label is not scrambled.
The labeled oxygen is never protonated twice and lost as water in base; it leaves bonded to the ethyl group as ethoxide.

q: Hydroxide converts acetone into its enolate. Which drawing shows correct curved arrows for this proton-transfer step?
h: Three bonds change: a new O–H bond, a new C=C, and the C=O π bond. Each arrow starts at electrons and ends where they go.
w: Enolate formation is an acid–base step. The hydroxide lone pair takes the α-hydrogen, the C–H bonding electrons become the new C=C π bond, and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen so the carbonyl carbon keeps four bonds. The three-arrow drawing (O⁻ → H, C–H → C=C, C=O → O) is correct and gives the enolate with the negative charge on oxygen.
x: The C=O π bond is never moved, so the carbonyl carbon would end up with five bonds once the new C=C forms.
Hydroxide adding to the carbonyl carbon is nucleophilic addition (hydrate formation), not removal of an α-hydrogen; no enolate forms.

The C=O π electrons are sent to carbon instead of oxygen, which would push the carbonyl carbon past an octet and leave oxygen electron-deficient; the π electrons should flow toward the electronegative oxygen.

q: In acid-catalyzed keto–enol tautomerization of acetone, the carbonyl oxygen is protonated first. Which drawing correctly shows the second step, in which water converts the protonated ketone into the enol?
h: The enol has a C=C and an O–H. Which hydrogen must water remove, and where must the C–H electrons go so that no carbanion appears in acid?
w: In acid, the enol forms by loss of an α-hydrogen from the O-protonated ketone. Water takes the α-H, the C–H electrons form the C=C, and the C=O π electrons return to the positive oxygen, which becomes the neutral OH of the enol. The drawing in which water removes the α-H and the C=O π bond moves onto O⁺ is correct. No carbanion is ever formed under acidic conditions.
x: Removing the O–H proton just reverses step 1 and gives back acetone; no C=C forms.
Water adding to the carbonyl carbon gives the hydrate (a gem-diol pathway), not the enol.
Leaving the C–H electrons on carbon creates a carbanion next to an oxonium ion. In acid the C–H electrons move straight into the C=C as the C=O π bond moves to O⁺.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is treated with LDA in THF at −78 °C. Which drawing shows correct arrows for the enolate-forming step under these conditions?
h: LDA is a very strong, very bulky base and the reaction is cold and irreversible. Which α-hydrogen can it reach fastest, and does it ever add to C=O?
w: LDA deprotonates irreversibly at −78 °C, so the enolate that forms fastest (kinetic control) is the one obtained. The bulky amide removes a hydrogen from the less hindered α-CH2 (C6), not from the methyl-bearing C2. The drawing in which N⁻ takes an H from the unsubstituted α-CH2, with the C–H electrons forming C=C and the C=O π bond moving to O is correct; it gives the less substituted enolate.
x: Removing the H on the methyl-bearing carbon gives the more substituted (thermodynamic) enolate, which forms under equilibrating conditions such as NaOEt/EtOH, not with LDA at −78 °C.
LDA is too hindered to add to a carbonyl carbon; it acts only as a base.
The correct hydrogen is removed, but without moving the C=O π bond the carbonyl carbon would have five bonds.

q: The lithium enolate of acetone reacts with iodomethane to give butan-2-one. Which drawing correctly shows the C–C bond-forming step?
h: The product has a new C–C bond to the α-carbon and a C=O. This is an S<sub>N</sub>2 step: what must happen at the carbon that is attacked?
w: The enolate reacts through its α-carbon. The oxygen lone pair re-forms the C=O, the C=C π electrons attack the CH3 carbon, and iodide leaves in the same SN2 step. The three-arrow drawing ending with the C–I bond moving onto iodine gives butan-2-one.
x: Attack through oxygen gives the enol ether 2-methoxypropene (O-alkylation), not butan-2-one; with lithium enolates and CH<sub>3</sub>I, C-alkylation dominates.
Without the C–I bond breaking, the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon would have five bonds; S<sub>N</sub>2 needs the leaving-group arrow.
The π electrons are aimed at iodine instead of carbon, and the C–I electrons are sent to carbon; this would make a C–I bond and a methyl anion, not alkylation.

q: In the aldol addition of acetaldehyde, the enolate adds to a second molecule of acetaldehyde. Which drawing correctly shows this step?
h: Arrows run from the nucleophile to the electrophile. Which atom of the enolate forms the new C–C bond, and what happens to the aldehyde's C=O?
w: The enolate is the nucleophile and reacts through its α-carbon: the O⁻ lone pair re-forms the C=O, the C=C electrons attack the aldehyde carbonyl carbon, and the aldehyde's C=O π electrons move onto its oxygen. The three-arrow drawing ending on the aldehyde oxygen gives the alkoxide of 3-hydroxybutanal.
x: Attack through the enolate oxygen would make a C–O bond (a hemiacetal-type alkoxide), not the aldol C–C bond.
The aldehyde C=O π bond is not moved, so the carbonyl carbon would have five bonds after the new C–C bond forms.
The arrows run backward, from the electrophilic carbonyl carbon toward the enolate; arrows must start at the electron-rich enolate.

q: In aqueous NaOH, 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one dehydrates to 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one by the E1cB mechanism. Which drawing correctly shows the step that forms the C=C?
h: E1cB means elimination through the conjugate base: which species is present before the leaving group departs, and why can hydroxide leave from it?
w: In E1cB the α-hydrogen is removed first, giving the enolate (the conjugate base). In a separate step the enolate pushes its electrons toward the β-carbon and expels hydroxide: O⁻ re-forms the C=O, the C=C π electrons shift to make the new Cα=Cβ bond, and the C–OH bond breaks onto oxygen. The drawing that starts from the enolate and ejects OH⁻ is correct. Hydroxide is normally a poor leaving group; it leaves here only because the enolate is a strong internal push and the product is a conjugated enone.
x: This is a concerted E2 drawing on the neutral β-hydroxy ketone. Under E1cB, deprotonation and loss of OH⁻ are separate steps, with the enolate as an intermediate.
This shows ionization to a tertiary carbocation (E1). In base, hydroxide does not leave on its own from a neutral alcohol.
The C–O electrons are sent to carbon instead of oxygen; the leaving group must take the bonding pair with it as OH⁻.

q: In the Claisen condensation of ethyl acetate, the ester enolate adds to a second ester molecule to give the tetrahedral intermediate shown. Which drawing correctly shows the step that forms ethyl acetoacetate?
h: Nucleophilic acyl substitution: the C=O re-forms and the best leaving group on that carbon departs. Compare CH<sub>3</sub>⁻, an ester enolate and ethoxide.
w: The alkoxide oxygen re-forms the C=O, and the carbon must lose one group to keep four bonds. The best leaving group is ethoxide (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 16). The drawing that expels CH3CH2O⁻ gives ethyl acetoacetate.
x: Expelling CH<sub>3</sub>⁻ (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50) is far too unfavorable; carbanions without stabilization are not leaving groups.
Re-forming the C=O with no bond breaking would give the carbon five bonds.
Expelling the ester enolate is the reverse of the addition step; it returns two molecules of ethyl acetate rather than the β-keto ester.

q: The last step before acid workup in a Claisen condensation is deprotonation of the β-keto ester product by ethoxide, which pulls the whole equilibrium toward product. Which drawing correctly shows this step for ethyl acetoacetate?
h: Find the hydrogen whose removal gives an anion delocalized over two carbonyl groups. Compare its pK<sub>a</sub> with that of ethanol.
w: The CH2 between the two carbonyls has pKa ≈ 11, far more acidic than ethanol (≈ 16), so ethoxide removes it essentially completely; this favorable step drives the reversible Claisen equilibria forward. The C–H electrons form a C=C to the ketone carbon and the ketone C=O π electrons move onto oxygen (the charge is also shared with the ester C=O). The drawing in which ethoxide removes an H from the central CH2 and the ketone C=O moves to O is correct.
x: The terminal CH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens are α to only one carbonyl (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 20). Ethoxide removes them only to a tiny extent, so this cannot drive the reaction.
Ethoxide adding to the ethyl ester carbonyl only exchanges OEt for OEt (degenerate transesterification); it is not the driving deprotonation.
The correct hydrogen is taken, but the ketone C=O π bond is not moved, leaving the ketone carbon with five bonds.

q: 3-Oxobutanoic acid loses CO<sub>2</sub> on gentle warming through a cyclic, six-membered transition state that gives the enol of acetone. Which drawing correctly shows the arrows for this step?
h: Six atoms form the transition-state ring. Three bonds break (O–H, C–C, C=O π) and three form. Where do the electrons of the breaking C–C bond end up?
w: Three pairs of electrons move around the ring at once: the ketone C=O π electrons bond to the acid hydrogen, the O–H bonding pair becomes the second C=O of CO2, and the C–C bond to the carboxyl carbon becomes the C=C of the enol. The three-arrow drawing that ends with the C–C bond forming the enol C=C is correct; the enol then tautomerizes to acetone.
x: The C–C bond electrons are sent onto the carboxyl carbon, which is already gaining a C=O π bond and would exceed its octet, while the CH<sub>2</sub> and former ketone carbons are left electron-deficient; those electrons must form the enol C=C.
The C–C bond never breaks, so the carboxyl carbon would carry five bonds and no CO<sub>2</sub> would be released.
These arrows run backward: they show an enol adding to CO<sub>2</sub> (carboxylation), the reverse of the decarboxylation.

q: In base-promoted α-bromination of acetone, the enolate reacts with Br<sub>2</sub>. Which drawing correctly shows this step?
h: Br<sub>2</sub> is the electrophile. Which atom of the enolate makes the new bond to Br, and which bromine leaves as bromide?
w: The enolate attacks through carbon: the O⁻ lone pair re-forms the C=O, the C=C electrons bond to the near bromine, and the Br–Br electrons leave on the far bromine as Br⁻. The three-arrow drawing ending on the distant bromine gives bromoacetone.
x: Attack through oxygen would give an O–Br compound (a hypobromite of the enol), not the α-bromo ketone.
The arrow starts at a bromine lone pair and ends at the enolate carbon, treating Br<sub>2</sub> as the nucleophile; arrows start at the enolate.
The Br–Br electrons are sent to the bromine that is forming the new C–Br bond, giving it too many electrons; they must go to the bromine that leaves.

q: In a Stork enamine alkylation, the pyrrolidine enamine of cyclohexanone reacts with iodomethane; hydrolysis later gives 2-methylcyclohexanone. Which drawing correctly shows the C–C bond-forming step?
h: An enamine is an enolate equivalent: the nitrogen lone pair plays the role of O⁻. Which carbon bonds to CH<sub>3</sub>, and what leaves?
w: The nitrogen lone pair pushes into the C–N bond (forming an iminium C=N⁺), the C=C electrons attack the CH3 carbon, and iodide leaves (SN2). The three-arrow drawing from N through the C=C to CH3, with I⁻ leaving is correct; the α-methyl iminium ion is later hydrolyzed to 2-methylcyclohexanone.
x: Attack by the nitrogen lone pair gives an N-methyl ammonium salt; it does not form the C–C bond needed for 2-methylcyclohexanone.
The C–I bond is not broken, so the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon would have five bonds.
The arrow starts at the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon, which has no lone pair; the electrophile receives electrons and never donates them.

q: The arrows convert the cyclohexanone enolate into its other resonance form. The enolate is then treated with chlorotrimethylsilane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>SiCl. Which statement correctly describes the new bond and why it forms?
c: An Si–O bond forms (a silyl enol ether): oxygen carries most of the charge and Si–O bonds are very strong
An Si–C bond forms at the α-carbon, because the carbanion form is the major resonance contributor of the enolate
An Si–C bond forms, because carbon is less electronegative and C–Si bonds are stronger than Si–O bonds
An Si–O bond forms, because enolates react through oxygen with all electrophiles, including CH<sub>3</sub>I
h: The enolate has two nucleophilic atoms. Which resonance form carries more of the charge, and how strong is an Si–O bond compared with an Si–C bond?
w: An enolate is an ambident nucleophile.
