The major resonance contributor puts the negative charge on the more electronegative oxygen (the form on the left), and silicon forms a very strong bond to oxygen (Si–O ≈ 450 kJ/mol, much stronger than Si–C). Hard, oxophilic electrophiles such as R3SiCl therefore react at oxygen. An Si–O bond forms, giving the trimethylsilyl enol ether of cyclohexanone.
x: The carbanion form, with the charge on the less electronegative carbon, is the minor contributor, and silicon prefers oxygen.
Si–O bonds are much stronger than Si–C bonds; the strong Si–O bond is a main reason the reaction occurs at oxygen.
With CH<sub>3</sub>I (a soft carbon electrophile) enolates react mainly at carbon; O-attack is specific to hard electrophiles such as silyl chlorides.

q: The step drawn is the C–C bond-forming step of a Michael addition between the diethyl malonate anion and but-3-en-2-one (methyl vinyl ketone). What species is formed directly in this step?
h: Follow each arrow: where does the new C–C bond form, where does the new π bond appear, and which atom ends up with the lone pair?
w: The malonate carbanion attacks the β-carbon (the terminal CH2) of the enone; the C=C electrons shift to make a new C=C between the α-carbon and the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. The product of this step is an enolate (1,4-addition), which is protonated afterward.
x: This alkoxide comes from attack at the carbonyl carbon (1,2-addition); the arrows show attack at the β-carbon.
This puts the new bond at the α-carbon of the enone and a carbanion on the end carbon; the arrows put the bond on the β-carbon and the charge on oxygen.
This neutral 1,5-dicarbonyl compound forms only after a later proton transfer to the enolate; it is not the direct product of the drawn step.

q: In the haloform reaction of acetophenone, hydroxide adds to PhCOCBr<sub>3</sub>, and the tetrahedral intermediate then collapses as drawn, expelling a carbon leaving group. Why can <sup>−</sup>CBr<sub>3</sub> leave here, when the tetrahedral intermediate from an ordinary methyl ketone does not expel <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>3</sub>?
c: Three bromines stabilize the carbanion inductively, so <sup>−</sup>CBr<sub>3</sub> is a far weaker base than <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>3</sub> (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 14 vs. 50)
The negative charge of <sup>−</sup>CBr<sub>3</sub> is delocalized by resonance into the C=O of the benzoic acid formed in this step
The C–CBr<sub>3</sub> bond breaks homolytically to give two radicals, so no carbanion ever has to form
Steric strain from three large bromines weakens the C–C bond, whatever the stability of the anion
h: A good leaving group is a weak base. Compare the acidity of CHBr<sub>3</sub> with that of CH<sub>4</sub>.
w: Leaving-group ability tracks the stability (weak basicity) of the departing anion. The three electronegative bromines pull electron density away from the carbanion carbon, so bromoform is about as acidic as water (pKa ≈ 14), while methane is around 50. −CBr3 is a weak enough base to leave, and the step is then pulled forward by proton transfer from benzoic acid to the anion, giving benzoate and CHBr3.
x: Once <sup>−</sup>CBr<sub>3</sub> has left it is no longer attached to the carbonyl, so there is no resonance with the C=O; its stability comes from induction by the bromines.
The arrows show a full (two-electron) arrow from the C–C bond onto CBr<sub>3</sub>; this is a heterolytic, ionic step in aqueous base.
Steric strain alone does not let a strongly basic anion leave; <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>3</sub> is not expelled however crowded the carbon is. Anion stability is the deciding factor.

q: The rate of acid-catalyzed bromination of acetone follows rate = k[acetone][H3O+]: it does not depend on [Br2], and chlorination and iodination run at the same rate. Which statement about the step drawn (the enol attacking Br2) is correct?
c: It is fast; the slow step is loss of an α-H from the O-protonated ketone to form the enol
It is the rate-determining step, so the rate law should be rate = k[enol][Br2]
It is fast; the slow step is protonation of the carbonyl oxygen by H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> before the enol forms
It is the rate-determining step, but Br<sub>2</sub> is regenerated, so [Br<sub>2</sub>] cancels from the rate law
h: If halogen concentration and identity do not affect the rate, the halogen must enter after the slow step. Which earlier step involves both the ketone and acid?
w: Because the rate is independent of [Br2] and of which halogen is used, the halogen reacts only after the rate-determining step. Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen is a fast equilibrium; the slow step is loss of an α-H from the protonated ketone to give the enol. The drawn step, the enol attacking Br2, is fast. Enol formation (α-C–H removal) is rate-determining, and the drawn step is fast.
x: If this step were slow, the rate would depend on [Br<sub>2</sub>] and on the halogen used, which the data rule out.
Proton transfer between oxygen atoms is very fast; the slow proton transfer is the one from carbon (the α-C–H).
Br<sub>2</sub> is consumed (it becomes C–Br and HBr), not regenerated; a step involving Br<sub>2</sub> that is slow would put [Br<sub>2</sub>] in the rate law.

q: In the second stage of a Robinson annulation, the enolate of 2-(3-oxobutyl)cyclohexanone cyclizes as drawn. What is formed directly in this step?
h: Count the atoms in the new ring, from the attacking CH<sub>2</sub> to the ring C=O carbon. How many are there, and where is the negative charge afterward?
w: The terminal CH2 of the enolate attacks the ring carbonyl carbon. The new ring contains that CH2, the side-chain C=O carbon, two CH2 groups, the ring CH and the former ring carbonyl carbon: six atoms. The ring C=O π electrons end on oxygen. The bicyclic β-alkoxy ketone (a fused six/six ring alkoxide) is formed; protonation and E1cB dehydration later give the octalone enone.
x: A four-membered ring would form only if the internal CH<sub>2</sub> (next to the side-chain C=O) attacked; the arrows start at the terminal CH<sub>2</sub>, and a strained four-membered ring is disfavored anyway.
This enone is the final Robinson product, formed after protonation and dehydration; it is not the direct product of the C–C bond-forming step.
This would come from the enolate oxygen attacking the C=O (a cyclic enol ether); the arrows show carbon attacking.

q: Diethyl 2-methylhexanedioate is treated with one equivalent of NaOEt in ethanol, then with dilute aqueous acid. What is the major product (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: Two enolates can cyclize, but every step before the last is reversible. Which cyclized β-keto ester still has a hydrogen between its two carbonyl groups for ethoxide to remove?
w: Either α-carbon could attack the other ester, and both pathways give a five-membered ring. The Dieckmann (like the Claisen) is reversible until the product is deprotonated at the carbon between the two C=O groups. If the methyl-bearing carbon attacked, that carbon would become quaternary with no H to remove, so that product reverts. Enolization at the unsubstituted CH2 and attack on the other ester gives a product with an acidic C–H between the carbonyls, which is trapped as its enolate. Ethyl 3-methyl-2-oxocyclopentane-1-carboxylate is formed after acidification.
x: This product has no hydrogen between its two carbonyls, so the final deprotonation that drives the Dieckmann cannot occur and it reverts to the diester.
Here the methyl is on the ring carbon next to the CH(CO<sub>2</sub>Et) rather than next to the ketone; that pattern would come from a 3-methyl diester, not this one.
Loss of the ester (hydrolysis and decarboxylation) needs heating in aqueous acid; cold, dilute acid only protonates the enolate.

q: When acetone and benzaldehyde are mixed with NaOH, the main C–C bond-forming step is the one drawn. Why does acetone's enolate add to benzaldehyde rather than to another acetone molecule?
c: An aldehyde C=O is more electrophilic than a ketone C=O, and benzaldehyde has no α-H to form an enolate
Benzaldehyde forms a more stable, conjugated enolate than acetone, so it is the better nucleophile in the mix
Acetone’s C=O is too hindered by its two methyl groups for any nucleophile to add to it
The phenyl ring of benzaldehyde donates electrons to the enolate and makes it a stronger nucleophile
h: Compare the two carbonyl compounds as electrophiles, and ask which of them can form an enolate at all.
w: Aldehydes are more reactive electrophiles than ketones (less steric hindrance, only one electron-donating alkyl group), so the acetone enolate attacks benzaldehyde faster than acetone. Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen and cannot form an enolate, so the only productive combination is acetone enolate + benzaldehyde. Benzaldehyde is the better electrophile and can act only as the electrophile.
x: Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot form an enolate at all.
Acetone does undergo aldol addition with its own enolate; it is simply slower and the equilibrium is unfavorable compared with addition to the aldehyde.
The phenyl ring belongs to the electrophile, not the enolate, so it cannot donate electrons to the nucleophile.

q: The drawing shows the C–C bond-forming step of the acid-catalyzed aldol reaction of acetaldehyde. Which statement correctly identifies the nucleophile and the electrophile?
c: The enol is the nucleophile, through its α-carbon; the O-protonated aldehyde is the electrophile
The enolate ion is the nucleophile through its α-carbon; the neutral aldehyde is the electrophile
The O-protonated aldehyde is the nucleophile; the enol, through its α-carbon, is the electrophile
The enol is the nucleophile, reacting through its oxygen; the O-protonated aldehyde is the electrophile
h: In acid, which carbonyl-derived species exists in small amounts, and which carbonyl has been made more electrophilic? Follow the middle arrow.
w: Acid gives two activated species: the enol (a weak, neutral nucleophile) and the O-protonated aldehyde (a strong electrophile). The arrows start at the enol O lone pair and C=C and end at the protonated carbonyl carbon, with the C=O+ π electrons moving onto oxygen. The neutral enol attacks through carbon, and the protonated aldehyde is the electrophile.
x: Enolate ions do not form in appreciable amounts in acid; this describes the base-catalyzed aldol.
The roles are reversed: arrows start at the electron-rich enol and end at the positively charged carbonyl carbon.
The O lone pair pushes into the C–O bond, but the new bond is made by the α-carbon of the enol; an O-attack would give an acetal-type C–O bond.

q: In base-promoted bromination of acetone, bromoacetone is deprotonated as drawn, at the CH<sub>2</sub>Br carbon rather than at the CH<sub>3</sub> group, and it does so faster than acetone itself. Why?
c: Bromine withdraws electrons inductively and stabilizes the enolate, so the CH<sub>2</sub>Br hydrogens are more acidic
Bromine donates lone-pair electrons by resonance and stabilizes the negative charge on the α-carbon
The CH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens of bromoacetone are not α to the carbonyl group, so base cannot remove them
Bromine’s large size blocks the CH<sub>3</sub> group, so hydroxide can reach only the CH<sub>2</sub>Br hydrogens next to it
h: Consider how a halogen affects the stability of a nearby negative charge.
w: Bromine is electronegative, so it pulls electron density through the σ bond and stabilizes the developing negative charge on the adjacent carbon. The CH2Br hydrogens are therefore more acidic than the CH3 hydrogens or acetone's own α-H. Inductive withdrawal by Br makes the CH2Br protons more acidic, so each bromination speeds up the next, and the same carbon is brominated three times (the start of the haloform reaction).
x: Lone-pair donation would put more electron density on a carbon that already carries negative charge, which destabilizes the anion; bromine's effect here is inductive withdrawal.
The CH<sub>3</sub> group is attached directly to the C=O carbon, so its hydrogens are α hydrogens too; they are just less acidic.
The CH<sub>3</sub> group is on the other side of the carbonyl and is not blocked; the choice is set by acidity, not sterics.

q: When 4-hydroxy-4-phenylbutan-2-one is warmed in aqueous NaOH, its alkoxide undergoes the step drawn. What are the products of this step?
h: Which C–C bond do the arrows break, and where do its electrons go? Read the arrows from the alkoxide oxygen to the far oxygen.
w: This is a retro-aldol step. The alkoxide oxygen forms a C=O (giving benzaldehyde), the C–C bond between the carbinol carbon and the CH2 breaks, and those electrons form a C=C to the ketone carbon while the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. Benzaldehyde and the enolate of acetone are produced: the exact reverse of the aldol addition.
x: This enone and hydroxide come from E1cB dehydration of the aldol, which starts by deprotonating the α-carbon; the drawn arrows break a C–C bond instead.
This would require breaking the bond between the CH<sub>2</sub> and the ketone carbon, giving an acyl anion; the arrows break the bond on the other side of the CH<sub>2</sub>.
This enolate keeps every C–C bond; it comes from removing an α-hydrogen, not from the arrows shown, which cleave a C–C bond.

q: Benzylmalonic acid loses CO<sub>2</sub> on heating through the cyclic step drawn. What is the final organic product after the enol tautomerizes?
h: Only one carboxyl group is lost. The other one's C=O takes the proton and ends up as a carboxylic acid again after tautomerization.
w: One CO2H leaves as CO2; the remaining carboxyl becomes an enediol (the enol of a carboxylic acid) that tautomerizes back to a C=O. The α-carbon keeps its H, gains another H and keeps the benzyl group. 3-Phenylpropanoic acid is the product.
x: Phenylacetic acid has one carbon too few; only the carboxyl carbon leaves, and the α-carbon stays with the benzyl group.
Only one carboxyl is lost; a carboxylic acid without a β-carbonyl group does not decarboxylate on simple heating.
Decarboxylation adds a hydrogen to the α-carbon; it does not create a C=C conjugated with the ring.

q: A student tries to run a Claisen condensation of ethyl acetate using NaOH in place of NaOEt, and the step drawn happens instead. Why does this ruin the Claisen?
c: Hydroxide saponifies the ester to acetate, a poor electrophile, in an essentially irreversible step
Hydroxide is too weak a base to remove an α-hydrogen of the ester, so no ester enolate can form
Hydroxide adds to the C=O to give a stable acetal that cannot react with an enolate afterward
Hydroxide replaces an α-hydrogen with OH, giving ethyl glycolate instead of the β-keto ester product
h: Follow the tetrahedral intermediate one more step. What acid–base reaction follows, and can the product go back?
w: Hydroxide adds to the ester C=O, the intermediate expels ethoxide, and the acetic acid formed is deprotonated at once (pKa 4.8). That last step makes saponification essentially irreversible, and the carboxylate is a very poor electrophile, so the ester is consumed. Saponification to acetate destroys the ester; that is why a Claisen uses the alkoxide that matches the ester.
x: Hydroxide (water pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.7) is about as strong a base as ethoxide; the problem is its addition to the C=O, not its basicity.
An acetal has two OR groups on a carbon that has lost its C=O; hydroxide addition gives a tetrahedral intermediate that expels ethoxide, not an acetal.
Bases do not substitute at the α-carbon; they either remove an α-H or add to the carbonyl carbon.

q: The anion of diethyl malonate is heated with 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. The step drawn is the main reaction. What does it produce, and what does it mean for a malonic ester synthesis?
c: E2: 2-methylpropene, Br<sup>−</sup> and diethyl malonate; tertiary halides eliminate instead of alkylating the enolate
SN2: diethyl tert-butylmalonate; tertiary halides are the best alkylating agents for enolates
E1: 2-methylpropene, formed after bromide leaves first and the enolate removes a proton from the carbocation
SN1: diethyl tert-butylmalonate, formed through the tert-butyl cation
h: Where does the first arrow end: at a carbon or at a hydrogen? Is the C–Br bond breaking in the same step?
w: The enolate takes a β-hydrogen, the C–H electrons form the C=C, and bromide leaves, all in one step: an E2 reaction. The products are 2-methylpropene, bromide and neutral diethyl malonate. Enolate alkylation is SN2 and works only with methyl, primary (and some secondary) halides. Tertiary halides undergo E2, so they cannot be used to alkylate malonate.
x: Backside attack at a tertiary carbon is blocked; tertiary halides do not undergo S<sub>N</sub>2, and the arrows show H removal, not attack at carbon.
The drawing shows one concerted step (H removal and C–Br cleavage together), which is E2, not a two-step E1 through a carbocation.
The arrows show the enolate removing a hydrogen, not bonding to carbon; no C–C bond forms.

q:
Which statements about forming enolates are correct?
I. Diisopropylamine (pKa ≈ 36) is a much weaker acid than a ketone (pKa ≈ 19–20), so LDA converts a ketone essentially completely and irreversibly into its enolate.
II. Because ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is a stronger acid than acetone (pKa ≈ 19), NaOEt converts only a small fraction of acetone into its enolate at equilibrium.
III. With LDA in THF at −78 °C, 2-methylcyclohexanone gives mainly the more substituted enolate, because that enolate has the more substituted C=C.
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of each base's conjugate acid with the ketone's. Then ask whether a cold, irreversible deprotonation can choose the more stable product.
w: I is true: the equilibrium lies about 1016 toward the enolate, so deprotonation is complete and irreversible. II is true: Keq ≈ 1016−19 = 10−3, so only a small fraction of enolate is present (enough for aldol or Claisen chemistry, which consume it as it forms). III is false: under kinetic control LDA removes the more accessible hydrogen on the CH2 and gives the less substituted enolate; the more substituted enolate is favored only under equilibrating conditions. I and II only.
x: This rejects II, but ethanol is about 1000 times more acidic than acetone, so with NaOEt the equilibrium lies on the side of the ketone and only a small fraction is enolate.
This rejects I, but LDA's conjugate acid (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 36) is far weaker than a ketone, so LDA deprotonates completely and irreversibly.
This accepts III, but LDA at −78 °C gives the kinetic (less substituted) enolate; the more substituted one forms under thermodynamic control.

q: Benzene reacts with the Br<sub>2</sub>·FeBr<sub>3</sub> complex. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the step that forms the arenium ion (σ complex) and FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>?
h: The ring is the nucleophile. Where does the first arrow start, and where must the Br–Br electrons go so the ring-bonded bromine keeps an octet?
w: The electron-rich ring is the nucleophile: one arrow starts at a ring π bond and ends at the terminal (outer) bromine. That bromine cannot hold a second bond, so the Br–Br bond breaks with both electrons moving to the bromine bonded to iron, which leaves as FeBr4−. Two arrows: ring π bond → outer Br, and Br–Br bond → the Br attached to Fe. The product is the arenium ion, whose positive charge is spread over three ring carbons.
x: This arrow starts at a bromine lone pair and ends at the ring, as if bromine were giving electrons to the ring. Arrows start at the nucleophile, and here the ring π bond is the electron source.
Without the Br–Br bond breaking, the outer bromine would have two bonds and three lone pairs (10 electrons). The leaving-group arrow is missing.

The Br–Br electrons are sent to the bromine that is gaining the new C–Br bond, which would give it an extra pair. They must go toward the FeBr<sub>3</sub> end, which becomes FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>.

q: In the nitration of benzene, the σ complex below loses a proton to water to restore the aromatic ring. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: Which carbon is sp<sup>3</sup>? Its C–H bond is the one that can supply electrons to the neighboring positive carbon.
w: Rearomatization is an acid–base step. A water lone pair takes the proton on the sp3 carbon (the one bearing NO2), and that C–H bond's electrons move into the ring bond to the cationic carbon, forming a C=C. The ring then has three C=C bonds again and is aromatic.
x: Water adding to the cationic carbon would give a nonaromatic addition product. EAS ends with loss of H<sup>+</sup>, because restoring aromaticity is strongly favored.
This removes a proton from an sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon. The sp<sup>3</sup> carbon would stay sp<sup>3</sup>, and the ring would get a cumulated C=C=C unit; no aromatic ring results.
The arrow runs from the C–H bond to water, as if water accepted electrons. The base must donate its lone pair to the H, and the C–H electrons must stay in the ring.

q: In HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, nitric acid is protonated on its OH group. Which set of curved arrows correctly converts this protonated nitric acid into the nitronium ion, O=N<sup>+</sup>=O, and water?
h: Water is the leaving group. Which way does the N–O bond's electron pair go, and how does nitrogen get back to four bonds?
w: Water leaves: the N–OH2+ bond breaks with both electrons going to that oxygen, which becomes neutral H2O. At the same time a lone pair on the O− forms a second N=O bond, so nitrogen keeps four bonds and an octet. Two arrows: N–OH2 bond → O, and O− lone pair → N–O bond, giving linear O=N+=O, the electrophile that attacks the ring.
x: Forming a second N=O bond while the N–OH<sub>2</sub> bond stays would give nitrogen five bonds (10 electrons). The water must leave in the same step.
Water leaves, but nothing replaces the lost bond: nitrogen would have only six electrons and a 2+ charge. The O<sup>−</sup> lone pair must form a π bond to nitrogen.
The arrow from the water oxygen points at nitrogen, so it describes water attacking, the reverse of leaving. A leaving-group arrow starts at the N–O bond and ends on the oxygen.

q: In Friedel–Crafts acylation, acetyl chloride binds AlCl<sub>3</sub> through chlorine. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this complex giving the acylium ion, CH<sub>3</sub>C≡O<sup>+</sup>, and AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>?
h: Which bond has to break to release AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, and what keeps the carbonyl carbon from being left with only six electrons?
w: The C–Cl bond breaks with both electrons going to chlorine, which stays on aluminum as AlCl4−. A lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen then forms a second π bond to carbon, so every atom has an octet in CH3C≡O+. Two arrows: C–Cl bond → Cl, and O lone pair → C–O bond. The acylium ion is resonance-stabilized and does not rearrange, which is why acylation avoids the rearrangements seen in Friedel–Crafts alkylation.
x: Forming C≡O while the C–Cl bond is intact would give the carbonyl carbon five bonds. The chloride must leave in the same step.
The C–Cl electrons are sent to carbon, making it a carbanion with five bonds' worth of electrons. A leaving group takes the bond electrons with it.
Breaking the Cl–Al bond simply undoes the Lewis acid–base complex and returns acetyl chloride and AlCl<sub>3</sub>; no electrophile forms.

q: Anisole is brominated at the para position. Which resonance contributor of the para σ complex has a complete octet on every carbon and oxygen and is the main reason the OCH<sub>3</sub> group directs ortho/para?
h: Para attack can place the positive charge on the carbon bonded to OCH<sub>3</sub>. What can the oxygen do for that carbon?
w: For para (or ortho) attack, one contributor puts the positive charge on the ring carbon that carries OCH3. An oxygen lone pair can then form a C=O+ π bond, giving an oxonium contributor in which every C and O has an octet. Meta attack never places the charge on that carbon, so it never gets this extra, especially stable contributor. That is why OCH3 is a strong ortho/para director.
x: This is a real contributor of the para σ complex, and it is what allows the oxonium form. But the cationic carbon has only six electrons, so it is not the all-octet structure asked for.
This contributor has the charge on a carbon next to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon. It has a six-electron carbon, and oxygen gives it no help.
This is the σ complex from meta attack (Br is meta to OCH<sub>3</sub>). Its cationic carbon has six electrons, and meta attack can never put the charge on the carbon bonded to oxygen.

q: 1-Fluoro-4-nitrobenzene reacts with sodium methoxide by addition–elimination (S<sub>N</sub>Ar). Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the addition step that forms the Meisenheimer complex, with the negative charge on a nitro oxygen?
h: Aryl carbons cannot be attacked from the back side. The ring has to make room for the new bond first; follow the π electrons until they reach the nitro group.
w: SNAr is two steps. In the addition step, methoxide attacks the carbon bearing F (the carbon with the leaving group, para to NO2). To keep that carbon at four bonds, the adjacent ring π bond shifts, the next π bond moves toward the nitro-bearing carbon, and an N=O π bond moves onto oxygen. Four arrows end with the charge on a nitro oxygen; this delocalization onto NO2 is why an ortho or para EWG is required. Fluoride leaves only in the second (elimination) step.
x: This is a concerted S<sub>N</sub>2 displacement. The back side of an aryl C–F bond points into the ring, so backside attack is impossible; S<sub>N</sub>Ar goes through an anionic intermediate instead.
Methoxide attacks the carbon bearing NO<sub>2</sub>, not the one bearing the leaving group, and the charge is left on a ring carbon instead of being delocalized onto the nitro group.
Only the attack arrow is drawn, so the ipso carbon would have five bonds. The ring π electrons must move away as methoxide bonds.

q: Chlorobenzene reacts with NaNH<sub>2</sub> in liquid NH<sub>3</sub>. After amide removes an ortho proton, the aryl anion below loses chloride to form benzyne. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows that step?
h: The carbanion lone pair becomes a new π bond to the neighboring carbon. What must that neighbor lose at the same time?
w: The sp2 lone pair on the anionic carbon forms a second π bond to the adjacent carbon, while the C–Cl bond breaks with both electrons going to chlorine. Two arrows: carbanion lone pair → C–C bond, and C–Cl bond → Cl. The new π bond uses sp2 orbitals in the plane of the ring, which overlap poorly, so benzyne is very reactive and is trapped by NH2− at either end of the triple bond.
x: Forming the new π bond without losing chloride gives the chlorine-bearing carbon five bonds. Chloride must leave in the same step.
The C–Cl electrons are sent to carbon instead of to chlorine. A leaving group departs with the bonding pair, here as Cl<sup>−</sup>.
The carbanion attacks chlorine itself, giving chlorine two bonds and three lone pairs (10 electrons). The lone pair has to form the C–C π bond instead.

q: Benzene with 1-chloropropane and AlCl<sub>3</sub> gives mainly isopropylbenzene. Which set of curved arrows shows a single step that converts the 1-chloropropane–AlCl<sub>3</sub> complex directly into the isopropyl cation and AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>?
h: A free primary carbocation is too unstable to form. Which drawing gives a secondary cation while every carbon keeps a legal number of bonds?
w: As the C–Cl bond lengthens, the hydrogen on C2 moves to C1 with its bonding electrons (a 1,2-hydride shift). C1 gains an H as it loses Cl, and C2 is left with three bonds and the positive charge. Two arrows: C2–H bond → C1, and C1–Cl bond → Cl, giving the secondary isopropyl cation, which alkylates the ring to give isopropylbenzene (cumene).
x: Breaking only the C–Cl bond gives the primary propyl cation, not the isopropyl cation. A primary cation does not form as a free intermediate; the shift happens as chloride leaves.
The hydride moves to C1 while chlorine is still bonded there, so C1 would have five bonds. The C–Cl bond must break in the same step.
Moving the CH<sub>3</sub> group from C2 to C1 just rebuilds a straight three-carbon chain and leaves a primary carbocation; a methyl shift gives no stability gain here.

q: 2,2-Dimethyloxirane is opened with CH<sub>3</sub>OH and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows methanol opening the protonated epoxide in the major pathway?
h: In the protonated epoxide, which C–O bond is longer and weaker, and which carbon carries more δ+?
w: After protonation, the C–O bond to the tertiary carbon is the weaker one, and that carbon carries most of the positive charge (SN1-like transition state). Methanol attacks the more substituted (tertiary) carbon from the back side as that C–O bond breaks onto oxygen. The product, after loss of H+, is 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol.
x: Attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon is the base-promoted (S<sub>N</sub>2) regiochemistry. Under acid, the tertiary carbon bears more δ+ and is attacked.
Methanol bonds to the tertiary carbon without any C–O bond breaking, so that carbon would have five bonds.

Methanol bonds to the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon while the other C–O bond breaks; the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon would have five bonds and the tertiary carbon would become a cation. The bond that breaks must be to the carbon being attacked.

q: (R)-2-Phenyloxirane is heated with NaOCH3 in CH3OH, then neutralized. What is the major product?
h: Under basic conditions the nucleophile attacks by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which epoxide carbon is less hindered, and is the stereocenter one of the carbons that gets attacked?
w: Methoxide is a strong nucleophile, so the epoxide opens by SN2 at the less hindered CH2 carbon. The benzylic stereocenter is not attacked; its C–O bond becomes the C–O− (then OH) with no bonds to it broken, so its configuration is retained. The product is (R)-2-methoxy-1-phenylethan-1-ol, PhCH(OH)CH2OCH3 (the descriptor stays R).
x: This is the enantiomer of the product. No bond to the stereocenter breaks under basic conditions, so its spatial arrangement cannot invert.
Methoxy on the benzylic carbon with inversion is the acid-catalyzed outcome (attack at the carbon best able to carry δ+). With methoxide and no acid, attack is at the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub>.
This places OCH<sub>3</sub> on the benzylic carbon with retention, which neither pathway gives: base attacks the CH<sub>2</sub>, and acid-catalyzed backside attack at the benzylic carbon inverts it.

q: Which drawing shows a workable Williamson step for making tert-butyl methyl ether, with correct curved arrows?
h: The Williamson synthesis is S<sub>N</sub>2. Which partner should carry the halide, and where must the alkoxide's arrow end?
w: An SN2 step needs an unhindered electrophilic carbon, so the halide goes on the methyl group and the bulky group comes in as the alkoxide. tert-Butoxide's lone pair attacks the CH3 carbon while the C–Br bond breaks onto bromine. CH3Br cannot undergo elimination, so substitution is clean.
x: The arrows are drawn correctly, but backside attack at a tertiary carbon is blocked. Methoxide acts as a base on tert-butyl bromide and gives 2-methylpropene by E2.
The C–Br electrons are sent to carbon. Bromide is the leaving group and departs with the bonding pair.
The alkoxide attacks bromine instead of carbon, which would give bromine two bonds and an expanded valence. The electrophilic atom is the δ+ carbon.

q: tert-Butyl methyl ether is heated with one equivalent of HI, and the ether oxygen is protonated first. Which set of curved arrows shows the C–O bond-breaking step of the major pathway?
h: Two C–O bonds could break. One leads to a very stable cation; the other would need S<sub>N</sub>2. Which is possible for each carbon?
w: Protonation makes methanol a good leaving group on the tert-butyl side. The C(tertiary)–O bond ionizes by SN1, with both electrons going to oxygen: one arrow, tert-butyl C–O bond → O, gives the tert-butyl cation and CH3OH. Iodide then captures the cation to give (CH3)3CI (some 2-methylpropene also forms by E1). Ethers with a tertiary group cleave on the tertiary side.
x: S<sub>N</sub>2 at the methyl carbon is how methyl primary ethers cleave, but here the tertiary side can ionize to a stable cation, which is much faster. The products are tert-butyl iodide and methanol, not CH<sub>3</sub>I and tert-butyl alcohol.
Backside attack at a tertiary carbon is sterically blocked; the tertiary C–O bond breaks first and iodide adds to the cation afterward.
Breaking the CH<sub>3</sub>–O bond would make a methyl cation, the least stable carbocation. It does not form.

q: Anisole is heated with concentrated HBr. After the ether oxygen is protonated, the curved arrows shown describe the next step. What are the products of this step?
c: anisole and HBr (a proton transfer only)
h: Follow each arrow: which atom gains a bond to bromine, and which bond's electrons end up on oxygen?
w: Bromide's lone pair forms a bond to the methyl carbon, and the CH3–O bond breaks with its electrons moving onto oxygen. This SN2 step gives phenol and bromomethane. Aryl–O bonds are not cleaved: an sp2 carbon cannot be attacked from the back side, and a phenyl cation is far too unstable for SN1.
x: This would need bromide to attack the ring carbon. The arrow goes to the methyl carbon, and aryl carbons do not undergo S<sub>N</sub>2 or S<sub>N</sub>1.
The arrows form a new C–Br bond and break a C–O bond; a proton transfer would move an H, which none of these arrows touches.
Bromide's arrow forms the C–Br bond as the C–O bond breaks, so the step is concerted S<sub>N</sub>2. A free methyl cation never forms.

q: 2-Methyl-2-butanol is dehydrated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and heat. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the step from the carbocation that gives the major alkene?
h: E1 ends with loss of a β proton. Which β hydrogen gives the more substituted C=C?
w: Water acts as a base on a β hydrogen, and that C–H bond's electrons form the π bond to the cationic carbon. Removing the H from the CH2 carbon gives 2-methyl-2-butene, the trisubstituted (Zaitsev) alkene, which is the more stable and major product under these thermodynamic conditions.
x: Removing an H from the CH<sub>3</sub> group is a correctly drawn E1 step, but it gives 2-methyl-1-butene, the less substituted, minor alkene.
Water adding to the carbocation is the reverse of the ionization step and leads back to the alcohol, not to an alkene.
The arrow goes from the C–H bond toward water, so water would be receiving electrons. The base must donate its lone pair to the proton.

q: In the pinacol rearrangement of 2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, loss of water gives the carbocation below. Which set of curved arrows converts it, in one step, into the protonated ketone (protonated pinacolone)?
h: A group on the carbinol carbon moves to the cation with its bonding pair. Which group should move, and how does oxygen then stabilize the new cation?
w: A methyl group on the carbon bearing OH shifts to the cationic carbon with its C–C bonding pair (1,2-methyl shift). As it leaves, an oxygen lone pair forms a C=O+ π bond to the carbon it left, so no carbon is ever without an octet in the product. Two arrows: C–CH3 bond → cationic carbon, and O lone pair → C–O bond. Loss of H+ then gives pinacolone, 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one.
x: This methyl shift is right, but without the oxygen arrow the product is a carbocation next to OH, not the protonated ketone the question asks for. The O lone pair forms the C=O<sup>+</sup> bond in the same step.
The first arrow starts at the positively charged carbon, which has no electrons to give. In a 1,2-shift the arrow starts at the migrating C–C bond.
An OH shift just moves the cation to the other carbon and gives an identical carbocation, with no C=O formed. The migrating group is methyl, so that oxygen can stabilize the new cation.

q: In a chromic acid (or PCC) oxidation of 2-propanol, the alcohol first forms a chromate ester. The arrows drawn show the next step. Which statement correctly describes it?
c: The C–H bond electrons form the C=O π bond, and the O–Cr electrons go to chromium, reducing it.
Water's lone pair forms the C=O π bond, and the O–Cr electrons go to oxygen, oxidizing chromium.
The C–O σ bond breaks to give a carbocation, and water then removes a proton from the CH<sub>3</sub> group.
The C–H electrons go to chromium as a hydride, and the O–Cr bond stays intact in the product.
h: Follow the arrow that starts at the C–H bond: where does it end? Then follow the arrow that starts at the O–Cr bond.
w: This is an E2-like elimination across C–O. Water removes the H on the carbinol carbon; those C–H electrons become the C=O π bond, and the O–Cr bond breaks with its electrons going to chromium. Chromium gains a pair of electrons, so it is reduced (Cr(VI) → Cr(IV)) while the carbon is oxidized to acetone. The same idea, a C–H on the carbinol carbon plus a leaving group on oxygen, underlies Swern and Dess–Martin oxidations, which is why 3° alcohols (no carbinol H) are not oxidized.
x: Water's lone pair forms an O–H bond to the proton, not the C=O bond, and chromium is reduced, not oxidized, when it gains the O–Cr electron pair.
No arrow breaks the C–O bond, and no carbocation forms; the H removed is on the carbinol carbon, not on a CH<sub>3</sub> group.
The C–H arrow ends at the C–O bond (forming C=O), not at chromium, and the O–Cr bond does break: the oxygen leaves chromium to become the ketone oxygen.

q: tert-Butyl alcohol is dehydrated with aqueous H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (the acid is H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>). Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the first step?
h: OH<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group. What has to happen to the OH before any C–O bond breaks?
w: The first step is protonation of the hydroxyl group. An oxygen lone pair of the alcohol takes the proton from H3O+, and the H–O bond of hydronium breaks onto its oxygen, giving the alkyloxonium ion and water. Now water, a weak base, is the leaving group in the next (rate-determining) step that forms the tert-butyl cation.
x: This has hydroxide leaving from the neutral alcohol. HO<sup>−</sup> is a strong base and a very poor leaving group; the OH must be protonated first.
The alcohol's lone pair bonds to the proton, but the H–O bond of hydronium does not break, so hydrogen would have two bonds.
This arrow pushes the H–O bond electrons of hydronium toward the alcohol oxygen. In a proton transfer the base donates a lone pair to H; the bond electrons stay on hydronium's oxygen.

q: Cyclopentadiene reacts with methyl acrylate in a Diels–Alder reaction. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this concerted [4+2] cycloaddition?
h: Count the π bonds that change: two in the diene, one in the dienophile. How many arrows does that take, and where does the new π bond form?
w: A Diels–Alder reaction moves three electron pairs around a six-atom ring at once. Three arrows: one diene end π bond → the dienophile CH2, the dienophile π bond → the other diene end, and the remaining diene π bond → the central C2–C3 bond. Two new σ bonds form, and the new π bond sits between the old C2 and C3 of the diene. No ions or intermediates form.
x: Only two arrows are drawn. The diene carbon that receives the new σ bond still has its C=C π bond, so it would have five bonds; the third arrow, into the C2–C3 bond, is missing.

This pushes the dienophile's π electrons onto the carbonyl oxygen, giving a zwitterion with a cationic diene carbon. That is a stepwise ionic (Michael-type) path, not the concerted cycloaddition, and the ring never closes.
The third arrow starts at the C2–C3 σ bond and pushes it toward C1. The electrons that move are the C1=C2 π electrons, which shift into the C2–C3 position.

q: 1,3-Butadiene is protonated by HBr at C1 to give an allylic cation. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this protonation step?
h: The nucleophile is a π bond of the diene. Which bond's electrons go to the proton, and what happens to the H–Br bond?
w: The C1=C2 π bond donates its electrons to the proton of HBr, and the H–Br bond breaks with both electrons going to bromine. Two arrows: C1=C2 π bond → H, and H–Br bond → Br. Adding H to C1 puts the positive charge on C2, next to the remaining C3=C4 π bond, so the cation is allylic and resonance-stabilized (charge shared by C2 and C4).
x: The arrow starts at the C2–C3 single (σ) bond. σ electrons are not donated in electrophilic addition; the π bond is the nucleophile.
This has bromine's lone pair attacking the electron-rich diene. HBr's bromine is not the electrophile; the δ+ proton is attacked first.
The H–Br bond is not broken, so the hydrogen would end up with two bonds. A bond-breaking arrow to bromine is missing.

q: 1,3-Butadiene and HBr at 40 °C give mainly the 1,4-adduct, 1-bromo-2-butene. Which set of curved arrows shows bromide converting the allylic cation into this product?
h: Draw the other resonance contributor of the cation. Which terminal carbon must bromide bond to for a 1,4-adduct, and what happens to the C=C next to it?
w: The allylic cation shares its charge between C2 and C4. For 1,4-addition, bromide bonds to C4 (the CH2 end), and the C3=C4 π bond shifts to C2–C3, giving BrCH2CH=CHCH3. At 40 °C the additions are reversible, so the more substituted, more stable internal alkene (the 1,4-product, thermodynamic control) dominates.
x: Bromide bonding to C2 gives 3-bromo-1-butene, the 1,2-adduct. It forms faster (kinetic product, favored at low temperature) but is not the 1,4-product.
Bromide bonds to C4 but the C3=C4 π bond does not move, so C4 would have five bonds.
C3 carries no positive charge in either resonance contributor, so it is not the electrophilic site; bonding there would also give C3 five bonds.

q: The allyl vinyl ether below is heated. The curved arrows show its [3,3]-sigmatropic (Claisen) rearrangement. What is the product?
h: Number the six atoms C1=C2–O3–C4–C5=C6. Which σ bond breaks, which forms, and where do the π bonds end up?
w: In the Claisen rearrangement the O3–C4 σ bond breaks and a new C1–C6 σ bond forms, while the π bonds shift to C2=O3 and C4=C5. The vinyl end (C1) bonds to the carbon that carries the CH3 (C6), so the methyl ends up next to the new bond and the CH=CH2 group is terminal. The product is 3-methylpent-4-enal, a γ,δ-unsaturated aldehyde (one new stereocenter, formed as a racemate).
x: Hex-4-enal would need C1 to bond to C4, the carbon that was attached to oxygen. In a [3,3] shift the new bond forms between the two ends of the six-atom chain, C1 and C6.
This keeps the C–O–C ether and only moves the allyl unit along oxygen, a [1,3] shift. The Claisen breaks the O–C(allyl) bond and makes a C–C bond.
The arrows form C2=O3 directly, giving an aldehyde, not an enol. An enol would need the π bond at C1=C2, but C1 becomes sp<sup>3</sup> when it forms the new σ bond.

q: (Butan-2-yl)trimethylammonium hydroxide is heated (Hofmann elimination). Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the E2 step that gives the major alkene?
h: The leaving group, N(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>, is large and leaves poorly, so the transition state has carbanion character. Which β hydrogens are most acidic and most accessible?
w: Hofmann elimination follows the Hofmann rule: the base removes a proton from the least substituted β carbon (the CH3). Hydroxide takes that H, the C–H electrons form the C=C, and the C–N bond breaks to release trimethylamine. Three arrows give 1-butene as the major alkene. The bulky NMe3+ group and the carbanion-like transition state favor removing the more accessible, less hindered primary hydrogens.
x: Removing an H from the CH<sub>2</sub> gives 2-butene, the Zaitsev product. With a trialkylammonium leaving group, the less substituted alkene is the major product.
This is S<sub>N</sub>2 at the secondary carbon bearing nitrogen. That carbon is hindered by the bulky NMe<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group, and on heating, E2 is the main pathway.
The C–N bond does not break, so the carbon bearing nitrogen would have five bonds once the C=C forms. Trimethylamine must leave in the same E2 step.

q: When aniline is treated with NaNO<sub>2</sub> and HCl at 0 °C, the first bond to nitrogen of the nitrosonium ion (NO<sup>+</sup>) forms. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: The amine is the nucleophile. Which atom of NO<sup>+</sup> is the electrophilic one, and what must give way when it gains a bond?
w: The amine nitrogen's lone pair attacks the nitrogen of NO+, and one N≡O π bond moves onto oxygen, so the nitroso nitrogen keeps an octet and oxygen becomes neutral. The product is an N-nitrosoanilinium ion (Ar–NH2+–N=O), which loses H+, tautomerizes, and loses water to give the arenediazonium ion, Ar–N≡N+.
x: This bonds the amine to oxygen. The N–N bond is what the diazonium ion needs, and the nitrogen end of NO<sup>+</sup> is the electrophilic site.
The new N–N bond forms but the N≡O π bond does not move, so the nitroso nitrogen would have 10 electrons.
This arrow starts at oxygen and goes to the amine, so the electrophile would be giving electrons to the nucleophile, the reverse of the real flow.

q: N-Methylacetamide is heated in aqueous HCl. The arrows show the tetrahedral intermediate (protonated on nitrogen) expelling methylamine. Why does the overall hydrolysis go essentially to completion instead of reaching an equilibrium mixture?
c: The expelled methylamine is protonated to CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, which has no lone pair to attack the carboxylic acid again.
Methylamine is a better leaving group than water, so the tetrahedral intermediate always expels it instead of water.
Water is a stronger nucleophile than methylamine, so it outcompetes methylamine for the protonated carboxylic acid.
Methylamine boils at −6 °C and escapes from the hot solution as a gas, which pulls the reaction forward.
h: What is the pK<sub>a</sub> of CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, and what form will methylamine take in strong aqueous acid?
w: In the drawn step, an O lone pair forms C=O+ and the C–N bond breaks, releasing CH3NH2. In aqueous HCl the amine (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 10.6) is converted completely to CH3NH3+, which has no lone pair and cannot add back to the carboxylic acid. Removing the nucleophile this way makes acid hydrolysis of amides effectively irreversible and consumes one equivalent of acid.
x: Leaving-group ability explains which group leaves from the intermediate, but not why the products do not recombine. It is protonation of the amine that prevents the reverse reaction.
Amines are stronger nucleophiles than water. The reverse reaction is shut off because the amine is protonated, not because water wins a competition.
In aqueous HCl, methylamine is present as the nonvolatile salt CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup>, so it does not boil off; the acid traps it in solution.

q: Dimethylamine reacts with acetyl chloride to give N,N-dimethylacetamide. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the first step, formation of the tetrahedral intermediate?
h: Nucleophilic acyl substitution is addition first, then elimination. In the addition step, which bond gives way so the carbonyl carbon keeps four bonds?
w: The amine's lone pair attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π bond moves onto oxygen. Two arrows: N lone pair → C, and C=O π bond → O, giving a tetrahedral intermediate with O− and N+. In the next step, the C=O re-forms and chloride is expelled, and a second equivalent of amine (or another base) removes the N–H proton.
x: This is a one-step S<sub>N</sub>2-style displacement of chloride. Substitution at a carbonyl carbon goes through the tetrahedral intermediate: the π bond, not the C–Cl bond, breaks first.
The amine attacks the carbonyl oxygen, the electron-rich end of the C=O. The electrophilic atom is the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
The amine bonds to the carbonyl carbon but no bond breaks, so that carbon would have five bonds. The C=O π electrons must move onto oxygen.

q: Which compounds are converted essentially completely to their conjugate bases by one equivalent of aqueous NaOH? (pK<sub>a</sub> of H<sub>2</sub>O = 15.7)
h: Compare each O–H pK<sub>a</sub> with 15.7. The equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid.
w: Hydroxide removes a proton completely when the acid is much stronger than water (pKa well below 15.7). I, 4-nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 7.2): true; the phenoxide is stabilized by resonance into the ring and onto the para nitro group. II, cyclohexanol (pKa ≈ 16–18): false; an alkoxide has no resonance stabilization, so Keq with hydroxide is about 1 or less and most of the alcohol stays protonated. III, 4-methoxyphenol (pKa ≈ 10.2): true; the electron-donating OCH3 makes it slightly weaker than phenol, but it is still about 105 times stronger than water, so Keq ≈ 105.5. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the methoxy group only slightly weakens a phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10), which is still far more acidic than water.
This misjudges I: the nitro group makes the phenol more acidic, not less, so 4-nitrophenol is deprotonated even more completely.
This misjudges II: a simple alcohol has pK<sub>a</sub> near or above that of water, so NaOH does not convert it fully to the alkoxide.

q:
(R)-Octan-2-ol (shown) is treated separately with the reagents below. Which statements about the products are correct?
I. TsCl, pyridine gives the tosylate with the (R) configuration.
II. PBr3 gives (R)-2-bromooctane.
III. SOCl2, pyridine gives (S)-2-chlorooctane.
h: Ask, for each reagent, whether a bond to the stereocenter is broken. If it is, how does the halide arrive?
w: I: true. Tosylation forms the O–S bond; the C–O bond to the stereocenter is untouched, so the configuration is retained, and OTs (like OH) is the top-priority group, so the label stays (R). II: false. PBr3 turns OH into a good leaving group (–OPBr2) that bromide displaces by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-2-bromooctane. III: true. With pyridine, SOCl2 forms a chlorosulfite that chloride displaces by SN2, again with inversion, giving (S)-2-chlorooctane. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: in pyridine, chloride attacks the chlorosulfite from the back side, so the chloride is inverted to (S).
This misjudges I: tosylation does not touch the C–O bond, so the tosylate keeps the (R) configuration.
This misjudges II: PBr3 converts a 2° alcohol by back-side SN2 attack, so the bromide is (S), not (R).

q:
Which reagents convert 3-phenylpropan-1-ol (shown) mainly to 3-phenylpropanal?
I. Na2Cr2O7, H2SO4, H2O
II. PCC, CH2Cl2
III. 1. (COCl)2, DMSO, −78 °C  2. Et3N
h: Which oxidants work without water? Water lets an aldehyde form a hydrate, which can be oxidized again.
w: A 1° alcohol stops at the aldehyde only under anhydrous conditions. I: false. Aqueous chromic acid forms the aldehyde, which hydrates and is oxidized further to 3-phenylpropanoic acid. II: true. PCC in CH2Cl2 is anhydrous, so the oxidation stops at the aldehyde. III: true. The Swern oxidation (activated DMSO, then Et3N) is also anhydrous and gives the aldehyde. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the Swern oxidation stops at the aldehyde just as PCC does.
This misjudges II: PCC in dichloromethane is the classic reagent for stopping a 1° alcohol at the aldehyde.
This misjudges I: aqueous dichromate over-oxidizes a 1° alcohol to the carboxylic acid through the aldehyde hydrate.

q:
Which combinations give 2-phenylbutan-2-ol (shown) after H3O+ workup?
I. methyl benzoate + excess CH3CH2MgBr
II. butan-2-one + C6H5MgBr
III. ethyl phenylacetate (C6H5CH2CO2Et) + excess CH3MgBr
h: Disconnect the target at the carbinol carbon. An ester plus excess Grignard puts two identical groups on that carbon.
w: The carbinol carbon of the target carries three different groups: CH3, CH2CH3 and C6H5. I: false. An ester adds two equivalents of the Grignard, so the carbinol carbon gets two ethyl groups plus the phenyl: 3-phenylpentan-3-ol. II: true. Phenyl adds to the ketone carbon of butan-2-one, which already holds CH3 and C2H5. III: false. Two methyls add to the ester carbon, which is bonded to a CH2Ph group, giving 2-methyl-1-phenylpropan-2-ol (a benzyl, not a phenyl, on the carbinol carbon). Answer: II only.
x: This misjudges I: excess ethyl Grignard adds twice to the ester, so the product has two ethyl groups and no methyl.
This misjudges III: the ester carbon of ethyl phenylacetate carries CH<sub>2</sub>Ph, so the product has a benzyl group and two methyls, not phenyl, methyl and ethyl.
This rejects the one correct route: phenyl Grignard adding to butan-2-one gives exactly the three groups the target needs.

q: Which ethers can be prepared in good yield by a Williamson ether synthesis, using the best choice of alkoxide and alkyl halide?
h: The Williamson step is S<sub>N</sub>2. For each ether, is there a disconnection that puts a methyl or primary carbon on the halide side?
w: The alkyl halide must be methyl or primary; a 2° or 3° halide with a strong alkoxide base mostly eliminates. I: false. Both sides are tertiary, so either route needs a 3° halide, which gives isobutylene by E2. II: false. Using cyclohexyl bromide (2°) with bulky tert-butoxide gives mainly cyclohexene by E2; the other route needs a 3° halide. III: true. tert-Butoxide + CH3I works because methyl iodide cannot eliminate. Answer: III only.
x: This misjudges II: the only available halide partners are a 2° halide (attacked by a bulky base, so E2) or a 3° halide (E2), so the yield is poor.
This misjudges I: di-tert-butyl ether would need a tertiary halide, which undergoes E2 with an alkoxide instead of S<sub>N</sub>2.
This misjudges I and II: each of them needs S<sub>N</sub>2 at a hindered (2° or 3°) carbon, where elimination wins.

q:
Consider the ring opening of 2,2-dimethyloxirane (shown). Which statements are correct?
I. With NaOCH3 in CH3OH, methoxide attacks the CH2 carbon of the ring.
II. With CH3OH and a catalytic amount of H2SO4, the major product is 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol.
III. Both conditions give the same constitutional isomer as the major product.
h: Under base the nucleophile does S<sub>N</sub>2 at the less hindered carbon. Under acid, which carbon of the protonated epoxide carries more positive charge?
w: I: true. A strong nucleophile opens an epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered carbon, the CH2, giving 1-methoxy-2-methylpropan-2-ol. II: true. In acid the protonated epoxide has much of its positive charge on the tertiary carbon (SN1-like transition state), so methanol attacks there, giving 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol. III: false. Because the two conditions attack different carbons, they give different constitutional isomers. Answer: I and II only.
x: This misjudges II: under acid catalysis the weak nucleophile attacks the more substituted carbon, so the OCH<sub>3</sub> ends up on the tertiary carbon, which is exactly the product named.
This misjudges I: basic (S<sub>N</sub>2) opening is controlled by sterics, so methoxide attacks the unhindered CH<sub>2</sub>.
This misjudges III: base and acid give opposite regiochemistry here, so the products are constitutional isomers, not the same compound.

q:
Ethoxybenzene (shown) is heated with excess concentrated HI. Which statements are correct?
I. Iodobenzene is one of the products.
II. Phenol is one of the products.
III. Iodide attacks the ethyl CH2 carbon of the protonated ether in an SN2 step.
h: After the oxygen is protonated, which carbon can iodide reach by back-side attack: the sp<sup>3</sup> ethyl carbon or the sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon?
w: HI protonates the ether oxygen, and iodide then attacks a carbon bonded to it. I: false. SN2 at an sp2 aromatic carbon is impossible (no back-side approach), and an aryl cation is far too unstable for SN1, so the ring C–O bond survives; phenol is not converted to iodobenzene even with excess HI. II: true. The leaving group is phenol. III: true. Iodide attacks the unhindered primary ethyl carbon, giving iodoethane. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the C–O bond that breaks is the ethyl one, by S<sub>N</sub>2 attack of iodide on the primary carbon.
This misjudges II: once iodide takes the ethyl group, the oxygen leaves still bonded to the ring as phenol.
This misjudges I: neither S<sub>N</sub>2 nor S<sub>N</sub>1 occurs at an aromatic carbon, so iodobenzene does not form.

q: Which dienes react with maleic anhydride in a Diels–Alder reaction?
h: Each diene here is held in one conformation by its ring. Is the conformation about the central single bond s-cis or s-trans?
w: A diene must be in the s-cis conformation, with C1 and C4 on the same side of the C2–C3 bond, to react. I: false. In 3-methylenecyclohexene the central bond lies in the ring, and the ring holds the exocyclic CH2 and the ring C=C on opposite sides: the diene is locked s-trans and cannot react. II: true. In 1,2-dimethylenecyclohexane both CH2 termini point the same way: locked s-cis. III: true. Cyclohexa-1,3-diene is locked s-cis by the ring. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the ring of cyclohexa-1,3-diene holds both double bonds s-cis, so it is a good Diels–Alder diene.
This misjudges II: both exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub> groups of 1,2-dimethylenecyclohexane point the same way, which is the s-cis geometry.
This misjudges I: 3-methylenecyclohexene is conjugated but locked s-trans, so its ends can never reach the dienophile together.

q: Rank compounds I–III by λ<sub>max</sub> in the UV spectrum, from shortest to longest wavelength.
h: Count the double bonds that are conjugated with each other in each compound.
w: Each added conjugated C=C narrows the HOMO–LUMO gap and moves λmax to longer wavelength. II, cyclohexa-1,4-diene, has two isolated C=C bonds (an sp3 CH2 separates them), so it absorbs below 200 nm like a simple alkene. I, cyclohexa-1,3-diene, is a conjugated diene (about 256 nm). III, octa-1,3,5,7-tetraene, has four conjugated C=C bonds and absorbs longest (near 300 nm). Order: II < I < III.
x: This puts the 1,3-diene below the 1,4-diene; the 1,4-isomer's double bonds are not conjugated, so it absorbs at shorter wavelength.
This places the tetraene below the diene; four conjugated double bonds absorb at longer wavelength than two.
This is the reverse order; longer conjugation means a longer λ<sub>max</sub>, not a shorter one.

q:
Buta-1,3-diene (shown) reacts with one equivalent of HBr. Which statements are correct?
I. At −80 °C, 3-bromobut-1-ene (the 1,2-adduct) is the major product.
II. At 40 °C, 1-bromobut-2-ene (the 1,4-adduct) is the major product because it has the more substituted, more stable C=C.
III. Both adducts form from the same resonance-stabilized allylic cation.
h: Protonate a terminal carbon and draw the resulting cation's resonance forms. Then think kinetic vs thermodynamic control.
w: I: true. At low temperature the reaction is under kinetic control; bromide bonds fastest to C2, which carries more of the positive charge (a 2° allylic carbon) and is closest to the bromide in the ion pair. II: true. At higher temperature the additions are reversible, so the more stable product wins: the 1,4-adduct has a disubstituted C=C, while the 1,2-adduct has a monosubstituted one. III: true. Protonation at C1 gives one allylic cation with positive charge shared by C2 and C4; attack at C2 gives the 1,2-adduct and attack at C4 the 1,4-adduct. Answer: I, II, and III.
x: This misjudges III: there are not two separate cations; one allylic cation with two resonance forms leads to both products.
This misjudges II: under equilibrating (warm) conditions the 1,4-adduct dominates because of its more substituted double bond.
This misjudges I: at −80 °C the faster-forming 1,2-adduct is the major product.

q:
(2E,4Z,6E)-Octa-2,4,6-triene (shown) undergoes 6π electrocyclic ring closure. Which statements are correct?
I. The thermal ring closure is disrotatory.
II. The thermal product is trans-5,6-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene.
III. The photochemical ring closure is conrotatory.
h: Find the HOMO of a hexatriene in the ground state (ψ<sub>3</sub>) and in the excited state (ψ<sub>4</sub>), and look at the phases of the end lobes.
w: I: true. A 6π (4n + 2) system closes thermally from its ground-state HOMO, ψ3, whose terminal lobes have the same phase on the same face, so the ends rotate disrotatory. II: false. With E,Z,E geometry both terminal methyls point outward; disrotatory closure turns both outward groups the same way, putting them on the same face: cis-5,6-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene. III: true. Light promotes an electron to ψ4, whose terminal lobes are out of phase, so the photochemical closure is conrotatory (and would give the trans product). Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: in the excited state the HOMO is ψ<sub>4</sub>, which has opposite end-lobe symmetry, so the photochemical closure is conrotatory.
This misjudges I: a thermal 6π electrocyclization is disrotatory, not conrotatory (conrotatory is the thermal mode for 4π systems).
This misjudges II: disrotatory closure of the E,Z,E triene gives the cis-dimethyl ring; the trans isomer is the photochemical product.

q: Which of these ions are aromatic? (Assume each ring is planar.)
h: Count π electrons: each C=C gives 2, a carbocation's empty p orbital gives 0, and a carbanion's lone pair gives 2. Then apply 4n + 2.
w: Each ring is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated, so the π-electron count decides. I: cyclopropenyl cation, one C=C and an empty p orbital: 2 π electrons (4n + 2, n = 0), aromatic. II: cyclopentadienyl cation, two C=C and an empty p orbital: 4 π electrons (4n), antiaromatic. III: cycloheptatrienyl anion, three C=C and a lone pair: 8 π electrons (4n), antiaromatic. Answer: I only.
x: This misjudges II: the cyclopentadienyl cation has 4 π electrons, a 4n count, so it is antiaromatic. (The cyclopentadienyl anion, with 6, is the aromatic one.)
This misjudges III: the cycloheptatrienyl anion has 8 π electrons, a 4n count. (The cation, tropylium, with 6, is the aromatic one.)
Only the cyclopropenyl cation has a 4n + 2 count; the other two ions have 4 and 8 π electrons and are antiaromatic.

q: Which of these heterocycles are aromatic?
h: First check that every ring atom has a p orbital. Then count π electrons, using one lone pair from the heteroatom if it is needed.
w: I: false. 4H-Pyran has an sp3 CH2 in the ring, which breaks the cyclic conjugation, so it is not aromatic. II: false. 1H-Azepine has three C=C bonds plus the N lone pair, 8 π electrons (4n); a planar ring would be antiaromatic, so the ring puckers and is nonaromatic. III: true. Furan has two C=C bonds plus one oxygen lone pair in a p orbital, 6 π electrons in a planar ring. Answer: III only.
x: This misjudges II: using the nitrogen lone pair, azepine has 8 π electrons, a 4n count, so it cannot be aromatic.
This misjudges I: the sp3 CH2 of 4H-pyran has no p orbital, so the ring is not fully conjugated.
This misjudges I and II: one has an sp<sup>3</sup> ring carbon and the other has 8 π electrons, so only furan meets Hückel's rule.

q: Rank these heterocycles in order of increasing basicity (weakest base first).
h: For each, find a lone pair that is NOT part of the aromatic sextet. Then ask whether the protonated form gains extra stabilization.
w: I, pyrrole: its only nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet, so protonation (which occurs at carbon) destroys aromaticity; pKa of the conjugate acid ≈ −4. Weakest. III, pyridine: the lone pair sits in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, outside the π system, so it is available; pKaH ≈ 5.2. II, imidazole: the pyridine-like N3 has an available sp2 lone pair, and the cation formed is symmetric, with the positive charge shared equally by both nitrogens through resonance; pKaH ≈ 7.0. Strongest. Order: I < III < II.
x: This puts pyridine above imidazole; the imidazolium ion is stabilized by resonance over two nitrogens, so imidazole is the stronger base by about 2 pK<sub>a</sub> units.
This puts pyrrole above pyridine; pyrrole's lone pair belongs to the aromatic sextet, so it is a far weaker base than pyridine.
This is the reverse order; pyrrole, with no available lone pair, is the weakest base, not the strongest.

q: Which of these ions are aromatic? (Assume each ring is planar.)
h: Count π electrons in each planar ring and test 4n + 2. A carbanion lone pair counts 2; a carbocation counts 0.
w: I: true. The cyclooctatetraene dianion has three C=C bonds plus two carbanion lone pairs, 10 π electrons (n = 2): aromatic, and it is in fact planar. II: true. The cyclononatetraenyl anion has four C=C bonds plus one lone pair, 10 π electrons: aromatic. III: false. The cyclononatetraenyl cation has four C=C bonds and an empty p orbital, 8 π electrons (4n): antiaromatic. Answer: I and II only.
x: This misjudges II: four C=C bonds plus the carbanion lone pair give 10 π electrons, a 4n + 2 count.
This misjudges I: the two negative charges add two lone pairs to the six π electrons of the C=C bonds, giving 10, which is aromatic.
This misjudges III: the cation has only 8 π electrons because the cationic carbon contributes an empty p orbital.

q:
Consider Birch reduction (Na, NH3(l), CH3CH2OH). Which statements are correct?
I. Benzene gives cyclohexa-1,4-diene.
II. Anisole (shown first) gives a diene in which the OCH3 group is on an sp3 carbon.
III. Benzoic acid (shown second) gives a diene in which the CO2H group is on an sp3 carbon.
h: Birch reduction adds electrons to the ring. Does an electron-donating group sit on a reduced carbon or stay on a C=C? What about an electron-withdrawing group?
w: I: true. Birch reduction adds two electrons and two protons to para positions, leaving the nonconjugated cyclohexa-1,4-diene. II: false. An electron-donating group avoids the carbons that pick up negative charge, so it stays on a ring double bond: anisole gives 1-methoxycyclohexa-1,4-diene, with OCH3 on an sp2 carbon. III: true. An electron-withdrawing group stabilizes the negative charge, so its carbon is reduced: benzoic acid gives cyclohexa-2,5-diene-1-carboxylic acid, with CO2H on the sp3 carbon. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: an electron-withdrawing group ends up on a reduced (sp<sup>3</sup>) carbon, because it stabilizes the radical anion and carbanion there.
This misjudges I: Birch reduction of benzene gives the 1,4-diene, not a conjugated diene and not cyclohexane.
This misjudges II: an electron-donating group like OCH<sub>3</sub> stays on a C=C after Birch reduction.

q: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, which of these compounds direct the incoming electrophile mainly to the ortho and para positions?
h: Is the atom bonded to the ring carrying a lone pair it can donate by resonance into the arenium ion?
w: An o/p director has an atom with a lone pair (or an alkyl group) attached to the ring, which stabilizes the ortho and para arenium ions. I: false. CF3 has no lone pair on the attached carbon and withdraws strongly by induction, so it is a deactivating meta director. II: true. Chlorine deactivates by induction but donates a lone pair by resonance, so it directs o/p. III: true. In phenyl acetate the ring is bonded to the ester oxygen, whose lone pair donates into the ring; it is a moderately activating o/p director (unlike methyl benzoate, where the carbonyl carbon is attached). Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the ring carbon of phenyl acetate is bonded to an oxygen with lone pairs, so the group is o/p directing, not meta.
This misjudges II: halogens deactivate the ring yet still direct o/p through lone-pair resonance.
This misjudges I: the CF<sub>3</sub> group has no lone pair to donate and pulls electron density away, so it directs meta.

q: Rank these compounds by rate of nitration with HNO3/H2SO4, from slowest to fastest.
h: Each nitro group strongly withdraws electron density. How does a halogen compare?
w: The rate of EAS falls as the ring loses electron density. I, 1,3-dinitrobenzene, carries two strongly deactivating nitro groups and is slowest. II, nitrobenzene, has one. III, fluorobenzene, is only weakly deactivated (F withdraws by induction but donates a lone pair by resonance) and reacts nearly as fast as benzene. Order: I < II < III.
x: This puts one nitro group below two; each nitro group deactivates further, so the dinitro compound is slowest.
This is the reverse order; nitro groups slow EAS, so the dinitro compound is slowest, not fastest.
This puts fluorobenzene below nitrobenzene; a halogen deactivates only weakly, while a nitro group deactivates strongly.

q:
Which statements about Friedel–Crafts reactions are correct?
I. Benzene with 1-chloropropane and AlCl3 gives mainly isopropylbenzene.
II. Friedel–Crafts acylation stops after one acyl group is added because the aryl ketone product is deactivated.
III. Nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts alkylation or acylation.
h: Think about what the electrophile is in each reaction, whether it can rearrange, and how reactive the ring must be.
w: I: true. The 1° chloride–AlCl3 complex undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable 2° (isopropyl) carbocation, so isopropylbenzene is the main product (the classic rearrangement problem of alkylation). II: true. The acyl group withdraws electron density by resonance, so the product ring is less reactive than benzene and does not react again; this is why acylation avoids the polysubstitution seen in alkylation. III: true. Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on rings more deactivated than a halobenzene, and nitrobenzene is so unreactive it is even used as a solvent for them. Answer: I, II, and III.
x: This misjudges III: a strongly deactivated ring such as nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions at all.
This misjudges I: the primary propyl electrophile rearranges by a hydride shift, so isopropylbenzene, not propylbenzene, is the main product.
This misjudges II: the ketone product is deactivated, which is exactly why acylation, unlike alkylation, stops after one substitution.

q:
Which sequences, starting from benzene, give 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene (shown) as the major product?
I. 1. HNO3, H2SO4  2. Br2, FeBr3
II. 1. Br2, FeBr3  2. HNO3, H2SO4
III. 1. HNO3, H2SO4  2. NBS, hν
h: The group already on the ring decides where the second group goes. Which group must be on first to direct meta?
w: The two groups are meta, so the first group must be a meta director. I: true. Nitrobenzene is brominated (Br2/FeBr3) at the meta position. II: false. Bromine is an o/p director, so nitrating bromobenzene gives mainly 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene (with some ortho), not the meta isomer. III: false. NBS with light brominates benzylic or allylic C–H bonds by a radical path; nitrobenzene has no such position and NBS does not perform ring EAS here. Answer: I only.
x: This misjudges II: bromine directs o/p, so the nitro group goes para or ortho to it, not meta.
This misjudges III: NBS/hν is a radical benzylic bromination, and nitrobenzene has no benzylic hydrogens.
This reverses the logic: brominating first gives the wrong (o/p) pattern, while nitrating first gives the meta product.

q: Which aryl halides react readily with NaOCH<sub>3</sub> in CH<sub>3</sub>OH (mild heating) by nucleophilic aromatic substitution (addition–elimination)?
h: Add methoxide to the carbon bearing the halogen and draw the anion. Can the negative charge reach the oxygens of a nitro group?
w: SNAr goes through an anionic (Meisenheimer) intermediate whose charge sits ortho and para to the attacked carbon, so a nitro group must be ortho or para to the leaving group. I: false. The nitro group is meta to Cl, so it cannot delocalize the charge by resonance. II: true. The nitro group is para to F; fluoride is an excellent SNAr leaving group because its electronegativity speeds the rate-determining addition step. III: true. Nitro groups ortho and para to Cl both stabilize the intermediate. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: two nitro groups ortho and para to the chlorine make 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene highly reactive in S<sub>N</sub>Ar.
This misjudges II: a para nitro group activates the ring, and fluoride is the best halide leaving group in S<sub>N</sub>Ar, not the worst.
This misjudges I: a meta nitro group cannot accept the negative charge by resonance, so the ring is not activated.

q: Rank these carbonyl compounds by the equilibrium constant for hydrate formation in water, from smallest to largest.
h: Hydration is favored when the C=O carbon is very electron-poor and when converting it to sp<sup>3</sup> costs little steric strain.
w: Alkyl groups donate electron density to the carbonyl carbon and crowd the sp3 hydrate, so they shift the equilibrium toward the carbonyl. I, acetone, has two alkyl groups: K ≈ 10−3, smallest. III, propanal, has only one alkyl group and an H: K ≈ 1. II, 1,1,1-trifluoroacetone, is a ketone, but the strongly electron-withdrawing CF3 group destabilizes the C=O and favors the hydrate: K well above 1, largest. Order: I < III < II.
x: This puts the aldehyde below the ketone acetone; an aldehyde has one fewer donating alkyl group and less steric crowding, so it hydrates more.
This puts the trifluoromethyl ketone below the aldehyde; the CF<sub>3</sub> group's strong inductive withdrawal outweighs the extra substituent and drives hydration.
This is the reverse order; acetone has the least electrophilic carbonyl and the smallest hydration constant.

q:
Which reagents reduce the ketone carbonyl of methyl 4-acetylbenzoate (shown) to a CH–OH group while leaving the ester unchanged?
I. 1. LiAlH4, ether  2. H3O+
II. NaBH4, CH3OH, 0 °C
III. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
h: Rank the reagents by hydride strength, and remember that one of these reagents removes the oxygen completely.
w: I: false. LiAlH4 is strong enough to reduce both carbonyls, so the ester also becomes a CH2OH group. II: true. NaBH4 reduces ketones and aldehydes readily but esters only very slowly, so it gives methyl 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoate. III: false. The Clemmensen reduction converts the ketone C=O all the way to CH2 (an ethyl group), not to an alcohol. Answer: II only.
x: This misjudges I: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> also reduces the ester to a primary alcohol, so it is not selective.
This misjudges III: Zn(Hg)/HCl removes the carbonyl oxygen entirely, giving CH<sub>2</sub>, not CH–OH.
This misjudges I and III: one reduces the ester as well, and the other deoxygenates the ketone to CH<sub>2</sub>.

q:
Cyclohexanone (shown) is treated with each reagent below and a catalytic amount of acid, with removal of water. Which give a product containing a C=N bond?
I. CH3NH2
II. (CH3)2NH
III. NH2OH
h: After the iminium ion forms, does the nitrogen still have an H it can lose?
w: A primary amine (or another NH2 compound) condenses with a ketone to an iminium ion that loses its N–H proton to give a neutral C=N. I: true. Methylamine gives the N-methyl imine. II: false. Dimethylamine is secondary; its iminium ion has no N–H to lose, so it loses an α C–H instead and forms an enamine (C=C–N), with no C=N in the neutral product. III: true. Hydroxylamine has an NH2 group and gives an oxime (C=N–OH). Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: hydroxylamine condenses through its NH<sub>2</sub> group to give an oxime, which contains a C=N bond.
This misjudges I: a primary amine such as methylamine gives an imine, the standard C=N product.
This misjudges II: a secondary amine cannot form a neutral C=N, so it gives an enamine instead.

q:
Which Wittig combinations give methylenecyclohexane (shown)?
I. cyclohexanone + Ph3P=CH2
II. formaldehyde + the ylide Ph3P=C(CH2)5 (cyclohexylidene)
III. cyclohexanecarbaldehyde + Ph3P=CH2
h: The Wittig reaction joins the carbonyl carbon and the ylide carbon with a C=C. Split the target's C=C into those two halves.
w: Cutting the target's C=C gives two halves: a CH2 and a ring carbon. Either half can come from the carbonyl and the other from the ylide. I: true. Cyclohexanone supplies the ring carbon and the methylene ylide supplies CH2. II: true. Formaldehyde supplies CH2 and the cyclohexylidene ylide supplies the ring carbon (a less common but valid route). III: false. The aldehyde carbon is outside the ring, so the new C=C is too: the product is vinylcyclohexane, an isomer of the target. Answer: I and II only.
x: This misjudges II: reversing the roles (formaldehyde plus the ring ylide) forms the same C=C bond.
This misjudges I: cyclohexanone with Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub> is the textbook route to methylenecyclohexane.
This misjudges III: the carbonyl carbon of cyclohexanecarbaldehyde is exocyclic, so the product is vinylcyclohexane, not methylenecyclohexane.

q: Rank these acyl compounds from least to most reactive toward hydrolysis by aqueous NaOH (nucleophilic acyl substitution).
h: All three are acetyl derivatives, so compare the leaving groups: the weaker the conjugate base that leaves (the stronger its conjugate acid), the more reactive the derivative.
w: Reactivity in nucleophilic acyl substitution follows leaving-group ability and how much the group donates into the C=O. III < II < I. III (N,N-dimethylacetamide) is least reactive: nitrogen donates its lone pair strongly into the carbonyl, and (CH3)2N− (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 38) is a terrible leaving group. II (ethyl acetate) is in the middle: ethoxide (pKa of ethanol ≈ 16) leaves reasonably well. I (phenyl acetate) is most reactive: phenoxide is resonance-stabilized (pKa of phenol ≈ 10), and the oxygen lone pair is partly delocalized into the ring, so it donates less to the C=O. Aryl esters are therefore more reactive than alkyl esters.
x: This puts the ester above the amide correctly but ranks ethyl acetate below the amide. Amides are the least reactive derivatives because N donates strongly and amide ion is a very poor leaving group.

This makes the phenyl ester less reactive than the ethyl ester. Phenoxide (from phenol, pK<sub>a</sub> 10) is a much better leaving group than ethoxide (pK<sub>a</sub> 16), so phenyl acetate is the more reactive ester.

This reverses the whole ladder. The amide is the least reactive and the phenyl ester the most reactive, because leaving-group ability runs PhO<sup>−</sup> > EtO<sup>−</sup> > R<sub>2</sub>N<sup>−</sup>.

q:
Which reagents, each followed by aqueous acid workup, convert ethyl benzoate into a tertiary alcohol?
I. excess C6H5MgBr
II. excess LiAlH4
III. excess CH3Li
h: An ester takes two equivalents of a carbon nucleophile. What kind of alcohol forms when the two new groups are carbon groups versus hydrogens?
w: An ester reacts twice with strong nucleophiles: the first addition expels ethoxide to give a ketone (or aldehyde), which is more reactive than the ester and adds a second equivalent. I is true: PhMgBr adds two phenyl groups, giving triphenylmethanol, a 3° alcohol. II is false: LiAlH4 delivers two hydrides, so the carbinol carbon gets two H and the product is benzyl alcohol, a 1° alcohol. III is true: CH3Li, like a Grignard reagent, adds twice to give 2-phenylpropan-2-ol, a 3° alcohol. The answer is I and III only.
x: This leaves out III. Organolithium reagents add to esters just as Grignard reagents do (twice), so CH<sub>3</sub>Li also gives a 3° alcohol.

This counts II as giving a 3° alcohol and leaves out I. LiAlH<sub>4</sub> adds two hydrogens, so the product is the 1° alcohol PhCH<sub>2</sub>OH, while PhMgBr adds two carbon groups and does give a 3° alcohol.
