This includes II. Hydride reduction of an ester puts two H on the former carbonyl carbon, giving a 1° alcohol, not a 3° one.

q: Rank these carboxylic acids from lowest to highest pKa.
h: Lowest pK<sub>a</sub> = strongest acid. How does the electron-withdrawing effect of Cl change as it moves farther from the carboxylate?
w: A chlorine stabilizes the carboxylate anion by induction, and the effect falls off quickly with the number of bonds between Cl and the CO2−. In I (2-chlorobutanoic acid) the Cl is on the α-carbon, so it is the strongest acid (pKa ≈ 2.9). In II (3-chlorobutanoic acid) the Cl is one carbon farther, so the effect is weaker (pKa ≈ 4.0). III (butanoic acid) has no withdrawing group (pKa ≈ 4.8). Lowest to highest pKa: I < II < III.
x: This puts the β-chloro acid ahead of the α-chloro acid. Induction weakens with distance, so Cl on the α-carbon (I) withdraws more and gives the lower pK<sub>a</sub>.
This ranks the acids from highest to lowest pK<sub>a</sub>, the reverse of what was asked.
This makes the β-chloro acid weaker than butanoic acid. Even one carbon farther away, the Cl still withdraws some electron density and lowers the pK<sub>a</sub> below 4.8.

q:
Which reactions give N-methylbenzamide as the main organic product?
I. benzoyl chloride + 2 equiv CH3NH2, 0 °C
II. methyl benzoate + excess CH3NH2, heat
III. benzoic acid + CH3NH2 + DCC, room temperature
h: An acid and an amine alone just form a salt. What does DCC do to the acid? Can an amine displace alkoxide from an ester with heat and time?
w: I is true: an acid chloride reacts quickly with an amine; the second equivalent of CH3NH2 neutralizes the HCl formed. II is true: aminolysis of an ester is slower (methoxide is a poorer leaving group than chloride), but heating an ester with excess amine does give the amide, and the amide is downhill because it is the least reactive derivative. III is true: DCC converts the carboxylic acid into an O-acylisourea, an activated ester with a good leaving group, which the amine attacks to give the amide plus dicyclohexylurea (the same coupling used in peptide synthesis). All three work: I, II, and III.
x: This rejects II and III. Esters do undergo aminolysis on heating, and DCC is a standard way to couple an acid and an amine directly.
This rejects III, likely because an acid plus an amine alone just forms an ammonium carboxylate salt. DCC changes that by activating the acid's OH into a good leaving group.
This rejects II. Ester aminolysis is slower than acid chloride aminolysis, but with heat and excess amine it goes to the more stable amide.

q:
Which sequences convert benzonitrile into acetophenone?
I. 1. CH3MgBr, ether  2. H3O+
II. 1. H3O+, heat  2. excess CH3MgBr  3. H3O+
III. 1. DIBAL-H, −78 °C  2. H2O
h: Follow each sequence one step at a time. What does a Grignard reagent do to a carboxylic acid's O–H? What does DIBAL-H give from a nitrile?
w: I is true: CH3MgBr adds once to the C≡N to give an imine anion (a second addition does not occur on a negatively charged nitrogen species), and aqueous acid hydrolyzes the imine to the ketone, acetophenone. II is false: acid hydrolysis gives benzoic acid, and CH3MgBr is a strong base, so it just removes the acidic O–H to make a carboxylate (and methane); the carboxylate does not add Grignard reagents, and workup returns benzoic acid. III is false: DIBAL-H delivers one hydride to the nitrile, and water hydrolyzes the imine to benzaldehyde, not a methyl ketone. The answer is I only.
x: This accepts II. A Grignard reagent deprotonates a carboxylic acid instead of adding to it, and the carboxylate salt is unreactive toward further Grignard addition.
This accepts II and rejects I. Grignard addition to a nitrile followed by hydrolysis is the standard nitrile-to-ketone route, while the acid in II just quenches the Grignard reagent.
This accepts III. DIBAL-H adds hydride, not a methyl group, so the nitrile becomes an aldehyde (benzaldehyde) after workup.

q: Which of these aldehydes can act as the enolate (nucleophilic) partner in a base-catalyzed aldol reaction?
h: An enolate forms by removing a hydrogen from the α-carbon, the carbon next to C=O. Count α-hydrogens in each.
w: Forming an enolate needs at least one α-hydrogen. I (benzaldehyde): false, its α-carbon is a ring carbon with no H. II (2,2-dimethylpropanal): false, its α-carbon is quaternary (three CH3 groups), so it has no α-H even though it has nine H on β-carbons. III (2-methylpropanal): true, its α-carbon carries one H, so it can form an enolate. The answer is III only. I and II can still serve as the electrophile in a crossed aldol.
x: This counts II, but its α-carbon is quaternary; the methyl H atoms are on β-carbons and are not acidic.
This counts I, but benzaldehyde's carbonyl is attached directly to the ring; the ring C–H bonds are not α to the C=O and are not acidic.
Neither benzaldehyde nor 2,2-dimethylpropanal has an α-hydrogen, so neither can form an enolate.

q: Which compounds give a yellow precipitate of iodoform (CHI<sub>3</sub>) with I<sub>2</sub> and aqueous NaOH?
h: The haloform reaction needs a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O group, or an alcohol that I<sub>2</sub>/NaOH can oxidize to one (CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)–).
w: The iodoform test needs a methyl ketone CH3C(=O)R or a CH3CH(OH)R group that is oxidized to one. I (pentan-3-one): false, both sides are ethyl groups; α-iodination happens but no CI3 group forms. II (acetophenone): true, a methyl ketone; the CH3 is triiodinated and cleaved, giving CHI3 and benzoate. III (2-methylpropan-2-ol): false, it has methyl groups but is a 3° alcohol, which cannot be oxidized to a ketone. The answer is II only.
x: This includes pentan-3-one. Its carbonyl carries two ethyl groups, so there is no CH<sub>3</sub>C=O unit to become CI<sub>3</sub>C=O.
This includes tert-butyl alcohol. It is a 3° alcohol, so it cannot be oxidized to a methyl ketone; having CH<sub>3</sub> groups is not enough.
This picks pentan-3-one, which has no methyl ketone, and misses acetophenone, which does.

q: Rank these compounds from least to most acidic at their most acidic C–H bond.
h: Ask how well each carbonyl group stabilizes the negative charge of the enolate, and whether the charge is spread over one C=O or two.
w: II (ethyl acetate, α-H pKa ≈ 25) is least acidic: the ester's OEt donates electrons into the C=O, so the carbonyl is less able to accept the enolate's charge. I (acetone, pKa ≈ 19–20) is more acidic because a ketone C=O stabilizes the enolate better. III (pentane-2,4-dione, pKa ≈ 9) is far more acidic: the central CH2 sits between two C=O groups, so the charge is delocalized onto both oxygens. Least to most acidic: II < I < III.
x: This makes the ester α-H more acidic than the ketone α-H. The ester's alkoxy oxygen donates into the C=O by resonance, so the ester enolate is less stabilized (pK<sub>a</sub> 25 vs about 20).
This puts the β-diketone below acetone. A CH<sub>2</sub> flanked by two carbonyls is about 10 pK<sub>a</sub> units more acidic, because both C=O groups share the charge.
This is the order from most to least acidic, the reverse of what was asked.

q:
Each pair of esters is treated with NaOEt in ethanol, then acid workup. Which pairs give mainly one crossed Claisen product?
I. ethyl acetate + ethyl propanoate
II. ethyl benzoate + ethyl acetate (added slowly)
III. diethyl carbonate (excess) + ethyl phenylacetate
h: A crossed Claisen is clean only when one partner has no α-hydrogens, so it can serve only as the electrophile.
w: I is false: both esters have α-hydrogens, so each forms an enolate and each is an electrophile; two self-condensation and two crossed products form. II is true: ethyl benzoate has no α-H, so it can only accept an enolate. Adding ethyl acetate slowly to the benzoate keeps its enolate meeting mostly benzoate, giving ethyl benzoylacetate. III is true: diethyl carbonate has no α-H; the enolate of ethyl phenylacetate attacks it to give diethyl phenylmalonate, a useful one-product acylation (excess carbonate suppresses self-condensation). The answer is II and III only.
x: This rejects II. Ethyl benzoate lacks α-hydrogens, so it acts only as the electrophile; with slow addition of ethyl acetate the crossed product dominates.
This accepts I. When both esters have α-hydrogens, each can be nucleophile and electrophile, so a mixture of four β-keto esters forms.
This accepts I. Ethyl acetate and ethyl propanoate both have α-hydrogens, which gives four products, not one.

q:
Which reagents add mainly in a 1,4- (conjugate) fashion to methyl vinyl ketone (shown)?
I. CH3Li, ether, then H3O+
II. the pyrrolidine enamine of cyclohexanone, then H3O+
III. C6H5MgBr, ether, then H3O+
h: Hard, highly reactive nucleophiles attack the carbonyl carbon directly; soft, stabilized nucleophiles attack the β-carbon.
w: I is false: organolithium reagents are hard, very reactive nucleophiles and add mainly 1,2 (to the C=O carbon), giving a 3° allylic alcohol. II is true: an enamine is a soft, neutral carbon nucleophile; its α-carbon adds to the β-carbon of the enone (the Stork enamine Michael reaction), and hydrolysis gives 2-(3-oxobutyl)cyclohexanone. III is false: Grignard reagents also add mainly 1,2 to simple enones; conjugate addition needs a cuprate (R2CuLi). The answer is II only.
x: This counts CH<sub>3</sub>Li as a conjugate-addition reagent. Organolithiums are hard nucleophiles that attack the carbonyl carbon directly (1,2-addition).
This counts PhMgBr. Grignard reagents add 1,2 to α,β-unsaturated ketones; a Gilman reagent such as Ph<sub>2</sub>CuLi is what gives 1,4-addition.
This picks the organolithium, which adds 1,2, and misses the enamine, the classic Michael donor.

q: Rank these nitrogen compounds from weakest to strongest base.
h: Is the nitrogen lone pair localized on N, delocalized into a ring, or delocalized into a C=O?
w: Basicity depends on how available the nitrogen lone pair is. II (acetanilide, an amide) is the weakest: its lone pair is delocalized into the C=O (and the ring), so amides are essentially non-basic (conjugate acid pKa near 0). III (aniline, conjugate acid pKa 4.6) is weak because its lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring. I (benzylamine, pKa 9.3) is strongest: the CH2 separates the nitrogen from the ring, so its sp3 lone pair is localized, like an ordinary alkylamine. Weakest to strongest: II < III < I.
x: This makes the amide more basic than aniline. Delocalization into a C=O is stronger than into a ring, so amides are far weaker bases than anilines.
This makes benzylamine weaker than aniline. In benzylamine the CH<sub>2</sub> keeps the lone pair out of conjugation with the ring, so it behaves like an alkylamine.
This is the order from strongest to weakest, the reverse of what was asked.

q:
Which routes give benzylamine (shown) cleanly, without a mixture of over-alkylated amines?
I. benzyl bromide + 1 equiv NH3
II. 1. benzyl bromide + potassium phthalimide  2. H2NNH2, heat
III. 1. benzonitrile + LiAlH4  2. H2O
h: After NH<sub>3</sub> is alkylated once, is the product more or less nucleophilic than NH<sub>3</sub>? Which methods avoid that problem?
w: I is false: the benzylamine formed is a better nucleophile than NH3, so it competes for benzyl bromide and gives di- and tribenzylamine (and even the quaternary salt). II is true: in the Gabriel synthesis the phthalimide nitrogen is alkylated once; its N–H is gone and the imide N is not nucleophilic, so no second alkylation occurs, and hydrazine releases the free 1° amine. III is true: LiAlH4 reduces C≡N to CH2NH2, and benzonitrile has the right carbon count (C6H5–C≡N → C6H5–CH2NH2). The answer is II and III only.
x: This rejects III. Reducing a nitrile with LiAlH<sub>4</sub> gives a 1° amine with no over-alkylation, and PhC≡N gives exactly PhCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.
This accepts I. The 1° amine product is more nucleophilic than ammonia, so direct alkylation with one equivalent of NH<sub>3</sub> gives a mixture.
This accepts I and rejects II. Direct alkylation of NH<sub>3</sub> over-alkylates; the Gabriel synthesis was invented to avoid exactly that.

q:
Benzenediazonium chloride (shown) is treated separately with each reagent. Which give the product named?
I. CuCl → chlorobenzene
II. KI → iodobenzene
III. H3PO2 → phenol
h: Recall what each reagent replaces the N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> group with. Which reagent is a reducing agent that supplies hydrogen?
w: I is true: CuCl replaces N2+ with Cl (Sandmeyer reaction). II is true: iodide is reactive enough to replace N2+ without a copper catalyst, giving iodobenzene. III is false: hypophosphorous acid replaces N2+ with H, giving benzene; phenol comes from warming the diazonium salt in water (or Cu2O/Cu2+ in water). The answer is I and II only.
x: This rejects II. KI converts aryldiazonium salts into aryl iodides directly; no CuI is needed.
This rejects I and accepts III. CuCl is the Sandmeyer reagent for aryl chlorides, while H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> reduces the diazonium salt to benzene, not phenol.
This accepts III. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> replaces the diazonium group with hydrogen; phenol needs water and heat instead.

q: Rank these anilines from weakest to strongest base.
h: A para substituent that pulls electron density out of the ring makes the NH<sub>2</sub> lone pair less available; one that pushes density in does the opposite.
w: I (4-nitroaniline, conjugate acid pKa ≈ 1.0) is the weakest base: the para NO2 withdraws by induction and resonance, and the amine lone pair can delocalize all the way onto the nitro oxygens. III (aniline, pKa 4.6) is in the middle. II (4-methoxyaniline, pKa ≈ 5.3) is the strongest: the para OCH3 donates by resonance, raising the electron density at nitrogen. Weakest to strongest: I < III < II.
x: This makes 4-nitroaniline more basic than aniline. The para nitro group strongly withdraws electrons and pulls the lone pair into conjugation, so it lowers the basicity by more than 3 pK<sub>a</sub> units.
This makes methoxy a base-weakening group. Although O is electronegative, a para OCH<sub>3</sub> donates by resonance, and resonance wins here, making 4-methoxyaniline more basic than aniline.
This is the order from strongest to weakest, the reverse of what was asked.

q:
Which sequences convert cyclohexanone into 1-methylcyclohexene?
I. 1. CH3MgBr  2. H3O+  3. H2SO4, heat
II. Ph3P=CH2
III. 1. CH3MgBr  2. H3O+  3. PCC
h: Where does the C=C end up in each route: inside the ring or outside it? And what does PCC do to a 3° alcohol?
w: I is true: the Grignard reagent gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, and acid-catalyzed E1 dehydration gives the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, the trisubstituted ring alkene 1-methylcyclohexene. II is false: the Wittig reaction puts the C=C exactly where the C=O was, giving methylenecyclohexane (an exocyclic C=CH2), a constitutional isomer of the target. III is false: PCC oxidizes 1° and 2° alcohols only; the 3° alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon and is unchanged, so no alkene forms. The answer is I only.
x: This accepts II. The Wittig reagent forms the C=C at the old carbonyl carbon, giving methylenecyclohexane, not the ring alkene.
This accepts II and rejects I. Dehydrating 1-methylcyclohexanol gives the endocyclic Zaitsev alkene, which is the target; the Wittig gives the exocyclic isomer.
This accepts III. PCC is an oxidant, not a dehydrating agent, and a 3° alcohol cannot be oxidized because its carbinol carbon has no H.

q:
Which sequences prepare 4-chloroaniline (shown) from benzene as the major product? (Separate ortho/para isomers where needed.)
I. 1. HNO3, H2SO4  2. Cl2, FeCl3  3. Fe, HCl; then NaOH
II. 1. Cl2, FeCl3  2. HNO3, H2SO4  3. Fe, HCl; then NaOH
III. 1. HNO3, H2SO4  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. (CH3CO)2O  4. Cl2, FeCl3  5. NaOH, H2O, heat
h: In each route, identify which substituent is on the ring when the second group goes on, and whether it directs ortho/para or meta.
w: I is false: NO2 is a meta director, so chlorinating nitrobenzene gives 3-chloronitrobenzene, and reduction gives 3-chloroaniline. II is true: Cl is an ortho/para director (deactivating), so nitration of chlorobenzene gives mainly 4-chloronitrobenzene (separated from the ortho isomer), and Fe/HCl reduces NO2 to NH2 without touching the aryl C–Cl. III is true: aniline is made first, then protected as acetanilide; NHCOCH3 is a moderate ortho/para director whose bulk favors para, so chlorination gives mainly 4-chloroacetanilide, and base hydrolysis of the amide frees 4-chloroaniline. The answer is II and III only.
x: This rejects III. Protecting aniline as its acetamide tames the strongly activating NH<sub>2</sub> (avoiding polyhalogenation and Lewis-acid complexation) and keeps it an o/p director, so III works.
This accepts I. Nitro is a meta director, so the chlorine goes meta to it and the route ends at 3-chloroaniline.
This accepts I. Chlorinating nitrobenzene places Cl meta, so route I makes the wrong isomer.

q:
Which sequences convert ethyl 4-oxopentanoate into 5-hydroxy-5-methylhexan-2-one, as shown?
I. 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH  2. excess CH3MgBr  3. H3O+
II. 1. excess CH3MgBr  2. H3O+
III. 1. NaBH4, CH3OH  2. excess CH3MgBr  3. H3O+  4. PCC
h: The ketone is more reactive than the ester toward CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr. Each route needs some way to keep the ketone carbon from gaining a methyl group.
w: I is true: ethylene glycol/TsOH protects the ketone as an acetal, which is inert to Grignard reagents; excess CH3MgBr adds twice to the ester to give the 3° alcohol, and aqueous acid removes the acetal, restoring the ketone. II is false: with no protection the ketone also adds CH3MgBr, so the product is the diol 2,5-dimethylhexane-2,5-diol. III is true: NaBH4 reduces the ketone but not the ester, giving a 2° alcohol (it may close to the γ-lactone, which reacts with the Grignard reagent the same way); excess CH3MgBr converts the ester (or lactone) into the 3° alcohol; PCC then oxidizes the 2° alcohol back to the ketone and leaves the 3° alcohol untouched. The answer is I and III only.
x: This rejects III. Reducing the ketone to a 2° alcohol is a valid protecting strategy here, because PCC later restores the ketone and cannot oxidize the 3° alcohol.
This rejects I. An acetal is the textbook protecting group for a ketone during a Grignard reaction, and the acid workup removes it.
This accepts II. Without protection, the more reactive ketone also adds CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, and both carbonyl carbons end up as 3° alcohols.

q:
Which sequences convert benzaldehyde into 1-phenylpropan-1-one (shown)?
I. 1. CH3CH2MgBr  2. H3O+  3. PCC
II. 1. CH3CH2MgBr  2. H3O+  3. NaBH4
III. 1. H2CrO4  2. excess CH3CH2MgBr  3. H3O+
h: After the Grignard step you have a 2° alcohol. Which reagent changes it into a ketone? And what does a Grignard reagent do to a carboxylic acid?
w: I is true: ethylmagnesium bromide adds to the aldehyde to give 1-phenylpropan-1-ol, a 2° alcohol, and PCC oxidizes it to the ketone. II is false: NaBH4 is a reducing agent; it does not change the 2° alcohol, so the product stays an alcohol. III is false: H2CrO4 oxidizes benzaldehyde to benzoic acid, and the Grignard reagent only deprotonates the acid to a carboxylate, which does not react further; workup returns benzoic acid. The answer is I only.
x: This accepts II. NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces carbonyls; it cannot turn an alcohol into a ketone, which needs an oxidant such as PCC.
This accepts III. A Grignard reagent is a strong base and just removes the carboxylic acid O–H; the carboxylate does not add it to give a ketone.
This accepts III and rejects I. Grignard addition followed by PCC oxidation is the direct aldehyde-to-ketone route; the acid in III quenches the Grignard reagent.

q:
Which sugars are reducing sugars (give a positive Tollens or Benedict's test)?
I. D-fructose
II. sucrose
III. lactose
h: A reducing sugar needs a free hemiacetal or hemiketal (an anomeric carbon that can open). Also, the tests are run in base, where ketoses can tautomerize.
w: I is true: D-fructose is a ketose, but in the basic test solution it tautomerizes through an enediol to aldoses (glucose and mannose), which are oxidized; its hemiketal also opens freely. So fructose is a reducing sugar. II is false: in sucrose the glucose C1 and the fructose C2 (both anomeric carbons) are joined in the glycosidic bond, so neither ring can open. III is true: lactose links galactose C1 to glucose C4, leaving the glucose anomeric carbon as a free hemiacetal that can open to an aldehyde. The answer is I and III only.
x: This rejects fructose because it is a ketone. Under the basic test conditions fructose isomerizes (via the enediol) to aldoses, so it gives a positive test.
This accepts sucrose. Both of sucrose's anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so it has no hemiacetal and is non-reducing.
This accepts sucrose and rejects fructose. Sucrose has no free anomeric carbon, while fructose reacts after base-catalyzed tautomerization.

q: Which of these amino acids has a net positive charge as its major form at pH 7.0? (Side-chain pK<sub>a</sub> values: arginine 12.5, glutamic acid 4.2, histidine 6.0.)
h: At pH 7 the α-CO<sub>2</sub>H is ionized (−1) and the α-NH<sub>2</sub> is protonated (+1). Then compare pH 7 with each side-chain pK<sub>a</sub>: below the pK<sub>a</sub> the group is protonated.
w: At pH 7 the backbone contributes +1 (NH3+) and −1 (CO2−), so the side chain decides. I (arginine): true, pH 7 is far below the guanidinium pKa of 12.5, so the side chain is protonated (+1) and the net charge is +1. II (glutamic acid): false, pH 7 is above the side-chain pKa of 4.2, so the side chain is CO2− and the net charge is −1. III (histidine): false, pH 7 is one unit above the imidazolium pKa of 6.0, so only about 10% of the side chains are protonated; the major form is neutral. The answer is I only.
x: This counts histidine as positive. With pH one unit above its side-chain pK<sub>a</sub>, about 90% of histidine has a neutral imidazole, so the major form has no net charge.
This counts histidine and misses arginine. Arginine's guanidinium (pK<sub>a</sub> 12.5) stays protonated at pH 7, while histidine is mostly neutral.
This counts glutamic acid as positive. Its side-chain CO<sub>2</sub>H (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.2) is ionized at pH 7, giving a net −1 charge.

q: Each D-aldohexose shown is oxidized with warm HNO3 to an aldaric acid (both C1 and C6 become CO2H). Which give an optically inactive aldaric acid?
h: Draw each aldaric acid and look for a horizontal mirror plane through the middle of the Fischer projection. Rotating the projection 180° in the plane is allowed.
w: Once both ends are CO2H, the aldaric acid is meso (optically inactive) if a horizontal mirror plane through the middle of the Fischer projection maps the top half onto the bottom half; that requires the OH on C2 to be on the same side as the OH on C5, and C3 the same side as C4. I (D-galactose): OH pattern right, left, left, right; C2/C5 match and C3/C4 match, so galactaric acid is meso: true. II (D-allose): all four OH on the right, so the halves match and allaric acid is meso: true. III (D-mannose): left, left, right, right; C2 (left) does not match C5 (right), so there is no mirror plane. Mannaric acid has only a C2 rotation axis, which does not make a molecule achiral, so it is optically active: false. The answer is I and II only.
x: This rejects II. With all four OH groups on the same side, the aldaric acid from D-allose has a mirror plane between C3 and C4 and is meso.
This rejects I and accepts III. Galactaric acid (mucic acid) is the classic meso aldaric acid; mannaric acid has only a C<sub>2</sub> axis, which does not make a molecule achiral.
This accepts III. Mannaric acid looks symmetric, but its symmetry is a C<sub>2</sub> rotation axis, not a mirror plane, so it is chiral.

q:
Rank these triacylglycerols from lowest to highest melting point.
I. tristearin (three C18 saturated chains)
II. triolein (three C18 chains, each with one cis C=C)
III. tripalmitin (three C16 saturated chains)
h: Melting point rises with stronger London forces, which need long chains that pack closely. What does a cis double bond do to packing?
w: II (triolein) melts lowest (it is the main component of olive oil, a liquid): each cis C=C puts a kink in the chain, so the chains cannot pack tightly and London forces are weak. III (tripalmitin) and I (tristearin) are both saturated, straight-chain fats that pack well; tristearin's longer C18 chains give more surface contact and a higher melting point than tripalmitin's C16 chains. Lowest to highest: II < III < I.
x: This puts triolein highest. Cis double bonds kink the chains and prevent close packing, so triolein has the lowest melting point.
This puts tristearin below tripalmitin. Longer saturated chains have more London-force contact, so C<sub>18</sub> tristearin melts higher than C<sub>16</sub> tripalmitin.
This puts tripalmitin below the unsaturated fat. Any cis double bond lowers the melting point much more than removing two CH<sub>2</sub> units from each chain.

q:
A compound C9H10O2 has a strong IR band at 1720 cm−1 and the 1H NMR spectrum shown. Which statements are correct?
I. The 4.38 ppm quartet comes from an O–CH2 group bonded to a CH3.
II. The aromatic signals show a para-disubstituted benzene ring.
III. The compound is a carboxylic acid.
h: Add up the aromatic integrations. Then ask what chemical shift a CH<sub>2</sub> would need to be next to oxygen, and where a CO<sub>2</sub>H proton appears.
w: I is true: a CH2 at 4.38 ppm is deshielded by an attached oxygen, and its quartet (and the 3H triplet at 1.39 ppm) shows it is bonded to a CH3: an ethoxy group. II is false: the aromatic signals integrate to 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 H, a monosubstituted ring (2 ortho H near 8.05, 1 para H, 2 meta H); a para-disubstituted ring would show 4 H as two 2H doublets. III is false: a carboxylic acid would show a broad 1H singlet near 10–13 ppm and a broad O–H band in the IR; neither is present. The data fit ethyl benzoate (DBE 5: ring + C=O). The answer is I only.
x: This accepts II. The aromatic region totals 5 H with a 2:1:2 pattern, which means one substituent on the ring, not two.
This accepts III. There is no 10–13 ppm acid proton; the oxygen-bearing CH<sub>2</sub> at 4.38 ppm points to an ester instead.
This rejects I and accepts II. The 4.38 ppm shift can only come from a CH<sub>2</sub> on oxygen, and the 5 aromatic H mean a monosubstituted ring.

q:
A compound C5H10O gives the 13C NMR spectrum shown. Which statements are correct?
I. The molecule contains only three carbon atoms.
II. The signal at 211.8 ppm is a ketone C=O carbon.
III. The spectrum fits pentan-3-one.
h: The formula fixes the number of carbons. If there are fewer signals than carbons, what must be true about the molecule?
w: I is false: the formula has five carbons; three signals mean some carbons are equivalent by symmetry. II is true: a signal above 200 ppm is an aldehyde or ketone C=O, and a value near 210 ppm fits a ketone. III is true: pentan-3-one (CH3CH2COCH2CH3) has a mirror plane through C=O, so its two CH2 carbons (35.5 ppm) are equivalent, as are its two CH3 carbons (7.9 ppm), giving exactly three signals. The answer is II and III only.
x: This rejects III. Pentan-3-one is symmetric, so its five carbons give exactly three signals, matching the C=O, CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub> peaks shown.
This accepts I. The formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O has five carbons; equivalent carbons share a signal, so the signal count is smaller than the carbon count.
This rejects II. A carbon at 211.8 ppm is in the ketone/aldehyde C=O range; nothing else in C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O appears that far downfield.

q:
The mass spectrum of an aromatic compound is shown. Which statements are correct?
I. The equal-height peaks at m/z 156 and 158 show the molecule contains one bromine atom.
II. The peak at m/z 77 is the phenyl cation, C6H5+.
III. Because there is an M+2 peak, the molecule contains two bromine atoms.
h: Bromine's two isotopes, <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br, are nearly equal in abundance. What pattern would one Br give, and what pattern would two Br give?
w: I is true: a single Br gives M+ and M+2 peaks of nearly equal height (about 1:1), as at 156/158 (C6H579Br = 156). II is true: losing Br· (79 or 81) from either molecular ion leaves m/z 77, the C6H5+ cation typical of monosubstituted benzenes. III is false: two Br atoms would give three peaks, M, M+2 and M+4, in about a 1:2:1 ratio; an M+2 peak about as tall as M means exactly one Br. The compound is bromobenzene. The answer is I and II only.
x: This rejects II. C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 77 is the classic fragment of a monosubstituted benzene, here formed by loss of a Br atom.
This accepts III and rejects I. One bromine gives the 1:1 M/M+2 pair; two bromines would add an M+4 peak and give a 1:2:1 pattern.
This accepts III. An M+2 peak alone does not mean two Br; two bromines would give a 1:2:1 triplet at M, M+2 and M+4.

q: Unknown A, C11H12O2, gives the IR, 1H NMR and 13C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The 1H doublets at δ 7.68 and 6.44 share J = 16.0 Hz. What is the degree of unsaturation of A, and which structural pieces account for it?
c: 6: a benzene ring, one C=C and one C=O
5: a benzene ring and one C=O
6: a benzene ring and two C=O groups
7: a benzene ring, one C=C, one C=O and a second ring
h: Use DBE = (2C + 2 − H)/2, ignoring O. Then spend the units on what the spectra show: benzene counts 4, each other ring or π bond counts 1.
w: DBE = (2(11) + 2 − 12)/2 = 6. A benzene ring uses 4 (aromatic H at δ 7.3–7.5, four aromatic 13C signals). The single C=O (δ 167.0, IR 1712 cm−1) uses 1, and the trans CH=CH (two 1H doublets with J = 16 Hz, IR 1640 cm−1, two sp2 CH carbons at δ 144.6 and 118.3) uses the last 1. So the pieces are a benzene ring, one C=C and one C=O.
x: DBE = 5 comes from miscounting the formula (for example using H = 14). With 12 H the value is 6, and the vinyl doublets at δ 7.68/6.44 need a C=C beyond the ring and C=O.
The DBE is right but the pieces are not: the <sup>13</sup>C spectrum has only one carbonyl signal (δ 167.0); the δ 144.6 and 118.3 signals are alkene CH carbons, not a second C=O.
DBE = 7 would need H = 10. With 12 H the total is 6, and there is no evidence for an extra ring: every sp<sup>3</sup> carbon belongs to an OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> group.

q: Unknown A, C11H12O2, gives the IR, 1H NMR and 13C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The 1H doublets at δ 7.68 and 6.44 share J = 16.0 Hz. Cinnamyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2CH=CHC6H5, is an isomer of A. Which IR observation rules it out?
c: The C=O stretch at 1712 cm<sup>−1</sup> is too low for an ester with an unconjugated C=O (1735–1750 cm<sup>−1</sup>)
There is no broad O–H band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>, so the compound is not a carboxylic acid at all
There is a C=C stretch at 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which fits a C=C conjugated with the benzene ring
There is a strong C–O stretch at 1165 cm<sup>−1</sup>, typical of the C–O single bond of an ester
h: Both compounds are esters with a C=C. Ask which band position depends on whether the C=O is next to the C=C.
w: An ester C=O that is not conjugated absorbs at 1735–1750 cm−1; conjugation with a C=C (an α,β-unsaturated ester) lowers it to about 1715–1730 cm−1. In cinnamyl acetate the C=C is on the alcohol side, separated from the C=O by O and CH2, so its C=O would appear near 1740 cm−1. The observed 1712 cm−1 band shows a C=O conjugated with the C=C, which fits ethyl cinnamate and rules out cinnamyl acetate.
x: The missing O–H band rules out a carboxylic acid, but cinnamyl acetate has no O–H either, so this does not tell the two esters apart.
Cinnamyl acetate also contains a C=C (a styrene-type CH=CH), so a band near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup> is expected for both isomers.
Every ester has strong C–O stretches in the 1300–1000 cm<sup>−1</sup> region, so this band appears for cinnamyl acetate too.

q: Unknown A, C11H12O2, gives the IR, 1H NMR and 13C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The 1H doublets at δ 7.68 and 6.44 share J = 16.0 Hz. A is the ester shown. Which hydrogen gives the 1H doublet at δ 6.44?
c: The H on carbon a, next to the C=O
The H on carbon b, next to the ring
The para H of the benzene ring
One of the two ortho H of the benzene ring
h: In an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl, draw the resonance form that puts + charge on one alkene carbon. Which vinyl H is deshielded, and which is not?
w: Both vinyl H are 1H doublets with J = 16 Hz (trans coupling to each other). Resonance (C=C–C=O ↔ +C–C=C–O−) puts partial positive charge on the β-carbon (b), which is also next to the ring, so Hb is strongly deshielded (δ 7.68) and its carbon appears at δ 144.6. The α-carbon (a) gains electron density, so Ha, next to the C=O, is the δ 6.44 doublet (carbon at δ 118.3).
x: H<sub>b</sub> sits on the β-carbon, which carries the partial + charge in the conjugated resonance form; it is the δ 7.68 doublet, not the upfield one.
Ring H appear at δ 7.3–7.5 and overlap as multiplets; a ring H would not show a clean 16 Hz doublet far upfield at δ 6.44.
The two ortho H are equivalent, so they would integrate for 2H, and they lie near δ 7.5, not at δ 6.44 as a 1H doublet.

q: Unknown A, C11H12O2, gives the IR, 1H NMR and 13C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The 1H doublets at δ 7.68 and 6.44 share J = 16.0 Hz. Which structure is A?
h: Three clues: the C=O position (conjugated or not), the ethyl group's shift (OCH<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>2</sub> on C=O), and the J value of the vinyl doublets.
w: The quartet at δ 4.27 (2H) and triplet at δ 1.34 (3H) are an O–CH2CH3 group, so the ester is an ethyl ester. The C=O at 1712 cm−1 (and δ 167.0, typical of a conjugated ester) shows the C=O is conjugated with the C=C. The two 1H vinyl doublets with J = 16 Hz show the alkene H are trans, and the 5H aromatic multiplets show a monosubstituted ring. A is ethyl (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enoate (ethyl trans-cinnamate).
x: The (Z) isomer has the same connectivity, but cis vinyl H couple with J ≈ 12 Hz, not 16 Hz.
Cinnamyl acetate has a CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.1 and an OCH<sub>2</sub> doublet near δ 4.7, not a quartet–triplet ethyl group; its unconjugated C=O would absorb near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Ethyl 4-vinylbenzoate has a para ring (two 2H doublets) and a vinyl group CH=CH<sub>2</sub> (one 1H dd plus two 1H doublets near δ 5.4 and 5.9), not two 1H doublets sharing J = 16 Hz.

q: Unknown B, C6H12O, gives the IR, 1H NMR and mass spectra shown. Which process forms the even-mass fragment at m/z 58?
c: A McLafferty rearrangement: a γ-H moves to the carbonyl O and propene (42 u) is lost
An α-cleavage that breaks the bond next to the C=O and loses a propyl radical (43 u)
An α-cleavage that loses a methyl radical (15 u) from beside the C=O
Loss of water (18 u) from the molecular ion, as for an alcohol
h: Subtract 58 from the molecular ion. Is the neutral piece lost an even-mass molecule or an odd-mass radical?
w: M+ = 100, so the m/z 58 ion forms by loss of 42 u, an even-mass neutral molecule (C3H6, propene). Simple cleavages lose radicals and give odd-mass ions from an ion like this one; an even-mass ion from an even-mass M+ points to a rearrangement. For a ketone with an H on the γ-carbon this is the McLafferty rearrangement: a six-membered transition state moves the γ-H to O and breaks the α–β bond, releasing propene and leaving the enol radical cation CH2=C(OH)CH3+• (m/z 58).
x: Losing a 43 u radical from m/z 100 gives m/z 57, not 58; that cleavage accounts for the separate m/z 57 and 43 peaks.
Loss of CH<sub>3</sub> (15 u) gives m/z 85, which is a different, small peak in the spectrum.
100 − 18 = 82, and there is no peak at 82; the IR also shows no O–H band, so B is not an alcohol.

q: Unknown B, C6H12O, gives the IR, 1H NMR and mass spectra shown. B is the ketone shown. Which hydrogens give the 2H doublet at δ 2.30?
h: Match each signal by integration first, then check its splitting with the n + 1 rule.
w: The 2H integration fits only the CH2 group. Its neighbors are the C=O (no H) and one CH (1 H), so n + 1 = 2: a doublet. Being α to the C=O puts it at δ 2.30. So the δ 2.30 doublet is the CH2 on carbon b. The other signals follow: δ 2.12 (s, 3H) is CH3 a (no neighbors with H), δ 2.17 (m, 1H) is CH c (8 neighboring H), and δ 0.92 (d, 6H) is the two CH3 d groups split by the one CH.
x: CH3 a is attached to the C=O, which has no H, so it is the 3H singlet at δ 2.12, not a 2H doublet.
The CH c has 2 + 6 = 8 neighboring H, so it is the 1H multiplet at δ 2.17.
The two CH3 d groups are equivalent and integrate for 6H; they are the doublet at δ 0.92, far from the C=O.

q: Unknown B, C6H12O, gives the IR, 1H NMR and mass spectra shown. Which structure is B?
h: Use the 6H doublet and the McLafferty peak together: which isomers have an isopropyl group, and which have a γ-H for the m/z 58 ion?
w: IR 1716 cm−1 with no O–H and no aldehyde C–H pair (2720/2820 cm−1) is a saturated ketone; DBE = 1. The 3H singlet at δ 2.12 is CH3C=O, the 6H doublet at δ 0.92 is (CH3)2CH, and the 2H doublet at δ 2.30 is a CH2 between the C=O and that CH. The McLafferty ion at m/z 58 (loss of propene) needs a γ-H, which the isobutyl chain has. B is 4-methylpentan-2-one.
x: Hexan-2-one also gives m/z 58 by McLafferty, but it has a straight chain: a 2H triplet at δ 2.42 and a 3H triplet near δ 0.90, with no 6H doublet.
3-Methylpentan-2-one has a 1H sextet-like CH next to the C=O near δ 2.45, a 3H doublet and a 3H triplet; its McLafferty ion loses ethene to give m/z 72, not 58.
3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one shows only two singlets (9H and 3H) and has no γ-H, so it cannot form a McLafferty ion at m/z 58.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Decide where the ethyl CH<sub>2</sub> is attached from its shift: next to O (δ ≈ 4.1) or next to C=O (δ ≈ 2.3).
w: IR 1740 cm−1 with no O–H is a saturated ester (DBE = 1). The 3H singlet at δ 3.67 is an O–CH3. The ethyl quartet is at δ 2.32, the shift of a CH2 on a C=O, not on O. So the ethyl group is on the acyl side: methyl propanoate, CH3CH2CO2CH3.
x: Ethyl acetate has the same three signals in a 2:3:3 ratio, but its quartet is an OCH<sub>2</sub> near δ 4.12 and its singlet is a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O near δ 2.05.
Propyl formate shows a formyl H singlet near δ 8.05 and four signals (OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet, CH<sub>2</sub> sextet, CH<sub>3</sub> triplet), not three.
2-Methylpropanoic acid would show a very broad O–H band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a 1H signal near δ 12 and a 6H doublet.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Either ester orientation gives two singlets. Use the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon shift: near δ 65 when bonded to O, near δ 40 when not.
w: DBE = 5: a benzene ring and one C=O. The 1740 cm−1 band is an unconjugated ester C=O, and the 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring. The CH3 singlet at δ 3.69 and the CH3 carbon at δ 52.0 are a methyl ester OCH3. The CH2 singlet at δ 3.62 with its carbon at δ 41.2 is a benzylic CH2 attached to the C=O, not to O. The compound is methyl phenylacetate.
x: Benzyl acetate has the reverse ester: its OCH<sub>2</sub> is a singlet near δ 5.1 (carbon near δ 66) and its CH<sub>3</sub>C=O is near δ 2.1 (carbon near δ 21).
Ethyl benzoate has an ethyl quartet and triplet, and its C=O is conjugated with the ring (near 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup>).
Methyl 4-methylbenzoate has a para ring (two 2H doublets, 4H total) and an aryl CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.4, with no CH<sub>2</sub> carbon.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two isomers here have an ethyl group on an ester. Check the C=O band (conjugated or aryl ester) and the CH<sub>2</sub> shift.
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). The C=O at 1725 cm−1 is an ester lowered by conjugation with the ring, and there is no O–H. The aromatic pattern 2H : 1H : 2H is a monosubstituted ring, and the 2H doublet at δ 8.05 is the ortho H deshielded by a C=O on the ring. The quartet at δ 4.38 is an O–CH2. The compound is ethyl benzoate.
x: Phenyl propanoate is an aryl ester: its C=O absorbs high, near 1760 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is next to C=O near δ 2.6, not at δ 4.38. Its ring H all lie near δ 7.1–7.4.
4-Ethylbenzoic acid would show a very broad O–H band (3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a 1H signal near δ 12, and two 2H doublets for the para ring; its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet would be near δ 2.7.
4-Methoxyacetophenone shows two singlets (OCH<sub>3</sub> near δ 3.9, CH<sub>3</sub>C=O near δ 2.6), a para pattern and a ketone C=O near 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: First decide aldehyde or ketone (look near δ 9–10 and at 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>). Then use the splitting of the δ 9.81 signal to find what the CHO is attached to.
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). The pair of bands at 2810 and 2710 cm−1 and the 1H signal at δ 9.81 show an aldehyde; the C=O at 1725 cm−1 is not conjugated. The CHO is a triplet, so it is next to a CH2. Two 2H triplets show a –CH2CH2– unit, and the 5H multiplet a monosubstituted ring. The compound is 3-phenylpropanal. (The CH2 at δ 2.78 is also split slightly by the CHO, J ≈ 1.5 Hz.)
x: Propiophenone is a ketone: no δ 9–10 signal, no 2710/2810 cm<sup>−1</sup> pair, a conjugated C=O near 1690 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and an ethyl quartet/triplet.
Phenylacetone is a ketone with two singlets (CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.7, CH<sub>3</sub> near δ 2.1) and no aldehyde H.
2-Phenylpropanal is an aldehyde, but its CHO is a doublet (next to a CH), and it shows a 1H quartet and a 3H doublet, not two 2H triplets.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown (the δ 11.9 signal disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake). Which structure fits?
h: A broad band spanning 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus an exchangeable H near δ 12 points to one functional group. Then count <sup>13</sup>C signals.
w: The very broad O–H band, the C=O at 1710 cm−1 and the exchangeable 1H at δ 11.9 identify a carboxylic acid. Only three 13C signals for four carbons means two carbons are equivalent; the septet (1H) and 6H doublet are an isopropyl group. The compound is 2-methylpropanoic acid.
x: Butanoic acid is also an acid, but it has four different carbons (four <sup>13</sup>C signals) and shows a triplet, a sextet and a triplet.
Ethyl acetate has no O–H (no broad band, no δ 12 signal); its C=O is near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Methyl propanoate has no O–H; its signals are a 3H singlet at δ 3.67, a quartet and a triplet.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 6.25 signal disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake, and the δ 2.99 doublet then becomes a singlet). Which structure fits?
h: Count the N–H bands (one or two) and ask what the CH<sub>3</sub> is coupled to, given that the doublet collapses when N–H becomes N–D.
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). The C=O at 1635 cm−1 plus the 1550 cm−1 band (N–H bend) is a secondary amide, and the single N–H stretch at 3335 cm−1 shows one N–H. The CH3 is a doublet (J ≈ 5 Hz) that becomes a singlet after D2O exchange, so it is coupled to the N–H: an N–CH3 group (δ 2.99). The 2H : 3H aromatic pattern with the 2H doublet downfield at δ 7.76 is a monosubstituted ring bonded to the C=O. The compound is N-methylbenzamide.
x: 4-Methylbenzamide is a primary amide (two N–H bands near 3350 and 3180 cm<sup>−1</sup>, 2H exchangeable), with a para ring and an aryl CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.4.
Acetanilide has one N–H, but its CH<sub>3</sub> is on the C=O: a singlet near δ 2.2 that has no N–H to couple with. Its ring H appear as 2H, 2H, 1H (δ 7.5, 7.3, 7.1).
2-Phenylacetamide is a primary amide (two N–H bands, NH<sub>2</sub>) and shows a 2H CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.6, not a 3H doublet.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NO gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: The 2220 cm<sup>−1</sup> band, the lack of an O–H band and the aromatic splitting pattern each remove one choice.
w: DBE = 6: a benzene ring (4) plus C≡N (2). The sharp band at 2220 cm−1 is a nitrile conjugated with the ring, and there is no O–H band. Two 2H doublets are a para-disubstituted ring, and the 3H singlet at δ 3.86 (carbon δ 55.5) is an aryl OCH3. Six 13C signals fit the para symmetry (δ 119.2 is the C≡N). The compound is 4-methoxybenzonitrile.
x: 3-Methoxybenzonitrile has no symmetry: four separate aromatic H signals and eight <sup>13</sup>C signals, not two 2H doublets and six carbons.
(4-Hydroxyphenyl)acetonitrile has an O–H (broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.7 (2H), not a 3H singlet.
4-(Hydroxymethyl)benzonitrile has an O–H band and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>O singlet near δ 4.8, not a 3H singlet at δ 3.86.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: No band at 3300–3500 cm<sup>−1</sup> means no N–H. Between the tertiary amines, ask whether the N is on the ring or on a CH<sub>2</sub>.
w: DBE = 4, a benzene ring. There is no N–H stretch, so the amine is tertiary. The 5H multiplet near δ 7.3 is a monosubstituted ring that is not attached to N (an N on the ring pushes the ortho/para H upfield to δ 6.6–6.8). The 2H singlet at δ 3.42 is a benzylic CH2 on N, and the 6H singlet at δ 2.24 is N(CH3)2. The compound is N,N-dimethylbenzylamine.
x: N-Ethyl-N-methylaniline is also tertiary, but it has an ethyl quartet/triplet, an N–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.9 (3H), and ring H split 2H : 3H with the ortho/para H near δ 6.7.
4-Isopropylaniline is a primary amine with two N–H bands near 3430 and 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a para ring (two 2H doublets), a septet and a 6H doublet.
N-Methyl-2-phenylethylamine is a secondary amine (one N–H band) and shows two 2H triplets plus a 3H singlet.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two isomers here have a para ring, an ethyl and a methyl. Which one, the CH<sub>2</sub> or the CH<sub>3</sub>, is on the oxygen? Compare δ 3.99 with δ 2.28.
w: DBE = 4 (a benzene ring); no O–H band, so the O is an ether (strong aryl C–O at 1245 cm−1). Two 2H doublets are a para ring. The quartet is at δ 3.99, the shift of an O–CH2, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.28 is an aryl CH3. So the ethyl is on O and the methyl is on the ring: 1-ethoxy-4-methylbenzene.
x: 4-Ethylanisole has the same signal pattern, but its O–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet is near δ 3.78 and its benzylic CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is near δ 2.6.
1-Ethoxy-2-methylbenzene is ortho-disubstituted: four different aromatic H that appear as a multiplet, not two 2H doublets.
1-(4-Methylphenyl)ethanol has an O–H (broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, exchangeable 1H), a 1H quartet near δ 4.85 and a 3H doublet near δ 1.47.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub> gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The δ 10.76 signal is sharp and disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake. Which structure fits?
h: Four 1H aromatic signals limit the substitution pattern. Methyl ester CH<sub>3</sub> (carbon near δ 52) or aryl ether (near δ 56)? Does the O–H look like an acid's?
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). Four different 1H aromatic signals (d, t, d, t) mean an ortho-disubstituted ring. The CH3 carbon at δ 52.2 is a methyl ester OCH3, not an aryl ether. The O–H is a band near 3200 cm−1 without the 3300–2500 cm−1 sprawl of an acid, and its sharp δ 10.76 signal is a phenol O–H held downfield by an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the ester C=O; that same hydrogen bond and conjugation lower the C=O to 1685 cm−1. The compound is methyl 2-hydroxybenzoate (methyl salicylate).
x: Methyl 4-hydroxybenzoate is para (two 2H doublets, six <sup>13</sup>C signals), and its phenol O–H, with no intramolecular hydrogen bond, is a broad signal near δ 6, not a sharp δ 10.76 singlet.
4-Methoxybenzoic acid is para (two 2H doublets), shows a very broad 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> acid O–H, and its aryl OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon is near δ 55.5.
2-Methoxybenzoic acid is also ortho, but its CH<sub>3</sub> is an aryl ether (carbon near δ 56) and its acid O–H gives a very broad 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> IR band.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. The vinyl signals at δ 6.85 and 6.10 share J = 16 Hz. Which structure fits?
h: A C=O near 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup> is lower than a normal ketone. What lowers it, and does the spectrum show an aldehyde H?
w: DBE = 2: one C=O and one C=C. The C=O at 1675 cm−1 (about 40 cm−1 below a saturated ketone) and the C=C at 1635 cm−1 show an α,β-unsaturated ketone. There is no aldehyde H. The CH3 singlet at δ 2.25 is CH3C=O; the 3H doublet at δ 1.90 is a CH3 on the alkene, split by the vinyl H at δ 6.85 (a multiplet, coupled to both the other vinyl H and the CH3). J = 16 Hz and the 970 cm−1 band fit a trans alkene. The compound is (E)-pent-3-en-2-one.
x: Cyclopentanone has no C=C or vinyl H; its C=O is raised by ring strain to about 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and its <sup>1</sup>H spectrum is two 4H signals near δ 2.0–2.2.
Pent-4-en-2-one is not conjugated: its C=O stays near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and it shows a terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> (2H near δ 5.1) and a CH<sub>2</sub> doublet near δ 3.2.
(E)-Pent-2-enal is an aldehyde: a 1H doublet near δ 9.5 and the C–H pair near 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>, with an ethyl group instead of two CH<sub>3</sub> signals.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 11.2 signal disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake). Which structure fits?
h: Identify the functional group from the broad IR band and δ 11.2, then read the CH/CH<sub>3</sub> splitting.
w: The very broad O–H band (3300–2500 cm−1), the C=O at 1705 cm−1 and the exchangeable 1H at δ 11.2 identify a carboxylic acid. DBE = 5 (ring + C=O), and the 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring. A 1H quartet and a 3H doublet are a CH–CH3 unit, with the CH (δ 3.74) both benzylic and α to the C=O. The compound is 2-phenylpropanoic acid.
x: 3-Phenylpropanoic acid has a –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– chain: two 2H triplets near δ 2.95 and 2.68, not a quartet and a doublet.
4-Ethylbenzoic acid has a para ring (two 2H doublets) and an ethyl group: a 2H quartet near δ 2.7 and a 3H triplet.
Methyl phenylacetate is an ester with no O–H band and no δ 11 signal; it shows two singlets (OCH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>).

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>ClO<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1750 cm<sup>−1</sup> and gives the mass spectrum and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: All four choices are chloro esters with M<sup>+</sup> 122/124. Use the multiplicities and integrations, then the shift of the quartet: is that CH<sub>2</sub> on O or on Cl?
w: The weak M+ at 122 with M+2 at 124 (about 3:1), like the 3:1 pairs at m/z 77/79 and 49/51, shows one Cl; 1750 cm−1 is an ester C=O made slightly higher by the α-Cl. The quartet (2H, δ 4.24) and triplet (3H, δ 1.30) are an O–CH2CH3, so the ester is an ethyl ester. The remaining 2H singlet at δ 4.06 is a CH2 between Cl and C=O with no neighbors. The acylium ion ClCH2CO+ (m/z 77/79, 3:1, from loss of ·OCH2CH3) fits. The compound is ethyl chloroacetate.
x: Methyl 3-chloropropanoate has an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet (3H) and two 2H triplets (ClCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>), with no quartet; its acylium ion would be at m/z 91/93.
2-Chloroethyl acetate has a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet near δ 2.1 (3H) and two 2H triplets for OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl; its base peak would be CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at m/z 43.
Methyl 2-chloropropanoate gives a quartet, a singlet and a doublet, but in a 1H : 3H : 3H ratio (CHCl near δ 4.4, OCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub> doublet), not 2H : 2H : 3H.

q: A compound C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>3</sub> gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two carbonyl carbons (δ 206 and 173) mean a ketone plus an ester. All four choices have 2H, 2H, 3H, 3H integrations, so the multiplicities decide.
w: DBE = 2: two C=O groups, a ketone (δ 206.6, IR 1717 cm−1) and an ester (δ 173.2, IR 1738 cm−1). The CH3 singlet at δ 3.67 (carbon δ 51.7) is a methyl ester OCH3; the CH3 singlet at δ 2.19 (carbon δ 29.8) is CH3C=O. Two 2H triplets are a –CH2CH2– unit with a carbonyl on each end (both near δ 2.6–2.8). The compound is methyl 4-oxopentanoate.
x: Ethyl acetoacetate has an ethyl ester (2H quartet near δ 4.2, 3H triplet) and an isolated CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.4 between the two C=O groups, not two triplets.
Methyl 3-oxopentanoate has a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.45 between the two C=O groups and an ethyl quartet/triplet on the ketone, not two triplets and two singlets.
Methyl 5-oxopentanoate is an aldehyde: a 1H triplet near δ 9.8 and a CHO carbon near δ 202 (a CH in DEPT), with no CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet.

q: A compound C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 3.42 signal disappears after a D<sub>2</sub>O shake). Which structure fits?
h: Two sharp-ish N–H bands mean one kind of amine. The aromatic pattern and the 3H singlet do the rest.
w: DBE = 4, a benzene ring. Two N–H bands at 3445 and 3370 cm−1 (symmetric and asymmetric stretches) and an exchangeable 2H signal mean a primary amine, NH2. Two 2H doublets are a para ring, shifted upfield (δ 6.6–6.8) by two electron-donating groups. The 3H singlet at δ 3.75 with the strong 1250 cm−1 aryl C–O band is an OCH3. The compound is 4-methoxyaniline.
x: 4-Aminobenzyl alcohol has an O–H (broad band) and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>O singlet near δ 4.5, not a 3H singlet near δ 3.75.
2-Methoxyaniline has the same groups but ortho: four different aromatic H as a multiplet, not two 2H doublets.
4-(Methylamino)phenol has one N–H and an O–H (a broad O–H band, not two sharp N–H bands) and an N–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.8.

q: A compound C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR (with DEPT) spectra shown. The vinyl signals at δ 6.98 and 6.01 share J = 10 Hz. Which structure fits?
h: Use the C=O position for conjugation, the vinyl CH carbons for how many H sit on the C=C, and each vinyl carbon's shift to find the β-carbon.
w: DBE = 3: C=O + C=C + one ring. The C=O at 1680 cm−1 and δ 199.9 (below the δ 205–212 of a saturated ketone) show conjugation with the C=C (1620 cm−1). DEPT shows two alkene CH carbons, and the β-carbon is strongly deshielded (δ 151.0) by resonance with the C=O, while the α-carbon is at δ 129.9. There is no aldehyde H, and three CH2 groups complete a six-membered ring. J = 10 Hz fits cis vinyl H in a ring. The compound is cyclohex-2-en-1-one.
x: Cyclohex-3-en-1-one is not conjugated: its C=O would be near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and δ 209, and both vinyl carbons would be near δ 125, with no strongly deshielded β-carbon.
Cyclopent-1-ene-1-carbaldehyde is an aldehyde: a 1H singlet near δ 9.8 and only one vinyl H (its other alkene carbon has no H).
2-Methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one has only one vinyl H and a CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 1.8; DEPT would show one alkene CH and a CH<sub>3</sub>, not two alkene CH.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O shows a strong IR band at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and gives the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Five carbons but only three <sup>13</sup>C signals: look for the symmetric choice.
w: DBE = 1 and 1715 cm−1 with δ 211.8 is a saturated ketone. Five carbons giving only three 13C signals, and only two 1H signals (4H quartet, 6H triplet), mean two identical ethyl groups on the C=O. The compound is pentan-3-one.
x: Pentan-2-one has no symmetry: five <sup>13</sup>C signals and four <sup>1</sup>H signals, including a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet near δ 2.1.
Pentanal is an aldehyde: a 1H triplet near δ 9.8, a CHO carbon near δ 202 and five <sup>13</sup>C signals.
2-Methylbutanal is an aldehyde with five different carbons and a 1H doublet near δ 9.6.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: All of these have two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Look at where neither singlet is (δ 3.8–3.9), and at how high the C=O band is.
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). Two 2H doublets are a para ring. Neither CH3 singlet is near δ 3.9, so there is no OCH3: δ 2.33 and 2.28 are an aryl CH3 and a CH3C=O. A C=O at 1765 cm−1 is higher than an alkyl ester (≈1740 cm−1), the mark of a phenyl ester, where the ring pulls the O lone pair away from the C=O. The ring H are fairly upfield (no C=O on the ring). The compound is 4-methylphenyl acetate.
x: Methyl 4-methylbenzoate has the ester reversed: an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.9, a ring doublet near δ 7.9 (ortho to C=O), and a conjugated C=O near 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Methoxyacetophenone has an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.9, a ring doublet near δ 7.9, and a conjugated ketone C=O near 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
2-Methylphenyl acetate is also an aryl ester (C=O near 1765 cm<sup>−1</sup>), but it is ortho-disubstituted: four different aromatic H as a multiplet, not two 2H doublets.

q: As a conjugated polyene gets longer (ethene → 1,3-butadiene → 1,3,5-hexatriene), its λ<sub>max</sub> moves to longer wavelength. Which explanation is correct?
c: Each added C=C adds π MOs, so the HOMO rises and the LUMO falls; the smaller gap is bridged by lower-energy, longer-wavelength light
Each added conjugated C=C lowers the HOMO and raises the LUMO; the larger HOMO–LUMO gap is then bridged by longer-wavelength light
Longer polyenes absorb through σ → σ* transitions, which need less energy than the π → π* transitions of short alkenes
Conjugation stabilizes the whole molecule, so a higher-energy photon is needed to excite it, which raises λ<sub>max</sub>
h: Picture the π MO ladder as p orbitals are added. What happens to the spacing in the middle, and how does photon energy relate to wavelength (E = hc/λ)?
w: Combining n p orbitals gives n π MOs spread over roughly the same total energy range, so the levels crowd together as n grows. The HOMO moves up and the LUMO moves down: ethene's gap is largest (λmax ≈ 171 nm), butadiene's smaller (217 nm), hexatriene's smaller still (≈ 258 nm). Because E = hc/λ, a smaller gap means a lower-energy photon, i.e. a longer wavelength. So: the HOMO rises and the LUMO falls, shrinking the gap, so longer-wavelength light is absorbed.
x: A larger gap would need a higher-energy photon, which is a shorter wavelength, not a longer one; and the direction of the HOMO and LUMO shifts is reversed.
The UV band of polyenes is a π → π* transition; σ → σ* transitions need far more energy (below about 150 nm) and do not change much with conjugation.
A higher-energy photon has a shorter wavelength (E = hc/λ), so this reasoning would lower λ<sub>max</sub>; overall stabilization of the molecule is not what sets the HOMO–LUMO gap.

q: Which compound has the longest-wavelength strong UV–vis absorption band (the π → π* λ<sub>max</sub>)? (One of them is a yellow solid.)
h: Count how many sp<sup>2</sup> atoms are in one unbroken conjugated π system in each compound. The bigger the system, the smaller the HOMO–LUMO gap.
w: λmax grows with the size of the conjugated π system. (1E,4E)-1,5-Diphenylpenta-1,4-dien-3-one (dibenzylideneacetone) joins two benzene rings, two C=C bonds and a C=O in one π system (17 sp2 atoms plus O); it absorbs near 330 nm, with the tail of the band reaching the violet, so it looks yellow. Benzalacetone (one ring + C=C + C=O) absorbs near 285 nm, acetophenone (ring + C=O) near 245 nm, and 4-phenylbutan-2-one, whose C=O is cut off from the ring by two sp3 carbons, has only benzene's own bands. Longest: dibenzylideneacetone.
x: (E)-4-Phenylbut-3-en-2-one has a good conjugated system (ring, C=C, C=O), but only half the size of dibenzylideneacetone's, so its λmax (≈ 285 nm) is shorter.
Acetophenone conjugates the ring with C=O only; with no C=C linker its λ<sub>max</sub> (≈ 245 nm) is shorter than either styryl ketone.
In 4-phenylbutan-2-one two CH<sub>2</sub> groups insulate the C=O from the ring, so there is no extended conjugation at all; it has the shortest strong band.

q: Rank the α,β-unsaturated ketones I–III by the λmax of their strong π → π* band, from shortest to longest wavelength.
h: Woodward-type trends for enones: each alkyl group on the C=C adds roughly 10–18 nm; one more C=C in conjugation adds about 30 nm plus its substituents.
w: All three share the C=C–C=O chromophore. I (but-3-en-2-one) has no alkyl groups on the C=C, so it absorbs at the shortest wavelength (≈ 210–220 nm). II (4-methylpent-3-en-2-one) has two β-methyl groups; each alkyl substituent raises λmax by roughly 12 nm (≈ 236 nm). III ((3E,5E)-hepta-3,5-dien-2-one) has a second C=C in conjugation, which extends the π system and adds about 30 nm, plus a terminal methyl (≈ 270 nm). Order: I < II < III.
x: Alkyl groups on the C=C raise λ<sub>max</sub> slightly (hyperconjugation raises the HOMO); they do not lower it, so II absorbs at longer wavelength than I.
Two β-methyl groups add only about 25 nm in total; an extra conjugated C=C adds about 30 nm on its own, so III is longer than II.
This is the reverse order: the most extended and most substituted π system has the smallest HOMO–LUMO gap and the longest λ<sub>max</sub>.

q: Lycopene, the pigment of tomatoes, is a C<sub>40</sub> hydrocarbon with 11 conjugated C=C bonds, and it looks red. Which statement explains its color?
c: Its long π system has a small HOMO–LUMO gap; it absorbs blue-green light (about 470 nm), and we see the complementary red
It absorbs red light (about 650 nm) strongly, and the absorbed color is the color that we see
Its π → π* band lies in the UV near 220 nm, and the red color comes from light that it emits afterward as it relaxes
Its C=C bonds are separated by sp<sup>3</sup> carbons, so each one absorbs on its own and the sum of all the bands looks red
h: First decide where an 11-unit polyene absorbs (UV or visible). Then remember that an object's color is made of the light it does not absorb.
w: Each added conjugated C=C narrows the HOMO–LUMO gap. With 11 in a row, the π → π* band moves all the way into the visible region (λmax ≈ 470 nm, blue-green). The light that reaches the eye is what remains: the complementary color, red-orange. So: a small HOMO–LUMO gap from extended conjugation gives absorption of blue-green light, and we see red.
x: An object shows the complementary color of the light it absorbs; a compound absorbing red light would look blue-green.
220 nm is typical of a single diene; 11 conjugated C=C bonds push λ<sub>max</sub> into the visible, and the color is from absorption, not emission.
Lycopene's 11 C=C bonds are conjugated (alternating with single bonds); isolated C=C bonds would each absorb near 170–180 nm, which is invisible.

q: 1,3-Butadiene (λ<sub>max</sub> 217 nm) reacts with maleic anhydride as shown. How does the UV spectrum of the purified Diels–Alder product compare with that of 1,3-butadiene?
c: The 217 nm band disappears: the product’s one C=C is isolated by sp<sup>3</sup> carbons, so no strong band remains above 200 nm
The band shifts to about 256 nm, because the product is a six-membered-ring conjugated diene like 1,3-cyclohexadiene
The band grows stronger, because the two new σ bonds of the ring extend the conjugation of the remaining C=C
The band does not change, because a Diels–Alder reaction keeps the total number of π bonds in the molecules the same
h: Count the π bonds before and after a [4+2] cycloaddition, and ask whether the C=C left in the ring is next to any other π bond.
w: In a Diels–Alder reaction three π bonds (two of the diene, one of the dienophile) become two new σ bonds and one new π bond, which sits between C2 and C3 of the old diene. In the product (cis-1,2,3,6-tetrahydrophthalic anhydride) that C=C is flanked by two CH2 groups, so it is not conjugated with anything, and an isolated C=C absorbs below 200 nm. So the strong 217 nm band disappears; this is why the loss of diene absorption is used to follow Diels–Alder reactions.
x: The product has only one C=C in the ring; 1,3-cyclohexadiene's 256 nm band needs two conjugated C=C bonds.
σ bonds do not extend a π system; the cycloaddition removes conjugation instead of adding it.
Three π bonds are replaced by two σ bonds and one π bond, so the π-bond count drops by two and the conjugated diene is destroyed.

q: Cyclohex-3-en-1-one is stirred with a trace of NaOEt in ethanol, and an isomer (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O) is isolated. Its IR spectrum is shown. Which statement correctly interprets the change?
c: The C=C moved into conjugation with C=O (cyclohex-2-en-1-one): the C=O stretch fell from about 1720 to 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a strong UV band near 225 nm appears
The C=C moved into conjugation with C=O: the C=O stretch fell to 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and the UV band moves to shorter wavelength because the conjugated isomer is more stable
The ketone tautomerized to its enol (cyclohexa-1,3-dien-1-ol), and the 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup> band is the enol C=C stretch
No isomerization occurred: 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup> is the normal C=O stretch of a six-membered-ring ketone
h: Base removes the α-H between C=O and C=C, and the enolate can reprotonate at another carbon. What does conjugation do to a C=O stretch and to UV absorption?
w: The α-H at C2 of cyclohex-3-enone is both α to the C=O and allylic, so it is unusually acidic; removing it gives a dienolate, and reprotonation at C4 gives the thermodynamically favored conjugated enone, cyclohex-2-en-1-one. Conjugation gives the C=O partial single-bond character (C=C–C=O ↔ +C–C=C–O−), lowering its stretch from about 1715–1720 cm−1 (nonconjugated) to 1680 cm−1, and the polarized C=C appears as a medium band near 1620 cm−1. The new C=C–C=O chromophore also gives a strong π → π* band near 225 nm, which the nonconjugated starting ketone lacks.
x: The IR part is right, but conjugation narrows the HOMO–LUMO gap, so the UV band moves to longer wavelength, not shorter.
An enol would show a broad O–H band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which is absent, and simple enols are only a trace component at equilibrium; the strong 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup> band is a C=O.
Cyclohexanone-type ketones absorb near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>; a value of 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup> with a 1620 cm<sup>−1</sup> C=C band signals conjugation.

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. The δ 7.70 and δ 6.44 doublets share a coupling constant of 16.0 Hz. Which structure fits?
h: What range of J is typical for two vinyl H that are trans to each other, cis to each other, or on the same carbon?
w: Two vinyl doublets coupled only to each other mean a disubstituted C=C with one H on each carbon. Typical vinyl couplings: trans 12–18 Hz, cis 6–12 Hz, geminal 0–3 Hz. J = 16.0 Hz is trans. The 3H singlet at δ 3.80 is an OCH3 ester and the 5H aromatic signals show a monosubstituted ring. The compound is methyl (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enoate (methyl cinnamate).
x: The (Z) isomer has the same signals but a cis coupling of about 12–13 Hz, and its vinyl H appear further upfield (about δ 6.9 and 5.9).
Methyl 2-phenylacrylate has two H on the same carbon (=CH<sub>2</sub>); geminal coupling is only about 1–2 Hz, so they would look like near-singlets, not 16 Hz doublets.
Phenyl (E)-but-2-enoate has a CH3 on the C=C: it would show a 3H doublet near δ 1.9 and a vinyl dq near δ 7.1, not an OCH3 singlet at δ 3.80.

q: The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of ethyl propanoate (400 MHz) is shown. The four lines of the δ ≈ 4.1 quartet appear at the positions in the table (Hz downfield of TMS). What are its chemical shift and coupling constant, and how far apart (in Hz) will adjacent lines of this quartet be on a 600 MHz instrument?
c: δ 4.12; J = 7.2 Hz; lines 7.2 Hz apart at 600 MHz
δ 4.12; J = 7.2 Hz; lines 10.8 Hz apart at 600 MHz
δ 4.12; J = 21.6 Hz; lines 21.6 Hz apart at 600 MHz
δ 2.75; J = 4.8 Hz; lines 4.8 Hz apart at 600 MHz
h: δ (ppm) = Hz from TMS ÷ spectrometer MHz, taken at the multiplet center. J is the spacing between adjacent lines in Hz. Which one depends on field strength?
w: The multiplet center is (1658.8 + 1637.2)/2 = 1648.0 Hz; δ = 1648.0 Hz ÷ 400 MHz = 4.12 ppm (the OCH2). Adjacent lines are 7.2 Hz apart, so J = 7.2 Hz, the same as in its CH3 triplet partner at δ 1.25. J comes from the bonds, not the magnet, so at 600 MHz the lines are still 7.2 Hz apart; only the shift in Hz changes (4.12 × 600 = 2472 Hz). Answer: δ 4.12; J = 7.2 Hz; 7.2 Hz apart at 600 MHz.
x: Scaling J by 600/400 treats the coupling like a chemical shift; coupling constants in Hz do not depend on the field strength.
21.6 Hz is the distance between the two outer lines, which spans three spacings (3J) in a quartet; J is the spacing between adjacent lines.
Dividing 1648.0 Hz by 600 uses the wrong spectrometer frequency; the line positions were measured at 400 MHz, so δ = 4.12 ppm.

q: The IR spectrum shown belongs to one of the four compounds. Which one?
h: All four have a C=O. Where does each derivative's C=O stretch fall? Electron-withdrawing groups on the carbonyl carbon raise the frequency; electron donation by resonance lowers it.
w: The C=O stretch follows how much single-bond character the C=O has. Cl withdraws electrons inductively and donates little by resonance, so an aroyl chloride C=O is stiff: about 1770–1775 cm−1. An aryl ester is near 1720–1725, an aryl ketone near 1685 and a primary amide near 1650–1670 cm−1 (with two N–H bands). The 1775 cm−1 band, with no N–H bands and no sp3 C–H, fits benzoyl chloride.
x: Methyl benzoate's C=O is near 1725 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and its OCH<sub>3</sub> would add sp<sup>3</sup> C–H bands just below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a strong C–O band near 1280 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Benzamide would show two N–H bands near 3370 and 3170 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=O near 1660 cm<sup>−1</sup>; strong N lone-pair donation lowers the amide C=O stretch.
Acetophenone's conjugated ketone C=O is near 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>, far below 1775, and its CH<sub>3</sub> would give sp<sup>3</sup> C–H bands.

q: Rank compounds I–III by the wavenumber of their C=O stretching band, from lowest to highest.
h: A stronger, more double-bond-like C=O vibrates at higher wavenumber. Which substituent donates most by resonance (more C–O single-bond character), and which withdraws most by induction?
w: Resonance donation from the heteroatom (X–C=O ↔ X+=C–O−) weakens the C=O; inductive withdrawal strengthens it. N donates strongly, so II (N,N-dimethylacetamide) absorbs lowest, near 1650 cm−1. In the ester I (ethyl acetate) O donates less and also withdraws inductively: about 1740 cm−1. Cl barely donates (poor 3p–2p overlap) and withdraws strongly, so III (acetyl chloride) is highest, about 1800 cm−1. Order: II < I < III.
x: This puts the amide above the ester. Nitrogen is a better π donor than oxygen, so the amide C=O has more single-bond character and the lower wavenumber.
This is the reverse of the true order; the acid chloride, with the least resonance donation, has the stiffest C=O and the highest wavenumber.
The acid chloride C=O (about 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is higher than the ester's (about 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>), not between the amide and ester.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Is the C=O conjugated with the ring (compare 1716 with about 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>)? Then read the splitting: what do two singlets say about the neighbors of the CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>?
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O). The C=O at 1716 cm−1 is a normal, nonconjugated ketone, and there is no aldehyde C–H (2820/2720 cm−1) or δ 9–10 signal. The 5H multiplet shows a monosubstituted ring. Both aliphatic signals are singlets, so the CH2 (δ 3.69, deshielded by both the ring and the C=O) and the CH3 (δ 2.15, a methyl ketone) have no H neighbors. The compound is 1-phenylpropan-2-one.
x: Propiophenone's C=O is conjugated with the ring (about 1688 cm<sup>−1</sup>), and its ethyl group would give a 2H quartet near δ 2.98 and a 3H triplet near δ 1.22.
2-Phenylpropanal is an aldehyde: it would show C–H bands near 2820 and 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a CHO doublet near δ 9.7, a 1H quartet and a 3H doublet.
4-Methylacetophenone is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets, not a 5H multiplet) and its conjugated C=O absorbs near 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the IR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Look for two bands just to the right of the sp<sup>3</sup> C–H region, near 2810 and 2715 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which functional group gives those plus a C=O?
w: There is a strong C=O at 1728 cm−1 and no O–H band. The pair of bands at 2810 and 2715 cm−1 is the aldehyde C–H stretch (a Fermi doublet), which ketones lack. A saturated aldehyde C=O is near 1730 cm−1, slightly above a ketone's 1715. The compound is pentanal.
x: Pentan-2-one has a C=O near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> but no aldehyde C–H, so the 2810/2715 cm<sup>−1</sup> pair would be missing.
Cyclopentanol has no C=O; it would show a strong, broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C–O band near 1050 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Pent-4-en-1-ol has no C=O; it would show a broad O–H near 3330 cm<sup>−1</sup>, =C–H above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a weak C=C near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 11.8 signal disappears after shaking with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: A very broad O–H band (3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>) plus a C=O near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup> points to one functional group. Then use the splitting to build the chain.
w: The extremely broad O–H (3300–2500 cm−1, from hydrogen-bonded dimers), the C=O at 1715 cm−1 and the exchangeable 1H at δ 11.8 identify a carboxylic acid. The rest is a propyl chain: CH3 triplet (δ 0.98), CH2 sextet (δ 1.68, five neighbors) and CH2 triplet next to C=O (δ 2.35). The compound is butanoic acid.
x: 2-Methylpropanoic acid would show a 1H septet near δ 2.58 and a 6H doublet near δ 1.20, not a triplet–sextet–triplet propyl pattern.
Ethyl acetate has no O–H: its ester C=O is near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and its NMR is a 2H quartet near δ 4.1, a 3H singlet near δ 2.0 and a 3H triplet.
1-Hydroxybutan-2-one has an alcohol O–H (a narrower band near 3450 cm<sup>−1</sup>, signal near δ 3), a 2H singlet near δ 4.25 and an ethyl quartet/triplet.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two 2H doublets point to one substitution pattern. Then compare the C=O wavenumber with ester and ketone values, and ask which ring H would be shifted upfield to δ 6.9.
w: Two 2H doublets in the aromatic region are the classic para-disubstituted pattern; ortho and meta isomers give four separate 1H aromatic signals. The C=O at 1685 cm−1 is a conjugated ketone, not an ester (about 1720 cm−1). The δ 6.93 doublet is upfield of benzene's δ 7.27, which fits H ortho to an electron-donating OCH3; the δ 7.93 doublet is ortho to the C=O. The 3H singlets are ArOCH3 (δ 3.87) and C(=O)CH3 (δ 2.55). The compound is 1-(4-methoxyphenyl)ethan-1-one (4-methoxyacetophenone).
x: Methyl 4-methylbenzoate is also para (two doublets) but is an ester: its C=O is near 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup>, its ring H are at δ 7.9 and 7.2 (no strong donor), and its ArCH<sub>3</sub> is near δ 2.40.
2-Methoxyacetophenone is ortho-disubstituted, so all four ring H differ and appear as four 1H signals, not two 2H doublets.
3-Methoxyacetophenone is meta-disubstituted; its four ring H are all different, including an isolated H between the groups, so it cannot give two 2H doublets.

q: Which technique would not readily distinguish pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one?
c: IR spectroscopy (position of the C=O stretch)
h: For each technique, predict what each ketone would give. Which one depends only on the functional group, which the two isomers share?
w: Both compounds are saturated, acyclic dialkyl ketones, so both show a C=O stretch near 1715 cm−1; IR cannot readily tell them apart. The other techniques can: pentan-3-one is symmetric and gives 3 13C signals while pentan-2-one gives 5; pentan-2-one has a CH3C=O singlet near δ 2.1 while pentan-3-one shows only a quartet and a triplet; and α-cleavage gives m/z 43 (CH3CO+) and 71 for pentan-2-one but m/z 57 (CH3CH2CO+) for pentan-3-one.
x: Pentan-3-one is symmetric (3 signals: C=O, CH<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>) while pentan-2-one has 5 different carbons, so <sup>13</sup>C NMR distinguishes them easily.
Pentan-2-one has a 3H singlet (CH<sub>3</sub>C=O near δ 2.1); pentan-3-one has no singlet at all, only a 4H quartet and a 6H triplet.
α-Cleavage gives different acylium ions: m/z 43 and 71 from pentan-2-one, m/z 57 from pentan-3-one, so the mass spectra differ.

q: A ketone C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O (IR 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>) gives the mass spectrum shown. Note the small even-mass peak at m/z 72. Which structure fits?
h: Find each candidate's two α-cleavage acylium ions and whether it has a γ-H for a McLafferty rearrangement (even-mass ion). Then match m/z 72, 71 and 57.
w: α-Cleavage of hexan-3-one (CH3CH2COCH2CH2CH3) loses a propyl radical to give CH3CH2CO+ (m/z 57) or an ethyl radical to give C3H7CO+ (m/z 71). The propyl chain has a γ-H, so a McLafferty rearrangement expels ethene (28) and gives the even-mass ion at m/z 100 − 28 = 72. The base peak, m/z 43, is the propyl cation C3H7+. Only hexan-3-one accounts for 57, 71 and 72 together.
x: 2-Methylpentan-3-one also gives m/z 57 and 71 by α-cleavage, but its isopropyl and ethyl groups have no γ-H, so it cannot form the McLafferty ion at m/z 72.
Hexan-2-one gives CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> (m/z 43) and C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> (m/z 85, absent here); its McLafferty ion (loss of propene) is at m/z 58, not 72.
3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one gives (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> at m/z 57 and m/z 85 and 43, but no m/z 71 and no McLafferty ion (the tert-butyl group has no γ-H).

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Br gives the 500 MHz <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. In each vinyl doublet (δ 7.11 and δ 6.78) the two lines are 0.028 ppm apart. Which structure fits?
h: Convert the line spacing to hertz with the spectrometer frequency (J = Δδ × MHz). Then compare with typical trans, cis and geminal vinyl couplings.
w: J = 0.028 ppm × 500 Hz/ppm = 14.0 Hz. Vinyl H trans to each other couple with J ≈ 12–18 Hz, cis with 6–12 Hz, geminal with 0–3 Hz, so 14.0 Hz is trans. The 5H multiplet shows a monosubstituted ring, so the compound is (E)-(2-bromovinyl)benzene ((E)-β-bromostyrene).
x: The (Z) isomer has a cis coupling of about 8 Hz. That value comes out only if 0.028 ppm is multiplied by 300 instead of the 500 MHz used here.
(1-Bromovinyl)benzene has both vinyl H on one carbon; geminal coupling is about 2 Hz, so its doublet lines would be only about 0.004 ppm apart.
4-Bromostyrene has a para-disubstituted ring (two 2H doublets, 4H total) and three vinyl H (a dd near δ 6.7 and two doublets near δ 5.7 and 5.3), not 5 aromatic H and 2 vinyl H.
