q: A compound C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Cl gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown, with DEPT results labeled. Which structure fits?
h: Count the signals each structure should give (symmetry), and use DEPT to decide whether the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon is CH<sub>3</sub> or CH<sub>2</sub>.
w: Five signals means symmetry: only the para isomer and benzyl chloride give 5. DEPT decides between them: the sp3 carbon at δ 20.8 is a CH3 (an ArCH3), not a CH2Cl, which would appear near δ 46. The aromatic region has two quaternary carbons (C–CH3 and C–Cl) and two CH signals of 2 C each. The compound is 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene (4-chlorotoluene).
x: Benzyl chloride also gives 5 signals, but its sp<sup>3</sup> carbon is a CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 46 and its ring has only one quaternary carbon (three CH signals).
2-Chlorotoluene has no symmetry, so all seven carbons differ (7 signals: 2 C and 4 CH aromatic plus CH<sub>3</sub>).
3-Chlorotoluene also has no symmetry plane through the ring, so it gives 7 <sup>13</sup>C signals.

q: Cyclohexanone is treated with the reagent shown. The product, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 1.53 multiplet contains overlapping signals). What is the product?
h: A Wittig reagent replaces C=O with C=C at exactly the carbonyl carbon. Which vinyl signal, and which IR band near 890 cm<sup>−1</sup>, would a C=CH<sub>2</sub> give?
w: The ylide adds to the C=O and the oxaphosphetane collapses to Ph3P=O and a C=C at the old carbonyl carbon, giving methylenecyclohexane. The spectra agree: no C=O or O–H band; =C–H at 3070 cm−1, C=C at 1650 cm−1 and the 890 cm−1 out-of-plane bend of a 1,1-disubstituted C=CH2; a 2H vinyl singlet at δ 4.58, 4 allylic H at δ 2.13 and the remaining 6 ring H at δ 1.53.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene has a trisubstituted C=C: one vinyl H near δ 5.4 (1H) and a 3H allylic methyl near δ 1.6, not a 2H vinyl singlet; the Wittig C=C forms exactly where the C=O was.
1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol is a Grignard (CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr) product; it would show a broad O–H near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a 3H singlet near δ 1.2 and no vinyl H.
Cyclohexanecarbaldehyde has C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O, a C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup>, aldehyde C–H bands near 2810/2710 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a CHO signal near δ 9.6.

q: Cyclohexanone is heated with ethane-1,2-diol and a catalytic amount of TsOH, with removal of water. The product (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. What is the product?
h: Removing water drives an equilibrium all the way to which carbonyl derivative? Check the IR for C=O and O–H, and ask what makes the four OCH<sub>2</sub> H a singlet.
w: Acid-catalyzed addition of a diol, with water removed, goes past the hemiketal to the cyclic ketal (dioxolane), 1,4-dioxaspiro[4.5]decane. The IR has no C=O (1715 cm−1) and no O–H, only C–O stretches at 1165 and 1110 cm−1. In the NMR the four OCH2CH2O H are equivalent (δ 3.94, 4H singlet) and the ten ring H appear at δ 1.60 and 1.40. This is the standard way to protect a ketone.
x: The hemiketal has C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and two O–H groups (broad IR near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>); with water removed the reaction goes on to the ketal.
The enol ether would show a vinyl H near δ 4.6, a C=C band near 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup> and an O–H band from the free CH<sub>2</sub>OH; its OCH<sub>2</sub> groups would be two triplets, not one singlet.
Unreacted cyclohexanone (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O) would show a strong C=O at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no signal near δ 3.9.

q: Cyclopentanone is treated with mCPBA. The product (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 1.88 multiplet contains two overlapping CH<sub>2</sub> signals). What is the product?
h: With a ketone, a peroxyacid inserts an O atom next to the C=O (Baeyer–Villiger). What new kind of CH<sub>2</sub> signal near δ 4.3 does that create?
w: In the Baeyer–Villiger oxidation the peroxyacid adds to C=O and an alkyl group migrates from carbon to oxygen, inserting O between the C=O and the ring carbon. A cyclic ketone becomes a lactone one atom larger: oxan-2-one (δ-valerolactone). The spectra fit: an ester C=O at 1745 cm−1 with a strong C–O at 1235 cm−1 and no O–H; a 2H triplet at δ 4.34 (CH2–O of the ester), a 2H triplet at δ 2.56 (CH2–C=O) and the two middle CH2 groups at δ 1.88.
x: 5-Hydroxypentanoic acid (the hydrolyzed lactone) is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and would show a very broad O–H band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a CH<sub>2</sub>OH near δ 3.6 and exchangeable H.
mCPBA epoxidizes C=C bonds, not C=O bonds; this spiro-epoxide (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O) has no C=O at all, and its ring CH<sub>2</sub> would appear near δ 2.7.
2-Hydroxycyclopentanone (α-hydroxylation) would show an O–H band near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a 1H CH(OH) signal near δ 4.0, not a 2H triplet.

q: Benzoyl chloride is treated as shown. The product gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. What is the product?
h: Both an O–CH<sub>2</sub> and a C(=O)–CH<sub>2</sub> give quartets. Where does each appear, and which C=O wavenumber matches an aryl ester versus an aryl ketone?
w: Ethanol attacks the acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution), Cl− leaves and pyridine takes up the HCl: the product is ethyl benzoate. The C=O drops from about 1775 cm−1 (acid chloride) to 1725 cm−1 (conjugated ester), with strong C–O bands at 1270 and 1105 cm−1. The CH2 quartet at δ 4.38 is on oxygen (an O–CH2 of an ester), and the 2H doublet at δ 8.05 shows ring H ortho to a C=O.
x: Propiophenone also has an ethyl quartet and triplet, but its CH<sub>2</sub> is on carbon next to C=O (δ ≈ 2.98, not 4.38) and its conjugated ketone C=O is near 1688 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Benzoic acid (from hydrolysis by water) would show a very broad O–H from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a δ 12 singlet, and it has no ethyl group.
Phenyl propanoate has the C=O on the ethyl side: its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is near δ 2.6, its phenyl ester C=O is near 1760 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and the ring H are not deshielded to δ 8.05.

q: Methyl 3-phenylpropanoate is treated as shown. The product (C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O) gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. What is the product?
h: At −78 °C, one equivalent of DIBAL-H gives a tetrahedral intermediate that survives until workup. Which δ 10 signal and IR pair near 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> would confirm the product?
w: DIBAL-H delivers one hydride to the ester; at −78 °C the aluminum-bound tetrahedral intermediate is stable and only releases the aldehyde on aqueous workup, so it is not reduced further. The product is 3-phenylpropanal. The spectra fit: aldehyde C–H at 2810/2710 cm−1, C=O at 1725 cm−1; CHO at δ 9.82 (a small triplet from the neighboring CH2), ArCH2 at δ 2.96 and CH2CHO at δ 2.78; the OCH3 singlet of the ester is gone.
x: 3-Phenylpropan-1-ol (from LiAlH<sub>4</sub> or excess DIBAL-H at higher temperature) has C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O, a broad O–H near 3330 cm<sup>−1</sup>, no C=O and a CH<sub>2</sub>OH triplet near δ 3.67.
Unreacted ester would show an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.67 and a C=O near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>, with no aldehyde C–H bands or δ 9.8 signal.
3-Phenylpropanoic acid would show a very broad O–H from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a broad δ 11–12 singlet; DIBAL-H reduces esters, it does not hydrolyze them.

q: Ethyl benzoate is treated with excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, then aqueous acid. The product (C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O) gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 1.80 signal disappears with D<sub>2</sub>O). What is the product?
h: How many equivalents of Grignard reagent does an ester consume, and why can't the reaction stop at the ketone? Then read the 6H singlet.
w: The first CH3MgBr adds to the ester C=O; the tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide to give acetophenone, which is more reactive than the ester and adds a second CH3MgBr at once. Acid workup gives the tertiary alcohol 2-phenylpropan-2-ol. The spectra fit: broad O–H at 3400 cm−1 and no C=O; a 6H singlet at δ 1.58 (two equivalent CH3 on a carbon with no H), an exchangeable OH at δ 1.80 and a monosubstituted ring.
x: Acetophenone cannot be isolated with excess Grignard reagent because the ketone reacts faster than the ester; it would also show a C=O near 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a 3H singlet near δ 2.6.
1-Phenylethanol would need a hydride, not a second methyl group; it would show a 1H quartet near δ 4.9 and a 3H doublet near δ 1.5, not a 6H singlet.
2-Phenylpropene (from dehydration) has no O–H; it would show two vinyl H near δ 5.4 and 5.1 and a 3H singlet near δ 2.15.

q: N,N-Dimethylbenzamide is reduced as shown. The product gives the IR spectrum (no bands above 3100 cm<sup>−1</sup> and none between 1650 and 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. What is the product?
h: In LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduction of an amide, which group leaves from the tetrahedral intermediate: the O (as an aluminate) or the NR<sub>2</sub>? What does that make before the second hydride adds?
w: Hydride adds to the amide C=O. In the tetrahedral intermediate the nitrogen lone pair pushes out the O–Al group (a better leaving group than R2N−), forming an iminium ion; a second hydride adds to it. The net change is C=O → CH2, giving N,N-dimethyl-1-phenylmethanamine (N,N-dimethylbenzylamine). The spectra fit: no C=O, no O–H or N–H (a 3° amine), C–H bands near 2820/2775 cm−1 typical of N–CH3/N–CH2, a 2H ArCH2N singlet at δ 3.42 and a 6H N(CH3)2 singlet at δ 2.24.
x: Benzyl alcohol would result if the amine left (as with esters), but R<sub>2</sub>N<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group; it would also show a broad O–H near 3330 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 4.65.
Benzaldehyde would show a C=O near 1700 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a CHO singlet near δ 10.0; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not stop at the aldehyde stage.
N-Methylbenzylamine would need loss of a methyl group, which LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not do; it would show an N–H band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and only a 3H N–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet.

q: Which carbocation is the most stable?
h: First ask whether the empty p orbital is next to a C=C. Then compare the carbons that share the charge in each resonance form.
w: An allylic cation spreads its charge over two carbons, and each alkyl group on those carbons adds more stabilization. In the 2-methylpent-3-en-2-yl cation the charge is shared by a tertiary carbon (C2) and a secondary carbon (C4), so both resonance forms are good ones. The other ions are either not conjugated or have their charge partly on a primary carbon.
x: This cation is tertiary, but the C=C is two carbons away (not allylic), so the charge cannot be delocalized; one resonance form only.
This cation is allylic, but its second resonance form puts the charge on a primary CH<sub>2</sub>, so the hybrid is a 2°/1° mix, weaker than a 3°/2° mix.
The C=C is separated from the cationic carbon by a CH<sub>2</sub>, so this is a plain secondary cation with no resonance stabilization.

q: Rank these benzylic chlorides from slowest to fastest S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis in aqueous ethanol.
h: The rate-determining step makes the carbocation. Ask how each group changes the stability of that cation.
w: SN1 rate follows carbocation stability. The benzyl cation from II is delocalized into one ring. In III the cation is shared over two rings (diphenylmethyl cation), so it forms much faster. In I the para nitro group withdraws electron density by induction and resonance, and one resonance form would put positive charge next to the positive nitro nitrogen, so that cation is destabilized and forms slowest. Order: I < II < III.
x: This is the reverse order; it treats the nitro group as stabilizing and the second ring as destabilizing.
This puts I ahead of II, but an electron-withdrawing nitro group slows cation formation compared with the unsubstituted benzyl chloride.
This misplaces III: a cation delocalized over two benzene rings is more stable than the simple benzyl cation, so III is fastest.

q: Which chloride reacts fastest with NaI in acetone (an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction)?
h: In the S<sub>N</sub>2 transition state the carbon under attack has a p-like orbital. What could overlap with it?
w: 3-Chloropropene (allyl chloride) is a primary halide whose SN2 transition state is lowered by overlap of the adjacent π bond with the partly formed and partly broken bonds, so allylic halides react much faster than ordinary primary halides.
x: 1-Chloropropane is primary and unhindered, but it has no π bond to stabilize the transition state, so it is slower than allyl chloride.
A vinylic chloride does not undergo S<sub>N</sub>2: backside attack is blocked by the π system and the C–Cl bond is stronger.
2-Chloropropane is secondary, so backside attack is more hindered than at a primary allylic carbon.

q: What is the major product of this dehydration?
h: E1 gives the most stable alkene. Which possible C=C can also be conjugated with the ring?
w: Protonation and loss of water give a secondary cation at C2. Losing a proton from the benzylic CH2 forms a C=C conjugated with the benzene ring, which is the most stable alkene available; the E isomer avoids the phenyl–methyl clash. The major product is (E)-1-phenylprop-1-ene.
x: The Z isomer is conjugated too, but the phenyl and methyl groups crowd each other on the same side, so the E isomer is favored under equilibrating E1 conditions.
Allylbenzene comes from removing a CH<sub>3</sub> proton; its C=C is monosubstituted and not conjugated with the ring, so it is a minor product.
2-Phenylpropene would need the phenyl to end up on C2, which this cation cannot reach without an unfavorable shift; it is not formed here.

q: 2,3-Dimethyl-1,3-butadiene reacts with one equivalent of Br2 at 40 °C, conditions where the products equilibrate. What is the major product? (The 1,4-adduct is drawn as its E isomer.)
h: Br<sup>+</sup> adds to a terminal carbon; the intermediate is allylic. Under equilibrium control, which product has the more substituted C=C?
w: Bromine adds at C1, giving an allylic cation (or bromonium ion) whose charge is shared by C2 and C4. Bromide can attack C2 (1,2-addition) or C4 (1,4-addition). At 40 °C the products equilibrate, so the more stable one dominates: the 1,4-adduct has a tetrasubstituted C=C (1,4-dibromo-2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene), while the 1,2-adduct keeps only a 1,1-disubstituted C=C.
x: This 1,2-adduct is favored at low temperature (kinetic control) but is less stable, so at 40 °C it converts to the 1,4-adduct.
The tetrabromide needs a second equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub>; with one equivalent the diene adds only once.
This allylic substitution product comes from radical bromination (NBS, light), not from Br<sub>2</sub> addition in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>.

q: (E)-Penta-1,3-diene reacts with one equivalent of HBr at −78 °C. What is the major product? (Ignore stereochemistry.)
h: Find the protonation site that gives the best allylic cation, then add Br<sup>−</sup> at each carbon that shares the charge. Compare the two products carefully.
w: Protonation at terminal C1 gives an allylic cation shared by C2 and C4, and both of these carbons are secondary, so this is the best cation. Bromide attack at C2 (1,2-addition) gives CH3CHBr–CH=CH–CH3; attack at C4 (1,4-addition) gives CH3CH=CH–CHBr–CH3, which is the same compound. So the kinetic and thermodynamic paths both give 4-bromopent-2-ene.
x: 3-Bromopent-1-ene comes from protonating C4, which gives an allylic cation shared by a secondary and a primary carbon; that cation is less stable.
1-Bromopent-2-ene is the 1,4-product of the same less stable cation (protonation at C4), with bromide on the primary carbon.
4-Bromopent-1-ene comes from protonating C3, giving a secondary cation that is not allylic; the diene reacts through the conjugated cation instead.

q: Which of these species are aromatic? (Assume each ring can be planar.)
h: For each ring check two things: does every ring atom have a p orbital, and is the π-electron count 4n+2?
w: I, pyrazole: every ring atom is sp2; the N–H nitrogen gives its lone pair to the π system and the other N gives one electron from its C=N bond, for 6 π electrons: aromatic (true). II, 4H-pyran: the CH2 carbon is sp3, so the cycle of p orbitals is broken: nonaromatic (false). III, the cyclononatetraenyl anion: four C=C bonds (8 electrons) plus the carbanion lone pair give 10 π electrons in a ring of nine p orbitals, a 4n+2 number (n = 2): aromatic (true). Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the anion has 10 π electrons (four C=C plus the lone pair), a Hückel number, so it is aromatic.
This misjudges I: pyrazole has 6 π electrons in a planar ring of five p orbitals, the same count as pyrrole.
This misjudges II: the sp3 CH2 interrupts the ring of p orbitals, so 4H-pyran cannot be aromatic.

q: Purine (shown) is the parent ring system of adenine and guanine. How many electrons are in its delocalized π system?
h: Count two electrons for each ring C=C or C=N. Then decide which nitrogen lone pairs are in p orbitals and which lie in the ring plane.
w: Purine has four double bonds in the fused rings (8 π electrons). The N–H nitrogen of the five-membered ring is pyrrole-like: its lone pair sits in a p orbital and adds 2 more. The other three nitrogens are pyridine-like: each is already in a C=N bond and its lone pair lies in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane. Total: 10 π electrons, a 4n+2 number, so purine is aromatic.
x: 8 counts only the double bonds and leaves out the N–H lone pair, which lies in a p orbital and is part of the π system.
12 adds a lone pair from a pyridine-like nitrogen as well; those lone pairs are sp<sup>2</sup> and lie in the ring plane, outside the π system.
16 counts every nitrogen lone pair; only the N–H nitrogen's lone pair is in a p orbital.

q: For the heptatrienyl anion shown (7 conjugated carbons), which π molecular orbital is the HOMO, and what kind of orbital is it?
h: Seven p orbitals give seven π MOs. With an odd number, the middle one is special. Then count the π electrons.
w: Seven p orbitals combine into seven π MOs: ψ1–ψ3 bonding, ψ4 nonbonding (the middle MO of an odd system), and ψ5–ψ7 antibonding. The anion has 8 π electrons (three C=C plus the lone pair), which fill ψ1 through ψ4. So the HOMO is ψ4, a nonbonding MO.
x: ψ<sub>3</sub> would be the HOMO of the 6-electron cation; the anion has two more electrons, which go into ψ<sub>4</sub>.
ψ<sub>5</sub> is the LUMO of the anion; it is empty in the ground state.
ψ<sub>4</sub> is the HOMO, but in an odd-numbered chain the middle MO is nonbonding, not antibonding.

q: Use a Frost circle (inscribed polygon) for the planar cyclopropenyl anion, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>. Which description of its π electrons is correct?
c: Two electrons fill the single bonding MO, and the other two occupy a degenerate pair of antibonding MOs, one electron in each, so it is antiaromatic
Four electrons fill two degenerate bonding MOs, so it is aromatic
Two electrons fill the bonding MO and two fill a nonbonding MO, so it is nonaromatic like the allyl anion
Two electrons fill the bonding MO and two are paired in one antibonding MO, so it is aromatic
h: Put a vertex of the triangle at the bottom of the circle. Where do the other two vertices fall relative to the center line?
w: With one vertex down, the triangle gives one MO below the center (bonding) and a degenerate pair above the center (antibonding); there is no nonbonding level. The anion has 4 π electrons (one C=C plus the lone pair). Two fill the bonding MO; the last two go into the degenerate antibonding pair, one in each by Hund's rule. A 4n count with unpaired electrons in antibonding orbitals means the planar anion is antiaromatic, which is why the cyclopropenyl anion is very hard to form.
x: A triangle has only one MO below the center line; the degenerate pair lies above it, so they are antibonding, not bonding.
A three-membered ring has no nonbonding level on its Frost circle; the open-chain allyl anion does, but the cyclic ion does not.
The two antibonding MOs are degenerate, so Hund's rule puts one electron in each; and 4 π electrons in a cyclic system is antiaromatic, not aromatic.

q: Rank these phenols from weakest to strongest acid.
h: Draw the resonance forms of each phenoxide. Can the negative charge reach the carbon bearing the nitro group?
w: A nitro group stabilizes the phenoxide. From the meta position (II) it works only by induction, so 3-nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 8.4) is more acidic than phenol (≈ 10.0). From the para position (III) the ring carbon bearing NO2 carries negative charge in one resonance form, so the charge can move onto the nitro oxygens; 4-nitrophenol (≈ 7.2) is the strongest acid. Order: I < II < III.
x: This makes 3-nitrophenol weaker than phenol, but the electron-withdrawing nitro group stabilizes the phenoxide even from the meta position.
This swaps II and III: only a para (or ortho) nitro group can accept the negative charge by resonance, so the para isomer is more acidic.
This is the reverse order; electron-withdrawing groups increase phenol acidity.

q: 1,3-Butadiene is heated with dimethyl maleate (the Z diester shown). Which description of the Diels–Alder product is correct?
c: The two ester groups are cis, and the product is a meso compound (optically inactive)
The two ester groups are trans, and the product forms as a racemic mixture
The two ester groups are cis, and the product forms as a racemic mixture of two enantiomers
A 1:1 mixture of cis and trans products forms because the cycloaddition is stepwise
h: Dienophile geometry is kept in the product. Then check whether the cis product has an internal mirror plane.
w: The Diels–Alder reaction is concerted and suprafacial on the dienophile, so the two groups that were cis on the alkene end up cis on the new ring: dimethyl cis-cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylate. Its two stereocenters are R and S, and a mirror plane passes between them, so the cis product is meso and optically inactive.
x: Trans esters would come from dimethyl fumarate, the E isomer; the cis geometry of maleate is kept.
The cis diester has a mirror plane (R,S), so it is a single meso compound, not a pair of enantiomers.
The reaction is concerted, so there is no intermediate that could rotate and scramble the geometry.

q: The allylic cation I is converted to its resonance form II. Which curved arrow correctly shows this?
h: Arrows start where electrons are (a bond or lone pair) and move toward the electron-poor atom. A positive carbon has no electrons to give.
w: The π electrons of C1=C2 shift to become a π bond between C2 and C3, the empty p orbital. C3 becomes neutral and C1 is left with the positive charge, giving II. So one arrow from the C1=C2 π bond to the C2–C3 bond is correct.
x: This arrow starts at the positive carbon, which has no electrons to move; arrows must begin at a bond or lone pair.
Moving the π electrons onto C1 would make C1 a carbanion, not move the positive charge; it does not give II.
This moves the C2–C3 σ bond; resonance forms move only π electrons and lone pairs, never σ bonds.

q: What is the hybridization of the nitrogen in pyrrole, and where is its lone pair?
c: sp<sup>2</sup>; the lone pair is in a p orbital
sp<sup>3</sup>; the lone pair is in an sp<sup>3</sup> orbital
sp<sup>2</sup>; the lone pair is in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital
sp; the lone pair is in a p orbital
h: Pyrrole is aromatic with 6 π electrons, but it has only two C=C bonds.
w: Pyrrole needs the nitrogen lone pair to complete its 6 π electrons (two C=C bonds give 4). For the lone pair to overlap with the ring p orbitals, nitrogen is sp2 with its lone pair in a p orbital; its three sp2 orbitals form the bonds to two carbons and H.
x: An sp<sup>3</sup> nitrogen would break the ring of p orbitals; pyrrole is planar and aromatic, so N is sp<sup>2</sup>.
This describes pyridine's nitrogen, whose lone pair lies in the ring plane; pyrrole's N–H uses all three sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals for σ bonds.
An sp nitrogen would be linear; the nitrogen in a five-membered ring is trigonal planar.

q: Which compound contains a conjugated π system?
h: Conjugated π bonds are separated by exactly one single bond, so their p orbitals line up side by side.
w: In but-3-en-2-one the C=C and C=O are joined by one single bond, so four p orbitals overlap in a row: a conjugated system.
x: The CH<sub>2</sub> between the C=C and C=O is sp<sup>3</sup>, so the two π bonds are isolated.
In an allene the two π bonds share a carbon and are perpendicular (cumulated), so they do not overlap with each other.
In cyclohexa-1,4-diene each pair of C=C bonds is separated by an sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>, so they are isolated.

q:
Which statements about the s-cis and s-trans conformations of 1,3-butadiene are correct?
I. The s-trans conformation is lower in energy.
II. The two interconvert by rotation about the C2–C3 single bond.
III. They are separate isomers that can be isolated at room temperature.
h: These are conformations, not configurations. How large is the barrier to rotation about the central bond?
w: I is true: in s-cis the inner hydrogens on C1 and C4 crowd each other, so s-trans is more stable. II is true: the 's' means rotation about the single (σ) bond C2–C3. III is false: the barrier is only about 25 kJ/mol, so they interconvert rapidly at room temperature and cannot be separated. Answer: I and II only.
x: This rejects II, but s-cis and s-trans differ only by rotation about the C2–C3 σ bond.
This rejects I and accepts III; s-trans is lower in energy, and the low rotation barrier means the forms cannot be isolated.
This accepts III, but conformers with a small rotation barrier interconvert many times per second at room temperature.

q: Rank these amines from least basic to most basic.
h: Basicity depends on how available the nitrogen lone pair is. Is it delocalized into a ring, and does the para group push or pull?
w: IV, cyclohexylamine, has a localized sp3 lone pair (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 10.6): most basic. In the anilines the lone pair is delocalized into the ring. The para methyl group of III donates a little density (pKa ≈ 5.1), so III is slightly more basic than aniline II (≈ 4.6). In I the para nitro group pulls the lone pair onto its oxygens by resonance (≈ 1.0), so I is least basic. Order: I < II < III < IV.
x: This makes 4-nitroaniline more basic than aniline, but the nitro group withdraws the lone pair by resonance, making it much less available.
This puts p-toluidine above cyclohexylamine; any aryl amine is far weaker as a base than an alkylamine because its lone pair is delocalized.
This is the reverse order; delocalizing the lone pair (and adding an electron-withdrawing group) lowers basicity.

q: Which labeled hydrogen-bearing carbon is the most acidic site in this compound?
c: All three are about equally acidic
h: Draw each conjugate base. Which one becomes aromatic?
w: Removing H from carbon b, the sp3 carbon of the cyclopentadiene ring, gives a cyclopentadienyl anion: a planar ring with 6 π electrons, which is aromatic. This makes that C–H unusually acidic (pKa about 16–18). The terminal alkyne C–H on a has pKa ≈ 25, and the CH2 on c is far less acidic. So carbon b is the most acidic site.
x: A terminal alkyne C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is acidic because of sp character, but the aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion is about a million times more stable.
The CH2 carbon is next to the alkyne and the ring, but its anion is not aromatic, so it is much less acidic than b.
The three sites differ by many pKa units because only the anion at b is aromatic.

q: (E)-1-Chlorobut-2-ene is warmed in ethanol (SN1 conditions). Which statement best describes the substitution products?
c: Only 1-ethoxybut-2-ene forms, because ethanol attacks the carbon that lost the chloride
Only 3-ethoxybut-1-ene forms, because the C=C cannot move
Only 2-ethoxybutane forms, after the C=C is protonated
h: Draw the cation formed when Cl<sup>−</sup> leaves, and then draw its resonance form.
w: Ionization gives an allylic cation whose positive charge is shared by C1 and C3. Ethanol can trap either carbon: at C1 it gives 1-ethoxybut-2-ene, at C3 it gives 3-ethoxybut-1-ene (an "allylic rearrangement" product). So a mixture of both ethers forms.
x: The S<sub>N</sub>1 intermediate is a delocalized cation, so the nucleophile is not limited to the carbon that held the chlorine.
The C=C does move in the resonance form; attack at C3 gives this product, but attack at C1 gives the other ether too.
No HCl adds to the C=C here; the reaction goes through the allylic cation and keeps a C=C in each product.

q: Oxepin (shown) has a seven-membered ring with three C=C bonds and an oxygen. It is not planar, and it reacts as an ordinary triene. What is the best explanation?
c: If it were planar with an oxygen lone pair in the π system, it would have 8 π electrons and be antiaromatic, so the ring puckers to avoid this
It has 6 π electrons and would be aromatic, but ring strain in a seven-membered ring prevents planarity
The oxygen is sp<sup>3</sup> in any geometry, so the ring can never have a continuous set of p orbitals
It would have 10 π electrons if planar, but oxygen is too electronegative to share both lone pairs
h: Count the π electrons if one oxygen lone pair joined the three C=C bonds in a planar ring.
w: Three C=C bonds give 6 π electrons; if the ring were planar, one oxygen lone pair would overlap with them, for 8 π electrons in a cyclic array: a 4n count, which would be antiaromatic. A flexible seven-membered ring can avoid this by bending into a boat, which breaks the cyclic overlap, so oxepin puckers to escape antiaromaticity and behaves as a nonaromatic triene.
x: With the oxygen lone pair included the count is 8, not 6; and seven-membered rings (as in the tropylium ion) can be planar when that is favorable.
An ether oxygen next to a C=C can rehybridize to sp<sup>2</sup>, as it does in furan; geometry, not a fixed sp<sup>3</sup> oxygen, is what decides.
Only one oxygen lone pair can lie in a p orbital, so the count would be 8, not 10.

q: Which reagents convert benzene into chlorobenzene?
h: Benzene is a weak nucleophile. What makes chlorine electrophilic enough to attack the ring?
w: Electrophilic aromatic chlorination needs a Lewis acid. FeCl3 binds Cl2 and polarizes it so the terminal Cl is strongly electrophilic; the ring attacks, the arenium ion loses H+, and aromaticity is restored. Cl2/FeCl3 is the reagent.
x: Light makes chlorine radicals; with benzene this leads to radical addition across the ring (hexachlorocyclohexane), not substitution.
HCl does not add to benzene: adding H<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> would destroy the aromatic ring, and there is no electrophilic chlorine.
Chloride is a nucleophile, and the electron-rich benzene ring does not react with nucleophiles.

q: Excess benzene is treated with 1-chloro-3-methylbutane and AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What is the major monoalkylation product?
h: A primary halide with AlCl<sub>3</sub> behaves like a primary carbocation. Follow hydride shifts until the cation cannot get more stable.
w: The AlCl3 complex of the primary chloride rearranges by a 1,2-hydride shift to the secondary cation at C2, and a second 1,2-hydride shift moves the charge to C3, which carries two methyls (a tertiary cation). Benzene traps this tertiary cation, so the major product is (2-methylbutan-2-yl)benzene (tert-pentylbenzene).
x: This keeps the original primary carbon skeleton; Friedel–Crafts alkylation with a primary halide rearranges before the ring attacks.
This product comes from stopping at the secondary cation; one more hydride shift gives a more stable tertiary cation.
(2-Methylbutyl)benzene would need a methyl shift that still leaves a primary carbon on the ring; the hydride shifts lead to a tertiary cation instead.

q: 4'-Methoxyacetophenone is nitrated with one equivalent of HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Find the positions ortho to OCH<sub>3</sub> and the positions meta to the acetyl group. Do the two groups agree?
w: OCH3 is a strong activating ortho/para director; its para position is taken, so it directs ortho. The acetyl group is a deactivating meta director, and its meta positions are the same carbons ortho to OCH3. The effects reinforce, giving 1-(4-methoxy-3-nitrophenyl)ethanone.
x: Ortho to the acetyl group is meta to OCH<sub>3</sub>; both groups disfavor this position.
With one equivalent of HNO<sub>3</sub>, and with the first nitro group deactivating the ring, the second nitration does not occur under these conditions.
Nitronium ion attacks the aromatic π system, not the CH<sub>3</sub> of the ketone; there is no α-nitration under EAS conditions.

q: How many constitutional isomers are possible for a benzene ring carrying one Br, one Cl and one NO<sub>2</sub> group (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>3</sub>BrClNO<sub>2</sub>)?
h: Sort them by pattern: 1,2,3-, 1,2,4- and 1,3,5-. In each pattern, how many different ways can three different groups be placed?
w: With three different groups: in the 1,2,3 pattern any of the three can be in the middle (3 isomers). In the 1,2,4 pattern any of the three can be at the isolated position 4, and the other two can be swapped between positions 1 and 2 (3 × 2 = 6 isomers). In the 1,3,5 pattern all arrangements are the same (1 isomer). Total: 3 + 6 + 1 = 10.
x: 6 is the count when two of the groups are the same (e.g., C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>3</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>Br); with three different groups the 1,2,4 pattern gives twice as many.
3 counts only the substitution patterns (1,2,3-, 1,2,4-, 1,3,5-), not the different ways the groups are placed in each one.
12 overcounts: rotating or flipping the ring can make some arrangements identical, especially in the 1,2,3 and 1,3,5 patterns.

q: Benzenesulfonic acid is heated in dilute aqueous H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> with steam. What is the main organic product?
h: Sulfonation is reversible. Which direction is favored with lots of water and little SO<sub>3</sub>?
w: Sulfonation is an equilibrium. In concentrated or fuming H2SO4 (high SO3) the sulfonic acid forms; in hot dilute acid, H+ adds to the ring carbon bearing SO3H and SO3 leaves (protodesulfonation), giving benzene. This is why SO3H works as a removable blocking group.
x: Phenol is made from sulfonates only by fusion with NaOH at very high temperature, not with dilute aqueous acid.
A second sulfonation needs high SO<sub>3</sub> concentration (fuming acid); dilute aqueous acid drives sulfonation backward.
Diphenyl sulfone is a by-product of sulfonation in concentrated acid; it does not form in dilute aqueous acid.

q: 4-Bromo-1-fluoro-2-nitrobenzene is stirred with excess dimethylamine in ethanol at 25 °C. What is the major product?
h: S<sub>N</sub>Ar needs the leaving group ortho or para to a nitro group. Check where each halogen is relative to NO<sub>2</sub>, and recall which halide is best for S<sub>N</sub>Ar.
w: Addition–elimination is fastest at a carbon ortho or para to NO2, because the Meisenheimer anion can put its charge on the nitro oxygens. F is ortho to NO2; Br is meta to it, so the bromine is not activated. Fluoride is also the best SNAr leaving group because its electronegativity speeds the rate-determining addition step. The product is N,N-dimethyl-4-bromo-2-nitroaniline.
x: Bromine is meta to the nitro group, so the anion from attack there cannot be delocalized onto NO<sub>2</sub>; that carbon is not activated.
Nitrite is rarely displaced when an activated fluoride is present; the C–F carbon ortho to NO<sub>2</sub> reacts instead.
Only the fluorine is activated; the meta bromine stays even with excess amine at room temperature.

q: 1-Bromo-3-(trifluoromethyl)benzene is treated with NaNH<sub>2</sub> in liquid NH<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Nothing activates S<sub>N</sub>Ar here, so think benzyne. Which ortho H is most acidic, and which way does NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> add so the carbanion sits next to CF<sub>3</sub>?
w: Amide removes the most acidic ortho proton, the one on C2 between Br and the inductively withdrawing CF3; loss of Br− gives a benzyne between C1 and C2. NH2− then adds to C1 so that the aryl anion forms on C2, right next to CF3, where induction stabilizes it best. Protonation gives 3-(trifluoromethyl)aniline.
x: The para isomer would need a benzyne between C1 and C6 with attack at C6; that route uses a less acidic proton and is minor.
Here NH<sub>2</sub> ends up next to CF<sub>3</sub>, which means the anion formed on the carbon away from CF<sub>3</sub>; that is the less stabilized anion.
Amide does not add to a ring that has no activating group while keeping the bromine; the reaction goes through elimination of HBr first.

q: What is the final organic product of this sequence?
h: Follow each step: diazotization, then a Sandmeyer reaction, then what does hot aqueous acid do to the new group?
w: Step 1 converts the ArNH2 into the arenediazonium salt ArN2+. Step 2, the Sandmeyer reaction with CuCN, replaces N2 with C≡N to give 4-methylbenzonitrile. Step 3 hydrolyzes the nitrile to a carboxylic acid, giving 4-methylbenzoic acid.
x: This is the product after step 2; hot aqueous acid in step 3 hydrolyzes the nitrile to COOH.
Phenols form when a diazonium salt is warmed in water without CuCN; here the cyanide is introduced first.
Nothing in the sequence oxidizes the methyl group, and the amino group is replaced in steps 1–2, not kept.

q: Which sequence converts 4-methylaniline into 1,3-dibromo-5-methylbenzene (3,5-dibromotoluene)?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub> (2 equiv), CH<sub>3</sub>COOH  2. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  3. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
1. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  2. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (2 equiv), FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub> (2 equiv), CH<sub>3</sub>COOH  2. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  3. CuBr
1. Br<sub>2</sub> (2 equiv), CH<sub>3</sub>COOH  2. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  3. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
h: The two bromines must end up meta to CH<sub>3</sub>. Which group in the starting material directs there, and how can you remove it afterward?
w: NH2 is the strongest director present; its para position is blocked by CH3, so Br2 goes to both positions ortho to NH2, which are meta to CH3. Diazotization and H3PO2 then replace N2+ with H, removing the directing group. The sequence Br2; NaNO2/HCl; H3PO2 gives 3,5-dibromotoluene.
x: Removing NH<sub>2</sub> first gives toluene, whose CH<sub>3</sub> directs bromine ortho/para, giving 2,4-dibromotoluene rather than the 3,5-isomer.
CuBr replaces the diazonium group with a third Br, giving 1,2,3-tribromo-5-methylbenzene instead of removing it.
Warming the diazonium salt in water replaces N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> with OH, giving 2,6-dibromo-4-methylphenol.

q: Which of these compounds are nitrated mainly at the meta position?
h: Look at the atom bonded directly to the ring. Does it carry a lone pair it can donate, or is it attached to electronegative atoms by multiple bonds?
w: I: the ring is bonded to sulfur of SO3H, which carries a strong partial positive charge and has no lone pair to donate: meta director (true). II: the ring is bonded to the carbonyl carbon of an amide (C(=O)NHCH3), which withdraws by resonance like any acyl group: meta director (true). III: the ring is bonded to the nitrogen of an acetamido group; its lone pair donates into the ring (less than in NH2), so it is an ortho/para director (false). Answer: I and II only.
x: This misjudges II: an amide attached through its carbonyl carbon is an electron-withdrawing acyl group and directs meta.
This confuses II and III: III is attached through nitrogen (donor, o/p), while I is a meta director.
This misjudges III: an –NHCOCH<sub>3</sub> group donates its nitrogen lone pair into the ring and directs ortho/para.

q: The arenium ion (σ complex) formed when NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> attacks benzene is shown with one resonance form. Which labeled carbons share the positive charge in the resonance hybrid?
h: Push the π electrons of each C=C toward the positive carbon and see where the charge moves.
w: Moving the Ca=Cb π bond toward Cc puts the charge on a; moving Cd=Ce toward Cc puts it on e. The positive charge is shared by a, c, and e, the carbons ortho and para to the sp3 carbon. This is why groups already on the ring at those positions can stabilize or destabilize the σ complex.
x: The carbons meta to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon never carry the charge in any resonance form.
The drawn form shows the charge on c, but two more resonance forms place it on a and e.
Only alternating carbons carry the charge; b and d do not.

q: Which sequence gives 2-chloro-4-nitrobenzoic acid from toluene?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate para)  2. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  3. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>
1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub> (separate para)  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate para)  2. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  3. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>
h: In the target, NO<sub>2</sub> is para and Cl is ortho to the carbon that was CH<sub>3</sub>. Which steps need the ortho/para-directing CH<sub>3</sub> still in place?
w: Nitrating toluene puts NO2 para to CH3. In 4-nitrotoluene, CH3 directs ortho to itself and NO2 directs meta to itself, and these are the same carbon, so chlorination gives 2-chloro-4-nitrotoluene. KMnO4 then oxidizes CH3 to COOH. The correct order is nitrate, chlorinate, then oxidize.
x: Oxidizing first gives benzoic acid, a meta director, so nitration puts NO<sub>2</sub> meta to COOH, not para.
In 4-chlorotoluene, nitration goes ortho to CH<sub>3</sub> (the stronger director), giving 4-chloro-2-nitrotoluene and then 4-chloro-2-nitrobenzoic acid, the wrong isomer.
In 4-nitrobenzoic acid both groups are meta directors; chlorination goes meta to COOH (ortho to NO<sub>2</sub>), giving 3-chloro-4-nitrobenzoic acid.

q: In aromatic sulfonation, benzene attacks SO<sub>3</sub> to form the σ complex. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: The ring π bond is the nucleophile. Sulfur is the electrophilic atom. When a new bond forms to sulfur, which bond must break?
w: A ring π bond (C1=C2) attacks the electron-poor sulfur, and at the same time one S=O π bond moves onto oxygen as a lone pair, giving the σ complex with an –SO3− group and a positive charge in the ring. So the correct drawing is ring π bond → S, and S=O π bond → O.
x: This shows oxygen attacking the ring. The aromatic ring is the nucleophile here and sulfur is the electrophile, not the reverse.
This attacks oxygen instead of sulfur; the electron-poor atom of SO<sub>3</sub> is sulfur, and the new C–S bond is what forms.
This pushes an oxygen lone pair toward sulfur while the ring also attacks it, adding electrons to sulfur twice; an S=O π bond must instead move onto oxygen.

q: Furan reacts with acetic anhydride and BF<sub>3</sub> to give one main acetylfuran. Where does substitution occur, and why?
c: At C2, because the σ complex from C2 attack has three resonance forms, including one with the charge on oxygen
At C3, because attack there keeps the positive charge away from the electronegative oxygen
At C2, because C2 is the most electron-poor carbon of the ring
At oxygen, because its lone pairs are the most nucleophilic site
h: Draw the σ complex for attack at C2 and at C3. How many resonance forms can you draw for each, and can oxygen share the charge?
w: Attack at C2 gives a cation delocalized over C3, C5 and the ring oxygen (three resonance forms; the oxonium form has every atom with an octet). Attack at C3 gives a cation shared only by C2 and the oxygen (two forms). The more delocalized intermediate forms faster, so furan, like pyrrole and thiophene, reacts at C2, through the σ complex with three resonance forms, giving 2-acetylfuran.
x: Placing positive charge on oxygen is actually stabilizing here, because the oxonium form gives every atom an octet; C3 attack has fewer resonance forms and is slower.
C2 is the most nucleophilic carbon of furan, not the most electron-poor; electrophiles attack where the ring is electron-rich.
Furan's oxygen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet; acylation at oxygen would destroy aromaticity and is not observed.

q: Which aryl chloride reacts fastest with NaOCH<sub>3</sub> in hot methanol by addition–elimination?
h: In S<sub>N</sub>Ar the anionic intermediate needs somewhere to put its charge. Can a ring atom accept it?
w: Addition of methoxide to the C–Cl carbon makes an anionic intermediate whose charge sits on the carbons ortho and para to the site of attack. In 4-chloropyridine the ring nitrogen is para to that carbon, so one resonance form puts the negative charge on the electronegative nitrogen, much like a para nitro group; it reacts readily.
x: In 3-chloropyridine the nitrogen is meta to the C–Cl carbon, so the anion cannot place its charge on nitrogen; it reacts far more slowly.
Chlorobenzene has no group to stabilize the anionic intermediate and does not undergo addition–elimination under these conditions.
The methyl group donates electron density and makes the anion even less stable; 4-chlorotoluene is unreactive.

q: What is the final product of this sequence?
h: Acetylation tames the amine. Where does the acetamido group direct the nitro group? Then follow the nitrogen through the diazonium step.
w: Acetylation gives acetanilide, whose NHCOCH3 is a moderate ortho/para director and is bulky, so nitration goes mainly para. Acid hydrolysis frees the amine (4-nitroaniline). Diazotization and the Sandmeyer reaction with CuBr replace N2+ with Br, giving 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene.
x: The meta product forms when free aniline is nitrated in strong acid (as the anilinium ion); acetylation prevents this and gives the para isomer.
This is the product after step 3; steps 4 and 5 convert the NH<sub>2</sub> to a diazonium salt and then to Br.
A phenol forms when the diazonium salt is heated in water; CuBr instead delivers bromide.

q: Benzene reacts with succinic anhydride and AlCl<sub>3</sub>, followed by aqueous workup. What is the product?
h: An anhydride is an acylating agent. After one carbonyl acylates the ring, what happens to the other end of the anhydride?
w: AlCl3 opens the cyclic anhydride to an acylium ion. Benzene attacks it (Friedel–Crafts acylation), and the other carbonyl ends up as a carboxylate that is protonated on workup. The product is the keto acid 4-oxo-4-phenylbutanoic acid. The new ketone deactivates the ring, so it reacts only once.
x: Nothing reduces the ketone; a separate Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner step would be needed to make 4-phenylbutanoic acid.
1-Indanone has only a two-carbon chain between the ring and the ketone and no carboxylic acid; the four-carbon anhydride acylates once and leaves the acid end free.
The second carbonyl ends up as a carboxylic acid, which does not acylate benzene under these conditions.

q: Toluene is sulfonated with SO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, and the para product is isolated. How many signals does its <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum show?
h: Use the mirror plane through the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon and the C–S carbon.
w: 4-Methylbenzenesulfonic acid has a mirror plane through C1 and C4. The two carbons ortho to CH3 are equivalent, and so are the two ortho to SO3H. Signals: CH3, C1, C2/C6, C3/C5 and C4: 5 signals.
x: 7 counts every carbon separately; symmetry makes the two pairs of ring CH carbons equivalent.
4 leaves out one carbon type; the two ipso carbons (bearing CH<sub>3</sub> and SO<sub>3</sub>H) are different from each other.
6 would fit an ortho or meta isomer with partial symmetry; the para isomer has two equivalent pairs, giving 5.

q: Dichloromethane is added to a large excess of benzene containing AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What is the main organic product?
h: Each C–Cl bond can alkylate a ring. Is the first product, a benzyl chloride, still a Friedel–Crafts alkylating agent?
w: The first alkylation gives benzyl chloride. A benzylic chloride ionizes even more easily with AlCl3 (resonance-stabilized benzyl cation), so it alkylates a second benzene. With excess benzene the product is diphenylmethane, Ph–CH2–Ph.
x: Benzyl chloride forms first, but it is a better alkylating agent than CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> and reacts again with the excess benzene.
AlCl<sub>3</sub> does not transfer chlorine to the ring from CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>; the carbon, not chlorine, becomes the electrophile.
CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> has only two C–Cl bonds, so it can join only two rings; triphenylmethane would require CHCl<sub>3</sub>.

q: Acetanilide reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> much more slowly than aniline does, although both are ortho/para directors. What is the best explanation?
c: The nitrogen lone pair of acetanilide is also delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen, so less of it is available to donate into the ring
The nitrogen of acetanilide is sp<sup>3</sup>, so its lone pair cannot overlap with the ring
The acetyl group makes the nitrogen a meta director, which competes with ortho/para attack
The acetyl group removes the nitrogen lone pair, so the ring is activated only by induction
h: Draw the amide resonance form. Where else can the nitrogen lone pair go?
w: In an amide, the nitrogen lone pair is shared with the adjacent C=O (amide resonance). In acetanilide the lone pair is pulled two ways, toward the carbonyl and toward the ring, so it donates less to the ring than the lone pair of aniline. The group is still an ortho/para director, but only a moderate activator. Competition from amide resonance is the reason.
x: Amide nitrogens are sp<sup>2</sup> and planar; the lone pair is in a p orbital that overlaps both the carbonyl and the ring.
The –NHCOCH<sub>3</sub> group still directs ortho/para through its nitrogen lone pair; it does not become a meta director.
The nitrogen keeps its lone pair; it is shared with the carbonyl, not removed, and it still donates into the ring by resonance.

q: Pentan-3-one is treated with hydroxylamine (NH<sub>2</sub>OH) in a weakly acidic buffer (pH ≈ 4.5). What is the major organic product?
h: Hydroxylamine carries an NH<sub>2</sub> group. Ask what a primary-amine-type nitrogen does with a ketone under mild acid.
w: Hydroxylamine reacts like a primary amine. Its nitrogen adds to the carbonyl carbon, proton transfers give a carbinolamine, and acid-promoted loss of water gives C=N. Because the nitrogen started with two N–H bonds, the last step removes an N–H proton and leaves a neutral C=N–OH group: the oxime of pentan-3-one, (CH3CH2)2C=N–OH. The N–O bond is not broken at any stage.
x: This carbinolamine is the tetrahedral intermediate. At pH 4.5 it loses water to give the C=N product, which is the compound isolated.
The N–O bond is not cleaved in oxime formation. The OH stays on nitrogen, so the product is C=N–OH, not C=NH.
A C=C–N (enamine-type) product forms only when nitrogen has no second H to lose, as with a secondary amine. NH<sub>2</sub>OH has two N–H bonds, so the C=N oxime forms.

q: 1-Phenylpropan-1-one is treated with propane-1,3-dithiol and BF<sub>3</sub>·OEt<sub>2</sub>, with removal of water. What is the product?
h: Thiols add to a C=O the way alcohols do, and a dithiol can close a ring. Which atom leaves the carbonyl carbon, and what replaces it?
w: The Lewis acid activates the C=O, and one SH group adds to give a hemithioacetal. Loss of water gives a sulfur-stabilized cation, and the second SH of the same molecule closes a six-membered ring. The carbonyl oxygen leaves as water, and the carbon ends up bonded to two sulfurs: the cyclic thioacetal 2-ethyl-2-phenyl-1,3-dithiane. Thioacetals are stable to aqueous acid, and Raney nickel later converts the C(SR)2 group to CH2.
x: This hemithioacetal is the first intermediate. With a Lewis acid and water removal it loses OH and closes the ring to the dithiane.
Losing H<sup>+</sup> from the cation would give this vinyl sulfide, but the second SH group of the same molecule is right there and captures the cation to form a six-membered ring.
This ring contains an oxygen bonded to CH<sub>2</sub>, but the dithiol supplies only sulfur. The carbonyl oxygen leaves as water, so the ring must contain two sulfurs.

q:
Acetophenone (shown) is heated with each reagent below and a catalytic amount of acid, with removal of water. Which reagents give an isolated product that contains a C=N double bond?
I. CH3NH2
II. (CH3)2NH
III. H2NNHC(=O)NH2 (semicarbazide)
h: Sort the nitrogen reagents by how many H atoms the attacking nitrogen carries.
w: A nitrogen with two H atoms (a primary-amine-type NH2) ends as C=N, because the last proton lost comes from nitrogen. A secondary amine has only one N–H, which is used up when the carbinolamine forms. Its iminium ion must lose an α C–H instead, giving an enamine (C=C–N). I. Methylamine is primary and gives the N-methyl imine, which has a C=N: true. II. Dimethylamine is secondary and gives an enamine, which has no C=N: false. III. The hydrazine-end NH2 of semicarbazide is a primary-amine-type nitrogen and gives a C=N semicarbazone: true. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III. The hydrazine-end NH<sub>2</sub> of semicarbazide has two H atoms, so it gives a C=N semicarbazone.
This misjudges I. Methylamine is a primary amine and gives the N-methyl imine, which contains C=N.
This misjudges II. Dimethylamine is secondary: its iminium ion cannot lose an N–H proton, so it loses an α C–H, and the isolated product is an enamine (C=C–N).

q: Which sequence converts ethyl 4-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylate into ethyl cyclohexanecarboxylate (ketone C=O → CH<sub>2</sub>) and leaves the ester intact?
h: Two classic deoxygenations use hot strong base or hot strong acid. Look for a route that runs under neutral conditions.
w: Ethane-1,2-dithiol with a Lewis acid converts the ketone into a cyclic thioacetal (a 1,3-dithiolane). Esters do not form thioacetals, so only the ketone reacts. Raney nickel (H2) then breaks both C–S bonds and replaces them with C–H bonds, turning the former carbonyl carbon into CH2. Neither step is strongly basic or acidic, so the ethyl ester survives. Answer: 1. HSCH2CH2SH, BF3; 2. H2, Raney Ni.
x: The Wolff–Kishner reduction does convert the ketone to CH<sub>2</sub>, but hot KOH also saponifies the ethyl ester to a carboxylate.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone only to a secondary alcohol (CH–OH), not to CH<sub>2</sub>.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone to CH–OH and the ester to CH<sub>2</sub>OH. Neither becomes CH<sub>2</sub>, and the ester is destroyed.

q: Methyl benzoate is treated with excess LiAlD<sub>4</sub> in ether, and the reaction is then worked up with ordinary H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the aromatic product?
h: Count how many deuteride ions the ester carbon receives. Then ask where the O–H hydrogen comes from.
w: An ester takes two hydride (here deuteride) ions. The first D− adds to the C=O; the tetrahedral intermediate expels CH3O− to give PhCDO. That aldehyde is more reactive than the ester and takes a second D−, giving the alkoxide PhCD2O−. Workup with H2O protonates the oxygen with ordinary H. Product: PhCD2OH (plus CH3OH).
x: One deuterium on carbon would mean the reduction stopped at the aldehyde. With excess LiAlD<sub>4</sub>, the aldehyde is reduced again, so the carbon carries two D atoms.
The O–H hydrogen comes from the workup water, not from LiAlD<sub>4</sub>. Because the workup uses H<sub>2</sub>O, the oxygen carries H, not D.
This structure has no deuterium on carbon. The deuterides are the nucleophiles that bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the workup supplies only the O–H hydrogen.

q:
Which combinations, each followed by aqueous acid workup, give 2-methyl-1-phenylpropan-2-ol (shown) as the main product?
I. C6H5CH2MgBr + acetone
II. C6H5MgBr + 2,2-dimethyloxirane
III. C6H5MgBr + 2-methylpropanal
h: For each pair, find which carbon of the Grignard reagent bonds to which carbon of the electrophile. For the epoxide, ask which ring carbon a strong nucleophile attacks.
w: The target is C6H5CH2–C(OH)(CH3)2. I. The benzylic CH2 of the Grignard reagent adds to acetone's carbonyl carbon, giving C6H5CH2C(CH3)2O−: true. II. Under basic conditions a Grignard reagent opens an epoxide by SN2 at the less substituted carbon. Phenyl bonds to the CH2, and the oxygen stays on the C(CH3)2 carbon, which gives the same alkoxide: true. III. Phenyl adds to the aldehyde carbon, giving C6H5CH(OH)CH(CH3)2, a secondary alcohol that is an isomer of the target: false. Answer: I and II only.
x: This misjudges II. The Grignard reagent attacks the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub> of the epoxide, so phenyl ends up on the CH<sub>2</sub> next to C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>O<sup>−</sup>, which is the target skeleton.

This misjudges I. Benzylmagnesium bromide adds its CH<sub>2</sub> carbon to acetone's carbonyl and builds exactly the C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–C(OH)(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> skeleton.
This misjudges III. Phenyl adds to the aldehyde carbon, giving the secondary alcohol C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, not the tertiary target.

q: Benzoic acid is treated with 2 equivalents of ethyllithium in ether. Which species is present in the flask before aqueous workup? (Li+ counterions are omitted.)
h: The first equivalent of ethyllithium does an acid–base reaction. Ask what the second equivalent does to the carboxylate, and whether the product has a leaving group it can expel.
w: The first equivalent of CH3CH2Li removes the acidic O–H and gives lithium benzoate. Organolithium reagents are reactive enough to add to a carboxylate (Grignard reagents are not), so the second equivalent adds to the carboxylate carbon. This gives the dianion PhC(O−)2CH2CH3. The dianion cannot collapse to a ketone because O2− is not a leaving group. No ketone exists while ethyllithium is present, so no tertiary alcohol forms. Aqueous workup gives the hydrate, which loses water to give propiophenone.
x: The ketone forms only after workup, when the dianion is protonated to a hydrate that loses water. If the ketone formed in the flask, it would react with more ethyllithium.
A tertiary alkoxide would need the ketone to exist in the presence of ethyllithium. The dianion cannot expel O<sup>2−</sup>, so a second addition never happens.
The lithium carboxylate forms after the first equivalent. Ethyllithium, unlike a Grignard reagent, is reactive enough for the second equivalent to add to it.

q: 3-Methylbutanoyl chloride is treated with lithium tri-tert-butoxyaluminum hydride, LiAlH(Ot-Bu)3, at −78 °C, followed by water. What is the main product?
h: This hydride reagent is a deliberately weakened LiAlH<sub>4</sub>. Which carbonyl is reactive enough to react with it at −78 °C, and which is not?
w: Three bulky tert-butoxy groups make LiAlH(Ot-Bu)3 a mild reagent that delivers one hydride. The acid chloride is the most reactive carbonyl compound: hydride adds, chloride is expelled, and an aldehyde forms. At −78 °C the aldehyde reacts much more slowly with this hindered reagent than the acid chloride does, so the reduction stops there. Product: 3-methylbutanal.
x: Reduction all the way to the primary alcohol is what LiAlH4 does. The hindered, milder LiAlH(Ot-Bu)3 at −78 °C stops at the aldehyde.
The reagent delivers hydride, not tert-butoxide. The tert-butoxy groups stay on aluminum.
Simple hydrolysis by the workup water would give the acid, but the acid chloride is reduced at −78 °C before any water is added.

q: Glutaric anhydride (shown) is stirred at room temperature with 2 equivalents of benzylamine, and the mixture is then acidified with dilute HCl. What is the main organic product?
h: When a nucleophile opens a cyclic anhydride, the carboxylate leaving group stays attached to the same molecule. What job does the second equivalent of amine do?
w: Benzylamine adds to one C=O of the anhydride. The tetrahedral intermediate expels the carboxylate, which opens the ring but stays on the chain. The second equivalent of amine acts as a base and neutralizes the new carboxylic acid as an ammonium carboxylate. A carboxylate is the least reactive acyl group and does not react with an amine at room temperature. Acidification gives 5-(benzylamino)-5-oxopentanoic acid, the amide–acid.
x: A diamide would need the carboxylate to undergo a second acyl substitution. A carboxylate does not react with an amine at room temperature, and the second equivalent of amine is used up as a base.
The cyclic imide (N-benzylglutarimide) forms only on strong heating with loss of water, not under these mild conditions.
Nothing in this sequence reduces a carbonyl group. This hydroxy amide would require a hydride reagent.

q: Methyl butanoate is heated in a large excess of ethanol containing a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What are the main products?
c: Butanoic acid and ethyl methyl ether
h: The mechanism is the same as Fischer esterification, but the nucleophile is ethanol and the starting acyl group already carries OCH<sub>3</sub>.
w: This is acid-catalyzed transesterification. The C=O is protonated, ethanol adds to the carbonyl carbon, a proton transfer makes the OCH3 group a good leaving group, and methanol leaves as the C=O re-forms. Each step is reversible; the large excess of ethanol drives the equilibrium toward the ethyl ester. Products: ethyl butanoate and methanol.
x: The bond that breaks is the acyl C–OCH<sub>3</sub> bond, not the O–CH<sub>3</sub> bond. No acid forms, because the nucleophile is ethanol, not water.
Water is the by-product when a carboxylic acid is esterified. Here the leaving group is methanol, because the acyl carbon already carries OCH<sub>3</sub>.
After ethanol adds, the tetrahedral intermediate still has a leaving group (OCH<sub>3</sub>), so it expels methanol and regains the C=O. An ester carbon does not end at an acetal oxidation state.

q:
Propanal (shown) is treated with each reagent below. For which reagents can the adduct readily return to propanal, because the addition to C=O is reversible?
I. H2O (hydrate formation)
II. CH3MgBr in ether, then aqueous NH4Cl
III. aqueous NaHSO3 (bisulfite addition)
h: An adduct can fall apart only if the group that added can leave again as a fairly stable species. Compare water, a carbanion and sulfite as leaving groups.
w: I. The hydrate (gem-diol) is in equilibrium with the aldehyde: water or hydroxide leaves easily, so hydrate formation is reversible: true. II. The Grignard reagent adds a methyl carbanion; CH3− (conjugate base of CH4, pKa ≈ 50) is never expelled, so butan-2-ol forms irreversibly: false. III. The bisulfite adduct is a crystalline salt, but sulfite is a weak base and a good leaving group; adding dilute acid or base regenerates the aldehyde (a classic way to purify aldehydes): true. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III. Bisulfite adducts revert to the aldehyde when treated with dilute acid or base, because sulfite is a good leaving group.
This misjudges I. Hydration of an aldehyde is a rapid equilibrium; the hydrate loses water to re-form propanal.
This misjudges II. A methyl carbanion is far too strong a base to leave, so Grignard addition is irreversible.

q: In acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of the imine formed from acetone and methylamine, water adds to the N-protonated imine (an iminium ion). Which drawing shows correct curved arrows for this addition step?
h: Water is the nucleophile. Find the electrophilic atom of the iminium ion, then decide where the C=N π electrons must go so that carbon keeps four bonds.
w: The iminium carbon is the electrophile, because the positive charge is shared with it (C=N+ ↔ C+–N). A water lone pair attacks that carbon, and the C=N π electrons move onto nitrogen, which neutralizes it. The product is the O-protonated carbinolamine, which later loses methylamine to give acetone. Correct drawing: water lone pair → carbon; C=N π bond → nitrogen.
x: With only the attack arrow, carbon would form a fifth bond. The C=N π bond must shift onto nitrogen.
Nitrogen is not the electrophile. It already has four bonds and a positive charge, so water adding to it would give an impossible pentavalent nitrogen. Water adds to carbon.
This arrow runs backward: it sends the C=N π electrons to water's oxygen. Water is the nucleophile, so the electrons must flow from its oxygen lone pair to the carbon.

q: Benzaldehyde is treated with the stabilized ylide Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CHCO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. What is the major organic product (besides Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O)?
h: A Wittig reaction puts a C=C where the C=O was. For the geometry, ask whether the ylide carbanion is stabilized by resonance with the ester.
w: The ylide carbon bonds to the carbonyl carbon. The oxaphosphetane then collapses to the alkene and Ph3P=O. When the ylide carbanion is conjugated with an ester (a stabilized ylide), the addition is reversible and the more stable trans intermediate wins, so the (E)-alkene is the major product. Simple alkyl ylides tend to give the (Z)-alkene instead. Product: ethyl (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enoate (ethyl (E)-cinnamate).
x: The (Z)-alkene is the usual major product of unstabilized (alkyl) ylides. An ester-stabilized ylide gives mainly the (E)-alkene.
A β-hydroxy ester is an aldol-type product. In a Wittig reaction the carbonyl oxygen ends on phosphorus as Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O, not as an OH group.
Epoxides come from sulfur ylides or the Darzens reaction. Phosphorus ylides give alkenes, because forming the strong P=O bond drives the reaction.

q: Each bromide below is to be converted into a Grignard reagent (Mg, ether) and then added to cyclohexanone. Which can be used directly, without first protecting or changing another functional group?
h: A Grignard reagent is a strong base and a strong nucleophile. Check each molecule for an acidic hydrogen or an electrophilic group.
w: I. The cyclic acetal is an ether-type group with no acidic H and no electrophilic carbon, so it is inert to Grignard reagents (that is why acetals are used to protect aldehydes): usable. II. The O–H (pKa ≈ 16) is vastly more acidic than the C–H of an alkane (pKa ≈ 50), so the Grignard reagent is protonated as soon as it forms: not usable without protection. III. The C≡N group is an electrophile that Grignard reagents attack, so the aryl Grignard would react with the nitrile of other molecules: not usable. Answer: I only.
x: This misjudges II. The alcohol O–H protonates the Grignard reagent and destroys it, so the OH must first be protected, for example as a silyl ether.
This misjudges III. Grignard reagents add to nitriles (that is how nitriles are turned into ketones), so this reagent would attack the C≡N of neighboring molecules.
This misjudges both II and III. Only the acetal is inert to a strongly basic, nucleophilic Grignard reagent.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O shows a strong IR band at 1728 cm<sup>−1</sup> and two weaker bands at 2820 and 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. What is the compound?
h: The IR bands identify the functional group. Then use the splitting of the δ 9.76 signal and the 6H signal to place the neighbors.
w: A C=O stretch near 1730 cm−1 together with the two aldehyde C–H bands at 2820 and 2720 cm−1 means an aldehyde, and the 1H signal at δ 9.76 is the CHO proton. That signal is a triplet, so the CHO is attached to a CH2 (δ 2.31, 2H). The 6H doublet at δ 0.98 is two equivalent CH3 groups on one CH (δ 2.21, 1H): an isopropyl group. Joining the pieces gives (CH3)2CH–CH2–CHO, 3-methylbutanal.
x: Pentanal would show a 3H triplet near δ 0.9 for its single CH<sub>3</sub>, not a 6H doublet, and it has no 1H methine signal.
In 2-methylbutanal the CHO is attached to a CH, so its signal would be a doublet. The spectrum would also show a 3H doublet and a 3H triplet rather than one 6H doublet.
A ketone has no CHO signal near δ 9.8 and no C–H bands at 2820/2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its CH<sub>3</sub>C=O would appear as a 3H singlet near δ 2.1.

q: Methyl 4-(chlorocarbonyl)benzoate (shown) is treated with 2 equivalents of diethylamine in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> at 0 °C. What is the main organic product?
h: Two acyl groups compete for the amine. Recall the reactivity order of carboxylic acid derivatives, and what the second equivalent of amine is for.
w: Acid chlorides are far more reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution than esters, because chloride is a much better leaving group than methoxide and Cl donates little electron density to the C=O by resonance. At 0 °C diethylamine reacts only at the COCl group. The second equivalent of amine traps the HCl as (CH3CH2)2NH2+ Cl−. The methyl ester is untouched. Product: methyl 4-(diethylcarbamoyl)benzoate.
x: A diamide is not formed. One equivalent of amine is used up neutralizing HCl, and an ester reacts with an amine far too slowly at 0 °C.
This product would need the ester to react while the acid chloride survives, which is the reverse of the reactivity order (acid chloride ≫ ester).
No water is present to hydrolyze the acid chloride. The amine is the nucleophile, so an amide forms.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexanecarboxylic acid into 2-cyclohexylbutan-2-ol (shown)?
h: The carbinol carbon of the target carries two different new groups (CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>). That means the route must stop at a ketone before the second group is added.
w: The target is a tertiary alcohol whose carbinol carbon holds the cyclohexyl group, a CH3, and a CH2CH3. The two different groups must be added one at a time, through a ketone. SOCl2 makes the acid chloride. The Gilman reagent (CH3)2CuLi adds one methyl and stops at cyclohexyl methyl ketone, because cuprates react with acid chlorides but not with ketones. Ethylmagnesium bromide then adds to the ketone, and workup gives the alcohol. Answer: 1. SOCl2 2. (CH3)2CuLi 3. CH3CH2MgBr 4. H3O+.
x: Excess Grignard reagent adds twice to an acid chloride, so both new groups are methyl. The product is 2-cyclohexylpropan-2-ol.
A Grignard reagent only deprotonates a carboxylic acid. The magnesium carboxylate does not react further, so the acid is recovered after workup.
Excess ethylmagnesium bromide adds twice to the ethyl ester, giving two ethyl groups (3-cyclohexylpentan-3-ol). This route never adds a methyl group.

q: Cyclopentylmagnesium bromide is added to formaldehyde (H<sub>2</sub>C=O), and the mixture is worked up with aqueous acid. What is the product?
h: The Grignard carbon bonds to the carbonyl carbon. How many carbons does formaldehyde bring, and how many R groups end up on the carbinol carbon?
w: The nucleophilic carbon of the Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde, forming a new C–C bond. The alkoxide C5H9CH2O− is protonated on workup. Formaldehyde has no R groups, so the product is a primary alcohol with one more carbon: cyclopentylmethanol.
x: Cyclopentanol has no new carbon. Grignard addition always forms a new C–C bond, so the product gains the CH<sub>2</sub> from formaldehyde.
1-Methylcyclopentanol is the product of CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr with cyclopentanone. Formaldehyde with a Grignard reagent gives a primary alcohol.
Grignard addition gives an alcohol after workup, not an aldehyde. No oxidizing agent is present.

q: Phenylacetaldehyde is heated with morpholine (a secondary amine) and a catalytic amount of TsOH, with removal of water. What is the major product?
h: Morpholine's nitrogen has only one H. After the iminium ion forms, which proton can be lost to give a neutral product?
w: The secondary amine adds to the aldehyde, and the carbinolamine loses water to give an iminium ion. Nitrogen has no H left to lose, so a proton is removed from the α-carbon (the benzylic CH2) instead. This gives an enamine whose C=C is conjugated with the benzene ring: 4-(2-phenylethenyl)morpholine.
x: This carbinolamine is an intermediate. With acid catalysis and removal of water, it dehydrates.
An amide would require oxidation of the aldehyde carbon, and no oxidant is present.
The saturated tertiary amine forms only if a reducing agent (such as NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN) is present to reduce the iminium ion, as in reductive amination.

q: Butanal is converted to its cyanohydrin with NaCN and HCl, and the cyanohydrin is then heated in aqueous H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the final organic product?
h: Step 1 adds a carbon. Step 2 is the usual fate of a nitrile in hot aqueous acid. Does anything remove the OH?
w: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde, and protonation gives the cyanohydrin CH3CH2CH2CH(OH)C≡N. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile, first to the amide and then to the carboxylic acid (with NH4+). The OH on the neighboring carbon is not affected. Product: 2-hydroxypentanoic acid (racemic), an α-hydroxy acid.
x: The amino alcohol (C–CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) is what LiAlH<sub>4</sub> gives from a cyanohydrin. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile instead of reducing it.
Hydrolysis of the nitrile does not remove the OH. The hydroxyl from cyanohydrin formation stays on the same carbon.
The amide is an intermediate of nitrile hydrolysis. Prolonged heating in aqueous acid converts it to the carboxylic acid.

q: 4-Methylpentan-2-one (shown) is stirred in D<sub>2</sub>O containing NaOD until no further exchange occurs. How many hydrogens per molecule are replaced by deuterium?
h: Exchange happens only through the enolate. Which carbons are directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon, and how many H atoms do they carry?
w: In NaOD/D2O, a hydrogen is exchanged only if removing it gives a resonance-stabilized enolate; the enolate then picks up D from D2O. Repeating this replaces every α-hydrogen. 4-Methylpentan-2-one has two α-carbons: C1 (CH3, 3 H) and C3 (CH2, 2 H). The C4–H is β to the carbonyl and is not acidic. Total: 5.
x: 2 counts only the CH<sub>2</sub>. The methyl group on the other side of the carbonyl (C1) is also α and also exchanges.
3 counts only the CH<sub>3</sub>. The CH<sub>2</sub> at C3 is also α to the carbonyl.
6 includes the C4–H, but C4 is β to the carbonyl. Its carbanion would not be stabilized by the C=O, so that H does not exchange.

q: Rank these compounds by the fraction present as the enol tautomer at equilibrium (neat liquid), from lowest to highest.
h: A simple ketone gains nothing by enolizing. A β-dicarbonyl enol gains conjugation and an internal hydrogen bond. Does an ester C=O gain as much from that as a ketone C=O?
w: I. For a simple ketone the C=O bond is much stronger than the C=C bond of the enol, so cyclohexanone has only a trace of enol (about 10−4%). II. The enol of 2,4-pentanedione has a C=C conjugated with the remaining C=O and a six-membered intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bond; it is about 80% enol. III. Ethyl acetoacetate also forms a conjugated, hydrogen-bonded enol. However, its ester C=O is already stabilized by resonance with the OEt lone pair, so it gains less, and the compound is only about 8% enol. Order: I < III < II.
x: This places the β-keto ester above the β-diketone. The ester oxygen's resonance donation already stabilizes the ester C=O, so ethyl acetoacetate gains less by enolizing (about 8% versus about 80%).
Cyclohexanone has far less enol (about 10<sup>−4</sup>%) than either β-dicarbonyl compound, which both gain conjugation and an intramolecular hydrogen bond.
This reverses the order. The simple ketone is almost entirely keto, and the β-diketone is mostly enol.

q: 2-Methylpentan-3-one is treated with LDA in THF at −78 °C, and then allyl bromide is added. What is the major product?
h: LDA is a bulky, very strong base used at low temperature. Which α-hydrogen can it reach fastest: the one on the CH<sub>2</sub> or the one on the CH?
w: The two α-carbons are the CH2 of the ethyl group and the CH of the isopropyl group. LDA at −78 °C removes a proton quickly and irreversibly, and the bulky base takes the more accessible CH2 proton (kinetic enolate). The enolate carbon then displaces bromide from allyl bromide by SN2. Product: 2,4-dimethylhept-6-en-3-one, CH2=CHCH2CH(CH3)C(=O)CH(CH3)2 (formed as a racemate).
x: Alkylation at the more substituted α-carbon comes from the thermodynamic enolate, formed with a weaker base under equilibrating conditions. LDA at −78 °C removes the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub> proton.
Lithium enolates react with alkyl halides mainly at carbon (C-alkylation). The O-allyl enol ether is at most a minor product.
LDA is a hindered, non-nucleophilic base and does not add to C=O. The allyl group is attached by S<sub>N</sub>2 at the enolate carbon, not by addition to the carbonyl.

q: Cyclohexanone is heated with NaOH in aqueous ethanol. Two molecules undergo aldol addition, and the aldol product then loses water by E1cB. Which structure is the enone formed directly in that dehydration step?
h: One molecule supplies the enolate (α-carbon), the other the C=O. In E1cB the new C=C forms between the α-carbon and the carbon that carried the OH.
w: The enolate of one cyclohexanone (at C2) adds to the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule, giving the β-hydroxy ketone 2-(1-hydroxycyclohexyl)cyclohexan-1-one. In E1cB dehydration, base removes the α-H between the C=O and the carbinol carbon, and the enolate then expels hydroxide. The new C=C therefore forms between that α-carbon and the former carbinol carbon, conjugated with the C=O: 2-cyclohexylidenecyclohexan-1-one. (On longer heating this enone partly isomerizes to the β,γ isomer, but that is a later equilibration, not the dehydration step.)
x: This β-hydroxy ketone is the aldol addition product. With heat it loses water to give the conjugated enone.

This enone is conjugated, but its C=C lies inside the ketone ring between C2 and C3. E1cB forms the C=C between the α-carbon and the former carbinol carbon, which is in the other ring, so this isomer would need a later double-bond shift.
This saturated ketone would need a reduction after dehydration. Nothing in NaOH/ethanol supplies hydrogen.

q: Nonane-2,8-dione (shown) is heated with aqueous NaOH. What is the major product of the intramolecular aldol condensation?
h: Number the chain C1–C9. List each possible enolate carbon (C1, C3, C7, C9) and count the ring size it would form by attacking the other carbonyl.
w: There are two kinds of enolate. An enolate at C1 (or C9) attacking the far carbonyl would close an eight-membered ring, which forms slowly. An enolate at C3 (or C7) attacking C8 (or C2) closes a ring of C3–C4–C5–C6–C7–C8: six atoms, the most favorable size. The ring carbon C8 carries the methyl (C9) and the new OH; C3 carries the acetyl group. Dehydration gives a C3=C8 double bond conjugated with the acetyl C=O. Product: 1-(2-methylcyclohex-1-en-1-yl)ethan-1-one.
x: This eight-membered enone (3-methylcyclooct-2-en-1-one) comes from the C1 enolate. An eight-membered ring forms far more slowly than the six-membered ring available from the C3 enolate.
This is the β-hydroxy ketone (aldol addition product). On heating with NaOH it dehydrates to the conjugated enone.

This miscounts the chain. A cyclopentene bearing a propanoyl group would come from nonane-2,7-dione (carbonyls five carbons apart); in nonane-2,8-dione the carbonyls are six carbons apart, which gives a six-membered ring.
