q: Cyclohexanone is treated with ethyl formate (HCO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) and NaOEt in ethanol, and the mixture is then acidified. What is the main product (drawn in its keto form)?
h: Ethyl formate has no α-hydrogens, so it can only be the electrophile. What does its tetrahedral intermediate expel?
w: This is a crossed Claisen condensation. The ketone α-H (pKa ≈ 20) is more acidic than an ester α-H, and ethyl formate has no α-H at all. The cyclohexanone enolate therefore adds to the formate C=O, and the tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide, transferring a formyl (CHO) group to C2. Ethoxide then removes the very acidic H between the two carbonyls, which drives the reaction; acid workup gives 2-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde (a β-keto aldehyde, largely present as its enol, 2-(hydroxymethylene)cyclohexanone).
x: Transferring a CO<sub>2</sub>Et group requires diethyl carbonate. Ethyl formate transfers a CHO group, because ethoxide is the group that leaves.
Enolates form at α-carbons. C3 is β to the ketone and is not deprotonated, so the new bond is made at C2.
After the formate carbonyl is attacked, the tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide, so the OEt does not stay on the product.

q: 2-Propylcyclohexan-1-one (shown) is to be made by (1) Dieckmann condensation with NaOEt, (2) alkylation of the resulting β-keto ester, and (3) hydrolysis and decarboxylation with H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and heat. Which diester and alkyl halide should be used?
h: In a Dieckmann condensation, the α-carbon of one ester attacks the other ester carbonyl. Count the ring atoms from the α-carbon to that carbonyl carbon.
w: Diethyl heptanedioate, EtO2C(CH2)5CO2Et, has a seven-carbon chain. The enolate at C2 attacks the C7 ester carbonyl, closing a ring of C2–C7 (six atoms) and giving ethyl 2-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylate. Its doubly activated C–H is removed by ethoxide, and the enolate is propylated with 1-bromopropane. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester to a β-keto acid, which loses CO2, leaving the propyl group α to the ketone. Answer: diethyl heptanedioate and 1-bromopropane.
x: Diethyl hexanedioate (adipate) closes a five-membered ring, so this route gives 2-propylcyclopentan-1-one.
The alkyl halide supplies the whole side chain. 1-Bromobutane would give 2-butylcyclohexan-1-one.
Diethyl octanedioate would close a seven-membered ring (a cycloheptanone), and seven-membered Dieckmann rings also form poorly.

q: Cyclohex-2-en-1-one is treated with thiophenol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>SH) and a catalytic amount of triethylamine. What is the major product?
h: Thiolate is a soft, weakly basic nucleophile. Which electrophilic carbon of an α,β-unsaturated ketone does it end up bonded to?
w: Triethylamine forms a little thiolate, C6H5S−. This soft, weakly basic nucleophile adds to the β-carbon of the enone (conjugate, 1,4-addition), giving an enolate. The enolate takes a proton from another PhSH, which regenerates thiolate, so only a catalytic amount of base is needed. Any 1,2-addition is reversible, so the 1,4-product, which keeps the strong C=O bond, accumulates. Product: 3-(phenylsulfanyl)cyclohexan-1-one.
x: 1,2-Addition of a weakly basic nucleophile is reversible. The more stable 1,4-adduct, which keeps the C=O, accumulates instead.
The nucleophile bonds to the electrophilic β-carbon, not the α-carbon. The α-carbon is where the enolate forms and is then protonated.
Keeping the C=C would require a leaving group on the β-carbon (addition–elimination). Here the enolate intermediate is simply protonated, so the ring becomes saturated.

q: (E)-4-Phenylbut-3-en-2-one is treated with methyllithium in ether at −78 °C, followed by aqueous NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. What is the major product?
h: Organolithium reagents are hard, very strongly basic nucleophiles. Do they react faster at the C=O carbon or at the β-carbon?
w: Methyllithium adds rapidly and irreversibly to the most electrophilic site, the carbonyl carbon (1,2-addition). Once the alkoxide forms, it does not revert, so the conjugate-addition product does not have a chance to form. Workup gives the allylic tertiary alcohol (E)-2-methyl-4-phenylbut-3-en-2-ol. A Gilman reagent, (CH3)2CuLi, would instead add 1,4.
x: This 1,4-adduct is the product of a cuprate, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CuLi. Methyllithium adds directly to the C=O.
This would need both a 1,4- and a 1,2-addition. After the fast 1,2-addition the C=O is gone, so there is no carbonyl left to activate the C=C.
Methylation at the α-carbon would need an enolate and an alkyl halide. Methyllithium is a nucleophile here and adds to the carbonyl carbon.

q: 2-Methylpropanal and but-3-en-2-one (methyl vinyl ketone) are heated with KOH in ethanol. A Michael addition is followed by an intramolecular aldol condensation. What is the final product?
h: Step 1: the aldehyde’s only α-carbon adds to the β-carbon of methyl vinyl ketone. Step 2: which CH<sub>3</sub> or CH<sub>2</sub> can reach the CHO to close a six-membered ring?
w: The enolate of 2-methylpropanal forms at its α-CH and adds to the β-carbon of methyl vinyl ketone. This gives the Michael adduct OHC–C(CH3)2–CH2CH2–C(=O)CH3. The enolate of the terminal CH3 of the ketone then attacks the CHO carbon. The ring formed contains the CHO carbon, C(CH3)2, two CH2 groups, the C=O, and the former CH3: six atoms. Dehydration puts the C=C between the former CHO carbon and the α-carbon, conjugated with the C=O. Product: 4,4-dimethylcyclohex-2-en-1-one.
x: This keto aldehyde is the Michael adduct. Under KOH and heat, it goes on to the intramolecular aldol condensation.

This places the gem-dimethyl carbon at C5, which miscounts the ring. In the product the C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is next to the former CHO carbon, which becomes C3 of the enone, so the gem-dimethyl is at C4.
This is the β-hydroxy ketone (aldol addition product). On heating with base it dehydrates to the conjugated enone.

q: In acid-catalyzed α-bromination of acetone, the enol reacts with Br<sub>2</sub>. Which drawing shows correct curved arrows for this step?
h: The enol's C=C is the nucleophile, pushed by the OH lone pair, and Br<sub>2</sub> is the electrophile. Every bond that breaks needs its own arrow.
w: An enol is an electron-rich alkene: the OH lone pair pushes into the C=C, which makes the α-carbon nucleophilic. Three arrows are needed: the O lone pair forms C=O+, the C=C π electrons attack one Br, and the Br–Br bond breaks to give bromide. The product is the O-protonated α-bromo ketone, which then loses H+ to give bromoacetone. Correct drawing: O lone pair → C–O bond; C=C π bond → Br; Br–Br bond → Br.
x: Here oxygen attacks bromine. The enol reacts at its α-carbon, because the C=C π electrons are the nucleophile; an O–Br hypobromite is not formed.
These arrows start at bromine and push electrons into the nucleophilic carbon. Br<sub>2</sub> is the electrophile, so the electrons must flow from the enol to Br.
The Br–Br bond is never broken in this drawing, so the attacked bromine would end with two bonds. A third arrow is needed to send the Br–Br electrons to the other Br as bromide.

q: Ethyl butanoate is treated with one equivalent of NaOEt in ethanol, and the mixture is then acidified with cold dilute acid. What is the product?
h: The α-carbon (C2) of one ester attacks the C=O of another, and ethoxide is expelled. Is any reducing agent or heat present?
w: This is a Claisen condensation. Ethoxide forms a small amount of enolate at C2 of ethyl butanoate. The enolate attacks the C=O of a second molecule, and the tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide, giving a β-keto ester. Ethoxide then removes the acidic C–H between the two carbonyls, which drives the reaction; cold acid restores the neutral product. Product: ethyl 2-ethyl-3-oxohexanoate.
x: This links the terminal carbon of the butanoyl chain to the second ester. Only the α-carbon (C2) is deprotonated, so the new C–C bond is at C2.
Heptan-4-one forms only if the β-keto ester is hydrolyzed and decarboxylated, which needs hot aqueous acid. Cold dilute acid only neutralizes the enolate.
A β-hydroxy ester would be an aldol-type product. In a Claisen condensation the tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide, so the new carbonyl remains a C=O.

q: Diethyl malonate is converted almost completely into its enolate by sodium ethoxide in ethanol, but ethyl acetate is not. What is the main reason?
c: The malonate CH<sub>2</sub> (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 13) is more acidic than ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16); ethyl acetate (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is much less acidic.
Ethoxide is too hindered to reach the α-hydrogens of ethyl acetate, but it can reach those of diethyl malonate.
Ethyl acetate reacts with ethoxide by transesterification, which uses up the base before any enolate forms.
The malonate enolate is stabilized by a hydrogen bond to ethoxide, which ethyl acetate's enolate cannot form.
h: An acid–base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid. Compare each α-C–H with ethanol, the conjugate acid of ethoxide.
w: Deprotonation goes essentially to completion only when the C–H acid is stronger than the conjugate acid of the base. The CH2 of diethyl malonate lies between two carbonyl groups, so its anion is delocalized onto two oxygens (pKa ≈ 13). That is more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), so Keq > 1. Ethyl acetate's α-H (pKa ≈ 25) is about 109 times weaker than ethanol, so only a trace of enolate forms. The malonate C–H is more acidic than ethanol; the acetate C–H is far less acidic.
x: Ethoxide is a small base and reaches α-hydrogens easily. The difference is thermodynamic (pK<sub>a</sub>), not steric.
Transesterification of an ethyl ester with ethoxide simply regenerates the same ethyl ester and ethoxide, so no base is consumed.
The extra stability of the malonate enolate comes from delocalizing the charge onto two carbonyl oxygens, not from hydrogen bonding to ethoxide.

q: The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of neat 2,4-pentanedione (shown) contains separate signals for the keto and enol tautomers, which interconvert slowly on the NMR time scale. The numbers on the peaks are relative integrals for the whole mixture, not H counts per molecule. What percentage of the molecules are present as the enol?
h: Pick one signal unique to each tautomer, and divide its integral by the number of H atoms that signal represents in one molecule.
w: Assign the signals. The enol has the O–H (δ 15.5), the vinyl C–H (δ 5.50, 1 H per molecule) and two CH3 groups that are averaged by fast proton shuttling (δ 2.04, 6 H). The keto form has the CH2 (δ 3.60, 2 H per molecule) and two CH3 groups (δ 2.24, 6 H). Molecules of enol ∝ 2/1 = 2. Molecules of keto ∝ 1/2 = 0.5. Enol fraction = 2 / (2 + 0.5) = 0.80. The methyl signals agree: 12/6 = 2 and 3/6 = 0.5. Answer: 80%.
x: 67% compares the raw integrals of the vinyl CH (2) and the keto CH<sub>2</sub> (1) without dividing the CH<sub>2</sub> integral by 2 H.
40% compares the enol vinyl CH integral (2) with the keto CH<sub>3</sub> integral (3) without correcting for the 1 H versus 6 H they represent.
20% is the keto fraction, not the enol fraction.

q: Ethyl acetate is treated with LDA in THF at −78 °C, then benzaldehyde is added, and the mixture is quenched with aqueous NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. What is the main product?
h: LDA converts all of the ester to its enolate before the aldehyde is added. What does an enolate do to an aldehyde C=O at low temperature?
w: LDA (pKa of diisopropylamine ≈ 36) deprotonates ethyl acetate completely and irreversibly at −78 °C. No neutral ester remains, so the ester cannot condense with itself. When benzaldehyde is added, the enolate adds to its C=O (a directed aldol addition), and the mild NH4Cl quench protonates the alkoxide. Product: ethyl 3-hydroxy-3-phenylpropanoate (racemic).
x: Dehydration to the cinnamate needs heat or acid or base for E1cB. At −78 °C with a mild NH<sub>4</sub>Cl quench, the β-hydroxy ester is isolated.
Ethyl acetoacetate is the self-Claisen product. With LDA all the ester is already enolate before the aldehyde is added, so no neutral ester is left to act as the electrophile.
A β-keto ester would form if the enolate attacked an ester such as ethyl benzoate. An aldehyde has no leaving group, so its addition product keeps an OH.

q: Optically active (R)-2-phenylpropanal (shown) slowly loses its optical activity in dilute aqueous NaOH. Which species is responsible?
c: The planar, achiral enolate formed by removing the α-hydrogen
The hydrate formed by adding hydroxide to the C=O
A carbocation formed by loss of hydroxide from the hydrate
An aldol dimer formed from two molecules of the aldehyde
h: The stereocenter is the α-carbon. What does hydroxide do to the C–H on that carbon?
w: The stereocenter carries the α-hydrogen. Hydroxide removes it to give an enolate, in which the former stereocenter is a planar sp2 carbon. Water reprotonates that carbon equally from either face, giving equal amounts of R and S. Repeating this racemizes the sample. Answer: the planar, achiral enolate.
x: Forming the hydrate changes the carbonyl carbon, not the α-carbon. The stereocenter is untouched, so the hydrate does not cause racemization.
Carbocations do not form in basic solution. Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, and the stereocenter is not involved.
An aldol reaction consumes the aldehyde rather than racemizing it. Loss of optical activity in the recovered aldehyde comes from reversible enolization.

q:
Which statements about the Claisen condensation of ethyl propanoate with NaOEt in ethanol are correct?
I. The overall reaction is driven by deprotonation of the β-keto ester product (pKa ≈ 11) by ethoxide.
II. A catalytic amount of NaOEt (about 5 mol %) is enough to give a high yield.
III. The ester must have at least two α-hydrogens, so that the β-keto ester product still has an acidic H to lose.
h: The addition and elimination steps of a Claisen condensation are uphill or close to even. What makes the last step favorable, and how much base does that step use up?
w: I. True: the β-keto ester has a C–H between two carbonyls (pKa ≈ 11), much more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16). Its essentially complete deprotonation pulls the earlier unfavorable equilibria forward. II. False: that final deprotonation consumes a full equivalent of ethoxide, so a stoichiometric amount of base is required; acid workup restores the neutral product. III. True: one α-H is used to form the enolate. A second α-H must remain on the carbon between the carbonyls of the product for the driving deprotonation; esters with only one α-H, such as ethyl 2-methylpropanoate, condense poorly with NaOEt. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III. With only one α-H, the product has no acidic H between the carbonyls, the driving deprotonation cannot occur, and the reaction does not go to completion with NaOEt.
This misjudges I. Deprotonation of the β-keto ester product is the step that drives the reaction.
This misjudges II. The driving deprotonation consumes ethoxide, so a full equivalent of base is needed, not a catalytic amount.

q: Which ketone, treated with excess I<sub>2</sub> in aqueous NaOH and then acidified, gives 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid (shown) as the organic acid product?
h: In the haloform reaction, which group of the ketone is lost as CHI<sub>3</sub>, and which group stays attached to the new CO<sub>2</sub>H?
w: The haloform reaction works on methyl ketones, RC(=O)CH3. In base the CH3 is iodinated three times, hydroxide adds to the C=O, and CI3− leaves, giving RCO2− and iodoform. Acidification gives RCO2H. The R group is unchanged, so R must be tert-butyl: 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one (pinacolone).
x: This ketone has no CH<sub>3</sub>C=O group. Its α-CH<sub>2</sub> can be iodinated, but no CI<sub>3</sub> group forms, so it does not undergo the haloform cleavage.
This methyl ketone does react, but its R group is (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>–, so the product is 3,3-dimethylbutanoic acid.
This methyl ketone does react, but its R group is isopropyl, so the product is 2-methylpropanoic acid.

q: Diethyl malonate is treated with 2 equivalents of NaOEt and 1 equivalent of 1,3-dibromopropane. The product is then heated in aqueous H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the final organic product?
h: The first enolate alkylates one end of the dibromide. The product still has an acidic C–H, and base remains. Then recall what hot aqueous acid does to a malonate.
w: The malonate enolate displaces one bromide (SN2). The monoalkylated malonate still has an acidic C–H, and the second equivalent of ethoxide removes it. That enolate displaces the other bromide intramolecularly, closing a ring of the malonate carbon plus three CH2 groups: diethyl cyclobutane-1,1-dicarboxylate. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes both esters; the 1,1-diacid has a CO2H β to a C=O and loses CO2. Product: cyclobutanecarboxylic acid.
x: This diester is the intermediate before step 2. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the esters and decarboxylates the malonic acid.
This assumes the second bromide never reacts. With a second equivalent of base, the monoalkylated malonate is deprotonated again and closes the ring intramolecularly.
A 1,1-dicarboxylic acid (a malonic acid) loses CO<sub>2</sub> readily on heating, through a cyclic transition state, so it does not survive step 2.

q: In the base-catalyzed aldol addition of propanal (carbons labeled a–c), which two carbons are joined by the new C–C bond?
c: Carbon b of one molecule and carbon a of another
Carbon a of one molecule and carbon a of another
Carbon b of one molecule and carbon b of another
Carbon c of one molecule and carbon a of another
h: One molecule acts as the nucleophile through its enolate. The other acts as the electrophile through its carbonyl carbon.
w: Hydroxide removes an α-hydrogen from carbon b, the carbon next to the C=O, to form the enolate. The nucleophilic α-carbon of that enolate attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon a of a second propanal molecule. Protonation gives 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal. Answer: carbon b of one molecule and carbon a of another.
x: Two carbonyl carbons are both electrophiles, and neither has electrons to donate, so they cannot bond to each other.
Joining two α-carbons would need both to act as nucleophiles. One partner must provide the electrophilic C=O carbon.
Carbon c is β to the carbonyl. Its hydrogens are not acidic, so no nucleophile forms there.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Track the carbon count: which steps add a carbon, and which only change the functional group?
w: Step 1 makes the aryl Grignard; CO2 then H3O+ give 4-methoxybenzoic acid (one new carbon). LiAlH4 reduces the acid to the primary benzylic alcohol, PBr3 converts it to ArCH2Br, and cyanide displaces bromide by SN2, adding a second new carbon: 2-(4-methoxyphenyl)acetonitrile. Net result: Ar–Br became Ar–CH2–C≡N, two carbons added.
x: This counts only one new carbon. The CO<sub>2</sub> carbon becomes the CH<sub>2</sub> after reduction and bromination, and cyanide brings a second carbon, so the nitrile sits on a CH<sub>2</sub>, not on the ring.
Nothing in the sequence hydrolyzes the nitrile; NaCN in DMSO stops at R–C≡N. Hydrolysis to the acid would need hot H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> or NaOH as a further step.
This adds three carbons. Only CO<sub>2</sub> and CN<sup>−</sup> add carbon here, so the chain off the ring has two carbons, not three.

q: What is the major final product of the sequence shown?
h: Dehydration of the tertiary alcohol can give an alkene inside the ring or outside it. Which is more stable, and what does ozone do to a ring C=C?
w: The Grignard adds to the ketone to give 1-ethylcyclohexan-1-ol. Hot H2SO4 dehydrates it by E1; the major alkene is the endocyclic 1-ethylcyclohexene (trisubstituted, in the ring, the more stable choice for a six-membered ring). Ozonolysis with a reductive (CH3)2S workup cuts the ring C=C, so the ring opens into one chain: the substituted carbon becomes a ketone and the CH becomes an aldehyde. Product: 6-oxooctanal, CH3CH2CO(CH2)4CHO.
x: Cyclohexanone plus acetaldehyde would come from the exocyclic alkene, ethylidenecyclohexane. Dehydration favors the endocyclic C=C, and cutting a ring alkene opens the ring instead of releasing the original ketone.
Dimethyl sulfide is a reductive workup, so the aldehyde end survives as CHO. A carboxylic acid would need an oxidative workup such as H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.
This is the product after step 2 only. Hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> dehydrates a tertiary alcohol readily, and O<sub>3</sub> then cleaves the alkene.

q: Which sequence gives 1-(3-chlorophenyl)propan-1-one (shown) from benzene as the major product?
c: 1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl
h: The two groups are meta to each other. Which of the two is a meta director, and so must go on first?
w: The acyl group (a ketone) withdraws electrons by resonance and is a meta director; chlorine is an ortho/para director. To get the 1,3 pattern, put the acyl group on first by Friedel–Crafts acylation (no rearrangement, no polyacylation), then chlorinate: Cl enters meta to the ketone. 1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3 2. Cl2, FeCl3.
x: Chlorine on first directs the acyl group ortho/para, mostly para, giving 1-(4-chlorophenyl)propan-1-one.
A primary propyl cation rearranges to the isopropyl cation, so this makes cumene, and an alkyl group would then direct Cl ortho/para. It also never makes a C=O.
The first two steps make the target, but the Clemmensen reduction removes the C=O and gives 1-chloro-3-propylbenzene.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexanol into N-methylcyclohexanamine (shown) as the major product?
c: 1. TsCl, pyridine  2. NaN<sub>3</sub>, DMSO  3. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>  4. H<sub>2</sub>O
h: The target is a secondary amine with exactly one methyl on N. Which route forms the C–N bond and stops cleanly at that stage?
w: PCC oxidizes the secondary alcohol to cyclohexanone. With methylamine at pH ≈ 6 the ketone forms an iminium ion, which NaBH3CN reduces much faster than it reduces the ketone. This reductive amination gives the secondary amine without over-alkylation: 1. PCC, CH2Cl2 2. CH3NH2, NaBH3CN, pH ≈ 6.
x: This forms the imine, N-cyclohexylidenemethylamine (C=N), but nothing reduces it, so no amine is obtained.
This route gives cyclohexanamine, a primary amine with no N-methyl group (and the 2° tosylate also loses some material to E2).
Excess CH3I does not stop at one methyl: the amine is methylated all the way to the quaternary ammonium salt, N,N,N-trimethylcyclohexanaminium iodide.

q: Which sequence converts methyl 4-acetylbenzoate into 1-[4-(hydroxymethyl)phenyl]ethan-1-one, as shown?
h: The ester must be reduced while the more reactive ketone is left alone. How can the ketone be hidden from the reducing agent?
w: Only LiAlH4 reduces the ester to a primary alcohol, but it would also reduce the ketone. Protect the ketone first as a cyclic acetal (ethylene glycol, TsOH); acetals do not react with hydride. LiAlH4 then reduces the ester to CH2OH, and aqueous acid removes the acetal to restore the ketone: 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH 2. LiAlH4 3. H3O+.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone, not the ester, giving methyl 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoate: the opposite of what is needed.
Without protection LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces both carbonyls, giving the diol 1-[4-(hydroxymethyl)phenyl]ethan-1-ol.
The protection step is right, but NaBH<sub>4</sub> is too weak to reduce an ester, so after deprotection the starting material comes back.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Each NaNH<sub>2</sub>/R–Br pair adds one alkyl group to the alkyne. What stereochemistry does a poisoned catalyst give?
w: The two acetylide alkylations build oct-3-yne, CH3CH2C≡C(CH2)3CH3. H2 with Lindlar's (poisoned) catalyst adds one equivalent of H2 syn across the triple bond and stops at the alkene, giving (Z)-oct-3-ene.
x: The E alkene comes from a dissolving-metal reduction (Na or Li in NH3). Lindlar hydrogenation adds both H atoms to the same face.
Full reduction to the alkane needs an active catalyst such as Pt or Pd/C. Lindlar's catalyst is poisoned so it stops at the alkene.
Step 5 reduces the triple bond. Lindlar's catalyst does react with alkynes; it is alkenes it leaves alone.

q: Which sequence converts acetylene into hexanal?
h: Count carbons first, then decide which hydration of a terminal alkyne puts the oxygen on the end carbon.
w: Acetylene (2 C) + 1-bromobutane (4 C) gives hex-1-yne. Hydroboration with a bulky borane, (sia)2BH, puts boron on the terminal carbon (anti-Markovnikov); oxidation gives an enol that tautomerizes to the aldehyde: 1. NaNH2 2. CH3(CH2)3Br 3. (sia)2BH 4. H2O2, NaOH gives hexanal.
x: Hg<sup>2+</sup>-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov: the oxygen goes to the internal carbon, giving the methyl ketone hexan-2-one.
1-Bromopentane gives hept-1-yne, so the anti-Markovnikov hydration makes heptanal, one carbon too many.
Ozonolysis cleaves the triple bond into pentanoic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>; it does not hydrate the alkyne.

q: Ethyl acetoacetate is treated with 1. NaOEt, 2. an alkyl halide R–X, and 3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat. Which R–X gives 5-methylhexan-2-one (shown) as the product?
h: The acetoacetic ester synthesis turns R–X into CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>–R. Cut the target at the bond between the CH<sub>2</sub> next to C=O and the rest.
w: Alkylation of the acetoacetate enolate, then ester hydrolysis and decarboxylation of the β-keto acid, gives CH3COCH2–R. In 5-methylhexan-2-one, CH3COCH2– is attached to –CH2CH(CH3)2, so R = isobutyl and the halide is 1-bromo-2-methylpropane. It is primary (though β-branched), so SN2 alkylation works.
x: An isopropyl group gives CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, 4-methylpentan-2-one, one carbon short. A secondary halide also alkylates poorly.
An isopentyl group gives CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, 6-methylheptan-2-one, one carbon too many.
A tertiary halide cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; the enolate acts as a base and gives 2-methylpropene by E2.

q: Which combination, followed by H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> workup, gives 1-phenylcyclopentan-1-ol (shown)?
h: Find the carbon bearing the OH. In a Grignard synthesis it was a carbonyl carbon, and the new C–C bond is one of its bonds.
w: The OH carbon is a ring carbon that also carries the phenyl group, so it was the C=O carbon of cyclopentanone, and the phenyl came from the Grignard reagent. Addition of PhMgBr to the ketone and acid workup give the tertiary alcohol: C6H5MgBr + cyclopentanone.
x: This gives cyclopentyl(phenyl)methanol, a secondary alcohol whose OH carbon lies outside the ring (it was the aldehyde carbon).
An alcohol has no C=O to attack. Its O–H proton simply destroys the Grignard reagent, giving benzene and a magnesium alkoxide.
Grignard reagents open epoxides at carbon, so this gives trans-2-phenylcyclopentan-1-ol, with OH and phenyl on adjacent carbons.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown? (It forms as a racemate; stereochemistry is not shown.)
h: NBS chooses the weakest C–H bond. A bulky base on that bromide can only remove one kind of β-hydrogen. What does OsO<sub>4</sub> add?
w: NBS/hν brominates the benzylic carbon, because the benzylic radical is resonance-stabilized: 1-bromo-1-phenylpropane. Potassium tert-butoxide is a strong, bulky base, so E2 wins over SN2; the only β-hydrogens are on C2, giving the conjugated alkene 1-phenylpropene. OsO4/NMO adds two OH groups syn across the C=C: 1-phenylpropane-1,2-diol.
x: This diol needs a terminal alkene, which would require bromination at the end carbon. NBS brominates the benzylic position, not the CH<sub>3</sub>.
This would be substitution of the bromide by water, which is not one of the steps; also OsO<sub>4</sub> would then have no alkene to react with.
tert-Butoxide is too hindered to be a good SN2 nucleophile at a secondary carbon; it acts as a base and eliminates.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Draw the Diels–Alder ring first and number it from the carbon that bears the ester. Where is the new C=C, and what happens when ozone cuts it?
w: The Diels–Alder reaction gives methyl cyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate: the ester carbon is C1 and the new C=C is C3=C4. Ozonolysis with a reductive workup cuts C3=C4 into two CHO groups and opens the ring. C1 is then joined to C2–C3 (CH2CHO) on one side and C6–C5–C4 (CH2CH2CHO) on the other: methyl 2-(2-oxoethyl)-5-oxopentanoate.
x: Two equal CH<sub>2</sub>CHO arms would need the C=C to be equally far from C1 on both sides. In the cyclohexene ring C1 is two bonds from one alkene carbon and three from the other.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S is a reductive workup, so the cleaved ends stay as aldehydes, not carboxylic acids.
This is only the Diels–Alder adduct. Ozone readily cleaves the isolated ring C=C in steps 2 and 3.

q: Which sequence converts 3-phenylpropanoic acid into 2-phenylethan-1-amine, with one fewer carbon, as shown?
c: 1. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; H<sub>2</sub>O  2. PBr<sub>3</sub>  3. NaN<sub>3</sub>  4. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; H<sub>2</sub>O
1. SOCl<sub>2</sub>  2. NH<sub>3</sub> (excess)  3. P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>, heat  4. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Only one amide reaction loses the carbonyl carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>.
w: SOCl2 makes the acid chloride and NH3 converts it to the primary amide, 3-phenylpropanamide. In the Hofmann rearrangement (Br2, NaOH, H2O) the N-bromoamide rearranges to an isocyanate, which is hydrolyzed with loss of CO2. The C=O carbon is lost, giving the amine with one fewer carbon: 1. SOCl2 2. NH3 3. Br2, NaOH, H2O.
x: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the amide C=O to CH<sub>2</sub> and keeps every carbon, giving 3-phenylpropan-1-amine.
This keeps all three chain carbons (acid → alcohol → bromide → azide → amine), giving 3-phenylpropan-1-amine.
Dehydration gives the nitrile and LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces it to RCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, again 3-phenylpropan-1-amine with no carbon lost.

q:
Which sequences convert 1-methylcyclohexene into 2-methylcyclohexan-1-one (shown)?
I. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH 3. PCC, CH2Cl2
II. 1. H2O, H2SO4 2. PCC, CH2Cl2
III. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH 3. Na2Cr2O7, H2SO4
h: The oxygen must end up on the less substituted alkene carbon, and the alcohol made must be one that can be oxidized.
w: Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov: OH goes on C2, giving (trans)-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, a secondary alcohol. Any oxidant for secondary alcohols then gives the ketone. I is true (PCC). III is true: chromic acid also oxidizes a 2° alcohol to a ketone, and there is no aldehyde to over-oxidize. II is false: acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov and gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, a tertiary alcohol that PCC cannot oxidize. I and III only.
x: This rejects III, but chromic acid oxidizes secondary alcohols to ketones cleanly; over-oxidation is a concern only for primary alcohols.
This accepts II. Acid hydration puts OH on the tertiary carbon, and a 3° alcohol has no C–H on the carbinol carbon to oxidize.
II fails: Markovnikov hydration gives a tertiary alcohol, which PCC does not oxidize.

q: The enone shown is made in one step by a crossed aldol condensation (NaOH, aqueous ethanol, heat). Which two starting materials are used?
h: Break the C=C. The alkene carbon on the ring was a C=O carbon; the other alkene carbon was the α-carbon of an enolate. Which partner has no α-H?
w: Disconnecting the C=C of the α,β-unsaturated ketone gives a CH=O on the aryl carbon and a CH3 next to the ketone C=O. So the electrophile is 4-methoxybenzaldehyde, which has no α-H and cannot enolize, and the enolate comes from acetone, CH3COCH3. Using excess acetone keeps the reaction from adding a second aryl group. Answer: 4-methoxybenzaldehyde + acetone, giving (E)-4-(4-methoxyphenyl)but-3-en-2-one.
x: Acetaldehyde's enolate gives (E)-3-(4-methoxyphenyl)prop-2-enal, an aldehyde with one carbon fewer; the target is a methyl ketone.
Butan-2-one adds an extra carbon: reaction at its CH<sub>3</sub> gives an ethyl ketone, and reaction at its CH<sub>2</sub> gives a branched enone. Neither is the target.
Acetaldehyde condenses mostly with itself, and the aryl ketone is the poorer electrophile. A cross product would be ArC(CH<sub>3</sub>)=CHCHO, an aldehyde, not the target ketone.

q: Which sequence converts bromobenzene into 2-phenylethan-1-ol?
h: The target has two carbons between the ring and the OH. Which electrophile adds two carbons and puts the oxygen on the far carbon?
w: Phenylmagnesium bromide opens ethylene oxide by SN2 attack at a ring carbon; the alkoxide is two carbons away, and acid workup gives 2-phenylethan-1-ol. Epoxides are the standard two-carbon extension that leaves a primary alcohol.
x: Formaldehyde adds only one carbon, giving benzyl alcohol (phenylmethanol).
Acetaldehyde adds two carbons, but the OH ends up on the carbon attached to the ring: 1-phenylethan-1-ol.
Ethanol is an acid toward a Grignard reagent; it simply protonates it to benzene.

q: A student plans to make cyclohexylmethanol from cyclohexanone as shown. Which statement about the plan is correct?
c: Step 2 is wrong: acid hydration is Markovnikov; BH<sub>3</sub>·THF then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH gives the primary alcohol.
Step 1 is wrong: a Wittig reagent adds to the C=O to give a tertiary alcohol, not an alkene.
Step 2 is wrong: acid hydration is anti-Markovnikov; Hg(OAc)<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O then NaBH<sub>4</sub> gives the primary alcohol.
The plan works as written, because the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub> is the less hindered carbon and takes the OH.
h: After the Wittig step the alkene is methylenecyclohexane. In acid, which carbocation forms?
w: The Wittig reaction correctly makes methylenecyclohexane. Aqueous acid protonates the CH2 end to give the tertiary carbocation, so water ends up on the ring carbon: 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, not the target. Hydroboration–oxidation adds OH to the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov, no carbocation), giving cyclohexylmethanol. Step 2 is wrong; use BH3·THF then H2O2, NaOH.
x: Phosphorus ylides convert ketones into alkenes (C=O → C=CH<sub>2</sub>); the oxaphosphetane collapses to the alkene and Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O.
Acid hydration is Markovnikov, and oxymercuration is also Markovnikov, so it too would give 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
Orientation in acid is set by carbocation stability, not by steric hindrance; the tertiary cation forms, so OH goes on the ring carbon.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown? (Stereoisomers are not distinguished.)
h: LDA makes an enolate. Where does the enolate carbon attack, and what does NaBH<sub>4</sub> then reduce?
w: LDA removes an α-H to give the lithium enolate, which is alkylated at carbon by allyl bromide (SN2), giving 2-allylcyclohexan-1-one. NaBH4 reduces the ketone to the secondary alcohol and leaves the isolated C=C alone: 2-allylcyclohexan-1-ol (cis/trans mixture).
x: This puts the allyl group and OH on the same carbon, as if an allyl Grignard had added to the C=O. The enolate reacts at the α-carbon, and NaBH<sub>4</sub> then supplies only H.
This is the product after step 2. NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces ketones readily.
O-Alkylation is minor for lithium enolates with alkyl halides; C-alkylation dominates. Also NaBH<sub>4</sub> would not change an enol ether.

q: Which sequence converts acetophenone into 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethan-1-one, as shown?
c: 1. Zn(Hg), HCl  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Fe, HCl  4. NaOH
h: Nitration goes meta to the acetyl group. Which reducing agent attacks the nitro group but not the ketone?
w: The acetyl group is a meta director, so nitration gives 3-nitroacetophenone. Iron (or tin) in HCl reduces an aryl NO2 to NH3+ and does not touch the ketone; NaOH frees the amine: 1. HNO3, H2SO4 2. Fe, HCl 3. NaOH.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone to a secondary alcohol and leaves the nitro group, the opposite of what is needed.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone, and with aryl nitro groups it gives azo compounds rather than a clean amine.
The Clemmensen reduction removes the C=O first, giving ethylbenzene; the ethyl group directs ortho/para, and the ketone is gone.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown? (It forms as a racemate.)
h: Find the weakest C–H bond for NBS, then follow the new carbon from cyanide.
w: NBS/hν brominates the benzylic CH2 (benzylic radical, resonance-stabilized), giving (1-bromoethyl)benzene. Cyanide displaces bromide (SN2 at a secondary benzylic carbon in DMSO), adding one carbon, and hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile to the carboxylic acid: 2-phenylpropanoic acid (racemic).
x: A straight chain would need bromination at the CH<sub>3</sub> end. NBS brominates the benzylic carbon, so CN and then COOH end up on the carbon next to the ring.
This is the product after step 2; hot H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> hydrolyzes the nitrile through the amide to the carboxylic acid.
This acid has one carbon fewer and no methyl branch. The ethyl group's CH<sub>3</sub> stays in the product as the branch.

q:
Which sequences give 1-bromo-4-tert-butylbenzene (shown) from benzene as the major product?
I. 1. (CH3)3CCl, AlCl3 2. Br2, FeBr3
II. 1. Br2, FeBr3 2. (CH3)3CCl, AlCl3
III. 1. (CH3)2CHCOCl, AlCl3 2. Br2, FeBr3 3. Zn(Hg), HCl
h: Bromine and alkyl groups are both ortho/para directors; a bulky group strongly favors para. An acyl group is a meta director, and a Clemmensen reduction cannot make a quaternary carbon.
w: I is true: tert-butylbenzene (activated, o/p) brominates almost only para, because the tert-butyl group blocks its ortho positions. II is true: bromobenzene is only weakly deactivated, so Friedel–Crafts alkylation still works; Br directs o/p and the bulky tert-butyl cation goes para. III is false on two counts: the acyl group directs Br meta, and Clemmensen reduction of the isobutyryl group gives an isobutyl group, CH2CH(CH3)2, not tert-butyl. I and II only.
x: This rejects II. Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on strongly deactivated rings (NO<sub>2</sub>, C=O, SO<sub>3</sub>H), but a halobenzene still reacts, and Br directs the new group para.
This rejects I and accepts III. III gives 1-bromo-3-isobutylbenzene (meta, wrong alkyl group), while I gives the target.
III fails: the acyl group sends Br meta, and reducing C=O to CH2 gives an isobutyl group, not tert-butyl.

q: What is the percent atom economy of this Wittig reaction for making methylenecyclohexane? Molar masses (g/mol): cyclohexanone 98.15, Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub> 276.32, methylenecyclohexane 96.17, Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O 278.29.
h: Atom economy = (mass of the desired product ÷ total mass of all reactants) × 100%. Which product is the one you want?
w: Atom economy = 96.17 ÷ (98.15 + 276.32) × 100% = 96.17 ÷ 374.47 × 100% = 26%. The large triphenylphosphine oxide by-product carries away about three quarters of the reactant mass. This is why the Wittig reaction scores poorly on atom economy even when its yield is high.
x: 74% is the mass fraction that ends up in Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O, the by-product. Atom economy uses the mass of the desired product, methylenecyclohexane.
98% divides the product by the ketone alone. Every reactant counts, and the ylide is by far the heaviest.
100% would require every reactant atom to end up in the product, as in an addition or Diels–Alder reaction. Here Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O is lost.

q:
Three routes to cyclohexanol are shown (catalysts not counted). Rank them from lowest to highest atom economy. Molar masses (g/mol): cyclohexanol 100.16, cyclohexene 82.15, H2O 18.02, bromocyclohexane 163.06, NaOH 40.00, cyclohexyl acetate 142.20.
I. cyclohexene + H2O (H2SO4 catalyst) → cyclohexanol
II. bromocyclohexane + NaOH → cyclohexanol + NaBr
III. cyclohexyl acetate + NaOH → cyclohexanol + CH3CO2Na
h: Divide 100.16 by the total reactant mass for each route. An addition reaction with a catalyst loses nothing.
w: I: 100.16 ÷ (82.15 + 18.02) = 100% (an addition; the catalyst is not counted). II: 100.16 ÷ (163.06 + 40.00) = 49%; the heavy Br leaves as NaBr. III: 100.16 ÷ (142.20 + 40.00) = 55%; sodium acetate is lost. II < III < I.
x: This swaps II and III. The bromide route loses the heavier by-product share (49% vs 55%), so it is the lowest.
This reverses the ranking. Substitutions and hydrolyses that release salts lose mass; the catalyzed hydration keeps every atom.
Hydration (I) is an addition with 100% atom economy, so it must be the highest, not in the middle.

q: A lab oxidizes cyclohexanol to cyclohexanone with stoichiometric Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> in aqueous H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which change best follows the principles of green chemistry?
c: Use catalytic TEMPO with aqueous NaOCl (bleach) as the oxidant, which leaves mainly NaCl and water as by-products
Use PCC in dichloromethane instead, so the oxidation does not need water
Use twice as much Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> so that all the alcohol reacts faster
Run the chromic acid oxidation in benzene so that the product is easier to separate
h: Look for the option that replaces a toxic, stoichiometric reagent with a catalyst and a benign oxidant.
w: Chromium(VI) reagents are toxic, carcinogenic and used in stoichiometric amounts, leaving chromium waste. Catalytic TEMPO with bleach oxidizes secondary alcohols to ketones using a catalyst (principle 9), a less hazardous reagent (principle 3) and gives mainly NaCl and water as waste (prevent waste, principle 1).
x: PCC is still a stoichiometric Cr(VI) reagent, and dichloromethane is a chlorinated solvent; this is not greener.
More chromium means more toxic waste and lower atom economy; it works against the principles.
Benzene is a carcinogenic solvent, and the toxic chromium reagent remains; this makes the process less green.

q: Ethane-1,2-diamine and benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl dichloride (terephthaloyl chloride) are combined. What repeat unit forms in the step-growth polymer, and what small molecule is released at each link?
h: Each link is a nucleophilic acyl substitution of an amine on an acid chloride. What leaves?
w: Each NH2 attacks a COCl carbon; chloride leaves and the N–H proton is lost, so each new amide bond releases one HCl. Alternating diamine and diacid units give a polyamide: –[NH–CH2CH2–NH–CO–C6H4–CO]n–, releasing HCl.
x: Water is released when a diamine is condensed with a dicarboxylic acid at high temperature. With an acid chloride the leaving group is Cl<sup>−</sup>, so HCl is lost.
This is a polyester, which would need a diol (ethane-1,2-diol). The monomer here has NH<sub>2</sub> groups, so amide links form.
Acyl substitution keeps the C=O carbon; only Cl leaves. Nitrogen bonds to the carbonyl carbon, not directly to the ring.

q: Poly(lactic acid), a compostable plastic made from corn sugar, has the repeat unit –[O–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CO]<sub>n</sub>–. Which monomer gives this polymer by step-growth condensation with loss of water?
h: Each ester link joins the OH of one monomer to the COOH of the next. Where is the CH<sub>3</sub> in the repeat unit?
w: In the repeat unit the CH bearing CH3 sits between the ester oxygen and the C=O. The monomer must have OH and COOH on adjacent carbons with a methyl on the OH carbon: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid). Head-to-tail esterification releases one H2O per link.
x: 3-Hydroxypropanoic acid would give –[O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–CO]<sub>n</sub>–, with no methyl branch.
Acrylic acid polymerizes by chain growth through its C=C and loses no water; it gives a C–C backbone with CO<sub>2</sub>H side groups, not an ester backbone.
Propane-1,2-diol has two OH groups and no carbonyl, so it cannot form ester links with itself.

q:
Which polymers are made by step-growth (condensation) polymerization?
I. polystyrene, from styrene (C6H5CH=CH2) with a radical initiator
II. a polyamide from ethane-1,2-diamine and decanedioyl dichloride, releasing HCl
III. poly(ethylene terephthalate), from dimethyl terephthalate and ethane-1,2-diol, releasing CH3OH
h: Step-growth polymers link two different functional groups and usually lose a small molecule; chain-growth polymers add monomers across C=C bonds.
w: I is false: styrene adds across its C=C in a radical chain reaction (chain growth), and nothing is lost. II is true: amine + acid chloride links form amides and release HCl. III is true: transesterification forms ester links and releases methanol. II and III only.
x: This leaves out II. Amide formation from an acid chloride is a condensation that releases HCl at every link.
This includes polystyrene, a chain-growth (addition) polymer with no by-product, and leaves out PET.
Polystyrene is not a condensation polymer; radical addition across C=C is chain growth.

q: The Fischer projection shows D-ribose. What are the CIP configurations of its stereocenters?
h: In a Fischer projection H is on a horizontal (toward you) bond. Find the 1→2→3 direction, then reverse it.
w: At each center, OH ranks first and H last. At C2 the order is OH > CHO > C3; at C3, OH > C2 (O,O,H) > C4 (O,C,H); at C4, OH > C3 > CH2OH. With all OH on the right and H on a horizontal bond, each 1→2→3 path appears counterclockwise; because H points toward the viewer, reverse it. Every center is R: 2R, 3R, 4R.
x: All-S is L-ribose, the mirror image. With H toward the viewer the apparent direction must be reversed.
This is D-xylose, which has its C3 OH on the left. In ribose all three OH groups are on the right.
This is D-arabinose, with its C2 OH on the left.

q: The Fischer projection shows D-allose. Which structure is β-D-allopyranose?
h: D-allose differs from D-glucose only at C3. In the β anomer of a D-pyranose, the anomeric OH is on the same face as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
w: Cyclization uses the C5 OH, so C2–C5 keep their configurations: in D-allose all four are R in the open chain, and in the pyranose C2, C3 and C5 are R while C4 is S. The β anomer has the C1 OH cis to the C5 CH2OH (C1 is R). The correct structure has C1 R, C2 R, C3 R, C4 S, C5 R: β-D-allopyranose. In a Haworth drawing, all four ring OH groups and the CH2OH point up.
x: This is the α anomer: only the anomeric carbon is inverted, so its OH is trans to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
This is β-D-glucopyranose. Its C3 OH is on the opposite face (C3 S); allose and glucose are C3 epimers.
Every stereocenter is inverted, so this is the enantiomer, β-L-allopyranose.

q:
Which compounds are reducing sugars (give a positive Benedict's test)?
I. maltose, α-D-Glcp-(1→4)-D-Glcp
II. methyl β-D-galactopyranoside
III. trehalose, α-D-Glcp-(1→1)-α-D-Glcp
h: A sugar is reducing only if some anomeric carbon is a hemiacetal (one ring O plus one free OH), which can open to the aldehyde.
w: I is reducing: the glycosidic bond uses C1 of the first glucose and C4 of the second, so the second unit's C1 is still a hemiacetal that opens to an aldehyde and reduces Cu2+. II is not: C1 carries OCH3, so it is an acetal (glycoside) that cannot open in base. III is not: the 1→1 link ties up both anomeric carbons as acetals. I only.
x: Trehalose is joined through both C1 atoms, so it has no hemiacetal left. Like sucrose, it is non-reducing.
This reverses I and II. The methyl glycoside is an acetal, while maltose keeps a free anomeric OH.
Glycosides (II) and 1→1-linked disaccharides (III) have no hemiacetal, so they cannot open to the aldehyde.

q: Amylose (starch) and cellulose are both unbranched polymers of D-glucopyranose joined 1→4. Why can humans digest amylose but not cellulose?
c: Amylose has α(1→4) glycosidic bonds, which human enzymes hydrolyze; cellulose has β(1→4) bonds, which they cannot
Amylose is made of D-glucose and cellulose is made of L-glucose
Cellulose links C1 to C6, which makes its chains too branched for enzymes
Amylose units are hemiacetals, while cellulose units are acetals
h: The two polymers share the same monomer and linkage positions. What is left to differ at the anomeric carbon?
w: Both polymers are made of D-glucose linked C1→C4. The difference is the anomeric configuration: α(1→4) in amylose and β(1→4) in cellulose. Human amylases hydrolyze α-glycosides only. The β links also let cellulose chains lie flat and H-bond into rigid fibers.
x: Both polymers are made of D-glucose; neither uses L-sugars.
Cellulose is linked 1→4, not 1→6, and it is unbranched. The 1→6 branches belong to amylopectin and glycogen.
In both polymers every internal link is an acetal (glycoside). Only the chain end has a hemiacetal.

q: L-Cysteine has pK<sub>a</sub> values of 1.96 (COOH), 8.18 (SH) and 10.28 (NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>). Which structure is the major form at pH 12?
h: A group is mostly deprotonated when the pH is above its pK<sub>a</sub>. Compare 12 with each pK<sub>a</sub>.
w: pH 12 is above all three pKa values, so each acidic group has lost its proton: CO2−, S− and neutral NH2. The dianion H2N–CH(CH2S−)–CO2−, net charge −2.
x: The thiol (pK<sub>a</sub> 8.18) is deprotonated at pH 12, almost four units above its pK<sub>a</sub>.
The ammonium group (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.28) is mostly deprotonated at pH 12, so the nitrogen is a neutral NH<sub>2</sub>.
This zwitterion is the major form near the isoelectric point (about pH 5), not in strong base.

q: A mixture of four amino acids is separated by electrophoresis in a buffer at pH 4.5. Which one moves toward the anode (the positive electrode)? Isoelectric points: aspartic acid 2.8, glycine 6.0, histidine 7.6, lysine 9.7.
h: An amino acid is negatively charged when the pH is above its pI, and negative ions move toward the positive electrode.
w: At a pH above its pI an amino acid carries a net negative charge; below its pI, a net positive charge. Only aspartic acid (pI 2.8) has a pI below 4.5, so only it is anionic and migrates to the anode: aspartic acid. Glycine, histidine and lysine are net positive at pH 4.5 and move toward the cathode, lysine fastest.
x: pH 4.5 is below glycine's pI (6.0), so glycine carries a small net positive charge and drifts toward the cathode.
With pI 7.6, histidine is net positive at pH 4.5 (its imidazole is protonated) and moves toward the cathode.
Lysine (pI 9.7) is the most positive of the four at pH 4.5 and moves fastest toward the cathode.

q: In an α-helix, what holds each turn of the helix in place?
c: Hydrogen bonds from each backbone C=O to the N–H of the residue four positions further along the same chain
Disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains on adjacent turns
Hydrogen bonds between backbone groups on two separate, side-by-side strands
Ionic attractions between the free N-terminal NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and C-terminal CO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> groups
h: Secondary structure is held by backbone–backbone interactions. In a helix, are they within one strand or between strands?
w: The α-helix is a secondary structure held together by backbone hydrogen bonds within one chain: the C=O of residue i accepts an H-bond from the N–H of residue i + 4. These bonds run almost parallel to the helix axis, about 3.6 residues per turn. Side chains point outward.
x: Disulfide bridges are covalent cross-links that help fix tertiary (or quaternary) structure. Many helices contain no cysteine.
H-bonds between neighboring strands describe a β-pleated sheet, not a helix.
There is only one N-terminus and one C-terminus per chain; they cannot hold every turn of a helix.

q: Proline residues are rarely found in the middle of an α-helix. Which feature of proline best explains this?
c: Its ring nitrogen forms a tertiary amide with no N–H for helix hydrogen bonding, and the ring restricts backbone rotation
Its side chain is ionized at pH 7 and repels neighboring residues
Its α-carbon is not a stereocenter, so it fits either helix sense
Its amide bond is not planar, because the ring nitrogen cannot share its lone pair with the C=O
h: Look at what is bonded to the nitrogen of proline once it forms a peptide bond.
w: Proline's side chain loops back onto its own α-nitrogen, forming a pyrrolidine ring. When it is acylated in a peptide, that nitrogen becomes a tertiary amide with no N–H, so it cannot donate the i → i + 4 hydrogen bond the helix needs. The ring also locks the N–Cα bond angle (φ), which does not fit the helix. No N–H and a rigid ring; proline acts as a helix breaker and is common in turns.
x: Proline's side chain is a neutral hydrocarbon ring; it is not ionized at any pH.
Proline's α-carbon is a stereocenter (L-proline is S); glycine is the achiral amino acid.
Tertiary amides are still planar and resonance-stabilized; the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the C=O just as in other peptide bonds.

q:
Which statements about nucleic acids are correct?
I. 2′-Deoxyribose in DNA lacks the OH group at C2′ that ribose in RNA has.
II. In double-stranded DNA, a purine base pairs with another purine.
III. Thymine and uracil differ only by a methyl group at C5 of the pyrimidine ring.
h: Recall the sugars, the base-pairing rule (one large base with one small base) and the structures of T and U.
w: I is true: DNA uses 2′-deoxyribose, with H instead of OH at C2′. II is false: each Watson–Crick pair joins a purine with a pyrimidine (A–T, G–C), which keeps the helix width constant. III is true: thymine is 5-methyluracil. I and III only.
x: This rejects III, but thymine is exactly uracil with a CH<sub>3</sub> at C5.
This accepts II. Purine–purine pairs would be too wide for the double helix; each pair is purine + pyrimidine.
II is false: base pairs always combine one purine (A or G) with one pyrimidine (T or C).

q: What is the nucleotide shown?
h: Identify three parts: the base (look at C5 and the C4 substituent), the sugar (OH at C2′?) and which carbon carries the phosphate.
w: The base is a pyrimidine with two C=O groups and a CH3 at C5: thymine. The sugar has only a CH2 at C2′, so it is 2′-deoxyribose. The phosphate is on the CH2O (C5′), while C3′ carries a free OH. 2′-Deoxythymidine 5′-monophosphate (dTMP).
x: Uridine has no methyl group on the base, and its ribose has an OH at C2′; this sugar is 2′-deoxy.
Cytosine has an NH<sub>2</sub> at C4 and only one C=O; this base has two C=O groups and a C5 methyl.
The phosphate is attached through the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub>O, which is C5′. C3′ (on the ring) carries the free OH.

q: In water, sodium stearate (a soap, one C17 tail) forms spherical micelles, while phosphatidylcholine (two C16–C18 tails on one head group) forms bilayer sheets that close into vesicles. What best explains the difference?
c: One tail per head gives a cone shape that packs into a sphere; two tails per head give a cylinder shape that packs into a flat bilayer
The phospholipid head group is nonpolar, so it must be buried inside the sheet
Soap tails are hydrophilic and face the water, while phospholipid tails are hydrophobic
Phospholipids are covalently linked to one another in the bilayer, but soap molecules are not
h: Both molecules hide their hydrocarbon tails from water. Think about how the shape (head size vs tail volume) packs.
w: Both are amphipathic: the polar head faces water and the hydrocarbon tails cluster away from it. A soap has a large head and one thin tail, a cone that packs into a sphere (micelle) with the tails in the core. A phospholipid's two tails take up about as much width as its head, a cylinder, which packs into a flat double layer with the tails inward. The shape set by the number of tails per head decides the aggregate.
x: The phosphocholine head group is ionic (phosphate − and ammonium +) and very polar; it faces the water on both surfaces.
Hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic in both molecules; in a micelle they form the core, away from water.
Bilayers are held together by noncovalent hydrophobic interactions; no covalent bonds join the lipids.

q: Biodiesel is made by heating a vegetable-oil triacylglycerol with methanol and a catalytic amount of NaOCH<sub>3</sub>. What are the products?
c: Three fatty acid methyl esters (RCO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) and glycerol
h: Methoxide attacks an ester carbonyl and the glycerol alkoxide leaves. What kind of reaction swaps one alcohol part of an ester for another?
w: This is base-catalyzed transesterification. Methoxide adds to each ester C=O (tetrahedral intermediate) and the glyceryl alkoxide leaves, giving a methyl ester; the alkoxide takes a proton from methanol, regenerating methoxide. Excess methanol drives all three esters over: three fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel) and glycerol. The scheme uses a short-chain model triglyceride.
x: Carboxylate salts form when water and a full equivalent of NaOH are used (saponification). Here methoxide is only a catalyst and methanol is the nucleophile.
The acyl groups move to methanol, so the fatty acid parts become methyl esters; glycerol is released as the free triol, not methylated.
Reduction to primary alcohols needs a hydride reagent such as LiAlH<sub>4</sub>. Methoxide only exchanges the alkoxy group.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no band above 3100 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. Which structure fits?
h: Five aromatic H means a monosubstituted ring. Where would a CH<sub>2</sub> appear if it were bonded to an ester oxygen and the ring at once?
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O); 1740 cm−1 and no O–H means an ester. The 5H multiplet at 7.35 ppm means C6H5–. A 2H singlet at 5.10 ppm is a CH2 bonded to both an ester oxygen and the ring (each shifts it downfield), and the 3H singlet at 2.09 ppm is CH3–C=O. Benzyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2C6H5.
x: Methyl phenylacetate also gives 5H, 2H and 3H singlets, but at about 3.6 (ArCH<sub>2</sub>C=O) and 3.7 ppm (OCH<sub>3</sub>). Nothing would appear at 5.1 ppm.
Ethyl benzoate would show a quartet (≈4.4 ppm, 2H) and a triplet (≈1.4 ppm, 3H) from the ethyl group, with aromatic H near 8.0 ppm.
A para-disubstituted ring gives two 2H doublets, not a 5H multiplet, and this compound has two CH<sub>3</sub> singlets and no CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O has a strong IR band at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Five carbons but only three signals: the molecule must have symmetry. Is the 211.8 ppm carbon a ketone or an aldehyde carbon?
w: 1715 cm−1 and a carbon at 211.8 ppm mean a ketone (aldehyde C=O carbons appear near 200 ppm). Only three signals for five carbons requires a mirror plane through the C=O, making the two ethyl groups equivalent: C=O (211.8), CH2 (35.5), CH3 (7.9). Pentan-3-one.
x: Pentan-2-one has no symmetry, so all five carbons are different and give five signals.
3-Methylbutan-2-one has two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the CH, but that still leaves four different carbons and four signals.
Pentanal gives five signals, its C=O carbon is near 202 ppm, and its IR would also show aldehyde C–H bands near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: (S)-Nicotine (shown) has two nitrogen atoms, a and b. When nicotine is dissolved in a buffer at pH 6, which nitrogen is mostly protonated, and why?
c: a, because its lone pair is in an sp3 orbital, held less tightly than the sp2 lone pair on b
b, because aromatic nitrogens are always more basic than amine nitrogens
a, because its lone pair is part of the aromatic π sextet and is easy to share
b, because its lone pair is delocalized into the ring, which stabilizes the cation
h: Compare a tertiary alkylamine (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> about 8–10) with pyridine (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> about 5). Which lone pair has more s character?
w: Nitrogen a is a tertiary alkylamine (in the pyrrolidine ring): its lone pair is in an sp3 orbital, and its conjugate acid has pKa ≈ 8. Nitrogen b is a pyridine-type nitrogen: its lone pair is in an sp2 orbital (more s character, held closer to the nucleus) and its conjugate acid has pKa ≈ 3. At pH 6, which is below 8 but above 3, a is mostly protonated, because its sp3 lone pair is more available. b stays mostly neutral.
x: Pyridine-type nitrogens are weaker bases than alkylamines (pK<sub>a</sub>H ≈ 5 vs ≈ 10) because the sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair is held closer to the nucleus.
Nitrogen a is in a saturated (pyrrolidine) ring, which is not aromatic; its lone pair is a localized sp3 pair.

The pyridine nitrogen's lone pair lies in the ring plane, perpendicular to the π system, so it is not delocalized; protonating it does not disrupt aromaticity, but the sp<sup>2</sup> pair is still the weaker base.
